stem: With reference to the judicial and executive adjustments introduced during the early phase of East India Company rule in Bengal, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Act of Settlement of 1781 exempted the Governor-General and the Council from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court at Calcutta for acts done by them in their official capacity, as well as matters concerning revenue collection.
Statement-II: Under the Act of Settlement of 1781, appeals from the Provincial Courts were directed to be taken to the Governor-General-in-Council rather than to the Supreme Court at Calcutta.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Act of Settlement of 1781 (Amending Act of 1781) resolved the acute jurisdictional paralysis created by the Regulating Act of 1773 by insulating the executive and revenue machinery from the Supreme Court at Calcutta and separating the Company's Mofussil appellate hierarchy from the Crown's Court.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The Regulating Act of 1773 had left the boundary between the executive authority of the Governor-General-in-Council and the judicial authority of the Supreme Court at Calcutta ambiguous, triggering bitter confrontations between Governor-General Warren Hastings and Chief Justice Elijah Impey (such as the Patna and Kasijora cases). To safeguard revenue administration and executive functioning, the Act of Settlement of 1781 explicitly exempted the Governor-General, the Council, and Company servants from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for acts performed in their official capacity, and barred the Court from exercising any jurisdiction in matters concerning revenue or its collection.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The Act of Settlement of 1781 recognized the Company's Mofussil judicial hierarchy by stipulating that appeals from the Provincial Courts would lie to the Governor-General-in-Council (sitting as the Sadar Diwani Adalat) and not to the Supreme Court. However, this appellate routing was a parallel structural reform to demarcate the Company's courts from the Crown's court, rather than the causal reason for granting sovereign immunity to the executive and revenue collection machinery in Statement-I.

ref: Act of Settlement, 1781; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1 (Historical Background)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional and administrative changes introduced during the late eighteenth century:
items: 1. Under Pitt's India Act of 1784, the Court of Directors was entrusted with supervising all civil, military, and revenue operations in India, while the newly created Board of Control was restricted to managing commercial affairs.
2. Pitt's India Act of 1784 empowered the Governor-General to override the majority decision of his Council in special cases and concurrently hold the office of Commander-in-Chief.

3. Pitt's India Act of 1784 formally designated the Company's territories in India as 'British possessions in India' for the first time and subordinated the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras to the Governor-General-in-Council of Bengal in all matters of war, revenue, and diplomacy.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Pitt's India Act of 1784 established the system of Double Government by separating commercial management (Court of Directors) from political superintendence (Board of Control), while the specific power of the Governor-General to override his Council was introduced later by the Amending Act of 1786.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the institutional roles under the system of Double Government created by Pitt's India Act of 1784. The pre-existing Court of Directors was restricted to managing the commercial affairs of the East India Company, whereas the newly created six-member Board of Control (representing the British Government) was empowered to supervise and direct all civil, military, and revenue operations of the British possessions in India.

Pitt's India Act of 1784 did not grant the Governor-General the power to override his Council; it merely reduced the strength of the Governor-General's Council from four to three members (one of whom was the Commander-in-Chief) so that the Governor-General could carry a decision with the support of just one member using his casting vote. It was the Amending Act of 1786—enacted specifically to fulfill the two preconditions demanded by Lord Cornwallis before accepting the post of Governor-General—that granted the Governor-General the power to override the decision of his Council in special cases and also serve as Commander-in-Chief.

Pitt's India Act of 1784 was constitutionally significant because it called the Company's territories in India 'British possessions in India' for the first time, laying the statutory claim of British parliamentary control over Indian territory, and tightened the control of the Governor-General-in-Council of Bengal over the subordinate Presidencies of Bombay and Madras on questions of war, diplomatic treaties, and revenue.

ref: Pitt's India Act, 1784 & Act of 1786; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the Charter Act of 1793 and the Charter Act of 1813, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Charter Act of 1813 introduced for the first time the statutory requirement that the salaries of the members and staff of the Board of Control be paid out of the Indian revenues rather than the British Exchequer.

2. The Charter Act of 1813 expressly asserted the undoubted sovereignty of the British Crown over the East India Company's territories in India and abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India except for trade in tea and trade with China.
3. The Charter Act of 1813 authorized the local governments in India to impose taxes on persons subject to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and to punish them in the event of non-payment.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Charter Act of 1793 initiated the fiscal burden of paying the London-based Board of Control out of Indian revenues, the Charter Act of 1813 asserted explicit Crown sovereignty, dismantled most of the Company's Indian trade monopoly, and empowered local governments to tax residents under Supreme Court jurisdiction.

exp.why: The provision requiring that the members and staff of the Board of Control be paid out of Indian revenues—a foundational component of the 'Home Charges' and Drain of Wealth—was introduced by the Charter Act of 1793, not the Charter Act of 1813. This practice continued for more than a century until the Government of India Act of 1919 transferred the salary of the Secretary of State for India back to the British Exchequer.

Pressured by the rise of laissez-faire ideology and Napoleon's Continental System in Europe, the British Parliament enacted the Charter Act of 1813 to abolish the East India Company's monopoly over Indian trade—throwing it open to all British merchants while retaining the Company's monopoly only over the trade in tea and trade with China—and explicitly declared the undoubted sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories in India.

The Charter Act of 1813 expanded the fiscal reach of the Company's administration in Presidency towns by empowering the local governments in India to levy taxes on persons subject to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (subject to the sanction of the Court of Directors and Board of Control) and to impose penalties for non-payment.

ref: Charter Act of 1793 & Charter Act of 1813; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the Charter Act of 1833, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It deprived the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers and vested the Governor-General of India in Council with exclusive legislative powers for the entire British India, leaving provincial governments with the authority only to submit drafts or proposals for laws.
2. Laws enacted under this Act were termed 'Acts', whereas laws enacted under the previous constitutional statutes were termed 'Regulations'.

3. The fourth member (Law Member) added to the Governor-General's Council under this Act was entitled from the outset to sit and vote as a full member in both executive and legislative meetings of the Council.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Charter Act of 1833 marked the climax of legislative centralization in British India by stripping the Madras and Bombay Presidencies of law-making power and adding a fourth Law Member to the Governor-General's Council purely for legislative deliberations.

exp.why: The Charter Act of 1833 was the final step toward complete legislative centralization in British India. It redesignated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India and vested in the Governor-General-in-Council exclusive legislative powers for the whole of British India. The Governors of Bombay and Madras were wholly deprived of their independent law-making powers and were left with the authority only to propose draft projects of laws to the Governor-General-in-Council where they deemed it expedient.

Because legislative power under the Charter Act of 1833 flowed from a centralized imperial authority applicable across all of British India and all classes of persons (both British and Indian, and callable in all courts including the Supreme Court), enactments made under the 1833 Act were officially styled as 'Acts', replacing the earlier nomenclature of 'Regulations' used under the 1773, 1793, and 1813 statutes.

Under the Charter Act of 1833, the fourth member added to the Governor-General's Council for legal expertise (initially Lord Macaulay) was not a full member of the Council. He was barred from sitting or voting in the Council except at meetings convened specifically for the purpose of making laws and regulations. It was only later, under the Charter Act of 1853, that the Law Member was elevated to a full member of the Governor-General's Executive Council with the right to sit and vote in executive business as well.

ref: Charter Act of 1833; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the institutional reforms introduced by the Charter Act of 1853, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council by adding six new members called legislative councillors to establish a distinct Indian (Central) Legislative Council.

2. It introduced local representation in the Indian Legislative Council by providing for the nomination of four non-official Indian members drawn from the provinces of Madras, Bombay, Bengal, and Agra.

3. A Bill passed by the Indian Legislative Council under this Act became law immediately without requiring the assent of the Governor-General, as the Governor-General personally presided over the Council's legislative sittings.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Charter Act of 1853 created a separate twelve-member legislative wing of the Governor-General's Council and introduced provincial representation through four British covenanted officials, while retaining the Governor-General's executive veto over all legislation.

exp.why: The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council for the first time. It provided for the addition of six new members called 'legislative councillors' (the Chief Justice and one puisne Judge of the Calcutta Supreme Court, plus four provincial representatives) to the existing six executive council members (Governor-General, Commander-in-Chief, and four ordinary members), creating a twelve-member Indian (Central) Legislative Council that operated as a mini-Parliament on the procedural lines of the British Parliament.

While the Charter Act of 1853 did introduce the principle of 'local representation' in the Indian (Central) Legislative Council by assigning four of the six new legislative seats to nominees of the provincial governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal, and the North-Western Provinces (Agra), these four members were NOT non-official Indians. Under the 1853 Act, they were required to be British covenanted civil servants of the Company with at least ten years' standing. The nomination of non-official Indians to the Legislative Council was introduced only later under the Indian Councils Act of 1861.

Despite the creation of a distinct Legislative Council under the Charter Act of 1853, executive supremacy over legislation was strictly preserved. No measure or Bill passed by the Legislative Council could acquire the force of law until it received the explicit assent of the Governor-General, who possessed an absolute veto over all Council legislation, and the Crown (acting through the Board of Control) retained the power to disallow any Act even after the Governor-General had assented to it.

ref: Charter Act of 1853; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the administrative and constitutional machinery established by the Government of India Act of 1858, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It constituted the Secretary of State-in-Council as a body corporate capable of suing and being sued in India and in England, while vesting ultimate political authority in the Secretary of State as a member of the British Cabinet accountable to the British Parliament.
opts.B: The fifteen-member Council of India created under the Act was an executive body whose majority decisions were legally binding on the Secretary of State in all administrative, diplomatic, and secret matters without exception.
opts.C: The Act abolished the system of Double Government in London and transferred the ultimate power of framing imperial policies directly to the Viceroy of India, making the Secretary of State merely a parliamentary spokesperson.
opts.D: All fifteen members of the Council of India were directly appointed by the British Crown on the advice of the Prime Minister, with no representation given to the outgoing Court of Directors of the East India Company.

core: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred Indian governance to the British Crown acting through the Secretary of State for India—a British Cabinet minister—assisted by an advisory fifteen-member Council of India, constituting the Secretary of State-in-Council as a legal body corporate.

exp.why: Option A is correct because Section 65 of the Government of India Act of 1858 constituted the Secretary of State-in-Council as a body corporate capable of suing and being sued in India and in England (assuming the legal liabilities and contracts of the erstwhile East India Company), while vesting complete political authority in the Secretary of State as a member of the British Cabinet ultimately responsible to the British Parliament. Option B is incorrect because the 15-member Council of India was primarily an advisory body; the Secretary of State could overrule its majority decisions in most ordinary administrative matters (except specific financial appropriations from Indian revenues) and could dispatch 'secret and urgent' orders relating to war, peace, and diplomacy to India without consulting the Council at all. Option C is incorrect because the Viceroy in India was strictly the subordinate agent of the Crown acting under the superintendence and control of the Secretary of State in London. Option D is incorrect because under the 1858 Act, only 8 of the 15 members of the Council of India were appointed by the Crown, while the remaining 7 were elected by the outgoing Court of Directors of the East India Company.

ref: Government of India Act, 1858; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the Indian Councils Act of 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances during an emergency only with the prior concurrence of the Legislative Council.
2. It initiated the process of legislative decentralization by restoring the law-making powers of the Bombay and Madras Presidencies.
3. It accorded statutory recognition to the 'portfolio system' introduced by Lord Canning.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 marked a major structural watershed by reversing the centralizing climax of the Charter Act of 1833 through legislative devolution to the provinces, while simultaneously fortifying executive authority via statutory recognition of the portfolio system and unilateral emergency ordinance powers for the Viceroy.

exp.why: Under Section 23 of the Indian Councils Act of 1861, the Viceroy was explicitly empowered to issue ordinances for the peace and good government of British India during an emergency WITHOUT the concurrence of the Legislative Council. The life of such an ordinance was restricted to a maximum of six months.

The Charter Act of 1833 had deprived the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers, centralizing all law-making in the Governor-General in Council. The Indian Councils Act of 1861 reversed this centralizing tendency by restoring legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, laying the foundation for provincial legislative autonomy.

The Act of 1861 gave statutory recognition to the 'portfolio system' first introduced by Lord Canning in 1859. Under this arrangement, a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council was placed in charge of one or more government departments and authorized to issue final orders on behalf of the Council on routine departmental matters.

ref: Indian Councils Act, 1861; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1 (Historical Background)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Councils Act of 1892:
items: Statement-I: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 empowered the non-official members of the Central Legislative Council to vote on budget demands and ask supplementary questions to the Executive.

Statement-II: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced a limited and indirect provision for the use of election in filling up some non-official seats on the recommendation of specified bodies, even though the word 'election' was not explicitly used in the statute.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 cautiously expanded legislative deliberation and representative composition without conceding control over the executive: it allowed budget discussion and prior-notice questions without supplementary questions or voting rights, and disguised indirect elections as 'nominations on recommendation'.

exp.why: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 only authorized the Legislative Councils to discuss the annual financial statement (budget) and address questions to the Executive with six days' prior notice. Non-official members were neither permitted to ask supplementary questions (which was introduced later under the Indian Councils Act of 1909) nor empowered to vote on budget demands (which was partially introduced under the Government of India Act of 1919).

Although the Indian Councils Act of 1892 carefully avoided the explicit term 'election', it laid the statutory seed for indirect elections by providing that certain non-official members of the Central and Provincial Legislative Councils would be nominated by the Viceroy and Governors on the recommendation of provincial legislative councils, district boards, municipalities, universities, trade associations, and zamindars.

ref: Indian Councils Act, 1892; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1 (Historical Background)

stem: With reference to the Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It retained an official majority in the Central Legislative Council while allowing the Provincial Legislative Councils to have a non-official majority.

2. It empowered members of the Legislative Councils to move resolutions on the budget before its final adoption and provided for the first time for the association of Indians with the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and Governors.

3. Alongside introducing communal representation for Muslims through a separate electorate, it also provided for the separate representation of Presidency Corporations, Chambers of Commerce, Universities, and Zamindars.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 combined incremental deliberative expansion and executive inclusion with institutional safeguards for colonial control—maintaining an official majority at the Centre while fragmenting the electorate along both communal (Muslim separate electorate) and special-interest (corporations, chambers of commerce, universities, zamindars) lines.

exp.why: While increasing the size of both Central and Provincial Legislative Councils (bringing the Central Council from 16 to 60 additional members), the 1909 Act deliberately retained an official majority in the Central Legislative Council to secure imperial legislation, while permitting non-official majorities (comprising both nominated and elected non-officials) in the Provincial Legislative Councils.

The Act enlarged the deliberative functions of the Legislative Councils at both levels by allowing members to ask supplementary questions and move resolutions on the budget (as well as matters of general public interest) before the budget was finally settled. It also permitted the appointment of Indians to the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and Governors, pursuant to which Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council as the Law Member.

Although best known for legalizing communalism by introducing a separate electorate for Muslims, the 1909 Act did not restrict separate representation solely to Muslims; it simultaneously instituted separate constituency representation for special interests, specifically Presidency Corporations, Chambers of Commerce, Universities, and Zamindars.

ref: Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the system of 'Dyarchy' introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act of 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 'Reserved' subjects were to be administered by the Governor with the aid of Ministers responsible to the Legislative Council, whereas the 'Transferred' subjects were to be administered by the Governor and his Executive Council without being responsible to the Legislative Council.

2. Crucial administrative subjects such as Law and Order, Land Revenue, Finance, and Irrigation were categorized as 'Transferred' subjects, while Education, Public Health, and Local Self-Government were placed under the 'Reserved' list.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Provincial Dyarchy under the Government of India Act of 1919 bifurcated provincial administration into two asymmetrically accountable halves: 'Reserved' subjects (core coercive and fiscal levers like Finance, Police, and Land Revenue) remained under the unaccountable Governor-in-Executive-Council, while 'Transferred' subjects (nation-building areas like Education and Health) were entrusted to Indian Ministers answerable to the legislature but starved of fiscal autonomy.

exp.why: The statement reverses the two categories of Provincial Dyarchy. Under the Government of India Act of 1919, 'Transferred' subjects were administered by the Governor with the aid of Ministers appointed from among the elected members of the Provincial Legislative Council and responsible to it. Conversely, 'Reserved' subjects were administered by the Governor and his nominated Executive Council without being responsible to the Legislative Council.

The allocation of subjects is reversed. Core sovereign and revenue portfolios—including Law and Order, Police, Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, and Irrigation—were kept in the 'Reserved' list under bureaucratic control, whereas developmental and welfare portfolios—such as Education, Public Health, Sanitation, Local Self-Government, Agriculture, and Excise—were placed in the 'Transferred' list.

ref: Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the institutional and financial reforms introduced by the Government of India Act of 1919, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It required that three of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council (other than the Commander-in-Chief) were to be Indians, and separated provincial budgets from the central budget for the first time.
2. While it created the new office of the High Commissioner for India in London, the salary of the Secretary of State for India continued to be paid out of Indian revenues.

3. In introducing bicameralism at the Centre, it vested both the Council of State (Upper House) and the Central Legislative Assembly (Lower House) with equal authority to vote on the votable demands for grants in the central budget.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Government of India Act of 1919 restructured imperial governance by expanding Indian representation in the Viceroy's Executive Council, separating provincial budgets from the Central budget, shifting the Secretary of State's salary from Indian revenues to the British Exchequer, and creating a bicameral Central Legislature where only the Lower House could vote on demands for grants.

exp.why: The Government of India Act of 1919 mandated that three out of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council (excluding the Commander-in-Chief) had to be Indians. It also separated provincial budgets from the Central budget for the first time and authorized the provincial legislatures to enact their own budgets.

Since the Government of India Act of 1858, the salary of the Secretary of State for India and his establishment in London had been charged to Indian revenues—a long-standing nationalist grievance. The Government of India Act of 1919 ended this practice by providing that the salary of the Secretary of State for India would henceforth be paid out of the British Exchequer, while transferring agency functions to a newly created High Commissioner for India in London.

Although the 1919 Act replaced the Imperial Legislative Council with a bicameral legislature comprising the Council of State (Upper House) and the Central Legislative Assembly (Lower House), the two Houses did not enjoy equal financial powers. The power to vote on the votable portion of the Demands for Grants in the Central Budget was vested exclusively in the Central Legislative Assembly (Lower House), and not in the Council of State.

ref: Government of India Act, 1919; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1; D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following groups in British India:
items: 1. Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans
2. Muslims
3. Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), Women, and Labour (Workers)
prompt: What is the correct chronological order in which the groups given above were statutorily accorded communal or special electorate representation (through separate electorates or reserved primary-electorate seats) by British Constitutional Acts?
core: The British colonial policy of electoral fragmentation via communal and special electorates unfolded in three distinct statutory stages: commencing with Muslims under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, extending to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans under the Government of India Act of 1919, and finally encompassing Depressed Classes, Women, and Labour under the Government of India Act of 1935.

exp.why: Stage 2 (1919): The Government of India Act of 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) extended the principle of communal representation by providing separate electorates for Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans.

Stage 1 (1909): The Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) first introduced the statutory system of communal representation for Muslims by accepting the concept of a 'separate electorate', under which Muslim members were to be elected only by Muslim voters.

Stage 3 (1935): The Government of India Act of 1935 further extended communal and special representation to the Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), Women, and Labour (Workers)—incorporating the Poona Pact's two-tier primary electorate mechanism for Scheduled Caste reserved seats alongside special/separate electorates for Women and Labour. Hence, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1909) -> 1 (1919) -> 3 (1935).

ref: Indian Councils Act, 1909; Government of India Act, 1919; Government of India Act, 1935; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the recommendations of the Indian Statutory Commission (Simon Commission) appointed in 1927:
items: Statement-I: The Simon Commission recommended the immediate replacement of separate communal electorates with joint electorates and universal adult franchise in the British Indian provinces.

Statement-II: The Commission recommended the abolition of Dyarchy in the provinces and the establishment of representative unitary governments in the provinces through the transfer of all provincial subjects to popular ministers.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In its 1930 report, the Simon Commission recommended abolishing the unworkable system of provincial Dyarchy introduced by the 1919 Act and replacing it with provincial autonomy, while rejecting universal adult franchise and advocating the continuation of separate communal electorates.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. The Simon Commission did not recommend abolishing separate communal electorates or introducing universal adult franchise. Instead, it recommended the retention and continuation of separate communal electorates (until communal tensions eased and Muslim consent was obtained) and only a limited extension of the property- and education-based franchise (roughly from 3% to 10–15% of the provincial population). It was the Nehru Report (1928) by Indian nationalists that demanded joint electorates and universal adult suffrage.

Statement-II is correct. The Simon Commission observed that the rigid division of provincial subjects into 'Reserved' and 'Transferred' under the Government of India Act of 1919 had blurred ministerial responsibility. It therefore recommended the abolition of provincial Dyarchy and the establishment of autonomous representative governments in the provinces (subject to the Governor's overriding special powers), which later formed the basis for Provincial Autonomy under the Government of India Act of 1935.

ref: Government of India Act 1935 & Simon Commission Report (1930); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the federal scheme proposed under the Government of India Act of 1935, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While joining the proposed All-India Federation was compulsory for the British Indian Provinces, accession was entirely voluntary for the Princely States.
2. The proposed All-India Federation never came into operation because the requisite number of Princely States failed to execute the Instrument of Accession.
3. To safeguard provincial autonomy within the federation, the Act vested residuary legislative powers in the Provincial Legislatures.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Government of India Act of 1935 envisaged an asymmetrical All-India Federation whose inauguration depended on the voluntary accession of a specified threshold of Princely States, while uniquely vesting unenumerated residuary legislative powers in the Governor-General rather than in any legislature.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 5 of the Government of India Act of 1935, the proposed All-India Federation was to comprise the Governor's Provinces and Chief Commissioner's Provinces (whose inclusion was automatic and mandatory) alongside those Indian Princely States whose rulers voluntarily signed an Instrument of Accession specifying the federal matters accepted by them.

Statement 2 is correct. For the Federation to be proclaimed, Rulers of Princely States entitled to fill at least half of the 104 seats allotted to the States in the Council of State (Upper House) and representing at least half of the aggregate population of all the Princely States had to accede. Because the Princely States refused to join, this statutory condition was never fulfilled and the All-India Federation never came into existence.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Because the framers could not reach a consensus between nationalists (who favored vesting residuary powers in the Centre) and the Muslim League (who favored vesting them in the Provinces), Section 104 of the Government of India Act of 1935 vested residuary legislative powers in the Governor-General (Viceroy). Acting in his discretion, the Governor-General could empower either the Federal Legislature or a Provincial Legislature to enact a law with respect to any matter not enumerated in any of the three lists.

ref: Government of India Act 1935 (Sections 5 & 104); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 1

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the implementation of the Government of India Act of 1935:
items: Statement-I: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, both Provincial Autonomy in the provinces and the system of Dyarchy at the Centre were simultaneously brought into operation in April 1937.

Statement-II: Because the conditions for the establishment of the All-India Federation under Part II of the 1935 Act were never fulfilled, the Central Government of British India continued to function under the transitional framework retaining the Central Executive and Legislature of the Government of India Act of 1919 up to 1946.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, Part III (Provincial Autonomy) became operational on 1 April 1937, whereas Part II (All-India Federation and Dyarchy at the Centre) remained a dead letter, forcing the Central Government to operate under the Ninth Schedule transitional provisions (the 1919 Act setup).

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. While Provincial Autonomy (Part III of the Government of India Act of 1935) came into operation on 1 April 1937 (with popular ministries functioning until the Congress ministries resigned in October–November 1939), the provision for Dyarchy at the Centre—which proposed dividing federal subjects into Reserved (defence, external affairs, ecclesiastical affairs, and tribal areas) and Transferred categories—was part of Part II of the Act and never came into effect at all.

Statement-II is correct. Since the operationalization of the Federal Executive and Federal Legislature (including Central Dyarchy) under Part II was legally contingent upon the proclamation of the All-India Federation, the non-accession of the Princely States meant Part II never took effect. Consequently, under Part XIII (Transitional Provisions) and the Ninth Schedule of the 1935 Act, the Central Government continued to be governed in accordance with the central machinery of the Government of India Act of 1919 until the Interim Government was formed in 1946.

ref: Government of India Act 1935 (Parts II, III & XIII); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the institutional changes introduced by the Government of India Act of 1935, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Federal Court established in 1937 replaced the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London as the final and ultimate court of appeal for British India.

2. While the Act provided for a Joint Public Service Commission for two or more provinces, the power to appoint its Chairman and members was vested jointly in the Governors of the participating provinces.
3. The 15-member Council of India created by the Government of India Act of 1858 was retained by the 1935 Act and was abolished only by the Indian Independence Act of 1947.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Government of India Act of 1935 established the Federal Court (though subject to Privy Council appellate jurisdiction), vested Joint Public Service Commission appointments in the Governor-General, and abolished the 1858 Council of India.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Although the Government of India Act of 1935 provided for the establishment of a Federal Court (set up in October 1937) with original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction, it did NOT replace the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as the highest court of appeal. Under Section 208 of the 1935 Act, appeals continued to lie from the Federal Court to the Privy Council in London (without leave in cases involving the interpretation of the 1935 Act or Instruments of Accession, and by leave in other cases). Privy Council jurisdiction was finally abolished only in 1949 by the Constituent Assembly through the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 265 of the Government of India Act of 1935, the Chairman and other members of a Joint Public Service Commission serving two or more provinces were appointed by the Governor-General acting in his discretion, not by the Provincial Governors acting jointly (a structural principle preserved in Article 316 of the Constitution of India, where the President appoints members of a Joint State Public Service Commission).

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Government of India Act of 1935 itself abolished the Council of India (established under the Government of India Act of 1858 to assist the Secretary of State for India). In its place, the Secretary of State for India was provided with a small body of advisers (not less than three and not more than six).

ref: Government of India Act 1935 (Sections 200–208, 264–265, 278); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the provincial legislatures and territorial reorganizations under the Government of India Act of 1935, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act introduced bicameralism in six out of the eleven British Indian provinces—namely Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, and the United Provinces—while leaving Punjab and the Central Provinces with unicameral legislatures.
2. Pursuant to the Act, Burma was separated from British India and Aden ceased to be part of British India to become a separate Crown Colony.
3. The Act gave constitutional effect to the creation of two new Governor's provinces—Sindh and Orissa.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Government of India Act of 1935 reorganized British India into eleven Governor's provinces (creating Sindh and Orissa, while separating Burma and Aden) and introduced bicameral legislatures (Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly) in six of those eleven provinces.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Section 60 of the Government of India Act of 1935 introduced bicameral legislatures (consisting of a Legislative Council as the Upper House and a Legislative Assembly as the Lower House) in six of the eleven Governor's provinces: Madras, Bombay, Bengal, the United Provinces, Bihar, and Assam. The remaining five provinces—Punjab, the Central Provinces and Berar, the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP), Orissa, and Sindh—were provided with unicameral legislatures (only a Legislative Assembly).

Statement 2 is correct. Under the Government of India Act of 1935 (which absorbed the Government of Burma Act, 1935 and Section 288 regarding Aden), Burma was formally separated from British India effective 1 April 1937, and the Chief Commissionership of Aden was detached from the administrative control of the Government of India to become the Crown Colony of Aden.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 289 of the Government of India Act of 1935, two new Governor's provinces were constituted in 1936: Sindh (by separating it from the Presidency of Bombay) and Orissa (by bifurcating the province of Bihar and Orissa and adding certain areas from the Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces).

ref: Government of India Act 1935 (Sections 46, 60, 288, 289); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the evolution of British constitutional proposals for a Constituent Assembly in India between 1940 and 1946, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the August Offer (1940) conceded that the framing of the new constitution should be 'primarily' the responsibility of Indians, the Cripps Proposals (1942) went further by proposing an elected constitution-making body composed 'solely' of Indians.

2. The Cripps Proposals stipulated that any British Indian province not prepared to accept the new constitution would have the right to retain its existing constitutional position and subsequently frame a separate constitution of its own.

3. Both the Cripps Proposals (1942) and the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) granted individual provinces the right to opt out of the proposed Indian Union prior to the commencement of the constitution and establish independent sovereign states.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The transition from the August Offer (1940) to the Cripps Mission (1942) shifted the proposed constitution-making responsibility from 'primarily' to 'solely' Indian hands, while the Cripps 'local option' clause permitting provincial non-accession was later reversed by the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) in favor of a single three-tier Union.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Lord Linlithgow's August Offer (August 1940) marked the first official British recognition of the right of Indians to frame their own constitution after the war, stating that the framing of a new constitutional scheme should be 'primarily' (mainly) the responsibility of Indians themselves. The Cripps Mission (March 1942) advanced this principle by declaring that the post-war constitution-making body would be composed 'solely' of Indians (elected by provincial legislative assemblies through proportional representation and nominated by the rulers of Princely States).

Statement 2 is correct. A central and controversial clause of the Cripps Proposals (1942) was the provincial non-accession ('local option') provision: His Majesty's Government undertook to accept the new constitution subject to the right of any province of British India that was not prepared to accept it to retain its present constitutional position, with the provision that His Majesty's Government would agree to a new separate constitution for such non-acceding provinces giving them the same full status as the Indian Union.

Statement 3 is incorrect. While the Cripps Proposals (1942) allowed individual provinces to refuse accession to the Indian Union and frame a separate constitution, the Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) explicitly rejected the partition of India and did NOT allow provinces to secede from the Union of India. Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, all provinces were part of a single Indian Union and grouped into three Sections (A, B, and C); a province only had the right to opt out of its 'Group' (not the Union itself) by a vote of its legislature after the first general elections under the new constitution.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 35 & 37; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the constitutional scheme proposed by the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It rejected the demand for a sovereign Pakistan on the rationale that partitioning British India would neither solve the communal minority problem nor preserve the strategic unity of defence and communications.

2. It proposed a three-tier federal structure in which the Union Government was restricted to Foreign Affairs, Defence, and Communications, while all residuary powers were vested in the Union Legislature to prevent secession.

3. Under the official interpretation of the Plan by the British Government, the initial grouping of Provinces into Sections A, B, and C was compulsory, though a province could opt out of a group after the first general elections under the new constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: To reconcile the Indian National Congress's demand for a united India with the Muslim League's demand for autonomy, the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) designed a weak three-tier federal Union limited to three subjects (Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Communications), vesting all residuary powers in the Provinces and mandating compulsory initial provincial grouping into Sections A, B, and C.

exp.why: The Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander) explicitly rejected the Muslim League's demand for a full-fledged sovereign Pakistan. It noted that a smaller Pakistan would require partitioning Punjab and Bengal against historic ties, while a larger Pakistan would still leave millions of non-Muslim minorities inside Pakistan and substantial Muslim minorities inside Remainder India, besides fracturing unified armed forces, railways, and posts and telegraphs.

Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, the Union of India was confined strictly to Foreign Affairs, Defence, and Communications (along with the powers necessary to raise finances for these three subjects). All subjects other than the Union subjects and all residuary powers were vested in the Provinces, not the Union Legislature. It was only after the Mountbatten Plan and Partition in June 1947 that the Constituent Assembly abandoned the Cabinet Mission's weak-Centre restriction and vested residuary powers in the Union (Article 248).

The Plan divided British Indian Provinces into Section A (Hindu-majority provinces), Section B (Muslim-majority provinces in the north-west), and Section C (Bengal and Assam). While the Congress argued that joining a group initially was optional for provinces like Assam and NWFP, the British Government clarified in its December 6, 1946 statement that the initial grouping into Sections A, B, and C was compulsory, and a province could decide to opt out of a group only by a vote of its legislature after the first general elections under the newly framed constitution.

ref: Cabinet Mission Statement of May 16, 1946; Laxmikanth Ch. 1 & 2

stem: With reference to the composition and election of the Constituent Assembly constituted in November 1946, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Seats were allotted to each British Indian Province and Princely State roughly in the proportion of one seat for every million of their respective populations.
2. The representatives of each British Indian Province were elected collectively by all members of the respective Provincial Legislative Assembly through the first-past-the-post system.
3. The Constituent Assembly was a partly elected and partly nominated body, as the representatives of the Princely States were to be nominated by the heads of those Princely States.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constituent Assembly of India (total allocated strength 389: 296 for British India and 93 for Princely States) combined indirect proportional election from communal legislative groups in British Provinces with nomination by the rulers of Princely States.

exp.why: To avoid the delay inherent in preparing adult franchise electoral rolls, the Cabinet Mission Plan allocated seats to every Province and Princely State (or group of states) in proportion to its population, roughly on the scale of one seat for every million population.

Seats allocated to each British province were first divided among the three principal communities—Muslims, Sikhs, and General (all except Muslims and Sikhs)—in proportion to their population. The representatives of each community were then elected only by the members of that respective community in the Provincial Legislative Assembly, and voting took place by the method of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (not collectively by first-past-the-post).

While the 296 seats allotted to British India (292 from eleven Governors' Provinces and 4 from Chief Commissioners' Provinces) were filled through indirect elections by Provincial Legislatures, the 93 seats allotted to the Princely States were to be filled by nominees of the heads of those Princely States, making the Assembly partly elected and partly nominated.

ref: Laxmikanth Ch. 2 (Making of the Constitution); Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Interim Government of India (1946–1947):
items: Statement-I: Because the Interim Government formed on September 2, 1946 operated legally as the Viceroy's Executive Council under the transitional statutory framework of the Government of India Act, 1919/1935, the Viceroy continued to be its formal President while Jawaharlal Nehru was designated as the Vice-President of the Council.

Statement-II: Even after five nominees of the All-India Muslim League joined the reconstituted Interim Government in October 1946 and assumed key portfolios including Finance, the Muslim League members refused to participate in the Constituent Assembly.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Prior to August 15, 1947, the Interim Government had no independent Dominion statute and legally functioned as the Viceroy's Executive Council (with the Viceroy as President and Nehru as Vice-President), while politically suffering from internal paralysis after the Muslim League joined the Executive Council in October 1946 without entering the Constituent Assembly.

exp.why: Since the All-India Federation envisaged under Part II of the Government of India Act, 1935 never came into operation, the Central Executive prior to August 15, 1947 continued to be governed by the transitional provisions (Ninth Schedule of the 1935 Act continuing the structure of the Government of India Act, 1919). Consequently, the Interim Government sworn in on September 2, 1946 was legally the Viceroy's Executive Council: Viceroy Lord Wavell (and later Lord Mountbatten) remained its formal President, and Jawaharlal Nehru held the official designation of Vice-President of the Executive Council.

Statement-II is also factually correct: on October 26, 1946, five Muslim League nominees (led by Liaquat Ali Khan, who took the Finance portfolio) joined the reconstituted Interim Government, yet the Muslim League persisted in boycotting the Constituent Assembly that met on December 9, 1946. However, this political boycott does not explain the statutory designation of the Viceroy as President and Nehru as Vice-President in Statement-I.

ref: Laxmikanth Ch. 1 & 2; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence

stem: With reference to the organizational setup and key office-bearers of the Constituent Assembly of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Following the French constitutional practice, Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member of the Assembly, was chosen as its temporary President for the inaugural sitting.
2. The Constituent Assembly had two Vice-Presidents during its tenure, namely H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari.

3. Sir B.N. Rau, who was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly and prepared the initial draft of the Constitution, was neither an elected member of the Constituent Assembly nor a member of the seven-member Drafting Committee.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constituent Assembly adopted the French seniority convention to install Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as Provisional President on December 9, 1946, subsequently elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad as permanent President alongside two Vice-Presidents (H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari), and relied on civil servant-jurist Sir B.N. Rau as non-member Constitutional Advisor.

exp.why: When the Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on December 9, 1946, it followed the French practice of selecting the senior-most member by age—Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha—as the temporary (provisional) President until Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on December 11, 1946.

To ensure representation of both British Indian Provinces and the Princely States in the presiding panel, the Constituent Assembly elected two Vice-Presidents: H.C. Mukherjee (elected in January 1947 from British India) and V.T. Krishnamachari (elected in July 1947 representing the Princely States after Jaipur joined the Assembly).

Sir Benegal Narsing Rau, a distinguished ICS officer and jurist, was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor (Legal Advisor) to the Constituent Assembly in July 1946. He prepared the original 243-article initial draft of the Constitution in October 1947 for the consideration of the Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, but Sir B.N. Rau himself was neither an elected member of the Constituent Assembly nor one of the seven members of the Drafting Committee.

ref: Laxmikanth Ch. 2 (Working of the Constituent Assembly); Constituent Assembly Debates Vol. I

stem: With reference to the changes introduced in the position and functions of the Constituent Assembly by the Indian Independence Act of 1947, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Assembly became a fully sovereign body empowered to abrogate or alter any law made by the British Parliament in relation to India, including the Indian Independence Act itself.
2. The Assembly assumed a dual role, functioning both as the constitution-making body and as the Dominion Legislature to enact ordinary laws for India on separate days.
3. Whenever the Assembly met as the Dominion Legislature to enact ordinary laws, it was presided over by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, whereas Dr. Rajendra Prasad presided when it met as the constituent body.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 6 and Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 emancipated the Constituent Assembly from the limitations of the Cabinet Mission Plan, conferring plenary legislative sovereignty and vesting it with the dual role of Constituent Assembly (chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad) and Dominion Legislature (chaired by G.V. Mavalankar).

exp.why: Before the Indian Independence Act of 1947, the Constituent Assembly was bound by the framework of the Cabinet Mission Plan. Section 6 of the 1947 Act conferred full legislative sovereignty on the Legislature of the Dominion (exercised by the Constituent Assembly), explicitly empowering it to frame any constitution it pleased and to repeal or amend any Act of the British Parliament extending to India, including the Indian Independence Act, 1947 itself.

Under Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the powers of the Federal Legislature for the Dominion were made exercisable in the first instance by the Constituent Assembly. Thus, the Assembly became the first Parliament of free India (Dominion Legislature), holding separate sessions for constitution-making and ordinary law-making until November 26, 1949.

Whenever the Assembly met as the constituent body to frame the Constitution, it was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad. However, whenever it met as the legislative body (Dominion Legislature), it was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar ( elected Speaker on November 17, 1947), not Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (who served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee and Union Law Minister).

ref: Indian Independence Act, 1947 (Sections 6 & 8); Laxmikanth Ch. 1 & 2

stem: With reference to the constitutional changes brought about by the Indian Independence Act of 1947 regarding executive authority and legislative assent during the Dominion period (1947–1950), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It deprived the British Monarch of the right to veto bills or ask for the reservation of certain bills for his approval, while empowering the Governor-General to give assent to any bill in the name of His Majesty strictly on the aid and advice of the Dominion Cabinet.
opts.B: It abolished the office of the Governor-General immediately upon the transfer of power on August 15, 1947, and vested the interim executive authority of the Dominion in the President of the Constituent Assembly.
opts.C: It retained the discretionary powers and 'individual judgment' of the Governor-General and Provincial Governors as originally provided under the Government of India Act, 1935, until the new Constitution was enforced.
opts.D: It required every constitutional statute passed by the Constituent Assembly to receive the formal royal assent of the Secretary of State for India in London before taking effect.

core: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 transformed the Governor-General and Provincial Governors from instruments of British imperial control into purely nominal constitutional heads bound in all matters by ministerial advice, while extinguishing the British Crown's reservation and disallowance powers over Indian legislation.

exp.why: Option A is correct because Section 6(3) and Section 8(2)(c) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 stripped the British Monarch of the power to disallow laws or require the Governor-General to reserve bills for the signification of His Majesty's pleasure. The Governor-General of the Dominion had full power to assent to any bill in His Majesty's name, and was reduced to a strictly constitutional head bound to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters. Option B is incorrect because the office of the Governor-General continued during the Dominion period (August 15, 1947 to January 26, 1950, held successively by Lord Mountbatten and C. Rajagopalachari), appointed by the British King on the advice of the Dominion Cabinet. Option C is incorrect because Section 8(2)(c) of the 1947 Act explicitly abolished all powers of the Governor-General or any Governor to act in his 'discretion' or exercise 'individual judgment' under the Government of India Act, 1935. Option D is incorrect because the Act abolished the office of the Secretary of State for India, and laws passed by the Constituent Assembly did not require royal assent from London.

ref: Indian Independence Act, 1947 (Sections 5, 6, 7 & 8); Laxmikanth Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the Committees and Sub-Committees of the Constituent Assembly of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas : J.B. Kripalani
2. Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee : Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
3. States Committee (Committee for Negotiating with States) : Jawaharlal Nehru
4. Steering Committee : Dr. Rajendra Prasad
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Constituent Assembly organized its work through major committees and specialized sub-committees. While Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel chaired the umbrella Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas, the specific Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee under it was chaired by J.B. Kripalani, and the States Committee for negotiating with princely states was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. The main Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas was chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, not J.B. Kripalani. This overarching committee had five sub-committees working under its purview.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee (which functioned within the larger Advisory Committee) was chaired by J.B. Kripalani, whereas the Minorities Sub-Committee was chaired by H.C. Mookherjee.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Although Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel headed the executive Ministry of States that oversaw the political integration of princely states, the Constituent Assembly's States Committee (Committee for Negotiating with States regarding their entry into the Assembly) was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
Pair 4 is correctly matched. Dr. Rajendra Prasad chaired both the Steering Committee and the Rules of Procedure Committee of the Constituent Assembly.

ref: Constituent Assembly Debates; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 2 (Making of the Constitution)

stem: With reference to the seven-member Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly set up on August 29, 1947, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. N. Madhava Rau : Appointed to the Committee following the demise of D.P. Khaitan in 1948
2. T.T. Krishnamachari : Appointed to the Committee after B.L. Mitter resigned due to ill health
3. Syed Mohammad Saadullah : Former Premier of Assam and the sole Muslim League representative on the Committee
4. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar : Former Advocate General of Madras who served as an original member of the Committee
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the seven-member Drafting Committee experienced two changes in its original composition: N. Madhava Rau replaced B.L. Mitter (who resigned due to ill health), and T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan (who passed away in 1948).

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. N. Madhava Rau (former Dewan of Mysore and Constitutional Advisor to the Eastern States) was appointed to the Drafting Committee to replace B.L. Mitter, who resigned from the Assembly due to ill health.
Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. T.T. Krishnamachari was inducted into the Drafting Committee in 1948 to fill the vacancy caused by the death of D.P. Khaitan.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Sir Syed Mohammad Saadullah, the former Premier of Assam, was the only member of the Drafting Committee who had been elected to the Constituent Assembly on a Muslim League ticket (note that N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, and Dr. K.M. Munshi were the other original members).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, an eminent jurist who had served as the Advocate General of Madras Presidency for fifteen years, was one of the original seven members of the Drafting Committee.

ref: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. V; Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the deliberative methodology and decision-making process of the Constituent Assembly of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Every contested clause during the Second Reading required a mandatory two-thirds majority of the total membership of the Assembly to prevent majoritarian imposition.
opts.B: The Assembly operated primarily through the twin principles of decision-making by consensus and the accommodation of diverse institutional concepts, circulated the February 1948 Draft for public critique for eight months, and avoided party whips during constitutional debates.
opts.C: Deadlocks between the Union Constitution Committee and the Provincial Constitution Committee on federal distribution of powers were resolved through binding provincial legislative referendums prior to the Third Reading.
opts.D: The Drafting Committee's initial text of February 1948 was treated as confidential parliamentary material and was opened to public inspection only after the completion of the clause-by-clause Second Reading.

core: As documented by constitutional historian Granville Austin, the Constituent Assembly of India distinguished itself by adopting two foundational decision-making principles: consensus (striving for unanimity rather than simple majority coercion) and accommodation (reconciling seemingly incompatible concepts like federalism and unitary strength). Furthermore, the Assembly actively solicited public participation by publishing the Draft Constitution in February 1948 for eight months of public feedback before beginning the clause-by-clause Second Reading.

exp.why: Option B is correct. The Constituent Assembly rejected strict party whips on constitutional questions and functioned through 'decision-making by consensus' and the 'principle of accommodation'. After the First Draft was published in February 1948, the people of India, the press, and provincial legislatures were given eight months (until October 1948) to propose criticisms and amendments before the Second Reading (clause-by-clause consideration, November 15, 1948 to October 17, 1949) commenced. Option A is incorrect because the Rules of Procedure did not mandate a two-thirds majority of total membership for passing every contested clause; formally, decisions could be taken by a simple majority of members present and voting, though the leadership consistently delayed votes to build broad consensus. Option C is incorrect because no provincial referendums were held to resolve federal deadlocks; instead, joint meetings of the Union and Provincial Constitution Committees resolved such issues. Option D is incorrect because the February 1948 Draft was widely published and circulated for public scrutiny well before the Second Reading began.

ref: Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, Ch. 13; NCERT Class XI: Indian Constitution at Work, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the enactment and commencement of the Constitution of India under Part XXII (Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 394, the provisions relating to citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament, and Fundamental Rights came into force immediately upon the enactment of the Constitution on November 26, 1949.

2. Article 395 explicitly repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935, while specifically exempting the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 from repeal.
3. Article 393 and Article 394 were themselves among the constitutional provisions that became operational on November 26, 1949 prior to the commencement of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 394 distinguishes between the date of adoption/enactment (November 26, 1949), when sixteen specific articles dealing with citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament, temporary/transitional provisions, and short title came into force at once, and the date of commencement (January 26, 1950), when the remaining provisions—including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles—became operational. Simultaneously, Article 395 repealed the 1935 and 1947 Acts while explicitly preserving the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 394, only Article 394 itself and fifteen other specified articles (Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, and 393)—which dealt with citizenship, the oath of the President, the Election Commission, definitions/interpretation, provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions, and the short title—came into force at once on November 26, 1949. Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) came into force only on the date of commencement of the Constitution, i.e., January 26, 1950.

Statement 2 is correct. Article 395 explicitly states: 'The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.' Preserving the 1949 Act ensured continuity in the termination of British Privy Council appellate jurisdiction over Indian courts.

Statement 3 is correct. Article 394 expressly begins with the words 'This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once', meaning both Article 393 (Short title) and Article 394 (Commencement) entered into force on November 26, 1949.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 393, 394 and 395; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following historic milestones performed by the Constituent Assembly of India:
items: 1. Adoption of the National Flag
2. Unanimous adoption of the Objectives Resolution
3. Election of Dr. Rajendra Prasad as the first President of India
4. Ratification of India's membership of the Commonwealth
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the above events from the earliest to the latest?
core: In addition to framing the Constitution and enacting ordinary laws as the Dominion Legislature, the Constituent Assembly performed sovereign nation-building acts between 1947 and 1950: adopting the Objectives Resolution (January 22, 1947), adopting the National Flag (July 22, 1947), ratifying Commonwealth membership (May 1949), and electing the first President of India along with adopting the National Anthem and National Song (January 24, 1950).

exp.why: The National Flag (horizontal tricolour of deep saffron, white, and dark green in equal proportion with the navy-blue Dharma Chakra at the centre) was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on July 22, 1947, making it the second milestone in the sequence.
The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946, was unanimously adopted by the Constituent Assembly on January 22, 1947, making it the earliest milestone in the sequence.

In its final session held on January 24, 1950 (two days before the commencement of the Constitution), the Constituent Assembly elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad as the first President of India and adopted the National Anthem and National Song, making it the latest milestone in the sequence.

Following the London Declaration of April 1949—which allowed a republican India to remain a full member of the Commonwealth while recognizing the British Monarch solely as the symbolic Head of the Commonwealth—the Constituent Assembly ratified India's continued membership of the Commonwealth in May 1949, placing it third in the sequence (2-1-4-3).

ref: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 2 (Other Functions Performed by the Constituent Assembly)

stem: With reference to the historical evolution of institutional mechanisms in the Indian constitutional framework, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Ordinance-making power of the Executive during emergencies : Indian Councils Act of 1861
2. Statutory recognition of the Portfolio System in the Executive Council : Indian Councils Act of 1861
3. First statutory provision for establishing a Public Service Commission in India : Government of India Act of 1935
4. Three-fold division of legislative subjects into Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent Lists : Government of India Act of 1919
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Tracing modern constitutional instruments to their British-era statutory precursors requires distinguishing between successive reforms: the Indian Councils Act of 1861 introduced both the Viceroy's six-month ordinance-making power and statutory recognition for Lord Canning's portfolio system; the Government of India Act of 1919 first mandated the creation of a Public Service Commission (realized in 1926); and the Government of India Act of 1935 first replaced the two-list system with a three-fold enumeration of Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent legislative lists.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Section 23 of the Indian Councils Act of 1861 first empowered the Viceroy to promulgate ordinances without the concurrence of the legislative council during an emergency, with the lifespan of such an ordinance fixed at six months.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. The Indian Councils Act of 1861 accorded statutory recognition to the 'portfolio system' (introduced by Lord Canning in 1859), under which a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council was placed in charge of one or more government departments and authorized to issue final orders on behalf of the Council.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. It was Section 96C of the Government of India Act of 1919 (not the 1935 Act) that first made a statutory provision for the establishment of a Public Service Commission in India, leading to the setting up of the Central Public Service Commission in 1926 on the recommendation of the Lee Commission (1923–24). The Government of India Act of 1935 subsequently expanded this architecture to provide for a Federal Public Service Commission, Provincial Public Service Commissions, and Joint Public Service Commissions.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The Government of India Act of 1919 provided only a two-fold classification of subjects into Central and Provincial Lists (with Provincial subjects further bifurcated into 'Transferred' and 'Reserved' under Dyarchy). The three-fold division of legislative subjects into Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent Lists—the direct precursor to the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India—was first introduced by the Government of India Act of 1935.

ref: D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 1 (The Historical Background); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: In the context of the Preamble to the Constitution of India, the characterisation of the Indian polity specifically as a 'Republic'—as distinct from merely being 'Democratic'—implies which of the following?

opts.A: The executive is collectively responsible to the popular chamber of the legislature elected through universal adult franchise.
opts.B: The Constitution establishes a federal distribution of powers between the Union and the States with an independent judiciary.
opts.C: The State possesses complete external independence to conduct its foreign affairs without subjection to any external authority.
opts.D: Political sovereignty vests in the people with an elected Head of State and all public offices are open to every citizen without any privileged class.

core: A democratic polity may be either a monarchy (where the Head of State is hereditary, as in the UK) or a republic (where the Head of State is elected directly or indirectly for a fixed term). In the Indian Preamble, the term 'Republic' signifies an elected Head of State, the vesting of political sovereignty in the people rather than a single individual, and the absence of any privileged class so that all public offices are open to every citizen without discrimination.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because the term 'Republic' in the Indian Preamble encompasses three core constitutional attributes: first, the Head of State (the President of India) is always elected (indirectly for a fixed term of five years) rather than occupying office through hereditary succession; second, political sovereignty is vested in the people of India and not in a single monarch; and third, there is a complete absence of any privileged class, meaning all public offices are open to every citizen without discrimination. Option (A) describes parliamentary representative democracy rather than republicanism (for instance, the United Kingdom has collective executive responsibility to an elected lower house, yet it is a constitutional monarchy and not a republic). Option (B) describes federalism, which is an institutional feature of the Constitution rather than the meaning of a republic. Option (C) defines external 'Sovereignty', not 'Republic'.

ref: Preamble to the Constitution of India; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 5 (Preamble of the Constitution)

stem: With reference to the historical evolution and procedural enactment of the Preamble to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Preamble is based on the 'Objectives Resolution' moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946 and unanimously adopted by the Constituent Assembly in January 1947.
2. To serve as a binding framework for the Drafting Committee, the Preamble was the very first part of the Constitution to be formally voted upon and enacted by the Constituent Assembly.
3. While the Preamble explicitly records November 26, 1949 as the date of adoption and enactment of the Constitution, the date of commencement of the Constitution is January 26, 1950.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the Preamble derives its philosophical foundation from the Objectives Resolution of 1946–47, the Constituent Assembly deliberately enacted the Preamble only after the rest of the Constitution had already been enacted so that it would remain in full conformity with the final constitutional text. Further, the Constitution distinguishes between its date of adoption (November 26, 1949, mentioned in the Preamble) and its date of commencement (January 26, 1950, defined under Article 394).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Preamble to the Indian Constitution is a modified version of the historic 'Objectives Resolution' drafted and moved by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946, and unanimously adopted by the Constituent Assembly on January 22, 1947.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it reverses the actual procedural sequence followed in the Constituent Assembly. The Preamble was enacted by the Constituent Assembly only after the rest of the Constitution had already been debated, voted upon, and enacted. President of the Constituent Assembly Dr. Rajendra Prasad specifically put the question 'That the Preamble stand part of the Constitution' at the end of the Second Reading (on October 17, 1949) so that the Preamble would accurately reflect the Constitution as finally framed.

Statement 3 is correct.
