The final paragraph of the Preamble explicitly records 'this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949' as the date on which the people of India in their Constituent Assembly adopted, enacted, and gave to themselves the Constitution. Under Article 394, while a few transitional and immediate provisions (such as citizenship and elections) came into force on November 26, 1949 itself, the remaining major provisions came into force on January 26, 1950, which Article 394 expressly designates as 'the date of the commencement of this Constitution'.

ref: Constituent Assembly Debates (Vol. X, Oct 17, 1949); Article 394 of the Constitution of India; Laxmikanth Ch. 2 & Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the ideals of Justice, Liberty, and Equality enshrined in the Preamble and other parts of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Preamble explicitly secures to all its citizens social, economic, political and religious justice, alongside equality of status and of opportunity.
2. While the Preamble enumerates liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, it does not mention economic or political liberty.
3. The phrase 'justice, social, economic and political' is unique to the text of the Preamble and does not appear verbatim in any Article of Part IV of the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The text of the Preamble is drafted with strict conceptual precision: it specifies three dimensions of Justice (social, economic, and political), five dimensions of Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship), and two dimensions of Equality (status and opportunity). Furthermore, the exact phrase 'justice, social, economic and political' is mirrored verbatim in Article 38(1) under the Directive Principles of State Policy.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Preamble specifies only three forms of Justice: social, economic, and political (an ideal inspired by the Russian Revolution of 1917). It does not mention 'religious justice'; matters of religion are instead covered under the five dimensions of Liberty (belief, faith, and worship) and Fundamental Rights (Articles 25–28).

Statement 2 is correct. The Preamble specifically enumerates five forms of Liberty for citizens: 'LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship'. It does not mention 'economic liberty' or 'political liberty', whereas 'economic' and 'political' are qualifiers attached to 'JUSTICE'.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The exact phrase 'justice, social, economic and political' is not restricted to the Preamble; it appears verbatim in Article 38(1) of Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), which mandates that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting a social order in which 'justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life'.

ref: Preamble and Article 38(1) of the Constitution of India; NCERT Class XI Indian Constitution at Work

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional validity and import of the terms 'Socialist' and 'Secular' in the Preamble to the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: The Supreme Court has upheld the 42nd Constitutional Amendment's insertion of the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble, holding that constitutional socialism in India neither restricts private enterprise nor mandates state nationalisation of all means of production.

Statement-II: Under the Indian constitutional scheme, the Preamble is an integral and amendable part of the Constitution under Article 368, where 'Socialism' denotes an evolving welfare state committed to eliminating inequality of opportunity within a mixed economy rather than a rigid dogmatic ideology, and 'Secularism' is an intrinsic facet of the Basic Structure.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court decisively upheld the 1976 insertion of 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble under Article 368, rejecting the argument that the retention of the original adoption date (November 26, 1949) barred retrospective textual amendment. The Court clarified that Indian 'Socialism' signifies an evolving welfare state and mixed economy that does not fetter private enterprise or bind elected governments to a rigid economic dogma.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (November 2024), the Supreme Court dismissed challenges to Section 2 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, which inserted the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble. The Court expressly ruled that the presence of the word 'Socialist' in the Preamble does not restrict private enterprise or tie the hands of elected governments to any static, state-monopoly economic model.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The Supreme Court explained that the Preamble is an inalienable part of the Constitution and is fully subject to Parliament's constituent power of amendment under Article 368 (notwithstanding that the Preamble bears the historical adoption date of November 26, 1949). Furthermore, in the Indian context, 'Socialism' represents the principle of economic and social justice embedded in a welfare state and mixed economy (eliminating inequality of status and opportunity without stifling private sector growth), while 'Secularism' (equal respect and neutrality towards all religions) was already an intrinsic part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

ref: Supreme Court Judgment in Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024 INSC 899); 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

stem: Consider the following landmark judicial pronouncements by the Supreme Court regarding the nature, status, and amendability of the Preamble to the Constitution of India:
items: 1. A nine-Judge Bench reiterated that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and invoked it to hold that secularism is a positive concept of equal treatment of all religions while adjudicating the scope of Article 356.
2. An advisory Bench opined that while the Preamble serves as 'a key to open the mind of the makers' where the text is ambiguous, it is nevertheless not a part of the Constitution.

3. An eleven-Judge Bench observed that the Preamble sets out the 'eternal and inalienable' ideals and aspirations of the Constitution in a nutshell while ruling that Parliament had no power to abridge Fundamental Rights.

4. A thirteen-Judge Bench formally overruled the earlier advisory opinion, declaring that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and is amendable under Article 368 subject to the Basic Structure doctrine.
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above judicial pronouncements, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The Supreme Court's jurisprudence on the Preamble evolved chronologically from treating it merely as an external interpretive aid in In re Berubari Union (1960), to celebrating its eternal ideals in I.C. Golaknath (1967), formally recognizing it as an integral and amendable part of the Constitution in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and applying its basic features directly to test executive action under Article 356 in S.R. Bommai (1994).

exp.why: Item 1 refers to S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), where a nine-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and relied upon it to establish that secularism is a part of the Basic Structure, the subversion of which by a State Government can justify President's Rule under Article 356.

Item 2 refers to the Presidential Reference in In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves (1960), where an eight-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court acknowledged that the Preamble is 'a key to open the mind of the makers', but erroneously held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.

Item 3 refers to I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), where Chief Justice K. Subba Rao (speaking for the majority of the eleven-Judge Bench) observed that the Preamble contains in a nutshell the ideals and aspirations of the Constitution andis not a mere platitude, while holding that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.

Item 4 refers to Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), where the thirteen-Judge Bench overruled the 1960 Berubari Union view, holding that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368 provided the basic elements or fundamental features enshrined in it are not destroyed. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1960) -> 3 (1967) -> 4 (1973) -> 1 (1994).

ref: In re Berubari Union (1960); Golaknath (1967); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); S.R. Bommai (1994); Laxmikanth Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the legal utility and limitations of the Preamble in constitutional adjudication in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Preamble is neither a source of substantive legislative power to the legislature nor is its content independently enforceable by a writ in a court of law.

2. The Preamble acts as an implied constitutional prohibition that can independently invalidate an ordinary statute passed by Parliament under the Seventh Schedule even if no operative Article of the Constitution is violated.

3. Where the language of an enacted Article of the Constitution is clear and unambiguous, the Preamble cannot be invoked to override or restrict its plain meaning, and serves as an interpretive aid only when a provision is capable of more than one construction.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and encapsulates elements of its Basic Structure for testing constitutional amendments under Article 368, it is neither a source of substantive legislative power nor a source of prohibition on legislative competence. For ordinary legislation and constitutional interpretation, the Preamble cannot override the clear language of an enacted Article and serves as an interpretive aid only when an operative provision is ambiguous.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. It is a settled principle of Indian constitutional law that the Preamble is non-justiciable: its ideals cannot be directly and independently enforced in a court of law through a writ petition, nor does it confer any substantive legislative or executive power upon any organ of the State.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Just as the Preamble is not a source of power, it is also not a source of prohibition or limitation upon the plenary legislative powers expressly granted by the Constitution. As held by the Supreme Court in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006), an ordinary statute enacted by a competent legislature cannot be struck down solely for violating the Preamble or the 'spirit of the Constitution' unless it transgresses a specific operative provision such as Part III (Fundamental Rights) or legislative competence under Part XI.

Statement 3 is correct. In constitutional adjudication (affirmed in Berubari Union, Kesavananda Bharati, and Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. Union of India, 1993), if the terms used in any substantive Article of the Constitution are plain, clear, and unambiguous, they must be given effect to directly, and the Preamble cannot be invoked to control, qualify, or restrict that plain meaning. Recourse to the Preamble as an aid to construction is permissible only when the language of an operative provision is ambiguous and reasonably admits of more than one interpretation.

ref: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973); Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideal of 'Liberty' enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: The ideal of 'Liberty' in the Preamble does not signify a mere absence of restraint or an unbridled license to do as one pleases, but encompasses positive opportunities for the fullest development of individual personality.

Statement-II: The liberties of expression, belief, faith, and worship proclaimed in the Preamble are operationalized in Part III of the Constitution as unqualified rights that can be curtailed only during the operation of a Proclamation of Emergency.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Indian constitutional philosophy, Liberty has both a negative dimension (absence of arbitrary restraint) and a positive dimension (providing conditions for the holistic development of an individual's personality). However, this liberty is never absolute and is subject to permanent constitutional qualifications and reasonable restrictions within Part III itself, even during normal peacetime.

exp.why: The framers of the Constitution conceived 'Liberty' in the Preamble not merely as the negative absence of state restraint, but as a positive enabling condition essential for the fullest development of every individual's personality and for the successful functioning of a democratic republic.

The liberties promised in the Preamble—such as liberty of expression, belief, faith, and worship—are explicitly qualified in Part III of the Constitution even during peacetime. Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), and freedom of conscience and religion under Article 25(1) is subject to public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part III.

ref: Constitution of India, Preamble, Art. 19 & 25; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the comparative constitutional and historical sources that inspired the Preamble to the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Practice of prefixing a written Constitution with a Preamble and the opening phrase 'We, the People' : Constitution of the United States of America
2. Foundational blueprint and substantive vision of the Preamble : Objectives Resolution moved in the Constituent Assembly (1946)
3. Ideals of social, economic, and political justice : French Revolution (1789)
4. Ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity : Russian Revolution (1917)
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: While the foundational blueprint and substantive vision of the Indian Preamble came directly from Jawaharlal Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946), its structural form and philosophical triads drew selectively from global milestones. Specifically, the American Constitution inspired the inclusion of a Preamble and the opening words 'We, the People', the 1917 Russian Revolution inspired the triad of Justice, and the 1789 French Revolution inspired the triad of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity.

exp.why: The American Constitution was the first written constitution in the world to begin with a Preamble, and India adopted both this constitutional practice and the opening declarative phrase 'We, the People' from the United States Constitution.

The Preamble to the Indian Constitution is directly based on the 'Objectives Resolution' drafted and moved by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and unanimously adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947.
The ideal of justice in its three dimensions—social, economic, and political—was inspired by the Russian Revolution of 1917, not the French Revolution of 1789.
The democratic trinity of liberty, equality, and fraternity in the Indian Preamble was inspired by the French Revolution of 1789, not the Russian Revolution of 1917.

ref: Subhash Kashyap, Our Constitution; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 3 & 4

stem: With reference to the legal and constitutional implications of the terms 'Sovereign' and 'Secular' in the Preamble to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. By virtue of India's sovereign status, international treaties ratified by the Union Executive do not automatically become enforceable as domestic law to override municipal statutes unless Parliament enacts enabling legislation under Article 253.

2. Unlike the strict wall of separation in Western negative secularism, the secularism envisaged in the Indian Preamble embodies a positive concept of equal respect for all religions alongside constitutional authority for the State to regulate secular activities associated with religious practice.

3. India's acquisition of foreign territory or cession of a part of its territory pursuant to a treaty is an exercise of sovereign power, though ceding national territory to a foreign state requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: External sovereignty empowers the Indian Union to enter into international treaties and acquire or cede territory, while internal sovereignty dictates a dualist legal framework under Article 253 whereby treaties affecting domestic rights require parliamentary legislation. Simultaneously, Indian secularism represents 'principled distance' and equal protection to all faiths (Sarva Dharma Sambhava) rather than rigid state hostility or isolation from religion.

exp.why: India follows the doctrine of dualism regarding international law and municipal law. Under Article 73 read with Article 253, while the Union Executive can ratify international treaties as an exercise of external sovereignty, such treaties are not self-executing if they modify domestic statutes or affect citizens' rights; Parliament must enact enabling legislation under Article 253.

As affirmed in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), Indian secularism does not erect an impassable wall between Church and State. Instead, it mandates equal treatment of all religions while empowering the State under Article 25(2) to regulate economic, financial, or political activities associated with religion and to enact social welfare reforms.

Being a sovereign state, India can acquire foreign territory or cede part of its territory according to international law. However, in the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that Article 3 does not cover the cession of Indian territory to a foreign state, which therefore requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

ref: Constitution of India, Preamble, Art. 25, 253 & 368; In re Berubari Union (1960); S.R. Bommai (1994)

stem: With reference to the concept of 'Fraternity' in the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Fraternity clause in the Preamble explicitly seeks to assure two interconnected values: the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.
2. Both the expressions 'dignity of the individual' and 'integrity of the Nation' were inserted into the Fraternity clause of the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
3. Beyond the Preamble, the constitutional commitment to promoting fraternity and upholding the dignity of citizens is reinforced as a Fundamental Duty in Part IVA of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar emphasized that without fraternity, liberty and equality would remain mere coats of paint. The Preamble expressly links fraternity to assuring both individual dignity (present since 1949) and national unity and integrity (with 'and integrity' added in 1976), a vision further operationalized through Fundamental Duties under Article 51A.

exp.why: The text of the Preamble expressly declares the resolve to promote among all citizens 'FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation'.

The expression 'dignity of the individual' and the phrase 'unity of the Nation' were present in the original Preamble adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 substituted 'unity of the Nation' with 'unity and integrity of the Nation', adding only the words 'and integrity' to the Fraternity clause.

Article 51A(e) in Part IVA of the Constitution makes it a Fundamental Duty of every citizen to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood (fraternity) amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic, and regional or sectional diversities, and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.

ref: Constitution of India, Preamble & Art. 51A(e); 42nd Amendment Act, 1976

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the procedure and scope for amending the Preamble to the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Since the Preamble embodies the foundational federal and democratic ideals of the Republic, a Constitutional Amendment Bill seeking to amend the Preamble requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States under the proviso to Article 368(2).

2. Because the Preamble precedes Part I of the Constitution and contains no numbered Articles, a Bill to amend the Preamble requires the prior recommendation of the President before its introduction in either House of Parliament.

3. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court held that while the operative Articles of the Constitution can be amended under Article 368, the text of the Preamble is immune from the amending power of Parliament.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Once the Supreme Court recognized the Preamble as an integral part of the Constitution in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), it became amendable under Article 368 subject to the Basic Structure limitation. Procedurally, since the Preamble is not listed in the entrenched proviso to Article 368(2), amending it requires only a special majority of Parliament without state ratification or prior presidential recommendation.

exp.why: Ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures is required only for bills seeking to amend the specific federal provisions exhaustively enumerated in Clauses (a) to (e) of the proviso to Article 368(2). Since the Preamble is not enumerated in the proviso to Article 368(2), it can be amended by a special majority of Parliament alone.

Under Article 368(2), a Constitutional Amendment Bill—including one seeking to amend the Preamble—can be introduced in either House of Parliament by a Minister or a Private Member without the prior recommendation of the President.

In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court reversed its earlier opinion in Berubari Union (1960) and explicitly ruled that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368, provided no amendment alters or destroys the Basic Structure reflected in it.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 368; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

stem: With reference to the constitutional vision of 'Economic Justice' in the Preamble and its judicial interpretation alongside Part IV of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The preambular ideal of 'Justice—social, economic and political' is directly echoed in Article 38 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, creating an interpretive bridge between the Preamble and Part IV of the Constitution.

2. According to the Supreme Court, the commitment to economic justice and a socialist welfare state in the Preamble does not bind the Constitution to any rigid economic dogma, leaving elected governments free to evolve flexible economic structures.

3. To realize distributive justice as envisioned in the Preamble, the Supreme Court has held that every privately owned resource automatically qualifies as a 'material resource of the community' available for state acquisition under Article 39(b).
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: The Preamble's goal of social, economic, and political justice is operationalized through Articles 38 and 39 in Part IV. In landmark 2024 rulings (Property Owners Association and Dr. Balram Singh), the Supreme Court clarified that Indian constitutional socialism signifies a welfare state and mixed economy rather than state monopoly, and not every private property automatically becomes a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b).

exp.why: Article 38(1) explicitly reproduces the preambular phrase by directing the State to strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting a social order in which 'justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life'.

In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (9-Judge Bench, 2024) and Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution deliberately avoids freezing any particular economic theory or rigid socialist dogma, allowing democratically elected governments the flexibility to adopt mixed-economy policies and encourage private enterprise alongside state welfare.

In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), a 9-Judge Constitution Bench overruled the expansive observations in State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) and Sanjeev Coke (1983), holding that NOT every privately owned resource automatically qualifies as a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b); whether a particular private resource falls within Article 39(b) depends on a context-specific inquiry into its nature, scarcity, impact on community well-being, and public trust characteristics.

ref: Constitution of India, Preamble, Art. 38 & 39(b); Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024)

stem: With reference to Article 1 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements accurately brings out the constitutional distinction between the expressions 'Union of India' and 'Territory of India'?

opts.A: The 'Union of India' includes only the States that are members of the federal system and share a distribution of powers with the Centre, whereas the 'Territory of India' is a wider expression encompassing the entire territory over which the sovereignty of India extends, including Union Territories and acquired territories.
opts.B: The 'Territory of India' refers solely to the existing States and Union Territories specified in the First Schedule, whereas the 'Union of India' is a broader constitutional term that also includes any foreign territories that may be acquired by the Government of India in the future.
opts.C: The Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States' rather than a 'Federation of States' primarily because the State Executives act solely as delegated agents of the Union Executive even during normal non-emergency times.
opts.D: Both 'Union of India' and 'Territory of India' are constitutionally synonymous terms under Article 1, as Union Territories also enjoy federal autonomy and constitutional division of legislative powers on par with the States.

core: Article 1 draws a structural distinction between the 'Union of States' (the federal compact comprising only the States) and the 'Territory of India' (the sovereign geographic domain comprising States, Union Territories, and acquired territories). Furthermore, the phrase 'Union of States' signifies an indestructible union not formed by an agreement among States.

exp.why: Option A is correct because under Article 1(1), 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.' The expression 'Union of India' includes only the States which are members of the federal system and share a constitutional distribution of legislative and executive powers with the Union. In contrast, under Article 1(3), the 'Territory of India' comprises: (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired. Thus, 'Territory of India' is a wider expression because it covers the entire geographic expanse over which Indian sovereignty is exercised, including directly administered Union Territories and newly acquired territories. Option B is incorrect as it inverts the relative scope of the two terms. Option C is incorrect because, as explained by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly, the Drafting Committee preferred 'Union of States' over 'Federation of States' for two specific reasons: first, the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among autonomous units like the American federation; and second, the States have no right to secede from the federation. In normal times, States are not mere agents of the Centre (S.R. Bommai v. Union of India). Option D is incorrect because the two terms are not synonymous and Union Territories are centrally administered units rather than autonomous federal partners.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 1(1) & 1(3); Constituent Assembly Debates Vol. VII (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the parliamentary power to reorganize territories under Articles 2 and 3 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 2 empowers Parliament both to admit existing foreign territories into the Union of India and to carve out a new State by separating territory from an existing State of the Indian Union.
2. A Bill seeking to alter the boundaries or name of an existing State under Article 3 can be introduced in either House of Parliament only on the prior recommendation of the President.

3. Unlike a Bill under Article 3, a Bill introduced under Article 2 for the admission or establishment of a new State from territory not previously part of India does not constitutionally require a prior reference by the President to any State Legislature.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 2 governs external territorial additions (admitting existing states or establishing new states that were not previously part of India), whereas Article 3 governs internal readjustment of existing Indian States and Union Territories. Consequently, the procedural preconditions in the Proviso to Article 3 apply only to Bills under Article 3.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect as it conflates the distinct scopes of Article 2 and Article 3. Article 2 grants two powers to Parliament: (a) the power to admit into the Union of India new States (duly formed political units already in existence outside India), and (b) the power to establish new States (territories not previously existing as states and not part of India). However, carving out a new State by separating territory from an existing State of the Indian Union is an internal territorial readjustment governed exclusively by Article 3(a), not Article 2.

Statement 2 is correct. Under the Proviso to Article 3, no Bill for the purpose of forming a new State or altering the areas, boundaries, or names of existing States shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President. Note that the bill can be introduced in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, but only with prior Presidential recommendation.

Statement 3 is correct. The procedural requirement of prior reference of the Bill by the President to the affected State Legislature for expressing its views within a specified period is contained in the Proviso to Article 3. Article 2 contains no such proviso; Parliament has broad discretion to admit or establish new States from territories not previously part of India on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 2 & 3; M.P. Jain, Indian Constitutional Law, Ch. V

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the procedural safeguards under the Proviso to Article 3 of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Under the Proviso to Article 3, the power to specify as well as to extend the time period within which a State Legislature must express its views on a State Reorganization Bill vests solely with the President of India.

2. A Bill under Article 3 may be validly introduced and passed by Parliament once the specified period has expired, even if the concerned State Legislature has failed to transmit its views or has unanimously rejected the proposal.

3. As held by the Supreme Court in Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960), if Parliament moves an amendment that substantially modifies the territorial arrangement envisaged in the original Bill, a fresh reference of the amended proposal to the concerned State Legislature is mandatory.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Proviso to Article 3 guarantees a procedural opportunity for the affected State Legislature to express its views within a President-specified timeframe, not a substantive veto over reorganization. Once the original Bill has been referred, germane parliamentary amendments to the Bill do not require a fresh reference to the State Legislature.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Proviso to Article 3 explicitly stipulates that where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries, or name of any of the States, the Bill shall be referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon 'within such period as may be specified in the reference or within such further period as the President may allow and the period so specified or allowed has expired.' This power was added by the 5th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1955.

Statement 2 is correct. The constitutional obligation of the President and Parliament is satisfied once the Bill is referred to the State Legislature and the specified or extended time period expires. Parliament is neither bound by the views expressed by the State Legislature nor prevented from proceeding if the State Legislature withholds its response within the stipulated time.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960), the original Bill proposed a three-unit split (Maharashtra, Gujarat, and a separate UT of Bombay), which Parliament subsequently amended during passage to create a composite bilingual State of Bombay. A 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that Article 3 does not require a fresh reference to the State Legislature every time an amendment to the Bill is moved and accepted in Parliament in accordance with Parliamentary Rules of Procedure, provided the amendment is germane to the subject matter of the original proposal.

ref: Constitution of India, Proviso to Article 3; 5th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1955; Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, AIR 1960 SC 51

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the applicability of Article 3 of the Constitution of India to Union Territories:
items: Statement-I: Parliament can pass a law under Article 3 to unite a Union Territory with an adjacent State or carve out a new Union Territory from an existing Union Territory, without referring the Bill to the Legislature of the affected Union Territory for its views.

Statement-II: Explanation I to Article 3 expressly clarifies that while the term 'State' in clauses (a) to (e) of Article 3 includes a 'Union Territory', it does not include a 'Union Territory' for the purpose of the Proviso to Article 3.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Inserted by the 18th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1966, Explanations I and II to Article 3 include 'Union Territory' within the meaning of 'State' in the substantive enabling clauses (a) to (e), while deliberately excluding 'Union Territory' from the Proviso to Article 3. Consequently, no consultation with a Union Territory's legislature is required to alter its boundaries.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 3 read with Explanations I and II, Parliament is empowered to form a new State or Union Territory by uniting a Union Territory with any State or separating territory from a Union Territory. When doing so, no reference of the Bill to the Legislature of the affected Union Territory (even if the Union Territory has an elected Legislative Assembly such as Puducherry, NCT of Delhi, or Jammu and Kashmir) is constitutionally required.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The 18th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1966 inserted Explanation I and Explanation II to Article 3 (in the wake of the Punjab Reorganization). Explanation I states: 'In this article, in clauses (a) to (e), "State" includes a Union territory, but in the proviso, "State" does not include a Union territory.' Because the requirement to refer a reorganization Bill to the concerned Legislature is situated inside the Proviso to Article 3, the deliberate exclusion of Union Territories from the word 'State' in the Proviso directly explains why Parliament need not refer such a Bill to a Union Territory's legislature.

ref: Constitution of India, Explanations I & II to Article 3; 18th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1966

stem: With reference to the constitutional jurisprudence governing the alteration of India's external boundaries and territory, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The power of Parliament under Article 3(c) to diminish the area of a State relates exclusively to internal territorial readjustments among the constituent units of the Indian Union and does not authorize the cession of Indian territory to a foreign country.

2. The cession of sovereign Indian territory to a foreign nation requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368, whereas the absorption of a foreign territory acquired by India under international law can be effected by ordinary parliamentary legislation.

3. As held by the Supreme Court in Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969), the settlement of a bona fide boundary dispute with a neighboring country—where the exact frontier was previously undemarcated—does not amount to cession of territory and can be executed by the Union Executive alone without any constitutional amendment.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Supreme Court jurisprudence distinguishes between three external territorial scenarios: (1) cession of undisputed Indian territory to a foreign state (requires an Article 368 amendment); (2) settlement of a bona fide undemarcated boundary dispute (can be done by Executive action alone); and (3) admission/merger of acquired foreign territory (can be done via ordinary legislation under Article 2 or 3).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In the Presidential Reference in In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves (1960), an 8-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court held that Parliament's power to 'diminish the area of any State' under Article 3(c) applies solely to internal adjustments where land taken from one Indian unit remains within the Territory of India under another unit. It does not cover the transfer or cession of sovereign Indian territory to a foreign nation.

Statement 2 is correct. Because cession reduces the Territory of India under Article 1(3) and the First Schedule in a manner not covered by Articles 2, 3, and 4, it can only be accomplished by amending the Constitution under Article 368 (as exemplified by the 9th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1960 for Berubari Union and the 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 for the Indo-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement). Conversely, foreign territory validly acquired under international law (by treaty, cession, or conquest) automatically becomes part of the Territory of India under Article 1(3)(c) upon acquisition and can be admitted as a new State under Article 2 or merged into an existing State/UT under Article 3 by ordinary parliamentary law (unless conferral of special structural autonomy requires an Article 368 amendment).

Statement 3 is correct. In Ram Kishore Sen v. Union of India (1966) and Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969, concerning the Rann of Kutch Tribunal Award), the Supreme Court distinguished outright cession of de jure Indian territory from the ascertainment and demarcation of an uncertain, disputed boundary. Settling a bona fide boundary dispute does not involve ceding territory that demonstrably belonged to India; hence, it falls within the treaty-making and executive power of the Union under Article 73 read with Entry 14 of the Union List, requiring neither a constitutional amendment under Article 368 nor parliamentary legislation.

ref: In re Berubari Union, AIR 1960 SC 845; Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India, (1969) 3 SCR 254; 9th & 100th Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to Article 4 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 4(1), any law enacted by Parliament under Article 2 or Article 3 must contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law.

2. While a law made under Article 3 can amend the First Schedule by a simple majority, any consequential alteration in the allocation of seats in the Council of States under the Fourth Schedule requires a special majority and ratification by half of the State Legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2).

3. Under Article 4(1), a State Reorganization Act passed by an ordinary legislative majority can also include supplemental and consequential provisions creating or abolishing High Courts, dividing assets and liabilities, and altering representation in the Legislature of the State affected by such law.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 4(1) mandates that laws made under Article 2 or 3 include necessary amendments to both the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule along with broad supplemental provisions. Article 4(2) expressly exempts all such laws from the purview of Article 368, enabling even Fourth Schedule seat reallocations to be passed by a simple majority.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 4(1) explicitly states: 'Any law referred to in article 2 or article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law...' Thus, amending the territorial entries in the First Schedule and the Rajya Sabha seat allocation in the Fourth Schedule is an integral statutory component of a State Reorganization Act.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Although the Fourth Schedule (allocation of seats in the Council of States) is generally listed as an entrenched provision under the Proviso to Article 368(2)(c), Article 4(2) carves out an explicit constitutional exception: 'No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.' Consequently, when the Fourth Schedule is amended as a consequence of a law enacted under Article 2 or Article 3, it is passed by a simple majority through the ordinary legislative process and does not require a special majority or ratification by the State Legislatures.

Statement 3 is correct. Article 4(1) empowers Parliament to include in any law under Article 2 or 3 'such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary.' In Mullaperiyar Environmental Protection Forum v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court affirmed that the power under Article 4(1) is wide enough to cover the establishment of High Courts, apportionment of river water rights, and division of assets and liabilities upon reorganization via ordinary legislative majority.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 4(1) & 4(2); Mullaperiyar Environmental Protection Forum v. Union of India, (2006) 3 SCC 643

stem: With reference to the commissions and committees appointed to examine the reorganization of States in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. S.K. Dhar Commission (1948) : Recommended the reorganization of States on the basis of administrative convenience, geographical contiguity, and financial self-sufficiency rather than linguistic considerations
2. JVP Committee (1948–49) : Accepted language as the primary basis for the reorganization of States while explicitly rejecting the doctrine of 'one language–one State'

3. Fazl Ali Commission (1953–55) : Formally rejected language as the criterion for reorganization at that juncture, while conceding that the matter could be re-examined if public sentiment was insistent and overwhelming
4. Shah Commission (1966) : Recommended the bifurcation of the composite State of Punjab to create the Hindi-speaking State of Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The evolution of State reorganization in India progressed from complete rejection of linguistic criteria in favour of administrative viability (Dhar Commission, 1948), to conditional deferment subject to overwhelming public sentiment (JVP Committee, 1949), to principled acceptance of linguistic homogeneity balanced against national unity and rejecting the 'one language–one State' dogma (Fazl Ali Commission, 1955).

exp.why: The Linguistic Provinces Commission (chaired by S.K. Dhar), appointed by the Constituent Assembly in June 1948, submitted its report in December 1948 recommending that the reorganization of provinces should be based on administrative convenience, geographical contiguity, financial self-sufficiency, and capacity for future development rather than linguistic considerations.

This describes the doctrinal position of the Fazl Ali Commission (States Reorganisation Commission, 1953–55), not the JVP Committee. The JVP Committee (comprising Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya) formally rejected language as the basis for reorganization at that time, though it noted that the issue could be reconsidered if public sentiment was insistent and overwhelming.

This describes the position of the JVP Committee (April 1949), not the Fazl Ali Commission. The Fazl Ali Commission (comprising Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar, and H.N. Kunzru) broadly accepted linguistic and cultural homogeneity as a primary basis for reorganization, while firmly rejecting the theory of 'one language–one State' and emphasizing the preservation of the unity and security of India.

In April 1966, the Government of India appointed the Punjab Boundary Commission under the chairmanship of Justice J.C. Shah. Acting on its recommendations via the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, the composite State of Punjab was bifurcated to create the State of Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh, while hilly areas were merged with the then Union Territory of Himachal Pradesh.

ref: States Reorganisation Commission Report (1955); Laxmikanth Ch. 6 (Union and its Territory)

stem: Consider the following constitutional and statutory milestones in the territorial integration and reorganization of the Indian Union after the enactment of the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956:
items: 1. De jure constitutional incorporation of Puducherry as a Union Territory into the Indian Union
2. Elevation of Himachal Pradesh from a Union Territory to the status of a full-fledged State
3. Incorporation of Dadra and Nagar Haveli as a Union Territory into the Indian Union
4. Conferment of the status of an 'Associate State' of the Indian Union on Sikkim by inserting Article 2A into the Constitution
prompt: Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the above milestones, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: Although the French territories of Pondicherry (Puducherry), Karaikal, Mahe, and Yanam were handed over to India for de facto administration in 1954, their de jure constitutional incorporation via the 14th Constitutional Amendment Act (1962) occurred after the incorporation of Dadra and Nagar Haveli via the 10th Constitutional Amendment Act (1961).

exp.why: While France transferred de facto administration of its establishments in India (Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe, and Yanam) in November 1954, the Treaty of Cession (signed in 1956) was ratified by the French Parliament only in 1962. Consequently, Puducherry was constitutionally incorporated into the Indian Union as a Union Territory by the 14th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962 (with effect from August 16, 1962).

Himachal Pradesh, which had been a Part C State and subsequently a Union Territory from 1956, was elevated to the status of the 18th full-fledged State of the Indian Union on January 25, 1971, through the State of Himachal Pradesh Act, 1970.

After liberation from Portuguese rule in 1954 and subsequent local administration until 1961, Dadra and Nagar Haveli was formally incorporated as a Union Territory into the Indian Union by the 10th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1961 (effective August 11, 1961), preceding the 12th Amendment (Goa, Daman and Diu, 1962) and the 14th Amendment (Puducherry, 1962).

Sikkim was first conferred the constitutional status of an 'Associate State' of the Indian Union through the 35th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1974, which inserted Article 2A and the Tenth Schedule into the Constitution (later repealed by the 36th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975, which made Sikkim a full-fledged State). Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 3 (1961) -> 1 (1962) -> 2 (1971) -> 4 (1974).

ref: Constitution 10th (1961), 14th (1962), and 35th (1974) Amendment Acts; State of Himachal Pradesh Act, 1970

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir as interpreted by the Supreme Court of India in In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution (2023):
items: Statement-I: The erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir did not retain any element of internal sovereignty after its accession to India and the issuance of the Proclamation of November 1949, as Article 1 of the Constitution applied to it directly through Article 370(1)(c), making it an integral part of the Union.

Statement-II: Under Article 370(3) of the Constitution, the President was empowered to issue a public notification declaring that Article 370 shall cease to be operative even after the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir in 1957.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In its December 2023 five-judge Constitution Bench judgment (In Re: Article 370), the Supreme Court held both that Jammu and Kashmir retained zero internal sovereignty post-accession (marking Article 370 as a manifestation of asymmetric federalism rather than sovereignty) and that the President's power under Article 370(3) survived the 1957 dissolution of the J&K Constituent Assembly; however, the survival of the abrogation power under Article 370(3) is a consequence of Article 370's transitional nature rather than the causal explanation for the absence of internal sovereignty.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The five-judge Constitution Bench held that with the execution of the Instrument of Accession in October 1947 and the Proclamation issued by Yuvraj Karan Singh on November 25, 1949 adopting the Constitution of India, Jammu and Kashmir surrendered its sovereignty completely. Moreover, Article 370(1)(c) explicitly mandated that Article 1 of the Constitution (which defines the Union and its territories) applied directly and unconditionally to Jammu and Kashmir from inception, leaving no vestige of internal sovereignty.

Statement-II is also correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The Supreme Court held that when the Constituent Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir ceased to exist in 1957, only the transitional proviso to Article 370(3) requiring its recommendation ceased to operate, while the substantive Presidential power under Article 370(3) to declare Article 370 inoperative survived. However, this procedural and substantive holding on Article 370(3) does not explain why J&K lacked internal sovereignty upon accession; rather, the absence of sovereignty and the temporary character of Article 370 together underpinned the survival of the President's power under Article 370(3).

ref: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution, 2023 INSC 1058 (5-Judge Constitution Bench); Articles 1 and 370

stem: With reference to the interplay between Article 3 and Article 356 of the Constitution in the reorganization of States, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The views expressed by a State Legislature on a Bill referred to it by the President under the Proviso to Article 3 are not binding on the President or Parliament.

2. During the operation of a Proclamation under Article 356 where the State Legislative Assembly is dissolved, the President may under Article 356(1)(c) suspend the operation of the Proviso to Article 3 requiring reference of a reorganization Bill to the State Legislature, and Parliament may exercise the consultative functions of the State Legislature.

3. In In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution (2023), the Supreme Court struck down Parliament's power to carve out a Union Territory from an existing State under Article 3(a) read with Explanation I, holding that Article 3 permits only the creation of full-fledged States.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 3, consultation with the State Legislature is procedural and non-binding; during President's Rule under Article 356, the Proviso to Article 3 can be suspended and Parliament can exercise the State Legislature's consultative role, and the Supreme Court in 2023 explicitly upheld the carving out of the Union Territory of Ladakh from Jammu and Kashmir under Article 3(a) read with Explanation I.

exp.why: As held by the Supreme Court in Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960), the Proviso to Article 3 only requires the President to refer the Bill to the concerned State Legislature to express its views within a specified period. Neither the President nor Parliament is bound to accept or act upon those views, nor is a fresh reference required if Parliament amends the Bill.

When a Proclamation under Article 356 is in force and the State Legislative Assembly has been dissolved, the President is empowered under Article 356(1)(b) to declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, and under Article 356(1)(c) to make incidental and consequential provisions suspending the operation of the Proviso to Article 3 insofar as it relates to referring a reorganization Bill to the State Legislature.

In its December 2023 judgment in In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution, the five-judge Constitution Bench explicitly UPHELD the validity of carving out the Union Territory of Ladakh from the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 3(a) read with Explanation I (inserted by the 18th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1966, which clarifies that 'State' in clauses (a) to (e) of Article 3 includes a 'Union Territory'). While the Court left open the broader question of whether an entire State can be permanently converted into Union Territories in view of the Union's assurance to restore J&K's statehood, it emphatically affirmed Parliament's power to carve a Union Territory out of a State.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 3 & 356; In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution (2023); Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960)

stem: With reference to the Zonal Councils and the North Eastern Council in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the North Eastern Council which was established by an Act of Parliament, the five Zonal Councils are constitutional bodies established by the President under Article 263 read with the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.

2. In each of the five Zonal Councils, the Chief Ministers of the States included in the zone act as the Vice-Chairperson of the Council by rotation, each holding office for a period of one year at a time.
3. The Chief Secretaries and Development Commissioners of the member States serve as Advisers to a Zonal Council and are entitled to participate in its discussions without the right to vote.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both the five Zonal Councils (created under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956) and the North Eastern Council (created under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971) are statutory advisory bodies rather than constitutional bodies under Article 263, and feature distinct rotational leadership and non-voting bureaucratic advisory mechanisms.

exp.why: Both the five Zonal Councils (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern) and the North Eastern Council are statutory bodies, not constitutional bodies. The five Zonal Councils were established under Part III (Sections 15–22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 passed by Parliament, whereas the Inter-State Council is a constitutional body established by Presidential Order under Article 263.

Under Section 16 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the Union Home Minister serves as the common Chairperson of each of the five Zonal Councils, while the Chief Ministers of the States included in each zone act as the Vice-Chairperson of the Zonal Council for that zone by rotation, each holding office for a period of one year at a time.

Under Section 16(4) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, each Zonal Council is assisted by Advisers—comprising one person nominated by the NITI Aayog (formerly Planning Commission), the Chief Secretary of each State in the zone, and the Development Commissioner of each State in the zone. These Advisers have the right to take part in the discussions of the Zonal Council or its committees, but do not have the right to vote.

ref: States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Part III, Sections 15–22); North Eastern Council Act, 1971; Laxmikanth Ch. 16

stem: With reference to the acquisition of foreign territory and the scope of Article 1(3)(c) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 1(3)(c) does not itself confer the power on the Union to acquire foreign territory; rather, the power to acquire foreign territory is an inherent attribute of sovereignty outside the Constitution, and Article 1(3)(c) merely recognizes the automatic constitutional absorption of territory once acquired according to international law.

2. A foreign territory under the mere de facto administrative control of the Government of India does not form part of the 'territory of India' under Article 1(3)(c) until there is a formal de jure transfer or sovereign assimilation.

3. When a foreign territory is acquired by the Union of India through an Act of State, its inhabitants cannot enforce pre-existing rights granted by the former sovereign in Indian municipal courts unless the new sovereign has recognized or assumed those obligations.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under settled Supreme Court jurisprudence (In Re: Berubari Union, 1960 and N. Masthan Sahib, 1962), the power to acquire foreign territory is an inherent sovereign attribute under international law outside Article 1(3)(c); constitutional assimilation under Article 1(3)(c) requires de jure acquisition rather than mere de facto administration, and an acquisition operates as an Act of State extinguishing unassumed municipal obligations of the prior sovereign.

exp.why: In In Re: Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves (1960), the Supreme Court held that Article 1(3)(c) ('such other territories as may be acquired') does not purport to confer power on India to acquire foreign territories. The power to acquire and cede territory is an inherent attribute of every sovereign State under international law outside the Constitution; Article 1(3)(c) merely makes a formal constitutional provision for the automatic absorption of such territories into the 'territory of India' once they are validly acquired under international law.

In N. Masthan Sahib v. Chief Commissioner, Pondicherry (1962), the Supreme Court ruled that the word 'acquired' in Article 1(3)(c) requires a transfer of full de jure sovereignty. Consequently, between 1954 (de facto transfer of administration) and August 1962 (ratification of the Treaty of Cession by France and the 14th Amendment), Pondicherry was not comprised within the 'territory of India' under Article 1(3)(c), and writ jurisdiction under Article 32 did not extend to quasi-judicial authorities functioning there outside India's de jure territory.

As established by the Supreme Court in Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. v. CIT (1958) and State of Gujarat v. Vora Fiddali (1964), the acquisition of foreign territory by conquest, cession, or annexation is an 'Act of State' in the exercise of sovereign power. Municipal courts of the new sovereign cannot enforce rights or concessions granted to inhabitants by the erstwhile sovereign unless the Union of India has expressly or impliedly recognized those pre-existing rights by law or agreement.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 1(3)(c); In Re: Berubari Union (1960); N. Masthan Sahib v. Chief Commissioner, Pondicherry (1962)

stem: With reference to the constitutional architecture of Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements accurately describes its temporal scope and enforcement?

opts.A: Articles 5 to 11 came into force only on January 26, 1950, and lay down an exhaustive constitutional code governing both pre-commencement and post-commencement acquisition of citizenship.
opts.B: While Articles 5 to 9 came into force immediately on November 26, 1949, Part II itself only identifies the classes of persons who became citizens at the commencement of the Constitution on January 26, 1950, leaving future regulation to Parliament.
opts.C: Under Article 394, the entirety of Part II (Articles 5 to 11) was brought into force on November 26, 1949, thereby fixing November 26, 1949 as the final cut-off date for determining Indian domicile at commencement.
opts.D: The Constitution vests concurrent legislative competence in Parliament and the Legislatures of border States to regulate post-1950 acquisition and termination of citizenship.

core: Part II of the Constitution does not lay down a permanent or comprehensive code for post-1950 citizenship; it merely identifies who became citizens at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950) and delegates plenary power to Parliament under Article 11. Under Article 394, Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 came into force immediately on November 26, 1949, whereas the legal benchmark of 'commencement of this Constitution' remained January 26, 1950.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. The framers of the Constitution intentionally avoided embedding a rigid, permanent code of citizenship in Part II, limiting Articles 5 to 8 to determining who qualified as citizens 'at the commencement of this Constitution' (defined under Article 394 as January 26, 1950) and empowering Parliament under Articles 10 and 11 to enact a comprehensive law (subsequently the Citizenship Act, 1955). Option (A) is incorrect because Articles 5 to 9 were enforced on November 26, 1949 itself, and Part II does not deal with post-commencement acquisition. Option (C) is incorrect on two counts: Article 394 brought into immediate force only Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 (not Articles 10 and 11), and the benchmark date for 'commencement of this Constitution' to assess domicile under Article 5 remained January 26, 1950, not November 26, 1949. Option (D) is incorrect because Citizenship (Entry 17, List I of the Seventh Schedule) and Article 11 fall within the exclusive legislative domain of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 5–11 and Article 394; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution under Article 5 and the constitutional doctrine of domicile in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To qualify as a citizen under Article 5, a person born in the territory of India had to additionally prove both domicile in India and ordinary residence in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding the commencement of the Constitution.
2. Unlike Articles 6 and 8, the acquisition of citizenship through lineage under Article 5 extends only to the birth of either parent in the territory of India and does not include grandparents.
3. As affirmed by the Supreme Court in Pradeep Jain v. Union of India, the Constitution recognises only a single 'domicile of India' and does not recognize a separate State domicile.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 5 requires two cumulative elements: (i) domicile in the territory of India at the commencement of the Constitution, and (ii) fulfillment of any ONE of the three alternative conditions under clauses (a), (b), or (c). Furthermore, India's federal setup recognizes only a single national domicile ('domicile of India') alongside single citizenship.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 5, having domicile in the territory of India is a mandatory threshold condition, but clauses (a), (b), and (c) are mutually independent alternatives separated by 'or': (a) born in the territory of India; OR (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; OR (c) ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding commencement. A person domiciled in India and born in India satisfied Article 5(a) directly without needing to prove five years' ordinary residence under clause (c).

Statement 2 is correct. Article 5(b) extends only to a person 'either of whose parents was born in the territory of India'. In contrast, Articles 6 and 8 explicitly extend lineage eligibility to a person who, or either of whose parents, or 'any of whose grandparents' was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935.

Statement 3 is correct. In Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984), the Supreme Court clarified that under Article 5 there is only one domicile in India—namely, domicile in the territory of India—and the legal system does not recognise a separate 'State domicile' distinct from Indian domicile (though residential requirements within a State may exist for limited statutory purposes).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 5; Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984) 3 SCC 654

stem: With reference to the special constitutional provisions governing citizenship amidst Partition and overseas residence in Part II of the Constitution, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Article 6 : Uses July 19, 1948 as the dividing cut-off date requiring six months of prior residence in India before registration for migrants from Pakistan
2. Article 7 : Overrides only Article 5 to derecognize the citizenship of persons who migrated from India to Pakistan after July 19, 1948 without a resettlement permit
3. Article 8 : Dispenses with both the requirement of Indian domicile and any final deadline for consular registration of Persons of Indian Origin residing outside undivided India
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 6, 7, and 8 form a carefully calibrated constitutional matrix: Article 6 overrides Article 5 and uses July 19, 1948 (the introduction of the Indo-Pakistan permit system) as the dividing line for migrants from Pakistan; Article 7 overrides BOTH Articles 5 and 6 using March 1, 1947 as the cut-off for migrants to Pakistan; and Article 8 governs PIOs residing outside undivided India without requiring Indian domicile.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Article 6(b), persons who migrated to India from Pakistan on or after July 19, 1948 (when the permit system was introduced) could become citizens at commencement only if registered by an appointed officer upon an application made before January 26, 1950, provided they had resided in India for at least six months immediately preceding the application.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched on two fundamental counts. First, the non-obstante clause of Article 7 overrides BOTH Articles 5 and 6 ('Notwithstanding anything in articles 5 and 6'), whereas Article 6 overrides only Article 5. Second, the cut-off date under Article 7 for migration from the territory of India to the territory included in Pakistan is March 1, 1947, not July 19, 1948.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Article 8 applies to any person who (or either of whose parents or any of whose grandparents) was born in undivided India (as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935) and who is ordinarily residing in any country outside India as so defined. Unlike Article 5, Article 8 does not require Indian domicile, and unlike Article 6(b), consular registration under Article 8 was permitted 'whether before or after the commencement of this Constitution'.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 6, 7, and 8; D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 6

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the termination of Indian citizenship upon voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship:
items: Statement-I: If a dispute arises as to whether, when, or how an Indian citizen has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State after January 26, 1950, that question is determined exclusively by the Central Government and cannot be initially adjudicated by ordinary civil courts.

Statement-II: Article 9 of the Constitution applies only to the voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship prior to the commencement of the Constitution, whereas post-commencement termination of citizenship upon foreign naturalisation is governed by Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 9 of the Constitution operates strictly on pre-January 26, 1950 acquisitions of foreign citizenship. Post-commencement voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship falls exclusively under Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, under which Section 9(2) vests exclusive initial jurisdiction in the Central Government—barring civil courts from deciding that question.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 9(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 read with Rule 40 and Schedule III of the Citizenship Rules, 2009, whenever any question arises as to whether, when, or how any citizen of India has acquired the citizenship of another country after January 26, 1950, it shall be determined by the Central Government. As consistently held by the Supreme Court (e.g., State of U.P. v. Rehmatullah; Bhagwati Prasad Dixit v. Rajeev Gandhi), the jurisdiction of civil courts to initially decide this question is barred.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Because Article 9 of the Constitution disables a person from claiming citizenship under Articles 5, 6, or 8 only if they voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship BEFORE the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950), cases where an existing Indian citizen acquires foreign citizenship AFTER January 26, 1950 are governed not by Article 9, but by Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 enacted under Article 11—which expressly creates the exclusive determinative machinery of the Central Government under Section 9(2).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 9; Citizenship Act, 1955, Section 9; State of U.P. v. Rehmatullah (1971) 2 SCC 113

stem: With reference to the nature of legislative power under Articles 10 and 11 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution, Parliament only, to the total exclusion of State Legislatures, has the competence to legislate on the acquisition and termination of citizenship.

2. By virtue of the non-obstante language in Article 11, Parliament is competent to terminate or restrict the citizenship even of persons who originally became citizens at the commencement of the Constitution under Articles 5 to 8.

3. Any parliamentary statute enacted under Article 11 that alters or abridges the conditions of citizenship set out in Articles 5 to 8 is deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution requiring a special majority under Article 368.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 10 and 11 vest plenary and exclusive legislative competence in Parliament to regulate all aspects of citizenship. Because Part II itself subjects constitutional citizenship at commencement to future laws made by Parliament, an ordinary statute enacted under Article 11 can modify or terminate citizenship without invoking Article 368.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 11 explicitly confers the power to make any provision regarding the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship on Parliament alone, reinforced by Entry 17 of List I (Union List: 'Citizenship, naturalisation and aliens'). State Legislatures have zero competence in this domain.

Statement 2 is correct. Article 10 states that every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen under Part II shall continue to be such citizen 'subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament', and Article 11 declares that 'Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament' to regulate acquisition and termination of citizenship.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Because Articles 10 and 11 expressly subordinate the continuation of citizenship under Articles 5 to 8 to ordinary parliamentary legislation, a law passed by Parliament under Article 11 (such as the Citizenship Act, 1955 or its amendments) is enacted by a simple majority through ordinary legislative procedure and does not require a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 10, 11, and 368; Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India, AIR 1962 SC 1052

stem: With reference to the acquisition of Indian citizenship by birth under Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 across its statutory amendments, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person born in India between January 26, 1950 and June 30, 1987 acquired Indian citizenship by birth irrespective of the nationality of the parents, unless at the time of birth the father enjoyed foreign diplomatic immunity or was an enemy alien in occupied territory.

2. A child born in India on or after December 3, 2004 to two foreign nationals does not acquire Indian citizenship by birth, even if both parents hold valid long-term visas and are lawfully residing in India at the time of the child's birth.

3. For a child born in India between July 1, 1987 and December 2, 2004 to acquire citizenship by birth, it was mandatory that at least one parent be a citizen of India at the time of birth, without any statutory disqualification based on whether the other parent was an illegal migrant.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 marks India's transition from unconditional jus soli (birth on soil, 1950–1987) to hybrid jus sanguinis (bloodline, post-1987). Since December 3, 2004, birth in India confers citizenship only if both parents are Indian citizens, or one parent is an Indian citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant—meaning children born in India to two foreign nationals never acquire citizenship by birth regardless of their lawful visa status.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 3(1)(a) read with Section 3(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, every person born in India on or after January 26, 1950, but before July 1, 1987, became a citizen of India by birth irrespective of the nationality of their parents, subject only to the two statutory exceptions in Section 3(2): where the father possessed diplomatic immunity as an envoy of a foreign power (and was not an Indian citizen), or where the father was an enemy alien and the birth occurred in a place then under enemy occupation.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Section 3(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (effective December 3, 2004), a person born in India on or after December 3, 2004 is a citizen by birth ONLY IF: (i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or (ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth. Consequently, if neither parent is an Indian citizen (i.e., both are foreign nationals), the child cannot acquire Indian citizenship by birth even if the foreign parents hold valid visas and reside legally in India.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 3(1)(b) (inserted by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1986 with effect from July 1, 1987), a person born in India on or after July 1, 1987, but before December 3, 2004, is a citizen of India by birth if 'either of his parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth'. The additional bar disqualifying a child whose other parent was an 'illegal migrant' was introduced only prospectively from December 3, 2004 by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955, Section 3 (as amended in 1986 and 2003); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the acquisition of Indian citizenship by descent and by registration under the Citizenship Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A minor who is a citizen of India by virtue of descent and also holds the citizenship of another country ceases to be an Indian citizen if they do not renounce the foreign citizenship within six months of attaining full age.

2. Every person of full age who applies for Indian citizenship by registration is statutorily required to take an oath of allegiance in the form specified in the Second Schedule before being registered.
3. Any person born outside India on or after December 3, 2004, automatically becomes an Indian citizen by descent at birth solely by virtue of both parents being citizens of India.
