prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Post-December 3, 2004, citizenship by descent under Section 4 is no longer automatic solely by parentage; it requires consular registration of birth within one year accompanied by a parental declaration that the minor does not hold a foreign passport. Additionally, Section 4(1A) mandates renunciation of any dual foreign nationality within six months of attaining majority, while Section 5(2) mandates an oath of allegiance for adult registration applicants.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 4(1A) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by the 2003 Amendment Act), a minor who is a citizen of India by virtue of descent under Section 4 and is also a citizen of any other country shall cease to be a citizen of India if they do not renounce the citizenship or nationality of that other country within six months of attaining full age.

Statement 2 is correct. Unlike acquisition by birth or descent, citizenship by registration under Section 5 is granted on an application to the Central Government, and Section 5(2) explicitly stipulates that no person of full age shall be registered as a citizen of India until they have taken the oath of allegiance in the form specified in the Second Schedule.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Section 4(1) as amended with effect from December 3, 2004, a person born outside India on or after that date does not become an Indian citizen by descent merely because either or both parents are Indian citizens. Such a person shall not be a citizen of India by descent unless their birth is registered at an Indian consulate within one year of the date of birth (or with the permission of the Central Government after one year) AND the parents declare in the prescribed form that the minor does not hold the passport of another country.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Sections 4 & 5; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the qualifications and conditions for acquiring Indian citizenship by naturalisation under Section 6 and the Third Schedule to the Citizenship Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person is ineligible for naturalisation as an Indian citizen if they are a subject or citizen of any country where citizens of India are prevented by the law or practice of that country from becoming citizens of that country by naturalisation.

2. Under the ordinary naturalisation framework, an applicant must have resided in India or been in the service of a Government in India throughout the continuous period of twelve months immediately preceding the date of the application, in addition to fulfilling the prescribed aggregate residence requirement during the fourteen years preceding those twelve months.

3. Where an applicant has rendered distinguished service to the cause of science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace or human progress, the Central Government may waive all the conditions specified in the Third Schedule except the requirement of possessing an adequate knowledge of a language specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Naturalisation under Section 6 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 is governed by the qualifications in the Third Schedule, which enforce strict reciprocity, a two-tier residence computation (12 months continuous immediately preceding the application plus aggregate residence over the preceding 14 years), and knowledge of an Eighth Schedule language. However, the proviso to Section 6(1) empowers the Central Government to waive all or any of the Third Schedule conditions—including the language requirement—for distinguished service.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Clause (a) of the Third Schedule to the Citizenship Act, 1955 codifies the principle of reciprocity: an applicant for naturalisation must not be a subject or citizen of any country where citizens of India are prevented by law or practice of that country from becoming subjects or citizens of that country by naturalisation.

Statement 2 is correct. Clauses (c) and (d) of the Third Schedule require that an applicant must have either resided in India or been in the service of a Government in India (or partly the one and partly the other) throughout the period of twelve months immediately preceding the date of the application, and during the fourteen years immediately preceding the said period of twelve months, must have resided in India or been in Government service for periods amounting in the aggregate to not less than eleven years (reduced to five years for specified categories under the 2019 Amendment).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the proviso to Section 6(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, if in the opinion of the Central Government the applicant is a person who has rendered distinguished service to the cause of science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace or human progress generally, it may waive 'all or any' of the conditions specified in the Third Schedule. There is no statutory exception barring the waiver of the Eighth Schedule language requirement.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Section 6 & Third Schedule; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the acquisition of citizenship upon the incorporation of a foreign territory into India:
items: Statement-I: Upon the incorporation of any foreign territory into India, every person residing in that territory does not automatically become a citizen of India merely by virtue of the territorial acquisition, but only in accordance with an executive notification issued by the Central Government.

Statement-II: Section 7 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 empowers the Central Government to notify in the Official Gazette the specific class of persons who shall become citizens of India from a specified date by reason of their connection with the incorporated territory, without requiring them to apply individually for naturalisation.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Indian constitutional and statutory law, the mere cession or incorporation of a foreign territory into the Union of India does not ipso facto confer Indian citizenship on all inhabitants. Instead, Section 7 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 authorizes the Central Government to issue an Official Gazette order specifying which persons connected with that territory become Indian citizens from a notified date, bypassing individual naturalisation procedures.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. When a foreign territory becomes part of India (such as Pondicherry in 1962, Sikkim in 1975, or the erstwhile Bangladeshi enclaves under the 100th Constitutional Amendment in 2015), its residents do not automatically acquire Indian citizenship by the bare act of territorial incorporation; their citizenship status is governed by the Citizenship Order notified by the Central Government.

Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Section 7 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 explicitly provides that if any territory becomes a part of India, the Central Government may, by order notified in the Official Gazette, specify the persons who shall be citizens of India by reason of their connection with that territory, and those persons shall be citizens of India as from the date to be specified in the order without needing to submit individual applications for naturalisation.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Section 7; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the loss of Indian citizenship through renunciation (Section 8) and termination (Section 9) under the Citizenship Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
items: 1. If an Indian citizen makes a declaration renouncing their Indian citizenship during a war in which India is engaged, the registration of such declaration is withheld until the Central Government otherwise directs.

2. Where a person ceases to be a citizen of India either by renunciation under Section 8 or by automatic termination under Section 9 upon voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship, every minor child of that person automatically ceases to be a citizen of India.

3. A minor child who loses Indian citizenship consequent to a parent's renunciation under Section 8 has the statutory right to resume Indian citizenship by making a declaration within one year after attaining full age.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While both Section 8 (renunciation) and Section 9 (termination) contain wartime provisos allowing the Central Government to suspend the loss of citizenship during a war in which India is engaged, the derivative loss of a minor child's Indian citizenship under Section 8(2) applies exclusively when a parent makes a declaration of renunciation under Section 8, and does not apply when a parent's citizenship terminates under Section 9.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under the proviso to Section 8(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, if a declaration of renunciation of Indian citizenship is made during any war in which India may be engaged, the registration of that declaration shall be withheld until the Central Government otherwise directs.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 8(2), derivative loss of Indian citizenship by a minor child occurs only where a parent ceases to be a citizen of India under Section 8(1) (i.e., by a formal declaration of renunciation). Section 9 (termination of citizenship upon voluntarily acquiring the citizenship of another country) contains no provision terminating the Indian citizenship of the minor child of that person.

Statement 3 is correct. Under the proviso to Section 8(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, any minor child who ceases to be an Indian citizen consequent to a parent's declaration of renunciation may, within one year after attaining full age, make a declaration in the prescribed form and manner that they wish to resume Indian citizenship and shall thereupon again become a citizen of India.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Sections 8 & 9; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the compulsory deprivation of Indian citizenship under Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Central Government is empowered to compulsorily deprive any citizen of India, including a citizen by birth or by descent, of their Indian citizenship if they have shown themselves by act or speech to be disloyal or disaffected towards the Constitution of India.

2. A naturalised citizen automatically ceases to be a citizen of India if they have been ordinarily resident out of India for a continuous period of seven years, even if they are residing abroad as a student at an educational institution or in the service of the Government of India.

3. Whenever the Central Government proposes to deprive a person of Indian citizenship on the ground of seven years' continuous residence outside India, the matter must mandatorily be referred to a Committee of Inquiry presided over by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Compulsory deprivation of citizenship under Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 applies only to citizens who acquired citizenship by naturalisation, registration, or domicile under Article 5(c); citizens by birth and by descent are statutorily immune from deprivation under Section 10. Furthermore, deprivation on the ground of seven-year continuous foreign residence is neither automatic nor applicable to students, Government servants, or persons who register annually at an Indian consulate.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Section 10(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 restricts the power of compulsory deprivation exclusively to citizens who are such by naturalisation, or by virtue only of Article 5(c) of the Constitution, or by registration (other than under Article 6(b)(ii) or Section 5(1)(a)). Citizens of India by birth (Section 3) or by descent (Section 4) cannot be deprived of their citizenship under Section 10 on any ground.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 10(2)(e) read with Section 10(3), deprivation for seven years' continuous residence outside India is not automatic; it requires an order by the Central Government satisfied that it is not conducive to the public good that the person should continue to be a citizen. Moreover, Section 10(2)(e) expressly exempts a person who during that period has been a student of any educational institution outside India, or in the service of a Government in India or of an international organisation of which India is a member, or who has registered annually at an Indian consulate their intention to retain Indian citizenship.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Section 10(4), when deprivation is proposed on the ground of seven years' continuous residence abroad [Section 10(2)(e)], reference to a Committee of Inquiry is discretionary ('the Central Government may, if it thinks fit'), whereas on other grounds (such as fraud or disloyalty) reference is mandatory if the affected person applies for it. Furthermore, under Section 10(5), the Chairman of the Committee of Inquiry is required to be a person who has for at least ten years held a judicial office, and not necessarily a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Section 10; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (enacted pursuant to the Assam Accord) and the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court of India thereon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Persons of Indian origin who entered Assam from the specified territory before January 1, 1966, and have been ordinarily resident in Assam since the date of their entry, are deemed to be citizens of India as from January 1, 1966.

2. Persons of Indian origin who entered Assam on or after January 1, 1966, but before March 25, 1971, and are detected as foreigners are granted limited civil rights as Indian residents, but remain permanently barred from having their names included in any electoral roll even after the expiry of ten years from the date of detection.

3. The Supreme Court has upheld the constitutional validity of Section 6A, ruling that the March 24, 1971 cut-off date satisfies the test of reasonable classification under Article 14 and does not violate the right to conserve distinct culture under Article 29(1).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 establishes a three-tier chronological framework for migrants entering Assam from the specified territory (Bangladesh): automatic citizenship from January 1, 1966 for pre-1966 entrants; registration with a 10-year disenfranchisement period followed by full citizenship (including voting rights) for entrants between January 1, 1966 and March 24, 1971; and illegal migrant status for entrants on or after March 25, 1971. In October 2024, a 5-Judge Constitution Bench upheld Section 6A against challenges under Articles 14, 29(1), and 355.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 6A(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, all persons of Indian origin who came before the 1st day of January, 1966 into Assam from the specified territory and who have been ordinarily resident in Assam since the dates of their entry into Assam shall be deemed to be citizens of India as from the 1st day of January, 1966.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 6A(3), (4), and (5) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person of Indian origin who entered Assam between January 1, 1966 and March 24, 1971 and is detected as a foreigner must register, and from the date of detection until the expiry of a period of ten years, enjoys the same rights and obligations as a citizen of India except the right to have their name included in any electoral roll. Upon the expiry of the ten-year period from the date of detection, they are deemed to be citizens of India for all purposes, including the right to vote.

Statement 3 is correct. In In Re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (2024), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 6A, holding that the special regime for Assam and the March 24, 1971 cut-off date (coinciding with the launch of Operation Searchlight) are based on intelligible differentia under Article 14, and that the provision does not violate Article 29(1) as the mere presence of diverse linguistic or ethnic groups does not per se abridge the right of locals to conserve their culture.

ref: Citizenship Act, 1955 Section 6A; In Re: Section 6A SC Constitution Bench Ruling (2024); Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the special provisions for citizenship introduced under Section 6B of the Citizenship Act, 1955 by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The provisions of Section 6B for granting citizenship to specified persecuted minority communities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan do not apply to the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura included in the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, nor to the areas covered under 'The Inner Line' notified under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873, though no such statutory exemption extends to Fifth Schedule areas in Peninsular India.

Statement-II: A person granted a certificate of registration or naturalisation under Section 6B is statutorily deemed to be a citizen of India retrospectively from the date of his or her entry into India, and any pending legal proceeding against such person in respect of illegal migration or citizenship stands abated.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Section 6B of the Citizenship Act, 1955 provides retrospective regularisation from the date of entry into India and abates pending illegal migration proceedings for eligible migrants who entered on or before December 31, 2014. However, to safeguard indigenous demographic and cultural autonomy in North-East India, Section 6B(4) explicitly exempts Sixth Schedule tribal areas and Inner Line Permit (ILP) areas, without extending this exemption to Fifth Schedule areas.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 6B(4) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019), nothing in Section 6B applies to the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, or Tripura as included in the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, and the areas covered under 'The Inner Line' notified under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873 (currently applicable across Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Manipur). The statute does not exempt Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule in Peninsular and Central India.

Statement-II is correct. Under Section 6B(2) and Section 6B(3) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, upon the grant of a certificate of registration or naturalisation under Section 6B, the person is deemed to be a citizen of India from the date of his or her entry into India (on or before 31 December 2014), and any proceeding pending against such person in respect of illegal migration or citizenship stands abated upon conferment of citizenship. However, Statement-II describes the legal effect of registration and does not explain the rationale for the territorial exemptions in Statement-I.

ref: Section 6B, Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by CAA 2019); Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the legal framework governing Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholders under Sections 7A and 7B of the Citizenship Act, 1955 and the rules made thereunder, consider the following statements:
items: 1. No person is eligible for registration as an OCI Cardholder if he, or either of his parents, grandparents, or great-grandparents is or had been a citizen of Pakistan or Bangladesh.

2. A person of foreign origin who is the spouse of a citizen of India becomes eligible to apply for registration as an OCI Cardholder immediately upon the legal solemnisation and registration of their marriage.

3. An OCI Cardholder requires prior special permission from the competent authority to undertake research, missionary, mountaineering, or journalistic activities in India, and foreign nationals who have served in a foreign military are generally barred from OCI registration unless specifically exempted.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 7A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 imposes strict national security guardrails on OCI eligibility, including an absolute bar on persons with Pakistani or Bangladeshi ancestry and a mandatory two-year marriage subsistence period for foreign spouses. Furthermore, under Section 7B notifications, OCI cardholders must obtain special permits for sensitive activities such as research, journalism, or missionary work in India.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The proviso to Section 7A(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 explicitly stipulates that no person shall be eligible for registration as an Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder if he or either of his parents or grandparents or great-grandparents is or had been a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, or such other country as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 7A(1)(d) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a spouse of foreign origin of a citizen of India or of an OCI Cardholder is eligible to apply for OCI registration only if the marriage has been registered and has subsisted for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the application, subject further to prior security clearance by a competent authority in India.

Statement 3 is correct. Under the consolidated statutory notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs in March 2021 under Section 7B(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, OCI Cardholders require a special permit from the FRRO or the Indian Mission concerned to undertake research, missionary or Tabligh, mountaineering, or journalistic activities, or an internship in any foreign diplomatic mission in India. Moreover, under MHA guidelines, foreign nationals who have served in any foreign military or police organisation are ineligible for OCI registration (with a narrow policy exception for Israeli citizens who underwent only mandatory conscription).

ref: Sections 7A & 7B, Citizenship Act, 1955; MHA Notification S.O. 1050(E) (2021)

stem: With reference to the renunciation and cancellation of registration of an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder under the Citizenship Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Central Government may cancel the registration of an OCI Cardholder if, within five years after registration, the cardholder has been sentenced to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years.

2. The Central Government is statutorily empowered to cancel an OCI registration if the cardholder has violated any provision of the Citizenship Act, 1955 or of any other law in force as may be notified by the Central Government.

3. Under the statutory proviso to Section 7D, no order cancelling an OCI registration on any specified ground can be passed unless the cardholder has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, whereas when a person voluntarily renounces OCI status under Section 7C, every minor child of that person registered as an OCI Cardholder automatically ceases to hold OCI status.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955 enumerates six distinct grounds for the cancellation of OCI registration (including fraud, disaffection towards the Constitution, assisting an enemy during war, sentencing to 2+ years imprisonment within 5 years, violation of notified laws, and sovereignty/security interests), while mandating a statutory opportunity of being heard across all grounds. Conversely, voluntary renunciation under Section 7C automatically terminates the OCI status of minor children.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 7D(d) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, the Central Government may, by order, cancel the registration granted under Section 7A if it is satisfied that the Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder has, within five years after registration under Section 7A(1), been sentenced to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years.

Statement 2 is correct. Clause (da) of Section 7D, inserted via the Finance Act, 2019, empowers the Central Government to cancel the registration of an OCI Cardholder if the cardholder has violated any of the provisions of the Citizenship Act, 1955 or of any other law for the time being in force as may be specified by the Central Government in the notification published in the Official Gazette.

Statement 3 is correct. The proviso to Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955 explicitly mandates a natural justice safeguard: 'Provided that no order under this section shall be passed unless the Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.' Furthermore, under Section 7C(2), where a person ceases to be an OCI Cardholder upon making a declaration of renunciation under Section 7C(1), every minor child of that person registered as an OCI Cardholder thereupon ceases to be an OCI Cardholder.

ref: Sections 7C & 7D, Citizenship Act, 1955; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following statements comparing the legal status of Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholders:
items: Statement-I: A Non-Resident Indian (NRI) who has not acquired the citizenship of any other country is eligible to be registered as an overseas elector in the electoral roll of his or her parliamentary or assembly constituency in India, whereas an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder is statutorily barred from registration as a voter.

Statement-II: In respect of economic and financial facilities in India, OCI Cardholders enjoy complete statutory parity with NRIs, including the unrestricted right to purchase agricultural land, plantation properties, and farmhouses in India.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) remain full citizens of India holding Indian passports and consequently enjoy political franchise as overseas electors under Section 20A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. By contrast, OCI Cardholders are foreign citizens barred from voting under Section 7B(2)(f) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, and barred from purchasing agricultural land, farmhouses, or plantation property in India.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 20A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (inserted by the 2010 Amendment Act), every citizen of India whose name is not included in the electoral roll, who has not acquired the citizenship of any other country, and who is absenting from his place of ordinary residence in India owing to employment, education, or otherwise outside India (an NRI), is entitled to have his name registered in the electoral roll. Conversely, under Section 7B(2)(f) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, an OCI Cardholder is expressly barred from registration as a voter under Section 16 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.

Statement-II is incorrect. Under the statutory notifications issued under Section 7B(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 as well as the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, parity with NRIs in respect of economic, financial, and educational fields explicitly excludes the acquisition of agricultural land, farmhouse, or plantation property. An OCI Cardholder cannot purchase agricultural or plantation property in India, though they may acquire such property by way of inheritance from a person resident in India.

ref: Section 7B, Citizenship Act, 1955; Section 20A, RPA 1950; FEMA Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory eligibility for holding high constitutional offices in India, such as the President of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court, which one of the following statements reflects the correct legal position?

opts.A: Both a citizen of India by birth and a foreign-born person who has acquired Indian citizenship by naturalisation or registration are equally eligible to hold the office of the President of India, whereas an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder is statutorily barred from holding such office.
opts.B: Unlike the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court which is open to naturalised citizens, the office of the President of India under Article 58 of the Constitution is restricted exclusively to citizens of India by birth or descent.
opts.C: A naturalised citizen of India becomes eligible for election as the President or Vice-President of India only after having held Indian citizenship for a minimum statutory cooling-off period of ten continuous years.
opts.D: While an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Cardholder is barred from being elected as the President or Vice-President of India, Section 7B of the Citizenship Act, 1955 permits an OCI Cardholder of eminent legal distinction to be appointed as the Attorney-General for India.

core: Unlike the United States Constitution which restricts the Presidency to a 'natural born Citizen', the Indian Constitution makes no distinction between citizens by birth and citizens by registration or naturalisation for eligibility to any constitutional office (including President under Article 58). Conversely, Section 7B(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 explicitly bars OCI Cardholders from holding high constitutional posts and public services.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because under Article 58(1)(a) of the Constitution, any 'citizen of India' who satisfies the age and Lok Sabha qualification criteria is eligible for election as President, whether such citizenship was acquired by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, or incorporation of territory. By contrast, Section 7B(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 explicitly bars an OCI Cardholder from enjoying the rights conferred on a citizen of India under Articles 58 (President), 66 (Vice-President), 124 (Supreme Court Judge), 217 (High Court Judge), 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment), and from appointment to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State. Option (B) is incorrect because India does not restrict the Presidency to citizens by birth. Option (C) is incorrect because neither the Constitution nor the Citizenship Act prescribes any post-naturalisation cooling-off period for contesting Presidential elections. Option (D) is incorrect because under Article 76(1), the Attorney-General for India must be qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court (which requires Indian citizenship under Article 124(3) and is expressly barred to OCI Cardholders under Section 7B(2)(c)).

ref: Articles 58, 66, 76, 124 & 217 of the Constitution; Section 7B(2), Citizenship Act, 1955; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following landmark statutory milestones in the evolution of the Citizenship Act, 1955:
items: 1. Abolition of pure jus soli by mandating that at least one parent must be a citizen of India at the time of birth for a child born in India to acquire citizenship by birth.
2. Insertion of Section 6A into the Citizenship Act, 1955 to give statutory effect to the cut-off dates of the Assam Accord.
3. Statutory merger of the Person of Indian Origin (PIO) Card scheme and the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme into a single 'Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder' framework.

4. Statutory disqualification of an 'illegal migrant' from acquiring citizenship by registration or naturalisation, alongside the initial statutory introduction of the Overseas Citizenship of India framework.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the above milestones from the earliest to the latest?
core: The statutory trajectory of the Citizenship Act, 1955 reflects a progressive shift from unconditional jus soli (birth on soil) to jus sanguinis (bloodline/parentage) and stricter border regularisation: the 1985 Amendment inserted Section 6A for Assam, the 1986 Amendment required at least one Indian citizen parent for citizenship by birth, the 2003 Amendment barred illegal migrants and introduced OCI, and the 2015 Amendment merged the PIO and OCI schemes.

exp.why: Item 1 occurred via the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1986 (Act 51 of 1986, effective 1 July 1987). Prior to 1 July 1987, anyone born in India on or after 26 January 1950 was a citizen of India by birth regardless of the nationality of their parents (pure jus soli). The 1986 Amendment amended Section 3 to require that for persons born in India on or after 1 July 1987, at least one parent must be a citizen of India at the time of birth.

Item 2 occurred via the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985 (Act 65 of 1985, effective 7 December 1985), which inserted Section 6A to implement the Assam Accord of August 1985, establishing 1 January 1966 and 25 March 1971 as the statutory cut-off dates for regularisation and detection of migrants entering Assam from Bangladesh (upheld by a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in October 2024).

Item 3 occurred via the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2015 (effective from 6 January 2015), which replaced the earlier OCI provisions to merge the Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card scheme and the OCI scheme into a unified 'Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder' category under Sections 7A to 7D.

Item 4 occurred via the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 (Act 6 of 2004, effective December 2004). It defined 'illegal migrant' in Section 2(1)(b), barred illegal migrants from acquiring citizenship by registration or naturalisation, tightened Section 3(1)(c) so that a child born in India is a citizen only if one parent is an Indian citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant, and initially introduced the Overseas Citizenship of India framework for persons of Indian origin in 16 specified countries. Thus, the chronological order is 2 (1985) -> 1 (1986) -> 4 (2003) -> 3 (2015).

ref: Citizenship (Amendment) Acts of 1985, 1986, 2003, and 2015; Laxmikanth Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the structural nature and enforceability of Fundamental Rights contained in Articles 12 to 18 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is most accurate?

opts.A: While most provisions in this group operate vertically as negative injunctions limiting State action, certain provisions like Articles 15(2) and 17 also operate horizontally against private individuals.
opts.B: All Fundamental Rights from Articles 14 to 18 are enforceable exclusively against the State and its instrumentalities as defined under Article 12, leaving violations by private individuals solely to ordinary tort or criminal law.
opts.C: Unlike the Fundamental Freedoms under Article 19, none of the equality provisions under Articles 14 to 18 are self-executory, and each requires an enabling parliamentary statute before a citizen can invoke writ jurisdiction.
opts.D: The rights guaranteed under Articles 14 to 18 are conferred exclusively upon citizens of India and cannot be invoked by foreign nationals or corporate legal entities even against arbitrary State action.

core: Fundamental Rights primarily impose negative obligations on the 'State' (vertical enforcement), but specific equality provisions like Article 15(2) (access to shops, public restaurants, wells, etc.) and Article 17 (abolition of untouchability) are enforceable horizontally against private individuals as well.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because although Fundamental Rights generally act as vertical limitations upon the powers of the State under Article 12 (such as Article 14, Article 15(1), and Article 16), Articles 15(2) and 17 explicitly bind private actors as well (horizontal application), prohibiting private discrimination in access to public resorts and the practice of untouchability in any form. Option (B) is incorrect because Articles 15(2) and 17 apply against private individuals too, as reaffirmed in the Supreme Court's jurisprudence including Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP (2023). Option (C) is incorrect because Fundamental Rights under Articles 14 to 16 and 18 are directly self-executory; only prescribing punishments for offences like untouchability under Article 17 read with Article 35 involves parliamentary legislation, which does not diminish the direct constitutional prohibition. Option (D) is incorrect because Article 14 ('any person') and Article 18(2)-(4) apply to both citizens and non-citizens.

ref: Constitution of India, Arts. 12–18; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Fundamental Rights)

stem: With reference to the definition of 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution of India and its applicability to the Judiciary, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A judicial order passed by a High Court or the Supreme Court on the judicial side adjudicating a dispute between private parties can be challenged through a writ petition under Article 32 as a violation of Fundamental Rights by the 'State'.

2. When the Supreme Court exercises its rule-making power under Article 145 or a High Court takes administrative decisions regarding the service conditions of its staff, it falls within the definition of 'State' under Article 12.

3. By virtue of Article 36, the expression 'State' in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) bears the same meaning as assigned to it in Article 12 under Part III, unless the context otherwise requires.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Judiciary exhibits a functional dichotomy under Article 12: courts are NOT 'State' when discharging judicial adjudication (Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar and Rupa Ashok Hurra cases), but they ARE 'State' when acting in an administrative or statutory rule-making capacity.

exp.why: In Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra (1966) and reaffirmed by a 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), the Supreme Court held that a superior court of justice, while acting in its judicial capacity to decide a lis between parties, is not 'State' under Article 12, and its judicial order cannot be challenged under Article 32 as violating Fundamental Rights.

As established in Prem Chand Garg v. Excise Commissioner (1962) and A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1988), when a court exercises its administrative functions (such as staff appointments under Articles 146 or 229) or statutory rule-making powers (such as Supreme Court Rules framed under Article 145), it acts as 'State' under Article 12 and such rules or administrative actions can be tested on the touchstone of Part III.
Article 36 explicitly stipulates that in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' has the same meaning as in Part III (Article 12).

ref: Constitution of India, Arts. 12, 36, 145; Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar (1966) & Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)

stem: In the context of judicial interpretation of the expression 'other authorities' under Article 12 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An entity need not be created by or under a statute in order to qualify as an instrumentality or agency of the 'State' under Article 12.

2. A society registered under the Societies Registration Act or a company incorporated under the Companies Act can be treated as 'State' if it is financially, functionally, and administratively dominated by, or under the pervasive control of, the Government.

3. A private body discharging a public function may be amenable to the writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 in respect of that public duty, without automatically becoming 'State' under Article 12 for all its internal private contractual or service disputes.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the R.D. Shetty, Ajay Hasia, and Pradeep Kumar Biswas (7-Judge Bench) doctrines, the test for 'other authorities' under Article 12 is functional, financial, and administrative domination by the Government rather than the mode of incorporation.

exp.why: In R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) and Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981), the Supreme Court clarified that it is immaterial whether a corporation or body is created by a statute or under a general law; the decisive inquiry is why it was created and whether it acts as an instrumentality or agency of the State.

In Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002, 7-Judge Bench), the Supreme Court consolidated the Ajay Hasia parameters and held that even a registered society or government company is 'State' under Article 12 when the cumulative facts establish that the body is financially, functionally, and administratively dominated by, or under the deep and pervasive control of, the Government.

As held in Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India (2005) and St. Mary's Education Society v. Rajendra Prasad Bhargava (2022), the scope of Article 226 ('to any person or authority... for any other purpose') is wider than Article 12/Article 32. A private body performing a public duty is amenable to Article 226 writs specifically where a public law element is involved, without becoming 'State' under Article 12 for purely private contracts of personal service.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 12 & Art. 226; Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002); Zee Telefilms (2005)

stem: With reference to Article 13 of the Constitution of India and judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 13(3), the term 'law' encompasses not only plenary enactments of Parliament and State Legislatures, but also ordinances, executive notifications, regulations, and customs or usages having the force of law.

2. The expression 'laws in force' under Article 13(3)(b) includes pre-constitutional laws passed by a competent authority in the territory of India and not previously repealed, even if such laws were not in operation at all or in particular areas at the commencement of the Constitution.

3. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court struck down Article 13(4) of the Constitution and held that a Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368 is ordinary 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 13(3) gives a wide, inclusive definition to 'law' (covering statutory instruments, ordinances, notifications, and customs), whereas Article 13(4)—upheld in Kesavananda Bharati—exempts Constitutional Amendments under Article 368 from Article 13, subjecting them instead to the Basic Structure test.

exp.why: Article 13(3)(a) expressly defines 'law' to include any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law.

Article 13(3)(b) explicitly states that 'laws in force' includes laws passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of the Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that any such law or any part thereof may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas.

In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the 13-Judge Bench overruled I.C. Golaknath (1967) and UPHELD the constitutional validity of the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, which inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3). Thus, a Constitutional Amendment Act is NOT 'law' under Article 13(2), although its validity can still be challenged if it alters or damages the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 13(3) & Art. 13(4); Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the operation of Article 13 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under the Doctrine of Eclipse, a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead altogether, but remains in a dormant state and can become operative again if a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency.
Statement-II: A pre-constitutional law that contravenes only a Fundamental Right guaranteed exclusively to citizens, such as Article 19, continues to operate validly against non-citizens.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Article 13(1) (Keshavan Madhava Menon and Bhikaji Narain Dhakras cases), pre-constitutional laws were validly enacted at their inception and are only overshadowed—not erased—to the extent of inconsistency with Part III, which explains both their revival upon constitutional amendment and their continued enforceability against non-citizens when the violated right is citizen-specific.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955), the Supreme Court propounded the Doctrine of Eclipse under Article 13(1), holding that because a pre-constitutional law was validly made by a competent legislature at its inception and Article 13(1) has no retrospective effect, the law is not dead ab initio; it is merely eclipsed by the Fundamental Right and revives as soon as the constitutional shadow is removed by an amendment.

Statement-II is also correct (Deep Chand v. State of U.P., 1959; State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, 1974). Since non-citizens cannot claim rights under Article 19, a pre-constitutional law inconsistent solely with Article 19 remains valid and enforceable against non-citizens. However, Statement-II is a parallel consequence of the prospective and partial operation of Article 13(1), not the underlying reason explaining why a constitutional amendment revives an eclipsed law against citizens in Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 13(1) & 13(2); Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955); Deep Chand v. State of U.P. (1959)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Doctrine of Waiver of Fundamental Rights in India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike in the United States of America, a citizen in India cannot voluntarily waive any of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution, even in exchange for a contractual settlement or statutory concession from the State.

Statement-II: Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are not enacted merely for the personal benefit of the individual, but are incorporated as a matter of public policy and as constitutional limitations upon the obligations and powers of the State.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959) and Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Supreme Court rejected the American doctrine of waiver, holding that Fundamental Rights are constitutional mandates of public policy binding on the State and cannot be bartered away by individuals.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959) and Olga Tellis v. BMC (1985), Constitution Benches of the Supreme Court held that no person can waive or estop themselves from asserting any Fundamental Right under Part III, even by an express agreement, compromise, or undertaking given to the State or a court.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The Supreme Court explained that Fundamental Rights under Part III are not mere private privileges conferrable or alienable at will, but represent a paramount constitutional policy that imposes a mandatory obligation and fetter upon the State under Article 13 not to transgress them, irrespective of an individual's consent.

ref: Constitution of India, Part III; Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959); Olga Tellis v. BMC (1985)

stem: Under Article 13 of the Constitution of India, if certain provisions of a newly enacted statute violate Fundamental Rights while the remaining provisions are constitutionally valid, but both the valid and invalid parts are so inextricably mixed into a single legislative scheme that the legislature would not have enacted the valid residue independently, what is the legal consequence under the judicial principles established in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India?

opts.A: The valid provisions remain enforceable in their entirety by applying the Doctrine of Pith and Substance to preserve the core legislative intent.
opts.B: The entire statute is placed in a state of temporary dormancy under the Doctrine of Eclipse until Parliament amends the invalid provisions.
opts.C: The entire statute must be struck down as unconstitutional because the Doctrine of Severability cannot be applied to salvage the truncated residue.
opts.D: The constitutional court is empowered to reconstruct the inseparable provisions so as to bring the entire legislative scheme into conformity with Part III.

core: Under the Doctrine of Severability derived from the words 'to the extent of such inconsistency/contravention' in Article 13(1) and 13(2), courts ordinarily invalidate only the offending portion of a statute. However, as settled in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957), when the valid and invalid provisions are so inextricably woven into a single scheme that the truncated residue cannot stand independently or reflect legislative intent, the entire statute must be struck down.

exp.why: Option C is correct: In R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957), the Supreme Court laid down the governing rules of the Doctrine of Severability under Article 13. While the general rule is that only the offending provision is declared void, if the valid and invalid provisions are so inextricably mixed up that they cannot be separated from one another, or if they form part of a single scheme intended to operate as a whole such that what is left is so thin and truncated that the legislature would not have enacted it independently, the invalidity of a portion results in the invalidity of the Act in its entirety. Option A is incorrect because the Doctrine of Pith and Substance applies to resolve questions of legislative competence between the Union and State Lists under Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule, not to save a statute that violates Fundamental Rights under Article 13. Option B is incorrect because the Doctrine of Eclipse applies when an otherwise valid law becomes dormant due to an inconsistent Fundamental Right, and does not rescue an inseparably defective post-constitutional scheme from invalidation. Option D is incorrect because courts cannot rewrite or redraft inseparable statutory provisions to make them constitutional, as doing so would amount to judicial legislation.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 13; R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (AIR 1957 SC 628); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the guarantee of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: The expression 'equality before the law' in Article 14 is of British origin and represents a negative concept implying the absence of any special privilege in favour of any individual and the equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land.

Statement-II: The expression 'equal protection of the laws' in Article 14 is borrowed from the American Constitution and represents a positive concept calling for equality of treatment in equal circumstances, permitting reasonable classification by the State.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 14 synthesizes two distinct constitutional traditions: 'equality before the law' (derived from A.V. Dicey's British Rule of Law, operating as a negative bar against special privileges) and 'equal protection of the laws' (derived from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, operating as a positive mandate for equal treatment among equals). Both statements accurately describe these two parallel, coordinate dimensions, so Statement-II does not serve as the causal explanation for Statement-I.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: The first limb of Article 14, 'equality before the law', owes its origin to British common law and A.V. Dicey's formulation of the Rule of Law. It is considered a negative concept because it forbids the conferment of arbitrary special privileges upon any individual and mandates that no person is above the ordinary law administered by ordinary courts.

Statement-II is correct, but does not explain Statement-I: The second limb of Article 14, 'equal protection of the laws', is adapted from Section 1 of the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution. It is a positive concept denoting that like should be treated alike without discrimination, which requires affirmative differential treatment where circumstances are unequal. Because Statement-II describes the second distinct phrase of Article 14 rather than explaining why 'equality before the law' is a British negative concept, both statements are independently correct without Statement-II explaining Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 14; State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the judicial doctrines governing Article 14 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the traditional classification test, the existence of an intelligible differentia between groups is by itself insufficient to validate a law unless that differentia bears a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

2. Under the E.P. Royappa doctrine, equality is treated as antithetical to arbitrariness, enabling courts to test the validity of State action under Article 14 even where no comparative class differentiation is involved.

3. While executive actions and subordinate legislation can be invalidated under Article 14 on the ground of manifest arbitrariness, primary plenary legislation enacted by Parliament can be struck down under Article 14 only if it fails the dual test of reasonable classification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 14 jurisprudence evolved from the old nexus test (requiring both intelligible differentia and rational nexus with the statutory object) to the E.P. Royappa non-arbitrariness doctrine. Furthermore, following Shayara Bano (2017), Navtej Singh Johar (2018), and the Electoral Bonds judgment (ADR v. Union of India, 2024), 'manifest arbitrariness' is an independent constitutional ground under Article 14 to strike down even primary plenary legislation enacted by Parliament or State Legislatures.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: To pass the traditional test of permissible classification under Article 14 (laid down in Charanjit Lal Chowdhury and Anwar Ali Sarkar), two cumulative conditions must be fulfilled: (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things grouped together from others left out, and (ii) that differentia must have a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. Mere differentiation without a rational nexus to the legislative object is unconstitutional.

Statement 2 is correct: In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court liberated Article 14 from the narrow confines of the classification test, holding that equality is a dynamic concept antithetical to arbitrariness. Thus, wherever a State action is arbitrary, whimsical, or irrational, it violates Article 14 even if it does not involve hostile discrimination between two comparable classes.

Statement 3 is incorrect: In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench overruled the narrower view in State of A.P. v. McDowell & Co. (1996) and held that 'manifest arbitrariness'—meaning something done by the legislature capriciously, irrationally, without adequate determining principle, or excessively and disproportionately—is a valid and independent ground under Article 14 to strike down primary plenary legislation as well as subordinate legislation. This doctrine was subsequently applied by Constitution Benches to invalidate primary statutory provisions in Joseph Shine (2018) and Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds case, 2024).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 14; E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974); Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017); ADR v. Union of India (2024)

stem: With reference to the constitutional exceptions to 'equality before the law' and immunities under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 361, while no criminal proceedings can be instituted or continued against the President or the Governor of a State in any court during their term of office, civil proceedings in respect of their personal acts can be instituted during their term of office after the expiration of two months' written notice.

2. Under Article 361A, no person is liable to any civil or criminal proceedings in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice.

3. Under Articles 105(2) and 194(2), a Member of Parliament or a State Legislature enjoys constitutional immunity from criminal prosecution for accepting a bribe in connection with a vote actually cast or a speech delivered on the floor of the House.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Articles 361 and 361A carve out valid constitutional immunities for the President/Governors and non-malicious media reporting of legislative proceedings as exceptions to Article 14, parliamentary privilege under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) is strictly tied to the collective functioning of the House. In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), a 7-Judge Bench overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) and held that lawmakers enjoy zero immunity from criminal prosecution for bribery.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Article 361(2) imposes an absolute bar against instituting or continuing any criminal proceedings whatsoever against the President or the Governor of a State in any court during their term of office. However, under Article 361(4), civil proceedings in which relief is claimed against the President or Governor in respect of any act done in their personal capacity (whether before or after entering office) can be instituted during their term of office, provided two months' written notice has been delivered stating the nature of the proceedings, the cause of action, and the relief claimed.

Statement 2 is correct: Article 361A (inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978) protects the freedom of the press by conferring immunity from any civil or criminal proceedings in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper (or wireless broadcast) of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or a State Legislature, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice (and excluding reports of secret sittings).

Statement 3 is incorrect: A 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024) overruled the 1998 majority ruling in P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State. The Court held that a legislator (MP or MLA) does NOT enjoy immunity under Article 105(2) or Article 194(2) from criminal prosecution for taking a bribe to vote or speak in the House or a committee thereof. The offence of bribery is complete at the moment the illegal gratification is accepted and does not depend on whether the legislator subsequently votes or speaks as agreed.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 105(2), 194(2), 361 & 361A; Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024 INSC 161); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the personal scope and applicability of the Fundamental Rights to Equality (Articles 14 to 18) under the Constitution of India:
items: 1. The Fundamental Rights against discrimination guaranteed under Articles 15 and 16 are available only to citizens of India and not to foreign nationals.

2. The guarantee of equality before the law under Article 14 applies to natural persons residing in India and does not extend to juristic persons such as statutory corporations or registered companies.
3. Under Article 18(3), a foreign national holding an office of profit or trust under the State in India may accept a title from a foreign State with the consent of the President of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Within the Equality Code (Articles 14–18), Articles 15 and 16 expressly restrict their protection to 'citizens' only, whereas Article 14 uses the broader phrase 'any person', thereby protecting citizens, foreign nationals, and juristic/legal persons (such as companies and statutory corporations) alike. Furthermore, while Article 18(2) imposes an absolute bar on Indian citizens accepting foreign titles, Article 18(3) imposes a qualified bar on foreigners holding an office of profit or trust under the State, allowing acceptance with Presidential consent.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The text of both Article 15 ('The State shall not discriminate against any citizen...') and Article 16 ('There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens...') explicitly confines the enjoyment of these Fundamental Rights exclusively to citizens of India. Foreign nationals cannot claim protection under Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, or 30.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Article 14 declares that the State shall not deny to 'any person' equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. The word 'person' is not limited to natural human beings; it includes legal or juristic persons such as statutory corporations, registered companies, and registered societies, as well as both citizens and foreigners.

Statement 3 is correct: Under Article 18(2), no citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State (an unconditional prohibition). In contrast, under Article 18(3), no person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 14, 15, 16 & 18; Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1951); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the prohibition of discrimination under Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 15(1) explicitly enumerates 'descent' and 'place of residence' among the prohibited grounds on which the State cannot discriminate against citizens in matters of admission to educational institutions.

2. Unlike Article 15(1) which is directed only against the State, the prohibition against discrimination in access to shops, public restaurants, and places of public entertainment under Article 15(2) is enforceable against both the State and private individuals.

3. While Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination on the ground of residence in public employment, Article 16(3) empowers Parliament exclusively—and not the State Legislatures—to prescribe residence within a State or Union Territory as a requirement for certain classes of public employment.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A precise textual comparison between Articles 15 and 16 reveals that Article 15(1) and 15(2) prohibit discrimination on five grounds only (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth), omitting 'descent' and 'residence' (which allows states to provide domicile/residence-based educational preferences unless barred by other provisions). In contrast, Article 16(2) lists seven prohibited grounds (adding 'descent' and 'residence'), subject to Parliament's exclusive power under Article 16(3) to prescribe residence requirements for public employment.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect: Article 15(1) prohibits the State from discriminating against any citizen on grounds only of 'religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them' (five grounds). It does NOT include 'descent' or 'residence'. As held by the Supreme Court in D.P. Joshi v. State of Madhya Bharat (1955), 'place of birth' is distinct from 'domicile/residence', which is why state rules prescribing bona fide residence criteria for educational admissions are not per se hit by the text of Article 15(1).

Statement 2 is correct: While Article 15(1) binds only 'the State', Article 15(2) states that no citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment, or the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public. Thus, Article 15(2) operates horizontally against private individuals as well as vertically against the State.

Statement 3 is correct: Article 16(2) includes 'descent' and 'residence' alongside religion, race, caste, sex, and place of birth (seven grounds in total) as prohibited grounds of discrimination in public employment. However, Article 16(3) carves out an exception by vesting the power exclusively in Parliament ('Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing...')—and expressly denying this power to State Legislatures—to prescribe residence within a State or Union Territory prior to employment as a requirement for any class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under that State or UT.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 15(1), 15(2), 16(2) & 16(3); D.P. Joshi v. State of Madhya Bharat (1955); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the exceptions to the rule of equality of opportunity in matters of public employment under Article 16 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 16(3), only the Parliament, and not the Legislature of a State, has the power to make a law prescribing residence within a State or Union Territory as a prior condition for certain classes of public employment.

2. While Article 16(3) empowers Parliament to prescribe 'residence' as a requirement for public employment in a State or Union Territory, it does not authorize Parliament to prescribe 'place of birth' or 'descent' as a qualification for such employment.

3. Under Article 16(5), a law may validly stipulate that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination in public employment on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence. However, Article 16(3) vests exclusive legislative competence in Parliament to prescribe 'residence' (and not 'place of birth' or 'descent') as a condition for certain state/UT appointments, while Article 16(5) exempts offices linked to religious or denominational institutions.

exp.why: Article 16(3) begins with 'Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing... any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment'. Combined with Article 35(a)(i), this legislative power is conferred exclusively on Parliament and explicitly denied to State Legislatures to prevent parochial fragmentation of national citizenship.

Although Article 16(2) bars discrimination on grounds of 'descent', 'place of birth', and 'residence', the exception carved out in Article 16(3) applies strictly to 'residence' within a State or Union Territory. Neither Parliament nor a State Legislature can prescribe 'place of birth' or 'descent' as a requirement for public employment.

Article 16(5) explicitly provides that nothing in Article 16 shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution, or any member of the governing body thereof, shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 16(2), 16(3), 16(5) & 35(a)(i); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Fundamental Rights).

stem: With reference to the constitutional validity of sub-classification within the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, as laid down by the 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. State Governments possess the constitutional competence under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) to sub-classify Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to grant preference to more backward subgroups among them, and such sub-classification does not violate Articles 341 and 342.

2. Any sub-classification of Scheduled Castes by a State must be backed by quantifiable and empirical data demonstrating both the inter-se backwardness of the subgroup and its inadequate representation in the public services of the State.

3. While exercising the power of sub-classification, a State Government is constitutionally permitted to earmark 100 per cent of the Scheduled Caste quota exclusively for the most backward subgroup, and such a policy decision is immune from judicial review.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), a 7-Judge Bench overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004), holding that Scheduled Castes are not a homogeneous class and States can sub-classify them under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) based on quantifiable empirical data of inter-se backwardness and inadequate representation, without allocating 100% of the quota to a single subgroup.

exp.why: Overruling the 5-Judge Bench decision in E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of A.P. (2004), the 7-Judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) held that sub-classification of SCs/STs for apportioning reserved seats among more backward subgroups does not add to or delete any caste from the Presidential Lists under Articles 341/342, and is a valid exercise of substantive equality under Articles 14, 15(4), and 16(4).

The Supreme Court laid down strict constitutional guardrails: a State cannot sub-classify SCs on political expediency or whim; it must collect quantifiable, empirical data proving both the inter-se social/educational backwardness of the sub-classified group and its inadequacy of representation across the State's public services.

The 7-Judge Bench explicitly ruled that while sub-classifying, a State cannot earmark 100 per cent of the reserved seats exclusively for a single sub-classified subgroup (as that would amount to de facto exclusion of all other castes in the Presidential List, violating Article 341(2)). Furthermore, the criteria and empirical basis of sub-classification are always subject to judicial review.

ref: Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench Judgment in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024); Articles 14, 15(4), 16(4), 341 & 342 of the Constitution.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the operational mechanics of vertical and horizontal reservations in India:
items: Statement-I: Under the constitutional jurisprudence governing public employment in India, candidates belonging to vertically reserved categories (SC, ST, or OBC) who secure marks higher than the cut-off for the Unreserved (Open) category on their own merit without availing any relaxation are still counted against their respective vertical reservation quota to preserve open seats for non-reserved candidates.

Statement-II: Interlocking horizontal reservations (such as for women or persons with benchmark disabilities under Articles 15(3) and 16(1)) cut across vertical categories so that candidates selected under a horizontal quota are placed within their respective vertical categories (SC, ST, OBC, or Open) by adjusting seats inside those vertical quotas without increasing the overall vertical reservation ceiling.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Indra Sawhney (1992) and Saurav Yadav (2020), the 'Open/Unreserved' category is not a quota for upper castes; Meritorious Reserved Category (MRC) candidates qualifying on own merit without relaxed standards must be adjusted in the Open category and not against the vertical reserved quota. Conversely, interlocking horizontal reservations are adjusted within each vertical category without breaching the vertical ceiling.

exp.why: As settled in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) and reaffirmed in Saurav Yadav v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2020), the Unreserved (Open) category is open to all citizens purely on merit and is not an exclusive quota for general category candidates. Consequently, reserved category (SC/ST/OBC) candidates who secure marks above the Open category cut-off on their own merit (without availing age, fee, or qualifying mark relaxations that bar migration) must be adjusted against the Open/Unreserved seats and cannot be counted against the vertical reserved quota.

Horizontal reservations (under Articles 15(3) and 16(1) for women, persons with disabilities, or ex-servicemen) are interlocking reservations that cut across vertical categories (SC, ST, OBC, and Open). As explained in Indra Sawhney (1992) and Rajesh Kumar Daria (2007), once horizontal quota candidates are selected, they are placed into their respective vertical categories (e.g., an SC woman selected under the women's quota is adjusted within the SC vertical quota), ensuring that horizontal adjustments never inflate the overall vertical reservation ceiling.

ref: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992); Rajesh Kumar Daria v. RPSC (2007); Saurav Yadav v. State of UP (2020).

stem: With reference to the constitutional framework and Supreme Court jurisprudence governing reservation in promotions in public employment, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 16(4A) of the Constitution confers an enforceable Fundamental Right to reservation in promotions upon Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, for which a High Court or the Supreme Court can issue a writ of mandamus directing the State to provide reservation.

2. In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), the Supreme Court held that while the 'creamy layer' principle cannot be applied to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in promotions, the State must still collect quantifiable data to prove the backwardness of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes before granting promotional reservation.

3. Under Article 16(4B) of the Constitution, unfilled reserved vacancies of a year that are carried forward to subsequent years as backlog vacancies must be clubbed together with the regular vacancies of the succeeding year for enforcing the 50 per cent annual ceiling on reservations.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 16(4) and 16(4A) are enabling provisions rather than enforceable Fundamental Rights. In Jarnail Singh (2018), the Supreme Court dropped M. Nagaraj's requirement of collecting quantifiable data on SC/ST backwardness (while retaining cadre-wise data on inadequacy of representation) and held that the creamy layer principle applies to SCs/STs in promotional reservation. Article 16(4B) exempts backlog vacancies from the 50% annual ceiling.

exp.why: In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) and Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand (2020), the Supreme Court settled that Articles 16(4) and 16(4A) are merely enabling provisions that vest discretionary power in the State. They do not confer a Fundamental Right to claim reservation in promotions, and Constitutional Courts cannot issue a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to provide reservation.

This statement reverses both holdings of the 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018). First, the Court struck down M. Nagaraj's requirement that States collect quantifiable data on the backwardness of SCs/STs (as SCs/STs are constitutionally presumed backward once notified under Articles 341/342), while retaining the requirement of cadre-wise quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation. Second, the Court held that the 'creamy layer' exclusion principle is grounded in Articles 14 and 16(1) and therefore applies to SCs and STs in reservation in promotions.

Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000, explicitly provides that unfilled reserved vacancies of a year carried forward to subsequent years shall be treated as a separate class of vacancies and shall NOT be considered together with the vacancies of the year in which they are being filled up for determining the 50 per cent ceiling on total vacancies of that year.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 16(4A), 16(4B) & 335; M. Nagaraj (2006), Jarnail Singh (2018 & 2022), Mukesh Kumar (2020).
