stem: With reference to the reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) introduced by the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 and upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 15(6), the State is empowered to make special provisions for the admission of Economically Weaker Sections to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in Article 30(1).

2. Citizens belonging to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Socially and Educationally Backward Classes covered under Articles 15(4), 15(5), and 16(4) are constitutionally excluded from availing EWS reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6).

3. Unlike Article 16(4A), Article 16(6) is an enabling provision that permits the State to provide EWS reservation subject to a maximum ceiling of 10 per cent in initial appointments or posts, and does not extend EWS reservation to promotions.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) as enabling provisions permitting up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (excluding SCs, STs, and OBCs already covered under Articles 15(4), 15(5), and 16(4)) in educational admissions (including unaided private non-minority institutions) and initial public appointments, but not in promotions.

exp.why: Article 15(6)(b) explicitly empowers the State to make special provision for the advancement of EWS regarding their admission to educational institutions, including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of Article 30.

Both Articles 15(6) and 16(6) define the beneficiary class as 'any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5)' (of Art. 15) and 'other than the classes mentioned in clause (4)' (of Art. 16). In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench upheld this exclusion of SCs, STs, and OBCs from the 10% EWS quota as a valid reasonable classification that does not violate the Basic Structure.

Article 16(6) is phrased as an enabling provision ('Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts... subject to a maximum of ten per cent'). It prescribes a ceiling of 'up to 10%' rather than a mandatory floor, and applies only to initial appointments/direct recruitment and not to promotions.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 15(6) & 16(6) (103rd Amendment Act, 2019); Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022).

stem: Consider the following pairs of Constitutional Amendment Acts relating to affirmative action under Articles 15 and 16 and the Supreme Court judgments that directly triggered their enactment:
items: 1. First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 (inserting Article 15(4)) : Enacted to overcome the ruling in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
2. 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005 (inserting Article 15(5)) : Enacted to overcome the ruling in P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005)
3. 77th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1995 (inserting Article 16(4A)) : Enacted to negate the 'catch-up rule' laid down in Virpal Singh Chauhan (1995) and Ajit Singh Januja (1996)
4. 85th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001 (amending Article 16(4A)) : Enacted first to overcome the bar on reservation in promotions laid down in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Affirmative action clauses in Articles 15 and 16 evolved through a dialogic process between Parliament and the Supreme Court: the 1st Amendment (Art 15(4)) responded to Champakam Dorairajan (1951); the 77th Amendment (Art 16(4A)) responded to Indra Sawhney (1992); the 85th Amendment (consequential seniority) responded to Virpal Singh Chauhan/Ajit Singh (1995/1996); and the 93rd Amendment (Art 15(5)) responded to P.A. Inamdar (2005).

exp.why: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court struck down the Madras Communal G.O. providing caste-based quotas in medical and engineering colleges as violative of Article 15(1) and Article 29(2). To overcome this ruling, Parliament enacted the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, inserting Clause (4) into Article 15.

In P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005), a 7-Judge Bench held that the State could not impose its reservation policy on unaided private educational institutions. Parliament enacted the 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005, inserting Article 15(5) to empower the State to provide reservation in admissions to private educational institutions (aided or unaided), excluding minority institutions under Article 30(1)—later upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008).

The 77th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1995 (which initially inserted Article 16(4A)) was enacted to overcome the 9-Judge Bench ruling in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), which had held that reservation under Article 16(4) is confined to initial appointments and does not extend to promotions. It was the 85th Amendment (2001), not the 77th Amendment, that negated the 'catch-up rule'.

In Union of India v. Virpal Singh Chauhan (1995) and Ajit Singh Januja v. State of Punjab (1996), the Supreme Court introduced the 'catch-up rule', whereby general category candidates promoted later would regain their seniority over earlier-promoted SC/ST candidates once they reached the same promotional level. To negate this 'catch-up rule' and confer 'consequential seniority' upon promoted SC/ST candidates retrospectively from 1995, Parliament enacted the 85th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001.

ref: Constitution of India, 1st, 77th, 85th & 93rd Amendment Acts; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 & Ch. 11.

stem: Consider the following landmark doctrinal milestones in the constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court of India concerning the Right to Equality and Affirmative Action:
items: 1. Recognition of Article 16(4) as an emphatic facet of substantive equality under Article 16(1) rather than a mere exception to equality of opportunity (State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas)
2. Judicial formulation of the 'Creamy Layer' principle requiring the exclusion of socially advanced members of Other Backward Classes from reservation benefits (Indra Sawhney v. Union of India)
3. Initial judicial pronouncement of the 50 percent ceiling rule on total reservations under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) (M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore)
4. Affirmation of the constitutional competence of States to sub-classify Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes based on quantifiable data of inter-se backwardness (State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the judicial milestones given above, from the earliest to the latest?
core: Indian equality jurisprudence evolved from treating reservation as an exception to formal equality (M.R. Balaji, 1962) to viewing it as an integral instrument of substantive equality (N.M. Thomas, 1975), before refining its internal rationality through the Creamy Layer rule (Indra Sawhney, 1992) and intra-group sub-classification (Davinder Singh, 2024).

exp.why: In State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (decided in September 1975; reported 1976), a 7-Judge Bench made a paradigm shift from formal to substantive equality, holding that Article 16(4) is not an exception to Article 16(1) but an emphatic illustration of the classification inherent in Article 16(1).

In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (decided in November 1992), a 9-Judge Bench upheld the 27% OBC reservation while mandating the exclusion of the socially and economically advanced 'Creamy Layer' among Other Backward Classes.

In M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (decided in September 1962; AIR 1963 SC 649), a 5-Judge Bench struck down a 68% reservation order and first laid down the constitutional rule that reservations, treated then as an exception to equality, should ordinarily be less than 50 percent.

In State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (decided in August 2024), a 7-Judge Bench overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) and held that Scheduled Castes do not form a homogeneous monolith, permitting States to sub-classify SCs and STs under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) based on empirical evidence of inadequate representation and inter-se backwardness. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 3 (1962) - 1 (1975) - 2 (1992) - 4 (2024).

ref: Constitution of India Articles 14–16; State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)

stem: With reference to the abolition of untouchability under Article 17 of the Constitution of India and the statutory framework governing it, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Neither the Constitution of India nor the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 defines the term 'untouchability'.

2. Under Article 35 of the Constitution, the power to make laws prescribing punishment for acts declared to be offences under Article 17 vests only in the Parliament and not in the Legislature of a State.

3. Under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, justifying untouchability on historical, philosophical, or religious grounds does not constitute a penal offence unless accompanied by physical obstruction or denial of access to a public place.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 17 is a self-executing absolute prohibition operating against both the State and private individuals, reinforced by Parliament's exclusive penal law-making competence under Article 35(a)(ii) through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

exp.why: The term 'untouchability' is not defined either in Article 17 of the Constitution or in the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (formerly the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955), leaving its historical and sociological import to judicial construction.

Article 35(a)(ii) explicitly provides that Parliament shall have, and the Legislature of a State shall not have, power to make laws for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under Part III (specifically Articles 17 and 23), ensuring uniform punishment across India.

Following the 1976 amendment to the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (Section 7(1)(c) combined with Explanation II), preaching untouchability or justifying it on historical, philosophical, or religious grounds, or on the ground of any tradition of the caste system, is by itself an independent and standalone punishable offence, even without physical obstruction.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 17 & 35(a)(ii); Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional and legal framework of Article 17 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Article 17 of the Constitution of India expressly stipulates that any person convicted of the offence of practicing untouchability shall stand disqualified from being chosen as a member of either House of Parliament or of a State Legislature.

Statement-II: In Indian constitutional jurisprudence, the term 'untouchability' in Article 17 is not construed in a literal or grammatical sense to include every form of social boycott or medical segregation, but refers to the historical caste-based practice of social disability imposed on certain classes of persons by reason of their birth.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 17 abolishes the historical caste-based institution of untouchability and declares its practice an offence punishable in accordance with law, the specific electoral disqualification for conviction stems from parliamentary statute (Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951) rather than the text of Article 17.

exp.why: Article 17 only declares that 'Untouchability' is abolished, its practice in any form is forbidden, and the enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law. It does not contain an express clause on electoral disqualification. The disqualification from contesting elections upon conviction under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 is prescribed by statute under Section 8(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 ( read with Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e)).

As held in Devarajiah v. B. Padmanna (AIR 1958 Mys 84) and consistently affirmed by the Supreme Court, the word 'Untouchability' in Article 17 is placed inside inverted commas to signify that it is not to be read in a literal or grammatical sense (such as quarantining persons with contagious diseases or ordinary individual boycotts), but refers to the historical social practice developed in India of relegating certain classes to social disabilities by birth.

ref: Constitution of India Article 17; Representation of the People Act, 1951 Section 8(1)(a); Devarajiah v. Padmanna

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the 'Abolition of Titles' under Article 18 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 18(4), both a citizen of India and a foreign national holding an office of profit or trust under the State are prohibited from accepting any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State without the consent of the President.
2. Under Article 18(3), a person who is not a citizen of India, while holding an office of profit or trust under the State, may accept a title from a foreign State with the consent of the President.

3. Under Article 18(2), a citizen of India who does not hold any office of profit or trust under the State may accept a title from a foreign State provided prior consent of the President of India is obtained.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 18 differentiates carefully between 'citizens' and 'persons holding an office of profit or trust under the State': while non-citizens in State service (Art. 18(3)) and any office-holder receiving foreign presents/emoluments (Art. 18(4)) may act with Presidential consent, the bar on an Indian citizen accepting a foreign title under Article 18(2) is absolute.

exp.why: Article 18(4) uses the broader phrase 'No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State', which applies equally to citizens and non-citizens holding such an office, requiring the consent of the President before accepting any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

Article 18(3) specifically provides that no person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State.

Article 18(2) declares simply and unconditionally: 'No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State.' Unlike Clauses (3) and (4), Clause (2) makes no exception for Presidential consent and applies to all Indian citizens regardless of whether they hold an office of profit under the State.

ref: Constitution of India Article 18(1)–(4); D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: In the context of the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench decision in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) regarding the validity of National Awards under Article 18 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: National awards such as the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards do not amount to 'titles' within the prohibition of Article 18(1) as they recognize excellence and merit in harmony with Article 51A(j), provided they are not used as prefixes or suffixes to the recipient's name.
opts.B: The Supreme Court upheld the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards by classifying all civilian honours as 'academic distinctions' within the explicit exception clause of Article 18(1).
opts.C: Article 18 itself prescribes mandatory forfeiture of citizenship and statutory imprisonment if a recipient uses a Padma award as an appellation before or after their name.
opts.D: While the Bharat Ratna is constitutionally valid under Article 18(1), the three-tier hierarchy of Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma Shri was held to be violative of the principle of equality under Article 14.

core: In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that Article 18(1) prohibits hereditary and aristocratic titles that create artificial social hierarchies, whereas National Awards recognize exemplary merit in furtherance of the Fundamental Duty to strive towards excellence under Article 51A(j).

exp.why: Option A is correct because in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), the 5-Judge Bench harmonized Article 18(1) with Article 51A(j) (the fundamental duty to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity), holding that National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma Shri) are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18(1) so long as they are not used as prefixes or suffixes to the awardee's name. Option B is incorrect because the Court explicitly rejected the argument that 'academic distinction' covers all civilian merit awards. Option C is incorrect because Article 18 contains no penal provision or forfeiture of citizenship; under executive regulations governing the awards, using an award as a prefix or suffix only invites cancellation/forfeiture of the award itself by the President. Option D is incorrect because the Court upheld the constitutional validity of all four awards.

ref: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India, (1996) 1 SCC 361; Constitution of India Articles 18(1) & 51A(j)

stem: Consider the following pairs of Constitutional Doctrines and their primary legal effect under Part III of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Doctrine of Manifest Arbitrariness : Invalidating plenary legislation under Article 14 when it is done capriciously, irrationally, or without an adequate determining principle
2. Doctrine of Eclipse : Rendering pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights dormant and inoperative rather than dead ab initio
3. Creamy Layer Principle : Excluding socially and economically advanced members of a backward class from affirmative action benefits to preserve substantive equality
4. Doctrine of Waiver : Permitting a citizen to voluntarily relinquish and contract out of the Fundamental Right to Equality under Article 14 in commercial dealings with the State
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 12 to 18 are anchored by key judicial doctrines—Eclipse (Art. 13(1)), Non-Waiver (Basheshar Nath), Manifest Arbitrariness (Art. 14), and Creamy Layer (Art. 15/16)—which ensure that Fundamental Rights operate as non-negotiable public policy limitations on State power.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. As crystallized in Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) and Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), even plenary legislation passed by Parliament or a State Legislature can be struck down under Article 14 on the ground of 'manifest arbitrariness' if it is capricious, irrational, or lacks an adequate determining principle.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Under Article 13(1) (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955), pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Part III are not wiped out from the statute book ab initio; they are merely overshadowed (eclipsed) by the Fundamental Right and can revive if the constitutional impediment is removed by amendment.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Originating in Indra Sawhney (1992) for OBCs and extended to SC/ST promotions in Jarnail Singh (2018) and SC/ST sub-classification in Davinder Singh (2024), the Creamy Layer doctrine ensures that the most advantaged members within a backward class do not corner benefits meant for the truly backward.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959) and Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Supreme Court decisively rejected the American Doctrine of Waiver in India, holding that Fundamental Rights—especially Article 14—are enacted in the interest of public policy as a direct admonition to the State, and no citizen can waive or contract out of their Fundamental Rights.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 13–16; Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959); Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)

stem: With reference to the applicability of the six fundamental freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The fundamental freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1) are available only to citizens of India and cannot be claimed by foreign nationals.

2. Because an incorporated company is a juristic person and not a citizen within the meaning of Part II of the Constitution, state action directed against a company can under no circumstances be challenged for violating Article 19.

3. The fundamental rights of Indian citizens who are shareholders or editors of a newspaper company under Article 19(1)(a) are not lost merely by reason of their associating together as a corporate body.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 19 freedoms are textually restricted to natural citizens of India and cannot be claimed by a corporation in its own name, the Supreme Court in R.C. Cooper (1970) and Bennett Coleman (1973) established that Indian citizens who are shareholders, directors, or editors can challenge state action against a company if the impact of that action directly impairs their personal rights under Article 19.

exp.why: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 confer Fundamental Rights exclusively on 'citizens', unlike Articles 14 and 21 which apply to 'any person'. Consequently, foreign nationals cannot invoke Article 19(1).

Although the Supreme Court held in State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1963) and Tata Engineering (TELCO) v. State of Bihar (1964) that a company itself is not a citizen, in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) and Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973) the Court clarified that state action directed at a company CAN be challenged under Article 19 by its shareholders, directors, or editors who are Indian citizens if their own fundamental rights are directly impaired by the state action.

In Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973), the Supreme Court held that the locus standi of shareholder-citizens and editors under Article 19(1)(a) is not extinguished merely because they carry on their business or publication through the medium of an incorporated company.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 19; R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970); Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8.

stem: With reference to the reasonable restrictions explicitly enumerated under Articles 19(2) to 19(6) of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs matching a Fundamental Freedom with a constitutionally specified ground of restriction:
items: 1. Freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India [Article 19(1)(d)] : Protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe
2. Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms [Article 19(1)(b)] : Decency or morality
3. Freedom to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business [Article 19(1)(g)] : Sovereignty and integrity of India and public order
prompt: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
core: Each sub-clause of Articles 19(2) to 19(6) contains a distinct, exhaustive list of permissible grounds for restricting the corresponding freedom in Article 19(1). Grounds such as 'public order', 'decency or morality', and 'sovereignty and integrity of India' do not apply uniformly across all six freedoms.

exp.why: Under Article 19(5), the State can impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of movement [Article 19(1)(d)] and residence [Article 19(1)(e)] only on two grounds: 'in the interests of the general public' or 'for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe'.

Under Article 19(3), the freedom of assembly [Article 19(1)(b)] can be restricted only in the interests of 'the sovereignty and integrity of India' or 'public order'. 'Decency or morality' is a valid ground under Article 19(2) [speech and expression] and Article 19(4) [associations or unions], but is absent from Article 19(3).

Under Article 19(6), the freedom of profession, occupation, trade, or business [Article 19(1)(g)] can be restricted 'in the interests of the general public' (along with prescribing professional/technical qualifications and creating State monopolies). Neither 'sovereignty and integrity of India' nor 'public order' is enumerated as an explicit textual ground in Article 19(6).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 19(2)–19(6); M.P. Jain, Indian Constitutional Law, Ch. XXIV.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the legal instruments through which Fundamental Rights under Article 19 can be restricted:
items: Statement-I: Reasonable restrictions on the freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1) cannot be imposed through mere departmental circulars or executive policy guidelines lacking the authority of an enacted legislature-backed law.

Statement-II: Under Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution, the inclusive definition of the term 'law' encompasses executive orders, notifications, rules, regulations, and customs or usages having the force of law.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' broadly to include executive notifications and customs so that citizens can challenge any state instrument violating Part III, the Supreme Court in Kharak Singh (1962) and Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) held that the term 'law' in Articles 19(2)–(6) has a narrower meaning: only a statutory law (or subordinate legislation backed by statute) can curtail Article 19 freedoms, not a mere executive circular.

exp.why: In Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962) and Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), the Supreme Court held that a 'law' restricting Article 19(1) freedoms under Articles 19(2) to 19(6) must be a valid statutory enactment or statutory rule, and cannot be a mere departmental instruction or non-statutory executive circular.

Statement-II is an accurate description of Article 13(3)(a). However, it does not explain Statement-I; in fact, if Article 13(3)(a)'s broad definition applied blindly to Articles 19(2)–(6), executive orders alone could restrict fundamental freedoms. The broad definition in Article 13(3)(a) exists strictly to bring executive actions under the scanner of judicial review under Article 13(2), whereas Articles 19(2)–(6) require legislative backing to restrict liberty.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 13(3)(a) & Art. 19(2)–(6); Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986); Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962).

stem: With reference to the constitutional principles laid down by the five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in the Electoral Bonds case (Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, 2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a) extends to disclosure of financial contributions made to political parties because economic inequality enables large donors to influence electoral outcomes and subsequent policy-making.

2. When resolving a conflict between two competing Fundamental Rights—specifically the voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a) and a donor's right to informational privacy of political affiliation under Article 21—the Court applies the 'double proportionality' standard rather than treating either right as hierarchically superior.

3. The Supreme Court held that financial contributions made by business corporations to political parties constitute a protected form of political speech under Article 19(1)(a) on par with donations by individual citizens, subject only to mandatory disclosure.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In striking down the Electoral Bonds Scheme (2024), the Supreme Court held that informational privacy of political affiliation under Article 21 must be balanced against the voter's right to know under Article 19(1)(a) using the double proportionality standard, while sharply distinguishing individual citizens' expressive donations from commercial corporate funding.

exp.why: The Constitution Bench held that money is closely intertwined with electoral politics and creates a legitimate possibility of quid pro quo in policy-making; therefore, information about the funding of political parties is essential for the effective exercise of the voter's freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a).

Since the Indian Constitution does not establish a rigid hierarchy between Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21, the Supreme Court applied the double proportionality standard to evaluate whether both fundamental rights could be realized to the maximum practicable extent and whether less restrictive alternatives (such as disclosure only above a statutory threshold through Electoral Trusts) existed.

Corporations are not citizens under Article 19. Furthermore, the Supreme Court expressly distinguished donations by individual citizens (which can be an expression of political support/affiliation) from contributions by companies, observing that corporate donations are essentially business transactions often made to secure quid pro quo benefits. The Court struck down the amendment to Section 182 of the Companies Act, 2013 that permitted unlimited corporate political donations (even by loss-making/shell companies) as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.

ref: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 113 (5-Judge Constitution Bench); Constitution of India, Art. 14, 19(1)(a) & 21.

stem: With reference to the horizontal application of Fundamental Rights and the freedom of speech of public functionaries as laid down by the five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023), consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Fundamental Right guaranteed under Article 19 or Article 21 can be enforced even against persons other than the State or its instrumentalities.

2. The grounds of restriction enumerated under Article 19(2) are exhaustive, and no additional restrictions can be imposed on a Minister's freedom of speech and expression by invoking the competing Article 21 rights of citizens.

3. A statement made by a Minister, even if traceable to any affairs of the State or made for protecting the Government, cannot be attributed vicariously to the Government by invoking the principle of collective responsibility.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court expanded the horizontal enforceability of Articles 19 and 21 against non-State actors, while affirming that Article 19(2) restrictions are strictly exhaustive and that collective ministerial responsibility does not make the Government vicariously liable for individual ministerial remarks.

exp.why: By a 4:1 majority in Kaushal Kishor (2023), the Constitution Bench expressly held that Fundamental Rights under Articles 19 and 21 are horizontally enforceable even against non-State actors (persons other than the State or its instrumentalities under Article 12), accompanied by a positive duty on the State to protect rights from private infringement.

The Court unanimously held that the eight grounds mentioned under Article 19(2) for restricting free speech under Article 19(1)(a) are exhaustive. Under the guise of protecting a citizen's dignity or right to life under Article 21, the Court cannot read additional unwritten restrictions into Article 19(2) against public functionaries or Ministers.

In its operative holding, the 4-judge majority clarified the scope of collective ministerial responsibility under Articles 75(3) and 164(2), ruling that collective responsibility flows from the Council of Ministers to the Legislature and that a statement made by a Minister, even if traceable to any affairs of the State or for protecting the Government, cannot be attributed vicariously to the Government by invoking the principle of collective responsibility.

ref: Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2023) 4 SCC 1 (5-Judge Constitution Bench); Constitution of India, Art. 19(1)(a), 19(2) & 21.

stem: With reference to the constitutional safeguards governing the suspension of internet and telecom services in India as laid down by the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to practice any profession or carry on any trade, business, or occupation over the medium of the internet enjoy constitutional protection under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(g) respectively.
2. Any executive order suspending internet services must satisfy the doctrine of proportionality, cannot be indefinite in duration, and must be proactively published so as to enable judicial review.
3. In this judgment, the Supreme Court explicitly declared the abstract right to access the internet as an independent and standalone Fundamental Right under Article 21 of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court refrained from declaring the right to access the internet as a standalone Fundamental Right, but held that using the internet as a medium for free speech and trade is constitutionally protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) and any suspension must pass the test of proportionality.

exp.why: The Supreme Court held that because the internet has become an indispensable medium for the expression of views as well as modern e-commerce and professions, exercising freedom of speech and expression and freedom of trade/occupation through the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2) and 19(6).

The Court ruled that indefinite suspension of internet services under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services (Public Emergency or Public Safety) Rules is impermissible, that every suspension order must satisfy the four-pronged proportionality test, and that all such orders must be published and subjected to periodic review.

In paragraph 28 of the Anuradha Bhasin judgment, the Supreme Court explicitly stated that none of the counsels had argued for declaring the right to access the internet as a standalone Fundamental Right and the Court declined to express a view on that broader question, confining its ratio solely to the protection of speech and trade exercised through the internet under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).

ref: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637; Constitution of India, Art. 19(1)(a) & 19(1)(g).

stem: With reference to the freedom of assembly guaranteed to citizens under Article 19 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is strictly in accordance with the constitutional text and judicial interpretation?

opts.A: While the requirement that an assembly must be peaceable and without arms is an intrinsic condition built into Article 19(1)(b) itself, external statutory restrictions under Article 19(3) can be imposed only in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order.
opts.B: The State can impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of peaceable assembly under Article 19(3) on the grounds of public order, decency, morality, or the interests of the general public.
opts.C: The fundamental right to assemble peaceably under Article 19(1)(b) carries a corresponding constitutional right for citizens to hold public meetings on any government-owned premises at their discretion.
opts.D: Because the maintenance of traffic regulations falls exclusively under the 'interests of the general public' rather than 'public order', the State cannot regulate public processions on thoroughfares under Article 19(3).

core: Article 19(1)(b) contains two intrinsic qualifications at the threshold ('peaceably' and 'without arms'), whereas Article 19(3) confines external statutory restrictions strictly to two exhaustive grounds: the sovereignty and integrity of India, and public order.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because Article 19(1)(b) itself limits the guaranteed right to assembling 'peaceably and without arms' (an intrinsic qualification), while Article 19(3) permits reasonable statutory restrictions only on two specified grounds: 'the sovereignty and integrity of India, or public order'. Option (B) is incorrect because 'decency or morality' (found in Articles 19(2) and 19(4)) and 'interests of the general public' (found in Articles 19(5) and 19(6)) are not permissive grounds under Article 19(3). Option (C) is incorrect because in Railway Board v. Niranjan Singh (1969) and Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020), the Supreme Court held that Article 19(1)(b) neither grants a right to hold meetings on arbitrary government/private premises nor permits the indefinite occupation of public roads. Option (D) is incorrect because in Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police (1972), the Supreme Court affirmed that regulating public processions and traffic on thoroughfares falls within the ambit of maintaining 'public order' under Article 19(3).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 19(1)(b) & 19(3); Himat Lal K. Shah (1972); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the freedom to form associations, unions, or co-operative societies under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The fundamental right to form an association under Article 19(1)(c) includes both the right to continue the association with its voluntary composition and the negative right of a citizen not to be compelled to join an association against their will.
2. Through the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, the right of citizens to form co-operative societies was elevated to the status of a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c).
3. According to the Supreme Court, the fundamental right to form a trade union under Article 19(1)(c) carries a concomitant fundamental right to effective collective bargaining and to go on strike.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 19(1)(c) guarantees both the positive and negative freedom of association (including co-operative societies added by the 97th Amendment), judicial precedent draws a strict line between the threshold right to form a union and the subsequent operational methods of that union, denying fundamental right status to strikes or collective bargaining.

exp.why: In Damyanti Naranga v. Union of India (1971) and Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1956), the Supreme Court held that the right to form an association under Article 19(1)(c) is not confined to the initial stage of formation; it protects the right to continue the association with its voluntary composition and necessarily implies the negative right not to be compelled to join or be forced into an association with others against one's volition.

The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 inserted the words 'or co-operative societies' into Article 19(1)(c), directly conferring Fundamental Right status on citizens to form co-operative societies (which part of the 97th Amendment remained completely valid even when Part IXB's application to state co-operatives was partially struck down in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah, 2021).

In All India Bank Employees' Association v. National Industrial Tribunal (1962) and T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the fundamental right to form a trade union under Article 19(1)(c) does not carry a concomitant fundamental right to achieve every object of the union, and therefore there is no fundamental right to effective collective bargaining, lock-out, or strike. The right to strike is at best a statutory right regulated by industrial laws.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 19(1)(c) & 19(4); Damyanti Naranga (1971); All India Bank Employees' Assn (1962); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the freedom of profession, occupation, trade, or business under Article 19(1)(g) and its exceptions under Article 19(6), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 19(6)(ii), when the State enacts a law creating a State monopoly in a trade or business to the complete or partial exclusion of citizens, the creation of the monopoly itself is presumed to be in the public interest and does not require separate justification under the general public interest test.

2. Under the judicial doctrine of 'res extra commercium', inherently pernicious activities such as gambling and trafficking in potable intoxicants enjoy threshold protection under Article 19(1)(g), subject to total prohibition by the State under Article 19(6).

3. The Constitution explicitly empowers the State under Article 19(6)(i) to make laws prescribing the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 19(6) carves out specific structural immunities for State monopolies and professional qualification laws, while the judicial doctrine of 'res extra commercium' excludes inherently pernicious activities from the threshold ambit of Article 19(1)(g) altogether.

exp.why: Inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, Article 19(6)(ii) clarifies that nothing in Article 19(1)(g) prevents the State from making any law relating to the carrying on by the State (or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State) of any trade, business, industry, or service, to the complete or partial exclusion of citizens. In Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa (1963), the Supreme Court held that the basic law creating a State monopoly is presumed to be in the public interest and the State does not have to separately prove its reasonableness in the interest of the general public.

Under the doctrine of 'res extra commercium' (things outside commerce), propounded by the Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957) and Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (1995), pernicious, immoral, or noxious activities such as gambling and trading in potable liquor do not constitute 'trade or business' at the threshold of Article 19(1)(g). Citizens have zero fundamental right to engage in them, so the State does not even need to invoke Article 19(6) to prohibit or monopolize them.

Article 19(6)(i) explicitly protects existing and future laws insofar as they relate to the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, or business.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 19(1)(g) & 19(6); Khoday Distilleries (1995); Akadasi Padhan (1963)

stem: With reference to the constitutional protection against ex-post-facto laws under Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The prohibition under Article 20(1) bars retrospective conviction or the retrospective enhancement of penalty for a substantive criminal offence, but it does not bar a retrospective change in the procedural rules or forum of a criminal trial.
2. The constitutional bar under Article 20(1) extends equally to prevent the legislature from enacting retrospective civil tax liabilities or fiscal penalties for past assessment years.

3. Because preventive detention restricts personal liberty, Article 20(1) prohibits the executive from passing a preventive detention order based on an individual's conduct prior to the enactment of the preventive detention statute.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Article 20(1) is strictly confined to substantive criminal law ('convicted of any offence' and 'penalty' for commission of an offence); it leaves untouched retrospective civil/tax legislation, retrospective changes in trial procedure, and precautionary preventive detention.

exp.why: In Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh (1953), the Supreme Court held that Article 20(1) prohibits only conviction or sentence under an ex-post-facto substantive criminal law, and does not give an accused a vested right to be tried by a particular procedure or forum. Thus, a trial conducted under a retrospectively altered criminal procedure does not violate Article 20(1).

Article 20(1) uses the strict words 'convicted of any offence'. Accordingly, the immunity against ex-post-facto laws applies only to criminal statutes and does not prohibit the retrospective imposition of civil liabilities, retrospective tax levies, or civil fiscal penalties (Hathising Manufacturing Co. v. Union of India, 1960).

Preventive detention is precautionary and interceptive rather than punitive; a detainee is neither 'convicted of any offence' nor subjected to a punitive 'penalty' for a proven crime. Therefore, Article 20(1) has no application to preventive detention orders.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 20(1); Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh (1953); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the application of Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under the constitutional jurisprudence of Article 20(1), if an ex-post-facto amendment enacted prior to the pronouncement of judgment reduces the statutory punishment for an offence already committed, the accused is constitutionally barred from claiming the benefit of the reduced punishment and must be sentenced under the harsher law in force on the date of the offence.

Statement-II: The text of the second part of Article 20(1) prohibits only subjecting a person to a penalty 'greater than' that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence, and does not prohibit the retrospective application of a lesser penalty.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the doctrine of beneficial retrospectivity (Rattan Lal and T. Barai rulings), Article 20(1) only bars retrospective enhancement of punishment ('penalty greater than'), thereby allowing an accused to avail the benefit of a subsequent ex-post-facto law that mitigates or reduces the punishment.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Under the doctrine of beneficial retrospectivity laid down by the Supreme Court in Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab (1965) and T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe (1983), an ex-post-facto law that mitigates or reduces the rigour of punishment for a previously committed offence is not barred by Article 20(1); unless the amending statute expressly indicates otherwise, an accused whose trial or appeal is pending can legitimately claim the benefit of the reduced punishment.

Statement-II is correct. The second clause of Article 20(1) explicitly states that no person shall 'be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence'. By restricting the prohibition to a 'greater' penalty, the constitutional text leaves full room for beneficial ex-post-facto laws that reduce penalties.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 20(1); Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab (1965); T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe (1983)

stem: With reference to the protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India and statutory criminal procedure, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the constitutional protection under Article 20(2) embodies only the principle of 'autrefois convict' by requiring both prior prosecution and punishment, the statutory bar under Section 337 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 is wider and covers both prior conviction and prior acquittal.

2. If a public servant is subjected to a departmental disciplinary inquiry and dismissed from service on charges of corruption, Article 20(2) bars his subsequent prosecution before a criminal court for the same offence.

3. The confiscation of smuggled goods and imposition of a fiscal penalty by Customs authorities under the Customs Act constitutes a judicial prosecution and punishment that bars a subsequent criminal trial before a Magistrate under Article 20(2).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 20(2) uses the conjunctive phrase 'prosecuted and punished' and applies only when the prior proceeding was a criminal prosecution before a court of law or judicial tribunal; consequently, neither prior acquittals nor departmental/customs penalties trigger the constitutional bar of Article 20(2).

exp.why: Article 20(2) states that 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.' Because 'prosecuted AND punished' is conjunctive, it embodies only the English common law rule of 'autrefois convict' (formerly convicted) and does not protect a person who was prosecuted and acquitted. In contrast, Section 337 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (which replaced Section 300 of the erstwhile CrPC, 1973) provides a wider statutory shield covering both 'autrefois convict' and 'autrefois acquit'.

In S.A. Venkataraman v. Union of India (1954), the Supreme Court held that to attract Article 20(2), the prior prosecution and punishment must have taken place before a court of law or a judicial tribunal in proceedings of a criminal nature. A departmental disciplinary inquiry conducted by administrative authorities is not a judicial prosecution for an offence, so subsequent criminal prosecution in a court is not barred.

In Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (1953) and Thomas Dana v. State of Punjab (1959), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled that Customs and Revenue authorities are administrative bodies, not courts of law or judicial tribunals. Therefore, confiscation of goods and imposition of departmental penalties under customs legislation do not amount to 'prosecution and punishment' under Article 20(2) and do not bar a subsequent criminal trial before a Magistrate.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 20(2); Section 337 of BNSS 2023; Maqbool Hussain (1953); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the protection against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India and the judicial pronouncements thereon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph examination, or Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP) test violates Article 20(3) because it compels an individual to impart personal knowledge involuntarily.

2. A judicial order directing an accused person to furnish specimen signatures, thumb impressions, DNA samples, or voice samples for forensic comparison does not amount to compelling the accused to 'be a witness against himself'.

3. The constitutional immunity under Article 20(3) applies uniformly to criminal prosecutions, civil suits for damages, and administrative fact-finding inquiries even prior to any formal accusation of an offence.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 20(3) prohibits only 'testimonial compulsion' (compelling an accused to communicate personal knowledge of relevant facts) and does not bar the compulsory collection of physical, biometric, or forensic identification material (Kathi Kalu Oghad and Ritesh Sinha cases). Furthermore, this guarantee is triggered only when a formal accusation of a criminal offence exists, excluding purely civil or administrative inquiries.

exp.why: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that the compulsory or non-consensual administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and BEAP tests intrudes into the subject's mental privacy and amounts to testimonial compulsion prohibited by Article 20(3), as well as a violation of substantive due process under Article 21.

In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961, 11-Judge Bench) and Ritesh Sinha v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019), the Supreme Court established that 'to be a witness' means imparting personal knowledge orally or in writing. Giving physical specimens like thumb impressions, handwriting/signature exemplars, blood/DNA, or voice samples merely furnishes static physical material for comparison and does not constitute self-incriminating testimony (a principle also codified in Section 349 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023).

Article 20(3) specifically states that 'No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.' The Supreme Court has consistently held that for Article 20(3) to apply, there must be a formal accusation relating to the commission of a criminal offence (such as an FIR or a formal complaint that may result in prosecution). It does not extend to civil proceedings or general administrative/departmental inquiries where the person does not stand formally accused of an offence.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 20(3); State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961); Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010); Ritesh Sinha v. State of UP (2019)

stem: Consider the following doctrinal milestones in the Supreme Court's constitutional interpretation of 'personal liberty' and Fundamental Rights under Part III of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Articulation of the 'Golden Triangle' linking Articles 14, 19, and 21, mandating that any procedure depriving personal liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India)

2. Interpretation of Fundamental Rights as mutually exclusive, isolated compartments where the validity of a preventive detention law under Article 21 could not be tested against the freedoms of Article 19 (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras)

3. Institutionalization of the structured four-pronged proportionality test to evaluate the validity of state intrusions into the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21 (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India)

4. Rejection of the 'mutual exclusivity' theory by holding that the constitutional validity of a state action must be judged by its direct effect on Fundamental Rights rather than its form or object (R.C. Cooper v. Union of India)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the doctrinal milestones given above, from the earliest to the latest?
core: The jurisprudence of Article 21 evolved from the formalistic 'isolated silos' doctrine in A.K. Gopalan (1950), through the dismantling of mutual exclusivity in the Bank Nationalisation / R.C. Cooper case (1970) and the substantive 'Golden Triangle' synthesis in Maneka Gandhi (1978), culminating in the structured proportionality standard in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

exp.why: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India was decided in 1978 (third in the sequence). The 7-Judge Bench established that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive and that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be right, just, and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive.

A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras was decided in 1950 (earliest in the sequence). The Court adopted a narrow positivist reading of Article 21 and treated each Fundamental Right as a distinct, self-contained code ('silo theory').

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India was decided in 2017 (latest in the sequence). The 9-Judge Bench reaffirmed the Golden Triangle and laid down the four-fold proportionality standard (legality, legitimate goal, rational nexus/necessity, and balancing safeguards) for testing limitations on privacy and personal liberty.

R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (the Bank Nationalisation case) was decided in 1970 (second in the sequence). An 11-Judge Bench overturned the Gopalan 'isolated silos' theory and substituted the 'object and form test' with the 'direct and inevitable effect test'.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 21; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Fundamental Rights)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the expression 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under the initial constitutional interpretation in the A.K. Gopalan case (1950), Article 21 protected personal liberty only against arbitrary executive action and offered no protection against an unreasonable or oppressive law enacted by a competent legislature.

Statement-II: Even after the Maneka Gandhi judgment (1978), the Indian Judiciary remains barred from examining the substantive fairness or non-arbitrariness of a duly enacted parliamentary statute depriving personal liberty, confining judicial review strictly to verifying whether the executive followed the statutory steps.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In A.K. Gopalan (1950), 'procedure established by law' was interpreted literally along the British concept of legislative supremacy, shielding only against ultra vires executive acts. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Supreme Court infused substantive due process into Article 21 via Article 14, empowering courts to strike down the legislative enactment itself if its procedure or substance is arbitrary, unfair, or unreasonable.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court distinguished the Indian phrase 'procedure established by law' from the American phrase 'due process of law', holding that as long as a law was enacted by a competent legislature, courts could not question its reasonableness or fairness; thus, Article 21 operated solely as a check against executive action lacking statutory backing.

Statement-II is incorrect. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court overruled the narrow Gopalan doctrine and held that 'law' in Article 21 does not mean merely an enacted piece of legislation, but must be a valid law that satisfies the test of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and reasonableness under Article 19. Consequently, Indian courts actively scrutinize both the procedural and substantive fairness of legislative enactments.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 21; A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950); Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

stem: With reference to the nine-Judge Bench judgment of the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) on the Right to Privacy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Court held that the fundamental right to privacy is strictly a spatial right attached to private residential premises and stands extinguished the moment an individual enters a public space or shares personal metadata on digital platforms.

2. Under the proportionality standard laid down in the judgment, once the State demonstrates the existence of a validly enacted statute pursuing a legitimate state aim, the judiciary cannot inquire into whether a less restrictive alternative measure was available.

3. To cure the absence of the word 'privacy' in the original constitutional text, the nine-Judge Bench issued a binding writ directing the insertion of a standalone Article 21B into Part III of the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), the 9-Judge Bench held that privacy is an intrinsic facet of Article 21 and Part III that 'attaches to the person, not the place', encompassing bodily integrity, informational self-determination, and decisional autonomy. Any state restriction on privacy must satisfy the rigorous four-pronged proportionality test, which explicitly includes the 'necessity' (least restrictive alternative) requirement.

exp.why: The Supreme Court explicitly rejected the narrow spatial conception of privacy, holding that 'privacy attaches to the person, not the place.' Even in public spaces or digital environments, individuals retain a reasonable expectation of privacy, including informational self-determination, bodily integrity, and decisional autonomy.

Under the structured proportionality test articulated in the Puttaswamy ruling (and applied in the Aadhaar judgment), a state measure infringing privacy must satisfy four cumulative prongs: (i) legality (existence of a law), (ii) legitimate state aim, (iii) rational nexus and necessity (demonstrating that the measure is the least restrictive alternative to achieve the objective), and (iv) balancing (procedural safeguards against abuse).

Under the Indian constitutional scheme, the judiciary cannot amend the text of the Constitution or direct the insertion of a new Article (which is the exclusive constituent power of Parliament under Article 368). Instead, the 9-Judge Bench declared that the right to privacy is an inalienable natural right intrinsic to the guarantee of life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the freedoms across Part III.

ref: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1; Constitution of India, Art. 21

stem: With reference to the landmark judgment of the Supreme Court in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Court ruled that any parliamentary statute enacted to give effect to Article 48A for climate change mitigation must be certified and passed exclusively as a Money Bill under Article 110.
2. The Court explicitly recognized the right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as a distinct fundamental right derived jointly from Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.

3. The Court observed that because climate vagaries disproportionately impair the health, livelihood, and food and water security of vulnerable communities unable to adapt, inaction on climate change implicates the right to equality under Article 14.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024, Great Indian Bustard case), the Supreme Court expanded environmental constitutionalism beyond the traditional 'right to a clean environment' by recognizing a distinct 'right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change' anchored simultaneously in Article 21 (life and health) and Article 14 (substantive equality for climate-vulnerable populations).

exp.why: The Supreme Court never held that environmental or climate mitigation statutes under Article 48A must be introduced as Money Bills under Article 110. A Money Bill is strictly confined to the fiscal matters enumerated in clauses (a) to (g) of Article 110(1). Instead, the Court read Articles 48A and 51A(g) as interpretive aids to expand the ambit of Articles 14 and 21.

While resolving the conflict between the conservation of the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard and the installation of overhead power transmission lines for renewable solar and wind energy, the three-Judge Bench explicitly recognized the 'right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change' as a distinct facet of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14 and 21.

The Court explained the nexus with Article 14 by highlighting that the adverse impacts of climate change—such as extreme heatwaves, water scarcity, crop failure, and displacement—fall disproportionately on underserved, tribal, and indigent communities who lack the resources to adapt, thereby violating their right to substantive equality.

ref: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors. (2024 INSC 280); Constitution of India, Arts. 14, 21, 48A & 51A(g)

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately reflects the constitutional and legal position in India regarding the 'Right to Die with Dignity' and euthanasia as laid down by the Supreme Court under Article 21?

opts.A: Article 21 encompasses the fundamental right to die with dignity through passive euthanasia by withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, and an Advance Medical Directive (Living Will) can be validly attested before a notary or a gazetted officer without requiring countersignature by a Judicial Magistrate.
opts.B: Both active euthanasia through the administration of a painless lethal substance and passive euthanasia through withdrawal of artificial life support are constitutionally valid for terminally ill patients, subject to approval by a High Court division bench.
opts.C: While passive euthanasia is permitted for patients in a permanent vegetative state upon the consent of immediate relatives, Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills) executed by healthy individuals in advance have no legal validity in India.
opts.D: Following the Gian Kaur and Common Cause judgments, the right to life under Article 21 includes both a general fundamental right to commit suicide and the right to passive euthanasia.

core: In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018, 5-Judge Bench), the Supreme Court held that the right to live with dignity under Article 21 includes the smoothing of the dying process (passive euthanasia) for terminally ill or PVS patients and legalized Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills), while maintaining that active euthanasia remains illegal. In January 2023, the Constitution Bench simplified the Living Will guidelines by replacing the cumbersome requirement of a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) countersignature with attestation before a notary or gazetted officer.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because the Constitution Bench in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) recognized passive euthanasia (withholding or withdrawing medical treatment/life support to allow natural death) and Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills) as intrinsic to the right to die with dignity under Article 21. Further, in its 2023 modification order, the 5-Judge Bench eliminated the impracticable requirement of having the Living Will countersigned by a Judicial Magistrate of First Class (JMFC), allowing attestation before a notary or a gazetted officer instead, alongside a streamlined two-tier medical board review in the hospital. Option (B) is incorrect because active euthanasia (positive act of administering a lethal drug to cause death) remains a criminal offence in India. Option (C) is incorrect because Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills) are legally valid and enforceable. Option (D) is incorrect because in Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996), the 5-Judge Bench explicitly held that Article 21 does not include a 'right to die' by suicide (unnatural termination of life), distinguishing it from the right to a dignified natural process of dying in terminal illness.

ref: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India (2018 & 2023 Modification); Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996); Constitution of India, Art. 21

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the right to education and early childhood care introduced by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 21A mandates that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

2. Following the 86th Constitutional Amendment, Article 45 directs the State to endeavour to provide early childhood care and free education for all children until they complete the age of fourteen years.
3. Article 51A(k) casts a Fundamental Duty upon a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 bifurcated the constitutional treatment of children's education by elevating elementary education (ages 6 to 14) to a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and a corresponding Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k). Simultaneously, it substituted Article 45 in the Directive Principles to focus specifically on early childhood care and education for children below the age of six years.

exp.why: Article 21A, inserted into Part III by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, explicitly states that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine. Parliament gave statutory effect to this mandate by enacting the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.

While the original (pre-2002) text of Article 45 referred to free and compulsory education until children complete the age of fourteen years, the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 substituted Article 45 entirely. The amended Article 45 directs the State to endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children 'until they complete the age of six years', not fourteen years.

The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added clause (k) to Article 51A in Part IVA, making it a Fundamental Duty of every citizen who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 21A, 45, and 51A(k); 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the interplay between Article 21A and Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: The provisions of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, including the statutory mandate to admit at least 25% children belonging to weaker sections and disadvantaged groups in entry-level classes, are inapplicable to both aided and unaided minority educational institutions.

Statement-II: The Supreme Court has held that compelling minority educational institutions under Article 21A to admit children belonging to other communities would alter and abrogate their special minority character protected under Article 30(1) of the Constitution.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that the RTE Act, 2009 is ultra vires the Constitution insofar as it applies to minority schools (whether aided or unaided) established under Article 30(1). The Court reasoned that Article 21A is a beneficial power that cannot be used to abrogate the basic structure protection of minority identity guaranteed under Article 30(1).

exp.why: While a 3-Judge Bench in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) had exempted only unaided minority schools from the RTE Act, 2009, a 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) went further and ruled that the entire RTE Act, 2009—including Section 12(1)(c) mandating 25% reservation for disadvantaged children—is inapplicable to both aided and unaided minority schools covered under Article 30(1).

Statement-II accurately states the constitutional reasoning behind Statement-I. In the Pramati judgment, the Constitution Bench explained that if minority schools (aided or unaided) are made to admit a fixed percentage of students not belonging to the minority community that established the institution, the minority character of such institutions can be destroyed, thereby violating their fundamental right under Article 30(1).

ref: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) 8 SCC 1; Constitution of India, Articles 21A and 30(1)

stem: With reference to the constitutional safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention under Article 22 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every person who is arrested and detained in custody under ordinary law must be produced before the nearest magistrate within twenty-four hours of such arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate.

2. Under Article 22(3), the procedural safeguards guaranteed by clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22—including the right to be defended by a legal practitioner of choice and production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours—do not apply to enemy aliens or to persons arrested or detained under any preventive detention law.

3. As interpreted by the Supreme Court, the procedural safeguards under Articles 22(1) and 22(2) apply strictly to arrests under criminal or quasi-criminal accusations and do not extend to arrests made under civil process or for the recovery of arrears of income tax.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 22(1) and 22(2) confer three core procedural safeguards against arbitrary punitive arrest: prompt communication of grounds, right to legal counsel of choice, and magisterial production within 24 hours (excluding transit time). However, Article 22(3) expressly excludes enemy aliens and preventive detenus from the purview of clauses (1) and (2), while judicial precedent confines their scope to criminal or quasi-criminal arrests.

exp.why: Under Article 22(2), every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate, and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.

Article 22(3) explicitly carves out two constitutional exceptions to clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22: nothing in those clauses shall apply (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention (whose separate procedural safeguards are governed instead by clauses (4) to (7) of Article 22).

In State of Punjab v. Ajaib Singh (1953), Purshottam Govindji Halai v. B.M. Desai (1955), and Collector of Malabar v. Erimmal Ebrahim Hajee (1957), the Supreme Court held that the language of Articles 22(1) and 22(2) relates exclusively to arrests made on allegations of a criminal or quasi-criminal nature or acts prejudicial to the public interest, and does not apply to arrests under civil process, failure to pay income tax arrears, or deportation orders.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 22(1), 22(2), and 22(3); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: In the context of recent Supreme Court jurisprudence on personal liberty and procedural safeguards under Article 22 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Supreme Court has drawn a clear constitutional distinction between 'reasons for arrest', which are general and formal parameters applicable to any arrestee, and 'grounds of arrest', which are personal and specific to the individual arrested.

2. To give meaningful effect to the fundamental rights under Articles 22(1) and 22(5), any person arrested under stringent special statutes such as the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act or the Prevention of Money Laundering Act must be furnished with the grounds of arrest in writing.

3. While written communication of the grounds of arrest is mandatory in preventive detention under Article 22(5), the Supreme Court has held that oral communication of the grounds of arrest at the time of remand satisfies the mandate of Article 22(1) in punitive arrests.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India (2023) and Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024), the Supreme Court harmonized Articles 22(1) and 22(5), holding that the right to be informed of the 'grounds of arrest' is not satisfied by reciting generic 'reasons for arrest' or through mere oral narration. Furnishing written grounds of arrest specific to the accused is a mandatory constitutional safeguard to enable effective legal representation and opposition to remand.

exp.why: In Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024), the Supreme Court delineated a fundamental difference between 'reasons for arrest' and 'grounds of arrest'. 'Reasons for arrest' (such as preventing further offences, ensuring proper investigation, or preventing tampering with evidence) are formal, general parameters contained in remand applications, whereas 'grounds of arrest' are personal facts in the exclusive knowledge of the investigating officer that specifically implicate the arrested individual.

In Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India (2023, regarding PMLA) and Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024, regarding UAPA), the Supreme Court held that because both Article 22(1) and Article 22(5) use identical constitutional language regarding informing the arrestee of the grounds of arrest 'as soon as may be', the grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing as a matter of course and without exception.

The Supreme Court explicitly rejected the contention that oral communication of the grounds of arrest satisfies Article 22(1). In Pankaj Bansal (2023) and Prabir Purkayastha (2024), the Court ruled that mere oral narration leaves the arrestee in a helpless position and boils down to the word of the arrested person against the investigating officer; therefore, communicating the grounds of arrest in writing is mandatory under Article 22(1) just as it is under Article 22(5).

ref: Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024 SC); Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India (2023 SC); Constitution of India, Articles 22(1) and 22(5)
