stem: With reference to the currently operative constitutional safeguards governing preventive detention under Articles 22(4) to 22(6) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the currently operative text of Article 22(4), no law providing for preventive detention can authorize the detention of a person for a period longer than two months unless an Advisory Board reports before the expiration of that period that there is sufficient cause for such detention.

2. Under the currently enforced provisions of Article 22(4), an Advisory Board must be constituted strictly in accordance with the recommendations of the Chief Justice of the appropriate High Court and cannot include persons who are merely qualified to be appointed as High Court judges.

3. Under Article 22(6), the detaining authority is constitutionally obligated to disclose all material facts to the detenu even if the authority considers such disclosure to be against the public interest, provided those facts are first submitted in a sealed cover to the Advisory Board.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although Section 3 of the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 sought to tighten Article 22(4) by reducing the initial preventive detention threshold from three months to two months and restructuring the Advisory Board, Section 3 has never been notified into force by the Central Government. Consequently, the original three-month limit and original Advisory Board composition remain the operative constitutional law, alongside the public-interest non-disclosure exception under Article 22(6).

exp.why: While Section 3 of the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 proposed reducing the maximum period of preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board from three months to two months, Section 3 has never been brought into force by Central Government notification (as upheld by the Constitution Bench in A.K. Roy v. Union of India, 1982). Therefore, the currently operative text of Article 22(4) continues to prescribe three months, not two months.

The requirement that an Advisory Board be constituted in accordance with the recommendations of the Chief Justice of the appropriate High Court and comprise only serving or retired High Court judges was also part of the un-notified Section 3 of the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978. Under the currently operative text of Article 22(4)(a), an Advisory Board consists of persons who 'are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court'.

Article 22(6) explicitly provides the exact opposite: nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any preventive detention order to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose. There is no constitutional obligation to disclose such privileged facts to the detenu.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 22(4), 22(5), and 22(6); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 (Section 3); A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982)

stem: With reference to the distribution of legislative powers regarding preventive detention under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Seventh Schedule, Parliament has exclusive competence to enact preventive detention laws for reasons connected with defence, foreign affairs, or the security of India, whereas both Parliament and State Legislatures can enact preventive detention laws for reasons connected with the maintenance of public order or essential supplies and services.

2. Where a State Legislature enacts a preventive detention law under the Concurrent List, both Parliament and the State Legislature possess concurrent power under Article 22(7) to prescribe the circumstances under which a person may be detained for more than three months without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board.

3. Under Article 22(7), only Parliament can prescribe by law the maximum period for which any person may in any class of cases be detained under any preventive detention law, including a law enacted by a State Legislature.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While legislative competence to enact preventive detention laws is divided between the Union List (Entry 9: defence, foreign affairs, security of India) and the Concurrent List (Entry 3: security of a State, public order, essential supplies), Article 22(7) vests overriding procedural and substantive control exclusively in Parliament. State Legislatures cannot dispense with the three-month Advisory Board requirement or fix the overarching maximum detention ceiling.

exp.why: Under Entry 9 of List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule, Parliament has exclusive power to make laws for preventive detention for reasons connected with Defence, Foreign Affairs, or the Security of India. Under Entry 3 of List III (Concurrent List), both Parliament and State Legislatures have competence to make laws for preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community.

Under Article 22(7)(a), Parliament alone—and not a State Legislature—is empowered to prescribe by law the circumstances under which, and the class or classes of cases in which, a person may be detained for a period longer than three months under any law providing for preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board. Even for a State preventive detention law, a State Legislature lacks this power.

Under Article 22(7)(b) and 22(7)(c), Parliament alone may by law prescribe the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained under 'any law providing for preventive detention' (which includes both Union and State laws), as well as the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board in an inquiry under Article 22(4)(a).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 22(7) and Seventh Schedule (List I Entry 9 & List III Entry 3); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the distribution of legislative powers regarding Preventive Detention under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs of Grounds for Preventive Detention and the Competent Legislature(s):
items: 1. Preventive detention for reasons connected with the Defence of India : Parliament exclusively
2. Preventive detention for reasons connected with Foreign Affairs : Both Parliament and State Legislatures
3. Preventive detention for reasons connected with the maintenance of public order : State Legislatures exclusively
4. Preventive detention for reasons connected with the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community : Both Parliament and State Legislatures
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Under the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, legislative competence over preventive detention is bifurcated between the Union List (Entry 9 of List I) and the Concurrent List (Entry 3 of List III), with no preventive detention entry in the State List. Consequently, while Parliament has exclusive power over preventive detention regarding defence, foreign affairs, and the security of India, both Parliament and State Legislatures share concurrent competence over preventive detention regarding the security of a State, maintenance of public order, and maintenance of essential supplies and services.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Entry 9 of List I (Union List) in the Seventh Schedule, Parliament has exclusive competence to enact laws providing for preventive detention for reasons connected with Defence, Foreign Affairs, or the Security of India.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Preventive detention for reasons connected with Foreign Affairs falls exclusively under Entry 9 of List I (Union List), meaning only Parliament—and not State Legislatures—is competent to legislate on this ground.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Although 'Public order' simpliciter is a State List subject (Entry 1 of List II), 'Preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community' is specifically placed under Entry 3 of List III (Concurrent List). Therefore, both Parliament and State Legislatures are competent to enact preventive detention laws on the ground of maintenance of public order.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Under Entry 3 of List III (Concurrent List), both Parliament and State Legislatures are competent to enact laws for preventive detention for reasons connected with the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community.

ref: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule (List I Entry 9 & List III Entry 3) and Art. 22; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the prohibition of 'forced labour' under Article 23 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Paying a worker remuneration less than the statutory minimum wage does not constitute 'forced labour' under Article 23(1) of the Constitution if the worker voluntarily entered into the contract of employment without any physical or legal coercion.

Statement-II: The Supreme Court in the People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India case held that economic compulsion arising from poverty and destitution strips away free choice just as much as physical or legal force, thereby bringing remuneration below the statutory minimum wage within the ambit of 'forced labour' under Article 23(1).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) v. Union of India (1982, the Asiad Workers Case), the Supreme Court gave an expansive purposive interpretation to the term 'forced labour' in Article 23(1). The Court held that 'force' is not restricted to physical or legal coercion; where a person is driven by hunger, poverty, or destitution to accept work for less than the statutory minimum wage, the labour he renders is 'forced labour' violative of Article 23(1) notwithstanding the ostensibly voluntary contract.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. The Supreme Court has expressly rejected the narrow argument that voluntary entry into an employment contract without physical or legal coercion immunizes an employer from Article 23(1) when paying less than the statutory minimum wage. Whenever a person provides labour or service for remuneration less than the minimum wage, it presumptively constitutes 'forced labour' violating Article 23(1).

Statement-II is correct. In People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court explained that in a society marked by widespread poverty and unemployment, economic compulsion arising from hunger and destitution leaves a worker with no real choice, making labour extracted below the statutory minimum wage a form of 'forced labour' prohibited by Article 23(1).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 23(1); PUDR v. Union of India (AIR 1982 SC 1473); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: With reference to the constitutional exception permitting 'compulsory service for public purposes' under Article 23(2) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 23(2), the State is empowered to impose compulsory service for public purposes, such as military conscription or social service, and is not constitutionally bound to pay remuneration for such service.

2. In imposing compulsory service for public purposes under Article 23(2), the State is expressly prohibited by the text of the Article from making any discrimination on the grounds of religion, race, caste, class, sex, or place of birth.

3. While the prohibition against forced labour under Article 23(1) operates against both the State and private individuals, the authority to impose compulsory service for public purposes under Article 23(2) is vested exclusively in the State.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 23(2) carves out a sovereign exception to the prohibition against forced labour by empowering the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes (whether remunerated or unpaid). Notably, the non-discrimination clause in Article 23(2) specifies only four prohibited grounds—'religion, race, caste or class'—deliberately omitting 'sex' so that the State may, for example, exempt women from compulsory military conscription.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 23(2) declares that nothing in Article 23 shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes (such as national defence/military conscription or essential social service). Because it is an exception to 'begar' and 'forced labour' in Article 23(1), the State is not constitutionally obligated to pay remuneration for such compulsory public service.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The text of Article 23(2) states: 'and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.' Unlike Article 15 or Article 16, Article 23(2) deliberately omits 'sex' and 'place of birth' (permitting the State, for instance, to differentiate on the basis of sex in military conscription).

Statement 3 is correct. While Article 23(1) has horizontal and vertical application (protecting individuals against both private actors and the State), the exception in Article 23(2) allowing compulsory service for public purposes is conferred exclusively on 'the State' and can never be invoked by private entities.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 23(1) & 23(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory framework governing the prohibition of child and adolescent labour in India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The text of Article 24 of the Constitution itself imposes a complete blanket prohibition on the employment of children below the age of fourteen years in both hazardous and non-hazardous occupations.
opts.B: The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (as amended in 2016) completely prohibits adolescents between fourteen and eighteen years of age from working in any establishment, whether hazardous or non-hazardous.
opts.C: Article 24 of the Constitution explicitly carves out a textual proviso permitting children below fourteen years of age to work in non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours.
opts.D: While Article 24 of the Constitution prohibits the employment of children below fourteen years of age in factories, mines, or other hazardous employment, the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (as amended in 2016) expands this prohibition to all occupations and processes, subject only to limited statutory exceptions such as helping in non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours.

core: Article 24 of the Constitution sets a constitutional floor by prohibiting the employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous employment. Parliament went beyond this constitutional minimum through the 2016 Amendment to the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, which banned the employment of children below 14 years across all occupations and processes (with narrow exceptions for non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours and child artists) and prohibited the employment of adolescents (14–18 years) in hazardous occupations.

exp.why: Option D is correct. Article 24 of the Constitution states: 'No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.' It does not by its own constitutional text prohibit non-hazardous work (making Option A incorrect) nor does it contain any textual proviso regarding family enterprises (making Option C incorrect). Instead, the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 expanded the statutory ban to prohibit the employment of children below 14 years in ALL occupations and processes (except helping his/her family in non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours or working as an artist in the audio-visual/sports sector), while prohibiting adolescents (aged 14 to 18 years) only from hazardous occupations and processes and regulating their conditions of service in non-hazardous work (making Option B incorrect).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 24; Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (as amended in 2016)

stem: With reference to the suspension of Fundamental Rights and their enforcement during the operation of a Proclamation of National Emergency under Articles 358 and 359 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 358, the six freedoms guaranteed by Article 19 are automatically suspended across the entire country only when a Proclamation of Emergency is declared on the grounds of war or external aggression, whereas a Presidential Order under Article 359 may extend to the whole or any part of the territory of India.

2. Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, a Presidential Order under Article 359 cannot suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Articles 20 and 21 even during a wartime Emergency.

3. During the operation of a Proclamation of Emergency, the immunity from challenge under Articles 358 and 359 extends to all legislative enactments passed by the State, even if such laws do not contain an explicit recital that they are in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 introduced three vital safeguards against the abuse of Emergency powers: first, Article 19 cannot be suspended under Article 358 during an Emergency declared on the ground of 'armed rebellion'; second, the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359; and third, only laws containing an explicit recital linking them to the Emergency (and executive actions taken under such laws) enjoy immunity from challenge under Articles 358 and 359.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 358(1), the automatic suspension of Article 19 occurs only when a Proclamation of Emergency is based on 'war' or 'external aggression' (not 'armed rebellion') and applies to the entire country. By contrast, a Presidential Order under Article 359(1) suspending the enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights may extend to the whole or any part of the territory of India.

Statement 2 is correct. By inserting the parenthetical exception '(except Articles 20 and 21)' in Article 359(1), the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 ensured that the right to move any court for the enforcement of the protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20) and the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) can never be suspended under any circumstances, reversing the ratio of ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 358(2) and Article 359(1B)—both inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978—immunity from challenge during an Emergency does NOT extend to any law which does not contain an explicit recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made, nor to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such a recital.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 19, 20, 21, 358 & 359; 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 & 17

stem: Consider the following pairs matching specific Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Constitution with their structural and constitutional attributes:
items: 1. Article 19 : Available exclusively to citizens of India and can be restricted only by a law enacted on the exhaustive grounds enumerated in clauses (2) to (6) of that Article
2. Article 20 : Available to all persons, but requires enabling penal legislation by Parliament under Article 35 to become operational
3. Article 22(1) and (2) : Available exclusively to citizens of India and inapplicable to persons detained under preventive detention laws

4. Article 23(1) : Available to both citizens and non-citizens, enforceable against both the State and private individuals, and its contravention is punishable under laws made exclusively by Parliament pursuant to Article 35(a)(ii)
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 19 to 24 vary significantly across three structural axes: who can claim the right (citizens only under Article 19 versus all persons under Articles 20–24), how the right can be restricted (exhaustive constitutional grounds in Articles 19(2)–(6)), and whether the right is a self-executory limitation on punitive power (Articles 20, 21, 22) or expressly declares its contravention to be an offence requiring parliamentary penal legislation under Article 35(a)(ii) (Article 23(1)).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The six freedoms under Article 19 are expressly conferred exclusively on 'citizens' ('All citizens shall have the right...') and cannot be claimed by foreigners. Furthermore, as reaffirmed by the 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023), the grounds for reasonable restrictions enumerated in clauses (2) to (6) of Article 19 are exhaustive and can only be imposed by a duly enacted 'law'.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. While Article 20 is indeed available to all persons (citizens, foreigners, and even legal persons like corporations where applicable), it is a direct, self-executory constitutional prohibition on State punitive power. It does NOT require any enabling legislation by Parliament under Article 35 to take effect.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Although Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons detained under preventive detention laws from the safeguards of Article 22(1) and (2), the rights under Article 22(1) and (2) are conferred on 'no person'—meaning they are available to both citizens and non-enemy foreigners, not exclusively to citizens of India.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Article 23(1) protects both citizens and non-citizens against both the State and private individuals. Furthermore, Article 23(1) expressly declares that 'any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law', and Article 35(a)(ii) vests exclusive power in Parliament (to the exclusion of State Legislatures) to make laws prescribing punishment for acts declared to be offences under Part III (namely Article 17 and Article 23(1)).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 19–24 & Art. 35(a)(ii); Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP (2023); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional relationship between individual religious freedom and denominational autonomy:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the individual freedom of religion under Article 25(1), the collective right of a religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion under Article 26 is explicitly subordinated by its opening text to all other Fundamental Rights in Part III.

Statement-II: In the event of a conflict between a religious denomination's right to manage its internal religious affairs under Article 26(b) and a State law enacted under Article 25(2)(b) throwing open public Hindu temples to all classes and sections of Hindus, the constitutional mandate of social reform and temple entry prevails.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 25(1) explicitly subjects individual religious freedom not only to public order, morality, and health, but also to 'the other provisions of this Part' (Part III), whereas the opening text of Article 26 subjects denominational rights only to public order, morality, and health. Nevertheless, through the doctrine of harmonious construction, the Supreme Court has held that Article 26(b) must yield to social welfare and temple-entry legislation enacted under Article 25(2)(b).

exp.why: Statement-I reverses the exact constitutional text of Articles 25(1) and 26. It is Article 25(1) that begins with the words 'Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part...', directly subordinating individual religious practice to egalitarian Fundamental Rights such as Articles 14, 15, and 17. Conversely, the opening clause of Article 26 states only 'Subject to public order, morality and health...', omitting the phrase 'and to the other provisions of this Part'.

Statement-II is correct. In Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. State of Mysore (1958), the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of harmonious construction to resolve the tension between Article 26(b) and Article 25(2)(b). The Court held that if a denominational right under Article 26(b) were allowed to completely exclude sections of Hindus from a public temple, Article 25(2)(b) would be rendered redundant; hence, Article 26(b) must be read subject to the State's social reform and temple-entry power under Article 25(2)(b).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 25 & 26; Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. State of Mysore (1958); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the freedom of religion under Article 25 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 25(2)(a), the State is empowered to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice.

2. Under Explanation II to Article 25, the reference to 'Hindus' for the purpose of throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character includes persons professing the Sikh, Jaina, Buddhist, and Zoroastrian (Parsi) religions.
3. Explanation I to Article 25 explicitly recognizes the wearing and carrying of kirpans as being included in the profession of the Sikh religion.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 25 separates the core spiritual doctrine of a religion from its associated secular activities and subjects the latter to State regulation under Article 25(2)(a). Its two constitutional Explanations explicitly protect the wearing and carrying of kirpans by Sikhs and define 'Hindus' for social reform/temple-entry purposes under sub-clause (2)(b) to include Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists—but not Parsis, Christians, Jews, or Muslims.

exp.why: Article 25(2)(a) expressly saves existing laws and empowers the State to make new laws regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political, or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice.

Explanation II to Article 25 states that in sub-clause (b) of clause (2), the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina, or Buddhist religion, and the reference to Hindu religious institutions shall be construed accordingly. It does not include persons professing the Zoroastrian (Parsi) religion.
Explanation I to Article 25 explicitly provides that the wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 25 (Clauses 1, 2 & Explanations I and II); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the freedom of religious denominations under Article 26 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To qualify as a 'religious denomination' under Article 26, a collective must satisfy three judicial conditions: a collection of individuals having a system of beliefs conducive to their spiritual well-being, a common organization, and designation by a distinctive name.

2. Under the text of Article 26, both the right of a religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion under clause (b) and its right to administer its property under clause (d) are exercisable only 'in accordance with law' enacted by the State.

3. While the State can regulate the secular administration of property belonging to a religious denomination under Article 26(d), a law that completely divests the denomination of its right of administration and vests it in a secular authority is unconstitutional.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 26 draws a sharp constitutional distinction between matters of religion under clause (b) and the administration of property under clause (d). Only clause (d) contains the qualifying words 'in accordance with law', permitting statutory regulation of property administration, provided such regulation does not altogether extinguish or confiscate the denomination's right to administer its institutions.

exp.why: In the Shirur Mutt case (1954) and S.P. Mittal v. Union of India (1983), the Supreme Court laid down the three-fold test for a 'religious denomination' under Article 26: (i) a collection of individuals who have a system of beliefs or doctrines which they regard as conducive to their spiritual well-being, (ii) a common organization, and (iii) designation by a distinctive name.

There is a vital textual distinction between clauses (b) and (d) of Article 26. Clause (b) grants the right 'to manage its own affairs in matters of religion' without the qualification 'in accordance with law'. In contrast, clause (d) grants the right 'to administer such property in accordance with law'. Hence, while property administration can be regulated by ordinary legislative enactments, matters of religion under clause (b) cannot be abridged by ordinary law except on grounds of public order, morality, health, or social reform under Article 25(2)(b).

As held in Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay (1954) and the Shirur Mutt case (1954), 'regulation' of property administration under Article 26(d) means that the law must leave the right of administration in the religious denomination itself, subject to regulatory safeguards. A law that takes away the right of administration altogether from the religious denomination and vests it in any other secular authority violates Article 26(d).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 26; Commissioner, HRE v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt (1954); S.P. Mittal v. Union of India (1983)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion under Article 27 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Article 27 prohibits both the levy of a regulatory fee on religious endowments and the utilization of general tax proceeds by the State for the reconstruction of places of worship damaged during communal disturbances.

Statement-II: The constitutional prohibition under Article 27 is directed specifically against the compulsory exaction of money without a quid pro quo whose proceeds are specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion or religious denomination.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 27 bars only the compulsion to pay 'taxes' whose proceeds are specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of any 'particular' religion. It neither prohibits the levy of a regulatory 'fee' backed by a secular quid pro quo nor bars the non-discriminatory expenditure of general tax revenues to repair shrines across multiple faiths damaged in riots or disasters.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect on both counts. First, Article 27 prohibits the levy of a 'tax', not a 'fee'. The State can validly levy a fee on religious endowments or pilgrims to defray the expenses of secular regulation, auditing, or safety services (Shirur Mutt case). Second, as held by the Supreme Court (K. Raghunath v. State of Kerala; Prafull Goradia v. Union of India), utilizing general tax funds to restore places of worship belonging to different communities damaged during communal riots does not promote any 'particular' religion and is therefore valid.

Statement-II accurately states the constitutional scope of Article 27. A 'tax' is a compulsory exaction of money by a public authority for public purposes without reference to any specific service rendered (quid pro quo). Article 27 specifically forbids compelling any person to pay taxes where the proceeds are earmarked for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 27; Shirur Mutt (1954); Prafull Goradia v. Union of India (2011); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in educational institutions under Article 28 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In an educational institution that is administered by the State but was established under an endowment or trust requiring religious instruction to be imparted, Article 28 imposes a complete prohibition on imparting any religious instruction.

2. In an educational institution recognized by the State or receiving aid out of State funds, no student can be compelled to take part in religious instruction or attend religious worship without their consent, or the consent of their guardian if the student is a minor.

3. As interpreted by the Supreme Court, the prohibition on 'religious instruction' in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds under Article 28(1) does not prohibit the comparative academic study of religions or value-based moral education.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 28 classifies educational institutions into distinct categories: while religious instruction is completely banned in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds under Article 28(1), Article 28(2) explicitly exempts institutions administered by the State that were established under an endowment or trust requiring religious instruction to be imparted.

exp.why: This statement inverts Article 28(1) and Article 28(2). While Article 28(1) completely prohibits religious instruction in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds, Article 28(2) creates an explicit exception: nothing in clause (1) applies to an educational institution administered by the State but established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution.

Under Article 28(3), no person attending any educational institution recognized by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction or attend any religious worship conducted in such institution or its premises unless such person or, if such person is a minor, their guardian has given consent.

In Ms. Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002), the Supreme Court distinguished between dogma-based 'religious instruction' (aimed at catechism or indoctrinating students into the tenets and rituals of a specific faith) and academic 'study of religions'. The Court held that Article 28(1) does not prohibit comparative academic study of religions, cultural heritage, or universal moral values.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 28; Ms. Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the Cultural and Educational Rights guaranteed under Article 29 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 29(2) prohibits the denial of admission to any citizen into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, language, or place of birth.

2. Despite the marginal heading of Article 29 referring to the protection of interests of minorities, the substantive right under Article 29(1) extends to 'any section of the citizens' residing in India having a distinct language, script, or culture, including the majority community.
3. The right to conserve a distinct language under Article 29(1) includes the right of citizens to agitate politically for the protection of that language.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike Article 30, which is confined strictly to religious and linguistic minorities, Article 29 protects 'any section of the citizens' under clause (1) and 'any citizen' under clause (2). However, Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission into State-maintained or State-aided educational institutions only on four specified grounds—religion, race, caste, or language—omitting 'sex' and 'place of birth'.

exp.why: Article 29(2) specifies only four prohibited grounds for denial of admission into educational institutions maintained or aided by the State: 'religion, race, caste, language or any of them'. Unlike Article 15(1), Article 29(2) deliberately omits the grounds of 'sex' and 'place of birth'.

Although the marginal note to Article 29 reads 'Protection of interests of minorities', the operative text of Article 29(1) explicitly vests the right in 'Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own'. The Supreme Court has confirmed that this includes both minority and majority sections of citizens.

In Jagdev Singh Sidhanti v. Pratap Singh Daulta (1964), the Supreme Court held that the right to conserve a language under Article 29(1) is an absolute constitutional right (not subject to reasonable restrictions like Article 19) and includes the right of citizens to agitate politically for the protection and conservation of their language.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 29; Jagdev Singh Sidhanti v. Pratap Singh Daulta (1964); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions under Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India, as interpreted by the seven-Judge Constitution Bench in Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. An educational institution incorporated by or under a parliamentary or state statute is constitutionally barred from claiming minority status under Article 30(1), as statutory incorporation extinguishes its minority character.

2. The words 'establish and administer' in Article 30(1) must be read conjunctively, meaning a religious or linguistic minority can claim the right to administer an educational institution only if it was also established by that minority.

3. Educational institutions established by a religious or linguistic minority prior to the commencement of the Constitution are entitled to the protection of Article 30(1) on par with those established after 1950.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench overruled S. Azeez Basha (1967), holding that an educational institution is not stripped of minority status under Article 30(1) merely because its legal existence or university status was conferred by a statute. Courts must pierce the statutory veil to examine the holistic indicia of establishment—namely, the genesis or brainchild of the institution, its purpose, and the steps taken to bring it into existence—even for pre-Constitution institutions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (November 2024), a seven-Judge Constitution Bench overruled the 1967 ruling in S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India. The Supreme Court held that a statute may merely recognize or incorporate an educational institution to enable its degrees to be legally valid; therefore, an institution is not barred from claiming minority status under Article 30(1) merely because it was established or incorporated by or under a statute.

Statement 2 is correct. Both in Azeez Basha and reaffirmed in AMU v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), the Supreme Court held that the words 'establish and administer' in Article 30(1) must be read conjunctively. A minority community cannot claim the constitutional right to administer an institution unless it is shown to have established it—determined by examining who conceived the idea (the 'brainchild'), whether it was founded predominantly for the minority community, and who mobilized the initial funds, land, and infrastructure.

Statement 3 is correct. Reaffirming In re Kerala Education Bill (1958), the seven-Judge Bench in AMU v. Naresh Agarwal (2024) held that Article 30(1) does not draw an artificial distinction between educational institutions established before January 26, 1950, and those established afterward; pre-Constitution minority institutions are equally entitled to the protection of Article 30(1).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 30(1); Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (7-Judge Bench, 2024); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the constitutional safeguards for minority educational institutions under Article 30 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. For the purpose of Article 30(1), both linguistic and religious minorities are determined by taking the respective State—and not the whole of India—as the unit of demographic assessment.

2. Under Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, the State must ensure that the amount fixed by law for the compulsory acquisition of any property of a minority educational institution does not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under Article 30(1).

3. In granting aid to educational institutions, the State is prohibited under Article 30(2) from discriminating against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a religious or linguistic minority.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 30 protects the educational rights of religious and linguistic minorities, whose numerical minority status is assessed with reference to the State where the institution is situated (T.M.A. Pai Foundation, 2002). Furthermore, when the 44th Amendment deleted the general right to property under Article 31, it specifically inserted Article 30(1A) to protect minority educational institutions against confiscatory property acquisition.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002), an eleven-Judge Constitution Bench held that since reorganization of States in India has been primarily along linguistic lines, for the purpose of determining who constitutes a minority (whether linguistic or religious) under Article 30(1), the unit of determination must be the State and not the whole of India.

Statement 2 is correct. When the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 omitted Article 31 (Right to Property) from Part III and shifted it to Article 300A, it simultaneously inserted Clause (1A) into Article 30 to ensure that any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of property of a minority educational institution fixes an compensation amount that does not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under Article 30(1).

Statement 3 is correct. Article 30(2) explicitly mandates that the State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 30(1), 30(1A) & 30(2); T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the saving of laws providing for the acquisition of estates under Article 31A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Second Proviso to Article 31A(1), if the State acquires any land within an estate held by a person under personal cultivation and within the statutory ceiling limit, the law must provide for compensation at a rate not less than its market value.

2. Article 31A immunizes the five specified categories of agrarian and corporate regulatory laws from being challenged on the ground of contravening any of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution.

3. A law enacted by a State Legislature falling within the ambit of Article 31A automatically enjoys constitutional immunity upon receiving the assent of the Governor under Article 200, without requiring reservation for the consideration of the President.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Inserted by the 1st Amendment (1951) and expanded by the 4th (1955) and 17th (1964) Amendments, Article 31A shields five specific categories of agrarian and corporate laws from challenge solely under Articles 14 and 19. However, this immunity is subject to two strict constitutional provisos: State laws must receive Presidential assent, and acquisition of personally cultivated land within ceiling limits requires full market-value compensation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Inserted by the 17th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1964, the Second Proviso to Article 31A(1) mandates that where any law makes provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force unless the law provides for payment of compensation at a rate which shall not be less than the market value thereof.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Article 31A does not grant blanket immunity against all Fundamental Rights in Part III; it only saves the five specified categories of laws from being declared void on the ground that they are inconsistent with, or take away or abridge, any of the rights conferred by Article 14 or Article 19.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the First Proviso to Article 31A(1), where a law falling under Article 31A(1) is made by the Legislature of a State, the protective immunity of Article 31A shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 31A; 1st, 4th & 17th Constitutional Amendment Acts; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike Article 31A, which is confined to five specific categories of laws, Article 31B is wider in scope and is capable of curing constitutional defects in any central or state enactment included in the Ninth Schedule with retrospective effect.

Statement-II: In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Supreme Court held that any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, is open to judicial review if it abrogates Fundamental Rights that form part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 31B begins with the phrase 'Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in article 31A', giving it a wider textual reach that is neither confined to agrarian reform nor merely prospective. However, the 9-Judge Bench in I.R. Coelho (2007) curtailed this breadth by subjecting all post-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule entries to the two-step Basic Structure and Golden Triangle (Articles 14, 19, 21) test.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Because Article 31B opens with the non-obstante/saving phrase 'Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in article 31A', its protection is not restricted to the five agrarian/corporate categories listed in Article 31A(1). Furthermore, Article 31B is curative and retrospective in operation: even if a statute was previously declared unconstitutional by a court for violating Part III, its subsequent inclusion in the Ninth Schedule cures the defect from its inception (subject to Basic Structure review).

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-Judge Bench ruled that there cannot be blanket immunity for laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment). Such laws must pass the 'rights test' and 'essence of rights test' under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 read with the Basic Structure doctrine. While Statement-I describes why Article 31B's textual scope is broader than Article 31A, Statement-II sets out the judicial limitation on Article 31B rather than explaining why its scope is wider than Article 31A.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 31B & Ninth Schedule; I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007); Laxmikanth Ch. 8 & 11

stem: With reference to the constitutional status and operational scope of Article 31C of the Constitution of India, as settled by the nine-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Upon the invalidation of Section 4 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act in Minerva Mills (1980), the unamended pre-1976 text of Article 31C stood revived, protecting only laws giving effect to the principles in Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
opts.B: Because the 42nd Constitutional Amendment substituted the words 'the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39' and that substitution was struck down in Minerva Mills, the entire protective safe harbour of Article 31C stands obliterated from the Constitution.
opts.C: Article 31C currently immunizes any legislation enacted to give effect to any of the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV from judicial challenge on the ground of violating Articles 14, 19, and 21.
opts.D: While Article 31C continues to protect laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c), the second limb of Article 31C—which bars courts from questioning whether a law actually gives effect to such policy—remains constitutionally valid and operative.

core: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (November 2024), a 9-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that Article 31C continues to exist in the Constitution in its original pre-1976 form (as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati). When Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment (which had expanded Article 31C to all Directive Principles), the unamended text protecting laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenges under Articles 14 and 19 automatically revived.

exp.why: Option A is correct. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), the nine-Judge Bench resolved a long-standing doctrinal question: whether the invalidation of Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) left Article 31C with a blank space (rendering it inoperative) or revived the pre-1976 text inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971). The Court unanimously held that when a court strikes down a constitutional amendment that substituted words in an existing article, the original unamended text automatically revives—otherwise the judicial invalidation of an unconstitutional amendment would paradoxically destroy the valid unamended provision. Hence, Option B is incorrect. Option C is incorrect because the expansion to all Directive Principles was struck down in Minerva Mills, and Article 31C only shields laws against Articles 14 and 19 (never Article 21). Option D is incorrect because the second limb of Article 31C (barring judicial review of the nexus between the law and the policy) was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) itself as violative of the Basic Structure.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 31C; Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (9-Judge Bench, Nov 2024); Laxmikanth Ch. 8 & 9

stem: With reference to the Right to Constitutional Remedies under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court under Article 32 for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights is both original and exclusive.

2. Under Article 32(3), only Parliament—and not a State Legislature—can by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the writ powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under Article 32(2).

3. Even during the operation of a Proclamation of Emergency, the President cannot under Article 359 suspend the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Articles 20 and 21.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is original (an aggrieved citizen can approach it directly), it is not exclusive because High Courts exercise concurrent original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights under Article 226. Furthermore, Article 32(3) vests the power to confer writ jurisdiction on subordinate courts exclusively in Parliament, and the 44th Amendment insulated the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 from suspension under Article 359.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is 'original' because an aggrieved citizen can directly approach the Supreme Court without having to come by way of appeal. However, it is not 'exclusive', because the High Courts also enjoy concurrent original jurisdiction under Article 226 to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 32(3), without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), only Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2). State Legislatures have no such competence.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 32(4), the right guaranteed by Article 32 shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by the Constitution. Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 359(1) explicitly stipulates that during a National Emergency, the President cannot suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Articles 20 and 21.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 32, 226 & 359; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the comparative writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 and the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Once a prima facie infringement of a Fundamental Right is established, the Supreme Court under Article 32 cannot decline relief merely on the ground that an alternative statutory remedy is available, because the right to move the Supreme Court is itself a guaranteed Fundamental Right.

2. Under Article 226, a High Court can issue a writ to an authority or government located outside its own territorial jurisdiction, provided the cause of action wholly or in part arises within its territorial limits.

3. While the remedy under Article 32 is discretionary, the exercise of writ jurisdiction by a High Court under Article 226 is constitutionally mandatory whenever an ordinary statutory right of a citizen is infringed.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right in Part III, making the Supreme Court's remedial duty mandatory for Fundamental Rights violations, whereas a High Court's jurisdiction under Article 226 is wider in subject-matter ('for any other purpose') but discretionary in nature, and extends extraterritorially under Article 226(2) if the cause of action arises wholly or in part within its territory.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Because Article 32 is enshrined in Part III as a Fundamental Right, the Supreme Court has been constituted as the defender and guarantor of Fundamental Rights (Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras; K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras). It cannot refuse to entertain an application seeking protection against the infringement of a Fundamental Right merely on the ground that an alternative remedy exists or that the petitioner did not approach the High Court first.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 226(2) (inserted by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963), the power conferred on a High Court to issue directions, orders, or writs may also be exercised in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises, notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories.

Statement 3 is incorrect. It reverses the constitutional position. The remedy under Article 32 is a guaranteed Fundamental Right and therefore mandatory when a Fundamental Right is violated, whereas the remedy under Article 226 is discretionary; a High Court may decline to exercise its writ jurisdiction if an effective alternative statutory remedy exists or if there is unexplained delay (laches), particularly when approached for the enforcement of ordinary legal rights.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32 & Art. 226(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Fundamental Rights)

stem: With reference to the writ of 'Habeas Corpus' in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike other prerogative writs under Articles 32 and 226, the writ of Habeas Corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals.

2. A High Court can issue a writ of Habeas Corpus even where a person is detained pursuant to a valid order of judicial remand or conviction passed by a court of competent jurisdiction, or where the detention takes place entirely outside its territorial jurisdiction with no part of the cause of action arising within it.
3. Under the strict rule of locus standi, a petition for Habeas Corpus can be filed only by the detained person himself and not by a stranger or next friend.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Habeas Corpus ('to have the body of') is the only prerogative writ available against both public authorities and private individuals and relaxes the strict rule of locus standi, but it cannot be issued where detention is lawful, pursuant to a valid judicial order of a competent court, or outside the court's territorial jurisdiction.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Habeas Corpus is an order issued by the court to a person who has detained another person, to produce the body of the latter before it so that the court may examine the cause and legality of detention. It is uniquely available against both public authorities and private individuals who unlawfully confine another person.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under settled constitutional jurisprudence (such as Kanu Sanyal v. District Magistrate and Manubhai Ratilal Patel v. State of Gujarat), a writ of Habeas Corpus cannot be issued where the detention is lawful, where a person is in custody pursuant to a valid order of judicial remand or conviction passed by a court of competent jurisdiction, where the proceeding is for contempt of a legislature or a court, or where the detention is entirely outside the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court with no part of the cause of action arising within it.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Because a person under unlawful detention is often physically incapacitated from approaching the court directly, the strict rule of locus standi is relaxed in petitions for Habeas Corpus. Any relative, friend, or even a public-spirited stranger who is aware of the facts of the detention can move the court on behalf of the detainee.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32 & 226; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Writs - Types and Scope)

stem: With reference to the writ of 'Mandamus' under the Indian Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It cannot be issued to enforce departmental instructions that do not possess statutory force, nor can it be issued to enforce a private contractual obligation.
2. By virtue of constitutional immunity, it cannot be issued against the President of India or the Governor of a State for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office.
3. It cannot be issued against the Chief Justice of a High Court acting in a judicial capacity, nor can it be issued when the duty in question is merely discretionary and not mandatory.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mandamus ('we command') lies only to compel the performance of a mandatory public duty created by the Constitution or a statute; it is barred against private individuals, non-statutory executive instructions, purely discretionary functions, the President/Governors under Article 361, and a High Court Chief Justice acting in a judicial capacity.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Mandamus is a command issued by a court to a public official asking him to perform his official duties that he has failed or refused to perform. Because the duty sought to be enforced must be a public duty of a statutory or constitutional nature, Mandamus cannot be issued to enforce administrative or departmental instructions that lack statutory force, nor to enforce purely contractual obligations.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 361(1) of the Constitution, the President, or the Governor of a State, is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties. Consequently, Mandamus does not lie against the President or the Governor.

Statement 3 is correct. A writ of Mandamus cannot be issued against the Chief Justice of a High Court acting in a judicial capacity (though administrative actions governed by statutory rules are amenable to judicial review). Furthermore, Mandamus lies only to compel the performance of an imperative/mandatory public duty and cannot be issued when the duty is merely discretionary.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32, 226 & 361; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8 (Fundamental Rights)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the writs of 'Prohibition' and 'Certiorari':
items: Statement-I: Unlike the writ of Prohibition which is strictly preventive and lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, the writ of Certiorari is both preventive and curative and can also be issued against administrative authorities affecting the rights of individuals.
Statement-II: Both the writs of Prohibition and Certiorari can be issued against legislative bodies as well as private individuals discharging public functions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Prohibition only prevents a judicial or quasi-judicial body from continuing proceedings in excess of jurisdiction, Certiorari additionally quashes an order already passed and extends to administrative authorities affecting individual rights; however, neither writ lies against legislative bodies or private individuals.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Prohibition ('to forbid') is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent the latter from exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping a jurisdiction it does not possess; thus, it is only preventive and is unavailable against administrative authorities. Certiorari ('to be certified' or 'to be informed') is both preventive and curative (as it quashes an order already made in excess of jurisdiction, error of law apparent on the face of the record, or violation of natural justice). Following the Supreme Court's jurisprudence (A.K. Kraipak and subsequent rulings), Certiorari can be issued even against administrative authorities whose decisions affect the rights of individuals.
Statement-II is incorrect. Neither the writ of Prohibition nor the writ of Certiorari is available against legislative bodies or private individuals and bodies.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32 & 226; A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the writ of 'Quo Warranto' under the Indian constitutional framework, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It can be sought only by a rival claimant whose personal legal or Fundamental Right to hold the public office has been directly infringed.
opts.B: It can be issued to inquire into the legality of a claim to a substantive public office of a permanent character created by a statute or by the Constitution, upon a petition filed by any public-spirited person even if not personally aggrieved.
opts.C: It lies equally against substantive constitutional offices, purely ministerial offices, and the managing committee of a private charitable trust registered under law.
opts.D: Once an appointment to a public office is made by the Governor, the doctrine of pleasure bars a High Court from issuing Quo Warranto even if statutory or constitutional qualifications are violated.

core: Quo Warranto ('by what authority or warrant') prevents illegal usurpation of a substantive public office of permanent character created by a statute or the Constitution, and unlike most other writs, can be sought by any public-spirited person regardless of personal grievance.

exp.why: Option B is correct. Quo Warranto literally means 'by what authority or warrant'. It is issued by the court to inquire into the legality of the claim of a person to a public office and prevents illegal usurpation of such office. It can be issued only when the office is a substantive public office of a permanent character created by a statute or by the Constitution. Unlike other writs (except Habeas Corpus), Quo Warranto dispenses with the strict requirement of personal aggrievement and can be sought by any interested or public-spirited person. Option A is incorrect because any interested person, not just a rival claimant or personally aggrieved person, can file it. Option C is incorrect because Quo Warranto cannot be issued in cases of purely ministerial office or private office. Option D is incorrect because even if an office (such as Advocate General) is held during the pleasure of the Governor, Quo Warranto lies if the appointee lacks the mandatory constitutional or statutory qualifications or if the appointment contravenes statutory provisions.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32 & 226; University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 8

stem: Suppose a citizen approaches a High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution alleging the violation of a Fundamental Right, and the High Court dismisses the writ petition by a speaking order on merits. In light of the Supreme Court's jurisprudence on the doctrine of res judicata (including Daryao v. State of U.P. and Ghulam Sarwar v. Union of India), which one of the following accurately states the constitutional position regarding a subsequent writ petition directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same facts?

opts.A: Because the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a guaranteed Fundamental Right in Part III, the doctrine of res judicata can never apply to any writ petition filed under Article 32.
opts.B: Dismissal of the petition under Article 226 on merits bars both a fresh original writ petition under Article 32 and an appellate challenge before the Supreme Court under Article 136.
opts.C: A fresh original writ petition under Article 32 on the same facts is barred by the rule of res judicata, except in the case of a writ of Habeas Corpus involving personal liberty.
opts.D: A fresh writ petition under Article 32 is barred even if the High Court had dismissed the earlier petition under Article 226 purely in limine on the ground of laches or availability of an alternative statutory remedy without entering into the merits.

core: In Daryao v. State of U.P. (1961) and Ghulam Sarwar v. Union of India (1967), the Supreme Court held that if a writ petition under Article 226 is decided on merits by a speaking order of a High Court, res judicata bars a fresh original petition under Article 32 on the same facts (though an appeal lies under Article 136), with a unique constitutional carve-out for the writ of Habeas Corpus.

exp.why: Option C is correct. In Daryao v. State of U.P. (1961), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the rule of res judicata is founded on sound public policy regarding the finality of judicial decisions of competent courts. Therefore, if a High Court entertains a writ petition under Article 226 for the enforcement of a Fundamental Right and dismisses it on merits by a speaking order, that decision binds the parties unless reversed in appeal, and the petitioner cannot institute a fresh original petition before the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same facts and grounds. However, in Ghulam Sarwar v. Union of India (1967) and Lallubhai Jogibhai Patel v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court carved out a crucial exception: the doctrine of res judicata (and constructive res judicata) does not apply to a writ of Habeas Corpus, as personal liberty is paramount. Option A is incorrect because res judicata does apply to Article 32 petitions for writs other than Habeas Corpus. Option B is incorrect because while an original petition under Article 32 is barred, an appellate remedy against the High Court's judgment (such as Special Leave Petition under Article 136) remains fully open. Option D is incorrect because in Daryao, the Court explicitly held that if the Article 226 petition is dismissed in limine without a speaking order, or dismissed on grounds of laches or availability of an alternative remedy without adjudicating the merits, it does not operate as res judicata to bar a petition under Article 32.

ref: Daryao v. State of U.P. (1961); Ghulam Sarwar v. Union of India (1967); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: With reference to the power to modify Fundamental Rights in their application to Forces under Article 33 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The power to enact laws under Article 33 restricting or abrogating Fundamental Rights is conferred only on the Parliament and not on State Legislatures, even in respect of State Police Forces charged with the maintenance of public order.

2. In respect of personnel employed in telecommunication systems set up for a State police force or intelligence bureau, the State Legislature concerned may by law restrict their Fundamental Rights with the prior assent of the President.
3. Non-combatant employees attached to the Armed Forces, such as barbers, carpenters, mechanics, and cooks, fall within the ambit of 'members of the Armed Forces' under Article 33.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 33 read with Article 35(a)(i) vests exclusive legislative competence in the Parliament—to the complete exclusion of State Legislatures—to restrict or abrogate the Fundamental Rights of armed forces, police forces, intelligence agencies, and their associated telecommunication personnel. Judicial interpretation extends this coverage to non-combatant employees integral to the functioning and discipline of the Armed Forces.

exp.why: Under Article 33 read with Article 35(a)(i) of the Constitution, the power to make laws restricting or abrogating Fundamental Rights for the maintenance of discipline and proper discharge of duties is vested exclusively in the Parliament. Even though 'Public Order' and 'Police' are State List subjects (Entries 1 and 2 of List II), a State Legislature cannot enact a law under Article 33 restricting the Fundamental Rights of its own State Police Force.

Under Article 33(c) and (d), persons employed in any bureau or other organization established by the State for purposes of intelligence or counter-intelligence, as well as persons employed in or in connection with the telecommunication systems set up for the purposes of any force, bureau or organization, are squarely covered by Parliament's exclusive legislative domain. State Legislatures have no power to legislate under Article 33 even with Presidential assent.

In Ous Kutilingal Achudan Nair v. Union of India (1976), the Supreme Court held that the expression 'members of the Armed Forces' in Article 33 covers not only combatant personnel but also non-combatant civilian employees (such as barbers, carpenters, mechanics, boot-makers, and cooks) who are integral to the operational efficiency and discipline of the Armed Forces.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 33 & 35(a)(i); Ous Kutilingal Achudan Nair v. Union of India (1976); Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the imposition of Martial Law under Article 34 and its structural comparison with a National Emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the operation of Martial Law suspends the ordinary law courts and civil administration in the affected area, ordinary law courts continue to function during a National Emergency under Article 352.
2. The Constitution explicitly defines the expression 'martial law' under Article 366 and enumerates the specific grounds on which the President may proclaim it in any area within India.

3. An Act of Indemnity passed by the Parliament under Article 34 to validate sentences passed or acts done under martial law can be declared void by the Supreme Court if it contravenes Articles 14 or 19.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Martial Law under Article 34 is an undefined common-law concept that temporarily supplants civil administration and ordinary courts in a specific disturbed area to restore order, unlike a National Emergency where ordinary courts continue to operate. Article 34 empowers Parliament to pass an Act of Indemnity that is constitutionally immunized from challenge on the ground of contravening Fundamental Rights.

exp.why: Martial Law affects only Fundamental Rights and suspends the ordinary government and ordinary law courts in the specific area where it is in force, subjecting civilians to military tribunals. Conversely, during a National Emergency under Article 352, ordinary courts of law continue to function and centre-state federal relations are modified.

The expression 'martial law' is nowhere defined in the Constitution of India (neither in Article 34 nor in Article 366), nor does the Constitution contain any explicit provision authorizing the executive to declare it or listing specific grounds for its imposition. The concept is borrowed from English common law and its possibility is implicitly recognized by Article 34.

Article 34 opens with a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part...'), empowering Parliament by law to indemnify any person in the service of the Union or a State for any act done in connection with the maintenance or restoration of order in any area where martial law was in force, and to validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted, or forfeiture ordered. Consequently, such an Act of Indemnity cannot be challenged for contravening Fundamental Rights such as Articles 14 or 19.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 34 & 352; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the legislative competence to give effect to certain provisions of Part III under Article 35 of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Prescribing residence within a State or Union Territory as a requirement for certain classes of public employment under Article 16(3) : Parliament exclusively
2. Empowering courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue prerogative writs within their local limits under Article 32(3) : State Legislature with the concurrence of the High Court
3. Prescribing punishment for acts declared to be offences under Part III, such as untouchability (Article 17) and traffic in human beings (Article 23) : Parliament exclusively
4. Altering, amending, or repealing any pre-constitutional law in force relating to a matter specified in Article 35(a) : Parliament exclusively
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Article 35 ensures nationwide uniformity in the application and enforcement of Fundamental Rights by granting exclusive legislative power to the Parliament—and expressly barring State Legislatures—over specific matters under Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33, and 34, as well as penalizing offences declared in Part III (Articles 17 and 23).

exp.why: Under Article 35(a)(i) read with Article 16(3), Parliament has the exclusive power (and the Legislature of a State shall not have power) to make laws prescribing residence within that State or Union Territory prior to employment as a requirement for any class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the Government or any local or other authority within a State or Union Territory.

Under Article 35(a)(i) read with Article 32(3), ONLY the Parliament—and not the Legislature of a State—has the power to make laws empowering any court other than the Supreme Court (without prejudice to the powers of the Supreme Court) to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the writ powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under Article 32(2).

Under Article 35(a)(ii), Parliament has the exclusive competence (and State Legislatures are barred) to make laws for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under Part III—specifically Untouchability under Article 17 and Traffic in human beings and forced labour under Article 23.
