Under Article 35(b), any law in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution in the territory of India with respect to any of the matters referred to in Article 35(a)(i) or (ii) continues in force subject to the terms thereof until altered or repealed or amended exclusively by the Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 35; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the prerogative writs issued under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Certiorari : Quashing an order already passed by an inferior court, tribunal, or quasi-judicial authority acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
2. Prohibition : Directing an inferior court or tribunal to cease ongoing proceedings where it lacks or exceeds jurisdiction
3. Quo Warranto : Inquiring into the legality of a person's claim to a substantive public office created by a statute or by the Constitution
4. Mandamus : Commanding a public official, statutory corporation, or the President of India to perform a mandatory public duty
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Each constitutional writ serves a distinct procedural and substantive function: Prohibition is preventive (stopping ongoing ultra vires judicial/quasi-judicial proceedings), Certiorari is curative (quashing a completed order), Quo Warranto prevents usurpation of a substantive public office, and Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public duty—subject to constitutional immunities such as Article 361.

exp.why: Certiorari ('to be certified') is issued by a higher court to an inferior court, tribunal, or quasi-judicial/administrative authority affecting rights of subjects, either to transfer a case pending with them or to quash their order already passed on grounds of excess or lack of jurisdiction or error of law apparent on the face of the record.

Prohibition ('to forbid') is a purely preventive writ issued by a higher court to an inferior court or tribunal directing it to stop ongoing proceedings that exceed its jurisdiction or usurp a jurisdiction it does not legally possess.

Quo Warranto ('by what authority or warrant') is issued by the court to inquire into the legality of the claim of a person to a public office. It can be issued only in respect of a substantive public office of a permanent character created by a statute or by the Constitution, and any public-spirited person (even if not personally aggrieved) can seek it.

While Mandamus ('we command') lies against public officials, public bodies, statutory corporations, inferior courts, tribunals, or the Government to compel the performance of a mandatory public duty, it CANNOT be issued against the President of India or the State Governors due to the express constitutional immunity under Article 361.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 32, 226 & 361; Laxmikanth Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following constitutional milestones concerning exceptions to Fundamental Rights and the right to property:
items: 1. Insertion of Article 31C into Part III to immunize laws giving effect to the Directive Principles specified in Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
2. Insertion of Articles 31A and 31B along with the Ninth Schedule to protect agrarian reform and zamindari abolition laws from judicial review on the ground of contravening Fundamental Rights.

3. Insertion of Clause (1A) in Article 30 mandating that the statutory amount fixed for the compulsory acquisition of property of a minority educational institution shall not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under Article 30(1).

4. Insertion of the Second Proviso to Article 31A(1) requiring payment of compensation at a rate not less than the market value for the acquisition of land held by a person under personal cultivation within the statutory ceiling limit.
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above constitutional developments, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The constitutional relationship between Fundamental Rights, agrarian property reforms, and minority institutional property evolved across four major amendments: the 1st Amendment (1951) introduced Articles 31A and 31B; the 17th Amendment (1964) added the market-value compensation proviso for land within ceiling limits; the 25th Amendment (1971) introduced Article 31C; and the 44th Amendment (1978) omitted Article 31 while inserting Article 30(1A).

exp.why: Milestone 1 occurred third in the sequence: Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 to give primacy to the socialist Directive Principles contained in Article 39(b) and (c) over Articles 14 and 19.

Milestone 2 occurred earliest: Articles 31A and 31B along with the Ninth Schedule were inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 to shield zamindari abolition and agrarian reform statutes from invalidation under Part III.

Milestone 3 occurred latest: When the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 abolished the Fundamental Right to Property (deleting Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and shifting property to Article 300A), it simultaneously inserted Clause (1A) in Article 30 to ensure that compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution does not abrogate its Fundamental Right under Article 30(1).

Milestone 4 occurred second: The Second Proviso to Article 31A(1) was inserted by the 17th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1964, prohibiting the State from acquiring land within the statutory ceiling limit held by a person under personal cultivation unless the law provides for payment of compensation at a rate not less than the market value. Thus, the exact chronological order is 2 (1951) -> 4 (1964) -> 1 (1971) -> 3 (1978).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 30(1A), 31A, 31B & 31C; 1st, 17th, 25th & 44th Amendment Acts

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional protection guaranteed to minority educational institutions under Article 30 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: By virtue of the express exclusion in Article 15(5) and the Supreme Court ruling in Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India, minority educational institutions covered under Article 30(1)—whether aided or unaided by the State—are exempt from the statutory mandate under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 to reserve twenty-five percent of seats in admissions for children belonging to weaker and disadvantaged sections.

Statement-II: An educational institution established by a religious or linguistic minority is not barred from claiming minority status under Article 30(1) merely on the ground that its legal incorporation was effected through a statute enacted by the Legislature.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 15(5) expressly carves out minority educational institutions referred to in Article 30(1) from state-mandated admission quotas, and in Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust (2014), the Supreme Court held that applying the 25% admission quota under the RTE Act, 2009 to aided or unaided minority schools would abrogate their minority character. Independently, in Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench overruled Azeez Basha (1967) and held that statutory incorporation does not preclude an institution from claiming minority status under Article 30(1).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 15(5) empowers the State to make special provisions regarding admission to educational institutions (including private aided and unaided institutions) for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs, and STs, 'other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30'. In Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench further held that compelling minority schools (whether aided or unaided) to admit 25% non-minority disadvantaged neighbourhood children under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009 would alter and destroy their special minority character protected by Article 30(1).

Statement-II is also correct. In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court overruled S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India (1967) and held that an educational institution is not barred from claiming minority status under Article 30(1) merely because it was incorporated or recognized through a statute enacted by the Legislature, provided its foundational genesis and ideation trace back to a religious or linguistic minority. However, Statement-II concerns the criteria for determining whether an institution was 'established' by a minority under Article 30(1), and does not explain why minority schools are exempt from mandatory admission quotas under Article 15(5) and the RTE Act, 2009.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 15(5), 21A & 30(1); Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust v. UoI (2014); Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (7-Judge Bench, 2024)

stem: With reference to the foundational provisions of the Directive Principles of State Policy under Part IV of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 36 of the Constitution, the definition of 'the State' for the purposes of Part IV is narrower than that under Article 12, as it excludes non-legislative statutory authorities.

2. Under Article 37, the provisions contained in Part IV are not enforceable by any court, yet the principles laid down therein are expressly declared to be fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

3. The Directive Principles resemble the 'Instrument of Instructions' enumerated in the Government of India Act, 1935, except that they are issued to the Legislature and the Executive rather than solely to the Governor-General and Governors.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 36 and 37 establish the constitutional parity of 'the State' across Parts III and IV while balancing judicial non-enforceability with a mandatory governance duty on legislative and executive authorities.

exp.why: Article 36 explicitly stipulates that in Part IV, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' has the exact same meaning as assigned to it in Part III (Article 12). Thus, it comprehensively includes the Union and State Governments, Parliament, State Legislatures, local authorities, and all other statutory and non-statutory authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

Article 37 expressly declares that the provisions contained in Part IV shall not be enforceable by any court, but that the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

As explained by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly, the Directive Principles are precisely like the 'Instrument of Instructions' issued to the Governor-General and the Governors of the colonies by the British Government under the Government of India Act, 1935; what are called Directive Principles is merely another name for the Instrument of Instructions addressed to the Legislature and the Executive.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 36 & 37; Constituent Assembly Debates Vol. VII; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 9

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding the ideological classification of the Directive Principles of State Policy:
items: 1. Promotion of cottage industries on an individual or co-operation basis in rural areas (Article 43) : Socialist Principle
2. Securing a living wage and a decent standard of life for all workers (Article 43) : Gandhian Principle
3. Separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State (Article 50) : Liberal-Intellectual Principle
4. Securing the participation of workers in the management of industries (Article 43A) : Socialist Principle
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Certain articles in Part IV, notably Articles 43 and 47, combine both Socialist and Gandhian ideological limbs within the same constitutional provision.

exp.why: While Article 43 contains two distinct limbs, its second limb—which directs the State to endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operation basis in rural areas—embodies the Gandhian vision of village self-sufficiency and decentralized rural economy, and is therefore classified as a Gandhian Principle rather than a Socialist Principle.

The first limb of Article 43—securing to all workers (agricultural, industrial or otherwise) work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure—reflects the ideology of a democratic socialist welfare state and is classified as a Socialist Principle, not a Gandhian Principle.

Article 50, which directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State, embodies the classic constitutional doctrine of separation of powers and independent administration of justice, placing it squarely under the Liberal-Intellectual Principles.

Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, directs the State to take steps by suitable legislation or in any other way to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings or establishments engaged in any industry. It promotes industrial democracy and is classified as a Socialist Principle.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 43, 43A & 50; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the text and scope of the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 49, the constitutional obligation of the State to protect monuments and places of artistic or historic interest applies only to those declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national importance.

2. Article 50 directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State, rather than mandating a separation between the legislature and the executive.

3. Under Article 48, the directive to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines is contained within the same article that directs the State to take steps for prohibiting the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A precise reading of the constitutional text of Articles 48, 49, and 50 reveals specific jurisdictional qualifiers—such as Parliamentary declaration of national importance in Article 49 and executive-judiciary separation in Article 50.

exp.why: Article 49 explicitly qualifies the State's obligation by stating that it shall be the obligation of the State to protect every monument or place or object of artistic or historic interest, 'declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national importance', from spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal or export. This phrase was inserted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, so it does not extend to every local monument.

Because India follows a parliamentary system of government founded on the fusion of legislative and executive powers, Article 50 does not mandate the separation of the legislature from the executive. Instead, it specifically directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State (given effect fully when executive magistrates were divested of judicial powers in criminal trials).

Article 48 combines both a Liberal-Intellectual scientific mandate and a Gandhian directive in a single sentence: 'The State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and shall, in particular, take steps for preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle.'

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 48, 49 & 50; 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956

stem: With reference to the scope of 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b) of the Constitution, as settled by the nine-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every privately owned property automatically qualifies as a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b) because individual private resources form part of the aggregate national wealth.

2. A privately owned resource may fall within the ambit of 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b) if it satisfies a context-specific inquiry based on factors such as its inherent nature, scarcity, impact on community well-being, and the consequences of its concentration in private hands.

3. Once a resource qualifies as a material resource of the community under Article 39(b), citizens can approach the High Court or the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus compelling the legislature to enact a law for its equitable redistribution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), a 9-Judge Bench overruled the sweeping doctrine that all private property is automatically a community resource under Article 39(b), replacing it with a nuanced multi-factor public-interest test.

exp.why: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), the 9-Judge Bench explicitly overruled Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view in State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) and the subsequent decision in Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. (1983). The Court held that not every resource owned by an individual can be considered a 'material resource of the community' merely because it meets the qualifier of 'material needs'.

The 9-Judge Bench held that while the phrase 'material resources of the community' may theoretically include certain privately owned resources (such as scarce natural resources, forests, mines, or spectrum), determining whether a specific private resource falls within Article 39(b) requires a context-specific inquiry guided by non-exhaustive factors: (i) the nature and characteristics of the resource, (ii) its impact on the well-being of the community, (iii) its scarcity, and (iv) the consequences of such a resource being concentrated in the hands of private individuals.

Article 39(b) is a Directive Principle of State Policy in Part IV of the Constitution. By virtue of Article 37, the provisions of Part IV are non-justiciable, and no constitutional court can issue a writ of mandamus directing the Parliament or a State Legislature to enact legislation to implement a Directive Principle.

ref: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (9-Judge Bench, Supreme Court, Nov 2024); Constitution of India, Article 39(b)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional status and scope of Article 31C of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Even when a legislation contains a declaration that it is enacted to give effect to the principles specified in Article 39(b) or Article 39(c), constitutional courts are not barred under Article 31C from examining whether the law bears a direct and reasonable nexus with those objectives.

Statement-II: In the Property Owners Association case (2024), a nine-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court held that the invalidation of Section 4 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act in Minerva Mills (1980) revived the original pre-1976 text of Article 31C, which restricts immunity from challenges under Articles 14 and 19 solely to laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 31C operates today in its post-Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and post-Minerva Mills (1980) form—confirmed by the 9-Judge Bench in 2024—protecting only laws having a judicially verifiable nexus with Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenges under Articles 14 and 19.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct because in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the 13-Judge Bench upheld the first part of Article 31C (inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971) but struck down its second part—which had declared that 'no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy'—as destructive of the Basic Structure of judicial review. Consequently, courts always retain the jurisdiction to examine whether a direct and reasonable nexus exists between the impugned law and Article 39(b) or 39(c).

Statement-II is also correct because in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), the 9-Judge Bench unanimously resolved a long-standing doctrinal question by holding that when Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment Act (which had expanded Article 31C to cover 'all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV'), Article 31C was not obliterated; rather, its narrower pre-1976 text protecting only Articles 39(b) and 39(c) automatically stood revived. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the court's power to examine nexus (Statement-I) derives from the invalidation of the finality clause in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), not from the revival of the pre-1976 text after Minerva Mills.

ref: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Minerva Mills (1980); Article 31C

stem: Consider the following pairs of Directive Principles of State Policy and the Constitutional Amendment Acts through which they were inserted into Part IV of the Constitution:
items: 1. Minimising inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities (Article 38(2)) : 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
2. Promoting equal justice and providing free legal aid to the poor (Article 39A) : 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
3. Securing the participation of workers in the management of industries (Article 43A) : 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978
4. Promoting voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies (Article 43B) : 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Tracking the specific Constitutional Amendments that expanded Part IV—specifically distinguishing the four directives added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) from the solitary directive added by the 44th Amendment (1978)—is essential for constitutional chronology.

exp.why: Clause (2) of Article 38—which directs the State to, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations—was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, not the 42nd Amendment.

Article 39A, which directs the State to promote justice on a basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid by suitable legislation or schemes to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities, was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

Article 43A, which directs the State to take steps to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry, was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (along with Articles 39(f), 39A, and 48A), not by the 44th Amendment.

Article 43B, directing the State to endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies, was inserted into Part IV by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 38(2), 39A, 43A & 43B; 42nd, 44th & 97th Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the provisions of Article 39 under Part IV of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The principle of 'equal pay for equal work for both men and women' is explicitly enumerated in the text of Part III as a Fundamental Right, in addition to being set out as a Directive Principle in Article 39(d).

2. The directive under Article 39(f) requiring the State to ensure that children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity was substituted in its present form by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

3. As laid down by the Supreme Court in the Property Owners Association case (2024), not every privately owned property automatically qualifies as a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 39 encapsulates the core principles of distributive justice and welfare state policy in Part IV. While 'equal pay for equal work' is textually located in Article 39(d) and read into Articles 14 and 16 by judicial interpretation, Article 39(b) was authoritatively interpreted in 2024 to mean that private property does not automatically become a community resource unless it meets specific public-nexus criteria.

exp.why: The text of Part III (Fundamental Rights) does not explicitly mention 'equal pay for equal work for both men and women'. Textually, it is a Directive Principle under Article 39(d). In Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court held that while it is not expressly declared a Fundamental Right in Part III, it is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d) that can be enforced through Articles 14 and 16.

The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 substituted clause (f) of Article 39 to direct the State to ensure that children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment.

In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), a nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court overruled the expansive view of Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy and held that not every privately owned resource automatically falls within the ambit of 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b); whether a private resource qualifies depends on context-specific factors such as its nature, scarcity, and community impact.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 39(b), 39(d), 39(f); Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024); Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: Consider the following constitutional and judicial milestones in the evolution of the relationship between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV):
items: 1. Invalidation by the Supreme Court of the finality clause of Article 31C which barred judicial review of any law containing a legislative declaration that it gives effect to Article 39(b) or (c).
2. Judicial pronouncement that Directive Principles of State Policy must conform to and run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights.
3. Judicial declaration that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
4. Insertion of Article 31C into the Constitution to immunize laws giving effect to the principles specified in Article 39(b) and (c) from challenges under Articles 14 and 19.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the above milestones from the earliest to the latest?
core: The doctrinal relationship between Part III and Part IV evolved from strict subordination of DPSPs (Champakam Dorairajan, 1951), through legislative attempts to confer primacy via Article 31C (25th Amendment, 1971) and judicial preservation of review (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), to the synthesis of 'harmony and balance' as Basic Structure (Minerva Mills, 1980).

exp.why: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (April 1973), the Supreme Court upheld the first part of Article 31C (protecting laws giving effect to Art. 39(b) and (c)), but struck down its second part ('no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court') on the ground that judicial review is a Basic Structure feature. This is the third milestone (1973).

In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (April 1951), the Supreme Court held that because Fundamental Rights are enforceable under Article 32 whereas DPSPs are expressly made non-enforceable by Article 37, the Directive Principles have to conform to and run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights. This is the earliest milestone (1951).

In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (July 1980), while striking down the 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C to all DPSPs, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Part III and Part IV, and that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the Basic Structure. This is the fourth milestone (1980).

The 25th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 31C into the Constitution, providing that no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles in Article 39(b) or 39(c) shall be deemed void on the ground that it is inconsistent with Articles 14, 19, or 31. This is the second milestone (1971), giving the chronological sequence 2-4-1-3.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 31C; Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980); Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the constitutional directives situated outside Part IV of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The direction to every State and local authority to endeavour to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups (Article 350A) is a constitutional directive located outside Part IV.

2. Both the mandate to consider the claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services and posts consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration (Article 335) and the duty of the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language (Article 351) are non-justiciable directives situated outside Part IV.

3. The direction to promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and in particular of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Article 46), is placed outside Part IV under Part XVI of the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Apart from the Directive Principles enumerated in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51), the Constitution contains three key non-justiciable directives to the State in other Parts: Article 335 in Part XVI, and Articles 350A and 351 in Part XVII. By contrast, Article 46 is an integral Gandhian Directive Principle located within Part IV itself.

exp.why: Article 350A (inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956) is located in Part XVII (Official Language), Chapter IV (Special Directives). It directs every State and local authority within the State to endeavour to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children of linguistic minority groups.

Article 335 is located in Part XVI (Special Provisions relating to Certain Classes) and directs that the claims of SCs and STs shall be taken into consideration, consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration, in the making of appointments to services and posts. Article 351 is located in Part XVII and directs the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language. Both operate as directives outside Part IV.

Article 46 ('Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections') is located directly inside Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), which spans Articles 36 to 51, and not in Part XVI.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 46, 335, 350A, 351; Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the constitutional architecture governing the enactment of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India, which one of the following statements correctly explains the legislative competence of a State Legislature to enact a law establishing a Uniform Civil Code regarding marriage, divorce, and succession within its territory?

opts.A: While Article 44 directs the 'State' to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code, actual legislative competence over personal law matters such as marriage, divorce, and succession flows from Entry 5 of the Concurrent List (List III), enabling a State Legislature to legislate subject to Article 254.
opts.B: Article 44 itself operates as an independent source of legislative power that confers concurrent jurisdiction on both Parliament and the State Legislatures to override Entry 97 of the Union List.
opts.C: Personal laws governing marriage, divorce, and succession fall within the residuary legislative powers of the Union under Article 248, but Parliament has delegated standing authority to State Legislatures under Article 252.
opts.D: Under Article 25(2), a State Legislature possesses exclusive primary competence to regulate secular activities associated with religious practice, whereas Parliament can legislate on personal laws only with the prior consent of the States.

core: Directive Principles under Part IV (such as Article 44) set out policy goals for the 'State' (which under Article 36 read with Article 12 includes both Union and State legislatures) but do not themselves confer legislative competence. The actual power of both Parliament and State Legislatures to enact laws on marriage, divorce, infants, minors, adoption, wills, intestacy, and succession derives from Entry 5 of List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule, governed by the repugnancy and Presidential-assent rules of Article 254.

exp.why: Option A is correct: Under Article 36 read with Article 12, the word 'State' in Article 44 includes both the Parliament of India and the Legislature of each State. More importantly, DPSPs are policy mandates, not sources of legislative competence. Legislative power over 'Marriage and divorce; infants and minors; adoption; wills, intestacy and succession; joint family and partition' is expressly placed in Entry 5 of List III (Concurrent List) in the Seventh Schedule. Under Article 246(2), both Parliament and State Legislatures are competent to legislate on Entry 5, and under Article 254(2), a State law on a Concurrent subject reserved for the consideration of the President and receiving Presidential assent prevails in that State even if repugnant to an earlier central law. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because Article 44 does not confer legislative power, personal law is not a residuary subject under Article 248, and Article 25(2) does not exclude Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 36, 44, 246(2), 254 & Seventh Schedule List III Entry 5; Laxmikanth Ch. 9 & 15

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional provisions on education:
items: Statement-I: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 simultaneously modified Part III, Part IV, and Part IVA of the Constitution to establish a tripartite framework for childhood care and education without duplicating the same age bracket between enforceable rights and non-enforceable directives.

Statement-II: While the Amendment inserted Article 21A in Part III and clause (k) in Article 51A of Part IVA to cover children between the ages of six and fourteen years, it substituted Article 45 in Part IV to direct the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 is unique for amending Fundamental Rights (Art. 21A), Directive Principles (Art. 45), and Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A(k)) together. By moving the 6–14 years age group into an enforceable Fundamental Right (Art. 21A) and parental Fundamental Duty (Art. 51A(k)), it restructured Article 45 in Part IV to focus specifically on early childhood care and education for children below the age of six years.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 modified all three chapters—Part III (Fundamental Rights), Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), and Part IVA (Fundamental Duties)—while neatly bifurcating the age groups between justiciable rights and non-justiciable policy directives.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Prior to 2002, original Article 45 covered free and compulsory education for children until they completed the age of 14 years. Once the 6–14 age group was elevated to a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and a parental duty under Article 51A(k), Article 45 was substituted so that the State's non-justiciable directive covers early childhood care and education for children until they complete the age of six years.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 21A, 45, 51A(k); 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002; Laxmikanth Ch. 8, 9 & 10

stem: With reference to Articles 47 and 48 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the directive to prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health and the directive to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle are contained within Article 47.

2. The constitutional directive under Article 47 to endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health is unqualified in the constitutional text and contains no exception for medicinal purposes.
3. The directive in Article 48 to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines was inserted into Part IV by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 47 addresses nutrition, standard of living, public health, and the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs (explicitly exempting medicinal purposes), whereas Article 48 (an original provision of the 1950 Constitution) addresses the organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines alongside the prohibition of slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle.

exp.why: These two directives are located in two separate articles. Article 47 deals with raising the level of nutrition, standard of living, public health, and prohibiting intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health. The directive to preserve and improve the breeds, and prohibit the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle is contained in Article 48.

Article 47 explicitly incorporates a textual exception for medicinal purposes: '...in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health.'

Article 48 ('Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry') has been part of the original Constitution since 1950. It was Article 48A ('Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life') that was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 47, 48 & 48A; Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the promotion of international peace and security under Article 51 of the Constitution of India and the domestic implementation of international treaties, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 51(c), any international treaty or convention ratified by the Union Executive automatically becomes enforceable municipal law binding on Indian courts even where it modifies existing domestic statutes without parliamentary legislation under Article 253.
2. Article 51 explicitly directs the State to endeavour to encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

3. Under Article 253, Parliament is empowered to enact legislation to give effect to an international agreement even with respect to a subject enumerated in the State List of the Seventh Schedule, without requiring the concurrence of the State Legislatures.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India follows a dualist approach to international treaties affecting domestic statutes or private rights: while Article 51(c) directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, treaties that alter domestic law require enabling parliamentary legislation under Article 253. Furthermore, Article 253 grants Parliament overriding legislative competence across the State List to implement international obligations.

exp.why: While Article 51(c) directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations and the Union Executive can ratify treaties under Article 73, India follows the dualist doctrine where treaties that modify existing domestic statutes, impose obligations on citizens, or affect private rights do not automatically become enforceable municipal law. They require enabling legislation by Parliament under Article 253 (Jolly George Varghese v. Bank of Cochin; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan allows reading in international conventions only when there is no inconsistency with domestic law).

Article 51(d) of the Constitution explicitly directs that the State shall endeavour to encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration, alongside promoting international peace and security (clause a), maintaining just and honourable relations between nations (clause b), and fostering respect for international law and treaty obligations (clause c).

Article 253 begins with a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter') and empowers Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any international treaty, agreement, or convention, even if the subject matter falls exclusively within List II (State List), without requiring State ratification.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 51 & Art. 253; Laxmikanth Ch. 9 & Ch. 14

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the justiciability and interpretive role of the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV):
items: Statement-I: A Constitutional Court cannot issue a writ of mandamus compelling the Parliament or a State Legislature to enact a law for implementing a Directive Principle of State Policy.

Statement-II: While exercising judicial review over an impugned statute, the Supreme Court relies on Part IV and regards a statutory restriction on a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1) that seeks to implement a Directive Principle as a primary indicator of a 'reasonable restriction' in the public interest.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although Article 37 expressly bars courts from enforcing Directive Principles or issuing mandamus to compel legislation, Part IV plays a vital role in judicial review as an interpretive benchmark for testing 'reasonable restrictions' under Article 19 and 'public purpose' under Article 14. The bar on mandamus stems from Article 37 and the doctrine of separation of powers, not from the interpretive use of Part IV in upholding enacted statutes.

exp.why: Under Article 37, the provisions contained in Part IV are expressly declared not to be enforceable by any court, and under the constitutional scheme of separation of powers, neither the Supreme Court nor a High Court can issue a writ of mandamus directing a Legislature to enact a statute implementing a Directive Principle.

Statement-II is also correct because the Supreme Court (in cases such as State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of J&K, and Minerva Mills v. Union of India) routinely relies on Part IV to uphold the constitutional validity of impugned statutes, holding that an executive or legislative action giving effect to a DPSP is prima facie a 'reasonable restriction' in the public interest under Articles 19(2)–(6) and satisfies 'public purpose' under Article 14. However, Statement-II explains how DPSPs assist in upholding enacted laws during judicial review, whereas Statement-I is explained by the express bar of non-justiciability in Article 37; hence Statement-II does not explain Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 14, 19 & 37; D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the recommendations of the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) and the provisions actually incorporated into Part IVA of the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Swaran Singh Committee recommended the inclusion of only eight Fundamental Duties, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act originally incorporated ten Fundamental Duties under Article 51A.
2. Acting on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act included the duty of citizens to pay taxes honestly as one of the Fundamental Duties in Part IVA.

3. Accepting the Swaran Singh Committee's proposal on enforceability, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act inserted a clause in Part IVA empowering Parliament to impose penalties for non-compliance with Fundamental Duties and barring judicial review of such penal laws.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended only eight Fundamental Duties alongside three major structural proposals: making the duty to pay taxes a Fundamental Duty, empowering Parliament to prescribe punishments for non-compliance, and immunizing such penal laws from judicial review. However, the 42nd Amendment Act enacted ten duties and rejected all three of those specific recommendations.

exp.why: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the inclusion of 8 Fundamental Duties in a separate chapter, whereas the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 actually enacted 10 Fundamental Duties under Article 51A(a) to (j) (with the 11th duty added later under clause (k) by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002).

Although the Swaran Singh Committee explicitly recommended that the duty to pay taxes should be made a Fundamental Duty of citizens, this recommendation was not accepted by the Government and was not incorporated into Article 51A by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act.

The Swaran Singh Committee recommended that Parliament be empowered by a constitutional clause in Part IVA to impose penalty or punishment for the refusal to observe any Fundamental Duty, and that no law imposing such penalty should be called in question in any court on the ground of infringement of any Fundamental Right or other constitutional provision. Neither of these recommendations was incorporated into Part IVA.

ref: Constitution of India Part IVA (Art. 51A); Laxmikanth Ch. 10 (Fundamental Duties)

stem: With reference to the text of the eleven Fundamental Duties enumerated under Article 51A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 51A(a) enjoins every citizen to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem, but does not expressly mention the National Song or the National Emblem.

2. Developing the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform, as well as safeguarding public property and abjuring violence, are explicitly enumerated as Fundamental Duties under Article 51A.
3. Casting one's vote in general elections to Parliament and State Legislatures is not enumerated among the Fundamental Duties in Part IVA of the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A precise textual reading of Article 51A(a)–(k) shows that while respecting the National Flag and National Anthem, developing scientific temper and humanism, and safeguarding public property are explicit constitutional duties, neither respecting the National Song/Emblem nor voting in elections is mentioned in Part IVA.

exp.why: Article 51A(a) states that it shall be the duty of every citizen of India 'to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.' It does not mention the National Song (Vande Mataram) or the National Emblem.

Article 51A(h) explicitly enumerates the duty 'to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform', and Article 51A(i) enumerates the duty 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence'.
Casting one's vote in elections and paying taxes are not included among the eleven Fundamental Duties listed under Article 51A(a) to (k) of Part IVA of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 51A(a)–(k); Laxmikanth Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the applicability and legal enforceability of the Fundamental Duties in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Fundamental Duties enshrined in Part IVA of the Constitution are applicable only to citizens of India and do not extend to foreigners residing in India.
2. The Supreme Court can directly issue writs under Article 32 against private individuals solely for breaching the duties under Article 51A even in the absence of an enabling parliamentary statute.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Unlike certain Fundamental Rights in Part III that extend to all persons, the Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are confined exclusively to citizens of India. Furthermore, Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable on their own and cannot be directly enforced against private individuals via writs under Article 32 unless backed by specific statutory legislation.

exp.why: The opening words of Article 51A expressly state, 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India...'. Thus, unlike Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28 which apply to all persons (citizens and foreigners alike), Fundamental Duties in Part IVA apply only to Indian citizens.

Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs specifically for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III, not for the direct enforcement of Fundamental Duties in Part IVA against private individuals. Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable per se and become legally enforceable against individuals only when operationalized through specific parliamentary or state statutes.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32 & Art. 51A; Laxmikanth Ch. 10

stem: Which one of the following statements best reflects the key finding of the Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) regarding the operationalization of Fundamental Duties of Citizens?

opts.A: It recommended a constitutional amendment to transfer environmental and educational duties from Part IVA to Part III so that citizens could directly approach High Courts under Article 226 for their enforcement.
opts.B: It identified that several Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are already legally enforceable indirectly through existing standalone statutes, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, without requiring a separate overarching enforcement statute.
opts.C: It proposed the establishment of a statutory National Fundamental Duties Commission vested with the powers of a civil court to penalize public servants and citizens for wilful breach of Article 51A.
opts.D: It concluded that since Part IVA was modelled on the erstwhile Soviet Constitution, no penal statute passed by Parliament can operationalize any clause of Article 51A unless Article 37 is first amended.

core: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee on Operationalization of Fundamental Duties of Citizens (1999) demonstrated that while Part IVA contains no direct penal sanction, numerous existing parliamentary laws already give statutory teeth to specific clauses of Article 51A. Consequently, operationalization requires civic education and strict implementation of existing laws rather than a single omnibus enforcement statute.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) catalogued existing legal provisions that already enforce several Fundamental Duties indirectly—such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (enforcing Art. 51A(a)), various criminal provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / erstwhile IPC and Representation of the People Act, 1951 against promoting enmity (enforcing Art. 51A(c) & (e)), the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (enforcing Art. 51A(g)). Option (A) is incorrect because the Committee did not recommend transferring Part IVA duties into Part III as justiciable Fundamental Rights. Option (C) is incorrect because it emphasized curriculum integration and sensitization rather than creating a penal National Fundamental Duties Commission. Option (D) is incorrect because Article 37 applies only to Part IV (DPSP), and Parliament is fully competent under its Seventh Schedule legislative powers to enact penal statutes giving effect to duties in Part IVA.

ref: Justice J.S. Verma Committee Report (1999); Laxmikanth Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the constitutional status of co-operative societies across Part III, Part IV, and Part IXB of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Fundamental Right to form co-operative societies under Article 19(1)(c) and the Directive Principle to promote co-operative societies under Article 43B, both inserted by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, continue to remain constitutionally valid and operative even though the Amendment was not ratified by one-half of the State Legislatures.

Statement-II: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of severability to hold that while Part IXB dealing with State co-operative societies required ratification under the proviso to Article 368(2) as it curtailed the exclusive legislative power of States under List II, the amendments to Part III and Part IV did not attract the ratification requirement.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court did not strike down the entirety of the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011. Applying the doctrine of severability, it struck down Part IXB only insofar as it applied to State-level co-operative societies for want of State ratification under Article 368(2), while upholding Article 19(1)(c), Article 43B, and Part IXB's application to multi-State co-operative societies.

exp.why: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 made three major changes: (i) it added the words 'or co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c) in Part III; (ii) it inserted Article 43B (promotion of co-operative societies) in Part IV; and (iii) it added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT). A common misconception is that the Supreme Court struck down the entire 97th Amendment in 2021 for lack of ratification by half of the State Legislatures. In reality, both the Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c) and the Directive Principle under Article 43B remain completely valid and operative.

In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court explained why Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B survived despite the absence of ratification under the proviso to Article 368(2). Part IXB dictated mandatory terms for State legislation on 'co-operative societies', a subject exclusively in Entry 32 of the State List (List II), thereby requiring ratification by half the States. However, amending Part III (Article 19(1)(c)) and Part IV (Article 43B), as well as regulating Multi-State Co-operative Societies (Entry 44 of List I), did not trench upon the entrenched federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) and were upheld via the doctrine of severability. Thus, Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 19(1)(c), Art. 43B & Part IXB; Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 9 & 60

stem: With reference to the Directive Principles relating to labour and social welfare in Part IV of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 41 explicitly qualifies the State's obligation to make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education, and to public assistance in cases of unemployment and old age with the phrase 'within the limits of its economic capacity and development'.

2. The directive requiring the State to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief is enshrined in Article 42, whereas the participation of workers in the management of industries is provided separately under Article 43A.

3. Article 43 directs the State to endeavour to secure to all workers a 'living wage'—a constitutional ideal broader than a statutory minimum wage—along with conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 41, 42, 43, and 43A form a cohesive cluster of socialistic labour directives in Part IV with precise textual boundaries: Article 41 contains an express fiscal-capacity caveat, Article 42 mandates maternity relief, Article 43 sets the aspirational benchmark of a 'living wage', and Article 43A (added in 1976) promotes industrial democracy.

exp.why: Article 41 explicitly states: 'The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of undeserved want.' The Supreme Court (e.g., in Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P.) has repeatedly highlighted this explicit economic-capacity qualification in Article 41.

Article 42 in the original Constitution directs that 'The State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief' (which serves as the constitutional foundation for the Maternity Benefit Act). In contrast, worker participation in management of industries was inserted separately as Article 43A by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

Article 43 expressly mandates the State to endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers—agricultural, industrial or otherwise—'work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities'. In Express Newspapers v. Union of India, the Supreme Court distinguished the aspirational 'living wage' under Article 43 (which includes comfort, education, and social needs) from a bare statutory 'minimum wage'.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 41, 42, 43 & 43A; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the environmental provisions enshrined in Part IV (Article 48A) and Part IVA (Article 51A(g)) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both Article 48A and Article 51A(g) expressly mention the protection of 'lakes and rivers' alongside forests and wildlife.

2. The moral and constitutional exhortation 'to have compassion for living creatures' is explicitly incorporated as a Fundamental Duty of every citizen under Article 51A(g), but does not appear in the text of Article 48A.
3. Both Article 48A and Article 51A(g) were introduced into the Constitution simultaneously by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While both Article 48A and Article 51A(g) were introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 to embed environmental constitutionalism, the text of Article 51A(g) is broader in enumeration: it explicitly mentions 'lakes, rivers' and 'compassion for living creatures', whereas Article 48A mentions only the 'environment' and 'forests and wild life'.

exp.why: A close reading of the constitutional text reveals a clear difference. Article 48A reads: 'The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.' It does not mention 'lakes and rivers'. In contrast, Article 51A(g) reads: 'to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures.'

The phrase 'and to have compassion for living creatures' (which was relied upon extensively by the Supreme Court in Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja, 2014) is explicitly present in Article 51A(g) under Part IVA, whereas Article 48A in Part IV contains no such phrase.

Following the 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment, Parliament enacted the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, which simultaneously inserted Article 48A into Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) and Part IVA containing Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duties).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 48A & Art. 51A(g); 42nd Amendment Act, 1976

stem: In the context of the constitutional relationship between the term 'Socialist' in the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV, as clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Indian constitutional framework, 'socialism' denotes the commitment to a welfare State that strives to eliminate inequalities in income, status, and opportunities rather than adherence to any rigid economic dogma.

2. The constitutional mandate of socialism read with Article 39(b) obligates the State to nationalize key means of production and precludes the adoption of market-oriented economic policies or private enterprise in core sectors.

3. The insertion of the word 'Socialist' into the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 made explicit the egalitarian socioeconomic vision that was already embedded in the original text of Articles 38 and 39 of Part IV.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024) and Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), the Supreme Court held that Indian constitutional socialism reflects a welfare State (as embodied in Part IV) and does not bind elected governments to state monopoly or restrict private enterprise.

exp.why: In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (November 2024), the Supreme Court upheld the 1976 insertion of the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' in the Preamble and clarified that in the Indian context, 'socialism' does not mean a totalitarian state-controlled economy; rather, it signifies a welfare state committed to social and economic justice and equality of opportunity as envisioned in Part IV.

Both in the 9-Judge Bench ruling in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) on Article 39(b) and in Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court rejected the contention that constitutional socialism or Part IV binds the State to nationalize private property or restricts private enterprise. The Court emphasized that the Constitution does not mandate a static economic ideology and allows elected governments full flexibility to pursue mixed or market-led economic growth alongside thriving private enterprise.

The Supreme Court observed that even prior to the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, the soul of Indian welfare socialism was already woven into the original Constitution through Articles 38 and 39 of Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy); the 1976 amendment merely made this implicit constitutional philosophy explicit in the Preamble.

ref: Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (SC, Nov 2024); Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (9-Judge Bench, Nov 2024)

stem: During the making of the Indian Constitution, the structural bifurcation of rights into two distinct categories—'justiciable' Fundamental Rights (subsequently placed in Part III) and 'non-justiciable' Directive Principles of State Policy (subsequently placed in Part IV)—was first formally recommended in Indian constitutional history by which of the following prior to being adopted on the advice of Sir B.N. Rau?

opts.B: The Tej Bahadur Sapru Committee Report (1945)

core: The Constitutional Proposals of the Sapru Committee (1945) first recommended dividing fundamental rights in India into two categories: justiciable rights enforceable by courts and non-justiciable directives guiding governance. Constitutional Adviser Sir B.N. Rau subsequently operationalized this scheme in his draft notes for the Constituent Assembly.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct: The Tej Bahadur Sapru Committee Report (published in 1945) examined the question of minority rights and fundamental rights and was the first committee in Indian constitutional history to recommend dividing fundamental rights into two distinct classes—'justiciable' and 'non-justiciable'. Drawing upon the 1937 Irish Constitution and the Sapru Report, the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly, Sir B.N. Rau, advocated placing justiciable rights in Part III and non-justiciable positive socio-economic obligations in Part IV. Option (A) is incorrect because the Nehru Report (1928) proposed a single unified list of Fundamental Rights without bifurcating them into justiciable and non-justiciable parts. Option (C) is incorrect because the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended the insertion of Fundamental Duties (Part IVA). Option (D) is incorrect because the Sarkaria Commission (1983) dealt with Centre-State relations.

ref: Constituent Assembly Debates; Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the enforceability and emergency operation of Part III, Part IV, and Part IVA of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: While the enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Part III (except Articles 20 and 21) can be suspended during the operation of a Proclamation of National Emergency under Articles 358 and 359, the Constitution contains no provision for the suspension of either Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) or Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) during an Emergency.

Statement-II: Unlike Fundamental Rights which always require specific parliamentary legislation under Article 35 before citizens can invoke them in a court of law, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties are self-executory constitutional injunctions that are directly enforceable through judicial writs without any enabling statute.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are predominantly self-executory negative injunctions enforceable by courts, which is why Articles 358 and 359 specifically provide for suspending their judicial enforcement during a National Emergency. Conversely, Part IV and Part IVA are non-justiciable positive mandates that depend on enabling legislation for legal enforcement and therefore require no constitutional suspension clause.

exp.why: Under Part XVIII of the Constitution, Article 358 provides for the automatic suspension of Article 19 during a National Emergency declared on grounds of war or external aggression, and Article 359 empowers the President to suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21). Because Directive Principles (Part IV) and Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) are non-justiciable and do not confer a right to move courts against the State in the first place, the Constitution neither provides nor needs any mechanism to suspend Part IV or Part IVA during an Emergency.

Statement-II reverses the constitutional position. Most Fundamental Rights in Part III are directly enforceable and self-executory (only a few specific provisions—such as prescribing punishments for offences under Articles 17 and 23, or making provisions under Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33, and 34—require parliamentary legislation under Article 35). Conversely, Directive Principles (Part IV, per Article 37) and Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) are non-justiciable and are NOT self-executory; they cannot be directly enforced through writs and require enabling statutes enacted by the appropriate legislature to create legally enforceable rights or penalties.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 32, 35, 37, 51A, 358 & 359; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 8, 9 & 10

stem: With reference to the initiation and introduction of a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An amendment of the Constitution can be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament and not in any State Legislature.
2. Such a Bill can be introduced either by a Minister or by a Private Member.

3. Similar to a Bill seeking to alter the boundaries of a State under Article 3, a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 requires the prior recommendation of the President before its introduction in Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 368(2) vests the power to initiate a Constitutional Amendment Bill exclusively in either House of Parliament, exercisable by both Ministers and Private Members without requiring prior Presidential recommendation.

exp.why: Under Article 368(2) of the Constitution, an amendment of the Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). State Legislatures have no power to initiate a Constitutional Amendment Bill (their role in creation/abolition of Legislative Councils under Article 169 is merely to pass a resolution enabling Parliament to legislate by simple majority outside Article 368).

Unlike a Money Bill (which can only be introduced by a Minister), a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 can be introduced either by a Minister (Government Bill) or by a Member of Parliament who is not a Minister (Private Member's Bill), subject to examination by the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions.

Unlike a Money Bill under Article 117(1) or a Bill for the reorganization of States under the proviso to Article 3, a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 does not require the prior recommendation or permission of the President for its introduction in Parliament, because requiring prior executive permission would fetter the constituent power of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 368(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 10 (Amendment of the Constitution)

stem: Under Article 368(2) of the Constitution of India, the 'special majority' required in each House of Parliament for the passage of a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandates that the Bill must be passed by:

opts.A: A majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House, irrespective of existing vacancies or absentees.
opts.B: A majority of the then members of that House excluding vacancies, and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
opts.C: A majority of the members present and voting, provided that such majority is not less than half of the total membership of that House.
opts.D: A majority of the total membership of that House, irrespective of vacancies or absentees, and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.

core: The special majority under Article 368(2) imposes a dual requirement at each effective stage of passage: an absolute majority of the total membership of the House (exceeding 50% of total sanctioned strength) AND a majority of at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because Article 368(2) stipulates two concurrent conditions: (1) a majority of the 'total membership of that House' (defined under Rule 158 of the Lok Sabha Rules as the total number of members comprising the House irrespective of whether there are vacancies or absentees on any account, i.e., more than 50% of total strength), and (2) a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House 'present and voting'. Option (A) is incorrect because it confuses Article 368 with the impeachment threshold of the President under Article 61 ('not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House'). Option (B) is incorrect because 'all the then members' (effective majority excluding vacancies) applies to the removal of the Vice-President, Speaker, and Deputy Speaker, not Article 368. Option (C) is incorrect because it omits the mandatory two-thirds requirement of members present and voting.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 368(2); Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, Rules 157-158; Laxmikanth Ch. 10

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the passage of a Constitutional Amendment Bill in Parliament:
items: Statement-I: In case of a deadlock between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha over a Constitutional Amendment Bill, the President cannot summon a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve the disagreement.

Statement-II: Article 368(2) explicitly mandates that a Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed in each House of Parliament separately by the prescribed special majority, thereby overriding the general provision for a joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Rajya Sabha enjoys complete parity with the Lok Sabha in exercising constituent power under Article 368; a Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed by each House separately and cannot be referred to a joint sitting under Article 108.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. If one House passes a Constitutional Amendment Bill and the other House rejects it or proposes amendments to which the originating House does not agree, the Bill comes to an end. There is no constitutional provision for holding a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve a deadlock over a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Article 368(2) constitutes a special self-contained code for constitutional amendments and mandates that a Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed 'in each House' by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting. Because Article 368(2) specifically requires separate passage in each House by a special majority (protecting the federal principle so the numerically larger Lok Sabha cannot outvote the Rajya Sabha in a simple-majority joint sitting), it overrides the general deadlock-resolution mechanism under Article 108 (which applies only to ordinary Bills and Financial Bills under Article 117).

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 108 & Art. 368(2); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 11

stem: With reference to the procedure for amending different provisions of the Constitution of India under Article 368(2), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Any Constitutional Amendment Bill seeking to alter the representation of States in Parliament or any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.
2. An amendment seeking to alter the provisions of Article 368 itself also requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.

3. Any amendment that seeks to abridge or modify a Fundamental Right guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before being presented to the President.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Only those entrenched federal provisions expressly enumerated in Clauses (a) to (e) of the Proviso to Article 368(2) require ratification by at least half the State Legislatures; Fundamental Rights (Part III) and DPSPs (Part IV) are amended by a special majority of Parliament alone.
