exp.why: Under Clauses (c) and (d) of the Proviso to Article 368(2), any amendment seeking to make a change in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule or the representation of States in Parliament affects the federal distribution of power and therefore requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.

Under Clause (e) of the Proviso to Article 368(2), the amending clause itself (the provisions of Article 368) is entrenched. Consequently, Parliament cannot unilaterally alter the procedure of constitutional amendment without ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.

Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are NOT included in the Proviso to Article 368(2). Therefore, amendments to Part III or Part IV require only a special majority of both Houses of Parliament under the main part of Article 368(2) (subject to the judicial limitation that they cannot damage or destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution), and do not require ratification by State Legislatures.

ref: Constitution of India, Proviso to Art. 368(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the ratification of a Constitutional Amendment Bill by the State Legislatures under the Proviso to Article 368(2), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The ratification by a State Legislature is effected through a resolution passed by a simple majority of the members of that Legislature present and voting.
2. The Constitution prescribes a mandatory time frame of six months within which the State Legislatures must communicate their ratification or rejection of the Bill to Parliament.

3. Once the Bill has been validly ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States, it can be presented to the President for assent even if some of the remaining State Legislatures have not yet taken any action on it.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: State ratification under the Proviso to Article 368(2) requires only a resolution passed by a simple majority of at least half the State Legislatures prior to Presidential presentation, with no constitutional time limit prescribed for the States.

exp.why: The Proviso to Article 368(2) stipulates that the amendment shall require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States 'by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures'. Since no special majority is specified for the State Legislatures, such a resolution is passed by an ordinary simple majority of members present and voting in the State Legislature.

The Constitution of India does not prescribe any time limit within which the State Legislatures must ratify or reject a Constitutional Amendment Bill referred to them under the Proviso to Article 368(2).

As long as the Amendment Bill has been validly ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before the Bill is presented to the President for assent, the constitutional requirement of the Proviso to Article 368(2) is satisfied. It is not necessary to wait for the remaining States to complete their deliberations once the threshold of half the States has been crossed.

ref: Constitution of India, Proviso to Art. 368(2); Jatin Chandra v. Union of India; Laxmikanth Ch. 10

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the assent of the President to a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368(2):
items: Statement-I: When a Constitutional Amendment Bill duly passed under Article 368 is presented to the President, the President is constitutionally bound to give assent and cannot withhold assent from the Bill.

Statement-II: While the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 took away the President's power to exercise an absolute veto on a Constitutional Amendment Bill, it preserved the President's power under the proviso to Article 111 to return the Bill once to the Houses for reconsideration.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 amended Article 368(2) to replace the discretionary phraseology of Article 111 with the mandatory command that the President 'shall give his assent to the Bill', eliminating all forms of Presidential veto (including returning the Bill for reconsideration).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 substituted the words 'it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill' in Article 368(2). Consequently, once a Constitutional Amendment Bill is duly passed by both Houses of Parliament (and ratified by State Legislatures, where required), the President is constitutionally obligated to give assent and cannot withhold it.

Statement-II is incorrect. The mandatory language inserted into Article 368(2) by the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 serves as a self-contained code for Presidential assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills, overriding the general veto options available under Article 111 for ordinary Bills. Therefore, the President can neither withhold assent nor return a Constitutional Amendment Bill for the reconsideration of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 368(2) & 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971; Laxmikanth Ch. 10 & Ch. 18

stem: With reference to the procedure for amending various provisions of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A parliamentary law enacted under Article 169 for the abolition or creation of a Legislative Council in a State contains supplemental provisions that modify the Constitution, yet it is expressly excluded from being deemed an amendment under Article 368.

2. A law made under Article 4 to alter the boundaries of a State that consequentially modifies the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha under the Fourth Schedule requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States under the proviso to Article 368(2).

3. Any addition, variation, or repeal of the provisions of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules governing the administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas can be effected only through a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by a special majority under Article 368(2).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Several constitutional provisions—such as Articles 4, 169, Paragraph 7 of the Fifth Schedule, and Paragraph 21 of the Sixth Schedule—contain self-contained flexibility clauses allowing Parliament to modify constitutional text by an ordinary legislative process (simple majority) while expressly declaring that such laws shall not be deemed amendments for the purposes of Article 368.

exp.why: Under Article 169(1), Parliament may by law provide for the abolition or creation of the Legislative Council of a State if the Legislative Assembly of that State passes a resolution to that effect by a special majority. Under Articles 169(2) and 169(3), any such parliamentary law contains such provisions for the amendment of the Constitution (such as amending Article 168) as may be necessary, and no such law is deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. Thus, Parliament passes it by a simple majority like an ordinary piece of legislation.

Although changes to the representation of States in Parliament generally fall under the entrenched proviso to Article 368(2) requiring special majority plus State ratification, Article 4 creates an express constitutional exception. Under Article 4(1) and 4(2), any law referred to in Article 2 or Article 3 (admission, formation, or alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of States) shall contain such supplemental provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule (allocation of seats in the Council of States) as may be necessary, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. Hence, it requires only a simple majority of Parliament and does not require ratification by the States.

Paragraph 7 of the Fifth Schedule and Paragraph 21 of the Sixth Schedule expressly empower Parliament to amend by law—by way of addition, variation, or repeal—any of the provisions of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules respectively. Both schedules explicitly stipulate that no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368, meaning they can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 4, 169, 368, Fifth Schedule (Para 7) & Sixth Schedule (Para 21); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 11

stem: With reference to the constitutional relationship between Article 13 and Article 368 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court struck down the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, holding that a Constitutional Amendment Act is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2).

2. The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) to create an explicit constitutional distinction between ordinary legislative enactments and constituent amendments made under Article 368.

3. Even though a Constitutional Amendment Act falls outside the purview of the bar under Article 13(2), Parliament's constituent power under Article 368(1) cannot be exercised to abrogate a Fundamental Right in a manner that destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the 13-Judge Bench overruled I.C. Golaknath (1967) and upheld the validity of the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, confirming that a Constitutional Amendment enacted in exercise of constituent power under Article 368 is not 'law' under Article 13(2). However, the Court simultaneously held that constituent power under Article 368 is subject to the implied substantive limitation of the Basic Structure Doctrine.

exp.why: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court did NOT strike down the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971. Instead, the Court overruled its earlier decision in I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) and unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of the 24th Amendment Act, affirming that the expression 'law' in Article 13(2) applies only to ordinary legislative enactments and does not include constituent amendments made under Article 368.

To neutralize the effect of the Golaknath ruling (which had treated constitutional amendments as 'law' under Article 13(2) and noticed that Article 368's marginal note referred only to the 'procedure for amendment'), the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 changed the marginal heading of Article 368 to include the 'power of Parliament to amend the Constitution', inserted Article 368(1) conferring constituent power, and added mutually reinforcing exclusions in Article 13(4) ('Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368') and Article 368(3) ('Nothing in article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article').

While Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) validly immunize Constitutional Amendment Acts from the specific threshold bar of Article 13(2), the majority in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the constituent power under Article 368(1) to 'amend by way of addition, variation or repeal' is inherently limited. Consequently, while Parliament can amend or abridge Fundamental Rights, it cannot alter or abrogate them to an extent that damages or destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 13(2), 13(4), 368(1) & 368(3); Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973); D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following doctrinal developments in the constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court of India regarding the power of Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights:
items: 1. Invocation of the doctrine of 'prospective overruling' to declare that Parliament lacks the power to abridge Fundamental Rights, while preserving the validity of earlier Constitutional Amendment Acts.

2. First judicial expression of doubt in concurring minority opinions by Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar questioning whether Fundamental Rights were intended to be 'playthings of a special majority' and whether the Constitution possesses permanent 'basic features'.

3. Unanimous judicial pronouncement by a Five-Judge Constitution Bench that the word 'law' in Article 13(2) denotes only ordinary legislative enactments and excludes constituent amendments enacted under Article 368.

4. Judicial formulation by a 7:6 majority of a Thirteen-Judge Bench that the constituent power to 'amend' under Article 368 carries an inherent limitation against altering the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the judicial developments given above, from the earliest to the latest?
core: The evolution of the Basic Structure Doctrine progressed through four landmark stages: unconditional upholdings of amending power in Shankari Prasad (1951), the famous minority doubts of Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar in Sajjan Singh (1964/1965), the 6:5 prospective bar on abridging Fundamental Rights in Golaknath (1967), and the 7:6 synthesis establishing the Basic Structure limitation in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

exp.why: Item 1 refers to I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (decided in February 1967, by an 11-Judge Bench in a 6:5 ruling led by Chief Justice K. Subba Rao), which imported the American doctrine of 'prospective overruling' to hold that Parliament would have no power from the date of the judgment to amend Part III so as to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights, while saving the 1st, 4th, and 17th Amendments.

Item 2 refers to Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (decided in October 1964, reported in 1965 SCR, by a 5-Judge Bench). While the 3-Judge majority led by CJI Gajendragadkar reaffirmed Shankari Prasad, Justice M. Hidayatullah and Justice J.R. Mudholkar authored historic separate opinions expressing grave doubts about whether Part III rights were mere 'playthings of a special majority' and Justice Mudholkar explicitly introduced the phrase 'basic features' of the Constitution (drawing from the Pakistan Supreme Court's decision in Fazlul Quader Chowdhry).

Item 3 refers to Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India (decided in October 1951 by a 5-Judge Constitution Bench), where the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, drawing a clear distinction between ordinary legislative power and constituent power to hold that 'law' in Article 13(2) does not include amendments made under Article 368.

Item 4 refers to Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (decided on April 24, 1973 by a 13-Judge Bench by a 7:6 majority), which overruled Golaknath on the scope of Article 13(2) but adopted the seed sown in Sajjan Singh to propound the Basic Structure Doctrine. Hence, the correct chronological order from earliest to latest is 3 (1951) -> 2 (1964/1965) -> 1 (1967) -> 4 (1973).

ref: Shankari Prasad (1951); Sajjan Singh (1965); I.C. Golaknath (1967); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Granville Austin, Working a Democratic Constitution

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Basic Structure Doctrine of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Neither the text of the Constitution of India nor the Supreme Court in its constitutional jurisprudence has laid down an exhaustive, closed catalogue of all the features that constitute the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

Statement-II: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Basic Structure limitation was derived not from an enumerated constitutional clause, but as an implied structural limitation inherent in the word 'amend' under Article 368—requiring the Court to determine on a case-by-case basis whether an impugned amendment destroys the overarching identity of the Constitution.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Because the Basic Structure Doctrine is not rooted in an explicit enumerated list in the constitutional text, but was judicially deduced in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) as an implied structural limitation inherent in the word 'amend' under Article 368 to preserve constitutional identity, its facets are necessarily illustrative and identified by the Supreme Court on a case-by-case basis.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The phrase 'Basic Structure' finds no mention anywhere in the text of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, both in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and in subsequent Constitution Bench rulings, the judges provided only illustrative examples of basic features (such as supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, federalism, judicial review, separation of powers, and parliamentary democracy) and purposefully refrained from framing an exhaustive, closed catalogue.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the majority deduced the Basic Structure Doctrine not from any explicit enumerated catalogue in the text, but from the structural and etymological meaning of the word 'amend' in Article 368—reasoning that a power to amend an existing Constitution does not encompass the power to destroy or abrogate its foundational identity. Because this limitation protects the overarching identity of the Constitution against unforeseen future inroads, the Supreme Court applies it holistically on a case-by-case basis rather than freezing it into a closed list.

ref: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225; M.P. Jain, Indian Constitutional Law

stem: With reference to the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 and the judgment of the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 formally repealed Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, which had been inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 to oust judicial review of constitutional amendments.

2. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that while Parliament possesses an unlimited constituent power under Article 368(5), any Constitutional Amendment Act remains subject to procedural judicial review for compliance with the special majority requirement under Article 368(2).

3. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the entirety of Article 31C, ruling that no Directive Principle of State Policy can ever be accorded constitutional protection against challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were never repealed by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978; rather, they were struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) on the ground that a 'limited amending power' is itself part of the Basic Structure. In the same case, the Court struck down only the 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C, restoring the pre-1976 scope of Article 31C protecting laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) (a position reaffirmed by the 9-Judge Bench in Property Owners Association, 2024).

exp.why: Section 55 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 to bar any court from questioning a constitutional amendment on any ground and to declare that there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament. However, the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 did NOT repeal Article 368(4) and (5). Instead, these clauses were judicially invalidated and declared void by the Five-Judge Constitution Bench in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980).

In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court emphatically rejected the claim of unlimited constituent power and struck down both Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368. Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud famously held that 'since the Constitution had conferred a limited amending power on the Parliament, the Parliament cannot under the exercise of that limited power enlarge that very power into an absolute power. Indeed, a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution.' Thus, judicial review of constitutional amendments is substantive (for violation of the Basic Structure) as well as procedural.

In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court did NOT strike down the entirety of Article 31C. It invalidated only Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, which had expanded Article 31C to grant primacy to all Directive Principles in Part IV over Articles 14 and 19, holding that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a basic feature. The original unamended text of Article 31C (inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971 and upheld in Kesavananda Bharati), which shields laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, remained valid—a constitutional position explicitly confirmed by the Nine-Judge Bench in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 31C, 368(4) & 368(5); Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980); Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024)

stem: With reference to the immunity enjoyed by laws placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B of the Constitution of India and the scope of judicial review, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court drew a line of demarcation at April 24, 1973, holding that all constitutional amendments inserting statutes into the Ninth Schedule prior to that date are valid and immune from Basic Structure challenge.

2. As per the Nine-Judge Bench ruling in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 loses the protective shield of Article 31B altogether and becomes automatically void if it abridges any Fundamental Right enumerated in Part III.

3. While examining whether a post-1973 Ninth Schedule statute violates the Basic Structure Doctrine, the Supreme Court applies the 'direct impact and effect test' (rights test) rather than the 'form of the amendment test'.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007), April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati verdict) serves as the cut-off date for Ninth Schedule immunity. Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are not automatically void merely for abridging a Part III right; rather, they are tested via a two-step inquiry using the 'direct impact and effect test' to see whether the violation of Fundamental Rights (especially Articles 14, 19, and 21) damages or destroys the Basic Structure.

exp.why: In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court applied the ratio of Kesavananda Bharati prospectively to the Ninth Schedule, establishing April 24, 1973 (the date on which the judgment in Kesavananda Bharati was pronounced) as the constitutional cut-off date. All amendments to the Constitution made before April 24, 1973 by which the Ninth Schedule was amended to include various Acts and Regulations were declared valid and immune from challenge, whereas inclusions made on or after that date were held open to challenge on the ground that they damage or destroy the Basic Structure.

In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the unanimous Nine-Judge Bench did NOT hold that Article 31B is rendered completely redundant or that any post-1973 Ninth Schedule law becomes automatically void if it abridges any Fundamental Right. Instead, the Court laid down a two-stage test: first, whether the Ninth Schedule law violates any Fundamental Right in Part III; and second, if it does, whether the extent of such violation damages or destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution (viewed through the 'essence of the rights' test and the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21 read with the underlying principles of Part III). Only if the violation crosses the threshold of damaging the Basic Structure will the law lose Article 31B protection and be struck down.

In I.R. Coelho (2007), the Nine-Judge Bench explicitly clarified that when testing whether a constitutional amendment placing laws in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 violates the Basic Structure, the determinative criterion is the 'direct impact and effect test' (also termed the 'rights test'), rather than the 'form and substance of the amendment test'. This means the Court examines the actual consequence and impact of the immunized statute on the overarching principles of Fundamental Rights, rather than merely looking at the formal nature of the constituent act.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 31B & Ninth Schedule; Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981); I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 2 SCC 1

stem: With reference to landmark judicial pronouncements on the Basic Structure Doctrine and constitutional amendments, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) : Struck down Clause (4) of Article 329A inserted by the 39th Amendment Act for abrogating free and fair elections and judicial review
2. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) : Struck down Clauses 2(d) of Article 323A and 3(d) of Article 323B inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act for excluding the writ jurisdiction of High Courts

3. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) : Struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act for ousting judicial review without State ratification under Article 368(2)
4. M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) : Upheld the constitutional validity of the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th Amendment Acts relating to reservation in promotions on the anvil of the Basic Structure
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Each landmark Basic Structure ruling targets a specific constitutional overreach: the 39th Amendment in Indira Nehru Gandhi, Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule in Kihoto Hollohan, tribunal exclusion clauses in L. Chandra Kumar, and reservation amendments in M. Nagaraj.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court invalidated Clause (4) of Article 329A (inserted by the 39th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975), which sought to place the election disputes of the Prime Minister and the Speaker beyond judicial scrutiny, holding that it violated free and fair elections, rule of law, and judicial review.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Clauses 2(d) of Article 323A and 3(d) of Article 323B (inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976), which excluded the jurisdiction of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 over tribunals, were struck down in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), not in Kihoto Hollohan.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule (inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985), which barred all courts from reviewing the Speaker's decision on disqualification for defection, was struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) because it encroached upon the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts under Articles 136, 226, and 227 without obtaining ratification by half of the State Legislatures under the Proviso to Article 368(2).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench upheld the validity of the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th Constitutional Amendment Acts (inserting and modifying Articles 16(4A), 16(4B), and the proviso to Article 335), holding that these enabling provisions do not violate the Basic Structure of equality so long as the ceiling limit, creamy layer exclusion, and backwardness/inadequacy criteria are respected.

ref: Constitution Art. 368; Laxmikanth Ch. 11 (Basic Structure of the Constitution)

stem: With reference to the judicial evolution of the Basic Structure Doctrine of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy has been judicially recognised as an essential feature of the Basic Structure.
2. The Parliamentary system of government, anchored in the collective responsibility of the Executive to the Legislature, constitutes a component of the Basic Structure.

3. In Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that the secret ballot system and the State domicile requirement for election to the Rajya Sabha are integral features of federalism under the Basic Structure.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While overarching constitutional principles like the Parliamentary system and the harmony between Part III and Part IV belong to the Basic Structure, specific electoral modalities such as secret ballot or domicile criteria for Rajya Sabha elections do not.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down sections of the 42nd Amendment that gave absolute primacy to all Directive Principles over Articles 14, 19, and 21, declaring that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Part III and Part IV, and that giving absolute primacy to one over the other would disturb the harmony of the Constitution, which is an essential feature of the Basic Structure.

Statement 2 is correct. Beginning with Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reiterated in S.R. Bommai (1994) and Kuldip Nayar (2006), the Supreme Court has consistently held that the Parliamentary system of government—characterised by the accountability and collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Legislature—forms part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench upheld the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2003, which replaced the secret ballot with an open ballot system for Rajya Sabha elections and removed the requirement that a candidate must be an elector in the specific State they seek to represent. The Court held that neither the secret ballot in indirect elections nor the State domicile qualification is a part of federalism or the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

ref: Minerva Mills v. UoI (1980); Kuldip Nayar v. UoI (2006); Laxmikanth Ch. 11

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the judicial review of legislation in India:
items: Statement-I: According to the settled constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court, an ordinary plenary statute enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature cannot generally be invalidated solely on the abstract ground that it violates the Basic Structure of the Constitution, unless the violation is traced to a specific constitutional provision.

Statement-II: The Basic Structure Doctrine operates as an implied limitation on the constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, whereas an ordinary statute cannot amend the Constitution and is tested on legislative competence and conformity with Part III and other express constitutional provisions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Basic Structure Doctrine is primarily a limitation on constituent power under Article 368; ordinary plenary legislation is subordinate to the Constitution and is tested against legislative competence (Articles 245-246) and express constitutional limitations including Part III.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977), Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006), and reaffirmed in Anjum Kadari v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that ordinary plenary legislation cannot be struck down merely for violating an overarching Basic Structure principle (like secularism or federalism) in the abstract; to invalidate an ordinary statute, the violation must be anchored in lack of legislative competence or breach of Part III or another express provision of the Constitution.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Because a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368 alters the text of the Constitution itself and is exempted from Article 13(2) via Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), the judiciary evolved the Basic Structure Doctrine to prevent the destruction of the Constitution's identity. Conversely, an ordinary law is subordinate to the existing constitutional text, cannot alter the Constitution, and is therefore fully checked by testing it against legislative competence and express constitutional provisions.

ref: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975); Anjum Kadari v. UoI (2024); D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: With reference to the amendability of the Preamble under Article 368 and recent Supreme Court jurisprudence thereon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and is subject to the constituent amending power of Parliament under Article 368, provided such amendment does not abrogate the Basic Structure.
2. The constitutional inclusion of the term 'Socialist' in the Preamble mandates state monopoly over key economic sectors and bars the expansion of private enterprise unless the Preamble is amended.

3. The presence of the original date of adoption (26th November, 1949) in the text of the Preamble does not fetter Parliament's power under Article 368 to subsequently insert new foundational terms into the Preamble.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court upheld the 1976 insertion of 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble under Article 368, clarifying that the 1949 adoption date does not freeze the Preamble and that Indian constitutional socialism signifies a welfare state within a mixed economy rather than a restriction on private enterprise.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Overruling its earlier view in the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368, subject to the condition that no amendment can destroy the basic features enshrined in the Preamble.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court upheld the 42nd Amendment's insertion of 'Socialist' and 'Secular' as part of the Basic Structure and clarified that in the Indian constitutional context, 'Socialism' does not mandate state monopoly or restrict private enterprise; rather, it denotes a welfare state committed to eliminating social and economic inequalities while allowing a flourishing private sector and mixed economy.

Statement 3 is correct. In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024), the petitioners contended that because the Preamble specifies a historical date of adoption (26th November, 1949), Parliament could not retrospectively or prospectively insert 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' via the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. The Supreme Court dismissed this argument, holding that the constituent power under Article 368 extends to the Preamble notwithstanding the historical adoption date recorded in its text.

ref: Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (SC 2024); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Laxmikanth Ch. 4 & 11

stem: Under the constitutional framework governing legislative procedures in India, which one of the following procedural features is common to both an Ordinary Bill under Article 107 and a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368?

opts.A: Both categories of Bills can be initiated either in a House of Parliament or through a resolution passed by a State Legislative Assembly.
opts.B: Both categories of Bills can be introduced in either House of Parliament by a Minister or by a Private Member without requiring the prior recommendation of the President.
opts.C: In the event of an unresolved deadlock between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, both categories of Bills can be referred to a joint sitting summoned by the President.
opts.D: When presented to the President after passage by both Houses, the President may return either category of Bill once for reconsideration by the Houses.

core: Both Ordinary Bills (under Article 107) and Constitutional Amendment Bills (under Article 368) share the procedural flexibility that they can be introduced in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, by either a Minister or a Private Member, without needing prior Presidential recommendation.

exp.why: Option B is correct because both an Ordinary Bill and a Constitutional Amendment Bill can be introduced in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, can be piloted by either a Minister or a Private Member, and do not require the prior recommendation of the President for introduction. Option A is incorrect because a Constitutional Amendment Bill can be initiated only in either House of Parliament and never in a State Legislature. Option C is incorrect because a joint sitting under Article 108 is available only for Ordinary Bills and Financial Bills, never for a Constitutional Amendment Bill, which must be passed by each House separately by special majority. Option D is incorrect because the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 amended Article 368(2) to make it mandatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill, removing both withholding of assent and suspensive veto (return for reconsideration).

ref: Constitution Art. 107, 108, 111 & 368; Laxmikanth Ch. 10 (Amendment of the Constitution)

stem: With reference to the procedural requirements under the Proviso to Article 368(2) and the judicial scrutiny of Constitutional Amendment Acts, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah, the Supreme Court struck down the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act in its entirety, holding that the Doctrine of Severability cannot be applied to an amendment that violates the procedural mandate of Article 368(2).

2. A Constitutional Amendment Bill that curtails the exclusive legislative domain of State Legislatures over a State List subject does not require State ratification under the Proviso to Article 368(2) if it refrains from textually altering the entries in the Seventh Schedule.

3. The Supreme Court invalidated the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act primarily on the procedural ground that it was presented to the President for assent without being ratified by one-half of the State Legislatures.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Proviso to Article 368(2) is triggered by the substantive impact of an amendment on federal provisions (substance over form), and in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court applied the Doctrine of Severability to strike down Part IXB only for State co-operative societies while retaining it for Multi-State co-operative societies.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court by majority explicitly applied the Doctrine of Severability to the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011. It struck down Part IXB only insofar as it applied to co-operative societies operating within a single State (for want of State ratification under the Proviso to Article 368(2)), while upholding the operation of Part IXB with respect to Multi-State Co-operative Societies as well as the amendments to Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Applying the 'direct impact and effect' test laid down in Sajjan Singh, Kihoto Hollohan, and Rajendra N. Shah, the Supreme Court held that if a Constitutional Amendment substantially restricts or regulates the exclusive legislative power of State Legislatures over a subject in the State List (such as Co-operative Societies under Entry 32 of List II), it brings about a 'change in' the Seventh Schedule in substance even without textually amending the entry, and therefore mandatorily requires ratification by at least one-half of the State Legislatures under the Proviso to Article 368(2).

Statement 3 is incorrect. The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 (which established the National Judicial Appointments Commission) had in fact been duly ratified by more than half of the State Legislatures before receiving Presidential assent. In the Fourth Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 2015), the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment on the substantive ground that it violated the Basic Structure (judicial independence and judicial primacy in appointments), not for non-compliance with the procedural ratification requirement.

ref: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021); Fourth Judges Case (2015); Constitution Art. 368(2)

stem: With reference to the structural balance between federal and unitary features in the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The division of legislative and executive powers between the Union and the States by a written Constitution, coupled with the supremacy of the Constitution, constitutes an essential federal feature of the Indian polity.
2. An integrated judicial system and single citizenship are essential structural hallmarks of a classical federal polity.
3. Bicameralism at the Union level, wherein the Council of States represents the constituent units of the federation, acts as a federal institutional design in the Indian constitutional framework.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Constitution combines classical federal features—such as a written supreme Constitution, division of powers under the Seventh Schedule, an independent judiciary, and a bicameral Parliament—with strong unitary features like single citizenship and an integrated judicial hierarchy. Understanding which institutional mechanisms preserve state autonomy versus which promote national integration is foundational to analyzing Indian federalism.

exp.why: A written Constitution that entrenches the demarcation of powers between the national government and regional governments, along with constitutional supremacy (preventing unilateral alteration of the federal distribution by ordinary legislation of either tier), is a foundational prerequisite of a federal polity.

This reverses federal and unitary characteristics. A classical federation (such as the United States) features dual citizenship (national and state) and a dual system of courts (federal courts enforcing federal laws and state courts enforcing state laws). India's single citizenship (Part II) and single integrated judicial system (with the Supreme Court at the apex enforcing both Central and State laws) are unitary features designed to counter centrifugal tendencies.

Bicameralism protects federal equilibrium by providing the States institutional representation in the Upper House (Rajya Sabha), whose special concurrence is required for amending federal provisions under the proviso to Article 368(2) or legislating on State List subjects under Article 249.

ref: Constitution of India Part I, Part V, Seventh Schedule; S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 13 (Federal System)

stem: With reference to asymmetric federalism and the Special Provisions for certain States under Part XXI of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Article 371A : Acts of Parliament in respect of ownership and transfer of land and its resources do not apply to Nagaland unless so decided by a resolution of the State Legislative Assembly
2. Article 371G : Acts of Parliament in respect of religious or social practices and customary law do not apply to Manipur unless so decided by a resolution of the State Legislative Assembly
3. Article 371H : The Governor of Arunachal Pradesh has special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State and acts in his individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers
4. Article 371J : The President may by order provide for any special responsibility of the Governor of Karnataka for establishing a separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Part XXI of the Constitution (Articles 371 to 371J) institutionalizes asymmetric federalism by accommodating historical agreements, socio-cultural autonomy of tribal communities in the North-East, and intra-state regional developmental imbalances. Only Nagaland (Article 371A) and Mizoram (Article 371G) enjoy the constitutional shield requiring a State Legislative Assembly resolution before Parliamentary Acts on customary laws and land ownership can take effect.

exp.why: Inserted by the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962, Article 371A(1)(a) stipulates that no Act of Parliament in respect of religious or social practices of the Nagas, Naga customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, and ownership and transfer of land and its resources shall apply to the State of Nagaland unless the Legislative Assembly of Nagaland by a resolution so decides.

Article 371G (inserted by the 53rd Amendment Act, 1986) applies to the State of Mizoram, not Manipur. Under Article 371G, Acts of Parliament relating to religious or social practices of the Mizos, Mizo customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice according to Mizo customary law, and ownership and transfer of land do not apply to Mizoram without a resolution of the Mizoram Legislative Assembly. Special provisions for Manipur are contained in Article 371C, which provides for the constitution and functions of a Committee of the Legislative Assembly consisting of members elected from the Hill Areas.

Under Article 371H(a) (inserted by the 55th Amendment Act, 1986), the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh has a special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State, and in the discharge of his functions in relation thereto, the Governor exercises his individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers, with the Governor's decision being final.

Inserted by the 98th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2012, Article 371J empowers the President to assign special responsibility to the Governor of Karnataka for the establishment of a separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka (now Kalyana-Karnataka) region, equitable allocation of funds, and reservation in educational and vocational training institutions and state government posts for persons belonging to that region.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 371A, 371C, 371G, 371H, and 371J (Part XXI); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 41

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the territorial extent of Central and State legislation under Article 245 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 245(2) of the Constitution, no law made by the Parliament can be deemed invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation outside the geographical territory of India.

Statement-II: Under the judicially evolved Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, a law enacted by a State Legislature is constitutionally valid even if it affects persons or objects located outside the territorial boundaries of that State, provided there is a real and sufficient connection between the State and the subject-matter.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 245 establishes an asymmetrical regime for territorial jurisdiction: while Parliament enjoys plenary power to enact laws with extra-territorial operation under Article 245(2) as an attribute of national sovereignty (subject to a constitutional nexus with India as clarified in GVK Industries v. ITO), a State Legislature is constitutionally confined to making laws for the whole or any part of the State. However, under the Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, a State law having incidental impact beyond its borders is upheld if a real and not illusory territorial connection exists.

exp.why: Article 245(1) empowers Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and Article 245(2) explicitly declares that no law made by Parliament shall be deemed to be invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation. In GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer (2011), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench clarified that Parliament may exercise this extra-territorial legislative power in relation to extra-territorial aspects or causes that have, or are expected to have, a direct or indirect nexus with or impact on India or the welfare of its citizens.

Although a State Legislature is not vested with general extra-territorial legislative power under Article 245(1), the Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957) established that a State law is not invalid merely because it affects persons residing outside the State, provided the connection (nexus) between the taxing/legislating State and the subject-matter is real and not illusory, and the liability sought to be imposed is pertinent to that connection. However, Statement-II explains the exception validating extra-territorial impact of State laws and does not explain why Parliamentary legislation is insulated from invalidity on grounds of extra-territorial operation under Article 245(2).

ref: Constitution of India Article 245; State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957); GVK Industries Ltd. v. ITO (2011)

stem: With reference to the constitutional exceptions to the plenary territorial jurisdiction of Acts of Parliament across the territory of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A regulation made by the President under Article 240 for the peace, progress and good government of the Union Territory of Lakshadweep or Andaman and Nicobar Islands has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament and may repeal or amend any Act made by Parliament in its application to that Union Territory.

2. Under the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution, the Governor of a State having Scheduled Areas is empowered to direct by public notification that any particular Act of Parliament shall not apply to a Scheduled Area in that State, or shall apply subject to specified exceptions and modifications.

3. Under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, the power to direct that an Act of Parliament shall not apply to an autonomous district in the State of Assam is vested exclusively in the President of India, whereas in Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, this power in respect of Parliamentary Acts is exercised by the respective State Governors.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although Article 245(1) empowers Parliament to legislate for the whole or any part of India, the Constitution carves out specific executive modification and non-applicability regimes under Article 240 (specified Union Territories), the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas), and the Sixth Schedule (Tribal Areas). Under the Sixth Schedule, there is a crucial divergence regarding Acts of Parliament: the Governor of Assam holds the power to exclude or modify Acts of Parliament in Assam's autonomous districts, whereas the President holds that power for Acts of Parliament in the autonomous districts of Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.

exp.why: Under Article 240(1) and (2) of the Constitution, the President can make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Puducherry (only when its Legislative Assembly is suspended or dissolved). Any regulation so made may repeal or amend any Act made by Parliament or any other law applicable to the Union Territory and, when promulgated by the President, has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.

Under Paragraph 5(1) of the Fifth Schedule, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, the Governor may, by public notification, direct that any particular Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of the State shall not apply to a Scheduled Area or any part thereof in the State, or shall apply to a Scheduled Area or any part thereof in the State subject to such exceptions and modifications as he may specify in the notification.

This statement swaps the constitutional authorities between Assam and the other three Sixth Schedule States. Under Paragraph 12(1)(b) of the Sixth Schedule, in the State of Assam, it is the Governor who may direct that any Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature (outside the matters specifically reserved to the District/Regional Councils) shall not apply to an autonomous district or region in Assam, or shall apply subject to exceptions and modifications. Conversely, under Paragraphs 12A(b), 12AA(b), and 12B(b), in respect of the autonomous districts or regions in Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, the power to direct that an Act of Parliament shall not apply (or shall apply with modifications) is vested in the President of India, while the Governor exercises this power only in respect of Acts of the State Legislature.

ref: Constitution of India Article 240, Fifth Schedule (Para 5), and Sixth Schedule (Paras 12, 12A, 12AA, 12B); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 14

stem: With reference to the distribution of legislative subjects under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India and the modifications enacted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 transferred 'Public health and sanitation' as well as 'Agriculture' from the State List (List II) to the Concurrent List (List III).

2. Following the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, the power to legislate on the constitution and organisation of all courts in India, including the Supreme Court and the High Courts, was placed in the Concurrent List (List III).

3. Under the scheme of Article 246, in the event of an irreconcilable overlapping between an entry in the Union List and an entry transferred to the Concurrent List, the Concurrent List entry prevails over the Union List entry.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 transferred exactly five entries from the State List to the Concurrent List: (1) Education, (2) Forests, (3) Protection of wild animals and birds, (4) Weights and measures (except establishment of standards), and (5) Administration of justice; constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and the High Courts. Core subjects like 'Public health and sanitation' (Entry 6) and 'Agriculture' (Entry 14) remain exclusively in the State List, while Article 246(1) secures the overarching predominance of the Union List over both the Concurrent and State Lists.

exp.why: Neither 'Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' (Entry 6 of List II) nor 'Agriculture, including agricultural education and research, protection against pests and prevention of plant diseases' (Entry 14 of List II) was transferred by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; both remain exclusively in the State List. The five subjects transferred from List II to List III were Education (Entry 25), Forests (Entry 17A), Protection of wild animals and birds (Entry 17B), Weights and measures except establishment of standards (Entry 33A), and Administration of justice; constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and the High Courts (Entry 11A).

Entry 11A inserted into the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment Act explicitly covers 'Administration of justice; constitution and organisation of all courts, except the Supreme Court and the High Courts'. The constitution and organisation of the Supreme Court (Entry 77 of List I) and of the High Courts (Entry 78 of List I) remain exclusively in the Union List.

This reverses the constitutional hierarchy of Lists under Article 246. Through the non-obstante clause in Article 246(1) ('Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3)') and the qualifying clause in Article 246(2) ('Notwithstanding anything in clause (3)... subject to clause (1)'), the Union List (List I) enjoys absolute predominance over both the Concurrent List (List III) and the State List (List II), while the Concurrent List prevails over the State List.

ref: Constitution of India Article 246 and Seventh Schedule; 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 14

stem: With reference to the residuary powers of legislation under the Indian constitutional framework, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 248 of the Constitution of India, the Parliament only has the exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or the State List, including the power of making any law imposing a tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.

2. Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the residuary powers of legislation were vested in the Federal Legislature, from which the framers of the Indian Constitution directly adopted the scheme of Article 248.

3. Whether a particular law falls within the residuary power of Parliament under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List is subject to judicial determination, and the Courts invoke the residuary clause only as a last resort when the subject cannot be reasonably comprehended within any specific entry of the three Lists.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List I vests residuary legislative and taxation powers exclusively in the Union Parliament, following the Canadian federal model rather than the US/Australian model (where residuary powers rest with the States) or the Government of India Act, 1935 (which vested residuary powers in the Governor-General). Judicial doctrine dictates that Entry 97 of List I cannot be invoked prematurely if a subject is covered under any entry in List II or List III upon a broad and liberal construction.

exp.why: Article 248(1) and (2) read with Entry 97 of List I confer exclusive competence on the Parliament—to the complete exclusion of State Legislatures—to legislate on any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or the State List, explicitly including the power to levy any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.

Under Section 104 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the residuary powers of legislation were vested neither in the Federal Legislature nor in the Provincial Legislatures, but in the Governor-General of India, who could in his discretion empower either the Federal Legislature or a Provincial Legislature to enact a law on an unenumerated matter. In departing from this colonial mechanism, the Constituent Assembly adopted the Canadian constitutional principle of vesting residuary powers in the Union Parliament.

As settled by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) and International Tourist Corporation v. State of Haryana (1981), the scope of residuary power is decided by the Judiciary. Before exclusive legislative competence can be claimed for Parliament by resort to the residuary power under Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I, the legislative Entry in the State List must first be given a wide and liberal interpretation to see whether the subject falls within the State's assigned domain; resort to the residuary power is permissible only as a last resort when all categories in the Lists are absolutely exhausted.

ref: Constitution of India Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I; Government of India Act, 1935 (Section 104); Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971)

stem: Under the constitutional scheme of distribution of legislative powers in India, suppose a State Legislature, lacking direct legislative competence over an entry exclusively reserved in the Union List, enacts a statute that ostensibly purports to regulate a subject in the State List, while in substance and practical effect usurping a subject within the exclusive domain of Parliament. Unlike a bona fide enactment that merely makes an incidental encroachment upon another List, this disguised transgression of constitutional limits is invalidated by the courts primarily by invoking which of the following judicial doctrines?
core: The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation tests legislative competence against covert or disguised transgressions based on the maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. Conversely, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance protects a bona fide law whose true character falls within the enacting legislature's allotted List despite incidental trenching upon another List.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation (derived from the Latin maxim 'Quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum'—what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, expounded in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa) applies when a legislature, lacking constitutional competence over a subject, disguises an ultra vires statute under the pretension or outward form of an entry within its own List. Note that 'colourable' here refers purely to a question of legislative competence under Article 246 and does not mean the judiciary investigates the mala fides or motives of the legislature. Option (A) is incorrect because the Doctrine of Pith and Substance validates (saves) a statute when its true nature and character ('pith and substance') genuinely fall within the enacting legislature's own List, even if it incidentally trenches upon an entry in another List. Option (B) is incorrect because Harmonious Construction is an interpretive rule used to reconcile apparent overlaps between different legislative entries or statutory provisions so that neither is rendered redundant. Option (C) is incorrect because the Doctrine of Territorial Nexus under Article 245 determines when a State law can validly have extra-territorial operation based on a real and sufficient connection between the State and the object of the law.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 246; K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 14

stem: With reference to the power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest under Article 249 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A resolution empowering Parliament under Article 249 must be passed by the Council of States and supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

2. Such a resolution remains in force initially for a period not exceeding one year, may be renewed any number of times for up to one year at a time, and any law made by Parliament under it ceases to have effect on the expiration of six months after the resolution ceases to be in force.
3. During the period a resolution under Article 249 remains in force, the power of a State Legislature to enact new laws on the specified matter in the State List stands suspended.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 249, a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds of members present and voting creates temporary concurrent competence for Parliament over a specified State List subject without stripping State Legislatures of their legislative power. Any conflict between a Parliamentary law enacted under Article 249 and a State law is resolved by the rule of federal supremacy under Article 251.

exp.why: Under Article 249(1), if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to any matter enumerated in the State List specified in the resolution, it becomes lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter.

Under Article 249(2), the resolution remains in force for such period not exceeding one year as may be specified therein, and under the proviso, if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force is passed in the same manner, it continues for a further period of one year from the date on which it would otherwise have ceased to be in force. Under Article 249(3), a law made by Parliament which it would not have been competent to make but for the passing of the resolution ceases to have effect on the expiration of six months after the resolution has ceased to be in force, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.

Article 251 explicitly stipulates that nothing in Articles 249 and 250 shall restrict the power of the Legislature of a State to make any law which under the Constitution it has power to make. Hence, State legislative power is not suspended; rather, if any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament under Article 249, the Parliamentary law (whether passed before or after the State law) prevails, and the State law to the extent of the repugnancy remains inoperative only so long as the law made by Parliament continues to have effect.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 249 & Art. 251; D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding legislation by Parliament on matters in the State List by consent of States under Article 252 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Once Parliament enacts an Act on a matter in the State List pursuant to resolutions passed by the Legislatures of two or more States under Article 252, none of the participating State Legislatures can subsequently amend or repeal that Act in its application to that State.

Statement-II: An Act passed by Parliament under Article 252 applies initially only to the States whose Legislatures passed the enabling resolutions, and extends to any other State only if subsequently adopted by a resolution passed by the House or Houses of the Legislature of that State.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Article 252(2), legislation by consent results in a surrender of legislative competence over that specific enactment by the participating State Legislatures, empowering only Parliament to amend or repeal it in the like manner. Separately, under Article 252(1), the territorial application of such a Central Act is confined to the initially consenting States and those States whose Legislatures subsequently adopt it by resolution.

exp.why: Under Article 252(2), any Act passed by Parliament pursuant to resolutions of two or more State Legislatures under Article 252(1) may be amended or repealed by an Act of Parliament passed or adopted in like manner, 'but shall not, as respects any State to which it applies, be amended or repealed by an Act of the Legislature of that State.' By passing the enabling resolution, the participating States surrender their legislative competence to alter or repeal the resulting Central Act so that uniformity of the common regulatory regime across consenting States is not unilaterally disrupted.

Statement-II is also correct because under Article 252(1), any Act so passed by Parliament applies initially only to the consenting States whose Legislatures passed the enabling resolutions, and to any other State by which it is adopted afterwards by a resolution passed in that behalf by the House or (where there are two Houses) by each of the Houses of the Legislature of that State. However, Statement-II describes the territorial applicability and adoption procedure under Article 252(1) and does not explain why participating States are constitutionally barred from amending or repealing the Act under Article 252(2).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 252(1) & 252(2); R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957)

stem: With reference to the power of Parliament to enact legislation for giving effect to international treaties, agreements, and conventions under Article 253 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements best describes the constitutional position?

opts.A: Parliament is competent to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India even on subjects enumerated in the State List without the consent of any State Legislature, subject to the limitations of Fundamental Rights under Part III.
opts.B: Parliament can legislate on a State List subject to implement an international treaty only after the treaty has been ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States.
opts.C: The Union Executive can enforce obligations altering domestic rights and liabilities arising out of an international convention on a State List subject solely through executive notifications under Article 73 without requiring parliamentary legislation.
opts.D: A parliamentary law enacted under Article 253 on a State List subject requires a prior authorization resolution passed by the Council of States by a special majority.

core: Article 253 begins with a non-obstante clause overriding the normal federal distribution of legislative powers in Articles 245 to 252, enabling Parliament to unilaterally legislate on State List subjects to implement international obligations. However, because Article 253 remains subject to the rest of the Constitution, such laws cannot contravene Fundamental Rights under Part III.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because Article 253 opens with the words 'Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter' (i.e., overriding the Seventh Schedule distribution of powers in Article 246), vesting Parliament with plenary power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement, or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association, or other body. As held in Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969), this overrides the State List without requiring State consent, though the power remains circumscribed by Part III (Fundamental Rights). Option (B) and Option (D) are incorrect because neither ratification by half the States nor a Rajya Sabha resolution is required under Article 253. Option (C) is incorrect because while the Union Executive can enter into treaties under Article 73, any treaty or convention that restricts the rights of citizens or modifies existing domestic laws requires enabling legislation by Parliament under Article 253.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 253; Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969); Laxmikanth Ch. 14

stem: Consider the following statements comparing the operational validity of laws enacted on matters in the State List during a National Emergency (Article 250) and during President's Rule (Articles 356 and 357):
items: 1. A law enacted by Parliament on a State List subject during the operation of a Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 250 continues to remain in force permanently even after the Emergency ceases to operate, unless expressly repealed by the concerned State Legislature.

2. A law made for a State by Parliament or the President during the operation of a Proclamation under Article 356 automatically ceases to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the Proclamation ceases to operate.

3. While a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, Article 250 does not suspend the legislative competence of a State Legislature over the State List, though in case of repugnancy, the Parliamentary law prevails so long as it remains in force.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Laws made by Parliament on the State List during a National Emergency under Article 250 automatically expire six months after the Emergency ceases, during which time State Legislatures retain concurrent legislative power. In contrast, under Article 357(2), laws enacted for a State during President's Rule survive the revocation of the Proclamation and remain in force until repealed or altered by a competent Legislature.

exp.why: Statement 1 swaps the rule of Article 357(2) with Article 250(2). Under Article 250(2), a law made by Parliament on the State List which Parliament would not, but for the issue of a Proclamation of National Emergency, have been competent to make shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.

Statement 2 swaps the rule of Article 250(2) with Article 357(2). Under Article 357(2) (as substituted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976), any law made in exercise of the power of the Legislature of the State by Parliament or the President during a Proclamation under Article 356 continues in force even after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other authority.

Under Article 251, nothing in Articles 249 and 250 restricts the power of the Legislature of a State to make any law which under the Constitution it has power to make. During a National Emergency, the State Legislature is NOT suspended; rather, Parliament acquires concurrent legislative competence over the State List, and if any provision of a State law is repugnant to the Parliamentary law made under Article 250, the Parliamentary law prevails so long as it continues to have effect.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 250, 251 & 357(2); 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 14 & 16

stem: With reference to the Doctrine of Repugnancy under Article 254 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 applies both when a State law on the Concurrent List conflicts with a Central law on the Concurrent List and when a State law enacted strictly within the State List incidentally trenches upon a Central law enacted under the Union List.

2. Where a law made by the Legislature of a State with respect to a matter enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to an earlier law made by Parliament on that matter, the State law prevails in that State if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received the President's assent.

3. Once a State law on a Concurrent List subject receives Presidential assent under Article 254(2), Parliament is barred from subsequently enacting a law that amends, varies, or repeals the law so made by the State Legislature without the prior concurrence of that State Legislature.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Constitutional repugnancy under Article 254 arises exclusively when both the Union law and the State law are enacted with respect to subjects in the Concurrent List (List III). Furthermore, while Presidential assent under Article 254(2) cures repugnancy in favour of a State law within that State against an earlier Central law, the Proviso to Article 254(2) empowers Parliament to unilaterally override, amend, or repeal that State law at any subsequent time.

exp.why: As consistently settled by Constitution Benches of the Supreme Court (e.g., M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India, Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar, and Vijay Kumar Sharma v. State of Karnataka), the question of repugnancy under Article 254 arises strictly and only when both the Union law and the State law operate in the same field with respect to a matter enumerated in the Concurrent List (List III). Where a State law enacted under List II incidentally touches upon a Central law enacted under List I, the issue is one of legislative competence under Article 246 and is resolved by the Doctrine of Pith and Substance, not Article 254.

Under Article 254(2), where a law made by the Legislature of a State with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State.

Under the Proviso to Article 254(2), nothing in clause (2) prevents Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter, including a law adding to, amending, varying, or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State. No prior concurrence of the State Legislature is required for Parliament to exercise this overriding power.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 254(1) & 254(2); Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1983); M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979)

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing State legislation and the requirement of Presidential sanction or assent, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the second proviso to Article 200, the Governor is constitutionally bound to reserve for the consideration of the President any Bill passed by the State Legislature which would so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by the Constitution designed to fill.
