2. Under the proviso to Article 304(b), a Bill or amendment imposing reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse within a State in the public interest can be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State only with the previous sanction of the President.

3. Under Article 255, no Act of the Legislature of a State shall be invalid by reason only that the previous sanction or recommendation of the President required by the Constitution was not given, if assent to that Act was subsequently given by the President.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the proviso to Article 304(b) requires prior Presidential sanction before introducing a State Bill restricting freedom of trade and commerce, Article 255 treats the requirement of prior recommendation or sanction as a matter of procedure only, curing its absence if the enacted Bill subsequently receives Presidential assent. Separately, the second proviso to Article 200 mandates reservation of State Bills that endanger the constitutional position of the High Court.

exp.why: Under the second proviso to Article 200 of the Constitution, the Governor shall not assent to, but shall reserve for the consideration of the President, any Bill which in the opinion of the Governor would, if it became law, so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by this Constitution designed to fill. This is the sole explicitly mandatory ground for reservation stated in the text of Article 200.

While Article 304(b) empowers the Legislature of a State to impose by law such reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse with or within that State as may be required in the public interest, its proviso expressly mandates that no Bill or amendment for the purposes of clause (b) shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President.

Article 255 provides a curative constitutional mechanism: requirements as to recommendations and previous sanctions are to be regarded as matters of procedure only. Consequently, no Act of Parliament or of a State Legislature is invalid merely because a constitutionally required prior recommendation or previous sanction of the Governor or the President was not obtained before introduction, provided the Act subsequently receives the assent of the Governor or the President (where the President's sanction was required).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 200, 255 and 304(b); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. on Centre-State Relations

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the distribution of executive powers between the Union and the States:
items: Statement-I: When Parliament enacts a law on a subject enumerated in the Concurrent List, the executive power to administer and implement that law ordinarily rests with the State Governments rather than the Union Government.

Statement-II: Under the proviso to Article 73(1) of the Constitution, the executive power of the Union does not extend to matters with respect to which the Legislature of a State also has power to make laws, save as expressly provided in the Constitution or in any law made by Parliament.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Articles 73 and 162, while executive power generally follows legislative competence, the Constitution creates a crucial federal safeguard for the Concurrent List (List III): even when Parliament legislates on a Concurrent subject, the executive power to implement that central law remains vested in the States unless the Constitution or the Parliamentary Act itself expressly confers that executive power on the Union.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Indian cooperative federalism, central laws enacted on Concurrent List subjects are by default executed through State administrative machinery unless Parliament specifically vests executive authority in Union authorities within the statute itself.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Article 73(1)(a) states that the executive power of the Union extends to the matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws, but the proviso to Article 73(1) explicitly carves out Concurrent List subjects (matters on which State Legislatures also have power to make laws), stipulating that Union executive power shall not extend to any State in such matters unless expressly provided in the Constitution or in any law made by Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 73 and 162; DD Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: With reference to the administrative relations between the Union and the States under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 257, the executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared to be of national or military importance, and as to the measures to be taken for the protection of the railways within the State.

2. Where a State incurs excess costs in carrying out executive directions of the Union under Article 257, any dispute regarding the sum to be paid by the Government of India to the State is determined by an arbitrator appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Inter-State Council.

3. Where any State has failed to comply with or give effect to any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under Articles 256 or 257, it is lawful for the President under Article 365 to hold that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 256 and 257 empower the Union to issue binding executive directions to States, backed by the coercive sanction of Article 365 (which links non-compliance to Article 356). To ensure impartiality when compensating States for extra costs incurred under Article 257(2) or (3), Article 257(4) vests the appointment of the arbitrator in the Chief Justice of India rather than the political executive.

exp.why: Under Article 257(2) and 257(3), the executive power of the Union expressly extends to giving directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared in the direction to be of national or military importance, and as to the measures to be taken for the protection of the railways within the State.

Under Article 257(4), where in carrying out any direction given to a State under clause (2) or clause (3), costs have been incurred in excess of those which would have been incurred in the discharge of the normal duties of the State, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India (not by the President or the Inter-State Council).

Article 365 provides the constitutional sanction behind Union executive directions: where any State has failed to comply with, or to give effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under any of the provisions of the Constitution, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution (thereby satisfying the precondition for President's Rule under Article 356).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 256, 257 and 365

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the mutual delegation of executive functions between the Union and the States:
items: 1. Under Article 258(2), a law made by Parliament which applies in any State may confer powers and impose duties upon that State or its officers and authorities in respect of a Union List subject even without the consent of the State Government.

2. Symmetrically, under Article 258A, a State Legislature may by law confer powers and impose duties upon the Union Government or its officers in respect of a State List matter without requiring the prior consent of the Government of India.
3. The Governor of a State can entrust functions relating to the executive power of the State to the Government of India or to its officers only with the consent of the Government of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 258 and 258A exhibit a deliberate federal asymmetry: while downward delegation of Union functions to a State can occur either by executive agreement with State consent under Article 258(1) or unconditionally by an Act of Parliament without State consent under Article 258(2), upward delegation of State functions to the Union under Article 258A can be effected only by the Governor with the consent of the Government of India.

exp.why: While executive entrustment by the President under Article 258(1) requires the consent of the State Government, Article 258(2) empowers Parliament by law to confer powers and impose duties upon a State or its officers and authorities in respect of matters outside the State Legislature's competence without requiring the consent of the State.

There is no provision in Article 258A equivalent to Article 258(2). A State Legislature cannot by law unilaterally impose duties or confer executive functions upon the Government of India or its officers without the Union's consent.

Inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956, Article 258A provides that the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 258 and 258A; 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956

stem: With reference to the 'Full Faith and Credit' clause under Article 261 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements accurately describes the constitutional position regarding judicial proceedings across States?

opts.A: Both civil decrees and criminal sentences passed by any court in a State require prior ratification by the High Court of the executing State before they can be enforced outside the originating State.
opts.B: The manner in which public acts, records and judicial proceedings of a State are to be proved and their effect determined across India is exclusively regulated by the respective State Legislatures under the State List.
opts.C: Article 261(3) mandates the automatic execution of both civil and criminal judgments across all States and compels the courts of one State to directly enforce the penal laws of another State.
opts.D: Final judgments or orders delivered by civil courts in any part of the territory of India are capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law without requiring a fresh suit on the judgment, whereas courts of one State are not required to enforce the penal laws of another State.

core: Article 261 ensures nationwide recognition of public acts, records, and judicial proceedings across the Indian federation. Crucially, Article 261(3) limits automatic cross-border execution to final judgments or orders of civil courts, adhering to the established legal principle that one State's courts do not directly enforce the penal laws of another State.

exp.why: Option D is correct. Under Article 261(1), full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State. Under Article 261(3), final judgments or orders delivered or passed by civil courts in any part of the territory of India shall be capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law, without the need to file a fresh suit upon the judgment. This clause applies specifically to civil judgments; criminal judgments and penal statutes of one State are not enforced directly by the courts of another State under Article 261(3). Option A is incorrect because civil decrees do not require High Court ratification in the executing State. Option B is incorrect because under Article 261(2), the manner of proof and effect is provided by law made by Parliament, not State Legislatures. Option C is incorrect because Article 261(3) is confined to civil courts.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 261; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. on Centre-State Relations

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the adjudication of inter-State river water disputes:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 262 of the Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of any inter-State river or river valley.

Statement-II: Because Section 6(2) of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 accords the published decision of a Water Disputes Tribunal the same force as an order or decree of the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court is also constitutionally barred from entertaining appeals by Special Leave under Article 136 against the Tribunal's final award.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 262(2) empowers Parliament by law to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and all other courts over inter-State river water disputes, which Parliament exercised via Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956. However, in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2016), the Supreme Court held that while this statutory bar excludes original suits under Article 131 over the water allocation dispute itself, Section 6(2) merely creates a legal fiction for enforcement and cannot oust the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 against a Tribunal's award.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 262(1) empowers Parliament to provide by law for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of any inter-State river or river valley, and Article 262(2) expressly states that notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint.

Statement-II is incorrect. In State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2016), the Supreme Court ruled that while Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 read with Article 262(2) bars original suits under Article 131 regarding water allocation disputes referred to a Tribunal, Section 6(2) of the Act (which states that the published decision of the Tribunal shall have the same force as an order or decree of the Supreme Court) merely creates a legal fiction to provide an effective enforcement mechanism. It does not and cannot extinguish the Supreme Court's constitutional appellate jurisdiction to hear appeals by Special Leave under Article 136 against a final order or award of a Water Disputes Tribunal.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 131, 136 and 262; Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2016)

stem: With reference to the Inter-State Council envisaged under Article 263 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It is a permanent constitutional body established through an Act of Parliament and is chaired by the President of India.
2. The Standing Committee of the Inter-State Council is chaired by the Prime Minister and includes the Chief Ministers of all States as its permanent members.
3. Its decisions on inter-State disputes are binding on the States concerned and bar the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 263, the President is empowered to establish an Inter-State Council by executive order (not by a parliamentary statute) to promote cooperative federalism; the Council is chaired by the Prime Minister, its Standing Committee is chaired by the Union Home Minister, and its mandate is purely advisory and complementary to the Supreme Court's binding original jurisdiction under Article 131.

exp.why: Article 263 empowers the President of India (and not Parliament by law) to establish an Inter-State Council by a Presidential Order if at any time it appears to the President that public interests would be served by its establishment. Exercising this power on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission, the President established the Inter-State Council in 1990. Furthermore, the Council is chaired by the Prime Minister (not the President) and consists of the Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of Union Territories having Legislative Assemblies, Administrators of Union Territories not having Legislative Assemblies, and six Union Cabinet Ministers (including the Home Minister) nominated by the Prime Minister.

The Standing Committee of the Inter-State Council, set up in 1996 for continuous consultation and processing of matters for the consideration of the Council, is chaired by the Union Home Minister (not the Prime Minister). Its membership comprises five Union Cabinet Ministers and nine Chief Ministers nominated on a rotational basis, rather than the Chief Ministers of all States permanently.

Under Article 263(a), the Inter-State Council's duty to inquire into and advise upon disputes which may have arisen between States is strictly advisory and recommendatory in nature. It cannot issue binding judicial decrees and does not oust or restrict the exclusive and binding original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 to adjudicate legal disputes between the Union and States or between States inter se.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 263; Presidential Order dated 28 May 1990; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16 (Inter-State Relations).

stem: With reference to the Regional Councils functioning as statutory instruments of cooperative federalism in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Eastern Zonal Council : Headquarters at Kolkata; comprises Bihar, West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Sikkim
2. Central Zonal Council : Established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 with headquarters at Prayagraj (Allahabad)
3. North-Eastern Council : Created by a separate Act of Parliament in 1971 with headquarters at Shillong; comprises eight States including Sikkim
4. Southern Zonal Council : Headquarters at Bengaluru; Chief Ministers of member States act as its Chairman by rotation for a term of two years
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Five Zonal Councils (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern) were established under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 with the Union Home Minister as common Chairman and Chief Ministers serving as Vice-Chairman by annual rotation, whereas the North-Eastern Council was created under a separate North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 and includes Sikkim since 2002.

exp.why: While the Eastern Zonal Council is headquartered at Kolkata and includes Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal, it no longer includes Sikkim. Following the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002, Sikkim was inducted as the eighth member State of the North-Eastern Council and excluded from the Eastern Zonal Council.

The five Zonal Councils (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern) are statutory bodies established under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. The Central Zonal Council comprises the States of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh, and Madhya Pradesh, with its headquarters located at Prayagraj (Allahabad).

Unlike the five Zonal Councils established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the North-Eastern Council (NEC) was created by a separate Act of Parliament—the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971. Headquartered at Shillong, it comprises eight States: Assam, Manipur, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Sikkim (added in 2002).

The headquarters of the Southern Zonal Council is located at Chennai (not Bengaluru). Furthermore, the Union Home Minister serves as the common Chairman of all five Zonal Councils, while the Chief Ministers of the member States in a zone act as Vice-Chairman of the Council by rotation, holding office for a period of one year at a time (not Chairman for two years).

ref: States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Part III); North-Eastern Council Act, 1971; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16 (Zonal Councils).

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing All-India Services under Article 312 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Parliament can create a new All-India Service common to the Union and the States if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest to do so.

2. The provision empowering the creation of an All-India Judicial Service (AIJS) was added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, and the Constitution explicitly stipulates that the AIJS shall not include any post inferior to that of a District Judge.

3. A law enacted by Parliament under Article 312 providing for the creation and regulation of an All-India Service is not deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

4. While the Central Government exercises immediate operational control over All-India Service officers serving in a State cadre, the ultimate authority to dismiss or remove such an officer rests jointly with the State Governor and the President.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 312 empowers Parliament to create new All-India Services (including an All-India Judicial Service not below the rank of District Judge) by ordinary legislative process once authorised by a special Rajya Sabha resolution; structurally, All-India Services follow a dual control mechanism where immediate operational control vests in the State Government, while ultimate disciplinary authority (dismissal or removal) vests exclusively in the Central Government.

exp.why: Under Article 312(1), if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest so to do, Parliament may by law provide for the creation of one or more All-India Services (including an All-India Judicial Service) common to the Union and the States.

The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 312 to explicitly include the 'All-India Judicial Service' (AIJS) within the ambit of All-India Services. Article 312(3) specifically mandates that the All-India Judicial Service shall not include any post inferior to that of a District Judge as defined in Article 236.

Under Article 312(4), even if a law creating an All-India Judicial Service contains provisions for amending Chapter VI of Part VI (Subordinate Courts), no such law enacted under Article 312 shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368, meaning it can be passed by Parliament by a simple majority like an ordinary law after the Rajya Sabha resolution.

The statement reverses immediate and ultimate control. All-India Services are controlled jointly by the Central and State Governments through a division of authority: the State Government under which the officer is serving exercises immediate control (postings, transfers, deputation, and power to institute inquiries or place the officer under suspension), whereas ultimate control—including the sole authority under Article 311(1) to impose the major penalties of dismissal, removal, or compulsory retirement—rests exclusively with the Central Government (President), not the State Governor.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 311 and 312; 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 15 & Ch. 65.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the federal dimension of Public Service Commissions in India:
items: 1. Unlike the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs) which are created directly by the Constitution, a Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC) can be created only by an Act of Parliament upon a resolution passed to that effect by the concerned State Legislatures.
2. Both the Chairman and members of a Joint State Public Service Commission are appointed as well as removed by the President of India.
3. The Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission are appointed by the Governor of the State, who is also empowered to remove them on the recommendation of the State High Court.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While UPSC and SPSCs are constitutional bodies created directly by Article 315(1), a Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC) is a statutory creation enacted by Parliament under Article 315(2) on the request of the concerned State Legislatures; to insulate SPSCs from state-level executive interference, their Chairmen and members are appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President.

exp.why: While Article 315(1) directly mandates the existence of a Public Service Commission for the Union and a Public Service Commission for each State, Article 315(2) provides that two or more States may agree that there shall be one Public Service Commission for that group of States, and if a resolution to that effect is passed by the House or each House of the Legislature of each of those States, Parliament may by law provide for the appointment of a Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC). Thus, a JSPSC is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament (as was done for Punjab and Haryana in 1966).

Under Articles 316(1) and 317(1)-(3), because a Joint State Public Service Commission serves more than one State, both the power of appointment and the power of removal of the Chairman and members of a JSPSC are vested in the President of India.

Although the Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission (SPSC) are appointed by the Governor of the State under Article 316(1), they can be removed ONLY by the President of India (and not by the Governor) under Article 317. Moreover, removal on the ground of misbehaviour requires the President to make a reference to the Supreme Court of India (not the State High Court), whose advice after inquiry is binding on the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 315, 316, and 317; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 44 & Ch. 45.

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory framework governing the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 239AA, while the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi is barred from making laws on Public Order, Police, and Land in the State List, Parliament retains plenary power to legislate for the NCT of Delhi on any matter in the State List and Concurrent List.

2. Under the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, the National Capital Civil Service Authority (NCCSA) is chaired by the Lieutenant Governor, and the Chief Minister has a veto over its recommendations regarding the transfer and posting of Group 'A' officers.

3. As held by the Supreme Court, the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi is constitutionally bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers even when exercising statutory power to nominate aldermen to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 239AA confers a sui generis asymmetric status on the NCT of Delhi where the Legislative Assembly can legislate on State and Concurrent List subjects (except Entries 1, 2, and 18 of the State List) subject to Parliament's overarching plenary legislative power; executive control over Group 'A' services is routed through the CM-chaired NCCSA by majority vote, and the Lieutenant Governor can act without ministerial aid and advice where a Parliamentary statute expressly requires independent action.

exp.why: Under Article 239AA(3)(a), the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi has power to make laws for the whole or any part of the NCT with respect to any of the matters enumerated in the State List or in the Concurrent List in so far as any such matter is applicable to Union Territories, except matters with respect to Entries 1 (Public Order), 2 (Police), and 18 (Land) of the State List (and Entries 64, 65, and 66 relatable to them). Crucially, under Article 239AA(3)(b)-(c), nothing derogates from the plenary power of Parliament to make laws with respect to ANY matter for the NCT of Delhi, and a law made by Parliament prevails over any repugnant law made by the Legislative Assembly.

Under Section 45E inserted by the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, the National Capital Civil Service Authority (NCCSA) is chaired by the Chief Minister of Delhi (not the Lieutenant Governor), with the Chief Secretary and the Principal Home Secretary of the GNCTD as ex-officio members (the Principal Home Secretary serves as Member-Secretary). All matters required to be decided by the Authority are decided by a majority of votes of the members present and voting—meaning the Chief Minister does not possess a veto and can be outvoted by the two senior civil servants. Furthermore, in case of a difference of opinion between the Lieutenant Governor and the Authority's recommendation, the decision of the Lieutenant Governor is final.

In Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Office of Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (August 2024), the Supreme Court held that the power of the Lieutenant Governor under Section 3(3)(b)(i) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (as amended by Parliament in 1993) to nominate ten persons with special knowledge or experience in municipal administration (aldermen) to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi is an independent statutory power conferred by a law made by Parliament. Consequently, it falls within the constitutional exception under Article 239AA(4) ('in so far as he is, by or under any law, required to act in his discretion'), and the Lieutenant Governor is NOT bound by the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers while making such nominations.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 239AA; GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023; Supreme Court Judgment in Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Office of Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (2024).

stem: Consider the following landmark milestones in the evolution of Centre-State relations in India:
items: 1. Adoption of the Anandpur Sahib Resolution demanding that the Centre's jurisdiction should be restricted only to defence, foreign affairs, communications, and currency, with all residuary powers vested in the States.
2. Appointment of the Rajamannar Committee by the Tamil Nadu Government, which recommended the abolition of All-India Services as well as Articles 356, 357, and 365 of the Constitution.
3. Constitution of the M.M. Punchhi Commission, which recommended a fixed five-year tenure for Governors and a procedure for their impeachment by the State Legislature.

4. Appointment of the Sarkaria Commission, which rejected the demand for structural curtailment of the Centre's powers and recommended the establishment of a permanent Inter-Governmental Council under Article 263.
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above milestones, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: Post-independence inquiries into Indian federalism progressed from strong state-autonomy assertions in the late 1960s and 1970s—beginning with Tamil Nadu's Rajamannar Committee (1969) and the Akali Dal's Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973)—to comprehensive Union-appointed commissions seeking balanced cooperative federalism inside the constitutional framework through the Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007).

exp.why: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution was adopted by the Akali Dal in October 1973. It demanded that the Central Government's jurisdiction be restricted solely to four subjects—defence, foreign affairs, communications, and currency—and that the entire residuary powers be vested in the States so as to make the Constitution federal in the strict sense.

The three-member Rajamannar Committee, chaired by Dr. P.V. Rajamannar, was appointed by the DMK Government of Tamil Nadu in September 1969 (submitting its report in 1971) to examine the entire question of Centre-State relations. Its radical recommendations included abolishing All-India Services (IAS, IPS, and IFS), deleting Articles 356, 357, and 365 (President's Rule), and vesting residuary legislative powers in the States.

The Second Commission on Centre-State Relations, chaired by former Chief Justice of India M.M. Punchhi, was set up by the Government of India in April 2007 (submitting its report in 2010). To safeguard gubernatorial independence and accountability, it recommended removing the 'doctrine of pleasure' for Governors, providing them a fixed tenure of five years, and laying down a procedure for their impeachment by the State Legislature along the lines of the President's impeachment.

The First Commission on Centre-State Relations, chaired by Justice R.S. Sarkaria, was appointed by the Central Government in June 1983 (submitting its report in 1988). While upholding the constitutional necessity of a strong Centre to preserve national unity and integrity, it made 247 recommendations to improve cooperative federalism, most notably the setting up of a permanent Inter-Governmental Council (Inter-State Council) under Article 263 and using Article 356 only sparingly as a measure of last resort. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1969) -> 1 (1973) -> 4 (1983) -> 3 (2007).

ref: Reports of the Sarkaria Commission (1988) and Punchhi Commission (2010); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 14 (Centre-State Relations).

stem: With reference to the constitutional architecture governing the levy, collection, and distribution of taxing powers in India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Concurrent List (List III) of the Seventh Schedule enumerates specific shared taxes that can be levied simultaneously by Parliament and the State Legislatures, in addition to Goods and Services Tax under Article 246A.
opts.B: Under Article 265, neither the Union nor a State can levy or collect any tax solely through an executive notification without the authority of a statute enacted by a competent Legislature, and the residuary power of taxation vests exclusively in Parliament.
opts.C: While the initial levy of a tax requires a legislative enactment under Article 265, the machinery for its assessment and collection can be validly established through purely executive instructions.
opts.D: If a subject of taxation is not enumerated in any of the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule, the power to levy such a tax is exercised concurrently by the Union and the States under Article 248.

core: Article 265 mandates that both the levy and collection of any tax require the authority of primary legislation enacted by a competent legislature, barring taxation by mere executive fiat. Furthermore, the Seventh Schedule completely separates Union and State taxing entries (with zero taxing entries in the Concurrent List) and vests residuary taxing powers exclusively in Parliament under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List I, making Article 246A (GST) a unique constitutional exception of simultaneous taxation outside the Seventh Schedule.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct: Article 265 of the Constitution stipulates that 'No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.' The Supreme Court has consistently held that 'law' in Article 265 means an Act of a competent Legislature (or valid subordinate legislation expressly authorized by a parent statute), meaning no tax can be imposed or collected by mere executive order or administrative notification. Further, under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List (List I), the residuary power of taxation (to levy any tax not mentioned in the State List or Concurrent List) vests exclusively in Parliament. Option (A) is incorrect (Trap T1) because the Concurrent List (List III) of the Seventh Schedule contains no head of taxation whatsoever (Entry 47 of List III relates only to 'fees', which are constitutionally distinct from taxes); simultaneous taxing power over Goods and Services Tax flows independently from the special override provision of Article 246A. Option (C) is incorrect because Article 265 explicitly covers both 'levied' and 'collected'—thus, the assessment and collection machinery must also be backed by statutory authority. Option (D) is incorrect because residuary taxing power under Article 248 belongs exclusively to Parliament, not concurrently to the States.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 246A, 248, 265 & Seventh Schedule; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 'Centre-State Relations'

stem: With reference to the distribution of tax revenues between the Union and the States under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (other than Goods and Services Tax) taking place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce under Article 269 are levied and collected by the Government of India, but their net proceeds do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India and are assigned to the States.

2. Under Article 270, all taxes and duties in the Union List—except those specified in Articles 268, 269, and 269A, surcharges under Article 271, and any cess levied for specific purposes—form part of the divisible pool shared between the Union and the States.

3. Stamp duties mentioned in the Union List under Article 268 are collected by the Government of India, credited initially to the Consolidated Fund of India, and subsequently distributed among the States on the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution distinguishes between three distinct mechanisms for non-GST taxes: duties levied by the Union but collected and retained directly by the States (Article 268), taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned wholly to the States outside the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 269), and taxes levied and collected by the Union that form the divisible pool shared with the States via Finance Commission recommendations (Article 270).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Under Article 269(1) and (2), taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (other than newspapers and except GST under Article 269A, i.e., the 6 items currently outside GST such as petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, ATF, and alcoholic liquor for human consumption) and taxes on the consignment of goods taking place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce are levied and collected by the Government of India, do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India, and are assigned to the States in accordance with principles formulated by Parliament by law.

Statement 2 is correct: Following the 80th Constitutional Amendment Act (2000) and the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act (2016), Article 270(1) establishes a single divisible pool comprising all taxes and duties referred to in the Union List EXCEPT duties and taxes referred to in Articles 268, 269, and 269A, surcharges on taxes and duties referred to in Article 271, and any cess levied for specific purposes under any law made by Parliament. The net proceeds of this divisible pool are distributed between the Union and the States as prescribed by the President after considering the recommendations of the Finance Commission.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Under Article 268(1) and (2), stamp duties mentioned in the Union List (Entry 91 of List I, such as stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, bills of lading, letters of credit, policies of insurance, transfer of shares, debentures, and proxies) are levied by the Government of India, but they are collected AND appropriated directly by the States within which such duties are leviable (except in Union Territories, where they are collected by the Government of India). Furthermore, Article 268(2) explicitly states that the proceeds in any financial year of any such duty leviable within any State shall NOT form part of the Consolidated Fund of India, nor does their appropriation require Finance Commission distribution.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 268, 269 & 270; 80th and 101st Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: Consider the following statements regarding surcharges on taxes and duties under the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 271 of the Constitution, the whole proceeds of any surcharge on taxes and duties levied by Parliament for the purposes of the Union form part of the Consolidated Fund of India and are not shared with the States.

Statement-II: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 amended Article 271 to expressly exclude Goods and Services Tax under Article 246A from the power of Parliament to levy a surcharge for the purposes of the Union.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 271 empowers Parliament to increase any of the duties or taxes referred to in Articles 269 and 270 by a surcharge for the purposes of the Union—whose entire proceeds go exclusively to the Consolidated Fund of India without State sharing—the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act explicitly carved out Goods and Services Tax (Article 246A) from Article 271 so that the Union cannot unilaterally impose a non-shareable surcharge on GST.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: Under Article 271, notwithstanding anything in Articles 269 and 270, Parliament may at any time increase any of the duties or taxes referred to in those articles by a surcharge for the purposes of the Union, and the whole proceeds of any such surcharge shall form part of the Consolidated Fund of India and are excluded from the divisible pool under Article 270.

Statement-II is correct, but does not explain Statement-I: Section 11 of the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 amended Article 271 by inserting the words 'except the goods and services tax under article 246A'. Consequently, Parliament cannot invoke Article 271 to levy a Union surcharge on GST (any GST Compensation Cess was levied separately under Section 18 of the 101st Amendment Act on the recommendation of the GST Council, not as a surcharge under Article 271). However, Statement-II states a substantive exception to the scope of taxes on which a surcharge can be levied, rather than explaining why the proceeds of valid surcharges under Article 271 are retained exclusively by the Union.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 271; Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016

stem: With reference to the legislative and fiscal framework of Goods and Services Tax (GST) under Articles 246A and 269A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 246A(2), Parliament only—to the exclusion of the State Legislatures—has the power to make laws with respect to Goods and Services Tax where the supply of goods, or of services, or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.

2. Under Article 269A, the supply of goods or services in the course of import into the territory of India is deemed to be a supply in the course of inter-State trade or commerce rather than an intra-State supply of the State where the port of entry is situated.

3. Goods and Services Tax on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States in the manner provided by Parliament by law on the recommendations of the Goods and Services Tax Council.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 246A(1) grants simultaneous legislative power to Parliament and State Legislatures over intra-State supplies of GST, Article 246A(2) and Article 269A confer exclusive legislative and taxing jurisdiction on Parliament over inter-State supplies and imports into India, ensuring that destination-based IGST is apportioned between the Union and the destination State without being retained by port States.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: While Article 246A(1) confers simultaneous power on Parliament and the Legislature of every State to make laws with respect to GST on intra-State supplies, Article 246A(2) explicitly provides that Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to Goods and Services Tax where the supply of goods, or of services, or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.

Statement 2 is correct: The Explanation to Article 269A(1) expressly stipulates that for the purposes of this clause, the supply of goods, or of services, or both in the course of import into the territory of India shall be deemed to be supply of goods, or of services, or both in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. This prevents coastal or port-of-entry States from taxing imports as intra-State supplies and ensures that Integrated GST (IGST) accrues to the Union and the destination State where the imported goods or services are eventually consumed.

Statement 3 is correct: Under Article 269A(1), Goods and Services Tax on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and such tax shall be apportioned between the Union and the States in the manner as may be provided by Parliament by law on the recommendations of the Goods and Services Tax Council. Furthermore, under Article 269A(2), the amount so apportioned to a State does not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 246A & 269A; IGST Act, 2017

stem: With reference to the composition, quorum, and decision-making procedure of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council under Article 279A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Due to the constitutional requirement of a three-fourths majority of weighted votes—where the Central Government holds one-third weightage and all State Governments together hold two-thirds weightage—neither the Union Government alone nor all the States voting unanimously without the Union can pass a decision in the Council.
2. One-third of the total number of Members of the Goods and Services Tax Council constitutes the quorum at its meetings, and its Vice-Chairperson is nominated by the President of India.

3. While the Union Finance Minister serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the Council, each State Government may nominate its Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister as its Member.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 279A institutionalizes fiscal federalism in the GST Council through an asymmetric yet mutually dependent voting design: because decisions require at least 75% of the weighted votes present and voting, and the Union holds 33.33% (1/3) while all States combined hold 66.67% (2/3), both the Union and the collective States possess an effective veto, necessitating consensus-building.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Under Article 279A(9), every decision of the GST Council shall be taken at a meeting by a majority of not less than three-fourths (75%) of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, where the vote of the Central Government has a weightage of one-third (33.33%) of the total votes cast, and the votes of all the State Governments taken together have a weightage of two-thirds (66.67%) of the total votes cast. Mathematically, since 33.33% < 75% and 66.67% < 75%, neither the Centre alone nor all the States voting together without the Centre can reach the 75% threshold.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Under Article 279A(7), one-half (50%)—not one-third—of the total number of Members of the Goods and Services Tax Council shall constitute the quorum at its meetings. Furthermore, under Article 279A(3), the Members of the GST Council representing the States (under sub-clause (c) of clause (2)) shall choose one amongst themselves to be the Vice-Chairperson of the Council for such period as they may decide; the Vice-Chairperson is not nominated by the President of India.

Statement 3 is correct: Under Article 279A(2), the GST Council consists of: (a) the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson; (b) the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance as a Member; and (c) the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government as Members.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 279A; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 'Goods and Services Tax Council'

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional relationship between the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council and the Legislatures of the Union and the States:
items: Statement-I: As laid down by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), all recommendations of the Goods and Services Tax Council under Article 279A(4) are constitutionally binding on both Parliament and the State Legislatures, rendering any deviating State GST enactment void on the ground of repugnancy.

Statement-II: Article 246A of the Constitution confers simultaneous and equal legislative power on both Parliament and the State Legislatures to enact laws on intra-State supplies of Goods and Services Tax without incorporating a repugnancy clause analogous to Article 254.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that because Article 246A vests simultaneous and equal legislative competence in Parliament and State Legislatures without an Article 254-style repugnancy clause, the recommendations of the GST Council under Article 279A(4) have only persuasive value over primary legislation and are binding only where the CGST/SGST Acts expressly make subordinate notifications contingent on Council recommendations.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect: In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022), the Supreme Court explicitly rejected the contention that all recommendations of the GST Council under Article 279A(4) are constitutionally binding on Parliament and the State Legislatures. The Court held that GST Council recommendations have only persuasive value regarding the exercise of primary legislative power under Article 246A, as treating them as mandatorily binding on legislatures would destroy fiscal federalism and reduce the simultaneous legislative power of States to a dead letter. (Recommendations are binding only on the executive when issuing secondary notifications where the parent CGST/SGST/IGST statute explicitly mandates acting 'on the recommendations of the Council'.)

Statement-II is correct: The Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals highlighted that Article 246A(1) confers a unique 'simultaneous' legislative power on both Parliament and the State Legislatures to enact laws on GST, treating the Union and the States as equal constitutional partners. Unlike Article 246(2) read with Article 254 (which governs the Concurrent List and makes Union law prevail over repugnant State law), Article 246A intentionally omits any repugnancy clause subordinating State GST laws to Union GST laws, instead relying on the GST Council under Article 279A as a forum of 'uncoercive cooperative federalism' to harmonize tax laws.

ref: Supreme Court Judgment in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022); Constitution of India, Articles 246A, 254 & 279A

stem: With reference to the distribution of legislative and taxing powers over minerals and mineral-bearing lands under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, as interpreted by the Nine-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in the Mineral Area Development Authority case (2024), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Royalty payable on mining leases under Section 9 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 is in the nature of a sovereign tax, and Entry 54 of the Union List empowers Parliament to levy taxes on mineral rights to the exclusion of State Legislatures.

2. While State Legislatures possess the legislative competence to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of the State List, Parliament can by law relating to mineral development impose statutory limitations—extending even to a prohibition—on the States' power to levy taxes under that Entry.

3. Under Entry 49 of the State List, State Legislatures are competent to levy taxes on mineral-bearing lands as a distinct head of taxation and may validly adopt the value of minerals produced or mineral yield as the measure of such tax.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (9-Judge Bench, 2024), the Supreme Court overruled India Cement (1989) and held that mining royalty is a contractual consideration rather than a tax, confirming that the power to tax mineral rights (Entry 50, List II) and mineral-bearing lands (Entry 49, List II) vests in the State Legislatures. While Parliament can statutorily limit the States' power under Entry 50 of List II through a law relating to mineral development, Entry 49 of List II is independent of Entry 50 and not subject to parliamentary curtailment under Entry 54 of List I.

exp.why: In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (2024), the 9-Judge Constitution Bench overruled the 7-Judge Bench ruling in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1989). The Court held that royalty under Section 9 of the MMDR Act, 1957 is a contractual consideration paid by the mining lessee to the lessor for parting with mineral rights, and is not a tax or impost. Further, under the constitutional scheme of the Seventh Schedule, taxing powers are specifically enumerated and never implied from general regulatory entries; therefore, Entry 54 of List I (regulation of mines and mineral development) is purely a regulatory entry and does not confer any power on Parliament to levy a tax on mineral rights.

Entry 50 of List II (State List) explicitly reads: 'Taxes on mineral rights subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development.' The 9-Judge Bench held that while Parliament cannot itself levy a tax on mineral rights, it possesses the legislative authority under Entry 50 of List II read with Entry 54 of List I to impose statutory limitations—which may include restrictions or even prohibition—on the States' fiscal power to tax mineral rights, provided such limitation is expressly enacted by Parliament by law.

The Supreme Court clarified that Entry 49 of List II ('Taxes on lands and buildings') encompasses all classes of land, including mineral-bearing and subterranean land, and operates as a separate taxing entry distinct from Entry 50 of List II. Consequently, limitations imposed by Parliament on Entry 50 of List II do not restrict the States' power to tax mineral-bearing land under Entry 49 of List II, and States may legitimately use mineral value or mineral produce as an economic measure to compute the land tax.

ref: Constitution Seventh Schedule (List I Entry 54; List II Entries 49 & 50); Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL (9-Judge Bench, 2024)

stem: In the scheme of Centre-State financial relations under Part XII of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements accurately describes the procedural safeguard provided under Article 274 to protect the fiscal interests of the States?

opts.A: No Bill or amendment which imposes or varies any tax or duty in which States are interested, or varies the meaning of the expression 'agricultural income' as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax, or imposes any surcharge for the purposes of the Union, shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President.
opts.B: Any parliamentary Bill that alters the principles on which moneys are distributable to the States out of the Consolidated Fund of India requires the prior concurrence of the Inter-State Council and at least half of the State Legislatures before its introduction in the Lok Sabha.
opts.C: A Bill passed by Parliament that diminishes the net proceeds of any tax assignable to the States cannot receive Presidential assent unless it has been referred to the Union Finance Commission for a binding fiscal impact assessment.
opts.D: Where a State Legislature passes a Bill imposing a tax on the sale or consumption of electricity generated by a Central Public Sector Undertaking, the Governor is mandatorily required under Article 274 to reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President.

core: Article 274 of the Constitution safeguards the revenue interests of the States against unilateral parliamentary legislation by mandating the prior recommendation of the President before any Bill or amendment affecting taxes in which States are interested can be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament. This safeguard covers four specific categories of parliamentary Bills without requiring ratification by State Legislatures or concurrence of the Inter-State Council.

exp.why: Option A is correct because Article 274(1) expressly mandates that no Bill or amendment shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President if it: (1) imposes or varies any tax or duty in which States are interested; (2) varies the meaning of the expression 'agricultural income' as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax; (3) affects the principles on which under any of the foregoing provisions of that Chapter moneys are or may be distributable to States; or (4) imposes any surcharge for the purposes of the Union under Article 271. Option B and Option C are incorrect because Article 274 neither requires ratification by State Legislatures nor a binding assessment by the Finance Commission or Inter-State Council. Option D is incorrect because the reservation of a State Bill imposing a tax on water or electricity stored, generated, or sold by an inter-State river authority falls under Article 288(2), whereas Article 274 applies solely to Bills or amendments in Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 274 & Art. 288(2); Laxmikanth Ch. 15 (Centre-State Relations)

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing Statutory Grants (Article 275) and Discretionary Grants (Article 282), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 282 of the Constitution, the power to make discretionary grants for any public purpose outside its ordinary legislative competence is vested exclusively in the Union Government and cannot be exercised by a State Government.

2. The first proviso to Article 275(1) mandates that there shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid of the revenues of a State such capital and recurring sums as may be necessary to enable that State to meet the costs of development schemes undertaken by it with the approval of the Government of India for promoting the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes or raising the level of administration of the Scheduled Areas therein.

3. While statutory grants under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and require the prior recommendation of the Inter-State Council, discretionary grants under Article 282 are made on the binding recommendation of the Union Finance Commission.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution distinguishes between statutory grants-in-aid of the revenues of States in need of assistance under Article 275 (which are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and tied to Finance Commission recommendations, alongside mandatory provisos for Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas) and the general spending power under Article 282. Crucially, Article 282 empowers both the Union and the States to make discretionary grants for any public purpose even outside their respective legislative competencies.

exp.why: Article 282 of the Constitution explicitly confers the discretionary grant-making power on both levels of government: 'The Union or a State may make any grants for any public purpose, notwithstanding that the purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament or the Legislature of the State, as the case may be, may make laws.' Therefore, both the Union Government and State Governments can make grants for any public purpose under Article 282.

While the main clause of Article 275(1) empowers Parliament to provide grants-in-aid of the revenues of such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance, the First Proviso to Article 275(1) creates a mandatory constitutional obligation to pay out of the Consolidated Fund of India such capital and recurring sums as may be necessary to enable a State to meet the costs of Centrally-approved development schemes for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes in that State or for raising the level of administration of the Scheduled Areas therein to that of the administration of the rest of the areas of that State (and the Second Proviso provides explicitly for the tribal areas of Assam).

Under Article 275(2), until Parliament makes provision under Article 275(1), powers are exercisable by the President by order after considering the recommendations of the Finance Commission (not the Inter-State Council). Conversely, grants under Article 282 are discretionary grants that fall outside the mandatory purview of the Finance Commission.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 275 & Art. 282; Laxmikanth Ch. 15 (Centre-State Financial Relations)

stem: With reference to the Union Finance Commission under Articles 280 and 281 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The qualifications requisite for appointment as members of the Union Finance Commission and the manner in which they shall be selected are not specified in the text of the Constitution, which instead empowers Parliament to determine them by law.

2. Under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c), the Union Finance Commission recommends measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities strictly on the basis of its own independent survey, without being constitutionally required to base them on the recommendations of the State Finance Commission.

3. Under Article 281, the President is constitutionally required to cause every recommendation made by the Finance Commission under the provisions of the Constitution, together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon, to be laid before each House of Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 280 establishes the Union Finance Commission as a quasi-judicial constitutional body whose members' qualifications and selection manner are left to be determined by Parliament by law. To ensure vertical fiscal linkages with the third tier of government without encroaching upon State autonomy, Articles 280(3)(bb) and (c) require the Union Finance Commission to recommend measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund for local bodies on the basis of the recommendations made by the respective State Finance Commission.

exp.why: Article 280(1) specifies the composition of the Finance Commission (a Chairman and four other members to be appointed by the President), while Article 280(2) expressly states that Parliament may by law determine the qualifications which shall be requisite for appointment as members of the Commission and the manner in which they shall be selected. Pursuant to this provision, Parliament enacted the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951.

Sub-clauses (bb) and (c) of Article 280(3), inserted by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992 respectively, explicitly mandate that the Union Finance Commission shall make recommendations to the President as to the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the State 'on the basis of the recommendations made by the Finance Commission of the State'.

Article 281 directly mandates that the President shall cause every recommendation made by the Finance Commission under the provisions of the Constitution, together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon, to be laid before each House of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 280 & Art. 281; Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951

stem: With reference to the doctrine of 'Mutual Immunity of Instrumentalities' embodied in Articles 285 and 289 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Article 285 exempts all property of the Union from all taxes imposed by a State or by any authority within a State unless Parliament by law provides otherwise, this constitutional immunity does not automatically extend to the property of Central Public Sector Undertakings registered as companies or statutory corporations having a distinct legal personality.

2. Unlike the broad immunity enjoyed by Union property under Article 285 irrespective of whether it is used for sovereign or commercial purposes, Article 289 does not exempt a State Government from Union taxation in respect of a trade or business of any kind carried on by or on behalf of that State, or any property used or occupied for the purposes of such trade or business.

3. Under Article 289(3), the authority to declare whether any particular class of trade or business carried on by a State is incidental to the ordinary functions of government—and therefore exempt from Union taxation—vests exclusively in Parliament by law.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 285 and 289 incorporate an asymmetric doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity. While Union Government property enjoys blanket immunity from State and municipal property taxation under Article 285 regardless of commercial use (though separate corporate entities like Central PSUs do not qualify as the Union itself), State property and income used for commercial trade or business are subject to Union taxation under Article 289(2) unless Parliament by law declares such business to be incidental to ordinary governmental functions.

exp.why: Under Article 285(1), the property of the Union is exempt from all taxes imposed by a State or by any authority within a State (such as municipalities or panchayats), save insofar as Parliament may by law otherwise provide. However, in a consistent line of rulings (e.g., Western Coalfields Ltd. and Food Corporation of India cases), the Supreme Court has held that a Government company registered under the Companies Act or a statutory corporation possesses an independent juristic personality distinct from the Union Government; even if 100% of its share capital is held by the Union, its property is owned by the corporate entity and is not 'property of the Union' under Article 285(1).

There is a deliberate constitutional asymmetry between Article 285 and Article 289. Under Article 285, property directly owned by the Union Government (such asdepartmental undertakings like Indian Railways) is immune from State taxation even when used commercially. In contrast, while Article 289(1) exempts the property and income of a State from Union taxation, Article 289(2) explicitly empowers the Union to impose taxes in respect of a trade or business of any kind carried on by or on behalf of the Government of a State, any operations connected therewith, any property used or occupied for such trade or business, or any income accruing therefrom.

Article 289(3) explicitly provides that the exception in Article 289(2) allowing Union taxation of State commercial activities 'shall not apply to any trade or business, or to any class of trade or business, which Parliament may by law declare to be incidental to the ordinary functions of government.' Thus, the Constitution vests this declaratory power exclusively in Parliament by law.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 285 & Art. 289; D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the borrowing powers of the Union and the States under Part XII of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 293 of the Constitution of India, the executive power of a State to borrow upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State is territorially restricted, and a State Government cannot directly raise a loan outside the territory of India even with the consent of the Government of India.

Statement-II: Article 293(3) stipulates that a State may not without the consent of the Government of India raise any loan if there is still outstanding any part of a loan which has been made to the State by the Government of India or by its predecessor Government, or in respect of which a guarantee has been given by the Government of India.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Constitution establishes a sharp asymmetry between the borrowing powers of the Union (Article 292) and the States (Article 293). First, Article 293(1) territorially confines a State's borrowing power to 'within the territory of India', barring external sovereign borrowing by States altogether; second, Article 293(3) requires a State even for domestic borrowing to obtain the prior consent of the Government of India whenever any part of a Central loan or Central guarantee to that State remains outstanding.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 293(1) expressly stipulates that 'Subject to the provisions of this article, the executive power of a State extends to borrowing within the territory of India upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State...' Unlike the Union Government under Article 292, which can borrow both inside and outside India, a State Government has no constitutional competence to raise a foreign loan outside the territory of India directly, and even Central consent cannot expand the territorial limitation fixed by Article 293(1) (which is why loans from multilateral agencies for State projects are borrowed by the Union Government and passed on via back-to-back arrangements).

Statement-II is also correct, as it states the exact constitutional mandate of Article 293(3). However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the prohibition on external borrowing by States stems from the express territorial limitation ('within the territory of India') in Article 293(1) read with exclusive Union competence over foreign loans under Entry 37 of the Union List, whereas Article 293(3) is a fiscal discipline mechanism regulating a State's domestic borrowing power whenever it remains indebted to the Centre.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 292 & Art. 293; Laxmikanth Ch. 15 (Borrowing by the Centre and the States)

stem: With reference to the financial provisions in Part XII of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Article 269A : Restrictions on States from imposing tax on the supply of goods or services where such supply takes place in the course of import into, or export out of, the territory of India
2. Article 274 : Prior recommendation of the President required for Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested
3. Article 286 : Levy and collection of Goods and Services Tax by the Government of India on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce
4. Article 290 : Adjustment between the Union and States in respect of certain expenses and pensions of courts and commissions
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Part XII of the Constitution establishes distinct fiscal boundaries and safeguards: Article 269A governs the levy and apportionment of IGST on inter-State supplies, whereas Article 286 restricts States from taxing supplies taking place outside the State or in the course of import and export. Furthermore, Article 274 acts as a procedural federal check requiring presidential recommendation for Union Bills that alter tax provisions in which States have a financial stake.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because the constitutional bar on States from imposing tax on the supply of goods or services taking place outside the State or in the course of import into, or export out of, the territory of India is contained in Article 286(1), not Article 269A.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Under Article 274(1), no Bill or amendment which imposes or varies any tax or duty in which States are interested, or which varies the meaning of the expression 'agricultural income', or affects the principles of distribution of moneys to States, shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched because the levy and collection of Goods and Services Tax (IGST) by the Government of India in the course of inter-State trade or commerce and its apportionment between the Union and the States on the recommendations of the GST Council is governed by Article 269A (inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016), not Article 286.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Article 290 provides for financial adjustments between the Consolidated Fund of India and the Consolidated Fund of a State in respect of certain expenses and pensions of a court or Commission that serves both the Union and a State, as determined by agreement or by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 269A, 274, 286 & 290; Laxmikanth Ch. 15

stem: With reference to the taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments under Article 276 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A law of the Legislature of a State relating to taxes on professions, trades, callings or employments for the benefit of the State or a municipality is valid notwithstanding that it relates to a tax on income.
2. The maximum ceiling of two thousand and five hundred rupees per annum per person on such tax can be periodically revised by the respective State Legislature through an ordinary Money Bill.

3. The exercise of the power by a State Legislature to levy a tax on professions and employments under Article 276 bars Parliament from levying taxes on income arising out of the same professions or employments.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 276 carves out a narrow constitutional exception allowing States and local bodies to levy a tax on professions, trades, callings, and employments without such levy being struck down as an encroachment on the Union's exclusive power to tax non-agricultural income. However, the ceiling of Rs. 2,500 per annum per person is constitutionally entrenched in Article 276(2) itself and does not curtail Parliament's power to levy income tax on those earnings.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 276(1) explicitly declares that notwithstanding anything in Article 246, no law of the Legislature of a State relating to taxes for the benefit of the State or of a municipality, district board, local board or other local authority therein in respect of professions, trades, callings or employments shall be invalid on the ground that it relates to a tax on income.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The maximum ceiling of Rs. 2,500 per annum in respect of any one person is explicitly hard-coded in Article 276(2) of the Constitution (having been raised from Rs. 250 by the 60th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988). Therefore, a State Legislature cannot enhance this ceiling through an ordinary Money Bill; any upward revision requires a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 276(3), the power of the Legislature of a State to make laws with respect to taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments shall not be construed as limiting in any way the power of Parliament to make laws with respect to taxes on income accruing from or arising out of professions, trades, callings and employments.

ref: Constitution of India Article 276; 60th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988

stem: With reference to the constitutional framework governing inter-State rivers and water disputes in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 262 of the Constitution by itself directly bars the Supreme Court and High Courts from exercising jurisdiction over any dispute relating to the waters of an inter-State river.
2. Under the Seventh Schedule, the power of a State Legislature to legislate on water supplies, irrigation, and canals is expressly subject to the provisions of Entry 56 of the Union List.

3. The River Boards Act, 1956 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 were enacted by Parliament pursuant to powers conferred under Entry 56 of the Union List and Article 262 of the Constitution, respectively.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Water is primarily a State subject under Entry 17 of List II, but it is constitutionally subordinated to Entry 56 of List I (Union regulation of inter-State rivers).
