Crucially, Article 262(2) does not automatically oust judicial jurisdiction on its own; rather, it is an enabling clause empowering Parliament to enact a statute excluding the jurisdiction of courts over inter-State water disputes.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Article 262(2) does not by its own force oust the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or other courts. Instead, it is an enabling provision stating that 'Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint.' The actual bar operates only because Parliament enacted Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956.

Statement 2 is correct. Entry 17 of List II (State List) covers 'Water, that is to say, water supplies, irrigation and canals, drainage and embankments, water storage and water power subject to the provisions of Entry 56 of List I.' Entry 56 of List I empowers Parliament to provide for the regulation and development of inter-State rivers and river valleys to the extent declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest.

Statement 3 is correct. Parliament enacted the River Boards Act, 1956 under Entry 56 of the Union List to establish advisory boards for the regulation of inter-State rivers, and enacted the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 under Article 262 for the adjudication of water disputes through ad-hoc tribunals.

ref: Constitution of India Article 262; Seventh Schedule List I Entry 56 & List II Entry 17

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in inter-State river water disputes:
items: Statement-I: Once Parliament enacts a law under Article 262(2) read with Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, the Supreme Court is completely barred from entertaining even a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against the final award of a Water Disputes Tribunal.

Statement-II: While Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 bars the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to adjudicate a water dispute referred to a Tribunal, the plenary constitutional appellate power under Article 136 against a Tribunal's final determination cannot be curtailed by a parliamentary statute.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the Cauvery Water Dispute judgment (State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu), the Supreme Court drew a fundamental constitutional distinction between the original adjudication of a 'water dispute' and appellate review of a Tribunal's final award. While Section 11 of the 1956 Act enacted under Article 262(2) validly bars original suits under Article 131, it does not extinguish the Supreme Court's plenary appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 once the Tribunal pronounces its award.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. As held by the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2016/2018 Cauvery judgment), the bar under Article 262(2) read with Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 does not prevent the Supreme Court from entertaining appeals via Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against the final decision/award of a Water Disputes Tribunal.

Statement-II is correct. The Supreme Court explained that Section 11 only excludes the Court's original jurisdiction (such as a suit under Article 131) to entertain and adjudicate a 'water dispute' or complaint that is referred to a Tribunal. Once the Tribunal has adjudicated the dispute and rendered its award, the constitutional appellate jurisdiction under Article 136—which is part of the basic structure—remains intact and cannot be taken away by Section 6(2) or Section 11 of the 1956 Act.

ref: State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (Cauvery Water Dispute); Constitution Articles 131, 136 & 262

stem: Consider the following stages in the resolution of an inter-State water dispute under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956:
items: 1. Reference by the Central Government or a State Government to the Tribunal for further explanation or guidance within three months of the report
2. Attempt by the Central Government to settle the water dispute by negotiations after receiving a request from a State Government
3. Publication of the decision of the Tribunal by the Central Government in the Official Gazette, giving it the same force as an order or decree of the Supreme Court
4. Constitution of a Water Disputes Tribunal by the Central Government consisting of a Chairman and two other members nominated by the Chief Justice of India
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the stages given above under the Act?
core: Under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (as amended in 2002), adjudication follows a strict statutory sequence: mandatory attempt at negotiated settlement by the Centre, constitution of a three-member Tribunal nominated by the CJI, submission of the primary report followed by a 3-month window for seeking clarification/supplementary report, and finally Official Gazette publication which accords the award the force of a Supreme Court decree.

exp.why: Under Section 5(3) of the Act, after the Tribunal investigates the matter and forwards its report setting out the facts and its decision to the Central Government (Step 3 in the overall sequence), the Central Government or any State Government may, within three months of the date of the decision, again refer the matter to the Tribunal for further consideration and explanation or guidance.

Under Section 4(1) of the Act, when the Central Government receives a request under Section 3 from any State Government in respect of any water dispute, it must first try to settle the dispute by negotiations (Step 1 in the sequence).

Under Section 6(1) and 6(2) of the Act, after the initial decision (or the modified decision following the Section 5(3) reference), the Central Government publishes the decision of the Tribunal in the Official Gazette, upon which the decision becomes final and binding on the parties and has the same force as an order or decree of the Supreme Court (Step 4 in the sequence).

Under Section 4(1) and 4(2) of the Act, if the Central Government is of the opinion that the water dispute cannot be settled by negotiations, it constitutes a Water Disputes Tribunal within a period not exceeding one year from the date of receipt of such request, consisting of a Chairman and two other members nominated by the Chief Justice of India from among persons who are Judges of the Supreme Court or of a High Court (Step 2 in the sequence).

ref: Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (Sections 3, 4, 5 & 6); Laxmikanth Ch. 16

stem: With reference to the alteration of Centre-State financial relations during Emergencies, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Order under Article 354 (National Emergency) : Modifies the constitutional provisions relating to the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States (Articles 268 to 279), but cannot extend beyond the expiration of the financial year in which the Proclamation ceases to operate

2. Direction under Article 354 (National Emergency) : Empowers the President to require all Money Bills and Financial Bills under Article 207 to be reserved for his consideration after they are passed by the Legislature of a State

3. Direction under Article 360 (Financial Emergency) : Authorizes the President to issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union, including the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 354 and 360 alter fiscal federalism in fundamentally different ways: during a National Emergency, Article 354 allows the President to modify or suspend tax devolution and grant provisions (Articles 268-279) only up to the end of the financial year in which the Proclamation ceases. Conversely, the power to compel reservation of State Money Bills for presidential consideration belongs exclusively to a Financial Emergency under Article 360.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Article 354(1), while a Proclamation of Emergency (National Emergency under Article 352) is in operation, the President may by order direct that all or any of the provisions of Articles 268 to 279 (distribution of revenues and grants between the Union and the States) shall have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as he thinks fit, provided that no such order shall extend beyond the expiration of the financial year in which the Proclamation ceases to operate.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. A Proclamation of National Emergency (Articles 352-354) does not empower the President to require all State Money Bills to be reserved for his consideration. That specific power is conferred exclusively during a Proclamation of Financial Emergency under Article 360(4)(a)(ii).

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Under Article 360(4)(b), during the period any Proclamation of Financial Emergency is in operation, the President is competent to issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union, including the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 354 & 360; Laxmikanth Ch. 15 & 17

stem: With reference to the proclamation of a National Emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: A proclamation of Emergency can be issued in respect of either the whole of India or only a specified part of its territory, even before the actual occurrence of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
opts.B: While a proclamation on grounds of war or external aggression can be issued in anticipation of imminent danger, a proclamation on the ground of armed rebellion can be issued only after the actual outbreak of violence.
opts.C: Once a proclamation of Emergency is in operation across the territory of India, the President is constitutionally barred from issuing a second proclamation on a different ground until the first proclamation is revoked.
opts.D: The power to restrict or vary the operation of a National Emergency to a specified part of the territory of India was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

core: Under Article 352(1) and its Explanation, a National Emergency can be proclaimed for either the whole of India or a specified part thereof, and it can be issued preemptively before the actual occurrence of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger thereof.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because Article 352(1) empowers the President to make a proclamation of Emergency in respect of the whole of India or such part of its territory as may be specified, and the Explanation to Article 352(1) clarifies that such a proclamation may be made before the actual occurrence of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger thereof. Option (B) is incorrect because preventive proclamation on the basis of 'imminent danger' applies equally to armed rebellion as it does to war and external aggression. Option (C) is incorrect because Article 352(9) (inserted by the 38th Amendment Act, 1975) explicitly empowers the President to issue different proclamations on different grounds even if a proclamation is already in operation. Option (D) is incorrect because the power to limit or vary a National Emergency to a specified part of India was introduced by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, not the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 352(1) & 352(9); 42nd & 44th Constitutional Amendment Acts; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16.

stem: With reference to the procedural safeguard regarding the 'Union Cabinet' under Article 352(3) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The President can issue a proclamation of National Emergency once the written recommendation of the Prime Minister on behalf of the Union Council of Ministers is communicated to him.
2. Article 352 is the only provision in the Constitution of India that explicitly mentions and defines the term 'Cabinet'.
3. For the purpose of Article 352(3), the 'Union Cabinet' consists exclusively of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75, excluding Ministers of State.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 352(3) is the sole provision in the Constitution mentioning the 'Cabinet', defining it strictly as the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75, whose collective written decision is mandatory before the President can proclaim a National Emergency.

exp.why: Under Article 352(3), introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 to prevent unilateral prime ministerial advice (as occurred in 1975), the President shall not issue a Proclamation of Emergency unless the decision of the Union Cabinet (and not merely the recommendation of the Prime Minister or the broader Council of Ministers) has been communicated to him in writing.

While Article 74 refers to the 'Council of Ministers', Article 352(3) is the only provision in the entire text of the Constitution of India where the word 'Cabinet' explicitly appears and is constitutionally defined.

Article 352(3) explicitly defines the Union Cabinet as the Council consisting of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75. Consequently, Ministers of State (whether with or without independent charge) and Deputy Ministers are constitutionally excluded from this specific decision-making body.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 74, 75 & 352(3); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the parliamentary approval and continuation of a National Emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. A proclamation of National Emergency ceases to operate at the expiration of two months from the date of its issue unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament.
2. Under Article 352(6), a resolution approving the continuation of a National Emergency requires a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of each House of Parliament.

3. If a proclamation of National Emergency is issued at a time when the Lok Sabha has been dissolved, the proclamation lapses at the end of one month even if it has been approved by the Rajya Sabha within that period.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the 44th Amendment safeguards in Article 352(4)–(6), a National Emergency requires parliamentary approval within one month (not two) by a special majority of total membership plus two-thirds present and voting, and survives dissolution of the Lok Sabha until 30 days after its reconstitution if approved by the Rajya Sabha in the interim.

exp.why: While the two-month parliamentary approval window still applies to President's Rule (Article 356) and Financial Emergency (Article 360), the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 reduced the period for parliamentary approval of a National Emergency under Article 352(4) from two months to one month from the date of its issue.

Under Article 352(6), a resolution approving a proclamation of Emergency or its continuation every six months requires a majority of the total membership of that House AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting. A majority of two-thirds of the total membership of the House is required only for the impeachment of the President under Article 61.

Under the proviso to Article 352(4), if a proclamation is issued when the Lok Sabha is dissolved (or dissolution takes place during the one-month period without the Lok Sabha passing the resolution) and the resolution is passed by the Rajya Sabha within that one-month window, the proclamation does not lapse at the end of one month; instead, it survives until 30 days from the date on which the reconstituted Lok Sabha first sits.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 352(4), 352(5) & 352(6); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16.

stem: With reference to the revocation of a proclamation of National Emergency under Articles 352(7) and 352(8) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A parliamentary resolution requiring the President to revoke a proclamation of National Emergency needs to be passed only by the Lok Sabha and does not require the approval of the Rajya Sabha.
2. Unlike a resolution approving the continuation of a National Emergency, a resolution disapproving its continuation is passed by a simple majority of the members present and voting.

3. Where one-tenth of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha give a written notice to move a resolution disapproving the Emergency when the House is not in session, the notice must be submitted to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha to convene a special sitting within 14 days.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Articles 352(7) and 352(8), the Lok Sabha alone can compel the President to revoke a National Emergency by passing a disapproval resolution by simple majority; a written notice by one-tenth of Lok Sabha MPs for a special sitting within 14 days goes to the Speaker if the House is in session, or to the President if it is not in session.

exp.why: Under Article 352(7), the President shall revoke a Proclamation of Emergency if the House of the People (Lok Sabha) passes a resolution disapproving its continuation. Unlike approval of an Emergency (which requires both Houses), legislative revocation rests exclusively with the Lok Sabha.

Article 352(6) restricts the requirement of a special majority strictly to resolutions under clauses (4) and (5) (approving the proclamation or its six-monthly continuation). A resolution disapproving the continuation of an Emergency under clause (7) requires only a simple majority of the Lok Sabha.

Under Article 352(8), a written notice signed by not less than one-tenth of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha must be given to the Speaker only if the House is in session; if the House is not in session, the notice must be given to the President, following which a special sitting of the House shall be held within 14 days from the date of receipt of the notice.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 352(7) & 352(8); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the impact of a National Emergency on Centre-State executive relations:
items: Statement-I: Upon the proclamation of a National Emergency under Article 352, the State Council of Ministers stands suspended and the executive power of the State is directly assumed by the President of India.

Statement-II: While a proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, Article 353(a) extends the executive power of the Union to giving directions to any State as to the manner in which its executive power is to be exercised on any matter.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike President's Rule under Article 356, a National Emergency under Article 352 does not suspend or dismiss the State Executive; instead, Article 353(a) converts the federal executive framework into a unitary one by empowering the Union to issue binding executive directions to a State on 'any matter'.

exp.why: Statement-I confuses the effect of a National Emergency (Article 352) with that of President's Rule (Article 356). During a National Emergency, State Governments and State Councils of Ministers are neither dismissed nor suspended; they continue to function, though under the overriding executive direction of the Union.

In normal times, the Union can issue executive directions to a State only on specific constitutional subjects (such as Articles 256 and 257). However, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Article 353(a) expands the Union's executive power to giving directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power thereof is to be exercised on any matter whatsoever.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 353(a) & 356; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16.

stem: With reference to the effect of a National Emergency on Centre-State legislative relations under Articles 250 and 353 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While a proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, the power of a State Legislature to make laws on the State List is suspended, and any law made by Parliament on the State List ceases to have effect six months after the Emergency ceases to operate.
2. During the operation of a National Emergency, if Parliament is not in session, the President can promulgate Ordinances on subjects enumerated in the State List.

3. Where a proclamation of National Emergency is in operation in only a specified part of the territory of India, the Union's expanded legislative and executive powers under Article 353 can also extend to any other State where the Emergency is not in operation, if the security of India is threatened by activities in or in relation to the emergency-affected part.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: During a National Emergency, State Legislatures are not suspended—Parliament merely acquires concurrent overriding power over the State List (with such laws expiring 6 months after the Emergency ends), the President's Ordinance power co-extensively covers the State List, and the Proviso to Article 353 extends Union emergency powers to unaffected States if security is threatened from the affected area.

exp.why: While it is true under Article 250(2) that laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to have effect on the expiration of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, the first part of the statement is incorrect. Under Articles 250(1) and 251, the legislative power of a State Legislature is NOT suspended during a National Emergency; rather, Parliament acquires concurrent overriding power to legislate on the State List while the State Legislature continues to exercise its legislative power subject to parliamentary supremacy.

Under Article 123(2), the President's power to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session is co-extensive with the legislative competence of Parliament. Because Article 250(1) empowers Parliament to make laws with respect to any matter in the State List while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, the President can validly promulgate Ordinances on State List subjects during this period.

Under the proviso to Article 353 (inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976), where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in a part of the territory of India, the Union's expanded executive power (clause a) and Parliament's expanded legislative power (clause b) shall also extend to any State other than a State in which the Emergency is in operation, if and in so far as the security of India or any part of its territory is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of India under Emergency.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 123, 250, 251 & Proviso to Article 353; 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

stem: With reference to the modification of Centre-State financial relations while a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation under Article 354 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The President may by order direct that all or any of the constitutional provisions relating to the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States (Articles 268 to 279) shall take effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as he thinks fit.
2. Any such Presidential Order modifying the devolution of taxes continues to remain in force for a maximum period of six months after the Proclamation of Emergency has ceased to operate.
3. Every such order made by the President must be laid before each House of Parliament as soon as may be after it is made.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 354, the President can modify or suspend the constitutional distribution of financial revenues between the Union and the States (Articles 268 to 279) during a National Emergency, subject to laying the order before both Houses of Parliament. Unlike parliamentary laws on State List subjects (which expire 6 months after the Emergency ceases), a financial order under Article 354 cannot extend beyond the expiration of the financial year in which the Proclamation ceases to operate.

exp.why: Under Article 354(1), the President may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, by order direct that all or any of the provisions of Articles 268 to 279 (governing the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States) shall for such period have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as he thinks fit.

Under Article 354(1), the period specified in such a Presidential Order cannot, in any case, extend beyond the expiration of the financial year in which the Proclamation of Emergency ceases to operate. The six-month post-emergency sunset rule applies to laws made by Parliament on State List subjects under Article 250(2), not to financial devolution orders under Article 354.
Article 354(2) explicitly mandates that every order made under clause (1) shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 354; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Emergency Provisions

stem: With reference to the extension of the normal five-year tenure of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies while a Proclamation of National Emergency (Article 352) is in operation, which one of the following statements is constitutionally correct?

opts.A: The President of India may, by executive order, extend the tenure of both the Lok Sabha and any State Legislative Assembly for a period not exceeding one year at a time.
opts.B: Parliament may by law extend the tenure of a State Legislative Assembly for a period not exceeding one year at a time, and such extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
opts.C: While the tenure of the Lok Sabha is extended by an Act of Parliament, the tenure of a State Legislative Assembly during a National Emergency is extended by a law passed by the respective State Legislature.
opts.D: Once Parliament extends the tenure of the Lok Sabha by one year during a National Emergency, the House continues for that full one-year period even if the Emergency is revoked immediately thereafter.

core: Under the provisos to Article 83(2) and Article 172(1), it is exclusively Parliament by law (and neither the President by executive order nor the State Legislature) that can extend the normal five-year tenure of the Lok Sabha or any State Legislative Assembly during a National Emergency. Such extensions can be granted for up to one year at a time, subject to a hard outer ceiling of six months after the Proclamation of Emergency ceases to operate.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because under the proviso to Article 172(1) (for State Legislative Assemblies) and the proviso to Article 83(2) (for the Lok Sabha), while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, the five-year period may be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time and not extending in any case beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate. Option (A) is incorrect because the extension requires an Act of Parliament, not a Presidential Order. Option (C) is incorrect because a State Legislature has no power to extend its own life; only Parliament by law can extend a State Assembly's tenure during a National Emergency. Option (D) is incorrect because any extension automatically terminates at most six months after the Proclamation of Emergency ceases to operate, even if the one-year statutory extension period has not yet elapsed.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 83(2) and 172(1); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Emergency Provisions

stem: With reference to the suspension of provisions of Article 19 during emergencies under Article 358 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The six Fundamental Rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended as soon as a Proclamation of National Emergency is issued on any of the three grounds mentioned in Article 352.

2. Unlike under Article 359, the suspension of the freedoms under Article 19 pursuant to Article 358 occurs automatically upon the operation of a qualifying Proclamation of Emergency without requiring a separate Presidential Order.

3. Any law enacted during the Emergency that is inconsistent with Article 19 ceases to have effect immediately upon the expiration of the Emergency, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 358 operates exclusively during an External Emergency (declared on the grounds of war or external aggression) and never during an Internal Emergency (armed rebellion). When triggered, it suspends Article 19 automatically without a separate Presidential Order, and Article 19 revives automatically the moment the Proclamation ceases to operate.

exp.why: By virtue of the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 358(1) operates ONLY when a Proclamation of National Emergency is declared on the grounds of 'war or external aggression'. It does NOT operate when a National Emergency is declared on the third ground of 'armed rebellion'.

Under Article 358(1), while a Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of its territory is threatened by war or by external aggression is in operation, nothing in Article 19 restricts the power of the State to make any law or take any executive action. This suspension is automatic and does not require a separate Presidential Order, unlike Article 359.

Under Article 358(1), any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the Proclamation ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 358; 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

stem: With reference to the Presidential Order issued under Article 359 of the Constitution of India during the operation of a Proclamation of National Emergency, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An order under Article 359 suspends the specified Fundamental Rights themselves for the duration of the Emergency, rather than merely suspending the right to move any court for their enforcement.

2. Similar to Article 358, a Presidential Order under Article 359 can be issued during an Emergency declared on the grounds of war or external aggression, but cannot be issued when the Emergency is declared on the ground of armed rebellion.

3. Under the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, the President is constitutionally barred from suspending the enforcement of Articles 19, 20, and 21 under Article 359, and orders issued under this Article are exempt from being laid before Parliament.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 359 empowers the President to suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of only those Fundamental Rights expressly mentioned in the Presidential Order (excluding Articles 20 and 21, which can never be suspended). Unlike Article 358, Article 359 operates during both External Emergencies (war/external aggression) and Internal Emergencies (armed rebellion), and every such Presidential Order must be laid before each House of Parliament.

exp.why: Textually and theoretically under Article 359(1), a Presidential Order does not suspend the Fundamental Rights themselves; rather, it declares that 'the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except Articles 20 and 21) as may be mentioned in the order and all proceedings pending in any court for the enforcement of the rights so mentioned shall remain suspended'.

Unlike Article 358 (which is confined to war or external aggression), Article 359 applies to a Proclamation of National Emergency declared on ANY of the three grounds—war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 barred the suspension of the enforcement of ONLY Articles 20 and 21 under Article 359(1) (Article 19 is not barred under Article 359). Furthermore, Article 359(3) explicitly mandates that every order made under clause (1) shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 359; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Emergency Provisions

stem: With reference to the protective shield against Fundamental Rights challenges under Articles 358(2) and 359(1B) of the Constitution of India (inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978), consider the following rows:
items: 1. An ordinary statute enacted during a National Emergency that does not contain an explicit recital stating that it is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency : Remains open to judicial challenge for violating Article 19 or other Fundamental Rights whose enforcement is suspended

2. A standalone executive action taken during a National Emergency without the authority of a law containing an explicit Emergency recital : Enjoys automatic immunity from Fundamental Rights challenges while the Proclamation is in force

3. A pre-existing ordinary law enacted prior to the Proclamation of Emergency that lacks an Emergency recital : Automatically becomes immune from challenge under Article 19 upon the declaration of an External Emergency
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the constitutional position correctly stated?
core: Articles 358(2) and 359(1B), inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, prevent blanket immunity for unrelated State actions during a National Emergency. Constitutional immunity from Fundamental Rights challenges applies ONLY to laws that contain an explicit recital that the law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation, and to executive actions taken under a law containing such a recital.

exp.why: Under Articles 358(2)(a) and 359(1B)(a), the suspension of Article 19 or the suspension of the enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights does NOT apply in relation to any law which does not contain a recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made. Hence, ordinary laws lacking this recital remain fully open to judicial review under Part III.

Under Articles 358(2)(b) and 359(1B)(b), immunity does NOT apply to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such an explicit Emergency recital. Standalone executive actions not backed by a recital-bearing statute enjoy zero immunity.

A pre-existing ordinary law enacted before the Emergency that does not contain a recital linking it to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made receives no protection under Articles 358(2) or 359(1B) and remains subject to Fundamental Rights challenges.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 358(2) and 359(1B); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the chronological and structural evolution of Part XVIII (Emergency Provisions) of the Constitution of India across successive Constitutional Amendments:
items: 1. Chronologically, the explicit constitutional power of the President to issue different Proclamations of National Emergency on different grounds simultaneously—even when an earlier Proclamation is already in operation—was enacted prior to the power to restrict a Proclamation of National Emergency to a specified part of India.

2. The periodic parliamentary approval block for the continuation of President's Rule under Article 356 was extended from six months to one year at a time by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, before being restored to six months by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

3. Both the requirement of a written decision of the Union Cabinet to proclaim a National Emergency and the empowerment of the President to vary or revoke a Proclamation in respect of only a specified part of India were introduced simultaneously by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Part XVIII evolved through three major amendments in the 1970s: the 38th CAA (1975) authorized simultaneous proclamations on different grounds; the 42nd CAA (1976) enabled part-of-India proclamations and extended the periodic renewal block of President's Rule from 6 months to 1 year; and the 44th CAA (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion', mandated written Cabinet communication, and restored the 6-month renewal block under Article 356.

exp.why: The power of the President to issue different Proclamations on grounds of war, external aggression, or internal disturbance whether or not there is a Proclamation already in operation (currently Article 352(9)) was inserted by the 38th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975, whereas the power to make a Proclamation in respect of only a specified part of the territory of India was inserted later by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 raised the period for which a Proclamation under Article 356 remains in force after each parliamentary approval from six months to one year; the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 restored the six-month periodic approval block.

While the requirement of a written decision of the Union Cabinet (Article 352(3)) and the substitution of 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance' were introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, the empowerment of the President to make or vary a Proclamation of Emergency in respect of only a specified part of India was introduced earlier by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

ref: Constitution of India, Part XVIII; 38th (1975), 42nd (1976), and 44th (1978) Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the imposition of President's Rule in a State, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, the President can issue a Proclamation imposing President's Rule in a State only upon receiving a formal written report from the Governor of that State.

2. Under Article 365, where any State has failed to comply with any valid executive directions given by the Union, it is lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.

3. Article 355 imposes a constitutional duty on the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that the government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 355, 356, and 365 form an integrated constitutional triad for safeguarding constitutional machinery in the States. Notably, Article 356(1) empowers the President to act 'on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise', meaning a Governor's report is not a mandatory prerequisite.

exp.why: Article 356(1) explicitly states that the President may issue a Proclamation if satisfied 'on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise' that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. Because of the phrase 'or otherwise', the President can act suo motu on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers even without receiving a report from the State Governor.

Article 365 creates a constitutional deeming presumption linking Union executive directions (such as under Articles 256 and 257) to Article 356: if a State fails to comply with or give effect to any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that the constitutional machinery in the State has failed.

Article 355 lays down the twin foundational obligations of the Union: first, to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance; and second, to ensure that the government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 355, 356(1) & 365; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16 (Emergency Provisions)

stem: With reference to the parliamentary approval and duration of a Proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Proclamation imposing President's Rule must be approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament passed by a simple majority within two months from the date of its issue.

2. Under Article 356(5), a resolution approving the continuation of President's Rule beyond one year cannot be passed by Parliament unless both a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation in the whole of India, or in the whole or any part of the State, and the Election Commission certifies that holding general elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State is difficult.
3. Under the existing provisions of Article 356(4), no Proclamation of President's Rule can in any case remain in force in a State for more than three years continuously.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While initial parliamentary approval and six-monthly extensions of President's Rule require only a simple majority within two months, the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 inserted Article 356(5) to impose two cumulative ('and') preconditions for any extension beyond one year, up to a strict maximum ceiling of three years.

exp.why: Under Article 356(3), a Proclamation of President's Rule ceases to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament. Unlike a National Emergency under Article 352 (which requires a one-month window and a special majority), a resolution under Article 356 is passed by a simple majority of members present and voting in each House.

Under Article 356(5), inserted by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978, a resolution for the continuance of a Proclamation beyond one year cannot be passed by either House of Parliament unless BOTH conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (a) a Proclamation of Emergency (under Article 352) is in operation in the whole of India or in the whole or any part of the State at the time of passing such resolution, AND (b) the Election Commission certifies that the continuance in force of the Proclamation is necessary on account of difficulties in holding general elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State.

The First Proviso to Article 356(4) lays down an absolute constitutional cap that no such Proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than three years. Historically, whenever President's Rule had to be extended beyond three years (such as in Punjab during the late 1980s and early 1990s), specific Constitutional Amendment Acts had to be enacted by Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 356(3), 356(4) & 356(5); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

stem: With reference to the exercise of legislative and financial powers under Article 357 during the operation of President's Rule in a State, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When the powers of the Legislature of a State are declared to be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, Parliament is competent to confer on the President the power of the State Legislature to make laws and to authorise the President to delegate such conferred power to any other authority.

2. Any law made by Parliament or by the President in exercise of the legislative powers of the State under Article 357 automatically ceases to have effect on the expiration of six months after the Proclamation of President's Rule has ceased to operate.

3. When the Lok Sabha is not in session during the operation of President's Rule, the President is empowered to authorise expenditure out of the Consolidated Fund of that State pending the sanction of such expenditure by Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 357 governs the delegation and lifespan of State legislative powers during President's Rule. Crucially, following the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, laws enacted under Article 357 do not automatically expire six months after President's Rule ends; they continue in force until altered or repealed by the restored State Legislature.

exp.why: Article 357(1)(a) explicitly provides that where by a Proclamation issued under Article 356(1) it has been declared that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, it shall be competent for Parliament to confer on the President the power of the Legislature of the State to make laws, and to authorise the President to delegate, subject to such conditions as he may think fit to impose, the power so conferred to any other authority to be specified by him.

While laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency under Article 250(2) expire six months after the Emergency ceases to operate, laws enacted under Article 357 during President's Rule are NOT coterminous with the Proclamation. Under Article 357(2) (as substituted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976), any law made in exercise of the power of the State Legislature under Article 357 continues in force even after the Proclamation ceases to operate, until altered, repealed, or amended by a competent Legislature or other authority.

Article 357(1)(c) explicitly states that when the House of the People (Lok Sabha) is not in session, it is competent for the President to authorise expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State pending the sanction of such expenditure by Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 357(1) & 357(2); 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the dissolution of a State Legislative Assembly under Article 356 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: According to the constitutional law laid down by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the President should not dissolve a State Legislative Assembly immediately upon issuing a Proclamation under Article 356, and may only keep it under suspended animation until both Houses of Parliament have approved the Proclamation.

Statement-II: Under Article 356(3), a Proclamation ceases to operate at the expiration of two months unless approved by both Houses of Parliament, and if the Proclamation is disapproved by Parliament or struck down by the Courts as unconstitutional, the status quo ante can be restored by reviving the Legislative Assembly.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the 9-Judge Bench harmonized the President's power to dissolve the State Assembly under Article 356(1)(a) with the parliamentary check in Article 356(3) and judicial review, holding that irreversible steps like dissolution must not be taken prior to approval by both Houses of Parliament.

exp.why: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that although Article 356(1)(a) empowers the President to assume functions of the State Government and implicitly carries the power to dissolve the Legislative Assembly, the President should not take the irreversible action of dissolving the Assembly until at least both Houses of Parliament have ratified the Proclamation under Article 356(3). Prior to parliamentary approval, the Assembly may only be kept under suspended animation.

Statement-II provides the exact constitutional reasoning behind Statement-I: because Article 356(3) makes the Proclamation conditional upon parliamentary ratification within two months and because the Proclamation is amenable to judicial review (where the Court has the power to restore the dismissed Ministry and revive the Legislative Assembly if the Proclamation is held mala fide or unconstitutional), keeping the Assembly in suspended animation prevents an irreversible constitutional fait accompli prior to parliamentary scrutiny.

ref: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) 3 SCC 1; Constitution of India, Article 356(1) & 356(3)

stem: With reference to the scope of judicial review over a Proclamation issued under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, as established by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Even after both Houses of Parliament have approved a Proclamation under Article 356(3), the Constitutional Courts can examine whether the President's satisfaction was based on wholly extraneous or irrelevant grounds, or was vitiated by mala fides, and can invalidate the Proclamation.
opts.B: Once both Houses of Parliament approve a Proclamation under Article 356(3), the Proclamation merges into a parliamentary resolution and becomes immune from judicial review.
opts.C: Article 74(2) completely bars the Supreme Court from calling upon the Union Government to produce the underlying material or reports on the basis of which the President's satisfaction under Article 356 was formed.
opts.D: A newly elected State Legislative Assembly cannot be constitutionally dissolved under Article 356 prior to holding its first sitting and the administration of oath to its members.

core: The satisfaction of the President under Article 356 is subjective in nature but conditioned on objective material; neither Article 74(2) nor subsequent approval by both Houses of Parliament under Article 356(3) immunizes an unconstitutional or mala fide Proclamation from judicial invalidation.

exp.why: Option A is correct: In S.R. Bommai (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad (2006), the Supreme Court held that although courts do not sit as an appellate forum over the sufficiency or correctness of the material, they can examine whether relevant material existed at all or whether the Proclamation was perverse, wholly extraneous, or actuated by mala fides. Option B is incorrect because parliamentary approval under Article 356(3) only extends the life of a valid Proclamation and does not cure the unconstitutionality of a Proclamation that was void ab initio. Option C is incorrect because the Court clarified that Article 74(2) only protects the actual ministerial advice tendered to the President from judicial inquiry, not the underlying material/record on the basis of which that advice was tendered and satisfaction formed. Option D is incorrect because in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the 5-Judge Bench explicitly held that a State Legislative Assembly is duly constituted upon the Election Commission's notification under Section 73 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and can constitutionally be dissolved under Article 356 even prior to its first meeting, though the specific dissolution in that case was struck down on grounds of mala fides.

ref: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994); Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) 2 SCC 1; Article 74(2) & Article 356

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the position of the State Judiciary during the operation of President's Rule under Article 356 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: During the operation of a Proclamation under Article 356(1), the President is empowered to assume to himself all executive functions of the State Government as well as the administrative and supervisory powers vested in the High Court of that State.

Statement-II: The Proviso to Article 356(1) of the Constitution of India expressly prohibits the President from assuming to himself any of the powers vested in or exercisable by a High Court, or from suspending in whole or in part the operation of any constitutional provision relating to High Courts.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: To preserve judicial independence and the Basic Structure even when a State's executive and legislative organs are taken over by the Union during President's Rule, the Proviso to Article 356(1) carves out an absolute constitutional immunity for the powers and constitutional provisions relating to High Courts.

exp.why: Under Article 356(1)(a), the President may by Proclamation assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor or any body or authority in the State other than the Legislature of the State. However, the President is strictly barred from assuming any power—judicial, supervisory, or administrative—vested in or exercisable by the High Court of the State.

The Proviso to Article 356(1) explicitly states: 'Provided that nothing in this clause shall authorise the President to assume to himself any of the powers vested in or exercisable by a High Court, or to suspend in whole or in part the operation of any provision of this Constitution relating to High Courts.' Thus, the constitutional position, jurisdiction, and powers of the State High Court remain completely untouched during President's Rule.

ref: Constitution of India, Proviso to Article 356(1); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 16

stem: Consider the following table comparing a National Emergency (Article 352) and President's Rule (Article 356):
items: 1. Impact on Fundamental Rights : Fundamental Rights are affected under Articles 358 and 359 during a National Emergency, whereas they remain completely unaffected during President's Rule.

2. Status of State Executive and Legislature : The State Council of Ministers and Legislative Assembly continue to function during a National Emergency, whereas the State Council of Ministers is dismissed and the Assembly is either suspended or dissolved during President's Rule.

3. Parliamentary Approval and Continuation : Both Article 352 and Article 356 require a special majority for initial parliamentary approval, while periodic six-monthly extensions require only a simple majority in both cases.

4. Revocation by Lok Sabha : The Lok Sabha can compel the revocation of a National Emergency by passing a disapproving resolution by a simple majority, whereas no such unilateral revocation mechanism by the Lok Sabha alone is prescribed for President's Rule.
prompt: In which of the rows given above is the constitutional comparison between Article 352 and Article 356 correctly stated?
core: A National Emergency (Article 352) converts the federal structure into a unitary one while keeping the State Executive and Legislature intact and requires a special majority for both initial approval and six-monthly extensions. In contrast, President's Rule (Article 356) displaces the State Executive and suspends or dissolves the State Legislature, leaves Fundamental Rights untouched, and requires only a simple majority for both initial approval and extensions.

exp.why: Row 1 is correct. During a National Emergency under Article 352, Fundamental Rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended (if declared on grounds of war or external aggression under Article 358) and the enforcement of other Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21) can be suspended by Presidential Order under Article 359. Under Article 356 (President's Rule), Citizens' Fundamental Rights remain wholly unaffected.

Row 2 is correct. Under Article 352, the State Executive and State Legislature are not suspended or dissolved; instead, the Union acquires concurrent executive and legislative powers over the State. Under Article 356, the State Council of Ministers is dismissed and the State Legislative Assembly is either placed under suspended animation or dissolved.

Row 3 is incorrect. Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, a resolution approving a National Emergency under Article 352 as well as every periodic six-monthly continuation resolution requires a special majority (majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting). Conversely, under Article 356, both initial parliamentary approval and periodic six-monthly continuation resolutions require only a simple majority in both Houses.

Row 4 is correct. Under Article 352(7) and (8), the President must revoke a Proclamation of National Emergency if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority disapproving its continuation. Article 356 contains no equivalent provision empowering the Lok Sabha alone to compel revocation by a unilateral resolution; a Proclamation under Article 356 may be revoked by the President at any time by a subsequent Proclamation.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 352, 356, 358 & 359; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter 16.

stem: With reference to the proclamation and parliamentary approval of a Financial Emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Proclamation of Financial Emergency must be approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament within two months from the date of its issue, failing which it ceases to operate.
2. A resolution approving a Proclamation of Financial Emergency requires only a simple majority of members present and voting in each House of Parliament.

3. Once approved by both Houses of Parliament, a Proclamation of Financial Emergency continues in force indefinitely until it is revoked by a subsequent Proclamation of the President, without requiring periodic six-monthly parliamentary renewals.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike Proclamations under Articles 352 and 356, a Proclamation of Financial Emergency under Article 360 is approved by a simple majority within two months and thereafter remains in operation indefinitely without any constitutional requirement for periodic six-monthly parliamentary renewals or any maximum outer time limit.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 360(2)(c), a Proclamation of Financial Emergency ceases to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament (subject to the 30-day survival proviso if the Lok Sabha is dissolved during that two-month window).

Statement 2 is correct. Unlike Article 352 (which requires a special majority), a resolution approving a Proclamation of Financial Emergency under Article 360 can be passed by either House of Parliament by a simple majority, that is, a majority of the members of that House present and voting.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 360(2), once approved by Parliament, a Financial Emergency continues indefinitely until revoked by a subsequent Proclamation by the President. No maximum period is prescribed for its operation, and repeated parliamentary approval every six months is not required.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 360(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter 16.

stem: With reference to the legal and fiscal consequences of a Proclamation of Financial Emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The executive authority of the Union extends to giving directions to any State to observe specified canons of financial propriety, including a provision for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the State.

2. The President is explicitly empowered to issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, notwithstanding the constitutional protection of their service conditions under Articles 125 and 221.

3. Any direction issued by the President may require that all Money Bills or other Financial Bills to which Article 207 applies shall be reserved for the consideration of the President after they are passed by the Legislature of the State.
4. During the operation of a Financial Emergency, the power of the State Legislature to pass the Annual Financial Statement (State Budget) stands automatically transferred to the Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 360(3) and (4), a Financial Emergency empowers the Union to enforce fiscal discipline by directing salary reductions across Union and State services—explicitly including Supreme Court and High Court Judges—and requiring State Money and Financial Bills to be reserved for Presidential consideration after passage by the State Legislature, without suspending the State Legislature itself.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 360(3) and Article 360(4)(a)(i), the executive authority of the Union extends to giving directions to any State to observe such canons of financial propriety as may be specified, and any such direction may include a provision requiring the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of a State.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 360(4)(b), the President is competent during a Financial Emergency to issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union, explicitly including the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution (such as Articles 125 and 221).

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 360(4)(a)(ii), Presidential directions during a Financial Emergency may include a provision requiring all Money Bills or other Bills to which the provisions of Article 207 apply (Financial Bills) to be reserved for the consideration of the President after they are passed by the Legislature of the State.

Statement 4 is incorrect. Unlike President's Rule under Article 356, a Financial Emergency under Article 360 does not suspend the State Legislature or transfer its budgetary powers to the Parliament. The State Legislature continues to pass its own Money Bills and Budget, subject to the requirement (if directed by the President) that such Bills be reserved for Presidential consideration after being passed by the State Legislature.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 360(3) & (4).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the status of Article 21 during a Proclamation of Emergency:
items: Statement-I: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a nine-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court formally overruled A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976) and held that the right to life and personal liberty inheres in human beings prior to the Constitution and is merely recognized, not created, by Article 21.

Statement-II: Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, a Presidential Order under Article 359(1) cannot suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 even during a wartime National Emergency, and immunity under Article 359(1A) extends only to laws containing an express recital relating to the Emergency.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 textually amended Article 359 to bar the suspension of the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21, the nine-Judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) went further on foundational constitutional philosophy to formally overrule A.D.M. Jabalpur (1976), holding that life and personal liberty are pre-constitutional natural rights that cannot be surrendered to the state.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), the nine-Judge Bench unanimously and formally overruled the majority decision in A.D.M. Jabalpur (1976) and affirmed Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent, holding that the right to life and personal liberty is an inalienable natural right inhering in every human being prior to the Constitution and is not a mere bounty conferred by the state.

Statement-II is correct, but does not explain Statement-I. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 amended Article 359(1) to exclude Articles 20 and 21 from the purview of Presidential suspension orders (thereby keeping habeas corpus maintainable) and inserted Article 359(1B) requiring an express Emergency recital. However, the Supreme Court in Puttaswamy (2017) overruled A.D.M. Jabalpur not because of the 1978 textual amendment, but because A.D.M. Jabalpur's underlying positivist premise—that the Constitution is the sole repository of the right to life—was fundamentally flawed under natural-rights jurisprudence.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 359(1), (1A) & (1B); Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1.

stem: With reference to the exercise of legislative and financial powers under Article 357 of the Constitution during the operation of President's Rule in a State, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When the Lok Sabha is not in session, the President is empowered to authorize expenditure out of the Consolidated Fund of the State pending the sanction of such expenditure by the Parliament.

2. When the powers of the Legislature of a State are declared to be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, the Parliament is barred from delegating the power to make laws for the State to the President.

3. Any law made by the Parliament or the President for the State during the operation of President's Rule ceases to have effect automatically upon the expiration of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 357, during President's Rule, Parliament can delegate State law-making power to the President, the President can authorize expenditure from the State Consolidated Fund when the Lok Sabha is not in session pending parliamentary sanction, and laws enacted under Article 357 continue in force indefinitely after President's Rule ends until repealed or altered by a competent Legislature.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 357(1)(c), it is competent for the President, when the House of the People (Lok Sabha) is not in session, to authorize expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State pending the sanction of such expenditure by the Parliament.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 357(1)(a), where a Proclamation under Article 356 declares that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, it is explicitly competent for Parliament to confer on the President the power of the Legislature of the State to make laws (known as President's Acts), and to authorize the President to delegate the power so conferred to any other authority.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 357(2) (as substituted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976), any law made in exercise of the power of the Legislature of the State by Parliament or the President during President's Rule continues in force even after the Proclamation ceases to operate, until it is altered, repealed, or amended by a competent Legislature or other authority. The six-month automatic sunset clause applies to State List laws enacted by Parliament under Article 250(2) during a National Emergency, not to laws made under Article 357.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 357(1) & (2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter 16.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional obligation of the Union under Article 355 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Article 355 imposes an independent constitutional duty on the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance, and read with Entry 2A of the Union List, empowers the Union to deploy its armed forces in any State in aid of the civil power without having to invoke President's Rule under Article 356.

Statement-II: Under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, the deployment of any armed force of the Union in a State in aid of the civil power is constitutionally permissible only with the prior concurrence of the concerned State Government unless a Proclamation under Article 352 or Article 356 is already in operation.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 355 serves both as the foundational justification for Articles 352 and 356 and as an autonomous source of Union obligation (Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India). Read with Entry 2A of List I (inserted by the 42nd Amendment), it enables the Union to deploy Central armed forces in any State in aid of the civil power without requiring State consent or a Proclamation under Article 356.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. As affirmed by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005), Article 355 imposes an affirmative duty on the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance. Further, read with Entry 2A of List I (Union List), the Union can deploy armed forces of the Union in a State in aid of the civil power to restore normalcy without having to resort to the extreme measure of invoking Article 356.

Statement-II is incorrect. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Entry 2A into List I (Union List) and simultaneously amended Entry 1 of List II (State List - 'Public order') to exclude the use of any naval, military, air force, or any other armed force of the Union in aid of the civil power. Consequently, while 'public order' is a State subject, the deployment and control of armed forces of the Union in any State in aid of the civil power falls exclusively within the Union's competence and does not legally require the prior concurrence of the State Government or a prior Proclamation under Article 352 or Article 356.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 355 & Seventh Schedule (List I Entry 2A, List II Entry 1); Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) 5 SCC 665.

stem: With reference to the Electoral College for the election of the President of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The election of a person as President cannot be called in question or postponed on the ground that a State Legislative Assembly is dissolved at the time of the election.

2. Under the Explanation to Article 54 of the Constitution, the expression 'State' includes the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territories of Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir for the purpose of constituting the Electoral College of the President.
3. Where a State Legislative Assembly is placed under suspended animation without being dissolved during President's Rule, its elected members are barred from voting in the Presidential election.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Article 54 defines the Presidential Electoral College to include elected MPs and elected MLAs of States, with its Explanation expressly including only the NCT of Delhi and the UT of Puducherry (excluding the UT of Jammu & Kashmir, as Article 54 has not been amended under Article 368(2) to include it). Under Article 71(4), vacancies in the Electoral College, including the dissolution of a State Assembly, do not invalidate or delay the Presidential poll.

exp.why: Under Article 71(4) of the Constitution (inserted by the 11th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1961) and affirmed by the Supreme Court in its Advisory Opinion in In Re: Presidential Poll (1974), the election of a person as President or Vice-President cannot be called in question on the ground of the existence of any vacancy for whatever reason among the members of the Electoral College, even if one or more State Legislative Assemblies are dissolved at the time of the election.

Under the Explanation to Article 54 (inserted by the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992), the term 'State' for the purposes of Articles 54 and 55 includes only the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry. Although the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 created a Legislative Assembly for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir under Section 13 (extending Article 239A), it did not amend the Explanation to Article 54 of the Constitution (which requires a constitutional amendment under the proviso to Article 368(2) with ratification by at least half of the States).

When a State Legislative Assembly is merely kept under suspended animation during a proclamation under Article 356 without being dissolved, the elected MLAs do not cease to be members of the Assembly. Consequently, they retain their constitutional right to vote in the Presidential election.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 54 & 71(4); In Re: Presidential Poll (1974); Laxmikanth Ch. 18

stem: With reference to the manner of election of the President of India under Article 55 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Presidential election, the value of the vote of an elected Member of the Lok Sabha is identical to the value of the vote of an elected Member of the Rajya Sabha, irrespective of the State or Union Territory they represent.

2. For calculating the value of the vote of an elected member of a State Legislative Assembly, the expression 'population' in Article 55 currently refers exclusively to the population ascertained at the 1971 Census.

3. A reduction in the total number of participating State Legislative Assemblies reduces the value of the vote of each elected Member of Parliament, even if the total elected strength of Parliament remains unchanged.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 55 ensures parity between the States as a whole and the Union Parliament in electing the President. While an MLA's vote value varies from State to State based on its 1971 Census population divided by its elected MLAs, every elected MP across both Houses has an identical vote value obtained by dividing the aggregate vote value of all MLAs across India by the total number of elected MPs (776).

exp.why: Under Article 55(2)(c), the value of the vote of each elected Member of Parliament is calculated by dividing the total value of votes assigned to all elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of all States (including Delhi and Puducherry) by the total number of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (543 in Lok Sabha + 233 in Rajya Sabha = 776). Thus, every elected MP, whether from the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha and regardless of their State, has the exact same vote value.

Under the proviso to the Explanation in Article 55 (as amended by the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001), the reference to the 'last preceding census' for determining the population of each State in Presidential elections is frozen exclusively at the 1971 Census until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published.

Because the numerator in the MP vote-value formula under Article 55(2)(c) is the sum of the vote values of all elected MLAs of participating Assemblies while the denominator is the fixed number of elected MPs (776), any reduction in the number of participating State Assemblies reduces the numerator. For instance, after Jammu and Kashmir ceased to be a State in 2019, the aggregate value of MLA votes fell from 5,49,495 to 5,43,231, which reduced the value of each MP's vote from 708 to 700.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 55; 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001

stem: Consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Although any citizen of India aged thirty-five years who is qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha and holds no office of profit fulfills the constitutional eligibility criteria under Article 58, such a person cannot validly file a nomination paper for the Presidential election without the formal backing of at least one hundred members of the Electoral College.

Statement-II: To prevent frivolous candidatures for the highest constitutional office—whose holder is uniquely bound under Article 60 by an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law rather than the general Third Schedule oath taken by Union Ministers—the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 mandates that every nomination paper must be subscribed by at least fifty electors as proposers and fifty electors as seconders.
