prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 58 lays down the basic constitutional qualifications for the Presidency and Article 60 sets out the President's unique constitutional oath ('to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law'), Parliament enacted Section 5B of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 under Article 71(3) requiring 50 electors as proposers and 50 electors as seconders to filter out non-serious candidates.

exp.why: Article 58 prescribes the constitutional qualifications for election as President (citizen of India, completed 35 years of age, qualified for election as a member of the House of the People, and not holding any office of profit). However, fulfilling Article 58 alone does not entitle a candidate to get on the ballot without sponsorship by at least 100 members of the Electoral College.

Unlike Union Ministers whose oath of office is in the Third Schedule ('to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution'), the President takes a special oath under Article 60 ('to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law'). To safeguard the dignity of this office against frivolous nominations, Section 5B(1)(a) of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 mandates that a candidate's nomination paper must be subscribed by at least 50 electors as proposers and 50 electors as seconders, which directly explains Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 58, 60 & 71(3); Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952

stem: With reference to the procedure for the impeachment of the President of India under Article 61 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Nominated members of either House of Parliament can participate in the impeachment of the President, whereas elected members of State Legislative Assemblies have no role in the impeachment process.

2. A resolution preferring the impeachment charge can be moved in either House of Parliament only after at least fourteen days' written notice signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of that House.

3. For the impeachment resolution to be passed by the initiating House and sustained by the investigating House, it must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Impeachment under Article 61 is a quasi-judicial parliamentary process restricted strictly to both Houses of Parliament (including nominated MPs, but excluding all MLAs). It requires the highest special majority known to the Indian Constitution: not less than two-thirds of the 'total membership' of each House, rather than two-thirds of members 'present and voting'.

exp.why: Under Article 61, impeachment is conducted entirely within the two Houses of Parliament. Because Article 61 refers to the 'total membership of that House' without excluding nominated members, nominated members of the Rajya Sabha participate and vote in the impeachment process even though they do not vote in the Presidential election. Conversely, elected MLAs of States and the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry vote in the election but have no role in impeachment.

Under Article 61(1) and 61(2)(a), either House of Parliament may prefer the charge of 'violation of the Constitution', provided the resolution is moved after at least 14 days' written notice signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of that House.

A majority of the total membership plus two-thirds of members 'present and voting' applies to constitutional amendments (Article 368) and the removal of Supreme Court Judges (Article 124(4)). In contrast, under Article 61(2)(b) and Article 61(4), the impeachment resolution of the President must be passed at both stages by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the 'total membership of that House'.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 61; Laxmikanth Ch. 18

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory provisions governing a vacancy in the office of the President of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: If the election of a new President is delayed beyond the expiration of the five-year term of the incumbent President, the Vice-President automatically assumes office as the Acting President.
opts.B: When a vacancy occurs in the office of the President due to death, resignation, or removal, the newly elected President holds office only for the remainder of the predecessor's five-year term.
opts.C: If the offices of both the President and the Vice-President fall vacant simultaneously, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha discharges the functions of the President until a new President is elected.
opts.D: While an election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the President's term must be completed before the expiration of the term, an election to fill a vacancy occurring due to death, resignation, or removal must be held within six months from the date of occurrence of the vacancy.

core: Article 62 distinguishes between a routine expiration of the President's 5-year term (where the outgoing President holds over under Article 56(1)(c) if the election is delayed, and the Vice-President never acts as President) and an abrupt mid-term vacancy due to death, resignation, or removal (where the Vice-President or CJI acts as President and an election must be held within 6 months for a full 5-year term).

exp.why: Option D is correct because Article 62(1) mandates that an election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the President's term shall be completed before the expiration of the term, while Article 62(2) mandates that an election to fill a vacancy occurring by reason of death, resignation, or removal shall be held as soon as possible and in no case later than six months from the date of occurrence of the vacancy. Option A is incorrect because under the proviso to Article 56(1)(c), the outgoing President continues to hold office beyond the five-year term until the successor enters upon office; to prevent an interregnum, the Vice-President does not become Acting President upon expiration of term. Option B is incorrect because under Article 62(2), the newly elected President holds office for a full term of five years from the date they enter upon office. Option C is incorrect because under the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, if both the President and Vice-President offices are vacant, the Chief Justice of India (or in their absence, the senior-most available Judge of the Supreme Court) discharges the functions of the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 56, 62 & 65; President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969

stem: With reference to the adjudication of doubts and disputes relating to the election of the President and the Vice-President of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of the President or the Vice-President are inquired into and decided exclusively by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final.

2. An election petition challenging the election of the President can be presented to the Supreme Court by any citizen registered as an elector in a Parliamentary constituency within thirty days of the declaration of the result.

3. If the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by them in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of that office on or before the date of the Supreme Court's decision are not invalidated.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 71(1), the Supreme Court exercises exclusive and final original jurisdiction over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election disputes, while Article 71(2) protects the validity of official acts performed prior to annulment. However, under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, locus standi to file an election petition is strictly restricted to a candidate or at least 20 members of the Electoral College (10 for Vice-President), excluding ordinary citizens.

exp.why: Under Article 71(1) of the Constitution, all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided exclusively by the Supreme Court, and its decision shall be final.

Under Section 14A of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, an election petition calling in question a Presidential election cannot be filed by an ordinary citizen/voter; it can only be presented to the Supreme Court by any candidate at such election, or by twenty or more electors (i.e., members of the Presidential Electoral College—elected MPs/MLAs) joined together as petitioners within 30 days of the publication of the declaration of the result (for a Vice-Presidential election, it requires a candidate or at least ten electors).

Under Article 71(2) of the Constitution, if the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by them in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office of President or Vice-President on or before the date of the decision of the Supreme Court shall not be invalidated by reason of that declaration.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 71; Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, Section 14A

stem: With reference to the election and constitutional position of the Vice-President of India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: While the Electoral College for the Vice-President includes both elected and nominated members of Parliament and excludes members of State Legislative Assemblies, a candidate for the office of Vice-President, like the President, must be qualified for election as a member of the House of the People.

Statement-II: Unlike the President, whose executive authority and constitutional role extend over both the Union and the States as the head of the Republic, the normal constitutional function of the Vice-President is to preside over the Council of States and only on rare occasions to temporarily discharge the functions of the President.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The composition of the Electoral College and the eligibility criteria for the Vice-President under Article 66 flow directly from the Vice-President's primary institutional role as the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). Consequently, State MLAs are excluded from the Electoral College, and a candidate for Vice-President must be qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha rather than the Lok Sabha.

exp.why: Under Article 66(1) of the Constitution, the Electoral College for the Vice-President indeed comprises both elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament and excludes members of the State Legislative Assemblies. However, the second half of the statement is incorrect: under Article 66(3)(c), a person is eligible for election as Vice-President only if they are qualified for election as a member of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), whereas under Article 58(1)(c), a candidate for the office of the President must be qualified for election as a member of the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

As explained by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly, the President is the head of the State whose powers extend over the administration of both the Union and the States, necessitating the participation of State MLAs in the Presidential election. In contrast, the Vice-President's primary function under Article 64 is merely to preside over the Council of States, and only on a rare occasion and for a temporary period (maximum six months under Article 65) to assume the duties of the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 58, 64, 65 and 66; Constituent Assembly Debates Vol. VII

stem: With reference to the constitutional procedure for the removal of the Vice-President of India under Article 67(b), consider the following statements:
items: 1. A resolution for the removal of the Vice-President can be introduced only in the Council of States and only after at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
2. The Constitution does not specify any grounds, such as 'violation of the Constitution' or 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity', for the removal of the Vice-President.

3. The removal resolution must be passed by the Council of States by a majority of all the then members of the Council and subsequently passed by the House of the People by a majority of the total membership of that House.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 67(b) prescribes a distinct, asymmetric removal procedure for the Vice-President reflecting their primary role as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The resolution must originate exclusively in the Rajya Sabha after a 14-day notice, requires an 'effective majority' in the Rajya Sabha, and needs only a 'simple majority' (agreed to) in the Lok Sabha, without any constitutionally specified grounds.

exp.why: Under Article 67(b) and its first proviso, a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President must originate exclusively in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and cannot be initiated in the House of the People (Lok Sabha). Furthermore, no such resolution can be moved unless at least fourteen days' advance notice has been given.

Unlike Article 61 (which specifies 'violation of the Constitution' for the impeachment of the President) or Article 124(4) (which specifies 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' for Supreme Court Judges), Article 67(b) lays down no grounds whatsoever for the removal of the Vice-President.

Article 67(b) stipulates that a Vice-President may be removed by 'a resolution of the Council of States passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council and agreed to by the House of the People'. While 'all the then members' in the Rajya Sabha denotes an Effective Majority (more than 50% of the total membership excluding vacancies), the phrase 'agreed to by the House of the People' requires only a Simple Majority (majority of members present and voting) in the Lok Sabha, not an absolute majority of its total membership.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 67(b); Laxmikanth Chapter on Vice-President

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the functions, voting rights, and emoluments of the Vice-President of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Regular emoluments of the Vice-President : Drawn strictly in the capacity of Ex-Officio Chairman of the Council of States under Article 97
2. Voting right while presiding over the Council of States : Cannot vote in the first instance, but exercises a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes
3. Vice-President acting as President under Article 65 : Continues to perform the duties of Chairman of the Council of States while drawing the emoluments of the President
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Constitution prevents a dual-office overlap when the Vice-President steps into the Presidency. Under the proviso to Article 64, whenever the Vice-President acts as President or discharges the functions of the President under Article 65, they cease to perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and do not draw the Chairman's salary under Article 97.

exp.why: The Constitution does not fix any separate salary or emoluments for the Vice-President in that capacity alone. Under Article 97 and the Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act, 1953, the Vice-President draws regular salary and allowances solely by virtue of being the Ex-Officio Chairman of the Council of States.

Under Article 100(1) of the Constitution, the Chairman of the Council of States (the Vice-President) is not a member of the House and therefore shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes.

Under the proviso to Article 64, during any period when the Vice-President acts as President or discharges the functions of the President under Article 65, the Vice-President shall NOT perform the duties of the office of Chairman of the Council of States and shall not be entitled to any salary or allowance payable to the Chairman of the Council of States under Article 97. During this period, those duties are performed by the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States under Article 91.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 64, 65, 91, 97 and 100(1)

stem: With reference to the executive power of the Union and the conduct of business of the Government of India under Articles 53 and 77 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Since the executive power of the Union is vested in the President under Article 53(1), Parliament is constitutionally barred from conferring by law any executive functions on authorities other than the President.

2. Any executive functions conferred by an existing law on the Government of any State or other authority are automatically deemed to have been transferred to the President upon the commencement of the Constitution.

3. Under Article 77(2), once an order or instrument made and executed in the name of the President is duly authenticated as per the rules made by the President, its substantive legality and constitutional validity cannot be challenged in any court on any ground.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 53(3) explicitly clarifies that vesting Union executive power in the President neither transfers existing statutory functions of States/other authorities to the President nor prevents Parliament from conferring functions by law on other authorities. Similarly, Article 77(2) only bars challenging the procedural authenticity of an order's execution, not its substantive validity.

exp.why: Article 53(3)(b) expressly states that nothing in Article 53 shall prevent Parliament from conferring by law functions on authorities other than the President. Thus, Parliament frequently creates statutory authorities and regulators and vests executive functions directly in them.

Article 53(3)(a) explicitly provides the exact opposite: nothing in Article 53 shall be deemed to transfer to the President any functions conferred by any existing law on the Government of any State or other authority.

Under Article 77(2), the validity of an order or instrument which is duly authenticated in accordance with rules made by the President shall not be called in question on the specific ground 'that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the President'. As repeatedly held by the Supreme Court, this bar applies only to the procedural question of due authentication/execution; it does not grant blanket immunity from judicial review on substantive grounds such as violation of Fundamental Rights, mala fides, or being ultra vires a statute.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 53(3) and 77(2); D.D. Basu Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: With reference to the constitutional evolution and judicial interpretation of Article 74 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 74(1) to explicitly state that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers, the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 added a proviso empowering the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice once.

2. As interpreted by the Supreme Court in the S.R. Bommai case, although Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into the advice tendered by Ministers to the President, it does not bar judicial scrutiny of the underlying material on the basis of which that advice was tendered.

3. Prior to the enactment of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, the Supreme Court held that the President could exercise the executive power of the Union independently of the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers whenever the House of the People stood dissolved.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Even prior to the 42nd Amendment, the Supreme Court established that the Indian Constitution embodies the Westminster parliamentary model where the President is bound by Ministerial advice, including when the Lok Sabha is dissolved (U.N.R. Rao, 1971; Samsher Singh, 1974). Furthermore, Article 74(2) shields the advice itself from judicial inquiry, but not the objective material forming the basis of that advice.

exp.why: Originally, Article 74(1) stated that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added that the President 'shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice'. Subsequently, the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 inserted the proviso allowing the President to return the advice once for reconsideration, while binding the President to act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court clarified that Article 74(2) only bars courts from inquiring into whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President. However, the relevant material on the basis of which the Council of Ministers formed its opinion is not part of the confidential advice itself and can be summoned and examined by the Court to test for mala fides or constitutional perversity.

Even before the 42nd Amendment (1976), the Supreme Court in U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971) and a 7-Judge Constitution Bench in Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) authoritatively held that Article 74(1) is mandatory, that the Council of Ministers continues in office even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved, and that the President cannot exercise executive functions without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 74; Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974); S.R. Bommai v. UoI (1994)

stem: With reference to the discretionary powers of the President of India in comparison with the Governor of a State, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Even though Article 74 of the Constitution of India, unlike Article 163 in the case of a State Governor, does not expressly confer any discretionary sphere of action upon the President, the President can still act without the advice of the Council of Ministers in certain exceptional political circumstances.

Statement-II: When no political party or pre-poll coalition secures a clear majority in the House of the People after a general election, or when an incumbent Council of Ministers loses its majority in the House and refuses to resign, there is no Council of Ministers enjoying the confidence of the House whose binding advice can guide the President in appointing a Prime Minister or dissolving the House.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike a State Governor who enjoys both explicit constitutional discretion under Article 163(1)-(2) and situational discretion, the President of India has no express constitutional discretion under Article 74. However, the President necessarily exercises situational discretion when the political link of collective responsibility breaks down, such as during a hung Lok Sabha or loss of majority by an incumbent Cabinet.

exp.why: Article 163(1) explicitly carves out an exception for the Governor ('except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'), and Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within their discretion final. Article 74 contains no such clause for the President. Nevertheless, constitutional conventions recognize that the President possesses situational (or circumstantial) discretion in exceptional political contingencies.

Statement-II directly explains why and how situational discretion arises for the President despite the text of Article 74. The binding nature of ministerial advice under Article 74(1) presupposes a Council of Ministers that commands the confidence of the House of the People under Article 75(3). When a general election yields a hung Parliament, or when an incumbent Prime Minister dies suddenly with no obvious successor, or when a Ministry loses the confidence of the Lok Sabha, the President must necessarily exercise situational discretion to appoint a Prime Minister or decide on dissolution.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 74, 75(3) and 163; Laxmikanth Chapters on President and Governor

stem: With reference to the veto powers of the President of India over Bills passed by the Parliament, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: If the President returns an Ordinary Bill for reconsideration under the proviso to Article 111, the Houses must re-pass it by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting to compel Presidential assent.
opts.B: While the President may either give or withhold assent to a Money Bill under Article 111, the Constitution expressly excludes the power to return a Money Bill to the Houses for reconsideration.
opts.C: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 first made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill without exercising any veto power.
opts.D: When the President withholds assent to a Private Member's Bill passed by both Houses, the Bill can be revived during the same session by summoning a joint sitting under Article 108.

core: Article 111 empowers the President to give or withhold assent to any Bill, but its proviso restricts the suspensive veto (returning a Bill for reconsideration) exclusively to Bills other than Money Bills. Moreover, Indian suspensive veto is overridden by an ordinary majority, and the 24th Amendment Act (1971) eliminated all Presidential veto powers over Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368(2).

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because under Article 111, when a Bill passed by the Houses of Parliament is presented to the President, the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill or that he withholds assent therefrom; however, the proviso to Article 111 explicitly states that the President may return the Bill for reconsideration 'if the Bill is not a Money Bill'. Thus, the President can give or withhold assent to a Money Bill, but cannot return it for reconsideration. Option (A) is incorrect because unlike the US President's 'qualified veto' which requires a two-thirds supermajority to override, the Indian President exercises only a 'suspensive veto' under Article 111, which is overridden if the Houses re-pass the Bill by an ordinary majority. Option (C) is incorrect because it was the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 (not the 42nd Amendment, 1976) that amended Article 368(2) by substituting the mandatory words 'the President shall give his assent to the Bill'. Option (D) is incorrect because once the President withholds assent (absolute veto), the Bill ends completely and cannot be revived; a joint sitting under Article 108 resolves inter-House deadlock prior to passage, not post-passage withholding of Presidential assent.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 111 and 368(2); 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter 18.

stem: With reference to the constitutional procedure governing State Bills presented to the Governor and reserved for the consideration of the President under Articles 200 and 201, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When a non-Money Bill reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President is returned on the President's direction and re-passed by the State Legislature, the President is still not constitutionally bound to accord assent to the re-passed Bill.

2. Where the President directs the Governor to return a reserved non-Money Bill to the State Legislature for reconsideration, it is mandatory for the House or Houses of the State Legislature to reconsider the Bill within six months from the date of receipt of such message.

3. If a Governor initially withholds assent to a Bill under the first proviso to Article 200 and returns it to the State Legislature, the Governor retains the discretion to reserve the Bill for the President if the State Legislature re-passes it without accepting the Governor's recommendations.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the proviso to Article 201, while a State Legislature must reconsider a returned reserved Bill within six months, the Constitution imposes no obligation on the President to assent to the re-passed State Bill. However, as settled by the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor, once a Governor elects to withhold assent and returns a Bill under Article 200, the Governor must grant assent if the State Legislature re-passes it and cannot subsequently reserve it for the President.

exp.why: Under the proviso to Article 201, when a reserved non-Money Bill is returned by the Governor on the President's direction and is reconsidered and passed again by the State Legislature (with or without amendment), it shall be presented again to the President for consideration. Crucially, unlike Article 111 and Article 200, Article 201 omits the mandatory stipulation that the President 'shall not withhold assent therefrom', leaving the President free to withhold assent even after reconsideration.

The proviso to Article 201 explicitly states that when a reserved Bill is so returned on the direction of the President, 'the House or Houses shall reconsider it accordingly within a period of six months from the date of receipt of such message'. No such six-month deadline exists under Article 111 for Parliament or under Article 200 when the Governor directly returns a Bill.

In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023) and subsequent rulings under Article 200, the Supreme Court held that the first proviso to Article 200 is structurally attached to the option of withholding assent. Once the Governor exercises the option of withholding assent, the Governor must return the non-Money Bill to the State Legislature 'as soon as possible', and if the State Legislature re-passes the Bill in its original or amended form, the Governor is constitutionally bound to grant assent ('shall not withhold assent therefrom') and cannot thereafter reserve the re-passed Bill for the consideration of the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 200 and 201; Supreme Court judgment in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023).

stem: With reference to the Ordinance-making power of the President of India under Article 123 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Where the two Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates after the promulgation of an Ordinance, the six-week period for the expiration of the Ordinance is reckoned exclusively from the later of those two dates.

2. Although the President's power to promulgate an Ordinance under Article 123 is co-extensive with the legislative competence of Parliament as to subject-matter, an Ordinance cannot be promulgated to amend the Constitution under Article 368.

3. As laid down by the Supreme Court, the laying of an Ordinance before both Houses of Parliament upon reassembly is a mandatory constitutional obligation, and the lapse of an Ordinance does not automatically create enduring legal rights.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Explanation to Article 123(2), the six-week life of an Ordinance upon parliamentary reassembly is counted from the later of the two dates when the Houses reassemble on different days. In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017, 7-Judge Bench), the Supreme Court held that laying an Ordinance before the Legislature is mandatory, repeated re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution, and lapsed ordinances do not automatically confer enduring rights.

exp.why: The Explanation to Article 123(2) explicitly provides that where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of determining when the Ordinance ceases to operate.

Under Article 123(3), an Ordinance is void if and in so far as it makes any provision which Parliament would not under the Constitution be competent to enact. While this makes the Ordinance-making power co-extensive with ordinary parliamentary legislation under the Union and Concurrent Lists (including retrospective tax or civil laws), constituent power under Article 368 requires a Bill to be initiated and passed by a special majority in each House of Parliament and therefore cannot be exercised via an executive Ordinance.

In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled that the requirement under Articles 123(2) and 213(2) to lay every Ordinance before the Legislature is mandatory, not directory; bypassing the Legislature through re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution; and unlike a temporary statute passed by the Legislature, actions taken under an Ordinance do not automatically survive or confer enduring rights after the Ordinance ceases to operate unless validated by public interest or constitutional necessity.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 123; Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench ruling in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the clemency powers of the President and the Governor under the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under the Constitution of India, while the President possesses the plenary power to pardon, commute, or remit a sentence of death, the Governor of a State is constitutionally barred from commuting or remitting a death sentence even where the offence is against a law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.

Statement-II: The clemency powers vested in the President under Article 72 and the Governor under Article 161 are exercised strictly on the aid and advice of the respective Council of Ministers, and the exercise or inordinate delay in the exercise of such power is amenable to judicial review on limited grounds.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While only the President can grant a complete 'Pardon' for a death sentence under Article 72(1)(c) or exercise clemency in Court-Martial sentences under Article 72(1)(a), the Governor's power under Article 161 does extend to suspending, remitting, or commuting a death sentence where the executive power of the State extends. Furthermore, clemency powers under both Articles 72 and 161 are exercised on ministerial advice and are subject to limited judicial review.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect because although only the President can grant a complete 'Pardon' in respect of a sentence of death under Article 72(1)(c) (and Article 72(3) expressly saves the power to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor of a State under any law for the time being in force), the Governor is NOT barred from suspending, remitting, or commuting a death sentence under Article 161 where the offence is against a law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends (reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in State of Haryana v. Raj Kumar, 2021).

Statement-II is correct because as established by the Supreme Court in Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980), Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1988), Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt. of A.P. (2006), and Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014), the President under Article 72 and the Governor under Article 161 act solely on the aid and advice of the respective Council of Ministers, and their decisions (as well as unexplained, inordinate executive delay in deciding mercy petitions) are subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, extraneous considerations, arbitrariness, or non-application of mind.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 72 and 161; Maru Ram v. UoI (1980); Shatrughan Chauhan v. UoI (2014); State of Haryana v. Raj Kumar (2021).

stem: With reference to the distinct forms of clemency powers exercisable by the President of India under Article 72 of the Constitution, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Commutation : Reducing the duration or quantum of a sentence without altering its legal character
2. Remission : Substituting one form of punishment for a lighter category of punishment
3. Respite : Awarding a lesser sentence in place of one originally awarded due to a special circumstance of the convict, such as physical disability or pregnancy
4. Reprieve : Stay of the execution of a sentence, especially that of death, for a temporary period to enable the convict to seek clemency
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Under Article 72, 'Commutation' alters the qualitative nature of punishment to a lighter form (e.g., rigorous imprisonment to simple imprisonment), whereas 'Remission' reduces only the quantitative period of the sentence without changing its character. 'Respite' reduces punishment due to special personal circumstances (like pregnancy), while 'Reprieve' is a temporary stay of execution.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because 'Commutation' denotes the substitution of one form of punishment for a lighter form (for example, commuting a death sentence to rigorous imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment to simple imprisonment). Reducing the duration of a sentence without changing its character is 'Remission'.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched because 'Remission' implies reducing the period/duration of a sentence without changing its legal character (for example, reducing a sentence of rigorous imprisonment for five years to rigorous imprisonment for two years). Substituting one form of punishment for a lighter form is 'Commutation'.

Pair 3 is correctly matched because 'Respite' denotes awarding a lesser sentence in place of one originally awarded due to some special fact or mitigating biological/physical condition of the offender, such as physical disability or pregnancy of a woman offender.

Pair 4 is correctly matched because 'Reprieve' implies a stay of the execution of a sentence (especially a sentence of death) for a temporary period, having the legal effect of postponing execution so the convict has time to seek pardon or commutation from the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 72; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter 18.

stem: With reference to the appointment and parliamentary rights of Union Ministers under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 75(5), a person who is not a member of either House of Parliament can be appointed as the Prime Minister or a Union Minister, provided that such person ceases to hold office at the expiration of six consecutive months unless he becomes a member of either House within that period.

2. During the six-month period in which a Union Minister holds office without being a member of either House of Parliament, Article 88 bars such a Minister from speaking or participating in the proceedings of the Lok Sabha until formally inducted into a House.

3. As laid down by the Supreme Court, an unelected person appointed as a Minister who fails to secure membership of the Legislature within six consecutive months cannot be re-appointed as a Minister during the term of the same Legislature without first getting elected.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 75(5) allows a non-member of Parliament to serve as Prime Minister or Minister for up to six consecutive months, and Article 88 grants every Minister the right to speak and participate (without voting) in either House during that tenure. However, in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001), the Supreme Court barred the repeated re-appointment of an unelected individual for successive six-month periods during the life of the same Legislature.

exp.why: Article 75(5) stipulates that a Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of either House of Parliament shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister. In Har Sharan Verma v. Tribhuvan Narain Singh (1971) and S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda (1996), the Supreme Court affirmed that the term 'Minister' includes the Prime Minister or Chief Minister, and membership of either House (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) within six months satisfies the constitutional requirement.

Under Article 88 of the Constitution, 'every Minister' and the Attorney-General of India shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote. Therefore, a Minister holding office under Article 75(5) has the full constitutional right to speak and participate in the proceedings of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, though he cannot vote until he becomes a member of that House.

In S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001), the Supreme Court held that Article 164(4) (and pari materia Article 75(5)) is in the nature of a one-time exception to the foundational principle of representative parliamentary democracy. Allowing a non-legislator who fails to get elected within six months to resign and be re-appointed repeatedly for another term of six months during the life of the same Legislature would subvert the democratic mandate and is unconstitutional.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 75(5) and 88; S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda (1996); S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001).

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions introduced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 and the limits on the size of the Council of Ministers across the Union, States, and Union Territories, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 75(1A), the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Union Council of Ministers shall not exceed fifteen per cent of the combined total membership of both Houses of Parliament.

2. While Article 164(1A) prescribes a ceiling of fifteen per cent of the Legislative Assembly strength alongside a minimum floor of twelve Ministers for a State, Article 239AA(4) restricts the Council of Ministers in the National Capital Territory of Delhi to ten per cent of the total members in its Legislative Assembly.

3. A member of either House of Parliament belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of that House on the ground of defection under the Tenth Schedule is also constitutionally barred from being appointed as a Union Minister for the remainder of their term unless re-elected.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 capped the Union Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha alone (not the entire Parliament) with no minimum floor, whereas States have a 15% cap of the Legislative Assembly with a minimum floor of 12 Ministers, and NCT of Delhi has a 10% cap under Article 239AA(4). Furthermore, Articles 75(1B) and 164(1B) bar legislators disqualified under the Tenth Schedule from holding ministerial office until they are re-elected.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Union Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the House of the People (Lok Sabha) alone—not the combined membership of both Houses of Parliament. Additionally, unlike States, there is no constitutional minimum floor on the number of Ministers at the Union level.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 164(1A), the total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in the Council of Ministers in a State cannot exceed 15% of the total membership of the Legislative Assembly of that State, provided that the number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, shall not be less than 12. In contrast, for the National Capital Territory of Delhi, Article 239AA(4) specifically caps the Council of Ministers at not more than 10% of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly (i.e., 7 Ministers in a 70-member House).

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 75(1B), a member of either House of Parliament belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of that House under Paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a Minister for the period commencing from the date of their disqualification till the date on which the term of their office as such member would expire or where they contest any election to either House of Parliament before the expiry of such period, whichever is earlier.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 75(1A), 75(1B), 164(1A) & 239AA(4); 91st CAA 2003; Laxmikanth Ch. 21

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional relationship between the President and the Union Council of Ministers:
items: Statement-I: Even after the dissolution of the House of the People, the Union Council of Ministers does not cease to hold office, and the President cannot exercise the executive powers of the Union without the aid and advice of a Council of Ministers.

Statement-II: Under Article 75(2) of the Constitution, although Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, the President can dismiss an individual Union Minister at his sole personal discretion without the advice of the Prime Minister whenever the House of the People stands dissolved.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: As settled by the Supreme Court in U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971), Article 74(1) is mandatory at all times, meaning the President cannot govern without a Council of Ministers even when the Lok Sabha stands dissolved. Furthermore, the 'pleasure of the President' under Article 75(2) is constitutionally exercised only on the advice of the Prime Minister to enforce collective responsibility, and never at the President's personal discretion.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that Article 74(1) ('There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President...') is mandatory. Because Article 53(1) requires the President to exercise executive power in accordance with the Constitution, the President cannot exercise executive functions without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers even after the House of the People is dissolved.

Statement-II is incorrect. Under Article 75(2), Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which embodies the principle of individual responsibility. However, the President cannot remove an individual Minister at his personal discretion—whether the Lok Sabha is in existence or dissolved—and can dismiss an individual Minister only on the advice of the Prime Minister. This provision constitutionally enables the Prime Minister to enforce collective responsibility under Article 75(3) by advising the removal of a Minister who differs from Cabinet policy.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 74(1), 75(2) & 75(3); U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971); Laxmikanth Ch. 21

stem: With reference to the parliamentary rights of Union Ministers under Article 88 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: A Union Minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha can participate in the debates of a Joint Sitting of both Houses under Article 108, but is barred from voting in that Joint Sitting.
opts.B: A Union Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament during the six-month period under Article 75(5) has the right to speak and participate in the proceedings of both Houses and any Joint Sitting of the Houses, without the right to vote in any of them.
opts.C: By virtue of being a Cabinet Minister, a Union Minister automatically acquires the right to participate and vote in the meetings of any Parliamentary Standing Committee, irrespective of whether the Minister is named a member of that Committee.
opts.D: During the vote on a Motion of No-Confidence in the Lok Sabha, every member of the Union Council of Ministers is entitled to cast a vote regardless of the House to which the Minister belongs, as the survival of the entire Council is at stake.

core: Under Article 88, every Union Minister has the right to speak and participate in the proceedings of either House, any Joint Sitting of the Houses, and any Parliamentary Committee of which the Minister is named a member, but is not entitled to vote 'by virtue of this article'. Consequently, a Minister's voting right flows solely from actual membership of the respective House or Joint Sitting, meaning a non-MP Minister serving under the six-month window of Article 75(5) can speak in either House or a Joint Sitting but cannot vote anywhere in Parliament.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. Under Article 88, every Minister has the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which they may be named a member, 'but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.' Thus, a Minister appointed without being a member of either House (under the 6-month window in Article 75(5)) can speak and participate in both Houses and in a Joint Sitting, but cannot vote in any of them because they are not a member of either House. Option (A) is incorrect because a Minister who is an elected or nominated member of the Rajya Sabha IS a member of a Joint Sitting of both Houses under Article 108 and therefore possesses the right to vote in a Joint Sitting by virtue of their Rajya Sabha membership. Option (C) is incorrect because Article 88 restricts a Minister's right of participation in a Parliamentary Committee to one 'of which he may be named a member' (and Ministers are barred under Parliamentary Rules from being appointed as members of Departmentally Related Standing Committees, Financial Committees, etc.). Option (D) is incorrect because on a No-Confidence Motion in the Lok Sabha, Ministers who are Rajya Sabha members (or non-MPs) can speak and defend the government in the Lok Sabha under Article 88, but only Ministers who are members of the Lok Sabha can vote.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 75(5), 88 & 108; Laxmikanth Ch. 21 & 23

stem: With reference to the constitutional duties of the Prime Minister under Article 78 of the Constitution of India as the channel of communication between the President and the Union Council of Ministers, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 78(a), the Prime Minister is under an explicit constitutional duty to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation.

2. Under Article 78(c), if an individual Minister has taken a decision on a matter that has not been considered by the Council of Ministers, the President is empowered to directly set aside that Minister's decision and refer the matter to the Supreme Court.

3. The Prime Minister's obligation to furnish information relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation is triggered under Article 78(b) whenever the President calls for such information.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 78 establishes the Prime Minister as the constitutional link between the President and the Union Council of Ministers regarding administrative decisions and legislative proposals. Crucially, under Article 78(c), when an individual Minister takes a decision without Cabinet consideration, the President cannot directly annul that decision; instead, the President may require the Prime Minister to submit the matter for the collective consideration of the Council of Ministers.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 78(a) explicitly lays down that it shall be the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 78(c), if the President so requires, it is the duty of the Prime Minister to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council. This clause safeguards the doctrine of collective responsibility by ensuring the entire Council deliberates on an individual Minister's unilateral decision; it does not empower the President to directly set aside the Minister's decision or refer it to the Supreme Court.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 78(b), it is the constitutional duty of the Prime Minister to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation as the President may call for.

ref: Constitution of India Article 78; Laxmikanth Ch. 20

stem: With reference to the distinction between the 'Union Council of Ministers' and the 'Union Cabinet' in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The term 'Cabinet' was incorporated into Article 74 of the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, to explicitly distinguish Cabinet Ministers from Ministers of State in the tendering of binding advice to the President.

2. For the purposes of the Constitution, the 'Union Cabinet' is explicitly defined under Article 352(3) as the Council consisting of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75.

3. While Ministers of State holding independent charge of ministries are members of the Union Council of Ministers, they do not attend meetings of the Union Cabinet as a matter of right and participate only when specially invited on matters concerning their departments.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Articles 74 and 75 refer only to the broader 'Council of Ministers', the term 'Cabinet' appears only once in the entire Constitution in Article 352(3), inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 to prevent the proclamation of a National Emergency without the written decision of the Cabinet. Functionally, the Cabinet is the core decision-making nucleus comprising the Prime Minister and Cabinet-rank Ministers, whereas Ministers of State attend Cabinet meetings only upon invitation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The word 'Cabinet' did not exist in the original Constitution and does not appear in Article 74 at all. Furthermore, it was inserted not by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976, but by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1978 exclusively into Article 352(3) to mandate that the President shall not issue a Proclamation of National Emergency unless the decision of the Union Cabinet has been communicated to him in writing.

Statement 2 is correct. Article 352(3) is the sole provision in the Constitution of India that defines and mentions the 'Cabinet', stating that the Union Cabinet is 'the Council consisting of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75'.

Statement 3 is correct. The Union Council of Ministers is a wider body encompassing Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (Independent Charge), Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers. Ministers of State with Independent Charge head their respective ministries/departments without working under a Cabinet Minister, but they are not members of the Union Cabinet and do not attend Cabinet meetings unless specially invited when a subject related to their ministry/department is under consideration by the Cabinet.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 74, 75 & 352(3); 44th CAA 1978; Laxmikanth Ch. 21

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the tenure and survival of the Union Council of Ministers:
items: Statement-I: The resignation or death of an incumbent Prime Minister automatically dissolves the entire Union Council of Ministers without requiring separate resignations from individual Ministers, whereas the death or resignation of any other Union Minister creates only a ministerial vacancy.

Statement-II: Upon the sudden death or resignation of a Prime Minister who commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, the Constitution mandates that the House of the People stands automatically dissolved alongside the Council of Ministers.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Because the Prime Minister is the constitutional head of the Council of Ministers under Article 74(1) and all other Ministers are appointed and continue in office solely on the Prime Minister's advice under Article 75(1), the death or resignation of the Prime Minister automatically dissolves the entire Council of Ministers. However, this dissolves only the Council of Ministers and does not dissolve the Lok Sabha, allowing the majority party or coalition to elect a new leader to be appointed Prime Minister.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 74(1), the Prime Minister stands at the head of the Council of Ministers, and under Article 75(1), all other Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. Because the Prime Minister is the 'keystone of the Cabinet arch' and the central axis around which the Council exists, the Prime Minister's death or resignation automatically dissolves the entire Council of Ministers without requiring individual resignations from other Ministers. Conversely, the death or resignation of any other Minister merely creates a vacancy.

Statement-II is incorrect. The death or resignation of an incumbent Prime Minister dissolves the Union Council of Ministers, NOT the House of the People (Lok Sabha). If the ruling party or coalition continues to command a majority in the Lok Sabha and elects a new leader, the President is constitutionally bound to invite that leader to be sworn in as the new Prime Minister and reconstitute the Council of Ministers without holding fresh general elections or dissolving the House.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 74(1), 75(1) & 85(2); Laxmikanth Ch. 20 & 21

stem: With reference to the Cabinet Committees in the Union Executive, consider the following statements:
items: 1. They are extra-constitutional in emergence and derive their institutional authority from the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961 framed under Article 77(3) of the Constitution.
2. The Prime Minister serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of all standing Cabinet Committees to maintain collective responsibility.
3. Ministers of State who do not hold Cabinet rank are not debarred from being appointed as members of Cabinet Committees.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Cabinet Committees are extra-constitutional bodies established under the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961 (framed under Article 77(3)) to reduce the workload of the Union Cabinet and facilitate in-depth policy coordination. While predominantly composed of Cabinet Ministers, non-Cabinet Ministers can be included as members, and the Prime Minister chairs only those committees of which he or she is a member.

exp.why: Cabinet Committees are not mentioned in the Constitution of India. Their establishment, nomenclature, and functions are governed by the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, which are framed by the President under Article 77(3) for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of India.

The Prime Minister does not chair all standing Cabinet Committees. While the Prime Minister chairs key committees such as the Cabinet Committee on Security, Economic Affairs, Political Affairs, and Appointments, committees such as the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs and the Cabinet Committee on Accommodation are ordinarily chaired by senior Union Cabinet Ministers like the Minister of Defence or the Minister of Home Affairs.

Although Cabinet Committees usually consist of Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (both those with Independent Charge and those attached to Cabinet Ministers) are not debarred from membership and are frequently appointed either as regular members or as special invitees when subjects pertaining to their ministries are deliberated.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 77(3); Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 'Cabinet Committees'

stem: Consider the following pairs of national bodies and their ex-officio Chairpersons:
items: 1. Inter-State Council : Prime Minister
2. Zonal Councils : Prime Minister
3. National Board for Wildlife : Union Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
4. Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority : Prime Minister
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Distinguishing the ex-officio headship of apex federal, statutory, and security bodies requires checking whether the governing statute or Presidential Order vests the chair in the Prime Minister or a senior Cabinet Minister. While the Prime Minister chairs the Inter-State Council, the National Board for Wildlife, and the Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority, the Union Home Minister chairs all Zonal Councils.

exp.why: Under the Inter-State Council Order, 1990 issued by the President pursuant to Article 263 of the Constitution, the Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairperson of the Inter-State Council, whereas the Union Home Minister serves as the Chairperson of the Standing Committee of the Inter-State Council.

Under Section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the Union Home Minister (and not the Prime Minister) is the common ex-officio Chairperson of all five statutory Zonal Councils, as well as the North-Eastern Council under the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.

Under Section 5A of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL), while the Union Minister in-charge of Environment, Forest and Climate Change serves as its Vice-Chairperson.

India's Nuclear Command Authority (NCA) comprises a Political Council and an Executive Council. The Political Council is chaired by the Prime Minister and is the sole body empowered to authorize the use of nuclear weapons, while the Executive Council is chaired by the National Security Advisor.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 263; States Reorganisation Act, 1956 Sec. 15; Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 Sec. 5A

stem: With reference to the requirement of prior recommendation or previous sanction in the legislative process in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Financial Bill under Article 117(3), which involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India without containing any of the matters specified in Article 110, cannot be introduced in either House of Parliament without the prior recommendation of the President.
2. A Bill seeking to amend the federal provisions of the Constitution under the proviso to Article 368(2) requires the prior recommendation of the President before its introduction in Parliament.

3. A Bill in a State Legislature that seeks to impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce, or intercourse under Article 304(b) requires the previous sanction of the Governor of the State before its introduction.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution draws fine distinctions regarding the stage at which Presidential recommendation is required and the authority granting it. Financial Bills (Category-II) under Article 117(3) require Presidential recommendation only for consideration (passing) and not for introduction, Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368 require no prior Presidential recommendation for introduction, and State Bills under Article 304(b) require the previous sanction of the President rather than the Governor.

exp.why: Unlike Money Bills and Financial Bills (Category-I) under Article 117(1), a Financial Bill (Category-II) under Article 117(3) can be introduced in either House of Parliament without the prior recommendation of the President. Under Article 117(3), the President's recommendation is required only for the consideration (passing) of the Bill by either House.

Under Article 368 of the Constitution, a Constitutional Amendment Bill—including one seeking to amend entrenched federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2)—does not require the prior recommendation of the President for its introduction in either House of Parliament. Consequently, even a private member can introduce a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

Under the proviso to Article 304(b), no Bill or amendment seeking to impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce, or intercourse in the public interest shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President of India (not the Governor of the State).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 117(1), 117(3), 304(b), and 368; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 'Parliament'

stem: With reference to the military and diplomatic powers vested in the President of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 53(2) of the Constitution, the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union is vested in the President as an autonomous prerogative that cannot be regulated by an ordinary law of Parliament.

2. While international treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded in the name of the President, a treaty that modifies domestic law or restricts the legal rights of citizens is not self-executing and requires enabling legislation by Parliament.

3. Under Article 253, Parliament has the exclusive power to enact laws for implementing any international treaty or convention made in the name of the President, even if the subject matter of such legislation falls wholly within the State List.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Constitution ensures parliamentary supremacy and civilian oversight over both military command and treaty implementation. Article 53(2) explicitly subjects the President's exercise of supreme command of the Defence Forces to regulation by law, while Article 253 empowers Parliament alone to enact enabling legislation to give domestic legal effect to international treaties, even over State List subjects.

exp.why: Article 53(2) explicitly stipulates that 'the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law.' Thus, far from being an autonomous prerogative immune from statute, the President's military command is expressly subordinated to regulation by laws enacted by Parliament (such as the Army Act, Navy Act, and Air Force Act).

While the Union Executive can negotiate and conclude international treaties in the name of the President under Article 73 read with Entry 14 of the Union List, the Supreme Court held in Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969) that if a treaty alters domestic law, restricts the rights of citizens, or involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, it cannot be enforced domestically without enabling legislation by Parliament under Article 253.

Notwithstanding the federal distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, Article 253 confers overriding power on Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any international treaty, agreement, or convention, even if the subject falls exclusively within the State List (List II), without requiring ratification by the States.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 53(2), 73, and 253; Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969)

stem: Consider the following procedural stages prescribed under Article 61 of the Constitution for the impeachment of the President of India:
items: 1. Investigation of the charge by the second House or a tribunal caused to be appointed by it, during which the President has the right to appear and to be represented.
2. Delivery of at least fourteen days' written notice of the intention to move the impeachment resolution, signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of the initiating House.
3. Adoption of the resolution preferring the charge by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the initiating House.
4. Adoption of a resolution by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the investigating House declaring that the charge preferred against the President has been sustained.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct sequential order of the stages given above?
core: Article 61 establishes a rigorous quasi-judicial two-stage bicameral procedure for the impeachment of the President for 'violation of the Constitution'. The initiating House first prefers the charge after a 14-day notice signed by one-fourth of its members and passes it by two-thirds of its total membership, after which the second House investigates the charge and must sustain it by the same two-thirds majority of total membership.

exp.why: Stage 3 (Item 1): Under Article 61(3), once a charge has been preferred by either House of Parliament, the other House shall investigate the charge or cause the charge to be investigated, and the President shall have the right to appear and to be represented at such investigation.

Stage 1 (Item 2): Under Article 61(2)(a), the impeachment process begins when a proposal to prefer a charge is contained in a resolution which is moved after at least fourteen days' notice in writing signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of the House has been given.

Stage 2 (Item 3): Under Article 61(2)(b), following the 14-day notice period, the resolution preferring the charge must be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the initiating House.

Stage 4 (Item 4): Under Article 61(4), if as a result of the investigation a resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House by which the charge was investigated or caused to be investigated, declaring that the charge has been sustained, such resolution has the effect of removing the President from office from the date on which the resolution is so passed.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 61; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 'President'

stem: Consider the following constitutional milestones that shaped the institutional relationship between the President and the Union Council of Ministers:
items: 1. Enactment of the constitutional amendment making it explicitly obligatory for the President to act in accordance with the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers under Article 74(1).

2. Supreme Court seven-Judge Constitution Bench judgment in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab establishing that the President and Governors are formal constitutional heads who exercise executive functions on ministerial aid and advice.
3. Enactment of the constitutional amendment inserting the word 'Cabinet' in Article 352(3) and empowering the President to return ministerial advice once for reconsideration.
4. Insertion of Article 75(1A) into the Constitution capping the total strength of the Union Council of Ministers at fifteen percent of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha.
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the milestones given above, from earliest to latest?
core: The parliamentary character of the Union Executive evolved sequentially through judicial doctrine and constitutional amendments: the Supreme Court first authoritatively settled the binding nature of ministerial aid and advice in Shamsher Singh (1974), which was codified into Article 74(1) by the 42nd Amendment (1976), refined with a one-time suspensive reconsideration by the 44th Amendment (1978), and structurally disciplined by the 15% size cap under the 91st Amendment (2003).

exp.why: Milestone 2 in sequence (1976): The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 74(1) to explicitly state that the President 'shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice' tendered by the Council of Ministers.

Milestone 1 in sequence (1974): Even prior to the 42nd Amendment, a seven-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (August 1974) authoritatively held that the Indian Constitution embodies the Westminster cabinet system and that both the President and the Governor are constitutional heads bound to act on the aid and advice of their Council of Ministers save in exceptional spheres of constitutional discretion.

Milestone 3 in sequence (1978): The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 added the proviso to Article 74(1) enabling the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice once (and binding the President to act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration), and also inserted the term 'Union Cabinet' into Article 352(3).

Milestone 4 in sequence (2003): The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 inserted Article 75(1A) and Article 164(1A), stipulating that the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister (or Chief Minister), in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the House of the People (or State Legislative Assembly).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 74(1), 75(1A), and 352(3); Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974); 42nd, 44th, and 91st Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the appointment, qualifications, and conditions of office of the Governor of a State under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Where the same person is appointed as Governor of two or more States, the emoluments and allowances payable to him are allocated among those States in such proportion as Parliament may by law determine.
2. The Constitution explicitly prescribes only two qualifications for the appointment of a person as a Governor: citizenship of India and completion of the age of thirty-five years.

3. In the absence of the Chief Justice of the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the State, the oath of office to the Governor is administered by the senior-most judge of that Court available.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Parliament determines the general emoluments and allowances of a Governor under Article 158(3), the specific proportional allocation of emoluments when one person serves as Governor of two or more States is determined by the President by order under Article 158(3A). The Constitution itself prescribes only citizenship and a minimum age of 35 years under Article 157.

exp.why: Under Article 158(3A), which was inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956, where the same person is appointed as Governor of two or more States, the emoluments and allowances payable to him are allocated among the States in such proportion as the President may by order determine (not Parliament by law).

Under Article 157 of the Constitution, no person shall be eligible for appointment as Governor unless he is a citizen of India and has completed the age of thirty-five years. Conventions such as being an outsider to the State are not written into Article 157.

Under Article 159, every Governor and every person discharging the functions of the Governor shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe an oath or affirmation in the presence of the Chief Justice of the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the State, or, in his absence, the senior-most Judge of that Court available.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 153 to 159; 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956; Laxmikanth Ch. 30

stem: With reference to the tenure of a State Governor and the constitutional doctrine of pleasure under Article 156, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Because a Governor is appointed by the President and holds office during his pleasure, the office of the Governor is constitutionally deemed to be an employment under the Government of India within the meaning of Article 319.

2. Under the doctrine of pleasure as interpreted by the Supreme Court, the Union Government cannot be called upon by a court to disclose the material for removing a Governor even when the aggrieved person demonstrates a prima facie case of arbitrariness or mala fides.
