3. The Constitution specifies that a Governor can be removed prior to the completion of a five-year term only on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: As held by Constitution Benches in Hargovind Pant (1979) and B.P. Singhal (2010), the Governor holds an independent constitutional office that is not an employment under the Government of India. While Article 156(1) specifies no grounds for removal, presidential pleasure is subject to limited judicial review if a prima facie case of arbitrariness or mala fides is established.

exp.why: In Hargovind Pant v. Dr. Raghukul Tilak (1979) and B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that the office of the Governor is an independent constitutional office and is neither subordinate to nor under the control of the Government of India; hence, it is not an 'employment under the Government of India' under Article 319.

In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench ruled that although the President need not assign reasons while withdrawing pleasure under Article 156(1), the power cannot be exercised in an arbitrary, capricious, or unreasonable manner. If the aggrieved person establishes a prima facie case of arbitrariness or mala fides, the Court can require the Union Government to produce the material on which the decision was made.

Article 156(1) simply states that the Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. The Constitution does not lay down any specific grounds (such as proved misbehaviour or incapacity) or impeachment/inquiry procedure for the removal of a Governor.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 156; B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) 6 SCC 331; Hargovind Pant v. Dr. Raghukul Tilak (1979)

stem: With reference to the constitutional immunity of the Governor under Article 361 and judicial review of gubernatorial actions, consider the following statements:
items: 1. No criminal proceedings whatsoever can be instituted or continued against the Governor of a State in any court during his term of office, even in respect of acts done in his personal capacity before entering upon office.

2. Civil proceedings claiming relief against the Governor for acts done in his personal capacity can be instituted during his term of office after the expiration of two months following a written notice.

3. The personal immunity conferred on the Governor under Article 361(1) bars the Supreme Court from examining the mala fides or constitutional validity of a Governor's report recommending action under Article 356.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 361 confers personal immunity on a serving Governor from criminal proceedings and requires a two-month notice for personal civil suits. However, as established in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), Article 361(1) only protects the Governor personally from being made a party in court and does not immunize official constitutional actions or reports under Article 356 from judicial review.

exp.why: Article 361(2) provides an absolute bar during the term of office: no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or the Governor of a State in any court during his term of office, whether for official or personal acts.

Under Article 361(4), civil proceedings in which relief is claimed against the Governor in respect of any act done or purporting to be done by him in his personal capacity, whether before or after he entered upon his office, can be instituted after the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered.

In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that the personal immunity of the Governor under Article 361(1) does not bar the Court from examining the validity of an action (such as a proclamation under Article 356 based on the Governor's report) on the ground of mala fides or ultra vires. While the Governor cannot be personally summoned, the Union Government is duty-bound to defend the action by producing the relevant material.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 361; Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) 2 SCC 1

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the discretionary powers of the Governor under the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 163(2) of the Constitution, the Governor enjoys an absolute and unfettered power to decide whether any matter falls within his discretion, and such a decision is completely immune from judicial review in all circumstances.

Statement-II: Unlike Article 74 relating to the President, Article 163(1) of the Constitution expressly provides for a sphere of constitutional discretion for the Governor where he acts without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 163(1)—unlike Article 74 for the President—explicitly recognizes that the Governor may act in his discretion 'by or under this Constitution', the 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Nabam Rebia (2016) clarified that Article 163(2) does not confer an overarching or unfettered discretion immune from judicial review.

exp.why: In Nabam Rebia & Bamang Felix v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly (2016), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that the finality clause in Article 163(2) must be read harmoniously with Article 163(1). The Governor cannot claim discretion in areas not envisaged by or under the Constitution, and the exercise of gubernatorial discretion is subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, or constitutional ultra vires.

Article 163(1) explicitly states that there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'. No such express exception clause exists in Article 74(1) for the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 74 and 163; Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016) 8 SCC 1

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Governor over State Bills under Article 200 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: A Governor cannot exercise an indefinite pocket veto under Article 200 by simply withholding assent to a non-Money Bill passed by the State Legislature without returning it to the House.

Statement-II: If the Governor withholds assent to a non-Money Bill and returns it to the State Legislature, and the House passes the Bill again without any amendments, the Governor is constitutionally empowered to reserve the re-passed Bill for the consideration of the President.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023), the Supreme Court held that the first proviso to Article 200 is constitutionally tethered to the option of withholding assent. Consequently, if a Governor withholds assent to a non-Money Bill, he must return it to the State Legislature 'as soon as possible', and if the House re-passes the Bill, he must grant assent and cannot reserve the unchanged re-passed Bill for the President.

exp.why: In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023), the Supreme Court ruled that the expression 'as soon as possible' in the first proviso to Article 200 attaches directly to the decision to withhold assent. An unelected Governor cannot thwart the normal course of lawmaking by an elected Legislature through an indefinite pocket veto; if assent is withheld, the Bill must be returned to the Legislature for reconsideration.

Under the first proviso to Article 200, if the Bill is passed again by the House or Houses with or without amendment and presented to the Governor for assent, 'the Governor shall not withhold assent therefrom'. Further, the Supreme Court clarified that once the Governor exercises the option of returning the Bill to the Legislature in the first instance, he exhausts his options and cannot subsequently reserve the re-passed unchanged Bill for the consideration of the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 200; State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023)

stem: With reference to the reservation of State Bills by the Governor for the consideration of the President under Articles 200 and 201 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the second proviso to Article 200, it is mandatory for the Governor to reserve a State Bill for the consideration of the President whenever the Bill seeks to impose any tax or duty affecting the financial interests of another State.

2. When a non-Money Bill reserved by the Governor is returned by the President for reconsideration and the State Legislature passes the Bill again within six months without any amendment, the President is constitutionally bound under Article 201 to give assent to the Bill.

3. Under the proviso to Article 201, the President may direct the Governor to return even a State Money Bill to the State Legislature for reconsideration if it conflicts with a central fiscal statute.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mandatory reservation under the second proviso to Article 200 applies only to Bills that derogate from the powers of the High Court so as to endanger its constitutional position. Under Article 201, the President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration, and even when a non-Money Bill is returned and re-passed by the State Legislature, the Constitution imposes no obligation on the President to grant assent.

exp.why: Under the second proviso to Article 200, the only ground on which the Constitution makes it obligatory ('shall reserve') for the Governor to reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President is where the Bill would, if it became law, so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by the Constitution designed to fill.

Under the proviso to Article 201, when a returned non-Money State Bill is reconsidered by the State Legislature within six months and passed again with or without amendment, it is presented again to the President for his consideration. However, unlike Article 111 (Union Bills) or the first proviso to Article 200 (State Bills before the Governor), Article 201 does not mandate that the President 'shall not withhold assent therefrom'.

The proviso to Article 201 explicitly begins with the words 'Provided that where the Bill is not a Money Bill, the President may direct the Governor to return the Bill...'. Thus, a State Money Bill reserved for the President can either be assented to or withheld assent from, but cannot be returned to the State Legislature for reconsideration.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 200 and 201; Laxmikanth Ch. 30

stem: With reference to the constitutional procedure governing Money Bills under Article 111 and Article 200 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements accurately describes a structural difference between the powers of the President and the Governor?

opts.A: Unlike the President who can either give or withhold assent to a Union Money Bill, the Governor has an additional constitutional option to reserve a State Money Bill for the consideration of the President, after which the Governor plays no further role in its enactment.
opts.B: While the President cannot return a Union Money Bill to the Houses of Parliament for reconsideration, the Governor is empowered under the first proviso to Article 200 to return a State Money Bill to the State Legislative Assembly once for reconsideration.
opts.C: When a State Money Bill is reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President under Article 201, the President may direct the Governor to return the Bill to the State Legislature for reconsideration within six months.
opts.D: Both the President and the Governor are constitutionally bound to grant assent to a Money Bill immediately upon its presentation because every Money Bill is introduced only with their respective prior recommendation.

core: While neither the President (under Article 111) nor the Governor (under Article 200) can return a Money Bill to the Legislature for reconsideration, the Governor possesses a third constitutional option unavailable to the President: reserving a State Money Bill for the consideration of the President under Article 200, which permanently terminates the Governor's role in that Bill's enactment.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because under Article 111, when a Union Money Bill is presented to the President, the President has only two choices: either declare that he assents to the Bill or that he withholds assent therefrom. In contrast, under Article 200, when a State Money Bill is presented to the Governor, the Governor has three choices: give assent, withhold assent, or reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President. Once reserved under Article 200, the Bill is governed by Article 201, under which the President either gives or withholds assent directly, and the Governor plays no further constitutional role. Option (B) is incorrect because the first proviso to Article 200 explicitly bars the Governor from returning a Money Bill for reconsideration. Option (C) is incorrect because the proviso to Article 201 explicitly restricts the President's power to direct the return of a reserved Bill to cases where the Bill is not a Money Bill. Option (D) is incorrect because although Money Bills are introduced with prior recommendation, the text of Articles 111 and 200 formally preserves the option of withholding assent rather than mandating automatic assent.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 111, 200 & 201; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapters on President & Governor

stem: With reference to the Ordinance-making power of the Governor under Article 213 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In a State having a unicameral legislature, the Governor can promulgate an Ordinance only when the Legislative Assembly is not in session.

2. Under the proviso to Article 213(1), the Governor requires prior instructions from the President before promulgating any Ordinance that involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State.

3. As laid down by the Supreme Court in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), the laying of an Ordinance before the State Legislature is mandatory, and the satisfaction of the Governor under Article 213 is subject to judicial review.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Governor's Ordinance-making power under Article 213 is strictly conditional upon the Legislature not being in session, is subject to judicial review and mandatory legislative tabling as held in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), and requires prior Presidential instructions only in the three federal-supervisory contingencies specified in the proviso to Article 213(1).

exp.why: Under Article 213(1), the Governor is empowered to promulgate Ordinances only during the recess of the Legislature. In a unicameral State, the Governor can promulgate an Ordinance only when the Legislative Assembly is not in session (and in a bicameral State, when both Houses are not in session, or when either of the two Houses is not in session because a law cannot be enacted by a single House sitting alone).

Under the proviso to Article 213(1), the Governor cannot promulgate an Ordinance without instructions from the President in only three specific cases: (a) if a Bill containing the same provisions would under the Constitution have required the previous sanction of the President for the introduction thereof into the Legislature; (b) if he would have deemed it necessary to reserve a Bill containing the same provisions for the consideration of the President; or (c) if an Act of the Legislature of the State containing the same provisions would under the Constitution have been invalid unless, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, it had received the assent of the President. A measure involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State requires the recommendation of the Governor under Article 207, not prior instructions from the President.

In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the requirement of placing an Ordinance before the Legislature under Article 213(2)(a) is mandatory and not directory, that repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution, and that the satisfaction of the President under Article 123 and of the Governor under Article 213 is not immune from judicial review.

ref: Constitution of India Article 213; Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench Judgment in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)

stem: With reference to the clemency powers of the President under Article 72 and the Governor under Article 161 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the power to grant a complete pardon in respect of a sentence of death vests exclusively in the President under Article 72, the Governor possesses the authority to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence of death.
2. Unlike the President, the Governor has no constitutional authority under Article 161 to grant pardon, reprieve, or remission in respect of punishments or sentences inflicted by a Court-Martial.

3. The constitutional power of the Governor under Article 161 to grant remission is sovereign in nature and remains untouched by the statutory minimum imprisonment restrictions prescribed under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While only the President can grant a complete pardon for a death sentence or grant clemency in Court-Martial cases under Article 72, the Governor retains the authority under Article 161 (and explicitly preserved by Article 72(3)) to suspend, remit, or commute a death sentence, and this constitutional power cannot be curtailed by statutory restrictions in the BNSS, 2023.

exp.why: Under Article 72(1)(c), only the President has the constitutional power to grant a complete pardon in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death. However, both Article 161 and Article 72(3) recognize that the Governor of a State possesses the power to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence of death whenever an offence relates to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends or where such power is conferred by law.

Article 72(1)(a) explicitly empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court-Martial. Article 161 confers no such power on the Governor regarding Court-Martial sentences.

As settled by the Supreme Court in Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980) and State of Haryana v. Raj Kumar (2021), statutory restrictions on premature release—such as the mandatory minimum 14-year actual imprisonment requirement under Section 475 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (which replaced Section 433A of the erstwhile CrPC)—bind only the statutory remission powers of the appropriate government and cannot fetter or override the sovereign constitutional power of the Governor under Article 161.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 72 & 161; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 Section 475; State of Haryana v. Raj Kumar (2021)

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding the special responsibilities of Governors under Part XXI of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Article 371A (Nagaland) : Special responsibility of the Governor to secure the proper functioning of the Committee of the Legislative Assembly consisting of members elected from the Hill Areas
2. Article 371C (Manipur) : Special responsibility of the Governor with respect to law and order in the State on account of internal disturbances
3. Article 371F (Sikkim) : Special responsibility of the Governor for peace and for an equitable arrangement for ensuring the social and economic advancement of different sections of the population
4. Article 371H (Arunachal Pradesh) : Special responsibility of the Governor with respect to law and order in the State, exercised in his individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 371 to 371-J tailor asymmetric federal responsibilities for State Governors: Article 371A (Nagaland) and Article 371H (Arunachal Pradesh) confer individual judgment regarding law and order, whereas Article 371C (Manipur) focuses on the Hill Areas Committee of the State Legislative Assembly and Article 371F (Sikkim) focuses on equitable socio-economic advancement.

exp.why: Under Article 371A(1)(b), the Governor of Nagaland has a special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State of Nagaland for so long as internal disturbances occurring in the Naga Hills-Tuensang Area immediately before the formation of the State continue, exercising his individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers. Securing the proper functioning of the Hill Areas Committee of the Legislative Assembly belongs to the Governor of Manipur under Article 371C.

Under Article 371C, the President may provide for a special responsibility of the Governor of Manipur to secure the proper functioning of the committee of the Legislative Assembly of the State consisting of members elected from the Hill Areas of that State, and the Governor must submit an annual report to the President regarding the administration of the Hill Areas.

Under Article 371F(g), the Governor of Sikkim has a special responsibility for peace and for an equitable arrangement for ensuring the social and economic advancement of different sections of the population of Sikkim, and in the discharge of this responsibility the Governor acts in his discretion, subject to such directions as the President may from time to time deem fit to issue.

Under Article 371H(a), the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh has a special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State, and in the discharge of his functions in relation thereto, the Governor exercises his individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers as to the action to be taken.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 371A, 371C, 371F & 371H; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Special Provisions for Some States

stem: Consider the following pairs of Constitutional Provisions and their specific mandates relating to Tribal Administration and the State Executive:
items: 1. Proviso to Article 164(1) : Mandates a Minister in charge of Tribal Welfare in the States of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Odisha
2. Paragraph 9 of the Sixth Schedule : Empowers the Governor to determine in his discretion the share of royalties from mineral licences payable to an Autonomous District Council in case of a dispute

3. Paragraph 20BB of the Sixth Schedule : Requires the Governor to consult the Council of Ministers, and if he thinks it necessary, the District or Regional Council concerned, while exercising his discretionary functions

4. Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule : Empowers the Governor to direct by public notification that any particular Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area in the State
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The 94th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2006 excluded Bihar from the proviso to Article 164(1), leaving Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha as the four States constitutionally required to have a Tribal Welfare Minister, while the Fifth and Sixth Schedules vest specialized legislative and discretionary functions in the Governor.

exp.why: By the 94th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2006, Bihar was excluded from the proviso to Article 164(1) and Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand were added. Currently, the proviso to Article 164(1) mandates a Minister in charge of Tribal Welfare (who may in addition be in charge of the welfare of the Scheduled Castes and backward classes) only in the four States of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha.

Under Paragraph 9(2) of the Sixth Schedule, if any dispute arises as to the share of royalties accruing each year from licences or leases for the purpose of prospecting for, or the extraction of, minerals granted by the State Government to be made over to a District Council, it shall be determined by the Governor acting in his discretion.

Under Paragraph 20BB of the Sixth Schedule, in the discharge of his functions under specified paragraphs of the Sixth Schedule in his discretion, the Governor shall consult the Council of Ministers, and if he thinks it necessary, the District Council or the Regional Council concerned, and take such action as he considers necessary in his discretion.

Under Paragraph 5(1) of the Fifth Schedule, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, the Governor may by public notification direct that any particular Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of the State shall not apply to a Scheduled Area or any part thereof in the State, or shall apply subject to such exceptions and modifications as he may specify.

ref: Constitution of India Proviso to Article 164(1) (94th Amendment Act, 2006), Fifth Schedule & Sixth Schedule

stem: With reference to the appointment, tenure, and constitutional duties of the Chief Minister and Ministers in a State, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person who is not a member of the State Legislature can be appointed as the Chief Minister or a Minister under Article 164, provided he or she becomes a member of the State Legislature within six consecutive months.

2. If a non-legislator appointed as a Minister under Article 164(4) ceases to hold office upon failing to get elected within six months, he or she can be re-appointed as a Minister for one more consecutive term of six months during the tenure of the same Legislative Assembly.

3. Under Article 167(c), if the Governor so requires, the Chief Minister is constitutionally obligated to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 164(4) permits a non-legislator to serve as a Chief Minister or Minister for up to six consecutive months, the Supreme Court in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001) held that this is a one-time exception during the term of a Legislative Assembly and cannot be abused through repeated re-appointments without getting elected.

exp.why: Under Article 164(4) of the Constitution, a Minister (including the Chief Minister) who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of the Legislature of the State shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister. Consequently, a non-member can be appointed as Chief Minister or Minister for up to six months, within which he or she must become a member of either House of the State Legislature.

In S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001), the Supreme Court explicitly ruled that re-appointing a non-legislator as a Minister after the expiry of the six-month period without getting elected to the State Legislature during the term of the same Legislative Assembly is unconstitutional. The Court held that Article 164(4) is in the nature of a one-time privilege during the life of an Assembly, and repeated re-appointments would subvert parliamentary democracy and collective responsibility under Articles 164(1) and 164(2).

Under Article 167(c), it is the constitutional duty of the Chief Minister of each State, if the Governor so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council. This provision reinforces the principle of collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 164 & 167; Supreme Court Judgment in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)

stem: With reference to the constitutional limits on the size of the Council of Ministers in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 164(1A) of the Constitution, the total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in the Council of Ministers in a State shall not exceed fifteen per cent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly of that State.

2. In the National Capital Territory of Delhi, the Constitution explicitly restricts the total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, to not more than ten per cent of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly.

3. The constitutional floor stipulating that the number of Ministers, including the head of the Council of Ministers, shall not be less than twelve applies uniformly to the Union, the States, and Union Territories having a Legislative Assembly.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 capped the size of the Council of Ministers at 15% of the lower House for both the Union (Article 75(1A)) and the States (Article 164(1A)), the minimum floor of 12 Ministers applies exclusively to States and has no parallel for the Union or for the NCT of Delhi (which is capped at 10% under Article 239AA(4)).

exp.why: Inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, Article 164(1A) mandates that the total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in the Council of Ministers in a State shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly of that State.

Under Article 239AA(4) (inserted by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991), the Council of Ministers for the National Capital Territory of Delhi shall consist of not more than ten per cent of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly (i.e., a maximum of 7 Ministers out of a 70-member Assembly).

The proviso stipulating that the number of Ministers shall not be less than 12 is contained exclusively in Article 164(1A) applicable to States. Neither Article 75(1A) (for the Union) nor Article 239AA(4) (for the NCT of Delhi, where the maximum itself is 7 Ministers) nor Section 44 of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 (which caps the UT of J&K Council of Ministers at 10% of the Assembly strength) prescribes a minimum floor of 12 Ministers.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 75(1A), 164(1A) & 239AA(4); 91st Amendment Act, 2003

stem: With reference to the Advocate General for a State under the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The remuneration of the Advocate General is determined by the State Legislature by law and is charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the State.
opts.B: He has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of any committee of the State Legislature of which he may be named a member, and enjoys all privileges and immunities available to a Member of the State Legislature while doing so.
opts.C: To be eligible for appointment as the Advocate General, a person must have completed at least thirty-five years of age and be qualified to be appointed as a Judge of a High Court.
opts.D: In a State having a bicameral Legislature, the Advocate General has the right to participate in the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly only and cannot address the Legislative Council unless summoned by its Chairman.

core: Under Articles 177 and 194(4) of the Constitution, the Advocate General has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of a State Legislature and any committee thereof of which he is named a member (without a right to vote), enjoying the parliamentary privileges of a legislator, while holding office during the Governor's pleasure at a remuneration determined by the Governor under Article 165(3).

exp.why: Option (B) is correct: Under Article 177, the Advocate General for a State has the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House or both Houses of the State Legislature and any committee of the State Legislature of which he may be named a member, though he is not entitled to vote. Under Article 194(4), the powers, privileges, and immunities of members of the State Legislature extend to persons who by virtue of the Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in the proceedings of, a House or its committees. Option (A) is incorrect because under Article 165(3), the Advocate General holds office during the pleasure of the Governor and receives such remuneration as the Governor may determine (not fixed by the State Legislature by law). Option (C) is incorrect because Article 165(1) read with Article 217(2) prescribes no minimum age limit of 35 years for appointment as a High Court Judge or Advocate General. Option (D) is incorrect because Article 177 explicitly confers the right to speak and participate in both Houses (the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council) in a bicameral State.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 165, 177 & 194(4); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity

stem: With reference to the conduct of business of a State Government and the constitutional position of the Governor, consider the following statements:
items: 1. As laid down by the Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), wherever the Constitution requires the 'satisfaction' of the Governor—such as for promulgating an ordinance under Article 213—it refers to the personal satisfaction of the Governor rather than the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers.
2. Under Article 166 of the Constitution, all executive action of the Government of a State shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor.

3. Once an order or instrument made in the name of the Governor is authenticated in the manner specified in the rules made by the Governor, its validity cannot be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the Governor.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the 7-Judge Constitution Bench ruling in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the Supreme Court established that the 'satisfaction' of the President or Governor required by the Constitution is not their personal satisfaction, but the institutional satisfaction of the Council of Ministers on whose aid and advice they function, while Article 166 governs the formal expression and authentication of State executive actions.

exp.why: In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court authoritatively ruled that wherever the Constitution requires the 'satisfaction' of the President or the Governor for the exercise of any power or function (including ordinance promulgation under Article 213), the satisfaction required by the Constitution is not the personal satisfaction of the President or the Governor, but the satisfaction in the constitutional sense under the Cabinet system of government—that is, the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers on whose aid and advice the Governor exercises powers and functions.
Article 166(1) explicitly states that all executive action of the Government of a State shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor.

Article 166(2) provides that orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the Governor shall be authenticated in such manner as may be specified in rules to be made by the Governor, and the validity of an order or instrument which is so authenticated shall not be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the Governor. (Note: While authentication bars challenging whether the Governor actually made the order, the substantive legality or constitutionality of the order itself remains subject to judicial review).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 166; Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) 7-Judge Bench

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional architecture of the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi:
items: Statement-I: Unlike full-fledged States, the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi is constitutionally barred under Article 239AA from making laws on matters relating to Public Order, Police, and Land in the State List, and the executive power of the Delhi Government is co-extensive with this restricted legislative domain.

Statement-II: Under the proviso to Article 239AA(4), the expression 'any matter' empowers the Lieutenant Governor to routinely refer every administrative decision of the Council of Ministers to the President whenever he disagrees with its policy merits, thereby exercising an independent executive veto over day-to-day governance.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Article 239AA, the legislative and co-extensive executive competence of the NCT of Delhi covers the State and Concurrent Lists excluding Entries 1 (Public Order), 2 (Police), and 18 (Land) of the State List; however, as held by the Supreme Court Constitution Benches (2018 & 2023), the proviso to Article 239AA(4) ('any matter') does not mean 'every matter' and cannot be used by the Lieutenant Governor to run a parallel administration.

exp.why: Under Article 239AA(3)(a), the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi has power to make laws with respect to any matter in the State List or Concurrent List applicable to Union Territories, except Entries 1 (Public Order), 2 (Police), and 18 (Land) of the State List (and Entries 64, 65, and 66 insofar as they relate to Entries 1, 2, and 18). Under Article 239AA(4), the Council of Ministers aids and advises the Lieutenant Governor in relation to matters on which the Assembly has power to make laws, making executive power co-extensive with legislative competence.

In Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018 5-Judge Constitution Bench, reaffirmed in May 2023), the Supreme Court held that the words 'any matter' in the proviso to Article 239AA(4) cannot be construed to mean 'every matter'. The Lieutenant Governor does not possess independent decision-making power over routine executive governance, cannot act mechanically as an obstructionist or parallel administration, and may invoke the reference to the President only in exceptional circumstances after attempts to resolve differences through dialogue have failed.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 239AA; Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018 & 2023 Constitution Bench)

stem: With reference to the National Capital Civil Service Authority (NCCSA) established under the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Authority consists of the Chief Minister of Delhi as its ex-officio Chairperson, along with the Chief Secretary and the Principal Home Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi as members.

2. All matters required to be decided by the Authority regarding transfers, postings, and vigilance matters of Group 'A' officers and DANICS officers serving in the affairs of the Government of NCT of Delhi are decided by a majority of votes of the members present and voting.

3. In case the Lieutenant Governor differs with the recommendation made by the Authority, the Act mandates that he must refer the matter to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, whose decision thereon shall be final.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Sections 45E to 45H inserted by the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, the 3-member NCCSA (chaired by the Chief Minister with two senior bureaucrats) decides matters by majority vote, but in the event of a difference of opinion between the Authority and the Lieutenant Governor, the decision of the Lieutenant Governor himself is statutorily final.

exp.why: Under Section 45E(2) of the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 (as inserted by the 2023 Amendment Act), the National Capital Civil Service Authority consists of the Chief Minister of the NCT of Delhi as Chairperson, the Chief Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi as Member, and the Principal Home Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi as Member-Secretary.

Under Section 45E(5) read with Section 45H(1) of the Act, the NCCSA makes recommendations regarding transfers, postings, vigilance, and disciplinary proceedings of Group 'A' officers and DANICS officers serving in the affairs of the Government of NCT of Delhi, and all questions at a meeting of the Authority are decided by a majority of votes of the members present and voting.

Under Section 45H(4) of the Act, the Lieutenant Governor may return the recommendation of the Authority for reconsideration, and in case of any difference of opinion between the Lieutenant Governor and the Authority, the decision of the Lieutenant Governor himself is final. There is no statutory requirement to refer such differences to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.

ref: Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, Sections 45E–45H

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in relation to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD):
items: Statement-I: As upheld by the Supreme Court, the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi is empowered to nominate ten persons with special knowledge or experience in municipal administration (aldermen) to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers of the NCT of Delhi.

Statement-II: Under Article 239AA(3)(a) of the Constitution, 'Local Government and Municipal Corporations' (Entry 5 of the State List) is an excluded subject on par with Public Order, Police, and Land, thereby completely barring the Delhi Legislative Assembly and the Council of Ministers from any constitutional jurisdiction over municipal bodies.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Government of NCT of Delhi v. Office of Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (August 2024), the Supreme Court held that the Delhi LG can independently nominate 10 aldermen to the MCD without the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers—not because Entry 5 (Local Government) is excluded under Article 239AA(3)(a), but because the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (a Parliamentary law enacted under Article 239AA(3)(b)) specifically vests a distinct statutory power in the LG, triggering the exception ('by or under any law, required to act in his discretion') in Article 239AA(4).

exp.why: In Government of NCT of Delhi v. Office of Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (2024), the Supreme Court ruled that under Section 3(3)(b)(i) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (as amended in 1993), the power to nominate ten aldermen (persons of at least 25 years of age having special knowledge or experience in municipal administration) to the MCD is a statutory power vested directly in the Administrator/Lieutenant Governor, which he exercises in his discretion without being bound by the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers.

Entry 5 of the State List ('Local government, that is to say, the constitution and powers of municipal corporations...') is NOT an excluded entry under Article 239AA(3)(a); only Entries 1 (Public Order), 2 (Police), and 18 (Land) (and related entries 64, 65, 66) are excluded. Instead, the LG's independent power arises because Article 239AA(4) requires the LG to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers 'except in so far as he is, by or under any law, required to act in his discretion'. Since Parliament, exercising its overarching legislative power for Delhi under Article 239AA(3)(b), amended the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 to specifically confer the nomination power on the Administrator/LG (as distinct from the 'Government'), that Parliamentary law satisfies the statutory discretion exception in Article 239AA(4).

ref: Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Office of Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (SC, August 2024); Article 239AA(3) & (4)

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory framework governing Union Territories with Legislatures in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi is established directly under Article 239AA of the Constitution, the Legislative Assemblies of both Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have been constituted through Parliamentary enactments under Article 239A.

2. Unlike the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi, the Legislative Assemblies of both Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir are empowered to make laws with respect to 'Public Order' and 'Police' enumerated in the State List.

3. Under Article 239B of the Constitution, the Lieutenant Governor of a Union Territory with a Legislature may promulgate an ordinance during the recess of the Assembly without prior instructions from the President if the ordinance pertains solely to a State List subject.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Union Territories with Legislatures do not follow a uniform model: NCT of Delhi is governed directly by Article 239AA, whereas Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir derive their legislative framework from Parliamentary laws enacted under Article 239A. Furthermore, ordinance-making in a UT under Article 239B strictly requires prior instructions from the President in every case.

exp.why: Article 239AA (inserted by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991) directly creates the Legislative Assembly for the NCT of Delhi in the text of the Constitution. Conversely, Article 239A empowers Parliament to create by law a body to function as a Legislature for a Union Territory; Parliament exercised this power via the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963 for Puducherry and Section 13 of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 (which expressly extends Article 239A to the UT of Jammu and Kashmir).

While the Puducherry Legislative Assembly can legislate on all matters in the State List (including Public Order and Police, subject to Parliament's overriding authority), Section 32(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 explicitly excludes Entries 1 and 2 of the State List—namely 'Public Order' and 'Police'—from the legislative competence of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, placing J&K on a footing similar to NCT of Delhi in respect of those two subjects.

Unlike a State Governor under Article 213 (who requires prior Presidential instructions only in three specified circumstances), the proviso to Article 239B(1) of the Constitution mandates that the Administrator/Lieutenant Governor of a Union Territory shall not promulgate any ordinance except after obtaining prior instructions from the President in that behalf. Additionally, no ordinance can be promulgated when the UT Legislature is dissolved or suspended.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 239A, 239AA & 239B; J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019, Sections 13 & 32; Laxmikanth Ch. 41.

stem: With reference to the Governor's power of nomination to the State Legislature, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 171(5) of the Constitution, the categories specified for the Governor's nomination of members to the State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, cooperative movement, sports, and philanthropy.

2. Under Article 333 of the Constitution as currently operative, the Governor may nominate one member of the Anglo-Indian community to the State Legislative Assembly if the community is not adequately represented.

3. The nomination of a member by the Governor to the State Legislative Council under Article 171(5) can be invalidated by a High Court on the ground that the Governor acted on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers rather than in his personal discretion.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 171(5), the Governor nominates one-sixth of the members of the State Legislative Council from five specific fields (literature, science, art, cooperative movement, and social service) strictly on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers. Meanwhile, the nomination of Anglo-Indians to State Legislative Assemblies under Article 333 ceased to operate following the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019.

exp.why: Article 171(5) of the Constitution enumerates exactly five fields from which the Governor nominates members to the Legislative Council: Literature, Science, Art, Co-operative movement, and Social service. 'Sports' and 'philanthropy' are not separately mentioned as constitutional categories in Article 171(5) (though individuals from such walks of life are sometimes nominated under the broader umbrella of 'art' or 'social service').

The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 (effective January 25, 2020) amended Article 334 and discontinued the reservation of seats by nomination for members of the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha (Article 331) and in the State Legislative Assemblies (Article 333). Consequently, the Governor no longer possesses any power to nominate an Anglo-Indian member to the State Legislative Assembly.

Nominating members to the State Legislative Council under Article 171(3)(e) read with Article 171(5) is an executive function of the Governor, not a discretionary power under Article 163(2). Courts have consistently held that the Governor must act on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers when making these nominations, and cannot act in his individual discretion.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 171(5), 333 & 334; 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019; Laxmikanth Ch. 30 & 33.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the legal and constitutional position of the Governor acting as the Chancellor of a State University:
items: Statement-I: When the Governor of a State exercises powers as the ex-officio Chancellor of a State University under a State University Act, the Governor is constitutionally bound by the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers under Article 163(1) of the Constitution, even where the statute vests independent authority in the Chancellor.

Statement-II: When discharging functions as the Chancellor of a State University by virtue of a State legislation, the Governor acts in a distinct statutory capacity rather than in the capacity of the constitutional head of the State Executive.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Supreme Court jurisprudence distinguishes between the Governor as the constitutional head of a State under Articles 154 and 163 and the Governor acting as an ex-officio Chancellor created by a State University statute. In the latter role, the Governor acts as a statutory authority (persona designata) and is not bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers unless the statute itself so provides.

exp.why: As affirmed by the Supreme Court in Bhuri Nath v. State of J&K (1997) and reiterated in recent rulings on Vice-Chancellor appointments (such as Prof. Sreejith P.S. v. Dr. Rajasree M.S., 2022), when the Governor acts as Chancellor under a State University Act, the office of Chancellor is statutory and distinct from the constitutional office of Governor. Therefore, Article 163(1) does not apply, and the Chancellor is not bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers where the statute confers independent authority on the Chancellor.

The Constitution does not make the Governor the Chancellor of State Universities; rather, State University Acts enacted by the State Legislature designate the Governor as the ex-officio Chancellor. Consequently, when exercising powers under such an Act, the Governor functions purely in a statutory capacity derived from the legislation rather than as the constitutional head of the State Executive.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 163; Supreme Court rulings in Bhuri Nath v. State of J&K (1997) & Sreejith P.S. v. Rajasree M.S. (2022); Punchhi Commission Report.

stem: With reference to the collective responsibility of the State Council of Ministers under Article 164(2) and the Governor's power to mandate a floor test, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution of India, the Governor's power to direct the Chief Minister to prove majority through a floor test can be exercised only at the stage of initial appointment of the Government, and cannot be invoked once a duly constituted Legislative Assembly is in session or adjourned.

2. The mandate under Article 164(2) that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State is a continuous constitutional requirement throughout the tenure of the Ministry.

3. While the Governor exercises constitutional discretion when calling for a floor test upon receiving objective material indicating a loss of majority, such a decision remains subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or absence of relevant material.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Collective responsibility under Article 164(2) is continuous, empowering the Governor under Articles 174 and 175(2) to direct a floor test even during an ongoing or adjourned session if cogent, objective material shows the incumbent government has lost the confidence of the House. However, as held in Subhash Desai (2023), the Governor's satisfaction is subject to judicial review and cannot be triggered merely by internal party dissension.

exp.why: In Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker, Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly (2020), the Supreme Court held that the Governor's power under Article 174 read with Article 175(2) to require a trust vote is not restricted to the initial formation of a government. Where objective circumstances (such as resignations of legislators) raise a prima facie doubt as to whether the incumbent Council of Ministers still commands a majority, the Governor can direct a floor test even during a running or adjourned session.

Under Article 164(2), the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State. This constitutional trust is not a one-time threshold at the time of swearing-in, but a continuous constitutional condition for the Ministry to remain in office.

In S.R. Bommai (1994), Shivraj Singh Chouhan (2020), and Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (5-Judge Constitution Bench, 2023), the Supreme Court held that although calling for a floor test is a discretionary constitutional power of the Governor when a government appears to have lost its majority, that discretion is not immune from judicial review. If the Governor calls a floor test without objective material indicating loss of confidence (for instance, merely to resolve an intra-party dispute), the decision is unconstitutional.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 164(2), 174 & 175(2); Shivraj Singh Chouhan (2020) & Subhash Desai (2023) SC Judgments.

stem: Suppose an ordinary non-Money Bill passed by a State Legislature contains provisions that would so derogate from the powers of the State High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by the Constitution designed to fill. Consider the following sequential stages under Articles 200 and 201 of the Constitution:
items: 1. Mandatory reservation of the Bill by the Governor for the consideration of the President under the Second Proviso to Article 200 without granting assent at the State level.
2. Issuance of a directive by the President to the Governor under the Proviso to Article 201 to return the Bill to the State Legislature together with a message requesting reconsideration.
3. Reconsideration of the Bill by the House or Houses of the State Legislature within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the presidential message.
4. Re-presentation of the reconsidered Bill directly to the Governor, who is thereafter constitutionally bound to grant assent to the Bill on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers.
prompt: Which one of the following correctly represents the valid constitutional sequence of stages under Articles 200 and 201?

opts.A: 1 -> 2 -> 3 only (followed by re-presentation of the Bill to the President for consideration)

core: Under the Second Proviso to Article 200, a State Bill endangering the constitutional position of the High Court must be reserved by the Governor for the President. Once reserved under Article 201, the Governor steps out of the assent chain: if the President directs its return for reconsideration, the State Legislature must reconsider it within six months and re-present it solely to the President.

exp.why: Under the Second Proviso to Article 200 of the Constitution, the Governor shall not assent to, but shall reserve for the consideration of the President, any Bill which in the opinion of the Governor would, if it became law, so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger the position which that Court is by the Constitution designed to fill. This is the only explicitly mandatory reservation clause in Article 200.

Under the Proviso to Article 201, where a reserved Bill is not a Money Bill, the President may direct the Governor to return the Bill to the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State together with a message requesting that the House or Houses will reconsider the Bill or any specified provisions thereof.

The Proviso to Article 201 explicitly stipulates that when a Bill is so returned upon a Presidential directive, the House or Houses of the State Legislature shall reconsider it accordingly within a period of six months from the date of receipt of such message.

Once a Bill has been reserved for the consideration of the President under Article 200, the Governor becomes functus officio with respect to granting assent to that Bill. Under the Proviso to Article 201, if the Bill is passed again by the State House or Houses with or without amendment after reconsideration, it shall be presented again to the President for his consideration—not to the Governor—and the Constitution does not bind the President to grant assent even upon such re-passage.

ref: Constitution of India, Second Proviso to Article 200 & Proviso to Article 201; Laxmikanth Ch. 30 & 33.

stem: With reference to the office of the Chief Secretary of a State in India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Chief Secretary is chosen by the Chief Minister from amongst senior Indian Administrative Service officers of the State cadre, and the office carries no fixed tenure prescribed by the Constitution.
opts.B: The Chief Secretary is appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of the Union Public Service Commission to ensure federal neutrality in State administration.
opts.C: The Constitution of India explicitly designates the Chief Secretary as the ex-officio Secretary to the State Council of Ministers with a minimum security of tenure of two years.
opts.D: During the operation of a Proclamation under Article 356, the Chief Secretary automatically assumes the constitutional powers of the State Legislature under the direction of the Governor.

core: The Chief Secretary is the apex civil servant and executive head of the State Secretariat, selected by the Chief Minister (and formally appointed in the name of the Governor) from senior IAS officers of the State cadre. The office is an administrative creation rather than a constitutional post, and the Constitution prescribes no fixed tenure for it.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because the Chief Secretary is selected by the Chief Minister from amongst senior IAS officers of the State cadre (with formal orders issued in the name of the Governor), and there is no fixed tenure prescribed by the Constitution. Option (B) is incorrect because although IAS officers are recruited through the UPSC and appointed to the service by the President, the posting as Chief Secretary of a State is the prerogative of the State Government/Chief Minister, not the President or UPSC. Option (C) is incorrect because the Constitution does not mention the office of the Chief Secretary or prescribe a two-year tenure (though the Chief Secretary acts as Secretary to the State Cabinet by administrative rules of business). Option (D) is incorrect because under Article 356(1)(b) and Article 357, the powers of the State Legislature during President's Rule are exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, whereas the Chief Secretary assists the Governor in running the executive administration.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 166 (Rules of Business); Laxmikanth Ch. 31 & 32.

stem: With reference to the composition of the House of the People (Lok Sabha) under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Following the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019, the maximum constitutionally permissible strength of the House of the People stands at 550 members.
2. The Constitution does not directly prescribe the mode of choosing representatives of the Union Territories to the House of the People and instead empowers the Parliament to provide for it by law.

3. While representatives of the States are chosen by direct election, representatives of Union Territories without a Legislative Assembly are nominated by the President on the recommendation of the respective Administrators.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 81(1), the Lok Sabha consists of not more than 530 representatives of the States and not more than 20 representatives of the Union Territories (totalling 550 after the 104th Amendment discontinued the Anglo-Indian nomination under Article 331). While Article 81(1)(a) mandates direct election for States, Article 81(1)(b) leaves the manner of choosing UT representatives to parliamentary law, under which Parliament enacted the Union Territories (Direct Election to the House of the People) Act, 1965 providing for direct elections across all Union Territories.

exp.why: Under Article 81(1), the House of the People consists of not more than 530 members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States and not more than 20 members to represent the Union Territories. The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 amended Article 334 to discontinue the reservation of seats for the nomination of up to two members of the Anglo-Indian community under Article 331 from January 25, 2020, reducing the maximum constitutional strength from 552 to 550.

Under Article 81(1)(b), the Constitution specifies that the representatives of the Union Territories in the House of the People shall be chosen 'in such manner as Parliament may by law provide', rather than mandating direct election in the constitutional text itself.

Exercising its power under Article 81(1)(b), Parliament enacted the Union Territories (Direct Election to the House of the People) Act, 1965, under which the representatives of all Union Territories—whether or not they have a Legislative Assembly—are chosen by direct election on the basis of universal adult suffrage, and not by presidential nomination.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 81, 331 & 334; 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It provides for the reservation of as nearly as may be one-third of the total number of seats for women in the House of the People, State Legislative Assemblies, and the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi, without extending such reservation to the Council of States or State Legislative Councils.

2. The one-third reservation for women within the seats already reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes operates as a horizontal sub-reservation rather than an additional vertical quota.

3. Under Article 334A, the reservation of seats for women shall come into effect after an exercise of delimitation is undertaken on the basis of the relevant figures for the first census taken after the commencement of the Act, and shall remain in force for a period of fifteen years from the date such reservation comes into effect, unless extended by Parliament by law.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 inserted Articles 330A, 332A, and 334A and amended Article 239AA to reserve one-third of directly elected seats (including one-third horizontal sub-reservation within SC/ST reserved seats) for women in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the NCT of Delhi Assembly. It does not apply to Upper Houses (Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils) and is contingent upon post-census delimitation with a 15-year renewable sunset clause.

exp.why: By amending Article 239AA and inserting Articles 330A and 332A, the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 mandates one-third reservation for women exclusively in the directly elected Houses—the Lok Sabha, the State Legislative Assemblies, and the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi. No such reservation is provided in the indirectly elected Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils.

Under Articles 330A(2) and 332A(2), as nearly as may be one-third of the total number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes under Articles 330 and 332 shall be reserved for women belonging to the SCs or the STs, operating horizontally within the existing SC/ST quota.

Under Article 334A(1) and 334A(2), the provisions relating to the reservation of seats for women shall come into effect after an exercise of delimitation is undertaken for this purpose after the relevant figures for the first census taken after the commencement of the 106th Amendment Act have been published, and shall cease to have effect on the expiration of 15 years from the commencement of such reservation unless extended for further periods by Parliament by law.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 239AA, 330A, 332A & 334A; 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023

stem: With reference to the composition of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) under Article 80 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The President nominates twelve members to the Council of States from amongst persons having special knowledge or practical experience in five specified fields—literature, science, art, cooperative movement, and social service.
2. The Fourth Schedule to the Constitution allocates seats in the Council of States to both the States and those Union Territories that have a Legislative Assembly.

3. Under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 enacted pursuant to Article 80(5), the electoral college for choosing representatives of a Union Territory to the Council of States consists of the elected members of the Legislative Assembly of that Union Territory, owing to which Union Territories like Ladakh and Chandigarh have no representation in the House.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 80(3) limits Presidential nominations to the Rajya Sabha to four fields (Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service), whereas 'Cooperative movement' is an additional fifth field reserved exclusively for the Governor's nominations to a State Legislative Council under Article 171(5). Under Article 80(5) read with Section 27A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, UT representatives to the Rajya Sabha are elected by an electoral college of elected MLAs of that UT, limiting Fourth Schedule representation to Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir.

exp.why: Under Article 80(3), the 12 members nominated by the President to the Council of States are drawn from only four specified fields: Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service. 'Cooperative movement' is not included in Article 80(3); it is the fifth field prescribed exclusively for the Governor's nominations to a State Legislative Council under Article 171(5).

Under Article 80(2), the allocation of seats in the Council of States to be filled by representatives of the States and of the Union Territories is governed by the provisions contained in the Fourth Schedule, which currently allocates seats to all 28 States and the 3 Union Territories having a Legislative Assembly (NCT of Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir).

Under Article 80(5), representatives of the Union Territories in the Council of States are chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law prescribe. Under Section 27A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the electoral college for a Union Territory consists of the elected members of its Legislative Assembly; consequently, Union Territories without a legislature (such as Ladakh, Chandigarh, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu) are not allocated seats in the Rajya Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 80, 171(5) & Fourth Schedule; Representation of the People Act, 1950 Sec. 27A

stem: Consider the following statements regarding elections to the Council of States (Rajya Sabha):
items: Statement-I: In elections to the Council of States, the 'None of the Above' (NOTA) option is inapplicable, and an elector belonging to a political party is required under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 to show their marked ballot paper to the authorized agent of their party before inserting it into the ballot box.

Statement-II: Following the 2003 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951, as upheld by the Supreme Court in the Kuldip Nayar case (2006), a candidate contesting an election to the Council of States from a particular State is no longer required to be registered as an elector in a parliamentary constituency within that same State.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The 2003 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951 introduced two distinct changes to Rajya Sabha elections, both upheld in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006): (1) an open ballot system for party MLAs to prevent cross-voting and corruption, and (2) removal of the State domicile requirement for candidates. Furthermore, in Shailesh Manubhai Parmar v. ECI (2018), the Supreme Court barred NOTA in Rajya Sabha polls because proportional representation by single transferable vote and party-whip accountability are incompatible with NOTA.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under the proviso to Section 59 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (inserted in 2003), votes in elections to the Council of States are given by open ballot where every elector belonging to a political party must show their marked ballot paper to their party's authorized agent. Moreover, in Shailesh Manubhai Parmar v. Election Commission of India (2018), the Supreme Court struck down the use of NOTA in Rajya Sabha elections, holding that NOTA is meant only for direct elections based on universal adult suffrage and secret ballot.

Statement-II is also correct, as the 2003 amendment to Section 3 of the RPA, 1951 removed the requirement that a candidate contesting to the Rajya Sabha from a State must be an elector in that specific State, making registration as an elector in any parliamentary constituency in India sufficient—a reform upheld in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006). However, Statement-II (eligibility of candidates) does not explain Statement-I (voting procedure for MLA electors, which is explained by the indirect proportional representation system and the need to enforce party discipline against cross-voting).

ref: Representation of the People Act, 1951 Sec. 3 & 59; Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006); Shailesh Manubhai Parmar v. ECI (2018)

stem: With reference to the readjustment and delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Articles 82 and 170 of the Constitution, the freeze on the readjustment of the total number of seats allocated to each State in the Lok Sabha and the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State continues until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published.

2. Pursuant to the 87th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, both the inter-state allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and the intra-state division of territorial constituencies were rationalized on the basis of the 2001 Census.
3. The number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People within each State remains frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census population proportions.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Articles 82 and 170 (as amended by the 84th and 87th Constitutional Amendment Acts), a dual census baseline operates until the first census after 2026: the total number of seats allocated to each State in the Lok Sabha and the total strength of each State Assembly remain frozen on the 1971 Census (to prevent penalizing states that stabilized population growth), whereas intra-state territorial division of constituencies and the reservation of seats for SCs and STs under Articles 330 and 332 were updated on the basis of the 2001 Census.

exp.why: The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001 amended the provisos to Articles 82 and 170(3) to extend the freeze on the readjustment of the total number of seats allocated to each State in the Lok Sabha and the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published.

Under the 84th and 87th Constitutional Amendment Acts, the inter-state allocation of total seats in the Lok Sabha remains frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census, not the 2001 Census. The 87th Amendment Act, 2003 only provided for the intra-state readjustment and rationalization of territorial constituencies within each State on the basis of the 2001 Census without altering the total number of seats allotted to any State.

Under the Explanation to Article 330(3) and the proviso to Article 332(3), as amended by the 87th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies within each State was refixed on the basis of the 2001 Census, rather than remaining frozen at the 1971 Census levels.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 82, 170, 330 & 332; 84th & 87th Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the creation, abolition, and functional composition of the Legislative Councils in States under Articles 169 and 171 of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Electorate of municipalities, district boards and specified local authorities (Article 171) : Elects one-third of the total members of the Legislative Council
2. Electorate of university graduates of at least three years' standing residing in the State (Article 171) : Elects one-twelfth of the total members of the Legislative Council
3. Nomination by the Governor from Literature, Science, Art, Cooperative Movement, and Social Service (Article 171) : Constitutes one-sixth of the total members of the Legislative Council

4. Parliamentary law for the creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council after a special-majority Assembly resolution (Article 169) : Requires a special majority under Article 368 in both Houses of Parliament
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Under Article 171(3), the composition of a State Legislative Council follows fixed fractions until modified by Parliament by law: 1/3 elected by local authorities, 1/3 elected by MLAs from non-MLAs, 1/12 elected by graduates of three years' standing, 1/12 elected by teachers of three years' standing (not lower than secondary schools), and 1/6 nominated by the Governor. Under Article 169, while the State Legislative Assembly must pass the resolution by a special majority, Parliament enacts the law for creating or abolishing the Council by a simple majority outside the scope of Article 368.

exp.why: Under Article 171(3)(a), as nearly as may be one-third of the total number of members of the Legislative Council of a State are elected by electorates consisting of members of municipalities, district boards and such other local authorities in the State as Parliament may by law specify.

Under Article 171(3)(b), as nearly as may be one-twelfth of the members are elected by electorates consisting of persons residing in the State who have been for at least three years graduates of any university in the territory of India or possess equivalent qualifications prescribed by law (with another one-twelfth elected by teachers of at least three years' standing in educational institutions not lower in standard than secondary schools under Article 171(3)(c), and one-third elected by MLAs under Article 171(3)(d)).
