Under Article 171(3)(e) read with Article 171(5), the remainder—which equals one-sixth of the total number of members of the Legislative Council—are nominated by the Governor from amongst persons having special knowledge or practical experience in Literature, Science, Art, Cooperative Movement, and Social Service.

Under Article 169(1), although the Legislative Assembly of the State must pass a resolution for the abolition or creation of the Legislative Council by a special majority (majority of the total membership of the Assembly and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting), Parliament passes the consequential law by a simple majority like an ordinary piece of legislation. Article 169(3) explicitly declares that no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 169 & 171; Laxmikanth Ch. 33

stem: With reference to the duration of the Houses of Parliament and the tenure of their members under the Indian constitutional and statutory framework, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Constitution of India explicitly fixes the term of office of a member of the Rajya Sabha at six years from the date of notification of election.
opts.B: While a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, the normal five-year term of the Lok Sabha can be extended by the President through an executive order for a period not exceeding one year at a time.
opts.C: A member elected in a by-election to fill a casual vacancy in the Rajya Sabha holds office for a fresh full term of six years.
opts.D: While the Constitution stipulates that as nearly as possible one-third of the members of the Rajya Sabha shall retire every second year, the six-year tenure of individual members is prescribed by a parliamentary statute.

core: Article 83(1) of the Constitution makes the Rajya Sabha a permanent body with one-third of its members retiring every second year, but leaves the exact term of individual members to be decided by Parliament by law (fixed at six years under Section 154 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951).

exp.why: Option (D) is correct. Under Article 83(1) of the Constitution, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) is not subject to dissolution, and as nearly as possible one-third of its members shall retire on the expiration of every second year in accordance with provisions made by Parliament by law. The Constitution itself did not fix the term of office of a member of the Rajya Sabha; Parliament prescribed the six-year tenure under Section 154(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Option (A) is incorrect because the six-year term is statutory, not constitutional. Option (B) is incorrect because under the proviso to Article 83(2), the five-year term of the Lok Sabha during a National Emergency can be extended only by Parliament by law (not by a presidential executive order) for a period not exceeding one year at a time, and not extending in any case beyond six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate. Option (C) is incorrect because under Section 154(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, a member chosen to fill a casual vacancy in the Rajya Sabha serves only for the remainder of their predecessor's term, unlike the President or Vice-President.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 83; Representation of the People Act, 1951 Sec. 154; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the qualifications for membership of Parliament and State Legislatures in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To contest an election to either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha from a particular State, a candidate need only be registered as an elector in any parliamentary constituency in India.
2. To contest an election to a State Legislative Assembly or a State Legislative Council, a candidate must be registered as an elector in an assembly constituency within that specific State.

3. The minimum age requirement of thirty years for the Rajya Sabha and twenty-five years for the Lok Sabha is prescribed purely by the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and not by the text of the Constitution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, Parliamentary candidates (for both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) can be registered electors in any parliamentary constituency across India, whereas State Legislature candidates (for both SLA and SLC) must be electors within that specific State.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Sections 3 and 4 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (as amended in 2003 and upheld by the Supreme Court in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, 2006), the requirement that a candidate contesting for the Rajya Sabha from a particular State must be an elector in that specific State was dispensed with. Consequently, for both the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha (except autonomous districts of Assam, Lakshadweep, and Sikkim as specified), a person only needs to be an elector for any Parliamentary constituency in India.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Sections 5 and 6 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, a person is not qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State unless they are an elector for any Assembly constituency in that specific State. Similarly, to be nominated by the Governor to the Legislative Council, the person must ordinarily reside in that State.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Article 84(b) of the Constitution of India itself explicitly mandates that a person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless they are not less than thirty years of age in the case of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and not less than twenty-five years of age in the case of the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 84 & 173; Representation of the People Act, 1951 Sec. 3–6; Kuldip Nayar v. UoI (2006)

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory provisions governing double membership and vacation of seats in Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. If a person who is not already a member of either House is elected simultaneously to both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha and fails to intimate within ten days in which House they wish to serve, their seat in the Lok Sabha becomes vacant.

2. If a person is elected both to Parliament and to the Legislature of a State, their seat in Parliament falls vacant at the expiration of fourteen days unless they have previously resigned their seat in the State Legislature.

3. In computing the period of sixty days of absence without permission of the House for declaring a member's seat vacant, no account is taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 101 of the Constitution read with Sections 68–70 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950 governs automatic seat vacation across dual election scenarios.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Section 68(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, any person who is chosen a member of both the House of the People (Lok Sabha) and the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and who has not taken their seat in either House must intimate in writing to the Election Commission within 10 days in which House they wish to serve; if they fail to give such intimation, their seat in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)—and not the Lok Sabha—becomes vacant at the expiration of that period. Note further that under Section 69, if a sitting member of one House is elected to the other House, their seat in the first House immediately falls vacant.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 101(2) of the Constitution read with Rule 2 of the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950 framed by the President, if a person is chosen a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State, their seat in Parliament becomes vacant at the expiration of fourteen days from the publication of the declaration unless they have previously resigned their seat in the State Legislature.

Statement 3 is correct. Under the proviso to Article 101(4) of the Constitution, if for a period of sixty days a member of either House of Parliament is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare their seat vacant; however, in computing the said period of sixty days, no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 101; Representation of the People Act, 1951 Sec. 68–70

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the oath of members and the validity of parliamentary proceedings:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 100(2) of the Constitution of India, any legislative proceeding or vote in either House of Parliament remains constitutionally valid even if it is subsequently discovered that an unqualified person or a member who had not subscribed to the constitutional oath sat and voted in the House.

Statement-II: Under Article 104 of the Constitution of India, a person who sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before making and subscribing the oath or affirmation under Article 99 is liable to a monetary penalty of five hundred rupees for each day they so sit or vote, to be recovered as a debt due to the Union.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Constitution separates collective legislative validity from individual liability: Article 100(2) protects the institutional integrity of parliamentary acts from being rendered void ab initio due to defective membership, while Article 104 imposes a personal daily pecuniary penalty on the erring individual.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 100(2) of the Constitution incorporates a saving clause (the de facto doctrine for legislative bodies) providing that either House of Parliament has power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in Parliament shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings. Thus, a Bill passed with such participation is not rendered void ab initio.

Statement-II is correct. Article 104 stipulates that if a person sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before complying with the requirements of Article 99 (oath or affirmation), or when they know that they are not qualified or that they are disqualified for membership thereof, they shall be liable in respect of each day on which they so sit or vote to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the Union. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: Article 100(2) saves parliamentary proceedings to prevent institutional paralysis and legal uncertainty for citizens, whereas Article 104 is an independent personal deterrent penalty against the individual.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 99, 100(2) & 104; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the election and tenure of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Whenever the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office immediately upon dissolution and continues to hold office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly constituted Lok Sabha.
2. While the date of election of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is fixed by the President of India, the date of election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker.
3. Upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the outgoing Speaker must formally tender their resignation in writing to the President of India before the Speaker Pro Tem assumes charge.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: To ensure institutional continuity of the Lok Sabha Secretariat even when the House is dissolved, the second proviso to Article 94 extends the Speaker's tenure until immediately before the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under the second proviso to Article 94 of the Constitution, whenever the House of the People (Lok Sabha) is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate their office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Rule 7 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the election of a Speaker is held on such date as the President may fix. Under Rule 8, the election of a Deputy Speaker is held on such date as the Speaker may fix.

Statement 3 is incorrect. First, under Article 94(b), whenever a Speaker resigns during their tenure, the resignation letter is addressed to the Deputy Speaker, never to the President of India. Second, upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, no resignation is required at all; the Speaker's term automatically comes to an end by operation of the second proviso to Article 94 immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected House.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 93 & 94; Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha Rules 7 & 8

stem: With reference to the constitutional procedure for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. At any sitting of the Lok Sabha while a resolution for the removal of the Speaker from office is under consideration, the Speaker shall not preside even though they are present in the House.

2. During the consideration of such a removal resolution, the Speaker has the right to speak in the House and is entitled to vote only in the first instance, and not in the case of an equality of votes.
3. A resolution for the removal of the Speaker under Article 94(c) requires to be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the Lok Sabha present and voting.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Articles 94(c) and 96, a Speaker facing a removal resolution cannot preside over the sitting, reverts to exercising an ordinary member's vote in the first instance (losing the casting vote), and can be removed by an 'effective majority' (majority of all the then members of the House).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Based on the principle of natural justice that no person shall be a judge in their own cause (nemo judex in causa sua), Article 96(1) of the Constitution mandates that at any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from their office is under consideration, the Speaker shall not, though they are present, preside.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 96(2) of the Constitution, the Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for their removal from office is under consideration in the House and shall, notwithstanding anything in Article 100, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings, but not in the case of an equality of votes.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 94(c) of the Constitution, the Speaker may be removed from office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of 'all the then members of the House' (known in parliamentary terminology as an effective majority, calculated after deducting actual vacancies from the total strength of the House), and not by a special majority of two-thirds of the members present and voting.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 94(c) & 96; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the member appointed by the President under Article 95(1) of the Constitution of India to perform the duties of the office of the Speaker when both the offices of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are vacant (commonly referred to as the Speaker Pro Tem), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The President is constitutionally bound to appoint only the oldest member of the newly elected Lok Sabha in terms of age to this office.
opts.B: Such a member possesses strictly ceremonial powers limited to administering the oath to newly elected members and is constitutionally barred from presiding over a floor test.
opts.C: While performing the duties of the vacant office of the Speaker, such a member exercises all the constitutional and procedural powers of the Speaker until the House elects a regular Speaker.
opts.D: Unlike the regular Speaker, the oath of office to such a member is administered by the outgoing Speaker of the dissolved Lok Sabha before vacating office.

core: Under Article 95(1), when the offices of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are vacant, the member appointed by the President to perform the duties of the Speaker (Speaker Pro Tem) possesses all the powers of the Speaker, including presiding over the first sitting, administering oaths, conducting the Speaker's election, and even presiding over a floor test if required.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct because under Article 95(1) of the Constitution (and analogously Article 180(1) for State Assemblies, as affirmed by the Supreme Court in the Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker, MP Legislative Assembly ruling), the member appointed to perform the duties of the vacant office of the Speaker steps into the shoes of the Speaker and exercises all powers vested in the Speaker until a regular Speaker is chosen. Option (A) is incorrect because appointing the senior-most member in terms of continuous legislative tenure (not biological age) is an unwritten parliamentary convention rather than a binding constitutional mandate. Option (B) is incorrect because the Constitution does not restrict the Speaker Pro Tem to ceremonial duties; they can legally conduct a floor test. Option (D) is incorrect because the President himself administers the oath to the Speaker Pro Tem.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 95(1) & 99; Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker (SC 2020); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the performance of duties of the presiding officers of the Lok Sabha:
items: Statement-I: A member of the Panel of Chairpersons nominated under the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha cannot preside over the House when the offices of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are vacant.

Statement-II: Under Article 95 of the Constitution of India, during a simultaneous vacancy in the offices of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, the senior-most member of the Panel of Chairpersons automatically assumes the duties of the office of the Speaker until a new election is held.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Constitution draws a sharp distinction between the 'absence' of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker from a sitting (Article 95(2)) and a 'vacancy' in both offices (Article 95(1)). The Panel of Chairpersons can preside only during the temporary absence of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, whereas during a simultaneous vacancy in both offices, only a member appointed by the President under Article 95(1) can perform the Speaker's duties.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 95(2) read with Rule 9 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, a member of the Panel of Chairpersons nominated by the Speaker is authorized to preside over the House only during the 'absence' of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker from any sitting. They have no constitutional authority to preside when both offices are formally 'vacant'.

Statement-II is incorrect. Under Article 95(1) of the Constitution, while the offices of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are vacant, the duties of the office of the Speaker shall be performed by 'such member of the House of the People as the President may appoint for the purpose'. There is no automatic assumption of office by any member of the Panel of Chairpersons.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 95(1) & 95(2); Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha Rule 9; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President of India is under consideration in the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman cannot preside over the sitting, though he is entitled to speak, take part in the proceedings, and vote in the first instance on such a resolution.
2. The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not subordinate to the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and is directly responsible to the Rajya Sabha.

3. A resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha needs to be passed only by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha and does not require the agreement of the Lok Sabha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because the Vice-President (ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) is not a member of the Rajya Sabha, Article 92(2) explicitly bars him from voting at all—even in the first instance—when a resolution for his removal is under consideration, unlike the Speaker of the Lok Sabha who votes in the first instance under Article 96(2).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 92(1), the Chairman cannot preside while a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President is under consideration. Under Article 92(2), while the Chairman has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of the Rajya Sabha during such consideration, he 'shall not be entitled to vote at all on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings' because he is not a member of the House. In contrast, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha (being a member of the House) can vote in the first instance during a removal resolution under Article 96(2).

Statement 2 is correct. Like the Deputy Speaker in the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a subordinate officer under the Chairman. He holds an independent constitutional office under Article 89(2) and is directly responsible to the Rajya Sabha.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 90(c), the Deputy Chairman may be removed from office by a resolution of the Council of States passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council (effective majority of the Rajya Sabha alone). Unlike the removal of the Vice-President under Article 67(b), the removal of the Deputy Chairman does not require the agreement or concurrence of the Lok Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 67(b), 89, 90 & 92; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following parliamentary functionaries with reference to a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament under Article 118(4) of the Constitution of India and the Rules made thereunder:
items: 1. Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
2. Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
3. Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
4. Speaker of the Lok Sabha
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct descending order of precedence among those who are constitutionally eligible to preside over a joint sitting?
core: Under Article 118(4) and Rule 5 of the Houses of Parliament (Joint Sittings and Communications) Rules, the order of precedence to preside over a joint sitting is: (1) Speaker of the Lok Sabha, (2) Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha, (3) Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and (4) any other member determined by the members present. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha never presides over a joint sitting as he is not a member of either House.

exp.why: The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha is eligible to preside over a joint sitting and ranks second in precedence, presiding during the absence of the Speaker.
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President of India) is NOT a member of either House of Parliament and therefore does not preside over a joint sitting of both Houses in any circumstance.
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is eligible to preside over a joint sitting and ranks third in precedence, presiding if both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are absent.

Under Article 118(4), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha ranks first in precedence to preside over a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament. Thus, excluding item 2, the valid descending order is 4 - 1 - 3.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 118(4); Houses of Parliament (Joint Sittings and Communications) Rules, Rule 5; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Secretariat of Parliament under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Constitution explicitly mandates that each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff, though it permits the creation of posts common to both Houses.
2. Parliament is empowered to regulate by law the recruitment and the conditions of service of persons appointed to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament.
3. The Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha is appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 98 guarantees the administrative autonomy of Parliament from the Executive by mandating a separate secretarial staff for each House under the control of the respective Presiding Officer, while authorizing Parliament to regulate their service conditions by law.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 98(1) explicitly provides that each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff, while its proviso clarifies that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 98(2), Parliament may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament. Until Parliament makes such a law, Article 98(3) empowers the President to make rules after consultation with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

Statement 3 is incorrect. To preserve the independence of the Legislature from the Executive, the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha is chosen and appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha (after consulting the leaders of the House and Opposition), and not by the President on the recommendation of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. Similarly, the Secretary-General of the Rajya Sabha is appointed by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 98; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the disqualification of a Member of Parliament on the ground of holding an 'office of profit' under Article 102(1)(a) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: A Member of Parliament holding an executive office under the Government to which pecuniary remuneration or profit is attached incurs disqualification even if the member voluntarily chooses not to draw any salary or allowance from that office.

Statement-II: Since the expression 'office of profit' is exhaustively defined in Article 102 of the Constitution, Parliament cannot exempt any profit-yielding office from disqualifying its holder without enacting a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Supreme Court jurisprudence (Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India), the decisive test for an 'office of profit' is whether the office is capable of yielding pecuniary gain, regardless of whether the holder actually draws it. While the Constitution does not define 'office of profit', Article 102(1)(a) explicitly empowers Parliament to declare by ordinary law which offices do not disqualify their holders.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. As laid down by the Supreme Court in Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006), an office of profit is an office that is 'capable of yielding a profit or pecuniary gain'. Whether a member actually receives or voluntarily forgoes the salary, honorarium, or compensatory allowance attached to the office is irrelevant once pecuniary gain is attached to the office itself.

Statement-II is incorrect on two counts. First, the expression 'office of profit' is neither defined in the Constitution of India nor in the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Second, Article 102(1)(a) itself explicitly empowers Parliament to declare by ordinary law (such as the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959) which offices of profit shall not disqualify their holders, requiring no constitutional amendment under Article 368.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 102(1)(a); Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006); Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959

stem: With reference to the statutory disqualification of legislators upon conviction for criminal offences under Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A sitting Member of Parliament convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more enjoys a three-month protection window against disqualification if an appeal is filed before the High Court within that period.

2. Once an appellate court grants bail and suspends the execution of the sentence of imprisonment under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the statutory disqualification of the convicted legislator ceases to operate automatically.
3. Under Section 8(3) of the Act, the total period of disqualification for a person sentenced to two years of imprisonment is limited to six years calculated from the date of such conviction.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Post-Lily Thomas (2013) and Lok Prahari (2018), a sitting legislator is disqualified instantaneously upon conviction and sentence of two or more years for a period extending throughout the imprisonment plus six years after release, which can only be halted by an express stay of the conviction itself rather than a mere suspension of sentence.

exp.why: In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 as ultra vires Articles 101(3)(a) and 190(3)(a) of the Constitution. Consequently, sitting MPs and MLAs no longer enjoy a three-month window to file an appeal; their seat falls vacant immediately on the date of conviction.

As clarified by the Supreme Court in Lok Prahari v. Election Commission of India (2018), a mere order granting bail or suspending the execution of the sentence of imprisonment under Section 430 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (formerly Section 389 of the CrPC) only halts incarceration and does not wipe out the operative conviction. Disqualification under Section 8 is stayed only when the appellate court passes a specific order staying the conviction itself.

Under Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, a person convicted of any offence (other than those in sub-sections 1 and 2) and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than two years is disqualified from the date of such conviction AND continues to be disqualified for a further period of six years since their release. Thus, the total duration is the term of imprisonment plus six years post-release.

ref: Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Section 8); Lily Thomas v. UoI (2013); Lok Prahari v. ECI (2018); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the vacation of seats and disqualification of Members of Parliament under the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Disqualification for holding an office of profit under Article 102(1)(a) : The President of India acting in accordance with the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India
2. Disqualification on the ground of defection under the Tenth Schedule : The President of India acting on the recommendation of the Presiding Officer of the House
3. Vacation of seat due to absence of sixty days without permission under Article 101(4) : The Presiding Officer acting suo motu upon the expiry of sixty sitting days
4. Vacation of seat upon resignation under Article 101(3)(b) : The Chairman or the Speaker after being satisfied that the resignation is voluntary and genuine
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Constitution distributes adjudicatory authority over parliamentary seats across four distinct mechanisms: the President bound by the Election Commission's opinion for Article 102(1) disqualifications, the Presiding Officer as a tribunal for Tenth Schedule defections, the House itself by resolution for 60-day absence, and the Presiding Officer after inquiry for resignations.

exp.why: Under Article 103 of the Constitution, any question as to whether a Member of Parliament has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in Article 102(1) (including holding an office of profit or statutory disqualifications under the RPA, 1951) is referred to the President, who shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and act according to such opinion.

Under Article 102(2) read with Paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule, any question regarding disqualification on the ground of defection is referred for the decision of the Chairman or the Speaker of such House directly, and not to the President of India.

Under Article 101(4), if for a period of sixty days a member of either House of Parliament is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the seat does not fall vacant automatically or by unilateral declaration of the Presiding Officer; rather, the House itself may declare his seat vacant by passing a resolution.

Under Article 101(3)(b), as amended by the 33rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1974, a member's seat becomes vacant when his resignation in writing is accepted by the Chairman or the Speaker, provided that the Chairman or the Speaker shall not accept the resignation if satisfied from information received or otherwise and after making such inquiry as he thinks fit that such resignation is not voluntary or genuine.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 101, 102, 103 & Tenth Schedule; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the grounds of disqualification for members of political parties under Paragraph 2(1) of the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Paragraph 2(1)(a), a legislator can be held to have voluntarily given up the membership of their political party only upon tendering a formal written resignation to the party leadership.

2. In adjudicating a petition under Paragraph 2(1)(a), the Presiding Officer is legally entitled to draw an inference of defection from the conduct of a member even outside the precincts of the House.

3. Under Paragraph 2(1)(b), a member who votes or abstains from voting in the House contrary to a party whip without prior permission escapes disqualification if the political party condones such act within fifteen days from the date of such voting or abstention.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Paragraph 2(1) of the Tenth Schedule establishes two distinct grounds of defection for party legislators: 'voluntarily giving up party membership' (which the Supreme Court interprets broadly to include anti-party conduct inside or outside the House without a formal resignation) and defying a party whip without prior permission or 15-day subsequent condonation.

exp.why: In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court authoritatively held that the words 'voluntarily gives up his membership' in Paragraph 2(1)(a) are not synonymous with 'resignation' and carry a much wider connotation. A member may be held to have voluntarily given up membership even without submitting a formal written resignation.

Reiterated in Ravi S. Naik (1994), Rajendra Singh Rana (2007), and Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary (2023), an inference that a member has voluntarily given up membership of their original political party can be legitimately drawn by the Speaker/Chairman from the member's conduct both inside and outside the Legislature (such as publicly campaigning for a rival party or petitioning the Governor to topple their own party's government).

Under Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the Tenth Schedule, a member incurs disqualification if he votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to any direction issued by his political party without obtaining prior permission, and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting or abstention.

ref: Tenth Schedule Paragraph 2(1); Ravi S. Naik v. UoI (1994); Laxmikanth Ch. 23 & 65

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes the constitutional position of an 'Independent Member' from that of a 'Nominated Member' under the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India?

opts.A: Both an independent member and a nominated member are allowed a six-month window from the date of taking their oath to join a political party without attracting disqualification.
opts.B: An independent member incurs disqualification under the Tenth Schedule the moment they vote in favour of a confidence motion moved by a ruling coalition, even without formally joining any political party.
opts.C: While an independent member is disqualified if they join any political party at any time after their election, a nominated member may join a political party within six months of taking their seat in the House without incurring disqualification.
opts.D: A nominated member who joins a political party within six months of taking their seat remains exempt from the whip of that political party for the remainder of their term in the House.

core: Paragraphs 2(2) and 2(3) of the Tenth Schedule treat independent and nominated legislators asymmetrically: an independent member is elected on a non-party mandate and is barred from joining any party at any point after election, whereas a nominated member has no electoral mandate and is granted a six-month window after taking their seat to choose a party affiliation.

exp.why: Option C is correct because under Paragraph 2(2) of the Tenth Schedule, an elected member who has been elected as such otherwise than as a candidate set up by any political party (an independent member) is disqualified if he joins any political party after such election. Conversely, under Paragraph 2(3), a nominated member of a House is disqualified only if he joins any political party after the expiry of six months from the date on which he takes his seat after complying with the oath requirements of Article 99 or Article 188. Option A is incorrect because independent members have no six-month window. Option B is incorrect because extending outside support to a government or voting on a confidence motion without formally joining a political party does not per se disqualify an independent member. Option D is incorrect because under Explanation (b) to Paragraph 2(1), once a nominated member joins a political party within six months, they are deemed to belong to that political party and are fully subject to its whip under Paragraph 2(1)(b).

ref: Tenth Schedule Paragraphs 2(1), 2(2) & 2(3); Laxmikanth Ch. 23 & 65

stem: With reference to the constitutional changes introduced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 to curb political defections, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It completely omitted Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule, thereby abolishing the defence of a one-third split in a legislature party and retaining protection for group defection only in the case of a valid merger under Paragraph 4.

2. While Article 164(1A) mandates both a fifteen per cent upper ceiling and a minimum floor of twelve Ministers for a State Council of Ministers, Article 75(1A) prescribes only the fifteen per cent upper ceiling for the Union Council of Ministers without stipulating any minimum numerical floor.

3. Under Articles 75(1B), 164(1B), and 361B, a legislator disqualified under the Tenth Schedule is barred from being appointed as a Minister and from holding any remunerative political post until the expiry of their term or until they are re-elected to the Legislature, whichever is earlier.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 closed the 'retail split' loophole by deleting Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule, capped the size of Councils of Ministers via Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A), and removed the incentive for defection by barring disqualified legislators from ministerial and remunerative political offices under Articles 75(1B), 164(1B), and 361B.

exp.why: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 omitted Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule, which previously protected a split by at least one-third of the members of a legislature party. Now, collective exemption from disqualification exists only under Paragraph 4 when a political party merges with another party and at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree to such merger.

Article 164(1A) stipulates that the total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in the Council of Ministers in a State shall not exceed 15 per cent of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly of that State, provided that the number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a State shall not be less than twelve. In contrast, Article 75(1A) caps the Union Council of Ministers (including the Prime Minister) at 15 per cent of the total strength of the House of the People without specifying any minimum number.

Articles 75(1B) and 164(1B) bar a member disqualified under the Tenth Schedule from being appointed as a Minister, and Article 361B bars them from holding any remunerative political post (defined as an office under the Central or State Government where salary or remuneration is paid out of public revenue), from the date of disqualification till the expiry of their term of office as a member or until they contest an election and are declared elected, whichever is earlier.

ref: 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003; Constitution Articles 75(1A), 75(1B), 164(1A), 164(1B), 361B & Tenth Schedule; Laxmikanth Ch. 21 & 65

stem: With reference to the exemption provided to Presiding Officers under Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule makes it constitutionally mandatory for a member elected as the Speaker of the House of the People to resign from their political party immediately upon assuming office.

2. If a Speaker who has voluntarily given up the membership of their political party upon election to the Chair rejoins that political party after ceasing to hold the office of Speaker, they do not incur disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

3. The exemption under Paragraph 5 expressly covers the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Chairman of a State Legislative Council, but does not mention the Chairman of the Council of States.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule confers an enabling exemption—not a mandatory compulsion—allowing Presiding Officers who are members of the House to sever their party ties during their tenure in the Chair and rejoin their party afterward without attracting disqualification.

exp.why: Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule does not compel a Speaker or other Presiding Officer to resign from their political party; it merely provides a protective exemption. It states that a person elected to such office shall not be disqualified under the Schedule IF he, by reason of his election to such office, voluntarily gives up the membership of his political party and does not rejoin it so long as he continues to hold such office.

Under Paragraph 5(b) of the Tenth Schedule, a Presiding Officer who has voluntarily given up the membership of the political party to which they belonged immediately before election to the Chair is protected from disqualification if they rejoin such political party after they cease to hold such office.

Paragraph 5 explicitly lists the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council of a State, and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of a State. It omits the Chairman of the Council of States because the Vice-President of India is not a member of either House of Parliament and therefore is not subject to the Tenth Schedule.

ref: Constitution of India, Tenth Schedule (Paragraph 5); Laxmikanth Ch. 23 & 65

stem: With reference to the adjudication of disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Notwithstanding the finality clause contained in Paragraph 6(1) of the Tenth Schedule, the final decision of the Speaker or Chairman on a question of disqualification on the ground of defection is subject to judicial review by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of constitutional mandate and natural justice.

Statement-II: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that the Presiding Officer adjudicating a Tenth Schedule dispute functions as a quasi-judicial Tribunal, and invalidated Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule for seeking to oust the jurisdiction of constitutional courts under Articles 136, 226, and 227 without obtaining ratification by half of the State Legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court severed and struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule for failing to comply with the federal ratification mandate of the proviso to Article 368(2), while upholding the remainder of the Tenth Schedule by characterizing the Speaker as a quasi-judicial Tribunal whose final orders are reviewable under Articles 136, 226, and 227.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Paragraph 6(1) of the Tenth Schedule states that the decision of the Chairman or the Speaker on whether a member of a House has become subject to disqualification under the Schedule shall be final. However, in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that this finality clause does not exclude the constitutional jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136 and the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227. While courts ordinarily refrain from quia timet (interlocutory) intervention prior to the Speaker making a final decision, once the final order is passed, it is amenable to judicial review on grounds of violation of constitutional mandate, mala fides, non-compliance with rules of natural justice, and perversity.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The reason the finality clause in Paragraph 6(1) and the procedural immunity of Paragraph 6(2) (which deems Tenth Schedule proceedings to be proceedings in Parliament/State Legislature under Articles 122/212) do not bar judicial review is two-fold: first, the Supreme Court held that the Speaker deciding a dispute under Paragraph 6(1) exercises quasi-judicial power as a Tribunal; second, Paragraph 7 of the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985—which explicitly barred the jurisdiction of all courts—effectively curtailed the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts under Articles 136, 226, and 227, thereby attracting the entrenched proviso to Article 368(2). Because the 52nd Amendment Bill was enacted without ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures, Paragraph 7 was struck down as unconstitutional through the doctrine of severability.

ref: Constitution of India, Tenth Schedule (Paras 6 & 7) and Art. 368(2); Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992); Laxmikanth Ch. 'Anti-Defection Law'

stem: With reference to the constitutional jurisprudence established by the Supreme Court of India regarding the operation of the Tenth Schedule, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Once a disqualification petition under the Tenth Schedule is instituted before the Speaker, any subsequent notice of intention to move a resolution for the removal of the Speaker under Article 179(c) stands constitutionally stayed until the pending disqualification petition is decided.

2. For the purposes of Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the Tenth Schedule, the Chief Whip and the Leader of the Party in the House are validly appointed by the autonomous majority resolution of the Legislature Party rather than by the organizational Political Party.

3. The existence of a bona fide intra-party leadership dispute within a political party operates as a valid constitutional defence under the Tenth Schedule for a faction of legislators voting contrary to the direction of the official party whip.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Nabam Rebia (2016) and Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023), a Speaker facing a pending removal notice under Article 179(c) is disabled from deciding disqualification petitions, and the authority to appoint the Whip and Leader in the House vests in the organizational 'political party' rather than the 'legislature party' in isolation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under the ratio of Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (5-Judge Bench, 2016), when a prior notice of intention to move a resolution for the Speaker's own removal under Article 179(c) (or Article 94(c) for the Lok Sabha Speaker) is pending, the Speaker is constitutionally disabled from adjudicating disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule until the removal motion is tested on the floor of the House (an issue subsequently referred to a 7-Judge Bench in Subhash Desai, 2023). Neither the Constitution nor Supreme Court precedent provides that the prior filing of a disqualification petition stays a removal notice against the Speaker.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (5-Judge Constitution Bench, 2023), the Supreme Court drew a fundamental constitutional distinction between the 'Political Party' (the organizational entity registered with the Election Commission) and the 'Legislature Party' (the group of MLAs or MPs inside the House). Interpreting the words 'political party to which he belongs' in Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the Tenth Schedule, the Court held that the Whip and the Leader of the Party in the House must be appointed by the organizational Political Party and not autonomously by a majority of the Legislature Party acting in isolation from the political party.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Following the deletion of Paragraph 3 (the one-third split exception) by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the Tenth Schedule no longer recognizes an internal split as a defence against defection. In Subhash Desai (2023), the Supreme Court explicitly held that participating in an intra-party leadership dispute or claiming rival factions within the party does not constitute a valid constitutional defence for violating a direction issued by the duly authorized whip of the political party unless the requirement of a two-thirds merger under Paragraph 4 is satisfied.

ref: Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023); Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016); Tenth Schedule, Para 2(1)(b)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the timeline for deciding disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Even though the text of the Tenth Schedule does not explicitly stipulate a fixed constitutional deadline within which the Presiding Officer must dispose of a defection petition, the Speaker cannot keep such disqualification petitions pending indefinitely across the tenure of the House.

Statement-II: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Hon'ble Speaker Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020), the Supreme Court held that since the Speaker functions as a Tribunal under the Tenth Schedule, the Speaker is constitutionally obligated to decide disqualification petitions within a reasonable period, which ordinarily should not exceed three months barring exceptional circumstances.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the text of the Tenth Schedule does not prescribe a fixed constitutional deadline for the Speaker to adjudicate defection petitions, the Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) operationalized judicial accountability by laying down an outer limit of three months as a 'reasonable period' barring exceptional circumstances.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The constitutional text of the Tenth Schedule (inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985) does not contain any explicit provision fixing a specific number of days or months within which the Speaker or Chairman must decide a disqualification petition under Paragraph 6. However, judicial precedent has established that the absence of an explicit textual deadline does not confer a licence on the Speaker to defeat the constitutional objective of the Tenth Schedule through pocket inaction until the expiry of the House's term.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Hon'ble Speaker Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020), the Supreme Court held that because the Speaker acts as a quasi-judicial Tribunal under the Tenth Schedule whose inaction undermines the constitutional mandate against defection, the Speaker must decide disqualification petitions within a 'reasonable period'. Considering that the tenure of a House is five years and a defecting member cannot be allowed to continue indefinitely in the House or as a Minister, the Court laid down that what is reasonable depends on the facts of each case, but barring exceptional circumstances for which there is good reason, this period must not exceed three months from the date on which the petition is filed.

ref: Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Hon'ble Speaker Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020); Tenth Schedule, Para 6

stem: With reference to the constitutional interplay between the resignation of a legislator and disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The acceptance of a voluntary and genuine resignation of a legislator by the Speaker under Article 190(3)(b) or Article 101(3)(b) does not extinguish a prior cause of action for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule arising from acts committed before the tendering of the resignation.

2. While passing an order of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, the Speaker possesses the concurrent authority to bar the disqualified legislator from contesting any by-election until the expiry of the remaining term of the existing House.

3. Under Article 164(1B) of the Constitution, a Member of a State Legislative Assembly who is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule remains eligible to be re-appointed as a Minister for up to six consecutive months without being re-elected to the Legislature.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil v. Speaker, Karnataka Legislative Assembly (2019), the Supreme Court held that a subsequent resignation does not wipe out prior acts of defection under the Tenth Schedule, and that the Speaker lacks the power to bar a disqualified legislator from contesting by-elections, though Article 164(1B)/75(1B) bars them from holding ministerial office until re-elected.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil v. Speaker, Karnataka Legislative Assembly (2019), the Supreme Court held that resignation and disqualification are distinct constitutional mechanisms. Even if a member tenders a voluntary and genuine resignation under Article 190(3)(b) (or Article 101(3)(b) for Parliament) which is accepted by the Speaker, such resignation operates only prospectively and does not wipe out or render infructuous a pending disqualification petition under the Tenth Schedule based on taint or disqualifying acts committed prior to the resignation.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil (2019), the Supreme Court struck down that portion of the Karnataka Speaker's order which had disqualified 17 MLAs until the end of the term of the 15th Legislative Assembly and barred them from contesting by-elections. The Court clarified that the Speaker's jurisdiction under Paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule is strictly confined to deciding whether a member has incurred disqualification from current membership; the Speaker has no constitutional or statutory power to specify the duration of disqualification or bar a disqualified member from contesting subsequent by-elections.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 164(1B) (and Article 75(1B) for the Union), inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, a legislator who is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule is also disqualified to be appointed as a Minister from the date of disqualification until the date on which the term of their office as such member would expire or until they contest an election to a Legislative House and are declared elected, whichever is earlier. Thus, the general six-month grace period under Article 164(4) for non-members cannot be invoked by a legislator disqualified under the Tenth Schedule to become a Minister without first winning re-election.

ref: Constitution of India, Arts. 75(1B), 101(3)(b), 164(1B) & 190(3)(b); Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil v. Speaker, Karnataka Legislative Assembly (2019)

stem: With reference to parliamentary privileges under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) of the Constitution of India and the law relating to legislative bribery, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Member of Parliament or a State Legislature who accepts illegal gratification to vote in a particular manner in the House enjoys constitutional immunity from criminal prosecution, provided the legislator actually casts the vote in accordance with the agreement.
2. The offence of bribery committed by a legislator is legally consummated only when the legislator performs the agreed speech or vote on the floor of the House or in a Parliamentary Committee.

3. While parliamentary privilege does not shield a legislator from bribery charges relating to floor debates, a Member of a State Legislative Assembly retains immunity under Article 194(2) in respect of votes cast in biennial elections to the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (7-Judge Constitution Bench, 2024), the Supreme Court overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) and held that legislators enjoy zero immunity under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) from criminal prosecution for bribery, as the offence of bribery is complete the moment illegal gratification is accepted regardless of subsequent legislative performance.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. This statement reflects the overruled 1998 majority ruling in P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (CBI/SPE), which had created an anomalous distinction whereby a bribe-taking MP who actually voted as agreed enjoyed immunity under Article 105(2), whereas one who took a bribe but abstained did not. In Sita Soren v. Union of India (7-Judge Constitution Bench, 2024), the Supreme Court unanimously overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao and held that MPs and MLAs do not enjoy any immunity under Articles 105(2) or 194(2) from criminal prosecution for taking a bribe to speak or vote in the Legislature or its committees, as bribery fails the two-fold test of being tethered to the collective functioning of the House and necessary for the fearless discharge of legislative duties.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the 7-Judge Bench explicitly held that under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the offence of bribery is agnostic to the performance of the agreed action and is crystallized and complete the very moment the legislator accepts or obtains the illegal gratification. Whether the legislator subsequently votes or speaks in the agreed direction, votes to the contrary, or abstains on the floor of the House has no bearing on criminal culpability.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court clarified that the denial of immunity for bribery under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) applies uniformly across both speeches/votes on the floor of the House and votes cast by legislators in elections to the Rajya Sabha (or Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections). Neither sphere of legislative activity affords any shield against criminal prosecution for corruption.

ref: Constitution of India, Arts. 105(2) & 194(2); Sita Soren v. Union of India (7-Judge Bench, 2024)

stem: Consider the following pairs of Parliamentary Functionaries in India and their primary institutional/legal basis:
items: 1. Leader of the House : Defined in the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of the respective House, but not mentioned in the Constitution of India.
2. Leader of the Opposition : Accorded statutory recognition and entitlements under a Parliamentary Act of 1977, without being mentioned in the original text of the Constitution of India.
3. Office of the Whip : Formally established and defined under the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of both Houses of Parliament, though omitted from the text of the Constitution of India.
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Among the three key parliamentary functionaries, the 'Leader of the House' derives formal definition from the Rules of Procedure of the Houses, the 'Leader of the Opposition' derives statutory status from the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977, whereas the 'Office of the Whip' is based on parliamentary convention and is mentioned neither in the Constitution nor in the Rules of the House.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The office of the 'Leader of the House' is not mentioned in the Constitution of India. Instead, it is explicitly defined under the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha (and Rajya Sabha), where it means the Prime Minister, if he is a member of the House, or a Minister who is a member of the House and is nominated by the Prime Minister to function as the Leader of the House.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. The office of the 'Leader of the Opposition' is not mentioned in the original text of the Constitution of India (though later statutory enactments and constitutional amendments on selection committees reference it). It was accorded formal statutory recognition in 1977 under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977, which defines the Leader of the Opposition as that member of the Council of States or the House of the People who is, for the time being, the Leader in that House of the party in opposition to the Government having the greatest numerical strength and recognized as such by the Chairman or the Speaker.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The office of the 'Whip' is mentioned neither in the Constitution of India nor in the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of the Houses. It is rooted in the conventions of parliamentary government (though statutory recognition of facilities is extended to recognized party whips under the Leaders and Chief Whips of Recognised Parties and Groups in Parliament (Facilities) Act, 1998, and Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the Tenth Schedule enforces compliance with directions issued by a political party without explicitly using the term 'Whip').

ref: Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha; Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977; Laxmikanth Ch. 'Parliament'

stem: With reference to the stages of passage of an Ordinary Bill in the Parliament of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill and the moving of substantive amendments by members take place during the Third Reading of the Bill.
2. The introduction of the Bill in the House and its publication in the Official Gazette together constitute the First Reading of the Bill.
3. During the Committee Stage of the Second Reading, a Select Committee can examine the Bill thoroughly and suggest amendments to its clauses without altering the underlying principles of the Bill.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: An Ordinary Bill passes through three readings in each House: the First Reading is formal introduction and Gazette publication; the Second Reading (comprising the Stage of General Discussion, Committee Stage, and Consideration Stage) is where detailed scrutiny and clause-by-clause amendments occur; and the Third Reading is restricted to voting on the Bill as a whole without substantive amendments.

exp.why: Clause-by-clause consideration, discussion, and voting on substantive amendments take place during the Consideration Stage of the Second Reading, not the Third Reading. During the Third Reading, debate is confined strictly to the acceptance or rejection of the Bill as a whole, and only formal, verbal, or consequential amendments are permitted.

Upon grant of leave by the House, the member or Minister introduces the Bill by reading its title and objectives, followed by its publication in the Gazette of India. Together, these steps constitute the First Reading. If a Bill is published in the Gazette with the prior permission of the presiding officer before introduction, leave of the House to introduce it is not even required.

Because the House accepts the underlying principles of the Bill when referring it to a Select or Joint Committee during the Second Reading, the Committee can scrutinize the text clause-by-clause, take expert testimony, and propose amendments, provided such amendments do not subvert the fundamental principles of the Bill.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 23 (Parliament)

stem: With reference to the distinction between Public Bills (Government Bills) and Private Members' Bills in the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Bill introduced by a Member of Parliament belonging to the ruling party who is not a Minister is classified as a Private Member's Bill.
2. While the introduction of a Government Bill in the House requires seven days' notice, the introduction of a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice.
3. Unlike the rejection of a Government Bill, the rejection of a Private Member's Bill in the Lok Sabha has no implication on the parliamentary confidence in the Council of Ministers.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The parliamentary classification of a Bill as a Public (Government) Bill or a Private Member's Bill depends solely on whether the member introducing it holds ministerial office, rather than on the member's political party affiliation.

exp.why: Any Member of Parliament who is not a Minister (whether from the opposition benches or from the ruling party/coalition) is defined as a Private Member. Consequently, a Bill introduced by a non-Minister MP of the ruling party is strictly a Private Member's Bill.

Under the Rules of Procedure of the Houses of Parliament, a Government Bill requires a minimum of 7 days' notice for introduction and is drafted by the concerned department in consultation with the Law Ministry, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice and is drafted under the responsibility of the member concerned.

Because a Government Bill reflects the official policy of the executive, its defeat in the Lok Sabha may signify a loss of parliamentary majority and require the resignation of the Council of Ministers. The defeat or withdrawal of a Private Member's Bill carries no consequence for the survival of the government.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 23 (Parliament)

stem: With reference to the constitutional definition of a Money Bill under Article 110 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Bill shall not be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences.

2. A Bill that deals exclusively with the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India, or the payment of moneys into or withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund, qualifies as a Money Bill.
3. A Bill that exclusively provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by a local authority or body for local purposes is deemed to be a Money Bill.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 110(1) enumerates the specific Union fiscal matters that constitute a Money Bill when a Bill deals 'only' with them, Article 110(2) carves out three explicit exclusions—pecuniary fines, licence/service fees, and local taxes imposed by local bodies for local purposes.

exp.why: Under Article 110(2) of the Constitution, a Bill is explicitly excluded from being deemed a Money Bill merely because it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences or fees for services rendered.

Under Article 110(1)(c), a Bill containing only provisions dealing with the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, or the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund, is a Money Bill.

Article 110(2) explicitly stipulates that a Bill shall NOT be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by any local authority or body for local purposes. Only Union taxation matters under Article 110(1)(a) qualify.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 110(1) and Article 110(2)

stem: With reference to the special constitutional procedure regarding Money Bills under Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The endorsement of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifying that a Bill is a Money Bill is constitutionally required both when it is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha and when it is presented to the President for assent.

2. If the Lok Sabha rejects all the recommendations made by the Rajya Sabha to a Money Bill, the Bill is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was originally passed by the Lok Sabha.

3. If the Lok Sabha accepts some of the amendments recommended by the Rajya Sabha, the modified Money Bill must be transmitted a second time to the Rajya Sabha for formal concurrence before being presented to the President.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 109, the Rajya Sabha exercises only a 14-day advisory role over Money Bills; once the Rajya Sabha returns the Bill with recommendations, the Lok Sabha's decision to accept or reject any of those recommendations immediately finalizes the passage of the Bill by both Houses without any second transmission.

exp.why: Article 110(4) expressly mandates that there shall be endorsed on every Money Bill when it is transmitted to the Council of States under Article 109, and when it is presented to the President for assent under Article 111, the certificate of the Speaker of the House of the People signed by him that it is a Money Bill.

Under Article 109(4), if the Lok Sabha does not accept any of the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the Lok Sabha without any of the amendments recommended by the Rajya Sabha.

Under Article 109(3), if the Lok Sabha accepts any of the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha, the Money Bill is immediately deemed to have been passed by both Houses with the amendments recommended by the Rajya Sabha and accepted by the Lok Sabha. No second transmission to the Rajya Sabha is required or provided for in the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 109 and 110(4)

stem: With reference to the certification of a Bill as a Money Bill by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the scope of its judicial review, consider the following statements:
items: 1. By virtue of Article 110(3) read with Article 122(1) of the Constitution, the Speaker's certification of a Bill as a Money Bill enjoys absolute immunity from judicial review even on grounds of substantive constitutional illegality.

2. The presence of the word 'only' in Article 110(1) implies that a Bill which bundles substantive non-fiscal legislative frameworks with fiscal provisions cannot be validly certified as a Money Bill unless those provisions are merely incidental to the matters specified in clauses (a) to (f) of Article 110(1).

3. Article 122(1) protects parliamentary proceedings only against challenges based on 'irregularity of procedure' and does not bar judicial scrutiny of a substantive violation of mandatory constitutional limits.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 110(3) accords textual finality to the Speaker's certification within the parliamentary arena, the Supreme Court has held in K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar-5J) and Roger Mathew that Article 122(1) shields only 'irregularity of procedure' and cannot immunize a substantive constitutional illegality that bypasses the Rajya Sabha in violation of Article 110(1).

exp.why: In K.S. Puttaswamy (5-Judge Bench, 2018) and Roger Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (5-Judge Bench, 2019), the Supreme Court held that although Article 110(3) states that the Speaker's decision shall be final, such finality operates internally between the two Houses and does not exclude the jurisdiction of Constitutional Courts if the certification suffers from gross constitutional illegality.

Article 110(1) states that a Bill is deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains 'only' provisions dealing with all or any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f), or any matter incidental to any of those specified matters under sub-clause (g). If the primary purpose of a Bill is non-fiscal (such as restructuring judicial tribunals, as struck down in Roger Mathew), incidental appropriation from the Consolidated Fund does not make the entire Bill a Money Bill.

Consistent with Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker (2007) and Roger Mathew (2019), Article 122(1) prohibits courts from inquiring into parliamentary proceedings strictly on the ground of 'any alleged irregularity of procedure', but it does not shield proceedings that are substantively unconstitutional or contrary to mandatory constitutional prohibitions.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 110(1), 110(3) & 122(1); Roger Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2019)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding a Financial Bill (Category-I) under Article 117(1) of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Like a Money Bill, a Financial Bill under Article 117(1) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the recommendation of the President.

Statement-II: Unlike a Money Bill, a Financial Bill under Article 117(1) can be either rejected or amended by the Rajya Sabha, and a deadlock between the two Houses over such a Bill can be resolved through a joint sitting under Article 108.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: A Financial Bill under Article 117(1) is a hybrid legislative instrument: because it contains Article 110(1)(a)-(f) fiscal clauses alongside general legislative matters, it requires Presidential recommendation and Lok Sabha introduction like a Money Bill, but once introduced, it is governed by the procedure of an Ordinary Bill during passage.

exp.why: Under Article 117(1), a Bill making provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f) of Article 110(1)—along with other matters of general legislation—shall not be introduced or moved except on the recommendation of the President, and a Bill making such provision shall not be introduced in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).

Once introduced in the Lok Sabha, a Financial Bill under Article 117(1) is governed by the same legislative procedure as an Ordinary Bill. Thus, the Rajya Sabha has full power to amend or reject it (subject to the proviso that no amendment other than for the reduction or abolition of a tax can be moved without the President's recommendation), and the President can summon a joint sitting under Article 108 in case of a deadlock. However, this passage mechanism does not explain why its introduction is restricted to the Lok Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 108 and 117(1); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Financial Bills under the Constitution of India:
