items: Statement-I: A Financial Bill (Category-II) under Article 117(3) of the Constitution, which involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India but does not include any of the matters specified in Article 110, requires the prior recommendation of the President for its introduction in either House of Parliament.

Statement-II: Under Article 117(3) of the Constitution, a Bill which, if enacted and brought into operation, would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be passed by either House of Parliament unless the President has recommended to that House the consideration of the Bill.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 117 draws a sharp procedural distinction between Financial Bills (Category-I) under clause (1) and Financial Bills (Category-II) under clause (3). While a Category-I Bill requires the President's recommendation at the threshold stage of introduction in the Lok Sabha, a Category-II Bill can be introduced in either House as an Ordinary Bill without prior recommendation, requiring the President's recommendation only at the stage of consideration and passing by either House.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Unlike a Money Bill (Article 110) and a Financial Bill Category-I (Article 117(1)), a Financial Bill Category-II under Article 117(3) is governed by the same legislative procedure as an Ordinary Bill at the introduction stage. It can be introduced in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, and the prior recommendation of the President is NOT required for its introduction.

Statement-II is correct. Article 117(3) explicitly mandates that a Bill which, if enacted and brought into operation, would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be passed by either House of Parliament unless the President has recommended to that House the consideration of the Bill.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 117(1) and Article 117(3); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the summoning of a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament under Article 108 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The provision of a joint sitting is applicable to Ordinary Bills and Financial Bills, but not to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.

2. If more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of a Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it, the President may notify his intention to summon both Houses to meet in a joint sitting.

3. In reckoning the period of six months for a legislative deadlock under Article 108(2), the entire duration from the date of reception of the Bill by the second House is counted continuously, without excluding periods when that House is prorogued.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 108 provides a mechanism to resolve inter-House legislative deadlocks over Ordinary and Financial Bills when the receiving House rejects the Bill, disagrees on amendments, or lets more than six months elapse without passing it. To ensure the receiving House gets six genuine months of functional time, Article 108(2) excludes any period during which that House is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 108(1) expressly excludes Money Bills (which are governed by Article 109, giving overriding powers to the Lok Sabha). Similarly, under Article 368(2), a Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by each House separately by a special majority, leaving no scope for a joint sitting.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 108(1)(c), one of the three situations constituting a deadlock is when more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of the Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 108(2), in reckoning any such period of six months, no account shall be taken of any period during which the House to which the Bill was sent is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 108(1) & 108(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the procedure and rules governing a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the absence of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides over a joint sitting, as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of either House of Parliament.

2. Where a Bill has been passed by the other House with amendments and returned, no new amendments can be proposed to the Bill at a joint sitting except those made necessary by the delay in its passage and those relevant to the matters on which the Houses have not agreed.
3. The quorum to constitute a joint sitting is one-tenth of the total strength of the Lok Sabha alone, and the sitting is governed by the Rules of Procedure of the House in which the Bill originated.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Article 118(4) and the Houses of Parliament (Joint Sittings and Communications) Rules, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting, followed in hierarchy by the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (excluding the Vice-President). Article 108(4) strictly limits the scope of permissible amendments at a joint sitting to prevent the reopening of settled clauses.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 118(4) and the Joint Sitting Rules, the Speaker presides over a joint sitting, and in his absence, the Deputy Speaker. If both are absent, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President of India) never presides over a joint sitting because he is not a member of either House of Parliament.

Statement 2 is correct. Under the proviso to Article 108(4), if the Bill has been passed by the other House with amendments and returned to the originating House, no amendment shall be proposed to the Bill at the joint sitting other than amendments made necessary by the delay in the passage of the Bill and amendments relevant to the matters with respect to which the Houses have not agreed. The decision of the presiding officer on the admissibility of such amendments is final.

Statement 3 is incorrect on both counts. First, the quorum to constitute a joint sitting is one-tenth of the total number of members of BOTH the Houses (not the Lok Sabha alone). Second, a joint sitting is always governed by the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha (with such modifications as the Speaker may make), irrespective of whether the Bill originated in the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 108(4) and 118(4); Houses of Parliament (Joint Sittings and Communications) Rules

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the effect of the dissolution of the Lok Sabha on pending legislative business:
items: Statement-I: A joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament may be held and a Bill passed therein notwithstanding that a dissolution of the Lok Sabha has intervened since the President notified his intention to summon the Houses to meet in a joint sitting.
Statement-II: Under Article 107(4) of the Constitution of India, a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha shall not lapse on a dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Article 107(4) saves Bills that originated in and remain pending in the Rajya Sabha without ever having been passed by the Lok Sabha, a deadlock requiring a joint sitting arises only after one House has already passed the Bill and transmitted it to the other. Such deadlocked Bills are saved from lapsing upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha not by Article 107(4), but by the independent overriding exception in Article 108(5) if the President notified the joint sitting prior to dissolution.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 108(5) specifically provides that a joint sitting may be held and a Bill passed thereat, notwithstanding that a dissolution of the House of the People has intervened since the President notified his intention to summon the Houses to meet therein.

Statement-II is correct as an independent constitutional rule under Article 107(4), which states that a Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People. However, Statement-II does NOT explain Statement-I: a Bill covered by Article 107(4) has not even been passed by one House and transmitted to the other to create an inter-House deadlock. By contrast, a deadlocked Bill pending in either House after passage by the other would ordinarily lapse under Article 107(5), and is saved in Statement-I solely by the non-obstante exception in Article 108(5).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 107(4), Article 107(5) and Article 108(5)

stem: With reference to the effect of the dissolution of the Lok Sabha on legislative business in Parliament under Article 107 of the Constitution of India, consider the following categories of Bills:
items: 1. A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha, in respect of which no joint sitting has been notified.
2. A Bill passed by both Houses of Parliament and pending the assent of the President.
3. A Bill passed by both Houses of Parliament but returned by the President for reconsideration of the Houses under the proviso to Article 111.
4. A Bill originated in and passed by the Rajya Sabha, which is transmitted to and pending in the Lok Sabha.
prompt: Which of the categories of Bills given above do not lapse on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
core: Under Article 107(5), any Bill that is pending in the Lok Sabha, or that has been passed by the Lok Sabha and is pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha (subject to Article 108). Once a Bill has been passed by both Houses and presented to the President under Article 111, it is no longer pending in Parliament and therefore neither lapses while awaiting assent nor lapses if returned by the President for reconsideration.

exp.why: Category 1 lapses. Under Article 107(5), a Bill which is pending in the Council of States after having been passed by the House of the People shall, subject to the provisions of Article 108, lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.

Category 2 does not lapse. Once a Bill is passed by both Houses and presented to the President for assent under Article 111, its parliamentary pendency has ended and the subsequent dissolution of the Lok Sabha does not affect the Bill.

Category 3 does not lapse. If a Bill passed by both Houses is returned by the President for reconsideration under the proviso to Article 111, it does not lapse upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha and can be reconsidered and passed by the newly constituted Lok Sabha (affirmed by the Supreme Court in Purushothaman Nambudiri v. State of Kerala).

Category 4 lapses. Under Article 107(5), any Bill which is pending in the Lok Sabha at the time of its dissolution lapses, regardless of whether it originated in the Lok Sabha or was transmitted to it after being passed by the Rajya Sabha.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 107(4), 107(5) and 111; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the termination of sittings and sessions of Parliament and their impact on parliamentary business, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 107(3) of the Constitution of India, a Bill pending in Parliament lapses upon the prorogation of the Houses and must be reintroduced in the subsequent session.
2. Upon the prorogation of a House of Parliament, all pending notices, other than those for introducing Bills, lapse and fresh notice must be given for the next session.
3. An adjournment sine die terminates both a sitting and a session of the House, and the power to declare it vests concurrently in the Presiding Officer of the House and the President of India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the British parliamentary convention where prorogation terminates all pending legislative business, Article 107(3) of the Indian Constitution explicitly insulates pending Bills from lapsing on prorogation. However, under Parliamentary Rules of Procedure, pending notices (except notices for introducing Bills) lapse upon prorogation and require fresh notice in the next session.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Article 107(3) of the Constitution of India explicitly stipulates that a Bill pending in Parliament shall NOT lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses. This is a deliberate departure from British parliamentary practice, where prorogation quashes all pending Bills.

Statement 2 is correct. While prorogation does not affect pending Bills or any business pending before a Parliamentary Committee, all pending notices (other than those for introducing Bills) lapse on prorogation and fresh notice must be given for the next session.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Adjournment sine die (adjournment without naming a day for reassembly) terminates only a sitting of the House, not a session. Furthermore, the power to adjourn or adjourn sine die lies exclusively with the Presiding Officer of the House, whereas the power to prorogue (terminate a session) lies exclusively with the President of India under Article 85(2)(a).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 85(2) and 107(3); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the assent to Bills under the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Under the Constitution of India, the President can return an Ordinary Bill to the Houses of Parliament for reconsideration once, but does not possess this suspensive veto power in respect of a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

Statement-II: Under the proviso to Article 111, if the President returns an Ordinary Bill to Parliament for reconsideration, the Houses can override the President's return only by passing the Bill again with a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the proviso to Article 111, the President may return any Bill that is not a Money Bill to the Houses for reconsideration, while the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 made Presidential assent obligatory for Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368(2). Unlike the qualified veto of the American President, the Indian President's suspensive veto is overridden if Parliament re-passes the Bill by an ordinary majority.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The proviso to Article 111 explicitly excludes a Money Bill from the President's power to return a Bill to the Houses for reconsideration. Further, under Article 368(2) as amended by the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, when a Constitutional Amendment Bill is presented to the President, the President 'shall give his assent to the Bill' and therefore cannot withhold assent or return it for reconsideration.

Statement-II is incorrect. The Indian Constitution confers a suspensive veto, not a qualified veto, on the President under the proviso to Article 111. If the Bill is passed again by the Houses with or without amendment by an ordinary majority (majority of members present and voting) and presented to the President for assent, the President shall not withhold assent therefrom. No special majority is required to override the return.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 111 and 368(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on President & Parliament

stem: With reference to the legislative procedure for passing an Ordinary Bill in a bicameral State Legislature under Articles 196 and 197 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. If an Ordinary Bill originates in the State Legislative Council, is passed by it, and is subsequently rejected by the State Legislative Assembly, the Governor is empowered to summon a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve the deadlock.

2. Where an Ordinary Bill originating in the State Legislative Council is rejected by the State Legislative Assembly, the Council may pass the Bill a second time after a lapse of three months to transmit it for the Governor's assent.

3. In respect of an Ordinary Bill originating in and passed by the State Legislative Assembly, the State Legislative Council can delay its passage for a maximum combined period of four months across two considerations.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Unlike the Rajya Sabha at the Union level, a State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) is strictly a dilatory chamber without coordinate legislative authority over Ordinary Bills, and the Constitution makes no provision for a joint sitting of a State Legislature. If an Ordinary Bill originates in the Council and is rejected by the Assembly, the Bill ends and dies immediately.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Unlike Article 108 for Parliament, the Constitution of India does not provide for the mechanism of a joint sitting of both Houses of a State Legislature to resolve a deadlock over an Ordinary Bill. The will of the directly elected Legislative Assembly ultimately prevails.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The overriding mechanism under Article 197 applies exclusively to an Ordinary Bill originating in the Legislative Assembly and transmitted to the Legislative Council. When an Ordinary Bill originates in the Legislative Council, is passed by it, and is rejected by the Legislative Assembly, the Bill comes to an end immediately and becomes dead.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 197(1) and (2), when an Ordinary Bill originating in the Legislative Assembly is transmitted to the Legislative Council, the Council can hold the Bill for a maximum of three months in the first instance and one month when passed again by the Assembly in the second instance, amounting to a maximum dilatory power of four months in total.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 196 and 197; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on State Legislature

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Governor of a State under Article 200 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: If the Governor of a State decides to withhold assent to a non-Money Bill passed by the State Legislature, the Governor cannot exercise an indefinite pocket veto to keep the Bill pending, nor can the Governor reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President after the State Legislature has reconsidered and re-passed it.

Statement-II: The first proviso to Article 200 is constitutionally coupled with the option of withholding assent, mandating that a Governor who withholds assent to a non-Money Bill must return the Bill to the State Legislature 'as soon as possible' with a message for reconsideration and shall not withhold assent if the House passes the Bill again.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023), the Supreme Court held that the first proviso to Article 200 qualifies the substantive power to withhold assent rather than creating an independent fourth option. Consequently, an unelected Governor cannot thwart the law-making power of elected State Legislatures by sitting indefinitely on Bills, and if the Governor WITHHOLDS assent, the Governor MUST return the non-Money Bill 'as soon as possible' to the Legislature and must grant assent once it is re-passed.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. As laid down by the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab, a Governor cannot exercise an indefinite pocket veto to stall Bills passed by the State Legislature. Furthermore, once the Governor exercises the option to return a Bill to the Legislature for reconsideration and the Legislature re-passes the Bill without material alteration, the Governor cannot then reserve that re-passed Bill for the consideration of the President.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The Supreme Court ruled that the phrase 'Provided that the Governor may, as soon as possible after the presentation to him of the Bill for assent, return the Bill if it is not a Money Bill' in the first proviso to Article 200 is inextricably attached to the option of withholding assent. In a parliamentary democracy, the word 'may' in the first proviso casts a constitutional duty to return the Bill 'as soon as possible' whenever assent is withheld, leaving no constitutional space for an indefinite pocket veto or subsequent reservation after re-passage.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 200; Supreme Court Judgment in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023/2024 baseline)

stem: With reference to the rules governing the Question Hour in the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Rules of Procedure of the Houses of Parliament, a parliamentary question can be addressed only to a Minister of the Union Government and never to a Private Member.
2. Unlike Starred Questions, Short Notice Questions are answered through written replies laid on the Table of the House and therefore do not permit any supplementary questions.

3. If the list of Starred Questions is exhausted before the end of the Question Hour, the presiding officer takes up Unstarred Questions for oral answers and supplementary questions during the remaining time.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: During Question Hour, questions are categorized into Starred (oral answer, supplementaries permitted), Unstarred (written answer laid on the Table, no supplementaries), and Short Notice Questions (urgent matters asked with less than 10 days' notice, answered orally with supplementaries permitted). Furthermore, questions can also be addressed to a Private Member if the subject matter relates to a Bill, resolution, or other business of the House for which that member is responsible.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. While questions are normally addressed to a Minister, the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business (such as Rule 40 of the Lok Sabha Rules) explicitly allow a question to be addressed to a Private Member provided the subject matter of the question relates to some Bill, resolution, or other matter connected with the business of the House for which that member is responsible.

Statement 2 is incorrect. A Short Notice Question relates to a matter of urgent public importance and is asked by giving a notice of less than ten days. It is answered orally on the floor of the House (typically immediately after the Question Hour or as the first item where there is no Question Hour), and supplementary questions are permitted thereon.

Statement 3 is incorrect. An Unstarred Question always requires a written answer, which is deemed to have been laid on the Table of the House at the end of Question Hour. It is never called for an oral answer on the floor of the House, nor can any supplementary question be asked on it.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, Rules 32–54; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Parliament

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes between the 'Question Hour' and the 'Zero Hour' in the Indian parliamentary system?

opts.A: While Question Hour is an informal Indian parliamentary innovation not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure, Zero Hour is explicitly regulated by the Rules of Procedure of both Houses.
opts.B: Zero Hour occupies the first hour of every parliamentary sitting, whereas Question Hour commences immediately after Zero Hour and continues until the regular legislative agenda is taken up.
opts.C: Unlike Question Hour, which is formally governed by the Rules of Procedure and takes place in the first hour of a sitting, Zero Hour is an informal Indian innovation that begins immediately after Question Hour and lasts until the agenda of the day is taken up.
opts.D: Both Question Hour and Zero Hour are explicitly codified under Article 118 of the Constitution of India and require a mandatory minimum notice period of ten days before any matter can be raised.

core: Question Hour occupies the first hour of every parliamentary sitting and is formally regulated by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in both Houses. By contrast, Zero Hour is an informal Indian parliamentary innovation emerging since 1962—not formally codified as 'Zero Hour' in the Rules of Procedure—representing the time gap between the end of Question Hour and the commencement of the regular agenda of the House.

exp.why: Option C is correct. The first hour of every parliamentary sitting is slotted for the Question Hour, which is formally mentioned and regulated in the Rules of Procedure of both Houses of Parliament. Zero Hour, on the other hand, is an Indian parliamentary innovation in practice since 1962 that allows members to raise matters of urgent public importance without prior ten-day notice. It starts immediately after the Question Hour and lasts until the regular business on the agenda of the day (Order Paper) is taken up. Options A and B reverse the procedural status and chronological sequence of the two devices, while Option D is incorrect because neither is directly codified inside the text of Article 118 nor does Zero Hour require a ten-day prior notice.

ref: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Parliament (Devices of Parliamentary Proceedings)

stem: With reference to the parliamentary device of 'Short Duration Discussion' (also known as a Two-Hour Discussion), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It must be initiated upon a formal substantive motion moved before the House and concludes with a mandatory division or voice vote to record the decision of the House.
opts.B: It can be raised only in the Lok Sabha because it involves an element of parliamentary censure against the Council of Ministers.
opts.C: It enables members to raise a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for a duration not exceeding two hours, without any formal motion before the House or any voting after the discussion.
opts.D: It is restricted exclusively to seeking factual elucidation on answers previously given to Starred or Unstarred Questions during the preceding three sittings of the House.

core: Under Rule 193 of the Lok Sabha Rules (and Rule 176 of the Rajya Sabha Rules), a Short Duration Discussion allows members to raise a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for up to two hours. Because its purpose is deliberative rather than decisional, there is neither a formal motion before the House nor any voting at the conclusion of the discussion.

exp.why: Option C is correct. Under a Short Duration Discussion (instituted in 1953 to give members an opportunity to discuss urgent public matters without disrupting the House via an Adjournment Motion), any member desirous of raising a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance may give notice in writing supported by at least two other members. The time allotted does not exceed two hours, and importantly, there is no formal motion before the House nor any voting; the member who gives notice makes a short statement, other permitted members speak, and the Minister replies. Option A is incorrect because there is no formal motion or vote. Option B is incorrect because this device exists in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha and carries no element of censure. Option D is incorrect because seeking elucidation on a matter of fact arising out of a recent Starred, Unstarred, or Short Notice Question is the specific scope of a 'Half-an-Hour Discussion', not a Short Duration Discussion.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, Rule 193; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Parliament

stem: Consider the following statements regarding parliamentary devices in India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike an Adjournment Motion, which can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, a Calling Attention Motion can be introduced in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha to draw a Minister's attention to a matter of urgent public importance.

Statement-II: While an Adjournment Motion involves an element of censure against the Council of Ministers—which is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha—a Calling Attention Motion seeks an authoritative ministerial statement without involving any debate-ending vote or censure.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: An Adjournment Motion is restricted exclusively to the Lok Sabha because it interrupts normal business and carries an element of censure against the Government, whereas a Calling Attention Motion is an Indian procedural innovation available in both Houses because it seeks an authoritative statement from a Minister without involving a vote of censure.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. An Adjournment Motion is an extraordinary device that sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance and can be moved only in the Lok Sabha. In contrast, a Calling Attention Motion (introduced in India in 1954 and explicitly provided for in the Rules of Procedure of both Houses) is available to both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Under Article 75(3) of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha. Because the passage of an Adjournment Motion involves an element of censure against the Government, the Rajya Sabha is not permitted to use this device. Conversely, a Calling Attention Motion merely requires the concerned Minister to make an authoritative statement on an urgent matter and permits members to seek brief clarifications without any motion being put to a vote of censure.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (Rules 56 & 197); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the admissibility and procedural rules governing an 'Adjournment Motion' in the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It requires the support of not less than 50 members for leave to be granted, and the discussion on the motion cannot last for less than two hours and thirty minutes.
2. It must be restricted to a single specific matter of recent occurrence that involves the administrative responsibility of the Government of India.
3. It can be moved to raise a question of breach of parliamentary privilege or a matter under adjudication by a court of law if the Speaker certifies it to be of urgent public importance.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because an Adjournment Motion disrupts the normal scheduled business of the Lok Sabha and carries an element of censure, the Rules of Procedure impose strict admissibility conditions, requiring the support of 50 members and barring matters of privilege, sub-judice issues, or multi-issue grievances.

exp.why: Because an Adjournment Motion interrupts the regular business of the House, Rule 60 of the Lok Sabha Rules mandates that at least 50 members must rise in their places in support of leave being granted. Once admitted, the discussion on the motion must last for at least 2 hours and 30 minutes.

Under Rule 58 of the Lok Sabha Rules, an Adjournment Motion must be restricted to a single specific matter of recent occurrence involving the direct responsibility of the Union Government; it cannot be framed in general terms or cover more than one distinct issue.

Rule 58 strictly prohibits an Adjournment Motion from raising a question of privilege, reviving discussion on a matter already discussed in the same session, dealing with any matter that is sub-judice (under adjudication by a court of law), or raising a question that can be brought on a distinct motion. The Speaker does not bypass these prohibitions.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (Rules 56–63); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to a 'No-Confidence Motion' in the Indian parliamentary system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Article 75 of the Constitution of India explicitly lays down the procedure for moving a 'No-Confidence Motion' in the Lok Sabha.
2. A No-Confidence Motion need not set out the specific grounds or reasons on which it is based.
3. It can be moved either against an individual Union Minister for specific policy failures or against the entire Council of Ministers.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 75(3) establishes the constitutional principle of collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha, the specific procedural mechanism of a 'No-Confidence Motion' derives from Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules rather than the text of the Constitution.

exp.why: The Constitution of India does not mention the term 'No-Confidence Motion' anywhere, including in Article 75. Article 75(3) merely states that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People. The procedural mechanism for moving a No-Confidence Motion (requiring the support of 50 members) is provided in Rule 198 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

Under Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules, a No-Confidence Motion simply expresses that 'this House expresses its want of confidence in the Council of Ministers' and is not required to state any specific grounds or reasons on which it is based.

Because a No-Confidence Motion enforces the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers under Article 75(3), it can be moved only against the entire Council of Ministers as a body, and never against an individual Minister.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 75(3); Rule 198 of Lok Sabha Rules; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the distinction between a 'Censure Motion' and a 'No-Confidence Motion' in the Lok Sabha:
items: Statement-I: If a Censure Motion is passed in the Lok Sabha against an individual Minister or a group of Ministers, the entire Union Council of Ministers is constitutionally bound to resign from office immediately.

Statement-II: Unlike a No-Confidence Motion, which can be moved only against the entire Council of Ministers without stating any specific reasons, a Censure Motion must state the reasons for its adoption and can be moved against an individual Minister, a group of Ministers, or the entire Council of Ministers.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: A Censure Motion is a targeted parliamentary rebuke for specific policies or acts and must state its grounds, but unlike a No-Confidence Motion, its passage in the Lok Sabha does not create an automatic constitutional obligation for the Council of Ministers to resign.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Even if a Censure Motion is passed in the Lok Sabha, the Council of Ministers is not constitutionally bound to resign from office immediately (though it is politically damaging and the government may have to prove its majority soon after). Mandatory resignation of the entire Council of Ministers occurs only upon the passage of a No-Confidence Motion or defeat on a Motion of Thanks / Money Bill.

Statement-II is correct. Because a Censure Motion is moved to censure the government or specific ministers for distinct policies or lapses, it must explicitly set out the reasons or charges for its adoption, and it can target an individual Minister, a group of Ministers, or the entire Council of Ministers. Conversely, a No-Confidence Motion requires no reasons to be stated and can only target the entire Council of Ministers.

ref: Laxmikanth Ch. 23 (Parliament: Censure Motion vs No-Confidence Motion)

stem: With reference to a 'Point of Order' in the Houses of Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It relates to the interpretation or enforcement of the Rules of Procedure or such Articles of the Constitution that regulate the business of the House, and its raising suspends the ongoing proceedings before the House.
2. Although it is an extraordinary device usually used to keep the government in check, both Opposition members and ruling party members are eligible to raise a Point of Order.
3. Once a Point of Order is raised, a brief debate not exceeding thirty minutes is permitted before the House votes on whether a breach of procedure has occurred.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Point of Order (Rule 376 of the Lok Sabha Rules) is an extraordinary procedural check that immediately suspends ongoing business to bring a breach of rules to the Presiding Officer's notice, and it is decided solely by the Chair without any debate or vote of the House.

exp.why: Under Rule 376 of the Lok Sabha Rules, a Point of Order relates to the interpretation or enforcement of the Rules of Procedure or such Articles of the Constitution as regulate the business of the House. When raised, it has the effect of suspending the proceedings before the House until the Presiding Officer gives a ruling.

While a Point of Order is commonly raised by an Opposition member to control the government and ensure adherence to rules, any member of the House—including a member belonging to the ruling party—can raise a Point of Order on a procedural lapse.

Under Rule 376(3), no debate is allowed on a Point of Order, nor is the matter put to a vote of the House. The question of whether a point raised is a valid Point of Order is decided exclusively by the Speaker/Chairman, whose decision is final (though the Chair may, if it thinks fit, hear a member briefly before giving its decision).

ref: Rule 376 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the different types of 'Closure Motions' used in Parliamentary proceedings to cut short a debate, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Closure by Compartments : Clauses of a bill or lengthy resolution are grouped into parts before the debate commences, and each part is put to vote as a whole
2. Kangaroo Closure : Undiscussed clauses of a bill or resolution are put to vote along with the discussed ones due to expiry of the allotted time
3. Guillotine Closure : Only important clauses are taken up for debate and voting, while the intervening clauses are skipped over and taken as passed
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Parliamentary closure motions take four distinct forms: Simple Closure, Closure by Compartments, Kangaroo Closure (leaping over less important intervening clauses), and Guillotine Closure (putting all remaining undiscussed clauses or demands to vote once the allotted time expires).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. In 'Closure by Compartments', the clauses of a bill or a lengthy resolution are grouped into parts before the commencement of the debate. The debate covers the part as a whole and the entire part is then put to vote. (Additionally, 'Simple Closure' is when a member moves that the 'matter having been sufficiently discussed be now put to vote').

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched because it describes 'Guillotine Closure', not 'Kangaroo Closure'. Under Kangaroo Closure, only important clauses are taken up for debate and voting, and the intervening clauses are skipped over ('leaped over' like a kangaroo) and taken as passed.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched because it describes 'Kangaroo Closure', not 'Guillotine Closure'. Under Guillotine Closure, when the time allotted for the discussion of a bill, resolution, or Demands for Grants expires, all the remaining undiscussed clauses or demands are put to vote together with the discussed ones without further debate.

ref: Laxmikanth Ch. 23 (Parliament: Closure Motion)

stem: With reference to the procedural devices reflected in the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Parliament, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Special Mention : Device in the Lok Sabha to raise matters that are not points of order and cannot be raised under other rules
2. Notice under Rule 377 : Motion moved by a member for the adjournment of the debate on a Bill, resolution, or motion
3. Dilatory Motion : Superseding motion whose primary object is to retard or delay the progress of a business under discussion in the House
4. No-Day-Yet-Named Motion : Motion admitted by the Speaker for which no date has been fixed for discussion
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Matters of public importance that are not points of order and cannot be raised under any other parliamentary rule are raised as a 'Notice under Rule 377' in the Lok Sabha and as a 'Special Mention' in the Rajya Sabha. A Dilatory Motion seeks to adjourn or delay debate on business currently before the House, whereas a No-Day-Yet-Named Motion is an admitted motion awaiting allotment of time on the recommendation of the Business Advisory Committee.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. A matter which is not a point of order or which cannot be raised during Question Hour, Half-an-Hour Discussion, Short Duration Discussion, or under an Adjournment Motion or Calling Attention Notice can be raised by way of a 'Special Mention' in the Rajya Sabha (under Rules 180A to 180E). The equivalent procedural device in the Lok Sabha is a 'Notice (Mention) under Rule 377'.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. 'Notice under Rule 377' is the procedural device in the Lok Sabha used by members to bring matters of urgent public importance that do not fall under any other parliamentary rule to the attention of the House. A motion for the adjournment of the debate on a Bill, motion, or resolution is a Dilatory Motion, not a Notice under Rule 377.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. A Dilatory Motion is a motion for the adjournment of the debate on a Bill, motion, or resolution, or a motion to retard or delay the progress of a business under consideration of the House. It can be moved by a member at any time after a motion has been made, and if the Presiding Officer is of the opinion that such a motion is an abuse of the rules of the House, they may either forthwith put the question thereon or decline to propose it.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. A No-Day-Yet-Named Motion is a motion that has been admitted by the Speaker, but no date has been fixed for its discussion. The Speaker, after considering the state of business in the House and in consultation with the Leader of the House or on the recommendation of the Business Advisory Committee, allots a day or days or part of a day for the discussion of any such motion.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (Rule 377, Rules 189–190, Rules 340–341) & Rajya Sabha (Rules 180A–180E); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the procedural distinction between 'Motions' and 'Resolutions' in the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every motion moved in either House of Parliament is a self-contained substantive proposal that must be put to the vote of the House, whereas a resolution is a procedural device that does not require a formal vote.
2. A member who has moved a resolution or an amendment to a resolution is entitled to withdraw it unilaterally at any stage prior to voting without seeking the leave of the House.
3. A Statutory Resolution can be moved only by a Minister and must be tabled in pursuance of an Act of Parliament rather than a provision of the Constitution.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: All resolutions fall into the category of substantive motions, meaning every resolution is a specific type of motion, but not all motions are substantive (they may be subsidiary or substitute motions). Furthermore, while not all motions are required to be put to the vote of the House, every resolution must be voted upon, and once moved, a resolution cannot be withdrawn except by leave of the House.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. It reverses the parliamentary rule. All resolutions fall into the category of substantive motions (self-contained independent proposals), whereas not all motions need to be of a substantive character—motions can also be subsidiary or substitute motions. Moreover, all motions are not necessarily put to the vote of the House, whereas all resolutions are required to be voted upon by the House.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Once a member has moved a resolution or an amendment to a resolution and it has been proposed by the Chair to the House, it passes into the possession of the House. Consequently, the member cannot withdraw the resolution or amendment except by the formal leave of the House.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Unlike a Government Resolution (which can be moved only by a Minister) or a Private Member's Resolution (which can be moved only by a private member), a Statutory Resolution can be moved either by a private member or by a Minister. It is called 'statutory' because it is always tabled in pursuance of a specific provision in the Constitution or an Act of Parliament.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (Ch. XIV & XV); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following stages in the enactment of the Union Budget in the Parliament of India:
items: 1. Presentation of the Budget
2. Scrutiny by Departmental Standing Committees
3. General Discussion on the Budget
4. Passing of the Finance Bill
5. Voting on Demands for Grants
6. Passing of the Appropriation Bill
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence in which the above stages take place?
core: The Union Budget goes through six distinct stages in Parliament: (1) Presentation of Budget, (2) General Discussion in both Houses, (3) Scrutiny by Departmental Standing Committees during the parliamentary recess, (4) Voting on Demands for Grants in the Lok Sabha, (5) Passing of the Appropriation Bill to authorize expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, and (6) Passing of the Finance Bill to give effect to the government's taxation proposals.

exp.why: Stage 1 (Item 1): The budgetary process begins with the Presentation of the Budget by the Finance Minister in the Lok Sabha with the Budget Speech, after which the Annual Financial Statement is laid on the table of the Rajya Sabha.

Stage 3 (Item 2): Scrutiny by the 24 Departmental Standing Committees takes place AFTER the General Discussion on the Budget is completed and the Houses are adjourned for a fixed recess period. During this recess, the committees examine the Demands for Grants of the concerned ministries in detail and submit their reports to both Houses.

Stage 2 (Item 3): A few days after the presentation of the Budget, the General Discussion on the Budget begins in both Houses of Parliament. During this stage, the Houses can discuss the Budget as a whole or any question of principle involved therein, but no Cut Motion can be moved and the Budget is not submitted to the vote of the House.

Stage 6 (Item 4): The Passing of the Finance Bill is the sixth and final stage of the budgetary enactment process, legalizing the income/taxation side of the Budget. Under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, the Finance Bill must be enacted (passed by Parliament and assented to by the President) within 75 days of its introduction.

Stage 4 (Item 5): In the light of the reports given by the Departmental Standing Committees, the Lok Sabha alone takes up the Voting on Demands for Grants. Each demand is voted separately by the Lok Sabha, and members can move Policy, Economy, or Token Cut Motions at this stage.

Stage 5 (Item 6): Immediately after the Demands for Grants have been voted by the Lok Sabha, the Appropriation Bill is introduced and passed under Article 114 of the Constitution to authorize the withdrawal of funds from the Consolidated Fund of India for both the grants voted by the Lok Sabha and the expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India. Thus, the Correct Chronological Sequence is 1 - 3 - 2 - 5 - 6 - 4.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 112–117; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the expenditure 'charged' upon the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3) of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the estimates relating to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India are not submitted to the vote of Parliament, either House of Parliament is competent to discuss any of these estimates.
2. The salaries, allowances, and pensions of the judges of both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. The list of expenditures charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3) is exhaustive and can be expanded only through a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Article 113(1), expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India is non-votable but can be discussed in either House of Parliament. Crucially, while the salaries, allowances, and pensions of Supreme Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, only the pensions of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112(3)(d)(iii)), whereas their salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 202(3)(d)).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 113(1) explicitly provides that so much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, but nothing in that clause shall be construed as preventing the discussion in either House of Parliament of any of those estimates.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 112(3)(d)(i), the salaries, allowances, and pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Supreme Court are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India. However, for Judges of any High Court, only their pensions are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3)(d)(iii) (since High Court judges may serve in multiple States during their tenure and retire at the national level), whereas their salaries and allowances during service are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the respective State under Article 202(3)(d).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Article 112(3)(f) explicitly includes 'any other expenditure declared by this Constitution or by Parliament by law to be so charged.' Therefore, Parliament is empowered to declare additional items of expenditure as charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India by enacting an ordinary statute, without requiring a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 112(3), 113(1) & 202(3)(d); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the constitutional procedure governing the Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) under Articles 112 and 113, consider the following parliamentary actions:
items: 1. Laying of the Annual Financial Statement before the House at the direction of the President
2. Holding a general discussion on the Budget as a whole and on questions of fiscal policy involved therein
3. Discussing the estimates of expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India
4. Voting on the Demands for Grants and moving Cut Motions to reduce the amount of a demand
prompt: Which of the parliamentary actions given above lie within the competence of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?
core: While the Annual Financial Statement is laid before both Houses of Parliament (Article 112(1)), and both Houses can conduct a General Discussion on the Budget as well as discuss expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 113(1)), the submission and voting of Demands for Grants—along with moving Cut Motions—is the exclusive constitutional prerogative of the Lok Sabha under Article 113(2).

exp.why: Action 1 lies within the competence of both Houses. Under Article 112(1) of the Constitution, the President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year.

Action 2 lies within the competence of both Houses. During the second stage of the Budget process, a General Discussion on the Budget as a whole and on any question of fiscal policy or principle involved therein takes place in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

Action 3 lies within the competence of both Houses. Under Article 113(1), although expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India is not submitted to the vote of Parliament, either House of Parliament (both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) is fully entitled to discuss any of those charged estimates.

Action 4 belongs exclusively to the Lok Sabha. Under Article 113(2), so much of the estimates as relates to other (votable) expenditure shall be submitted in the form of Demands for Grants to the House of the People (Lok Sabha) alone, and only the Lok Sabha has the power to assent, refuse to assent, or assent subject to a reduction of the amount (via Cut Motions). The Rajya Sabha has no power to vote on Demands for Grants.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 112(1), 113(1) & 113(2); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to 'Cut Motions' moved during the voting on Demands for Grants in the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Policy Cut Motion seeks to ventilate a specific grievance within the sphere of responsibility of the Government of India and states that 'the amount of the demand be reduced by Rs 100'.

2. A Token Cut Motion represents the disapproval of the policy underlying the demand and states that 'the amount of the demand be reduced to Re 1', requiring the member to indicate an alternative policy.

3. An Economy Cut Motion may be admitted by the Speaker not only to reduce a voted Demand for Grant by a specified lump-sum amount, but also to reduce an item of expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Policy Cut Motion expresses total disapproval of the policy underlying a demand by stating that 'the amount of the demand be reduced to Re 1', whereas a Token Cut Motion ventilates a specific grievance by stating that 'the amount of the demand be reduced by Rs 100'. Furthermore, no Cut Motion of any kind can relate to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India because charged expenditure is not submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. It describes a Token Cut Motion rather than a Policy Cut Motion. A Policy Cut Motion represents the disapproval of the policy underlying the demand and states that 'the amount of the demand be reduced to Re 1', where the members can also advocate an alternative policy.

Statement 2 is incorrect. It describes a Policy Cut Motion rather than a Token Cut Motion. A Token Cut Motion is moved to ventilate a specific grievance that is within the sphere of responsibility of the Government of India, and it states that 'the amount of the demand be reduced by Rs 100'.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Rule 210 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, one of the strict conditions for the admissibility of any Cut Motion (whether Policy, Economy, or Token Cut) is that it cannot relate to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India, as charged expenditure is non-votable under Article 113(1) of the Constitution.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha (Rules 209–210); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the constitutional discipline governing the passage of the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill in the Parliament of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 114 of the Constitution, no amendment can be proposed to an Appropriation Bill in either House of Parliament that would have the effect of varying the amount or altering the destination of any grant already voted by the Lok Sabha.
2. Unlike in the case of an Appropriation Bill, members of the Lok Sabha can move amendments to the annual Finance Bill seeking to reject or reduce a tax proposed by the Executive.

3. Since expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is not submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha during the Demands for Grants stage, either House of Parliament may move an amendment during the consideration of the Appropriation Bill to reduce the amount of such charged expenditure.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 114(2) imposes an absolute bar on moving amendments in either House of Parliament to an Appropriation Bill that vary the amount or alter the destination of any voted grant or vary the amount of any expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. By contrast, during the consideration of the Finance Bill, Parliament retains the power to move amendments to reject or reduce a proposed tax.

exp.why: Under Article 114(2) of the Constitution, once the Demands for Grants have been voted by the Lok Sabha, the Appropriation Bill simply gives legal authority to withdraw those sums from the Consolidated Fund of India. No amendment can be proposed to such a Bill in either House of Parliament which will have the effect of varying the amount or altering the destination of any grant so made, and the decision of the person presiding as to whether an amendment is inadmissible under this clause is final.

The Finance Bill gives effect to the financial proposals of the Government of India for the following financial year. Unlike the Appropriation Bill, where substantive amendments to quantum or destination are constitutionally barred, amendments can be moved in the House during the consideration of the Finance Bill seeking to abolish or reduce any tax (though an amendment to increase a tax or introduce a new tax requires the prior recommendation of the President under Article 117(1)).

Article 114(2) explicitly prohibits proposing any amendment to an Appropriation Bill in either House of Parliament that has the effect of 'varying the amount of any expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India'. Charged expenditure can be discussed in either House under Article 113(1), but its amount cannot be varied by amending the Appropriation Bill.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 114; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament (Budget in Parliament)

stem: With reference to the extraordinary financial grants provided under Article 116 of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Vote on Account : A grant made in advance by the Lok Sabha in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of any financial year, pending the completion of the voting of demands and passing of the Appropriation Bill.
2. Vote of Credit : A grant made for a special purpose that forms no part of the current service of any financial year.

3. Exceptional Grant : A grant made for meeting an unexpected demand upon the resources of India when, on account of the magnitude or indefinite character of the service, the demand cannot be stated with the details ordinarily given in an annual financial statement.
prompt: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
core: Article 116 empowers the Lok Sabha to make three special types of grants: Vote on Account (advance grant for part of a financial year pending regular appropriation), Vote of Credit (an executive 'blank cheque' for an unexpected demand of indefinite character or magnitude such as a war emergency), and Exceptional Grant (for a special purpose forming no part of the current service of any financial year).

exp.why: Under Article 116(1)(a), the Lok Sabha has the power to make any grant in advance in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of any financial year pending the completion of the procedure prescribed in Article 113 for the voting of such grant and the passing of the law in accordance with Article 114.

This description belongs to an 'Exceptional Grant' under Article 116(1)(c). A Vote of Credit under Article 116(1)(b) is granted for meeting an unexpected demand upon the resources of India when, on account of the magnitude or the indefinite character of the service, the demand cannot be stated with the details ordinarily given in an annual financial statement.

This description belongs to a 'Vote of Credit' under Article 116(1)(b), which functions like a blank cheque given to the Executive during national emergencies. An Exceptional Grant under Article 116(1)(c) is made for a special purpose and forms no part of the current service of any financial year.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 116; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament (Other Grants)

stem: With reference to Supplementary, Additional, Excess, and Token Grants in the Parliamentary financial procedure of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A demand for an Excess Grant under Article 115 is presented to the Lok Sabha only after the financial year has ended and actual expenditure has been found to exceed the amount originally granted for that service.
2. Before demands for Excess Grants are submitted to the Lok Sabha for voting, they must first be examined and recommended for regularisation by the Estimates Committee of Parliament.

3. When funds to meet proposed expenditure on a new service can be made available by re-appropriation of savings within an existing grant without involving any net addition to total expenditure, a demand for the grant of a token sum is submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Excess Grants under Article 115(1)(b) regularise money already spent during a financial year in excess of the voted grant; to prevent executive abuse, they can be presented to the Lok Sabha for voting only after the CAG has audited the accounts and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has examined and recommended their regularisation.

exp.why: Under Article 115(1)(b), if any money has been spent on any service during a financial year in excess of the amount granted for that service and for that year, the President causes to be laid before both Houses of Parliament a demand for such excess. By definition, this occurs after the financial year has closed and the final accounts have been compiled and audited.

Demands for Excess Grants must be examined and approved by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament—not the Estimates Committee—based on the audit findings of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) before they are brought before the Lok Sabha for voting and regularisation.

A Token Grant is sought when the Executive proposes to incur expenditure on a 'new service' not contemplated in the budget, and the required funds can be met by re-appropriating savings from another head within the same grant. To uphold parliamentary control over new services, a demand for a token sum (conventionally Rs. 1 lakh) is submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha, and upon its approval, the funds are made available by re-appropriation.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 115; Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the composition of the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 266(1) of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Subject to the constitutional provisions regarding the Contingency Fund and the assignment of the net proceeds of certain taxes and duties to the States, all revenues received by the Government of India form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. Short-term funds raised by the Union Government through the issue of treasury bills or ways and means advances form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.

3. All moneys received by the Union Government in repayment of loans previously advanced by it to State Governments are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India rather than the Public Account of India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 266(1) explicitly specifies three streams of inflow that constitute the Consolidated Fund of India: (i) all revenues received by the Government of India (subject to Article 267 and provisions regarding assignment of net proceeds of certain taxes/duties to States), (ii) all loans raised by that Government by the issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances, and (iii) all moneys received by that Government in repayment of loans.

exp.why: Under Article 266(1), subject to the provisions of Article 267 (Contingency Fund) and the provisions of Chapter I of Part XII with respect to the assignment of the whole or part of the net proceeds of certain taxes and duties to States (such as under Article 269), all revenues (both tax and non-tax) received by the Government of India form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.

Article 266(1) expressly includes 'all loans raised by that Government by the issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances' within the Consolidated Fund of India. Unlike small savings and provident funds (which enter the Public Account), market loans, treasury bills, and ways and means advances flow directly into the Consolidated Fund.

Article 266(1) explicitly states that 'all moneys received by that Government in repayment of loans' shall form part of the Consolidated Fund of India. Since the original loans were disbursed out of the Consolidated Fund, their principal recoveries return to the Consolidated Fund as non-debt capital receipts.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 266(1); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament (Funds)

stem: Under the constitutional scheme governing public finance in India, while no money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under an Appropriation Act passed by Parliament, disbursements from the Public Account of India under Article 266(2) do not require parliamentary appropriation. Which one of the following best explains the constitutional rationale for this distinction?

opts.A: The Public Account of India is audited exclusively by the Reserve Bank of India rather than the Comptroller and Auditor General, placing its daily operations outside parliamentary oversight.
opts.B: In relation to moneys credited to the Public Account, the Union Government acts in a fiduciary capacity as a banker or trustee for funds that do not belong to it as revenue and carry an existing obligation to be paid back to the rightful depositors.
opts.C: The corpus of the Public Account consists solely of statutory grants-in-aid earmarked for State Governments under the recommendations of the Finance Commission, which are treated as charged expenditure.
opts.D: All withdrawals from the Public Account require the prior personal sanction of the President of India on the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee, rendering a separate Appropriation Bill redundant.

core: Under Article 266(2), all other public moneys received by or on behalf of the Government of India (such as provident funds, judicial deposits, small savings, and remittances) are credited to the Public Account of India. Because the Government merely holds these funds in trust as a fiduciary/banker and is legally bound to return them to depositors or remitters upon maturity or demand, executive disbursements from this account do not require a Parliamentary Appropriation Act.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because the Public Account of India under Article 266(2) comprises transactions where the Government incurs a liability to repay the money received (e.g., Provident Fund deposits, Small Savings collections, judicial deposits, departmental deposits, and remittances). Since these moneys do not belong to the Government as sovereign revenue or sovereign borrowing for general appropriation, the Government acts merely as a fiduciary banker/trustee, and disbursements are made by executive action in accordance with relevant rules without requiring parliamentary appropriation under Article 114. Option (A) is incorrect because the CAG audits all transactions relating to the Public Account under Article 149 and the CAG's (DPC) Act, 1971. Option (C) is incorrect because Finance Commission grants-in-aid under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Option (D) is incorrect because the Public Account is operated by executive action without requiring prior PAC recommendation.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 266(2); NCERT Indian Constitution at Work & M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory mechanism governing the Contingency Fund of India under Article 267(1) of the Constitution, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Contingency Fund of India is created directly by the Constitution with a fixed constitutional corpus that can be enhanced only by a Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368.
opts.B: The Fund is placed at the disposal of the Prime Minister and is operated by the Cabinet Secretary to meet unforeseen national security and disaster relief expenditures without subsequent reporting to Parliament.
opts.C: Once an advance is made from the Contingency Fund to meet an unforeseen expenditure, that expenditure is treated as permanently charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and does not require a vote of the Lok Sabha.
opts.D: The Fund is established by Parliament by law in the nature of an imprest placed at the disposal of the President to make advances for unforeseen expenditure pending its subsequent authorisation by Parliament under Article 115 or Article 116, after which the Fund is recouped.

core: Article 267(1) empowers Parliament to establish by law a Contingency Fund in the nature of an imprest placed at the disposal of the President (held by the Finance Secretary on behalf of the President). It does not bypass parliamentary control over public finance; rather, it allows the Executive to make advances for urgent, unforeseen expenditure *pending* ex-post-facto authorisation by Parliament under Article 115 or 116, after which the Fund is recouped from the Consolidated Fund of India.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct. Under Article 267(1), the Constitution does not itself establish the Contingency Fund of India; instead, it empowers Parliament to establish it by law (enacted as the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950). The Fund is in the nature of an imprest placed at the disposal of the President of India (administratively held by the Finance Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs, on behalf of the President) to enable advances to be made for the purpose of meeting unforeseen expenditure *pending* authorisation of such expenditure by Parliament by law under Article 115 (Supplementary/Additional Grant) or Article 116. Once Parliament subsequently votes the grant and passes the relevant Appropriation Bill, the amount advanced is resumed into the Contingency Fund to restore its full corpus. Option (A) is incorrect because its corpus is determined by ordinary parliamentary law (and ordinances/Finance Acts amending the 1950 Act), not under Article 368. Option (B) is incorrect because it is placed at the disposal of the President, operated by the Finance Secretary, and strictly requires subsequent parliamentary authorisation. Option (C) is incorrect because advances must be regularised through parliamentary authorisation (voting of supplementary demands by the Lok Sabha unless the unforeseen item itself happens to be a constitutionally charged item).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 267(1); Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Parliament

stem: With reference to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the Parliament of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Its members are elected annually by both Houses of Parliament from amongst their members according to the principle of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and a Minister cannot be elected as its member.
2. The Constitution of India mandates the Speaker of the Lok Sabha to appoint the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha as the ex-officio Chairman of the Committee.

3. While scrutinizing the appropriation accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the Committee examines not only the legal and formal regularity of expenditure, but also its wisdom, faithfulness, and economy.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Public Accounts Committee is a bicameral financial committee elected annually via proportional representation whose Chairman is appointed by the Speaker from the Opposition strictly by a parliamentary convention established in 1967 rather than a constitutional mandate. Assisted by the CAG as its 'friend, philosopher, and guide', the PAC scrutinizes both technical regularity and the wisdom, faithfulness, and economy of public expenditure.

exp.why: The Public Accounts Committee consists of 22 members (15 elected by the Lok Sabha and 7 associated from the Rajya Sabha). They are elected every year from amongst the members of the respective Houses according to the principle of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote so that all parties receive due representation. Under Rule 309 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, a Minister is ineligible to be elected as a member of the Committee, and if a member is appointed a Minister after election, they cease to be a member of the Committee.

The Constitution of India does not contain specific provisions regarding the composition or Chairmanship of the Public Accounts Committee; it is governed by Rules 308 and 309 of the Lok Sabha Rules. The Chairman of the Committee is appointed by the Speaker from amongst its members. Until 1966–67, a senior member of the ruling party was appointed Chairman; since 1967, a parliamentary convention (not a constitutional or statutory requirement) has developed whereby the Speaker appoints a member of the Opposition among the elected PAC members as its Chairman, who need not necessarily be the Leader of the Opposition.

In examining the appropriation accounts, finance accounts, and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the PAC does not restrict itself merely to verifying whether money has been disbursed legally within the scope of the demand granted by Parliament. Its inquiry extends 'beyond the formality of expenditure to its wisdom, faithfulness and economy' to bring to light cases of waste, loss, extravagance, corruption, and nugatory expenditure, although it cannot question the broader policy underlying the estimates.

ref: Rules 308 & 309, Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23 (Parliamentary Committees)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Estimates Committee of the Parliament:
items: Statement-I: The Estimates Committee is required to examine the budget estimates and submit its recommendations before the Demands for Grants are finally voted upon by the Lok Sabha.

Statement-II: The Estimates Committee consists exclusively of thirty members from the Lok Sabha, with no representation from the Rajya Sabha, reflecting the Lower House's exclusive constitutional authority to vote on the Demands for Grants.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike Departmentally Related Standing Committees that scrutinize Demands for Grants during the budgetary recess prior to voting, the Estimates Committee examines budget estimates only after they have been voted by the Parliament and functions throughout the year as a 'continuous economy committee'. Its membership is restricted solely to 30 Lok Sabha MPs because the Rajya Sabha has no voting power over Demands for Grants under Article 113.

exp.why: The Estimates Committee does not examine the budget estimates prior to the voting of Demands for Grants, nor is the voting on Demands for Grants contingent upon the submission of its report. Under Rule 311 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Committee continues the examination of selected estimates from time to time throughout the financial year and reports to the House as its examination proceeds. It examines budget estimates only after they have been voted by the Parliament.

All 30 members of the Estimates Committee are drawn exclusively from the Lok Sabha and elected annually by the Lok Sabha from amongst its members via proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. The Rajya Sabha has no representation on this committee because, under Article 113(2) of the Constitution, the power to assent to, refuse, or reduce Demands for Grants vests exclusively in the Lok Sabha.
