ref: Constitution of India Art. 113; Rules 310–312, Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was originally constituted in 1954 on the recommendation of the John Mathai Committee.
2. The Chairman of the Committee is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha from amongst any of its twenty-two members belonging to either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.

3. The Committee is empowered to investigate the day-to-day administration of public undertakings as well as matters for which special statutory machinery is established under the statute governing a particular undertaking.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Constituted in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee, the 22-member Committee on Public Undertakings is subject to two key structural rules: its Chairman must be appointed by the Speaker exclusively from among its Lok Sabha members, and its jurisdiction explicitly excludes day-to-day administration, major government policy, and matters covered by dedicated statutory machinery.

exp.why: The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee (1959). By contrast, it was the Estimates Committee that was set up in 1950 on the recommendation of the then Finance Minister John Mathai.

While the Committee on Public Undertakings comprises 22 members (15 elected by the Lok Sabha and 7 elected by the Rajya Sabha), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha appoints the Chairman of the Committee exclusively from amongst its members who are drawn from the Lok Sabha. A member of the Committee belonging to the Rajya Sabha cannot be appointed as its Chairman.

Under the proviso to Rule 312A of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Committee on Public Undertakings is expressly barred from examining and investigating: (i) matters of major government policy as distinct from business or commercial functions of the public undertakings, (ii) matters of day-to-day administration, and (iii) matters for the consideration of which machinery is established by any special statute under which a particular public undertaking is established.

ref: Rule 312A & 312B, Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) of the Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Each of the twenty-four Standing Committees consists of thirty-one members who are elected annually by the respective Houses according to the principle of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
2. While considering the Demands for Grants of the concerned Ministries during the budgetary recess, the reports of these Committees shall not suggest anything of the nature of cut motions.
3. The recommendations contained in the reports of these Committees are advisory in nature and are not legally binding on the Parliament or the Executive.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the three Financial Committees whose members are elected via proportional representation, the 31 members of each of the 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees (21 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha) are nominated by the respective Presiding Officers. During the budgetary recess, DRSCs scrutinize Demands for Grants without proposing cut motions, and their reports have persuasive rather than binding force.

exp.why: Each of the 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees consists of 31 members (21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha), but they are not elected by the Houses. Instead, under Rule 331D of the Lok Sabha Rules, the 21 Lok Sabha members are nominated by the Speaker from amongst the members of the Lok Sabha, and the 10 Rajya Sabha members are nominated by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha from amongst the members of the Rajya Sabha, for a term not exceeding one year.

After the general discussion on the Budget in the two Houses is concluded, the Houses are adjourned for a fixed period during which the DRSCs consider the Demands for Grants of the related Ministries and make their reports. Under Rule 331E(1)(b) of the Lok Sabha Rules, these reports shall not suggest anything of the nature of cut motions, as cut motions can only be moved by individual members on the floor of the Lok Sabha.

Under Rule 331N of the Lok Sabha Rules, the reports of the Standing Committees have persuasive value and are treated as considered advice given by the Committees. They are not legally binding on the Parliament or the Government, though the Government is required to submit Action Taken Notes explaining the implementation of accepted recommendations and reasons for any non-acceptance.

ref: Rules 331C–331N, Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the committees relating to the day-to-day business of the Houses of Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, the Presiding Officer of the House acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee, and the General Purposes Committee.

2. Both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha constitute a separate standing Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions, presided over by the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman respectively, to classify bills and allocate time for their discussion.
3. The General Purposes Committee in each House advises on matters concerning the affairs of the House that do not fall within the jurisdiction of any other parliamentary committee.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In both Houses of Parliament, the Presiding Officer (Speaker in Lok Sabha and Chairman in Rajya Sabha) serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee, and the General Purposes Committee. However, a dedicated Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions exists exclusively in the Lok Sabha (chaired by the Deputy Speaker), whereas in the Rajya Sabha this function is performed by its Business Advisory Committee.

exp.why: In the Lok Sabha, the Speaker is the ex-officio Chairman of the Business Advisory Committee (15 members), the Rules Committee (15 members), and the General Purposes Committee. Correspondingly, in the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the ex-officio Chairman of the Business Advisory Committee (11 members), the Rules Committee (16 members), and the General Purposes Committee.

The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions is a special committee constituted exclusively in the Lok Sabha (comprising 15 members with the Deputy Speaker as its Chairman). The Rajya Sabha does not have a separate Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions; the function of allocating time for the discussion of Private Members' Bills and Resolutions in the Rajya Sabha is discharged by its Business Advisory Committee.

The General Purposes Committee in each House consists of the Presiding Officer, the Deputy Presiding Officer, members of the panel of chairpersons/vice-chairpersons, Chairpersons of all standing parliamentary committees of the House, leaders of recognized parties and groups, and such other members as nominated by the Presiding Officer. Its mandate is to consider and advise on matters concerning the affairs of the House that do not fall within the specific jurisdiction of any other parliamentary committee.

ref: Rules 287–297 & 329–331, Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure; Rajya Sabha Rules of Procedure; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following pairs of Parliamentary Committees and their primary institutional mandates and composition:
items: 1. Committee on Subordinate Legislation : Consists of ten members in the Rajya Sabha to scrutinize the promises and undertakings given by Ministers on the floor of the House and report on their implementation

2. Committee on Government Assurances : Consists of fifteen members in each House to examine whether the powers to make regulations, rules, and bye-laws delegated by the Parliament are being properly exercised by the Executive within statutory limits

3. Committee on Papers Laid on the Table : Examines all papers laid on the table of the House by Ministers to verify compliance with constitutional or statutory provisions and to check for any unreasonable delay in laying them

4. Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes : Consists of thirty members drawn from both Houses of Parliament to consider the reports of the National Commissions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and examine matters relating to constitutional safeguards
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Parliament exercises day-to-day oversight over the Executive through specialized scrutiny committees: the Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks executive delegated legislation (15 members in each House), while the Committee on Government Assurances tracks ministerial promises made on the floor (15 members in Lok Sabha, 10 in Rajya Sabha). Meanwhile, the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks delays in laying statutory notifications, and the 30-member joint Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs oversees constitutional safeguards.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because both the composition and mandate have been interchanged with the Committee on Government Assurances. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation consists of 15 members in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha (nominated by the Speaker and Chairman respectively), and its mandate is to examine and report to the House whether the powers to make regulations, rules, sub-rules, and bye-laws delegated by the Parliament or conferred by the Constitution are being properly exercised by the Executive within the scope of such delegation.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched because its mandate and Rajya Sabha strength have been swapped with the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. The Committee on Government Assurances consists of 15 members in the Lok Sabha and 10 members in the Rajya Sabha, and its mandate is to scrutinize the assurances, promises, and undertakings given by Ministers from time to time on the floor of the House and report on the extent to which they have been implemented and whether such implementation has taken place within the minimum time necessary for the purpose.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Constituted in 1975 (with 15 members in the Lok Sabha and 10 members in the Rajya Sabha), the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table examines all papers laid on the table of the House by Ministers to ascertain whether they comply with the provisions of the Constitution or the relevant Act or Rule, whether there has been any unreasonable delay in laying the paper, and whether both Hindi and English versions have been laid.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. The Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes consists of 30 members (20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha) elected by the respective Houses via proportional representation. Its functions include considering the reports submitted by the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A) and examining all matters relating to the welfare and constitutional safeguards of SCs and STs.

ref: Rules 317–324 & 331A–331B, Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the constitution and functioning of a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) in India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It is a permanent standing committee constituted at the commencement of every new Lok Sabha to investigate financial irregularities across Union Ministries.
opts.B: It can be constituted only through a Presidential notification issued under Article 85 of the Constitution on the formal aid and advice of the Union Cabinet.
opts.C: It is an ad-hoc committee set up for a specific purpose when a motion is passed by one House and agreed to by the other House, or by agreement between the Presiding Officers of both Houses.
opts.D: Unlike a Joint Committee on a Bill, a Joint Parliamentary Committee is statutorily required to comprise an equal number of members from the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

core: A Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is an ad-hoc committee of Parliament constituted to investigate a specific issue of public importance or policy/financial irregularity. It is brought into existence through parliamentary consensus—either via a motion adopted by one House and concurred in by the other, or through mutual agreement between the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct because a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is an ad-hoc (temporary) committee constituted for a specific inquiry or subject, and it ceases to exist once it submits its report to Parliament. Procedurally, a JPC is constituted when a motion is passed by one House and agreed to by the other House, or when the Presiding Officers of both Houses (the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) agree to set it up. Option (A) is incorrect because a JPC is an ad-hoc committee, not a permanent standing committee. Option (B) is incorrect because the President under Article 85 summons, prorogues, and dissolves Parliament, and plays no role in constituting a JPC. Option (D) is incorrect because there is no statutory requirement of equal membership; by convention, the number of Lok Sabha members in a JPC is twice that of the Rajya Sabha (typically in a 2:1 ratio).

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha; Laxmikanth Ch. 23 (Parliamentary Committees)

stem: With reference to the Committee of Privileges and the Ethics Committee of the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Rajya Sabha was the first House of the Indian Parliament to constitute a permanent Ethics Committee to oversee the moral and ethical conduct of its members.
2. Both the Committee of Privileges and the Ethics Committee possess the jurisdiction to examine complaints against non-member citizens whose conduct brings the House into disrepute.

3. While every breach of parliamentary privilege by a Member of Parliament involves misconduct, every unethical act examined by the Ethics Committee does not necessarily amount to a breach of privilege.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Committee of Privileges safeguards the constitutional immunities and authority of the House against breaches or contempt by either members or non-members, the Ethics Committee enforces the internal Code of Conduct strictly applicable to sitting Members of Parliament.

exp.why: The Rajya Sabha constituted a permanent Ethics Committee in March 1997 (inaugurated in May 1997) as the first such institutional mechanism in Parliament. The Lok Sabha initially constituted an ad-hoc Ethics Committee in 2000 and made it a permanent standing committee under its Rules of Procedure only in 2015.

There is a fundamental jurisdictional difference between the two committees regarding non-members. A non-member citizen can commit a breach of privilege or contempt of the House (such as obstructing an MP or casting libellous reflections on the House) and can be proceeded against by the Committee of Privileges. However, the Ethics Committee's jurisdiction is strictly confined to examining allegations of unethical conduct against Members of Parliament; it cannot investigate or punish non-members for unethical behaviour.

The concept of unethical conduct is broader than a breach of parliamentary privilege. Every breach of privilege by an MP involves misconduct, but not every violation of the ethical code of conduct (such as failure to declare a pecuniary conflict of interest or conduct unbecoming of an MP outside the House) constitutes a technical breach of parliamentary privilege.

ref: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following stages in the context of parliamentary scrutiny of public finances across a fiscal cycle:
items: 1. General discussion on the Annual Financial Statement in both Houses of Parliament without voting on any demand.
2. Detailed scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of Ministries by the respective Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) during the parliamentary recess.
3. Mandatory approval of the Demands for Grants by the Estimates Committee prior to the voting on Demands in the Lok Sabha.
4. Examination by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the appropriation and finance audit reports submitted by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).
prompt: Which one of the following options represents the correct chronological sequence of valid parliamentary stages in the enactment and ex-post scrutiny of the Union Budget?
core: During the budget enactment phase, Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs)—and not the Estimates Committee—examine the Demands for Grants during the inter-session recess before the Lok Sabha votes on them. The Estimates Committee examines budget estimates only after they have been voted by Parliament, while the Public Accounts Committee conducts ex-post scrutiny based on CAG audit reports.

exp.why: Following the presentation of the Union Budget under Article 112, the first parliamentary stage is a general discussion on the Budget as a whole in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. No cut motion is moved and no voting takes place at this stage.

At the end of the general discussion, Parliament adjourns for a fixed recess period during which the 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) examine and deliberate in detail upon the Demands for Grants of the concerned ministries and submit their reports to the House before voting on Demands begins.

This is an invalid procedural stage. The Estimates Committee does not examine or approve the Demands for Grants prior to voting by the Lok Sabha. Under the Rules of Procedure, the Estimates Committee can examine budget estimates only after they have been voted by Parliament, and its work continues throughout the financial year without holding up the voting on Demands for Grants or the passage of the Appropriation Bill.

After the financial year concludes and the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) submits audit reports to the President (who causes them to be laid before Parliament under Article 151), the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) conducts an ex-post facto examination of public expenditure to verify that money was spent legally and for the purpose for which it was granted.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 112–114 & 151; Laxmikanth Ch. 22 & 23

stem: With reference to the constitutional architecture of Parliamentary Privileges in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 105 of the Constitution, parliamentary privileges extend to persons who are constitutionally entitled to speak and take part in the proceedings of a House of Parliament or any of its committees, even if they are not members of either House.

2. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 codified all parliamentary privileges into a comprehensive statutory list under Article 105(3) to replace the conventions of the British House of Commons.
3. Since the President of India is a constituent part of Parliament under Article 79, the President enjoys the same parliamentary privileges under Article 105 as the Members of Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Article 105(4) explicitly extends parliamentary privileges to non-member constitutional participants like the Attorney General and Union Ministers speaking in the other House, but not to the President. Furthermore, the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 only dropped the explicit textual reference to the British House of Commons in Article 105(3) without codifying privileges by statute.

exp.why: Under Article 105(4) of the Constitution, the provisions of clauses (1), (2), and (3) of Article 105 apply in relation to persons who by virtue of the Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, a House of Parliament or any committee thereof (such as the Attorney General for India under Article 88 and Union Ministers) in the same manner as they apply to Members of Parliament.

The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 did NOT codify parliamentary privileges into a statute. It merely made a verbal modification to Article 105(3) (and Article 194(3) for States) by dropping the direct textual reference to the 'British House of Commons' and stating that until defined by Parliament by law, the privileges of each House shall be those existing immediately before the coming into force of Section 15 of the 44th Amendment Act, 1978. Parliament has still not enacted a comprehensive law codifying all privileges.

Although the President is an integral constituent part of the Parliament under Article 79, the President does not sit or participate in the deliberations of either House and does not enjoy parliamentary privileges under Article 105. The personal and official immunities of the President are separately governed by Article 361 of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 79, 88, 105 & 361; 44th Amendment Act 1978

stem: With reference to the constitutional immunity of legislators under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. If a Member of Parliament accepts a bribe to vote in a particular manner and subsequently casts the vote in the House in accordance with that agreement, the member enjoys immunity from criminal prosecution under Article 105(2).

2. The offence of bribery by a legislator is complete at the point in time when the illegal gratification is accepted, irrespective of whether the legislator subsequently speaks or votes in the House as agreed.

3. The constitutional principles denying legislative immunity for bribery apply equally to speeches and votes on the floor of the House as well as to votes cast by elected Members of Legislative Assemblies in elections to the Rajya Sabha.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) and held that MPs and MLAs enjoy zero immunity under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) from criminal prosecution for bribery, because bribery fails the two-fold test of being tethered to collective legislative functioning and is complete the moment illegal gratification is accepted.

exp.why: This statement reflects the overruled 1998 majority ruling in P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State. In March 2024, a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Sita Soren v. Union of India unanimously overruled the 1998 judgment and held that a legislator who accepts a bribe to speak or vote in a particular manner in the House is NOT immune from criminal prosecution under Articles 105(2) or 194(2), even if the legislator actually votes or speaks in accordance with the bribe.

In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that the offence of bribery under the Prevention of Corruption Act is agnostic to the performance of the agreed action. The offence is complete at the very moment the legislator accepts or agrees to accept illegal gratification, independent of whether the vote or speech is later delivered on the floor of the House.

The 7-Judge Bench in Sita Soren (2024) clarified that parliamentary privilege is meant to protect the integrity of free deliberation within the House, not to create islands of immunity from the general criminal law of the land. Consequently, the absence of immunity for bribery applies both to floor proceedings (speeches/votes) and to votes cast by MLAs in Rajya Sabha elections.

ref: Sita Soren v. Union of India (7-Judge Bench, 2024); Constitution of India Art. 105(2) & 194(2)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the freedom of speech of Members of Parliament:
items: Statement-I: The freedom of speech enjoyed by a Member of Parliament inside the House under Article 105(1) of the Constitution is distinct from a citizen's fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and is not subject to the reasonable restrictions enumerated under Article 19(2).
Statement-II: The Constitution of India places no textual restriction on the subject matter of discussions inside Parliament other than the Rules of Procedure framed by each House under Article 118.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While a Member of Parliament's freedom of speech inside the House under Article 105(1) is independent of the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), it is explicitly made 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution'—most notably Article 121, which prohibits discussion on the conduct of Supreme Court and High Court judges except upon a removal motion.

exp.why: As settled by the Supreme Court in M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (Searchlight Case), the freedom of speech in Parliament conferred by Article 105(1) is a special constitutional privilege distinct from the general fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), and is therefore not controlled by the reasonable restrictions listed in Article 19(2).

Article 105(1) begins with the words: 'Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament.' Thus, freedom of speech inside Parliament is subject not only to the Rules of Procedure framed under Article 118, but also to other provisions of the Constitution—specifically Article 121, which expressly prohibits any discussion in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties except upon a motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the removal of the Judge.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 105(1), 118 & 121; M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha

stem: A sitting Member of the Lok Sabha is arrested by a central law enforcement agency outside the precincts of Parliament in connection with a cognizable criminal offence and remanded to judicial custody fifteen days prior to the commencement of the Monsoon Session of Parliament. In the context of Parliamentary Privileges in India, which one of the following statements accurately represents the constitutional and legal position in this scenario?

opts.A: The arrest constitutes a breach of parliamentary privilege unless prior sanction of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha was obtained before executing the warrant, since the arrest occurred within forty days before the commencement of a session.
opts.B: The arrest does not violate parliamentary privilege because the immunity from arrest during a session and forty days before its commencement or after its conclusion is restricted exclusively to civil cases and does not extend to criminal offences or preventive detention.
opts.C: While the initial arrest is lawful, the Member acquires a constitutional right under Article 105 to be released on interim custody once the session begins so as to participate and vote in the proceedings of the House.
opts.D: Because parliamentary privilege does not extend to criminal cases, the arresting authority is neither legally required to intimate the Speaker regarding the arrest nor prohibited from executing an arrest warrant inside the precincts of the House without the Speaker's permission.

core: Individual parliamentary privilege of freedom from arrest during a session and 40 days before its commencement or after its conclusion (codified under Section 135A of the Code of Civil Procedure) applies solely to civil arrests and never to criminal offences, contempt of court, or preventive detention. However, the arresting authority must promptly inform the Presiding Officer, and no arrest (civil or criminal) can be executed within the precincts of the House without the Presiding Officer's permission.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because parliamentary privilege exists to ensure the uninterrupted functioning of the House, not to place legislators above the ordinary criminal law of the land. Freedom from arrest during a session and 40 days before its start and 40 days after its prorogation (under Section 135A of the Code of Civil Procedure) is strictly limited to civil cases. Option (A) is incorrect because no prior permission of the Speaker is required to arrest an MP in a criminal or preventive detention case outside the precincts of the House. Option (C) is incorrect because in K. Ananda Nambiar v. Chief Secretary (1966) and subsequent rulings, the Supreme Court held that a validly detained MP has no constitutional privilege to attend parliamentary sessions while in lawful custody. Option (D) is incorrect because under Rules 229 and 230 of the Lok Sabha Rules, the arresting magistrate or executive authority must immediately intimate the Speaker about the reason and place of arrest, detention, or release of a Member; moreover, no arrest—even in a criminal case—can be made within the precincts of the House without the explicit permission of the Presiding Officer.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 105; Section 135A CPC; Rules 229-233 of Lok Sabha Rules; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the collective privileges of the Houses of Parliament and State Legislatures and the scope of judicial review over legislative proceedings, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Each House of Parliament and of a State Legislature possesses the collective privilege to punish both its own members and non-members for breach of privilege or contempt of the House, including the power to expel a sitting member.

2. When a House of Legislature commits a person to prison for contempt of the House for a specified term, the sentence remains continuously enforceable even after the prorogation or dissolution of that House until the fixed term expires.

3. Under Articles 122 and 212 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is completely barred from exercising judicial review over a resolution of a State Legislative Assembly suspending its members beyond the remainder of an ongoing session.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: While a Legislature can punish members and outsiders for contempt (including expulsion of members as upheld in Raja Ram Pal, 2007), its power to commit a contemnor to prison terminates automatically upon the prorogation or dissolution of the House. Furthermore, Articles 122 and 212 shield only mere procedural irregularities and do not bar judicial review of substantive unconstitutionality or irrationality, such as prolonged suspension of MLAs beyond an ongoing session (Ashish Shelar, 2022).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Acting as a guardian of its own authority and dignity, each House of Parliament (under Article 105) and State Legislature (under Article 194) holds the collective privilege to punish both members and non-members (strangers) by reprimand, admonition, or imprisonment for breach of privilege or contempt of the House. In Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional power of a House to expel its members for conduct unbecoming of a legislator.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under established parliamentary law and convention in India, the power of a House to commit a contemnor to custody is co-terminus with the duration of the ongoing session. Prorogation of the House (or dissolution in the case of the Lower House) automatically terminates any sentence of imprisonment imposed by that House for contempt, and the prisoner must be released forthwith.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In Raja Ram Pal (2007) and Ashish Shelar v. Maharashtra Legislative Assembly (2022), the Supreme Court held that Articles 122 and 212 only immunize legislative proceedings from judicial scrutiny on the ground of mere 'irregularity of procedure', and do not bar judicial review where a resolution suffers from substantive illegality, unconstitutionality, or mala fides. In Ashish Shelar (2022), the Supreme Court struck down the one-year suspension of 12 MLAs as unconstitutional and irrational, holding that suspension is a disciplinary measure limited to the ongoing session and cannot operate as a de facto expulsion leaving a constituency unrepresented beyond the six-month constitutional limit under Article 190(4).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 105, 122, 194 & 212; Raja Ram Pal v. Speaker (2007); Ashish Shelar v. Maharashtra Legislative Assembly (2022)

stem: With reference to the constitutional scope and applicability of Parliamentary Privileges under Article 105 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Attorney General of India enjoys all the parliamentary privileges and immunities available to a Member of Parliament when participating in the proceedings of either House or any parliamentary committee of which he is named a member.
2. A Union Minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha enjoys the same parliamentary privileges and immunities under Article 105 while speaking in the Lok Sabha as an elected Member of the Lok Sabha.

3. Because the President of India is a constituent part of Parliament under Article 79, the parliamentary privileges and immunities under Article 105 extend equally to the President in the discharge of legislative functions.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 105(4), parliamentary privileges extend not only to MPs but also to all persons who by virtue of the Constitution have the right to speak in and otherwise take part in the proceedings of a House or its committees (specifically the Attorney General of India and Union Ministers under Article 88). However, the President of India does not enjoy parliamentary privileges under Article 105, as presidential immunities are governed separately by Article 361.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 88 of the Constitution, the Attorney General of India has the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, without a right to vote. Article 105(4) explicitly extends all parliamentary privileges and immunities under clauses (1), (2), and (3) of Article 105 to every person who bears this constitutional right.

Statement 2 is correct. Reading Article 88 alongside Article 105(4), a Union Minister who is a member of one House has the constitutional right to speak and participate in the proceedings of the other House (though without voting rights there) and consequently enjoys the full protection of parliamentary privileges under Article 105 while participating in that other House.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Although the President of India is an integral constituent part of Parliament under Article 79, the President does not sit or take part in the ordinary debates and proceedings of either House. Consequently, the parliamentary privileges under Article 105 do not apply to the President; instead, the personal and official immunities of the President (and Governors) are separately guaranteed under Article 361 of the Constitution.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 79, 88, 105(4) & 361; Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the constitutional protection regarding the publication of proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures under Article 361A of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It confers absolute immunity from civil and criminal proceedings in any court for publishing a substantially true report of legislative proceedings, even if the publication is proved to have been made with malice.
opts.B: Its constitutional protection extends only to reports of the proceedings of either House of Parliament, leaving the protection for reporting proceedings of State Legislatures to ordinary statutes enacted by the respective States.
opts.C: It protects the publication in a newspaper or broadcast via wireless telegraphy of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or of a State Legislature from civil or criminal court proceedings, unless proved to be made with malice, but does not apply to secret sittings of any House.
opts.D: It was present in the original Constitution enacted in 1950 and applies solely to print newspapers, excluding reports broadcast by means of wireless telegraphy.

core: Inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 361A grants constitutional immunity from civil and criminal court proceedings for publishing in a newspaper (or broadcasting via wireless telegraphy) a substantially true report of the proceedings of either House of Parliament or a State Legislature. This immunity ceases if the publication is proved to be actuated by malice, or if it relates to the proceedings of a secret sitting of any House.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct as it accurately states the scope and three constitutional qualifiers of Article 361A: (1) the report of the proceedings of either House of Parliament or of a State Legislature must be 'substantially true', (2) the immunity from civil or criminal proceedings in any court is lost if the publication is proved to have been made with malice, and (3) under the Proviso to Article 361A(1), the protection does not apply to the publication of any report of the proceedings of a secret sitting of any House. Furthermore, Article 361A(2) explicitly extends this protection to broadcasts by means of wireless telegraphy as part of any programme or service provided by a broadcasting station. Option (A) is incorrect because malice forfeits the protection. Option (B) is incorrect because Article 361A explicitly covers both Parliament and State Legislatures. Option (D) is incorrect because Article 361A was not in the original Constitution; it was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 to give constitutional status to the principle earlier embodied in the statutory Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1956 (the Feroze Gandhi Act).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 361A (44th Amendment Act, 1978); Laxmikanth Ch. 23

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the creation and abolition of State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishads) under Article 169 of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: A resolution by a State Legislative Assembly seeking the creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council must be passed by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting.

Statement-II: Once a State Legislative Assembly passes such a resolution, it is constitutionally binding upon Parliament to enact the corresponding legislation by a special majority under Article 368.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 169 establishes an asymmetric majority procedure for creating or abolishing a State Legislative Council: the State Legislative Assembly must initiate the proposal via a resolution passed by a special majority, whereas Parliament may thereafter enact the law by a simple majority. Moreover, the Assembly's resolution is not binding on Parliament, and under Article 169(3), such an Act of Parliament is not deemed a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 169(1) of the Constitution, the Legislative Assembly of the concerned State must pass a resolution for the creation or abolition of the Legislative Council by a special majority—that is, by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting.

Statement-II is incorrect on two distinct constitutional counts. First, Article 169(1) uses the permissive phrase 'Parliament may by law provide', meaning a resolution passed by the State Legislative Assembly is merely an enabling condition and is not binding upon Parliament (which may choose to accept, defer, or not act upon the resolution). Second, Article 169(3) explicitly states that no such law passed by Parliament shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368; hence, Parliament passes the law by a simple majority like an ordinary legislative enactment.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 169; Laxmikanth Ch. 34

stem: With reference to the composition and manner of selection of members of a State Legislative Council under Article 171 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Five-sixths of the total number of members of a State Legislative Council are indirectly elected in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, while one-sixth are nominated by the Governor.

2. Unlike the President's nomination power to the Rajya Sabha, the Governor is constitutionally empowered to nominate persons having special knowledge or practical experience in the 'cooperative movement' to the State Legislative Council, in addition to literature, science, art, and social service.

3. While one-third of the members of the Council are elected by members of local authorities in the State, one-sixth are elected by graduates of three years' standing and another one-sixth by teachers of secondary schools and above.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 171(3), the composition of a State Legislative Council follows a strict fractional distribution: 1/3rd elected by local bodies, 1/3rd elected by MLAs, 1/12th elected by graduates, 1/12th elected by teachers (totalling 5/6th indirectly elected by proportional representation via STV), and the remaining 1/6th nominated by the Governor from five fields (Literature, Science, Art, Cooperative Movement, and Social Service).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 171(3) and 171(4), five-sixths (1/3 + 1/3 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 5/6) of the total number of members of a State Legislative Council are indirectly elected in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, while the remaining one-sixth (1/6) are nominated by the Governor.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 80(3), the President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from four fields: Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service. In contrast, under Article 171(5), the Governor nominates 1/6th of the members of the State Legislative Council from five fields, adding 'Cooperative Movement' to Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 171(3)(b) and (c), the electorates consisting of university graduates of three years' standing and teachers of at least three years' standing in educational institutions not lower in standard than a secondary school elect one-twelfth (1/12th) each—not one-sixth each—of the total members of the Legislative Council. Together, the graduates' and teachers' constituencies account for one-sixth (1/12 + 1/12 = 1/6) of the Council's strength.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 80(3) & 171; Laxmikanth Ch. 34

stem: With reference to the passage of an Ordinary Bill in a State having a bicameral Legislature under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In case of a deadlock over an Ordinary Bill between the State Legislative Assembly and the State Legislative Council, the Governor is empowered to summon a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve the disagreement.
2. The State Legislative Council can delay the passage of an Ordinary Bill passed by the State Legislative Assembly for a maximum period of six months across both rounds of consideration.

3. When an Ordinary Bill originating in and passed by the State Legislative Council is rejected by the State Legislative Assembly, it is returned to the Council for reconsideration within three months.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the Rajya Sabha at the Union level, a State Legislative Council is strictly a dilatory chamber regarding Ordinary Bills under Article 197: there is no provision for a joint sitting in a State Legislature, the Council can delay an Assembly-passed Bill for at most four months (three months in the first instance plus one month in the second), and a Council-originated Bill dies immediately if rejected by the Legislative Assembly.

exp.why: Unlike Article 108 of the Constitution which empowers the President to summon a joint sitting of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha to resolve a deadlock over an Ordinary Bill, the Constitution makes no provision for a joint sitting of both Houses of a State Legislature. Under Article 197, the will of the directly elected State Legislative Assembly ultimately prevails without any joint sitting.

Under Article 197(1) and (2), the State Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill transmitted by the Legislative Assembly for a maximum period of four months in total: three months in the first instance and one month in the second instance after the Assembly passes the Bill again. The six-month period applies to the Rajya Sabha under Article 108, not to the State Legislative Council.

The overriding mechanism under Article 197 applies exclusively to Bills originating in the State Legislative Assembly and transmitted to the Legislative Council. If an Ordinary Bill originates in the Legislative Council and is rejected by the Legislative Assembly, the Bill ends immediately and becomes dead; it is not returned to the Council for a second passage.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 196 & 197; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on State Legislature.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the financial powers of a State Legislature:
items: Statement-I: In a State having a bicameral Legislature, the Annual Financial Statement is laid solely before the State Legislative Assembly, and the State Legislative Council is constitutionally barred from discussing the general provisions of the Budget.
Statement-II: Under Article 203 of the Constitution of India, the Demands for Grants in the State Budget can be submitted to the vote only of the State Legislative Assembly.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In a bicameral State Legislature, the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) is laid before both Houses under Article 202 and the Legislative Council is fully entitled to discuss it, but the exclusive power to vote on Demands for Grants vests only in the State Legislative Assembly under Article 203(2).

exp.why: Under Article 202(1) of the Constitution, the Governor causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses of the Legislature in a bicameral State. Furthermore, Article 203(1) explicitly clarifies that nothing prevents the discussion in the Legislature of any of the budget estimates; therefore, the State Legislative Council can hold a general discussion on the Budget.

Under Article 203(1) and (2) of the Constitution, estimates relating to expenditure other than charged expenditure are submitted in the form of Demands for Grants exclusively to the State Legislative Assembly, and only the Legislative Assembly has the constitutional power to assent, refuse to assent, or reduce any demand for grant.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 198, 202 & 203; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on State Legislature.

stem: With reference to the constitutional role of the Members of a State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Election of the President of India under Article 54 : Neither elected nor nominated members of the State Legislative Council participate
2. Election of representatives of the State to the Rajya Sabha under Article 80(4) : Elected members of the State Legislative Council participate alongside elected members of the Legislative Assembly

3. Ratification of a Constitutional Amendment Bill by a State Legislature under the proviso to Article 368(2) : Both the State Legislative Assembly and the State Legislative Council participate in passing the ratification resolution
4. Election of the Vice-President of India under Article 66 : Neither elected nor nominated members of the State Legislative Council participate
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Members of a State Legislative Council do not participate in electing the President, the Vice-President, or the State's representatives to the Rajya Sabha; however, because the 'Legislature of a State' in a bicameral State comprises both Houses, the Legislative Council does participate in ratifying Constitutional Amendment Bills under the proviso to Article 368(2).

exp.why: Under Article 54 of the Constitution, the Electoral College for the President consists only of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including NCT of Delhi and Puducherry). Because the Legislative Council itself is largely indirectly elected and nominated, neither its elected nor its nominated members participate.

Under Article 80(4) of the Constitution, the representatives of each State in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) are elected solely by the elected members of the Legislative Assembly of the State. Members of the State Legislative Council have no voting role in Rajya Sabha elections.

The proviso to Article 368(2) requires ratification by the 'Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures'. In a State having a bicameral Legislature under Article 168, the Legislature comprises both the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council, so a ratification resolution must be passed by both Houses.

Under Article 66(1) of the Constitution, the Vice-President is elected by an electoral college consisting exclusively of the members (both elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament. Members of State Legislatures, whether of the Assembly or the Council, do not participate.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 54, 66, 80(4) & 368(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity.

stem: With reference to the Presiding Officers of the State Legislative Council under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. On the analogy of the Rajya Sabha where the Vice-President serves as the ex-officio Chairman, the Governor of the State appoints a person who is not a member of the State Legislature to serve as the Chairman of the State Legislative Council.

2. A resolution for the removal of the Chairman of the State Legislative Council is passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council and does not require the concurrence of the State Legislative Assembly.

3. While a resolution for the removal of the Chairman of the State Legislative Council is under consideration, he cannot preside over the sitting of the Council, though he has the right to speak in its proceedings and vote in the first instance on such resolution.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the Rajya Sabha which is presided over by an ex-officio Chairman (the Vice-President of India) who is not a member of the House, the State Legislative Council elects both its Chairman and Deputy Chairman from amongst its own members under Article 182, and removes them by an effective majority of the Council alone under Article 183(c).

exp.why: Under Article 182 of the Constitution, the Legislative Council of every State having such Council shall choose two members of the Council to be respectively Chairman and Deputy Chairman thereof. Thus, unlike the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman of a State Legislative Council is always a member of the Council elected by the Council itself.

Under Article 183(c), the Chairman of the State Legislative Council may be removed from office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council (effective majority) after a 14-day notice. Because he is chosen solely by the Council, the State Legislative Assembly has no role in his removal.

Under Article 185(1) and (2), while any resolution for the removal of the Chairman from his office is under consideration, he shall not preside even though he is present, and he shall have the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of the Legislative Council and shall be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution (and not in the case of an equality of votes).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 182, 183 & 185; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on State Legislature.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the tenure and qualifications of members of a State Legislative Council:
items: Statement-I: To be chosen to fill an elected seat in a State Legislative Council, a candidate must be registered as an elector for a Legislative Assembly constituency in that State, whereas a person nominated by the Governor to the Council must be ordinarily resident in that State, and both hold office for a six-year term—even though none of these three specific requirements is explicitly written into the text of the Constitution of India.

Statement-II: Exercising its constitutional mandate under Articles 172(2) and 173(c), Parliament enacted the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which statutorily fixes the six-year tenure of Legislative Council members and prescribes the Assembly constituency elector qualification for elected seats and the ordinary residency requirement for nominated seats.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Articles 172(2) and 173(c) of the Constitution only stipulate the biennial retirement of one-third of the Legislative Council's members and basic age/citizenship qualifications, leaving the specific six-year tenure, the Assembly elector qualification for elected members, and the ordinary residency qualification for nominated members to be prescribed by Parliament under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

exp.why: The text of the Constitution (Articles 172 and 173) does not directly specify the six-year term of office of members of the State Legislative Council, nor does it state the electoral roll or residency requirements. Yet in law, a candidate contesting an election to the Legislative Council must be an elector for an Assembly constituency in that State, a person nominated by the Governor under Article 171(5) must be ordinarily resident in that State, and both serve a six-year term.

Statement-II directly explains Statement-I: Article 172(2) and Article 173(c) empower Parliament to regulate retirement/tenure and prescribe additional qualifications by law. Under this authority, Parliament enacted the Representation of the People Act, 1951, wherein Section 156 fixes the term of office of Council members at six years, Section 6(1) mandates that a person chosen to fill an elected seat in the Legislative Council must be an elector for any Assembly constituency in that State, and Section 6(2) mandates that a person nominated by the Governor to the Legislative Council must be ordinarily resident in that State.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 171, 172(2) & 173(c); Representation of the People Act, 1951, Sections 6(1), 6(2) & 156.

stem: With reference to the constitutional status and functioning of a State Legislative Council under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Minister who is a member of the State Legislative Council has the constitutional right to speak, participate in the proceedings, and vote in the State Legislative Assembly specifically when a Motion of No-Confidence against the Council of Ministers is put to vote.

2. In a bicameral State Legislature, the resolution recommending to Parliament the abolition of the State Legislative Council must be passed by a special majority of both the State Legislative Assembly and the State Legislative Council.

3. While the resolution of the State Legislative Assembly for the abolition of the State Legislative Council requires a special majority of the Assembly, the subsequent law of Parliament giving effect to such abolition is passed by a simple majority and is not deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 177, a Minister who is a member of the Legislative Council can speak and participate in the Legislative Assembly but can never vote there (even on a No-Confidence Motion); furthermore, under Article 169, the abolition of a Legislative Council requires a special-majority resolution of the State Legislative Assembly alone, followed by an ordinary law of Parliament passed by simple majority outside the scope of Article 368.

exp.why: Under Article 177 of the Constitution, every Minister of a State has the right to speak in and otherwise take part in the proceedings of either House, but is explicitly barred from voting in a House of which he is not a member. Therefore, a Minister who is an MLC can participate in the debate on a No-Confidence Motion in the Legislative Assembly, but cannot vote on it.

Under Article 169(1), the resolution for the abolition (or creation) of the Legislative Council of a State needs to be passed only by the Legislative Assembly of the State (by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting). The Legislative Council itself has no role in passing the resolution for its own abolition.

Under Article 169(1) and (3) of the Constitution, once the State Legislative Assembly passes the resolution by a special majority, Parliament may by law provide for the abolition or creation of the State Legislative Council, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. Hence, Parliament passes such a law by a simple majority like ordinary legislation.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 169 & 177; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on State Legislature.

stem: With reference to the qualifications and tenure conditions for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution of India, a person who is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist is eligible to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court, whereas no corresponding provision exists for appointment as a Judge of a High Court.
2. The Constitution prescribes a minimum age of 35 years and an upper age limit of 65 years for a person to be appointed and hold office as a Judge of the Supreme Court.

3. In computing the ten-year qualifying period as an advocate of a High Court for appointment to the Supreme Court, any period during which the person held a judicial office after becoming an advocate is excluded.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Article 124(3) provides three alternative eligibility pathways for appointment to the Supreme Court—including being a 'distinguished jurist' in the President's opinion (a category absent in Article 217 for High Courts)—while prescribing no minimum age in the Constitution.

exp.why: Under Article 124(3)(c) of the Constitution, a person is eligible to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court if they are, in the opinion of the President, a 'distinguished jurist'. In contrast, Article 217(2) does not contain a 'distinguished jurist' category for appointment as a High Court Judge (the 42nd Amendment Act had inserted it for High Courts, but the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted it).

While Article 124(2) stipulates that a Judge of the Supreme Court holds office until attaining the age of 65 years, the Constitution prescribes no minimum age for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court.

Under Explanation II to Article 124(3), for the purpose of computing the ten-year period during which a person has been an advocate of a High Court, any period during which a person has held judicial office not inferior to that of a district judge after becoming an advocate is explicitly included, not excluded.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 124(2), 124(3) and 217(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 26 (Supreme Court).

stem: With reference to the constitutional evolution of the Collegium System in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) : Held that 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India under Article 124(2) means 'concurrence' and is binding on the President
2. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993) : Held that 'consultation' does not mean 'concurrence' and granted primacy to the Executive in judicial appointments
3. In re Special Reference 1 of 1998 : Institutionalized a Collegium consisting of the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court
4. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) : Struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act to preserve judicial primacy as part of the Basic Structure
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Collegium system evolved through four landmark judicial pronouncements: the First Judges Case (1981) gave primacy to the Executive, the Second Judges Case (1993) overruled it by equating 'consultation' with 'concurrence', the Third Judges Case (1998) expanded the Collegium to five judges, and the Fourth Judges Case (2015) invalidated the NJAC.

exp.why: In S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case, 1981), the Supreme Court held that the word 'consultation' in Articles 124(2) and 217(1) does not mean 'concurrence', implying only an exchange of views and granting ultimate primacy to the Executive in judicial appointments.

In the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Second Judges Case, 1993), a nine-judge Constitution Bench overruled the First Judges Case and held that 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India actually means 'concurrence', establishing judicial primacy through a Collegium of the CJI and the two senior-most judges.

In re Special Reference 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case), answering a Presidential Reference under Article 143, the Supreme Court expanded the Collegium for Supreme Court appointments and High Court transfers to a body comprising the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court.

In the Fourth Judges Case (2015), a five-judge Constitution Bench by a 4:1 majority struck down both the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, 2014, holding that judicial primacy in appointments is essential to the independence of the judiciary under the Basic Structure doctrine.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 124(2); Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998) & NJAC Judgment (2015); M. Laxmikanth, Ch. 26.

stem: With reference to the internal functioning and consultation norms of the Supreme Court Collegium as laid down in the Third Judges Case (1998), consider the following statements:
items: 1. If the successor Chief Justice of India is not among the four senior-most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court, they must still be made part of the Collegium for appointments to the Supreme Court.
2. Even if two Judges of the five-member Collegium express an adverse opinion against a proposed appointment to the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India should not press for such an appointment.

3. For the transfer of a Judge or Chief Justice from one High Court to another, the Supreme Court Collegium comprises only the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Third Judges Case (1998), the Supreme Court Collegium operates on a plurality principle with a two-judge veto rule, mandatory inclusion of the CJI-designate in the seniority line, and a five-member composition for both Supreme Court appointments and High Court transfers.

exp.why: In In re Special Reference 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case), the Supreme Court held that while the Collegium ordinarily consists of the CJI and the four senior-most puisne Judges, if the Judge who is to succeed the CJI by seniority is not one of the four senior-most puisne Judges, that Judge must invariably be made part of the Collegium.

The Third Judges Case established a specific dissent threshold: if two or more Judges in the five-member Collegium express strong and cogent adverse opinions against a candidate's appointment, the Chief Justice of India should not persist with the recommendation.

While the Supreme Court Collegium for the initial appointment of a High Court Judge consists of the CJI and the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court, for the transfer of a High Court Judge or Chief Justice under Article 222, the Collegium consists of the CJI and the four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court (in addition to consulting the Chief Justices of the two High Courts concerned).

ref: In re Special Reference 1 of 1998, (1998) 7 SCC 739; Memorandum of Procedure for Appointment of Supreme Court and High Court Judges.

stem: With reference to the role of the Executive and the scope of judicial review in the appointment of Judges to the higher judiciary in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The President may return a recommendation of the Supreme Court Collegium once for reconsideration on cogent grounds, but if the Collegium unanimously reiterates the recommendation, the President is bound to make the appointment.
2. A recommendation made by the Chief Justice of India without complying with the norms and requirements of the consultation process with the Collegium is not binding on the Government of India.
3. Judicial review of a judicial appointment is permissible on the ground of the candidate's comparative suitability and merits, but not on the ground of lack of constitutional eligibility.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In judicial appointments, the Executive can ask the Collegium to reconsider a recommendation once, is not bound if the CJI bypasses Collegium consultation norms, and judicial review of appointments is strictly confined to 'eligibility' and 'effective consultation' rather than 'suitability'.

exp.why: Under the law laid down in the Second and Third Judges Cases and incorporated in the Memorandum of Procedure, the Union Executive may return a Collegium recommendation once with specific reasons for reconsideration. However, if the Collegium unanimously reiterates its recommendation after considering those reasons, the appointment must be made.

In the Third Judges Case (1998), the Supreme Court explicitly clarified that the sole opinion of the Chief Justice of India does not constitute the 'consultation' required under Articles 124(2) and 217(1); therefore, any recommendation made by the CJI without complying with the Collegium consultation norms is not binding on the Government.

The statement reverses the settled constitutional position. As held in the Second and Third Judges Cases and reaffirmed in Anna Mathews v. Supreme Court of India (2023), judicial review is permissible only on the narrow grounds of lack of constitutional 'eligibility' or lack of effective consultation with the Collegium, whereas the subjective assessment of a candidate's 'suitability' or comparative merit is entirely outside the scope of judicial review.

ref: In re Special Reference 1 of 1998; Anna Mathews v. Supreme Court of India (2023); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 26.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the post-retirement constitutional position of a Judge of the Supreme Court:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 124(7) of the Constitution of India, no person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court shall plead or act in any court or before any authority within the territory of India.

Statement-II: A retired Judge of the Supreme Court is legally eligible to be appointed as the Chairperson of statutory bodies such as the National Human Rights Commission or to preside over quasi-judicial tribunals.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 124(7) imposes a complete constitutional ban on retired Supreme Court Judges pleading or acting as counsel before any court or authority in India to safeguard judicial impartiality, but this bar on legal practice does not prohibit holding statutory or quasi-judicial offices.

exp.why: Article 124(7) of the Constitution expressly prohibits any person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority within the territory of India. The constitutional rationale behind this prohibition is to preserve the dignity and impartiality of the judiciary so that sitting judges do not favour future employers or feel embarrassed when former peers appear before them as advocates.

Both statements are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. Statement-II states a distinct legal rule: presiding over a statutory commission (like the NHRC or Lokpal) or a quasi-judicial tribunal (like the NGT or NCLAT) involves discharging public adjudicatory/statutory functions and does not constitute 'pleading or acting' before an authority as prohibited under Article 124(7).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 124(7); Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 26.

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 124(4) of the Constitution, a Judge of the Supreme Court can be removed from office on the grounds of violation of the Constitution, proved misbehaviour, or incapacity.

2. An address for the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court must be supported by a majority of the total membership of each House of Parliament and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.
3. The address by both Houses of Parliament for the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court must be presented to the President in the same session.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 124(4), a Supreme Court Judge can be removed only on the grounds of 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' via an address passed by both Houses of Parliament with a dual special majority and presented to the President within the same parliamentary session.

exp.why: Article 124(4) specifies only two grounds for the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court: 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'. 'Violation of the Constitution' is the specific ground prescribed under Article 61 for the impeachment of the President of India, not for the removal of a Supreme Court Judge.

Article 124(4) mandates a rigorous dual special majority in each House of Parliament: a majority of the total membership of that House AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.

Article 124(4) explicitly requires that the address passed by each House of Parliament must be 'presented to the President in the same session for such removal' before the President can pass the removal order.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 124(4) and 124(5); Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 26.

stem: Consider the following procedural stages in the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968:
items: 1. Constitution of a three-member Committee comprising a Judge of the Supreme Court, a Chief Justice of a High Court, and a distinguished jurist to investigate the grounds.
2. Exercise of statutory discretion by the Presiding Officer of the House to either admit the motion or refuse to admit it after consulting such persons as he thinks fit.
3. Submission of a written notice of motion signed by not less than 100 members in the case of the Lok Sabha or 50 members in the case of the Rajya Sabha.

4. Adoption of an address for removal by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting in the same session.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the stages given above?
core: While Article 124(4) prescribes the substantive grounds and parliamentary special majority for removing a Supreme Court Judge, the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 lays down the mandatory pre-voting inquiry procedure. Crucially, the Presiding Officer is not bound to admit a notice merely because it satisfies the numerical signature threshold; the three-member Inquiry Committee is constituted only if and after the Presiding Officer admits the motion.

exp.why: This is the third chronological stage. Under Section 3(2) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, the Presiding Officer constitutes the three-member Inquiry Committee (a Supreme Court Judge or CJI, a High Court Chief Justice, and a distinguished jurist) only after formally admitting the motion, not before.

This is the second chronological stage. Under Section 3(1) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, upon receiving a validly signed notice, the Speaker or the Chairman may, after consulting such persons and examining such relevant material as he thinks fit, either admit the motion or refuse to admit the same. Admission is discretionary, not automatic.

This is the first chronological stage. The statutory removal process is initiated only when a notice of motion is given to the Speaker or the Chairman signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or at least 50 members of the Rajya Sabha.

This is the fourth chronological stage among the listed items. Only if the three-member Committee's report finds the Judge guilty of misbehaviour or suffering from incapacity is the motion taken up for consideration and passed by both Houses of Parliament by the special majority under Article 124(4) in the same session for presentation to the President.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 124(4)-(5); Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, Sections 3-6

stem: With reference to the constitutional safeguards ensuring the independence of the Supreme Court of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 121, no discussion shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court in the discharge of his duties except only upon a motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the removal of the Judge.
2. Once appointed, the salaries and allowances of the Judges of the Supreme Court cannot be reduced during their term of office under any provision of the Constitution.

3. The administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including all salaries, allowances, and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court, are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution insulates the Supreme Court from legislative and executive interference through security of tenure, non-votable charged expenditure (Article 146(3)), and immunity from parliamentary discussion on judicial conduct except on a removal motion (Article 121). However, financial protection under Article 125 is subject to the explicit constitutional exception of a Financial Emergency under Article 360(4)(b).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 121 creates an absolute bar on parliamentary discussion regarding the official conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge, carving out a sole exception: such conduct can be discussed in Parliament only upon a substantive motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the Judge's removal.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the proviso to Article 125(2) stipulates that neither the privileges nor the allowances of a Judge nor his rights in respect of leave of absence or pension shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment, Article 360(4)(b) explicitly empowers the President, during the operation of a Financial Emergency proclamation, to issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union, including the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 146(3) read with Article 112(3)(d), the administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including all salaries, allowances, and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court, are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India and are therefore not subject to the vote of Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 112(3)(d), 121, 125, 146(3) and 360(4)(b)

stem: With reference to the appointment of Acting Chief Justice, ad hoc Judges, and retired Judges in the Supreme Court of India, consider the following statements:
