items: 1. If at any time there is a lack of quorum of the permanent Judges of the Supreme Court to hold or continue any session, the President of India directly appoints a duly qualified Judge of a High Court as an ad hoc Judge of the Supreme Court in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

2. Under Article 128, the Chief Justice of India may request a retired Judge of the Supreme Court or a duly qualified retired Judge of a High Court to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court without requiring the prior consent of the President.

3. A retired Judge sitting and acting in the Supreme Court under Article 128 draws the same statutory salary under the Second Schedule as a permanent Judge and is deemed for all constitutional purposes to be a Judge of the Supreme Court.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 126, 127, and 128 allocate appointing authority differently: while the President directly appoints an Acting Chief Justice of India under Article 126, it is the Chief Justice of India—acting with the previous consent of the President—who appoints ad hoc Judges (Article 127) and requests retired Judges to sit and act (Article 128). Moreover, Article 128 explicitly clarifies that a retired Judge sitting on the Court has all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a Supreme Court Judge, 'but shall not otherwise be deemed to be a Judge of that Court'.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 127(1), when there is a lack of quorum of the Judges of the Supreme Court to hold or continue any session, it is the Chief Justice of India (and not the President of India) who appoints a High Court Judge duly qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge to be an ad hoc Judge of the Supreme Court, after obtaining the previous consent of the President and after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 128, the Chief Justice of India may at any time request a retired Judge of the Supreme Court (or of the Federal Court or a High Court Judge duly qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge) to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court only with the previous consent of the President (as well as the consent of the retired Judge concerned).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the concluding clause of Article 128, every retired Judge so requested shall, while sitting and acting, be entitled to such allowances as the President may by order determine and have all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of, 'but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that Court'.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 126, 127 and 128

stem: With reference to the seat of the Supreme Court of India and the establishment of its benches outside Delhi under Article 130 of the Constitution, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Parliament is empowered to establish regional benches of the Supreme Court outside Delhi by enacting an ordinary law after consulting the Chief Justice of India.
opts.B: The President of India may by notification appoint any other place as the seat of the Supreme Court solely on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers.
opts.C: Establishing regional benches of the Supreme Court in different parts of India requires a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368 ratified by at least half of the State Legislatures.
opts.D: Article 130 is an enabling provision that empowers the Chief Justice of India, with the approval of the President, to appoint any other place or places as the seat of the Supreme Court.

core: Article 130 declares that the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, appoint. The provision is discretionary and enabling, vesting the power of initiation exclusively in the Chief Justice of India rather than Parliament or the Union Executive alone.

exp.why: Option D is correct because Article 130 explicitly vests the authority to appoint any place or places other than Delhi as the seat of the Supreme Court in the Chief Justice of India, acting with the approval of the President. It is an enabling, discretionary provision, meaning neither the President nor Parliament can compel the CJI to establish regional benches. Options A and B are incorrect because neither Parliament by law nor the President acting without a decision initiated by the CJI holds the power to designate a seat under Article 130. Option C is incorrect because no Constitutional Amendment under Article 368 is required if the CJI, with Presidential approval, exercises power under Article 130.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 130; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Supreme Court

stem: Consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: When a two-judge or three-judge Bench of the Supreme Court finds that a case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution—which under Article 145(3), like a Presidential Reference under Article 143, must be heard by a minimum of five Judges—it cannot constitute a five-judge Constitution Bench on its own and must place the matter before the Chief Justice of India.

Statement-II: In the constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India is the sole 'Master of the Roster' vested with the exclusive administrative prerogative to constitute Benches and allocate cases among the Judges.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Article 145(3), the minimum number of Judges who are to sit for the purpose of deciding any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or for hearing any Reference under Article 143 shall be five. Because the Chief Justice of India is the exclusive 'Master of the Roster' on the administrative side, smaller Benches cannot constitute larger Benches suo motu and must refer the papers to the CJI for constituting an appropriate Constitution Bench.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 145(3) mandates a minimum Bench strength of five Judges (a Constitution Bench) both for deciding any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution and for hearing a Presidential Reference under Article 143. Under the proviso to Article 145(3) and the Supreme Court Rules, when a smaller Bench is satisfied that such a question is involved, it must refer the case to the Chief Justice of India for constituting a larger Bench rather than constituting one itself.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. As authoritatively settled by the Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand (1998), Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms v. Union of India (2017), and Asok Pande v. Supreme Court of India (2018), the Chief Justice of India is the 'Master of the Roster' and alone holds the administrative prerogative to constitute Benches of the Court and allocate cases. It is precisely because of this exclusive roster prerogative that a Division Bench cannot directly assign a case to a specific five-judge Bench and must place the matter before the CJI.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 145(3); Asok Pande v. Supreme Court of India (2018)

stem: With reference to the original and exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India under Article 131, consider the following statements:
items: 1. This jurisdiction extends only to intergovernmental disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between two or more States, and cannot be invoked by or against a private citizen or corporation.
2. To be maintainable under Article 131, the dispute must involve a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends, and cannot be purely political in nature.

3. This jurisdiction also extends to disputes arising out of pre-constitutional treaties, covenants, or sanads executed with former Indian princely states, provided the Union Government is currently a party to the dispute.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 131 confers original and exclusive federal jurisdiction on the Supreme Court subject to two strict tests: a 'party limitation' (only the Union Government and State Governments can be parties, excluding private individuals or bodies) and a 'subject-matter limitation' (the dispute must involve a question of law or fact on which a legal right depends, and must not fall within constitutional exclusions such as pre-constitutional treaties under the Proviso to Article 131 or inter-state river water disputes barred under Article 262).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 131 explicitly limits the parties before the Supreme Court in an original federal suit to three categories: (a) between the Government of India and one or more States; (b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other; or (c) between two or more States. Private citizens, statutory corporations, or non-state entities cannot be impleaded as parties under Article 131 (State of Bihar v. Union of India, 1970).

Statement 2 is correct. The opening text of Article 131 mandates that the dispute must involve 'any question (whether of law or fact) on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends'. Purely political controversies that do not involve the determination of a constitutional or legal right of a State or the Union are outside the ambit of Article 131.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Proviso to Article 131 explicitly excludes from the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction any dispute arising out of any treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad, or other similar instrument which was entered into or executed before the commencement of the Constitution and continues in operation after such commencement, or which provides that the said jurisdiction shall not extend to such a dispute. Instead, under Article 143(2), the President may refer such pre-constitutional treaty disputes to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 131 and Article 143(2); State of Bihar v. Union of India (1970)

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory exclusions from the exclusive Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India under Article 131, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Any dispute arising out of a treaty, agreement, covenant, or sanad executed before the commencement of the Constitution and continuing in operation is expressly barred from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under the Proviso to Article 131.

2. Disputes regarding the adjustment of certain administrative expenses and pensions between the Union and the States under Article 290 are excluded from Article 131 and are instead determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.

3. An ordinary commercial lawsuit involving an autonomous statutory corporation or government company owned by a State Government against the Union of India does not fall within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 131 begins with the qualifying clause 'Subject to the provisions of this Constitution', which allows other constitutional articles (such as the Proviso to Art. 131, Art. 262, Art. 280, and Art. 290) to carve out exceptions from the Supreme Court's original federal jurisdiction. Furthermore, Article 131 is strictly limited to disputes involving constituent units of the federation regarding legal rights arising in their constitutional relationship, excluding separate corporate personalities.

exp.why: The Proviso to Article 131 explicitly stipulates that the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court shall not extend to a dispute arising out of any treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad, or other similar instrument which, having been entered into or executed before the commencement of the Constitution, continues in operation after such commencement. Such disputes may instead be referred by the President to the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion under Article 143(2).

Because Article 131 is 'Subject to the provisions of this Constitution', Article 290 overrides it with respect to adjustments of certain expenses and pensions between the Union and the States. Under Article 290, in default of agreement as to the contribution sum, the determination is made by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, rather than through an original suit before the Supreme Court.

In State of Bihar v. Union of India (1970), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that a dispute under Article 131 must solely involve the Government of India and one or more States (not any private party or separate legal entity joined either jointly or alternatively) and must concern a legal right relating to their federal constitutional relationship. An autonomous statutory corporation or government company has a separate legal personality distinct from the 'State' for the purposes of Article 131.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 131 & Art. 290; State of Bihar v. Union of India (1970); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes the constitutional scope of the Writ Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 from that of a High Court under Article 226?

opts.A: While the Supreme Court can issue writs throughout the territory of India only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, a High Court possesses a wider subject-matter scope to issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and any other legal right, making the remedy under Article 32 guaranteed and non-discretionary unlike the discretionary remedy under Article 226.
opts.B: Both Article 32 and Article 226 are guaranteed Fundamental Rights under Part III of the Constitution, meaning neither the Supreme Court nor a High Court can decline to entertain a writ petition on the ground that an effective alternative statutory remedy exists.
opts.C: A High Court under Article 226 cannot issue a writ to any government or authority located outside its state territorial limits, even if the cause of action wholly or in part arises within its territorial jurisdiction.
opts.D: Under Article 139 of the Constitution, only a State Legislature by law can confer on the Supreme Court the power to issue writs for purposes other than the enforcement of Fundamental Rights within that State.

core: The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is narrower in subject-matter scope (restricted to Fundamental Rights unless enlarged by Parliament under Art. 139) but wider in territorial reach and mandatory in nature because Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right. Conversely, a High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is wider in subject-matter scope ('for any other purpose') but discretionary in nature.

exp.why: Option A is correct because the Supreme Court under Article 32 can issue writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (unless Parliament confers additional power by law under Article 139), whereas a High Court under Article 226 can issue writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also 'for any other purpose' (enforcement of ordinary legal rights). Furthermore, because Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, the Supreme Court is constituted as the guarantor and protector of Fundamental Rights and cannot refuse to exercise its jurisdiction when a breach of a Fundamental Right is established, whereas the remedy under Article 226 is discretionary. Option B is incorrect because Article 226 is a constitutional right in Part VI, not a Fundamental Right in Part III, and High Courts regularly decline petitions where an efficacious alternative remedy exists. Option C is incorrect because under Article 226(2) (inserted by the 15th Amendment, 1963), a High Court can issue writs to an authority outside its territorial jurisdiction if the cause of action wholly or in part arises within its territory. Option D is incorrect because Article 139 empowers Parliament by law—not State Legislatures—to confer power on the Supreme Court to issue writs for purposes other than Part III.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 32, Art. 139 & Art. 226; Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the Appellate Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in constitutional and civil matters under Articles 132 and 133 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 133, an appeal in a civil proceeding lies to the Supreme Court only if the monetary valuation of the subject-matter in dispute meets a minimum pecuniary threshold prescribed by Parliament by law.

2. Under Article 132, an appeal lies to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree, or final order of a High Court whether in a civil, criminal, or other proceeding, if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
3. Unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, no appeal lies to the Supreme Court under Article 133 from the judgment, decree, or final order of a single Judge of a High Court.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972 abolished the pecuniary limit of Rs. 20,000 for civil appeals to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1), replacing it with a requirement that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance needing a decision by the Supreme Court. Simultaneously, Article 133(3) bars direct civil appeals to the Supreme Court from the judgment of a single Judge of a High Court unless Parliament provides otherwise.

exp.why: Originally, Article 133(1) provided for a civil appeal as a matter of right if the amount or value of the subject-matter of the dispute was not less than Rs. 20,000 (or such other sum as Parliament might specify). However, the 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972 removed the monetary/pecuniary valuation threshold altogether so that access to the apex court depends on the legal importance of the question rather than the wealth of the litigants. Today, an appeal under Article 133(1) requires a High Court certificate that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance and that in the opinion of the High Court the said question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.

Article 132(1) explicitly states that an appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree, or final order of a High Court in the territory of India, whether in a civil, criminal, or other proceeding, if the High Court certifies under Article 134A that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution.

Article 133(3) expressly mandates that notwithstanding anything in that Article, no appeal shall, unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, lie to the Supreme Court from the judgment, decree, or final order of one Judge of a High Court.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 132 & Art. 133; 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972; D.D. Basu Ch. 22

stem: With reference to the Appellate Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in criminal matters under Article 134 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 134(1), an appeal lies to the Supreme Court as a matter of right without a High Court certificate if the High Court has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death, or has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from a subordinate court and in such trial convicted the accused and sentenced him to death.

2. Exercising its power under Article 134(2), Parliament enacted the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, extending the right to appeal without a certificate to cases where a High Court reverses an acquittal or withdraws a case for trial and sentences the accused to imprisonment for life or for a period of not less than ten years.

3. No appeal lies to the Supreme Court as a matter of right without a certificate under Article 134 where a High Court reverses an order of conviction passed by a subordinate court and orders the acquittal of the accused.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 134(1)(a) and (b) coupled with the Parliamentary enlargement under Article 134(2) in 1970 confer a statutory and constitutional right of criminal appeal without a High Court certificate when a High Court reverses an acquittal or withdraws a subordinate trial and imposes death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment of 10 or more years. Conversely, if the High Court reverses a conviction and acquits the accused, there is no appeal as of right under Article 134.

exp.why: Under clauses (a) and (b) of Article 134(1), an appeal lies to the Supreme Court as a matter of right (without requiring a certificate of fitness under clause (c)) in two situations: (a) if the High Court has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death; or (b) if the High Court has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from any court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused person and sentenced him to death.

Article 134(2) empowers Parliament by law to confer on the Supreme Court any further powers to entertain and hear appeals from any judgment, final order, or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court. Acting under this provision, Parliament enacted the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, which allows an appeal without a certificate if the High Court (on reversal of acquittal or withdrawal of trial) sentences the accused to imprisonment for life or to imprisonment for a period of not less than ten years.

The automatic right of appeal under Article 134(1)(a)-(b) and the 1970 Act protects an accused whose acquittal has been turned into a severe conviction by the High Court for the first time. It does not apply in reverse: if a High Court reverses an order of conviction and acquits the accused, no appeal lies as of right under Article 134(1)(a) or (b) (though the State may seek a certificate under Art. 134(1)(c) or petition for Special Leave under Art. 136).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 134; Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970; Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Special Leave to Appeal by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution:
items: Statement-I: Article 136 confers a plenary and discretionary residuary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed by any court or tribunal in the territory of India, including interlocutory orders.

Statement-II: Because the power of judicial review is part of the basic structure of the Constitution, Article 136 places no express constitutional restriction on the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to grant special leave against orders passed by a court-martial or tribunal constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 136(1) vests an extraordinary, discretionary, and plenary residuary appellate power in the Supreme Court that applies even to interlocutory orders and quasi-judicial tribunals. However, Article 136(2) carves out an explicit constitutional exception barring the application of Article 136(1) to any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.

exp.why: Unlike Articles 132 to 134—which apply only to 'final orders' of a High Court—Article 136(1) uses sweeping language ('any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal'). Consequently, the Supreme Court can grant special leave against both final and interlocutory orders of any court or quasi-judicial tribunal, though it remains a discretionary privilege rather than a right of the litigant.

Statement-II is incorrect because Article 136(2) contains an express constitutional exclusion: 'Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to any judgment, determination, sentence or order passed or made by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.' Note, however, that writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 for violation of Fundamental Rights or jurisdictional errors is separate from appellate jurisdiction under Article 136(2).

ref: Constitution of India Art. 136(1) & Art. 136(2); Pritam Singh v. The State (1950); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution:
items: Statement-I: While the Supreme Court may respectfully decline to tender its advisory opinion to the President on a general question of law or fact of public importance, it is constitutionally bound to report its opinion when the President refers a dispute arising out of a pre-constitutional treaty, agreement, covenant, or sanad.

Statement-II: Whereas Article 143(1) uses permissive language ('may report to the President its opinion') for general references of public importance, Article 143(2) uses mandatory language ('shall report to the President its opinion') to provide a constitutional forum for examining pre-constitutional treaty disputes that are expressly barred from the Court's original jurisdiction under the Proviso to Article 131.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 143 bifurcates Presidential References into two distinct categories: discretionary responses under Article 143(1) ('may report') for general questions of law or fact of public importance, and mandatory responses under Article 143(2) ('shall report') for pre-constitutional treaty/covenant disputes excluded from Article 131's original jurisdiction. Regardless of the clause invoked, the resulting opinion remains advisory and does not bind the President.

exp.why: In Re: Special Courts Bill (1978) and the Ismail Faruqui (Ayodhya Reference, 1994) cases, the Supreme Court held that under Article 143(1), it is not bound to answer a reference and may decline to express an opinion for good and cogent reasons (such as if the question is purely socio-political, hypothetical, or superfluous). However, in a reference made under Article 143(2) regarding pre-constitutional treaties or sanads, the Court is constitutionally obligated to report its opinion to the President.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains the constitutional mechanism behind Statement-I. The framers of the Constitution deliberately used 'may' in Article 143(1) and 'shall' in Article 143(2). Because the Proviso to Article 131 barred original suits over pre-constitutional treaties, covenants, and sanads entered into with former Princely States, Article 143(2) mandated that if the President refers such a dispute to the Supreme Court, the Court 'shall' report its opinion thereon so that the executive has authoritative judicial guidance.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 143(1), Art. 143(2) & Proviso to Art. 131; In Re: Special Courts Bill (1978); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the status of the Supreme Court of India as a 'Court of Record' and its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, consider the following statements:
items: 1. As a Court of Record under Article 129 of the Constitution, the judgments, proceedings, and acts of the Supreme Court are recognized as having evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any court.
2. The Supreme Court is empowered to punish for contempt not only of itself, but also of High Courts, subordinate courts, and tribunals functioning throughout the territory of India.

3. The substantive power of the Supreme Court to punish for contempt of itself originates from the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, and can therefore be abridged or extinguished by an ordinary parliamentary law.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 129 read with Article 142(2) confers an inherent, inalienable constitutional power on the Supreme Court as a Court of Record to punish for contempt of itself as well as lower courts across India. While Parliament can regulate contempt procedure via the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, no ordinary statute can abridge or abolish this substantive constitutional jurisdiction.

exp.why: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a 'Court of Record'. In constitutional jurisprudence, a Court of Record possesses two defining traits: first, its acts and judicial proceedings are enrolled for perpetual memory and testimony, carrying unquestionable evidentiary value before any court; second, it has the summary power to punish for contempt.

In Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991), the Supreme Court held that as the apex Court of Record at the head of a unified national judiciary under Article 129, its contempt jurisdiction extends to protecting the dignity and administration of justice not merely of itself, but also of High Courts, subordinate courts, and tribunals across India.

The substantive power of the Supreme Court to punish for contempt is a constitutional power vested directly by Article 129 and Article 142(2), not a statutory creation of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. As affirmed in Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) and In Re: Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995), Parliament's legislative power under Entry 77 of List I and Article 142(2) is regulatory and cannot abridge, dilute, or extinguish the Court's inherent constitutional power under Article 129.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 129 & 142(2); Delhi Judicial Service Assn. v. State of Gujarat (1991); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the Review Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India under Article 137 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments under Article 137 is an absolute constitutional prerogative that is not subject to any law enacted by Parliament.
2. Under the Supreme Court Rules, a review petition operates as a second open-court hearing on merits where a judgment can be reversed merely because an alternative legal interpretation was possible.
3. The Constitution mandates that every review petition must be heard by a Bench of greater numerical strength than the Bench that delivered the original judgment.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 137 explicitly subjects the Supreme Court's review power to parliamentary laws and rules framed under Article 145. A review is not a disguised rehearing of an appeal; it is normally disposed of by circulation in chambers before the same Bench and is confined strictly to patent errors on the face of the record or discovery of new evidence.

exp.why: Article 137 expressly begins with the qualifying clause: 'Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under article 145, the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it.' Thus, the constitutional text itself makes the exercise of review jurisdiction subject to statutory conditions and procedural rules framed under Article 145.

As settled in Kamlesh Verma v. Mayawati (2013), a review is not an appeal in disguise where an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected because another view is possible. Under Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013, review is restricted to three narrow grounds (discovery of new and important evidence, mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or any other sufficient analogous reason) and is ordinarily disposed of by circulation without oral arguments in open court (with an exception carved out for death penalty cases in Mohd. Arif v. Registrar, Supreme Court of India, 2014).

Neither the Constitution nor the Supreme Court Rules mandate a larger Bench for hearing a review petition. On the contrary, Order XLVII Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules mandates that a review application shall, as far as practicable, be circulated to the same Judge or Bench of Judges that delivered the original judgment or order.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 137 & 145; Order XLVII, Supreme Court Rules, 2013; Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the 'Curative Petition' in the Indian judicial system, evolved by the Supreme Court in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It is a judicially innovated remedy anchored in Articles 129, 137, and 142 to prevent abuse of process and cure a gross miscarriage of justice after the dismissal of a review petition, requiring mandatory certification by a Senior Advocate and circulation to the three senior-most Judges along with the Judges who passed the impugned judgment, if available.
opts.B: It is an extraordinary statutory remedy introduced by an amendment to the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, allowing any aggrieved party a second review as a matter of right before a five-Judge Constitution Bench.
opts.C: It can be entertained directly before filing a review petition under Article 137 if the petitioner demonstrates that a subsequent judgment of a coordinate Bench has taken a different legal view on the same statutory provision.
opts.D: Unlike a review petition which is disposed of by circulation in chambers, every curative petition must mandatorily be heard in open court with oral arguments in the presence of the Attorney General for India.

core: Evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) under Articles 129, 137, and 142, a Curative Petition balances the principle of finality of judgments with ex debito justitiae (obligation to cure gross miscarriage of justice or violation of natural justice). To prevent floodgates of litigation, it requires Senior Advocate certification and initial in-chamber scrutiny by the three senior-most Judges plus the original Bench.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), a five-Judge Constitution Bench invoked the Supreme Court's inherent and plenary powers under Articles 129, 137, and 142 to fashion the 'Curative Petition' so that technical finality does not perpetuate a gross miscarriage of justice (such as violation of natural justice where a party was not heard, or judicial bias/non-disclosure of conflict of interest). To prevent abuse, the Court mandated strict procedural guardrails (now codified in Order XLVIII of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013): it lies only after the dismissal of a review petition, requires certification by a Senior Advocate confirming fulfillment of the Rupa Ashok Hurra conditions, and is first circulated in chambers to a Bench of the three senior-most Judges plus the Judges who passed the judgment under challenge (if still in office). Option (B) is incorrect because it is a judicial innovation, not a statutory creation. Option (C) is incorrect because exhaustion of a review petition is a mandatory prerequisite, and a subsequent change in law is not a ground for a curative petition. Option (D) is incorrect because curative petitions are also initially considered by circulation in chambers, and an open-court hearing is granted only if the majority of the Bench concludes that the matter needs hearing.

ref: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) 4 SCC 388; Order XLVIII, Supreme Court Rules, 2013

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the plenary power of the Supreme Court of India under Article 142 of the Constitution:
items: Statement-I: While the Supreme Court can invoke Article 142 to relax procedural requirements or fill legislative vacuums—such as dissolving a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown—it cannot invoke Article 142 to pass an order that directly contravenes an express prohibition in a substantive statute or violates Fundamental Rights.

Statement-II: The equitable power to do 'complete justice' under Article 142(1) is constitutionally structured as a supplementary residual power to bridge legal gaps where existing law is silent or inadequate, rather than as a super-legislative authority to supplant valid substantive enactments.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 142(1) empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree necessary for doing 'complete justice', enabling it to depart from procedural rigours or fill legislative voids (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023). However, as settled in Supreme Court Bar Association (1998), this equitable power is meant to supplement the law and not to supplant substantive statutory prohibitions or Fundamental Rights.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023), a five-Judge Constitution Bench affirmed that the Supreme Court can invoke Article 142(1) to depart from procedural requirements (such as waiving the 6-to-18-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act) and grant divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. Simultaneously, the Bench reiterated the foundational rule laid down in Prem Chand Garg (1963) and Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) that Article 142 cannot be exercised to contravene Fundamental Rights or override specific prohibitions in substantive public policy statutes.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The reason Article 142 permits relaxing procedural bottlenecks or filling legislative gaps (like the Vishaka guidelines or irretrievable breakdown of marriage) while forbidding the violation of express substantive statutes is rooted in the very nature of Article 142(1): it is a corrective, equitable jurisdiction designed 'to supplement the law and not to supplant it', ensuring that the absence or rigidity of procedural law does not defeat justice, without turning the judiciary into a parallel legislature that can nullify valid substantive enactments.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 142; Supreme Court Bar Assn. v. UoI (1998); Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023)

stem: With reference to the Constitution Bench judgment of the Supreme Court in High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2024) concerning Article 142 and interim stay orders, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Interim stay orders granted by High Courts in civil and criminal cases do not automatically stand vacated upon the expiry of six months unless extended by a speaking order.

2. The Supreme Court held that its plenary power under Article 142 cannot be invoked to issue blanket time-bound directions that divest High Courts of their judicial discretion to grant or vacate interim relief under Article 226.

3. In the constitutional scheme of India's integrated judiciary, High Courts are constitutionally subordinate to the Supreme Court in the exercise of their original writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: In High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of UP (2024), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench overruled Asian Resurfacing (2018), holding that interim stay orders of High Courts do not automatically expire after six months. The Court emphasized that High Courts are autonomous constitutional courts (not subordinate to the Supreme Court) whose judicial discretion cannot be curtailed by blanket directions under Article 142.

exp.why: In High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2024), a five-Judge Constitution Bench overruled the 2018 three-Judge Bench ruling in Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd. v. CBI. The Constitution Bench held that a direction mandating the automatic vacation of interim stay orders of High Courts in civil and criminal trials after six months defeats justice, punishes litigants for systemic delays over which they have no control, and violates principles of natural justice by vacating judicial orders without a hearing.

The 2024 Constitution Bench explicitly ruled that the Supreme Court should not exercise its plenary jurisdiction under Article 142 to issue blanket, across-the-board guidelines that fetter or take away the judicial discretion of High Courts in deciding when to grant, extend, or vacate interim orders under Articles 226 and 227.

Reiterating Tirupati Balaji Developers (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar (2004), the five-Judge Bench in High Court Bar Association, Allahabad (2024) underscored that High Courts are independent constitutional Courts of Record and are NOT constitutionally or administratively subordinate to the Supreme Court. While the Supreme Court occupies the apex position in the appellate hierarchy, High Courts enjoy wider original writ jurisdiction under Article 226 than the Supreme Court under Article 32 and exercise sovereign judicial power within their constitutional sphere.

ref: High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024 INSC 150); Constitution of India, Articles 142 & 226

stem: With reference to the binding nature of judicial precedents under Article 141 and enforcement of judicial authority under Article 144 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The expression 'all courts within the territory of India' in Article 141 does not include the Supreme Court itself, leaving the Supreme Court free to depart from or overrule its previous judgments in appropriate cases.

2. What is binding on all courts under Article 141 is the ratio decidendi of a Supreme Court judgment, and not obiter dicta or fact-specific relief granted solely in exercise of equitable power under Article 142.
3. Under Article 144 of the Constitution, all authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India are constitutionally mandated to act in aid of the Supreme Court.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 141, the ratio decidendi of Supreme Court judgments binds all courts in India except the Supreme Court itself (Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar, 1955), while purely fact-specific directions under Article 142 do not constitute binding precedent. Complementing this, Article 144 obligates all civil and judicial authorities across India to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

exp.why: In the landmark seven-Judge Bench ruling in Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1955), the Supreme Court held that the words 'all courts within the territory of India' in Article 141 do not include the Supreme Court itself. If the Supreme Court were bound by its own decisions under Article 141, constitutional interpretation would become frozen and erroneous precedents could only be corrected by constitutional amendment.

Under the doctrine of stare decisis embedded in Article 141, only the ratio decidendi (the underlying legal principle and reasoning essential to decide the issue) has the force of 'law declared by the Supreme Court'. Passing observations not necessary for the decision (obiter dicta) and equitable, one-time directions issued purely on the peculiar facts of a case under Article 142 (as clarified in State of Punjab v. Rafiq Masih, 2014 and Indian Bank v. Abs Marine Products, 2006) do not constitute binding precedent under Article 141.

Article 144 of the Constitution explicitly provides: 'All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.' This imposes a direct constitutional duty on every executive and judicial functionary at both the Union and State levels to enforce and assist in the execution of the Supreme Court's orders and writs.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 141 & 144; Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar (1955); Laxmikanth Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the enlargement of the jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 138(1), Parliament can by law confer further jurisdiction and powers on the Supreme Court with respect to any of the matters in the Union List without requiring the consent of State Legislatures.

2. Under Article 138(2), the Supreme Court can exercise further jurisdiction with respect to any matter outside the Union List solely on the basis of an executive agreement between the Government of India and a State Government, without requiring any parliamentary enactment.

3. Under Article 139, Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court the power to issue directions, orders, or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus and quo warranto, for any purposes other than the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the baseline jurisdiction of the Supreme Court Cannot be curtailed by ordinary legislation, the Constitution under Articles 138, 139, and 140 explicitly empowers Parliament to enlarge the Court's jurisdiction by law, subject to specific federal safeguards when matters outside the Union List are involved.

exp.why: Under Article 138(1) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any of the matters in the Union List as Parliament may by law confer. Since legislative competence over the Union List vests exclusively in Parliament, an ordinary parliamentary statute suffices without requiring ratification by State Legislatures.

Article 138(2) imposes a dual requirement for conferring further jurisdiction with respect to any matter outside the Union List: first, a special agreement between the Government of India and the Government of a State, and second, an enabling law passed by Parliament providing for the exercise of such jurisdiction and powers by the Supreme Court. An executive agreement alone is insufficient.

While Article 32(2) originally restricts the Supreme Court's constitutional writ jurisdiction to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III, Article 139 explicitly empowers Parliament to confer by law on the Supreme Court the power to issue directions, orders, or writs (including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari) for any purposes other than those mentioned in Article 32(2).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 138, 139 & 140; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 26 (Supreme Court)

stem: With reference to the constitutional mechanisms relating to the transfer of cases and exercise of judicial powers under the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Article 139A(1) : Power of the Supreme Court to withdraw cases involving the same or substantially the same questions of law of general importance pending before one or more High Courts and dispose of all such cases itself
2. Article 139A(2) : Power of the President of India, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, to transfer any suit, appeal, or other proceeding from one High Court to another High Court
3. Article 32(3) : Exclusive power of the Supreme Court to authorize any subordinate court within India to exercise the writ powers conferred upon the Supreme Court under Article 32(2)
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Article 139A vests the judicial power to withdraw or transfer cases between High Courts strictly in the Supreme Court itself, whereas Article 32(3) vests the legislative competence to authorize other courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights strictly in Parliament.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Article 139A(1) (inserted by the 42nd Amendment and modified by the 44th Amendment), where cases involving the same or substantially the same questions of law of general importance are pending before the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts, or before two or more High Courts, the Supreme Court may withdraw the case or cases pending before the High Court(s) and dispose of all the cases itself—either on its own motion (suo motu), or on an application made by the Attorney-General of India or by a party to any such case.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Under Article 139A(2), the power to transfer any case, appeal, or other proceedings pending before any High Court to any other High Court (if deemed expedient for the ends of justice) vests exclusively in the Supreme Court of India, not in the President of India. The President, after consultation with the CJI under Article 222, has the executive power to transfer High Court Judges, not judicial cases.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Under Article 32(3), it is Parliament by law—and not the Supreme Court—that may empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the writ powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under Article 32(2), without prejudice to the powers of the Supreme Court.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 32(3) and 139A; D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the judicial review of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: Any law placed in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution after April 24, 1973 does not enjoy blanket immunity under Article 31B and is open to judicial review if it damages or destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution as reflected in Articles 14, 19, and 21.

Statement-II: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 amended the text of Article 31B to insert an explicit proviso subjecting all Ninth Schedule enactments inserted after April 24, 1973 to judicial scrutiny under the Golden Triangle of Part III.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The subjection of post-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule laws to the Basic Structure test stems entirely from the Supreme Court's constitutional interpretation in Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007) rather than any textual amendment to Article 31B.

exp.why: In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that all laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the date on which the landmark Kesavananda Bharati judgment propounding the Basic Structure doctrine was delivered) are open to challenge on the ground that they abrogate Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 in a manner that damages or destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution, evaluated through the 'direct impact and effect' (rights test / essence of rights) standard.

The text of Article 31B has never been amended since its original insertion by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 did not insert any proviso into Article 31B. The cut-off date of April 24, 1973 is a judicially evolved line of demarcation established in Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) and reaffirmed in I.R. Coelho (2007), based on the date the Basic Structure limitation on Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 was declared in Kesavananda Bharati.

ref: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 2 SCC 1; Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981); Constitution Art. 31B

stem: With reference to the judicial doctrines applied by the Supreme Court of India in constitutional adjudication, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Doctrine of Eclipse as applied to Article 13(1), a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not wiped out from the statute book ab initio, but remains in a dormant condition and revives automatically if a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency.

2. Under the Doctrine of Prospective Overruling first invoked in I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court declares that its new constitutional interpretation will govern only future transactions while preserving the validity of past actions taken under the overruled law.

3. Under the Doctrine of Severability, even where the valid and invalid provisions of an impugned statute are so inextricably interwoven that the remainder cannot stand independently, the Court must rewrite the invalid clauses to save the legislation rather than striking down the entire statute.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Constitutional adjudication balances the supremacy of Part III with legal continuity: the Doctrine of Eclipse preserves dormant statutes pending constitutional amendments, Prospective Overruling protects settled past transactions, and Severability excises only separable unconstitutional provisions without judicial rewriting.

exp.why: As laid down in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), a pre-constitutional law that becomes inconsistent with Part III under Article 13(1) is not dead for all purposes or obliterated from the statute book ab initio. It is merely overshadowed ('eclipsed') by the Fundamental Right and remains dormant. Once a constitutional amendment removes the shadow or impediment, the law becomes free from the infirmity and becomes enforceable again without requiring fresh re-enactment.

In I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court adopted the Doctrine of Prospective Overruling to avoid administrative and legal chaos. Under this doctrine, when the Court overrules an earlier precedent or invalidates a long-standing legal position, it restricts the operation of the new ruling to future cases and transactions while leaving past transactions and vested rights undisturbed.

As settled by the Supreme Court in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957), the Doctrine of Severability applies only when the valid and invalid parts of a statute are distinct and separable. If the valid and invalid provisions are so inextricably mixed up that they cannot be separated from one another, the invalidity of a portion results in the invalidity of the entire Act; moreover, the judiciary cannot usurp legislative power by rewriting inextricably flawed statutory text.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 13; M.P. Jain, Indian Constitutional Law (Doctrines of Eclipse, Severability & Prospective Overruling)

stem: With reference to the doctrines of constitutional interpretation applied by the Supreme Court to resolve disputes concerning the federal distribution of legislative powers, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Doctrine of Pith and Substance, if an enactment falls substantially within the legislative competence assigned to a Legislature under the Seventh Schedule, it does not become invalid merely because it incidentally encroaches upon a matter assigned to another Legislature.
2. When applying the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation, the Supreme Court conducts an inquiry into the mala fide motives or bad faith of the Legislature that passed the impugned statute.

3. Under the Doctrine of Territorial Nexus flowing from Article 245, a State law is not invalid on the ground of extra-territorial impact if there exists a real and sufficient connection between the legislating State and the subject-matter located outside its geographical boundaries.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Federal interpretation doctrines examine the substantive character (Pith and Substance), disguised transgression of competence (Colourable Legislation), and real connection (Territorial Nexus) of a statute, while strictly refraining from inquiring into the subjective motives or bona fides of a coordinate Legislature.

exp.why: Because legislative entries in the Three Lists of the Seventh Schedule inevitably overlap, the Supreme Court applies the Doctrine of Pith and Substance (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, 1951). If the 'true nature and character' (pith and substance) of the legislation falls within the enacting Legislature's allotted List, incidental trenching upon an entry in another List does not invalidate the law.

As authoritatively settled by the Constitution Bench in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953), the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation (founded on the maxim 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly') does NOT involve any question of bona fides or mala fides on the part of the Legislature. Courts never impute bad faith or improper motives to a sovereign Legislature; the doctrine resolves itself purely into a question of legislative competence—whether the Legislature has transgressed its constitutional limits in a disguised or covert form.

While Article 245(1) empowers a State Legislature to make laws for the whole or any part of the State, the Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla (1957) held that under the Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, a State law affecting persons or objects outside its borders is valid if the connection (nexus) between the State and the subject-matter is real and sufficient (not illusory), and the liability sought to be imposed is pertinent to that connection.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 245 & 246; K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953); State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla (1957)

stem: With reference to the procedural innovations evolved by the Supreme Court of India in the exercise of its constitutional and Public Interest Litigation (PIL) jurisdiction, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Relaxation of Locus Standi : Permitting any bona fide public-spirited citizen or social action group to move the Court under Article 32 to enforce the Fundamental Rights of socially or economically disadvantaged persons unable to approach the Court themselves
2. Epistolary Jurisdiction : Treating letters or postcards addressed to the Court highlighting grave violations of Fundamental Rights as formal writ petitions by relaxing strict rules of pleading
3. Continuing Mandamus : Quashing an already executed judicial order of an inferior court or statutory tribunal on the ground of a patent error of law apparent on the face of the record

4. Curative Jurisdiction : Extraordinary jurisdiction exercised under Articles 137 and 142 after the dismissal of a review petition to prevent gross miscarriage of justice arising from a violation of natural justice or apprehension of bias
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Through judicial procedural innovations—such as relaxing locus standi, epistolary petitions, continuing mandamus, and curative petitions—the Supreme Court transformed Article 32 from an adversarial individual remedy into an accessible instrument of structural and corrective justice.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. In S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) and Peoples Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982), the Supreme Court relaxed the traditional Anglo-Saxon rule of locus standi (which restricted standing solely to the aggrieved individual), allowing any public-spirited citizen acting bona fide to petition the Court on behalf of persons who, due to poverty, disability, or socially disadvantaged position, cannot approach the Court for relief.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Epistolary jurisdiction (a term popularized by Prof. Upendra Baxi and applied by Justice P.N. Bhagwati in Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India and Sunil Batra II) refers to the Court's practice of treating letters, postcards, or telegrams addressed to it regarding human rights violations as formal writ petitions under Article 32.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Quashing an already executed judicial or quasi-judicial order of an inferior court or tribunal for an error of law apparent on the face of the record or want of jurisdiction is the classical function of the writ of Certiorari. In contrast, 'Continuing Mandamus' (evolved in Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997) is a procedural mechanism whereby the Court, instead of disposing of a writ petition with a one-time final command, keeps the petition pending and issues periodic interim directions requiring executive/investigating agencies to report ongoing compliance.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Evolved by a 5-Judge Constitution Bench in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) under Articles 129, 137, and 142, a Curative Petition lies even after the dismissal of a Review Petition on extremely narrow grounds—specifically, violation of the principles of natural justice (not being heard) or reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of a Judge—to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriage of justice.

ref: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981); Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997); Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002); M. Laxmikanth, Ch. 29 (PIL)

stem: With reference to the appointment and constitutional qualifications of Judges of a High Court in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Constitution does not prescribe a minimum age for appointment as a Judge of a High Court, it empowers the President to appoint a distinguished jurist as a High Court Judge.
2. For recommending appointments of Judges to a High Court, the Supreme Court Collegium comprises the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court.

3. While computing the ten-year period required to qualify for appointment as a High Court Judge, the period during which a person has held a judicial office in India can be combined with the period for which they have been an advocate of a High Court.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 217(2) of the Constitution does not include the 'distinguished jurist' category for High Court appointments (unlike Article 124(3) for the Supreme Court), and the Supreme Court Collegium for High Court appointments comprises the CJI plus two senior-most Supreme Court Judges.

exp.why: Although the Constitution does not prescribe a minimum age for appointment as a High Court Judge, Article 217(2) contains no provision for appointing a 'distinguished jurist' as a Judge of a High Court. The 'distinguished jurist' qualification exists exclusively for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court under Article 124(3)(c).

Under the Second and Third Judges Cases (1993 and 1998), the Supreme Court Collegium that recommends appointments to High Courts consists of the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court (whereas for Supreme Court appointments and High Court transfers, the Collegium consists of the CJI and four senior-most Judges).

Under Explanations (a) and (aa) to Article 217(2), in computing the ten-year period during which a person has held judicial office in the territory of India or has been an advocate of a High Court, any period during which the person has held judicial office after becoming an advocate, or been an advocate after holding judicial office, is combined.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 217(2); Third Judges Case (1998); Laxmikanth on High Courts

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the expenditure on salaries and pensions of High Court Judges:
items: Statement-I: While the salaries and allowances of the Judges of a State High Court are determined by Parliament by law and charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Statement-II: High Court Judges belong to a single integrated judicial system and are constitutionally liable to be transferred from one High Court to another across different States during their tenure.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Articles 221, 202(3)(d), and 112(3)(d)(iii), Parliament determines the salaries, allowances, and pensions of High Court Judges by law; salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State where they serve, whereas pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India because judges may serve in multiple states through transfers.

exp.why: Under Article 221, the salaries, allowances, and pensions of High Court Judges are determined by Parliament by law (not by the State Legislature). Under Article 202(3)(d), their salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, whereas under Article 112(3)(d)(iii), their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Because India has an integrated judicial system where High Court Judges can be transferred between different State High Courts under Article 222, charging a retired judge's entire pension to the Consolidated Fund of the last State where they served (or apportioning it across multiple States) would be fiscally anomalous; hence the Constitution charges their pension on the Consolidated Fund of India.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 112(3)(d)(iii), 202(3)(d), 221 & 222

stem: With reference to the oath, resignation, and post-retirement restrictions of High Court Judges, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person appointed as a Judge of a High Court subscribes to an oath or affirmation before the Governor of the State, but addresses their resignation in writing to the President of India.

2. A retired permanent Judge of a High Court is constitutionally permitted to plead or act before the Supreme Court and before any High Court other than the High Court(s) in which they held office as a permanent Judge.

3. An Additional Judge of a High Court who demits office upon the expiry of their term without being made a permanent Judge is not barred under Article 220 from returning to legal practice before the same High Court.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Governor administers the oath to a High Court Judge under Article 219, the President is the appointing and resignation-receiving authority under Article 217; further, the post-retirement restriction on pleading under Article 220 applies exclusively to those who have held office as a 'permanent' Judge.

exp.why: Under Article 219, every person appointed to be a Judge of a High Court makes and subscribes an oath or affirmation before the Governor of the State (or some person appointed in that behalf by the Governor). However, under Proviso (a) to Article 217(1), a Judge may resign their office by writing under their hand addressed to the President.

Under Article 220 (as amended by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956), no person who has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court shall plead or act in any court or before any authority in India except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts where they did not serve as a permanent Judge.

Article 220 specifically uses the phrase 'has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court'. This phrasing was deliberately introduced by the 7th Amendment Act, 1956, so that advocates appointed for temporary terms up to two years as Additional or Acting Judges under Article 224 are not barred from resuming legal practice in the same High Court if not confirmed as permanent Judges.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 217, 219, 220 & 224

stem: With reference to the constitutional framework and binding Supreme Court precedents governing the transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another under Article 222 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Chief Justice of India is required to consult only the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court and the Governor of the receiving State before recommending a transfer.
opts.B: In addition to the Collegium of four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India must consult the Chief Justices of both the High Court from which the Judge is being transferred and the High Court to which the transfer is proposed.
opts.C: A Judge of a High Court cannot be transferred to another High Court without their prior written consent, even if the transfer is proposed in public interest.
opts.D: Once the President issues a transfer order after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the transfer is completely immune from judicial review on all grounds.

core: Under Article 222 read with the Third Judges Case (1998), for transferring a High Court Judge, the CJI must consult the four senior-most Supreme Court Judges as well as the Chief Justices of both the transferor and transferee High Courts; the consent of the judge is not required, though the transfer must be in public interest and non-punitive.

exp.why: Option B is correct because in the Third Judges Case (In re Special Reference 1 of 1998), the Supreme Court held that for the transfer of a High Court Judge (including a Chief Justice), the Chief Justice of India must consult the four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court and, in addition, the Chief Justices of the two High Courts concerned (one from which the Judge is being transferred and the other receiving them). Option A is incorrect because the Collegium for transfers comprises four (not two) senior-most SC Judges and does not require the Governor's consultation in the Collegium process. Option C is incorrect because the prior consent of the Judge being transferred is not constitutionally required under Article 222 if the transfer is made in public interest. Option D is incorrect because a transfer order is subject to limited judicial review (at the instance of the transferred judge alone) if it is punitive or made without the mandatory plurality consultation.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 222; Third Judges Case (1998)

stem: With reference to the appointment of Additional, Acting, and Retired Judges in the High Courts, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 224 of the Constitution, the Chief Justice of a High Court, with the previous consent of the President, appoints Additional Judges for a period not exceeding two years to clear temporary arrears of business.

2. An Acting Judge appointed to perform the duties of a permanent High Court Judge who is temporarily unable to perform the duties of their office cannot hold office after attaining the age of sixty-two years.

3. A retired High Court Judge who sits and acts as a Judge of a High Court under Article 224A enjoys all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a Judge of that High Court, but is not otherwise deemed to be a Judge of that High Court.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Additional and Acting Judges under Article 224 are appointed directly by the President (up to 2 years and subject to the 62-year age limit), whereas under Article 224A, it is the Chief Justice of the High Court who, with the previous consent of the President, requests a retired High Court Judge to sit and act.

exp.why: Statement 1 confuses Article 224 with Article 224A. Under Article 224(1), it is the President (and not the Chief Justice of the High Court with the previous consent of the President) who appoints duly qualified persons as Additional Judges of the High Court for a period not exceeding two years due to temporary increase in business or arrears of work. The mechanism of the Chief Justice of the High Court acting with the previous consent of the President applies to requesting retired judges to sit and act under Article 224A.

Under Article 224(2) and 224(3), the President may appoint a duly qualified person to act as a Judge of a High Court when any permanent Judge (other than the Chief Justice) is unable to perform the duties of their office or is appointed to act temporarily as Chief Justice, and no person appointed as an Additional or Acting Judge shall hold office after attaining the age of 62 years.

Under Article 224A, every retired High Court Judge who sits and acts as a Judge of a High Court upon the request of the Chief Justice of that High Court (with the previous consent of the President and the consent of the retired judge) is entitled to allowances determined by the President by order and has all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of, 'but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that High Court'.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 223, 224 & 224A

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the writ jurisdiction of High Courts in India:
items: Statement-I: A High Court exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226 can issue directions, orders, or writs not only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights, but also against a government or authority whose seat is located outside its territorial jurisdiction.

Statement-II: Article 226 explicitly empowers every High Court to issue writs 'for any other purpose' in addition to Part III rights, and extends this jurisdiction to any authority outside its territory if the cause of action arises wholly or in part within its territorial limits.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 is wider in subject-matter scope than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32 because of the phrase 'for any other purpose' in Article 226(1), and under Article 226(2), it can reach respondents located outside the State if the cause of action arises wholly or in part within its territorial limits.

exp.why: Unlike the Supreme Court under Article 32 (which can issue writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights), a High Court under Article 226 can issue writs for enforcing both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights, and can also issue writs to any Government, authority, or person located outside its territorial jurisdiction under specified constitutional conditions.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Article 226(1) includes the words 'for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose', which enables the enforcement of non-fundamental legal rights. Furthermore, Article 226(2) (originally inserted by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963) provides that a High Court may exercise this power in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises, notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 226(1) & 226(2); L. Chandra Kumar v. UoI (1997)

stem: With reference to the power of superintendence of a High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It encompasses both administrative and judicial superintendence over all courts and tribunals functioning within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court, and can be exercised suo motu even without an application by an aggrieved party.

2. Unlike a writ of certiorari under Article 226 which primarily enables the High Court to quash or annul an impugned order, the supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 further empowers the High Court to issue substantive directions guiding the subordinate court or tribunal on the manner in which it must proceed.

3. Because judicial superintendence under Article 227 forms a part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution, this supervisory power under Article 227 extends without exception to tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 227 vests every High Court with plenary administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its territory to keep them within the bounds of their authority. However, Article 227(4) explicitly carves out a constitutional exception excluding any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces from the High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227.

exp.why: Under Article 227(1), every High Court has superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction. The Supreme Court has consistently held (including in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997) that this power is both administrative and judicial in nature, is a basic feature of the Constitution, and can be invoked suo motu to prevent miscarriage of justice.

As clarified by the Supreme Court in Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Ahmad Ishaque (1955) and Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai (2003), while in a writ of certiorari under Article 226 the High Court can only demolish or quash the offending order of an inferior court or tribunal and cannot substitute its own order, under the supervisory jurisdiction of Article 227 the High Court can additionally guide, direct, or remand the matter with positive procedural instructions to the subordinate forum.

Article 227(4) contains an explicit constitutional exception: 'Nothing in this article shall be deemed to confer on a High Court powers of superintendence over any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.' Thus, while judicial review under Article 226 is available against orders of the Armed Forces Tribunal (Union of India v. Parashotam Dass, 2023), supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227(4) remains constitutionally barred over military courts-martial and the Armed Forces Tribunal.
