ref: Constitution of India, Article 227; L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997); Laxmikanth Ch. 34

stem: With reference to the status and powers of a High Court as a Court of Record under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 215, the judgments, proceedings, and acts of a High Court are preserved for perpetual memory and testimony, and their evidentiary truth cannot be questioned when produced before any court subordinate to it.

2. Even in the absence of a specific constitutional provision analogous to Article 137, a High Court, as a superior court of record of plenary jurisdiction, possesses an inherent power to review its own orders passed under Article 226 to correct palpable errors and prevent miscarriage of justice.

3. Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, a High Court is empowered to punish not only for contempt of itself, but also for contempt of courts subordinate to it, provided such contempt of the subordinate court does not already constitute a punishable offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 215 designates every High Court as a Court of Record with all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself. By virtue of being a superior Court of Record, a High Court inherently possesses the power to correct its own records and review orders passed under Article 226, while Section 10 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 extends its contempt jurisdiction to protect subordinate courts.

exp.why: Article 215 declares that every High Court shall be a court of record. A defining attribute of a court of record is that its judicial records and proceedings carry unimpeachable evidentiary value and cannot be challenged when produced before any subordinate court.

While Article 137 explicitly confers the power of review on the Supreme Court, no separate article uses the word 'review' for High Courts. However, in Shivdeo Singh v. State of Punjab (1963) and M.M. Thomas v. State of Kerala (2000), the Supreme Court held that a High Court, being a superior Court of Record under Article 215 and exercising plenary jurisdiction under Article 226, has the inherent power and duty to review its own decisions to correct errors apparent on the face of the record.

Under Section 10 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, every High Court has the same jurisdiction, powers, and authority in respect of contempt of courts subordinate to it as it exercises in respect of contempt of itself. The proviso to Section 10 stipulates that no High Court shall take cognizance of a contempt alleged to have been committed in respect of a subordinate court where such contempt is an offence punishable under the general penal code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 215; Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (Section 10); M.M. Thomas v. State of Kerala (2000)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional jurisdiction and orders of the High Courts:
items: Statement-I: Interim stay orders granted by a High Court in pending civil and criminal trials do not automatically expire or stand vacated upon the lapse of six months.

Statement-II: The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution is wider in its subject-matter scope than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32, as a High Court can issue writs not only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights but also for any other purpose.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench overruled Asian Resurfacing (2018) and held that interim stay orders of High Courts cannot automatically stand vacated after six months, as automatic vacation without judicial application of mind violates natural justice and the constitutional autonomy of High Courts. Separately, Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ subject-matter jurisdiction than Article 32 by covering non-fundamental legal rights.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court overruled the 2018 judgment in Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd. v. CBI. The Court held that constitutional courts should not fix blanket time-bound schedules leading to the automatic vacation of interim stay orders passed by High Courts after six months, because automatic vacation without hearing the parties violates the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem), prejudices litigants for institutional delays beyond their control, and infringes upon the judicial discretion of High Courts, which are constitutional courts and not administratively subordinate to the Supreme Court.

Statement-II is also correct, because Article 32 can be invoked only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 226 empowers a High Court to issue writs both for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose' (i.e., enforcement of ordinary legal rights). However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: the prohibition on automatic six-month expiry of stay orders in civil and criminal trials stems from principles of natural justice, judicial application of mind, and the limits of Article 142, rather than the distinction between Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights in writ jurisdiction.

ref: High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (5-Judge Bench, 2024); Constitution of India, Articles 142 and 226

stem: Under the Constitution of India, with reference to the establishment of a common High Court for two or more States and the extension of the jurisdiction of a State High Court to a Union Territory, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The President of India is empowered to establish a common High Court for two or more States by issuing a public notification after consulting the Chief Justice of India and the Governors of the concerned States.
opts.B: Where the High Court of a State exercises jurisdiction in relation to a Union Territory, the Legislature of that State may by law expand or modify the territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction of the High Court over that Union Territory.
opts.C: Parliament alone is empowered by law to establish a common High Court for two or more States and a Union Territory, and the Legislature of the concerned State has no power to increase, restrict, or abolish the High Court's jurisdiction in relation to that Union Territory.
opts.D: The jurisdiction of a State High Court can be extended to or excluded from an adjoining Union Territory only after a resolution to that effect is ratified by the Legislature of the concerned State.

core: Under Articles 230 and 231 of the Constitution, Parliament enjoys exclusive legislative competence to extend or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court over any Union Territory and to establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States and a Union Territory. Article 230(2) expressly bars a State Legislature from increasing, restricting, or abolishing the jurisdiction of its High Court in relation to a Union Territory.

exp.why: Option C is correct. Under Article 231(1), Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States and a Union Territory. Under Article 230(1), Parliament may by law extend the jurisdiction of a High Court to, or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court from, any Union Territory. Furthermore, Article 230(2) explicitly provides that where the High Court of a State exercises jurisdiction in relation to a Union Territory, nothing in the Constitution shall be construed as empowering the Legislature of the State to increase, restrict, or abolish that jurisdiction. Option A is incorrect because this power vests in Parliament by law, not in the President by executive notification. Options B and D are incorrect because the State Legislature has neither the power to modify the High Court's jurisdiction over a Union Territory nor a veto/ratification role under Article 230.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 230 and 231; Laxmikanth Ch. 34

stem: With reference to the constitutional relationship between a High Court and the Subordinate Courts in a State, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the initial appointment, posting, and promotion of District Judges are made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court under Article 233, the subsequent control over subordinate courts—including the posting, promotion, and grant of leave to persons in the judicial service holding any post inferior to that of a District Judge—vests exclusively in the High Court under Article 235.

2. In exercising disciplinary control under Article 235, the High Court alone is competent to hold departmental inquiries against subordinate judicial officers, and its recommendation for dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank is binding on the Governor.

3. Under Article 228, if a High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, it is mandatory for the High Court to withdraw the case to itself.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 233 and 235 establish a clear constitutional demarcation to insulate the subordinate judiciary from executive interference: while the Governor issues the formal order of initial appointment of District Judges in consultation with the High Court, operational and disciplinary control over all subordinate courts rests wholly with the High Court under Article 235. Additionally, Article 228 uses the mandatory term 'shall withdraw' whenever a subordinate court case hinges on a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.

exp.why: Under Article 233(1), appointments of persons to be, and the posting and promotion of, District Judges in any State are made by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court. Once appointed, and for all posts inferior to the post of District Judge, Article 235 vests complete control over district courts and courts subordinate thereto—including posting, promotion, and grant of leave—exclusively in the High Court.

The Supreme Court (e.g., in State of West Bengal v. Nripendra Nath Bagchi and Registrar, High Court of Orissa v. Sisir Kanta Satapathy) has held that 'control' under Article 235 includes complete disciplinary jurisdiction. To preserve judicial independence, only the High Court can initiate and conduct disciplinary inquiries against subordinate judges; while the formal order of major punishment (dismissal, removal, compulsory retirement, or reduction in rank) is issued in the name of the Governor as the appointing authority under Article 311, the High Court's recommendation is binding on the Governor.

Article 228 states that if the High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, 'it shall withdraw the case' and may either dispose of the case itself or determine the said question of law and return the case to the subordinate court. Subordinate courts have no jurisdiction to finally adjudicate substantial questions of constitutional interpretation.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 228, 233, and 235; Laxmikanth Ch. 35

stem: Consider the following constitutional provisions governing the recruitment, scope, and composition of the Subordinate Judiciary under Chapter VI of Part VI of the Constitution of India:
items: 1. In the recruitment of persons other than District Judges to the judicial service of a State under Article 234, the Governor is constitutionally required to consult both the State Public Service Commission and the High Court, whereas the State Public Service Commission has no constitutional role in the appointment of District Judges under Article 233.

2. Under Article 236(a), the constitutional expression 'District Judge' is not confined to civil jurisdiction alone and explicitly includes a Sessions Judge, an Additional Sessions Judge, and an Assistant Sessions Judge; further, under Article 237, the Governor may by public notification direct that the provisions of Chapter VI of Part VI shall apply to any class or classes of Magistrates in the State.

3. Under Article 236(b), the constitutional expression 'judicial service' includes both civil judicial officers inferior to the post of District Judge and Executive Magistrates exercising preventive jurisdiction under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution prescribes distinct consultation procedures for District Judges (Article 233: Governor in consultation with High Court) and other subordinate judges (Article 234: Governor in consultation with State PSC and High Court). While Article 236(a) broadly defines 'District Judge' to include Sessions Judges, Article 236(b) strictly restricts 'judicial service' to posts of District Judge and inferior civil judicial posts, excluding Executive Magistrates unless specifically notified under Article 237.

exp.why: Under Article 233(1), District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court alone. In contrast, under Article 234, appointments of persons other than District Judges to the judicial service of a State are made by the Governor in accordance with rules made by him after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to such State.

Under Article 236(a), the expression 'district judge' explicitly includes judge of a city civil court, additional district judge, joint district judge, assistant district judge, chief judge of a small cause court, chief presidency magistrate, additional chief presidency magistrate, sessions judge, additional sessions judge, and assistant sessions judge. Furthermore, Article 237 empowers the Governor by public notification to direct that the provisions of Chapter VI of Part VI and rules made thereunder shall apply in relation to any class or classes of magistrates in the State as they apply to persons appointed to the judicial service.

Under Article 236(b), the expression 'judicial service' is strictly defined to mean 'a service consisting exclusively of persons intended to fill the post of district judge and other civil judicial posts inferior to the post of district judge.' Executive Magistrates belong to the executive cadre of the State administration and do not form part of the 'judicial service' under Article 236(b).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 233, 234, 236, and 237; Laxmikanth Ch. 35

stem: With reference to the structural organisation and sentencing powers of the subordinate criminal judiciary under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, consider the following statements:
items: 1. State Governments are mandated to notify every city or town with a population exceeding one million as a Metropolitan Area served by a separate cadre of Metropolitan Magistrates.
2. In every district, the High Court appoints a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to serve as the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
3. Judicial Magistrates of the First Class and Second Class are statutorily empowered to impose community service as a sentence for specified minor offences.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 abolished the colonial-era classification of 'Metropolitan Areas' and 'Metropolitan Magistrates' (as well as Assistant Sessions Judges) to establish a uniform hierarchy of Criminal Courts across all districts in India, while formally introducing 'community service' as a statutory punishment imposable by Magistrates.

exp.why: Under the erstwhile Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, cities with a population exceeding one million were notified as Metropolitan Areas with a separate cadre of Metropolitan Magistrates. Section 6 of the BNSS, 2023 completely abolished the category of Metropolitan Areas and Metropolitan Magistrates to create a uniform pan-India hierarchy of Judicial Magistrates of the First Class and Second Class under the Sessions Court.

To safeguard judicial independence at the district level, Section 10(1) of the BNSS, 2023 mandates that in every district, the High Court (and not the State Executive) shall appoint a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to be the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

Section 23(2) and Section 23(3) of the BNSS, 2023 explicitly empower Judicial Magistrates of the First Class and Second Class to pass sentences of 'community service'—defined as unpaid work ordered by the Court that benefits the community—for minor offences specified under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023.

ref: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 Sections 6, 10 & 23; Laxmikanth Ch. 36

stem: With reference to the procedural and evidentiary reforms governing subordinate courts under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the BSA, 2023, electronic or digital records that are created or stored simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files are classified as primary evidence.

2. Under the BNSS, 2023, police officers are statutorily bound to register a First Information Report (FIR) irrespective of the territorial jurisdiction where the cognizable offence was committed, and must mandatorily cause a forensic expert to visit the crime scene for all offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more.

3. The BNSS, 2023 empowers a trial court to conduct a trial in absentia and pronounce judgment against a proclaimed offender who has absconded to evade trial, after a lapse of ninety days from the date of framing of charges.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The BNSS, 2023 and BSA, 2023 modernise trial procedure in district courts by conferring primary evidence status on electronic records, institutionalising Zero FIRs, mandating forensic crime-scene examination for serious offences (punishable with 7 years or more), and enabling trials in absentia for proclaimed offenders.

exp.why: Explanation 4 to Section 57 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023 explicitly stipulates that where an electronic or digital record is created or stored simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence. Section 61 further accords electronic records the same legal validity and enforceability as traditional documents.

Section 173(1) of the BNSS, 2023 gives statutory recognition to 'Zero FIR' by requiring the registration of information relating to a cognizable offence irrespective of the area where it is committed. Further, Section 176(3) makes it mandatory for a forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence and videograph the process on a mobile phone or other electronic device for all offences punishable with imprisonment for seven years or more.

Section 356 of the BNSS, 2023 introduces trial in absentia for proclaimed offenders. When a person declared as a proclaimed offender absconds to evade trial with no immediate prospect of arrest, it operates as a deemed waiver of the right to be tried in person, allowing the Court to proceed with the trial and pronounce judgment after ninety days have elapsed from the framing of charges.

ref: BSA, 2023 Sections 57 & 61; BNSS, 2023 Sections 173, 176(3) & 356

stem: Part XIV-A of the Constitution of India (inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976) draws a clear structural distinction between Administrative Tribunals under Article 323A and Tribunals for Other Matters under Article 323B. In this context, consider the following comparative pairs:
items: 1. Legislative Competence : Under Article 323A, only Parliament can establish tribunals, whereas under Article 323B, both Parliament and State Legislatures can establish tribunals within their legislative competence.

2. Subject-Matter Scope : Article 323A deals exclusively with recruitment and service matters of public servants, whereas Article 323B covers disputes relating to taxation, foreign exchange, industrial labour, and land reforms.

3. Structural Hierarchy : Article 323A explicitly authorizes a multi-tiered hierarchy of administrative tribunals, whereas Article 323B restricts creation to a single tribunal per State without any hierarchy.
prompt: Which of the comparative pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 323A and 323B differ fundamentally in three constitutional dimensions: legislative competence (Parliament exclusively under 323A vs. both Parliament and State Legislatures under 323B), subject matter (public service disputes vs. taxation, land, labour, etc.), and institutional architecture (single-tier per Union/State under 323A vs. a permissible hierarchy of tribunals under 323B).

exp.why: Under Article 323A(1), only Parliament is empowered to establish administrative tribunals for both the Centre and the States. Conversely, under Article 323B(1), the 'appropriate Legislature' (meaning either Parliament or a State Legislature, within their respective spheres of legislative competence) may establish tribunals by law.

Article 323A is strictly confined to disputes and complaints regarding recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts. Article 323B(2) enumerates a wide range of non-service matters including taxation, foreign exchange, import and export, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, ceiling on urban property, elections to legislatures, foodstuffs, and rent/tenancy rights.

This statement reverses the constitutional text. Under Article 323A(1), only one tribunal for the Union and one for each State (or two or more States) may be established, leaving no scope for a hierarchy of tribunals. By contrast, Article 323B(3)(a) explicitly states that a law made under Article 323B may 'provide for the establishment of a hierarchy of tribunals'.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 323A & 323B; Laxmikanth Ch. 35

stem: Consider the following statements regarding judicial review over the decisions of Administrative Tribunals in India:
items: Statement-I: An aggrieved party cannot directly appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution against an order of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) without first approaching the jurisdictional High Court.

Statement-II: In the L. Chandra Kumar case (1997), the Supreme Court held that whereas the power of judicial review vested in the Supreme Court under Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution, the writ and supervisory jurisdiction of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 can be constitutionally transferred to statutory appellate tribunals.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench held that the power of judicial review vested in both the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Articles 226/227) forms an inviolable part of the Basic Structure; consequently, Tribunals play only a supplemental role and their orders must first be challenged before a Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 136.

exp.why: Following the 7-Judge Bench ruling in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), all decisions of Tribunals created under Articles 323A and 323B are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the concerned Tribunal falls. Aggrieved litigants are not permitted to bypass the High Court and approach the Supreme Court directly by way of Special Leave Petition under Article 136.

In L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the Supreme Court categorically declared that the power of judicial review over legislative and executive action vested in BOTH the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral feature of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. The Court struck down Article 323A(2)(d) and Article 323B(3)(d) to the extent they excluded the jurisdiction of High Courts, holding that Tribunals are 'supplemental' to—and can never be constitutional 'substitutes' for—the High Courts.

ref: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 261; Laxmikanth Ch. 35

stem: With reference to the jurisdiction and procedure of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The CAT exercises original jurisdiction over recruitment and all service matters concerning members of the All-India Services, even while they are serving under a State Government cadre.
2. In discharging its adjudicatory functions, the CAT is not bound by the strict procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and is guided instead by the principles of natural justice.
3. The statutory jurisdiction of the CAT extends to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament as well as the officers and servants of the Supreme Court of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, the CAT exercises original jurisdiction over All-India Services and Central Civil Services while operating on principles of natural justice unencumbered by the CPC, 1908; however, to preserve legislative and judicial autonomy, parliamentary secretarial staff, judicial staff of the Supreme Court/High Courts, and members of the armed forces are statutorily excluded from its purview.

exp.why: Under Section 14(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, the Central Administrative Tribunal exercises exclusive original jurisdiction in relation to recruitment and all service matters of members of the All-India Services (IAS, IPS, and IFoS), regardless of whether the officer is on central deputation or serving in a State cadre.

Under Section 22(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, the CAT is not bound by the technical procedural rules of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is guided by the principles of natural justice, enabling speedy and inexpensive adjudication where applicants may appear either in person or through legal practitioners.

Section 2 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 explicitly excludes three categories of personnel from the purview of the CAT: (a) any member of the naval, military, or air forces or any other armed forces of the Union; (b) any officer or servant of the Supreme Court or of any High Court or courts subordinate thereto; and (c) any person appointed to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament or of any State Legislature.

ref: Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 Sections 2, 14 & 22; Laxmikanth Ch. 35

stem: With reference to the rationalisation and administration of tribunals under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act abolished several existing statutory appellate bodies, including the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, and transferred their appellate jurisdiction to High Courts or Commercial Courts.

2. The Search-cum-Selection Committee constituted for recommending appointments of Chairpersons and Members of Central Tribunals is chaired by the Union Minister of Law and Justice, who exercises a casting vote in the event of a tie.

3. Under the Act, the Chairperson and Members of a Tribunal hold office for a fixed statutory tenure of six years or until they attain the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, with no minimum age prescribed for appointment.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 dissolved multiple domain-specific appellate tribunals (transferring their functions back to High Courts/Civil Courts) and instituted a uniform appointment and tenure framework featuring a Search-cum-Selection Committee chaired by the CJI (or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by the CJI) with a 4-year tenure and a 50-year minimum age threshold.

exp.why: The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished several statutory appellate bodies across various enactments—including the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB), the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal (FCAT), the Airport Appellate Tribunal, and the Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal—and transferred their appellate functions directly to High Courts or Commercial/Civil Courts to reduce delays and administrative overlap.

To comply with Supreme Court directives on judicial independence in the Madras Bar Association cases, Section 3(3) of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 provides that the Search-cum-Selection Committee for Central Tribunals is chaired by the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by the CJI (not the Union Law Minister), who holds the casting vote. For State Administrative Tribunals, the Committee is chaired by the Chief Justice of the respective High Court.

Section 5 of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 prescribes a term of office of four years (not six years), subject to an upper age limit of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for other Members (not 65 years). Additionally, Section 3(1) explicitly mandates that a person who has not completed the age of 50 years shall not be eligible for appointment as a Chairperson or Member.

ref: Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 Sections 3 & 5; Madras Bar Association v. Union of India

stem: With reference to the jurisdiction and functioning of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Being a statutory tribunal rather than a constitutional court of record, the NGT cannot take suo motu cognizance of environmental violations based on media reports or letters unless a formal application is filed.
opts.B: Its original civil jurisdiction extends to substantial questions relating to the environment arising out of the implementation of both the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
opts.C: In adjudicating environmental disputes, the Tribunal is strictly bound by the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and its final orders are statutorily appealable only to the jurisdictional High Court.
opts.D: Despite being a creature of statute, the Tribunal is empowered to exercise suo motu jurisdiction in environmental matters and is statutorily mandated to apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and the polluter pays principle.

core: The National Green Tribunal is a sui generis environmental forum vested with suo motu jurisdiction to protect the right to a healthy environment under Article 21 and is guided by Section 20 of the NGT Act, 2010. However, its statutory jurisdiction is strictly confined to the seven laws listed in Schedule I, which excludes the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct: In Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021), the Supreme Court held that the NGT is not a passive tribunal; given its preventive, ameliorative, and remedial role in safeguarding the environmental dimension of Article 21, it possesses suo motu power to initiate proceedings based on letters, representations, or media reports. Furthermore, Section 20 of the NGT Act, 2010 explicitly mandates the Tribunal to apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and the polluter pays principle when passing any order, decision, or award. Option (A) is incorrect because Ankita Sinha affirmed the NGT's suo motu powers. Option (B) is incorrect (Trap T5) because the NGT exercises jurisdiction only over the seven laws listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act (which includes the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the Biological Diversity Act, 2002), whereas the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 are excluded from Schedule I. Option (C) is incorrect because under Section 19(1), the NGT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (it is guided by principles of natural justice), and under Section 22, statutory appeals against NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court within 90 days (though High Courts retain constitutional writ jurisdiction under Article 226 per L. Chandra Kumar).

ref: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Sections 14, 19, 20, 22 & Schedule I); Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (SC, 2021)

stem: With reference to the constitutional and statutory framework of free legal aid in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, women, children, and members of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes are entitled to free legal services irrespective of their annual income.

2. Article 39A, which directs the State to provide free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities, was inserted into the Constitution by the Forty-second Amendment Act, 1976.
3. The Union Minister of Law and Justice serves as the Patron-in-Chief of the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), while the Chief Justice of India serves as its Executive Chairman.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 operationalizes Article 39A by granting automatic entitlement to free legal services to marginalized groups—including women, children, and SC/ST members—without an income threshold. At the apex institutional level, NALSA is headed by the Chief Justice of India as Patron-in-Chief and a senior Supreme Court Judge as Executive Chairman.

exp.why: Under Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, specific categories of persons—including a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, a woman or a child, a victim of trafficking or begar, a person with disability, and a person in custody—are statutorily entitled to free legal services regardless of their income. The annual income ceiling prescribed by the State/Central Government under Section 12(h) applies only to persons who do not fall within the specially protected categories in clauses (a) to (g).

Article 39A ('Equal justice and free legal aid') was added to Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) of the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, forming the constitutional foundation for the enactment of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

Under Section 3(2) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, the Chief Justice of India serves as the Patron-in-Chief of the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), while a serving or retired Judge of the Supreme Court (by convention, the second senior-most judge of the Supreme Court) is nominated by the President, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, to serve as its Executive Chairman.

ref: Constitution of India, Art. 39A; Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Sections 3 & 12); Laxmikanth Ch. 37

stem: With reference to the jurisdiction and awards of Lok Adalats organized under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Lok Adalat has jurisdiction to determine and arrive at a compromise or settlement in any civil dispute as well as in any criminal offence, provided both parties file a joint application for compounding the offence.
2. Every award made by a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court, and if a pending court case is settled at a Lok Adalat, the court fee originally paid by the plaintiff is refunded.

3. Since the Act declares the award of a Lok Adalat to be final and binding, even the writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Articles 226 and 227 cannot be invoked to challenge such an award on grounds of fraud.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lok Adalats operate on consensual compromise and cannot entertain non-compoundable criminal offences even with mutual consent of the parties. While Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 equates a Lok Adalat award to a civil court decree and bars all statutory appeals, it cannot oust the basic-structure writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227.

exp.why: Under the proviso to Section 19(5) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Lok Adalat has no jurisdiction in respect of any case or matter relating to an offence not compoundable under any law. Even if both the complainant and the accused mutually consent to settle a non-compoundable offence, a Lok Adalat cannot take cognizance of or compound it.

Under Section 21(1) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, every award of the Lok Adalat shall be deemed to be a decree of a civil court, or as the case may be, an order of any other court. Furthermore, where a compromise or settlement is arrived at by a Lok Adalat in a case referred to it, the court fee paid in such a case is refunded in the manner provided under the Court Fees Act, 1870.

While Section 21(2) of the Act provides that every award made by a Lok Adalat shall be final and binding on all the parties to the dispute and no statutory appeal shall lie to any court against the award, the Supreme Court (in State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh and Bhargavi Constructions v. Kothakapu Muthyam Reddy) held that a party can challenge a Lok Adalat award on limited grounds such as fraud or misrepresentation by filing a writ petition under Articles 226 and/or 227 of the Constitution before the High Court, as constitutional judicial review is part of the Basic Structure and cannot be barred by statute.

ref: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Sections 19 & 21); State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh (SC, 2008); Laxmikanth Ch. 37

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Lok Adalats and Permanent Lok Adalats in India:
items: Statement-I: Like a regular Lok Adalat organized under Chapter VI of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Permanent Lok Adalat established for public utility services has no adjudicatory authority and must refer the dispute back to a regular court if the parties fail to reach an amicable settlement.

Statement-II: While a regular Lok Adalat exercises only conciliatory jurisdiction based on mutual consent of the parties, a Permanent Lok Adalat is vested with both conciliatory and adjudicatory powers in respect of pre-litigation disputes relating to specified public utility services.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Regular Lok Adalats (Chapter VI) are purely conciliatory forums that cannot decide a dispute on merits without mutual compromise. In contrast, Permanent Lok Adalats for Public Utility Services (Chapter VIA, inserted in 2002) possess a hybrid mechanism: they first attempt conciliation, and if the parties fail to settle, they are empowered to adjudicate the dispute on merits.

exp.why: Under Section 20(5) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a regular Lok Adalat has no power to decide a case on merits if no compromise or settlement is arrived at; it must return the record of the case to the court (or advise pre-litigation parties to seek a remedy in a court). However, under Section 22C(8) (inserted by the 2002 Amendment Act in Chapter VIA), a Permanent Lok Adalat established for public utility services is expressly empowered to decide the dispute on merits if the parties fail to reach an agreement during conciliation, provided the dispute does not relate to any offence.

Permanent Lok Adalats (PLAs) were created under Chapter VIA specifically to remedy the structural weakness of regular Lok Adalats, where public utility providers could frustrate pre-litigation proceedings simply by refusing to consent to a settlement. Thus, PLAs exercise a two-stage hybrid jurisdiction over public utility disputes (such as transport, postal, power, water, sanitation, insurance, and banking services) within their pecuniary limit: mandatory conciliation first, followed by binding adjudication on merits if conciliation fails.

ref: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Chapter VI & Chapter VIA, Section 22C); Bar Council of India v. Union of India (SC, 2012); Laxmikanth Ch. 37

stem: With reference to the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The presiding officer of a Gram Nyayalaya, known as the Nyayadhikari, is appointed by the District Collector from among experienced members of the Gram Panchayat or retired revenue officers.

2. Unlike the traditional Nyaya Panchayats, a Gram Nyayalaya is a formal court of the subordinate judiciary that exercises jurisdiction over both civil and criminal cases specified in the Schedules to the Act.

3. An appeal against a judgment of a Gram Nyayalaya lies to the Court of Session in criminal matters and to the District Court in civil matters, and such appeals are statutorily required to be heard and disposed of within six months.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Gram Nyayalayas are mobile grassroots judicial courts—not elected panchayat tribunals—presided over by a Nyayadhikari who holds the status and qualifications of a First Class Judicial Magistrate appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court. They exercise summary civil and criminal jurisdiction, with appeals to the District/Sessions Court subject to a six-month disposal mandate.

exp.why: Under Sections 5 and 6 of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, the State Government, in consultation with the High Court, appoints a Nyayadhikari for every Gram Nyayalaya. A person is not eligible to be appointed as a Nyayadhikari unless they are eligible to be appointed as a Judicial Magistrate of the first class, and they draw the same salary and allowances as a First Class Judicial Magistrate.

Under Section 11 of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, notwithstanding anything contained in the criminal or civil procedural codes, a Gram Nyayalaya exercises both civil and criminal jurisdiction. It tries criminal offences specified in the First Schedule (including offences not punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding two years) and civil suits or claims of the classes specified in the Second Schedule.

Under Sections 33 and 34 of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, subject to specified limitations (such as where an accused has pleaded guilty or in petty sentences/fines or small civil claims below the statutory threshold), an appeal in criminal cases lies to the Court of Session and an appeal in civil cases lies to the District Court. Both sections mandate that the appeal shall be heard and disposed of within six months from the date of filing.

ref: Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 (Sections 5, 6, 11, 33 & 34); Laxmikanth Ch. 37

stem: With reference to the Mediation Act, 2023, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A mediated settlement agreement resulting from mediation (other than community mediation) is final, binding on the parties, and enforceable in the same manner as a judgment or decree passed by a court.

2. A mediated settlement agreement cannot be challenged on merits, and an application to challenge it can be filed only on the limited grounds of fraud, corruption, impersonation, or where the dispute was not fit for mediation under the Act.
3. Under the First Schedule to the Act, disputes relating to the levy or collection of any direct or indirect tax and disputes involving prosecution for criminal offences are excluded from mediation.
4. The Act makes pre-litigation mediation mandatory in all civil and commercial disputes before a party can file any suit or proceeding in a court or tribunal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Mediation Act, 2023 accords statutory enforceability as a court decree to mediated settlement agreements (excluding community mediation) and restricts challenges strictly to fraud, corruption, impersonation, or non-mediability under the First Schedule. Crucially, the enacted law kept general pre-litigation mediation voluntary and consensual rather than universally mandatory.

exp.why: Under Section 27 of the Mediation Act, 2023, a mediated settlement agreement resulting from mediation signed by the parties and authenticated by the mediator is final and binding on the parties and is enforceable in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in the same manner as if it were a judgment or decree passed by a court. (Section 44(4) explicitly carves out community mediation settlements, which are not enforceable as a civil court decree).

Under Section 28(2) of the Mediation Act, 2023, a mediated settlement agreement may be challenged only on four specific grounds: (a) fraud, (b) corruption, (c) impersonation, or (d) where the mediation was conducted in disputes or matters not fit for mediation under Section 6 (read with the First Schedule).

Section 6 read with the First Schedule to the Mediation Act, 2023 enumerates the indicative list of disputes or matters not fit for mediation. This expressly excludes disputes involving prosecution for criminal offences, disputes relating to claims against minors or persons with intellectual disabilities, disputes affecting rights of third parties, and disputes relating to the levy, collection, penalties, or offences in relation to direct or indirect taxes.

While the initial 2021 draft Bill proposed mandatory pre-litigation mediation, following the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, Section 5(1) of the enacted Mediation Act, 2023 made pre-litigation mediation voluntary and consensual in general civil and commercial matters ('the parties before filing any suit or proceedings of civil or commercial nature in any court, may voluntarily and with mutual consent take steps to settle the disputes by pre-litigation mediation'). Mandatory pre-litigation mediation remains applicable only where required by specific statutes, such as commercial disputes of specified value not contemplating urgent interim relief under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015.

ref: The Mediation Act, 2023 (Sections 5, 6, 27, 28, 44 & First Schedule)

stem: Consider the following committees and working groups constituted to examine rural decentralization, district planning, and Panchayati Raj Institutions in India:
items: 1. G.V.K. Rao Committee on Administrative Arrangements for Rural Development (CAARD)
2. Hanumantha Rao Working Group on District Planning
3. L.M. Singhvi Committee on Revitalisation of Panchayati Raj Institutions for Democracy and Development
4. V.N. Gadgil Committee on Policy and Programmes
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the constitution of the above committees/groups, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The institutional evolution of Panchayati Raj in the 1980s progressed systematically from decentralized district planning (Hanumantha Rao, 1982–84) and administrative debureaucratization (G.V.K. Rao, 1985) to the demand for constitutional recognition (L.M. Singhvi, 1986) and the concrete legislative blueprint for the 73rd Amendment (Gadgil Committee, 1988).

exp.why: The G.V.K. Rao Committee on Administrative Arrangements for Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation Programmes (CAARD) was appointed by the Planning Commission in March 1985. It famously concluded that developmental administration had become overly bureaucratized, reducing Panchayati Raj to 'grass without roots'.

The Working Group on District Planning under the chairmanship of C.H. Hanumantha Rao was set up by the Planning Commission in 1982 (submitting its report in May 1984), preceding the G.V.K. Rao Committee. It advocated decentralized district planning under the District Collector with holistic integration of sector-wise schemes.

The L.M. Singhvi Committee was appointed by the Rajiv Gandhi government in June 1986 to prepare a concept paper on the revitalization of Panchayati Raj Institutions for democracy and development. It strongly advocated that PRIs should be constitutionally recognized, protected, and preserved by inserting a new chapter in the Constitution.

The Committee on Policy and Programmes chaired by V.N. Gadgil was constituted in 1988 (shortly after the P.K. Thungon Sub-Committee of 1988) to answer how Panchayati Raj Institutions could be made effective. Its blueprint (uniform three-tier system, five-year fixed tenure, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission, and reservation for SCs, STs, and women) directly formed the basis of the 64th Amendment Bill (1989) and eventually the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2-1-3-4.

ref: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj - Evolution of Panchayati Raj); Report of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (6th Report: Local Governance).

stem: With reference to the structural recommendations made by various committees on Panchayati Raj in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Ashok Mehta Committee : Creation of the post of District Development Commissioner to act as the Chief Executive Officer of the Zila Parishad

2. G.V.K. Rao Committee : Replacement of the three-tier structure with a two-tier system comprising Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat, along with official participation of political parties at all levels
3. L.M. Singhvi Committee : Establishment of Nyaya Panchayats for a cluster of villages and judicial tribunals in each State to adjudicate disputes relating to Panchayat elections and dissolution
4. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee : Transfer of all executive planning and development functions at the district level to an executive Zila Parishad headed by an elected non-official Chairperson
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Each major committee on Panchayati Raj proposed a distinct institutional locus of power: Balwant Rai Mehta favored an executive Block-level Panchayat Samiti with an advisory Zila Parishad; Ashok Mehta championed a two-tier Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat model with open political party participation; and G.V.K. Rao recommended a District Development Commissioner as CEO of the Zila Parishad.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. The creation of the post of a District Development Commissioner (of senior rank, above or equal to the District Collector in developmental matters) to act as the Chief Executive Officer of the Zila Parishad and take charge of all developmental departments at the district level was a signature recommendation of the G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985), not the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977).

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The replacement of the three-tier system by a two-tier system—consisting of the Zila Parishad at the district level and the Mandal Panchayat (covering a group of villages with a total population of 15,000 to 20,000) below it—along with open and official participation of political parties at all levels of Panchayat elections, was recommended by the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977), not the G.V.K. Rao Committee.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended that Nyaya Panchayats should be established for a cluster of villages for accessible grassroots justice, and specifically proposed the establishment of judicial tribunals in each State to adjudicate controversies regarding elections to Panchayati Raj Institutions, their dissolution, and other matters related to their functioning.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Under the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) scheme of 'democratic decentralization', the Panchayat Samiti at the block level was designated as the primary executive body, whereas the Zila Parishad at the district level was conceived merely as an advisory, coordinating, and supervisory body with the District Collector serving as its Chairman.

ref: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj); Reports of the Balwant Rai Mehta (1957), Ashok Mehta (1978), G.V.K. Rao (1985), and L.M. Singhvi (1986) Committees.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional status of Panchayati Raj Institutions in India:
items: Statement-I: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 brought the mandatory provisions relating to the constitution and regular five-yearly elections of Panchayats under the purview of the justiciable part of the Constitution, removing the discretion earlier enjoyed by State Governments regarding their survival.

Statement-II: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act repealed Article 40 from Part IV of the Constitution and transferred the subject of 'Local Government' from the State List to the Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the 73rd Amendment gave constitutional teeth to Article 40 by adding a justiciable Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O), it neither repealed Article 40 from the Directive Principles nor shifted 'Local Government' out of Entry 5 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Prior to the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992, the organization of village panchayats rested solely on Article 40 in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), which is non-justiciable under Article 37. By inserting Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O), the 73rd Amendment transformed the constitution of three-tier Panchayats (Article 243B) and regular elections every five years (Article 243E) into mandatory, justiciable constitutional obligations enforceable through the higher judiciary.

Statement-II is incorrect on two counts. First, the 73rd Amendment did not repeal Article 40; Article 40 continues to exist in Part IV of the Constitution, and Part IX was added to actualize its mandate. Second, 'Local government, that is to say, the constitution and powers of municipal corporations, improvement trusts, district boards, mining settlement authorities and other local authorities for the purpose of local self-government or village administration' continues to remain exclusively in Entry 5 of List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule, and was never transferred to the Concurrent List.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 40, Part IX (Articles 243–243O), and Seventh Schedule (List II, Entry 5).

stem: With reference to the 'Gram Sabha' under Part IX of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is strictly in accordance with the constitutional text?

opts.A: It is a body consisting of all adult residents residing within the territorial area of a Panchayat at the village level, regardless of whether their names are entered in the electoral rolls.
opts.B: It is a statutory deliberative body consisting solely of the elected ward members and the Sarpanch of a Village Panchayat.
opts.C: It is a body consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level, and it exercises such powers as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide.
opts.D: Its specific executive and financial powers over the Village Panchayat are directly enumerated in the Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution, operating uniformly across all States without requiring State legislation.

core: Under Article 243(b), membership of the Gram Sabha is strictly tied to registration in the village electoral rolls (not mere adult residence), and under Article 243A, its powers and functions are not fixed by the Constitution itself but are determined by the respective State Legislature by law.

exp.why: Option C is correct because Article 243(b) explicitly defines 'Gram Sabha' as a body consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of Panchayat at the village level. Furthermore, Article 243A stipulates that a Gram Sabha may exercise such powers and perform such functions at the village level as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide. Option A is incorrect because mere adult residence (18 years or above) does not confer membership of the Gram Sabha unless the person is registered on the electoral roll of that village. Option B is incorrect because the elected ward members and Sarpanch constitute the Village Panchayat (the executive body), whereas the Gram Sabha is the entire village electorate. Option D is incorrect because the Constitution does not enumerate the powers of the Gram Sabha (except specific statutory mandates later enacted for Fifth Schedule areas under the PESA Act, 1996); the Eleventh Schedule lists 29 functional subjects that may be devolved to Panchayats under Article 243G by State law.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 243(b) and Article 243A.

stem: With reference to the structural composition and mode of election of Panchayats under Part IX of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A State having a population not exceeding twenty lakhs is constitutionally permitted to omit the constitution of Panchayats at the intermediate level.
2. All the seats in a Panchayat at the village, intermediate, and district levels representing territorial constituencies in the Panchayat area must be filled by persons chosen by direct election.

3. While the Chairpersons of Panchayats at the intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly by and from amongst the elected members thereof, the Constitution mandates that the Chairperson of a Panchayat at the village level shall be elected directly by the voters of the Gram Sabha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 73rd Amendment establishes a vital distinction between members and Chairpersons: while direct election is constitutionally mandatory for territorial constituency seats across all three tiers (Article 243C(2)), the mode of election of the Village Panchayat Chairperson is left to the discretion of the State Legislature (Article 243C(5)(a)).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. While Article 243B(1) mandates a uniform three-tier system of Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels in every State, Article 243B(2) provides an explicit exception that Panchayats at the intermediate level may not be constituted in a State having a population not exceeding twenty lakhs.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 243C(2), all the seats in a Panchayat at all three levels (village, intermediate, and district) shall be filled by persons chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the Panchayat area. This is a compulsory (mandatory) provision binding on all States to which Part IX applies.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 243C(5)(b), the Chairperson of a Panchayat at the intermediate level or district level must compulsorily be elected indirectly—by, and from amongst, the elected members thereof. However, under Article 243C(5)(a), the Chairperson of a Panchayat at the village level shall be elected 'in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide'. Thus, the Constitution does not mandate direct election of the Sarpanch/Village Panchayat Chairperson; a State Legislature is free to provide for either direct election by the village electorate or indirect election by the ward members.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 243B and Article 243C.

stem: With reference to the composition of Panchayats and the voting rights of their members under Article 243C of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Legislature of a State may, by law, provide for the representation of the Chairpersons of the Village Panchayats in the Panchayat at the intermediate level, and of the Chairpersons of the Intermediate Panchayats in the Panchayat at the district level.

2. The Legislature of a State may, by law, provide for the representation of Members of both Houses of Parliament and both Houses of the State Legislature in Panchayats at the intermediate and district levels, subject to territorial nexus conditions.

3. Under Article 243C(4) of the Constitution, members of a Panchayat who are not chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies are constitutionally barred from exercising the right to vote in the meetings of the Panchayats.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike nominated experts in Municipalities who are constitutionally barred from voting under the proviso to Article 243R(2)(a), Article 243C(4) explicitly grants the Chairperson and other members of a Panchayat—whether or not chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies—the right to vote in the meetings of the Panchayats.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 243C(3)(a) and (b), the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide for the representation of the Chairpersons of the Panchayats at the village level in the Panchayats at the intermediate level (or in the case of a State not having intermediate Panchayats, in the Panchayats at the district level), and of the Chairpersons of the Panchayats at the intermediate level in the Panchayats at the district level.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 243C(3)(c) and (d), the State Legislature may, by law, provide for the representation in Panchayats at the intermediate and district levels of: (i) the members of the House of the People and the members of the Legislative Assembly of the State representing constituencies which comprise wholly or partly a Panchayat area at that level; and (ii) the members of the Council of States and the members of the Legislative Council of the State where they are registered as electors within the Panchayat area at the intermediate level or within the district, respectively.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The verbatim text of Article 243C(4) states: 'The Chairperson of a Panchayat and other members of a Panchayat whether or not chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the Panchayat area shall have the right to vote in the meetings of the Panchayats.' While Article 243C(5)(b) restricts voting in the election of the Chairperson of an intermediate or district Panchayat strictly to the 'elected members thereof' (those directly elected from territorial constituencies), Article 243C(4) explicitly affirms rather than bars the right of non-directly elected members to vote in general meetings of the Panchayats. This is a crucial constitutional contrast with Municipalities, where nominated persons having special knowledge under the proviso to Article 243R(2)(a) explicitly 'shall not have the right to vote in the meetings of the Municipality'.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 243C(3), Article 243C(4), Article 243C(5)(b), and Article 243R(2).

stem: With reference to the constitutional architecture of reservation of seats and offices in Panchayats under Part IX of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 243D, the mandate of reserving not less than one-third of the total number of seats for women applies both to seats filled by direct election (including those reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes) and to the offices of Chairpersons in Panchayats at each level.
2. By virtue of Article 243M(3A), the constitutional requirement relating to the reservation of seats in Panchayats for the Scheduled Castes does not apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.

3. Part IX of the Constitution makes it obligatory for every State Legislature to reserve not less than twenty-seven percent of seats and offices of Chairpersons in Panchayats for the Backward Classes of citizens.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 243D mandates population-proportionate reservation for SCs and STs and a minimum one-third horizontal reservation for women across all Panchayat seats and Chairperson offices, while keeping OBC reservation entirely discretionary for State Legislatures under Article 243D(6). Additionally, the 83rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000 inserted Article 243M(3A) exempting Arunachal Pradesh from SC reservation in Panchayats as the State is inhabited entirely by indigenous tribes with no indigenous Scheduled Castes.

exp.why: Under Article 243D(2), not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved for SCs and STs must be reserved for women belonging to SCs and STs. Under Article 243D(3), not less than one-third (including the number of seats reserved for SC/ST women) of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in every Panchayat shall be reserved for women. Furthermore, under the proviso to Article 243D(4), not less than one-third of the total number of offices of Chairpersons in the Panchayats at each level shall also be reserved for women.

The 83rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000 inserted Clause (3A) in Article 243M, explicitly providing that nothing in Article 243D relating to reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes shall apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.

Under Article 243D(6), reservation of seats in any Panchayat or offices of Chairpersons in the Panchayats at any level in favour of Backward Classes of citizens is a purely voluntary (enabling) provision left to the discretion of the State Legislature, and the Constitution neither mandates it nor prescribes a 27% quota.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243D and 243M(3A); 83rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the tenure and premature dissolution of Panchayats:
items: Statement-I: Unlike a newly elected Lok Sabha or State Legislative Assembly constituted after a premature dissolution, a Panchayat reconstituted upon premature dissolution does not enjoy a fresh full term of five years.

Statement-II: To maintain an uninterrupted and predictable five-year local body electoral cycle, Article 243E(4) of the Constitution stipulates that a Panchayat constituted upon premature dissolution shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued had it not been so dissolved.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike the Lok Sabha (Article 83(2)) or a State Legislative Assembly (Article 172(1)), which receive a fresh full five-year term whenever reconstituted after premature dissolution, a Panchayat (Article 243E(4)) or Municipality (Article 243U(4)) reconstituted after premature dissolution serves only for the unexpired remainder of the dissolved body's five-year term.

exp.why: When the Lok Sabha or a State Legislative Assembly is dissolved before the completion of its five-year term, the newly elected House enjoys a fresh full term of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting. In contrast, a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution does not get a fresh five-year term.

Article 243E(4) explicitly provides that a Panchayat constituted upon the dissolution of a Panchayat before the expiration of its duration shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued had it not been so dissolved (and under the proviso to Article 243E(3)(b), if the remainder of the period is less than six months, it is not necessary to hold any election for constituting the Panchayat for such period). This directly explains Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 243E; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj).

stem: With reference to the disqualifications for membership of Panchayats under Article 243F of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of a Panchayat if he is so disqualified by or under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the Legislature of the State concerned, or under any law made by the Legislature of the State.
2. No person shall be disqualified on the ground that he is less than twenty-five years of age, if he has attained the age of twenty-one years.

3. If any question arises as to whether a member of a Panchayat has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in Article 243F, the question shall be referred for the final decision of the Governor, who shall act according to the opinion of the State Election Commission.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 243F aligns Panchayat membership disqualifications with State Legislature election laws and specific State statutes while lowering the qualifying age threshold from 25 years to 21 years. Crucially, unlike Article 192 (where the Governor decides MLA disqualifications in consultation with the ECI), Article 243F(2) vests the adjudication of Panchayat member disqualifications in such authority and in such manner as the State Legislature may, by law, provide.

exp.why: Article 243F(1)(a) and (b) explicitly stipulate that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of a Panchayat if he is so disqualified by or under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the Legislature of the State concerned, or by or under any law made by the Legislature of the State.

Because Article 243F(1)(a) applies the disqualifications for State Legislature elections (where the minimum age is 25 years under Article 173(b)), the proviso to Article 243F(1)(a) carves out a constitutional protection stating that no person shall be disqualified on the ground that he is less than 25 years of age, if he has attained the age of 21 years.

Under Article 243F(2), if any question arises as to whether a member of a Panchayat has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in Clause (1), the question shall be referred for the decision of such authority and in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide—not to the Governor acting on the opinion of the State Election Commission (which is the mechanism for MLAs under Article 192 with the ECI).

ref: Constitution of India, Article 243F; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj).

stem: With reference to the distinction between the compulsory (mandatory) and voluntary (discretionary) provisions of Part IX of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the constitution of Panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels (in States having a population exceeding twenty lakhs) is a mandatory constitutional obligation under Article 243B, the actual devolution of powers and responsibilities with respect to the 29 functional matters listed in the Eleventh Schedule under Article 243G is left to the discretion of the State Legislature.

2. Providing representation in Panchayats at the intermediate and district levels to Members of Parliament and Members of the State Legislature under Article 243C, as well as reserving seats for the Backward Classes under Article 243D, are voluntary provisions that a State Legislature may choose whether or not to enact.

3. While the Governor is constitutionally mandated under Article 243I to constitute a State Finance Commission at the expiration of every fifth year, authorizing a Panchayat to levy, collect and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls and fees under Article 243H is an enabling provision dependent on legislation passed by the State Legislature.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act bifurcates Part IX into mandatory structural guarantees (Gram Sabha, 3-tier structure, direct election of members, 21-year minimum age, SC/ST and 1/3rd women reservation, 5-year tenure, SEC, and SFC) and discretionary functional/fiscal provisions left to State legislation (devolution over the 29 subjects of the 11th Schedule under Art 243G, fiscal taxation powers under Art 243H, MP/MLA representation under Art 243C(3), and OBC reservation under Art 243D(6)).

exp.why: Article 243B uses mandatory language ('There shall be constituted in every State, Panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels...'), excluding only the intermediate level in States with a population not exceeding 20 lakhs. Conversely, Article 243G uses enabling language ('the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow the Panchayats with such powers and authority...'), making devolution across the 29 matters of the Eleventh Schedule discretionary.

Both Article 243C(3) (providing representation of Chairpersons of lower-tier Panchayats and MPs/MLAs/MLCs in intermediate and district Panchayats) and Article 243D(6) (reservation of seats or Chairperson offices in favour of Backward Classes) explicitly state that the Legislature of a State 'may, by law, provide' or 'Nothing in this Part shall prevent the Legislature of a State from making any provision', making them strictly discretionary.

Under Article 243I(1), the Governor 'shall, as soon as may be within one year from the commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992, and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year, constitute a Finance Commission'. In contrast, Article 243H states that the Legislature of a State 'may, by law, authorise a Panchayat to levy, collect and appropriate such taxes, duties, tolls and fees', making fiscal devolution voluntary.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243B, 243C, 243D, 243G, 243H, and 243I; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the institutional independence of the State Election Commissioner:
items: Statement-I: Under Article 243K of the Constitution of India, although the State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor, he or she can be removed from office only by an order of the Governor passed after an address by the State Legislative Assembly supported by a special majority on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Statement-II: Interpreting Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution, the Supreme Court of India has held that a serving government official holding an office of profit under the State Government cannot be appointed or given additional charge to function as the State Election Commissioner.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the proviso to Article 243K(2), the State Election Commissioner can be removed only in the like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of a High Court—meaning removal is exclusively by the President of India following an address passed by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority, not by the Governor or the State Legislature. Furthermore, in State of Goa v. Fouziya Imtiaz Shaikh (2021), the Supreme Court ruled that the SEC must be completely independent of the State Executive and cannot be a serving government bureaucrat.

exp.why: Under the proviso to Article 243K(2), the State Election Commissioner shall not be removed from his office except in like manner and on the like ground as a Judge of a High Court. Under Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4), a Judge of a High Court is removed by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a special majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Neither the Governor nor the State Legislative Assembly has the constitutional power to remove the State Election Commissioner.

In State of Goa v. Fouziya Imtiaz Shaikh (2021), the Supreme Court held that paramount constitutional independence is vested in the State Election Commission under Articles 243K and 243ZA, and directed that no serving government employee or bureaucrat under the State Government can be appointed or given additional charge as the State Election Commissioner.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243K and 243ZA; Supreme Court Judgment in State of Goa v. Fouziya Imtiaz Shaikh (2021); Laxmikanth Ch. 39.

stem: With reference to the State Finance Commission and its constitutional interface with the Union Finance Commission, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Just as Article 280 specifies that the Union Finance Commission shall consist of a Chairman and four other members, Article 243I directly prescribes in the text of the Constitution that every State Finance Commission shall consist of a Chairman and four other members.

2. The State Finance Commission constituted by the Governor under Article 243I for Panchayats is also constitutionally mandated under Article 243Y to review the financial position of the Municipalities and make recommendations to the Governor.

3. Under Clauses (3)(bb) and (3)(c) of Article 280, the Union Finance Commission is constitutionally bound to adopt the exact quantum of grants-in-aid recommended by the respective State Finance Commissions without any independent modification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
