core: Unlike Article 280(1) which fixes the numerical strength of the Union Finance Commission in the Constitution, Article 243I(2) leaves the composition, qualifications, and manner of selection of the State Finance Commission entirely to the State Legislature by law. The same SFC serves both Panchayats (Art 243I) and Municipalities (Art 243Y), and while the Union Finance Commission under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c) makes recommendations 'on the basis of' SFC recommendations, it is not bound to mechanically accept the exact quantum proposed by an SFC.

exp.why: While Article 280(1) directly specifies that the Union Finance Commission shall consist of a Chairman and four other members, Article 243I(2) does not specify the numerical strength of the State Finance Commission in the Constitution. Instead, Article 243I(2) empowers the Legislature of a State, by law, to provide for the composition of the Commission, the qualifications requisite for appointment as members thereof, and the manner in which they shall be selected.

Article 243Y(1) explicitly stipulates that the Finance Commission constituted under Article 243I shall also review the financial position of the Municipalities and make recommendations to the Governor as to the principles governing the distribution of net tax proceeds, assignment of taxes, and grants-in-aid to the Municipalities.

Under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c), inserted by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, it is the duty of the Union Finance Commission to make recommendations to the President as to the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and Municipalities in the State 'on the basis of the recommendations made by the Finance Commission of the State'. This requires the Union Finance Commission to consider SFC reports as the basis, but does not bind it to rubber-stamp their exact monetary figures without applying its own normative assessment.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243I, 243Y, and 280(3)(bb)-(c); Laxmikanth Ch. 39 & 40.

stem: With reference to the financial administration, taxation powers, and auditing of accounts of Panchayats under Part IX of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Constitution directly vests Panchayats with the mandatory right to levy and collect property taxes and professional taxes within their territorial jurisdiction without requiring an enabling State legislation.
opts.B: The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions with respect to both the maintenance of accounts by the Panchayats and the auditing of such accounts.
opts.C: Under Article 243J of the Constitution, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is constitutionally mandated to conduct the statutory audit of the accounts of all three tiers of Panchayati Raj Institutions.
opts.D: The recommendations of the State Finance Commission regarding the distribution of net proceeds of State taxes between the State and the Panchayats are constitutionally binding on the State Government.

core: Articles 243H and 243J are voluntary/enabling provisions that leave both the fiscal devolution of taxation powers to Panchayats and the framework for maintaining and auditing Panchayat accounts entirely to the discretion of the State Legislature by law.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because Article 243J of the Constitution explicitly provides that the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions with respect to the maintenance of accounts by the Panchayats and the auditing of such accounts. Option (A) is incorrect because Article 243H is an enabling (discretionary) provision whereby the State Legislature may, by law, authorise a Panchayat to levy, collect, and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, and fees; the Constitution does not confer self-executing taxation powers directly on Panchayats. Option (C) is incorrect (Trap T2: Authority Swap) because Article 243J does not mandate the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India to audit Panchayat accounts; each State Legislature determines the auditing agency (such as the Director of Local Fund Audit), though States may entrust Technical Guidance and Support (TGS) to the CAG. Option (D) is incorrect because under Article 243I(4), the Governor causes every recommendation made by the State Finance Commission together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon to be laid before the State Legislature, making its recommendations advisory rather than constitutionally binding.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 243H, 243I & 243J; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 (Panchayati Raj)

stem: With reference to the exemptions from the application of Part IX of the Constitution of India and the mechanisms for its extension under Article 243M, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 243M, Parliament is empowered to extend the provisions of Part IX to the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram by enacting an ordinary law subject to specified exceptions and modifications.

2. The provisions of Part IX relating to the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes under Article 243D apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh unless exempted by a public notification issued by the Governor.

3. Any law enacted by Parliament to extend the provisions of Part IX to the Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas referred to in Article 244 is deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 243M establishes distinct extension mechanisms: exempted States (Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram) can extend Part IX to themselves via a special majority resolution of their own State Legislative Assembly under Article 243M(4)(a), whereas Scheduled and Tribal Areas require a parliamentary law under Article 243M(4)(b) that is explicitly excluded from the purview of Article 368.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 243M(2)(a), nothing in Part IX applies to the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram. Under Article 243M(4)(a), it is NOT Parliament by law, but the Legislative Assembly of the concerned State (Nagaland, Meghalaya, or Mizoram) that may extend Part IX to that State by passing a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 243M(3A), inserted by the 83rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000, nothing in Article 243D relating to the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes shall apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh. This is an absolute constitutional exemption operating directly by virtue of Article 243M(3A)—because Arunachal Pradesh is inhabited entirely by indigenous tribal communities with zero notified Scheduled Castes—and does not depend on any discretionary exemption notification by the Governor.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 243M(4)(b), Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of Part IX to the Scheduled Areas and the Tribal Areas referred to in clause (1) and clause (2) of Article 244 subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and Article 243M(4)(b) explicitly stipulates that 'no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of Article 368'.

ref: Constitution of India Article 243M; 83rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000; Laxmikanth Ch. 39

stem: With reference to the statutory powers and functions of the Gram Sabha under the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Panchayat at the village level can take up plans, programmes, and projects for social and economic development for implementation only after they are approved by the Gram Sabha, and must obtain a certification of utilisation of funds from the Gram Sabha.
2. The responsibility for the identification and selection of persons as beneficiaries under poverty alleviation and other programmes is statutorily vested in the Gram Sabha.
3. While the Gram Sabha has the right to regulate the collection of Minor Forest Produce (MFP), the statutory ownership of MFP in the Scheduled Areas remains vested in the State Forest Department.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 4 of the PESA Act, 1996 places the Gram Sabha at the fulcrum of tribal self-governance by vesting it with prior approval over village development plans, selection of poverty alleviation beneficiaries, certification of fund utilization, and direct ownership of Minor Forest Produce (MFP).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 4(e)(i) of the PESA Act, 1996, every Gram Sabha shall approve of the plans, programmes, and projects for social and economic development before such plans, programmes, and projects are taken up for implementation by the Panchayat at the village level. Furthermore, under Section 4(f), every Panchayat at the village level is required to obtain from the Gram Sabha a certification of utilisation of funds by that Panchayat for the plans, programmes, and projects referred to in clause (e).

Statement 2 is correct. Under Section 4(e)(ii) of the PESA Act, 1996, every Gram Sabha shall be responsible for the identification or selection of persons as beneficiaries under the poverty alleviation and other programmes.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Section 4(m)(ii) of the PESA Act, 1996, while endowing Panchayats in the Scheduled Areas with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government, a State Legislature shall ensure that the Panchayats at the appropriate level and the Gram Sabha are endowed specifically with the ownership of minor forest produce (MFP)—not merely collection rights with ownership retained by the State Forest Department.

ref: Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, Section 4; Laxmikanth Ch. 39

stem: With reference to the mandatory structural and administrative safeguards under Section 4 of the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Tribes in every Panchayat in the Scheduled Areas shall not be less than one-half of the total number of seats, all seats of Chairpersons of Panchayats at all levels shall be reserved only for the Scheduled Tribes.

2. While the Gram Sabha or the Panchayats at the appropriate level must be consulted before acquiring land in the Scheduled Areas for development projects, their prior recommendation is mandatory before granting a prospecting licence, mining lease, or concession by auction for minor minerals.

3. The State Legislature shall endeavour to follow the pattern of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution while designing the administrative arrangements in the Panchayats at the district level in the Scheduled Areas.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 4 of the PESA Act, 1996 provides heightened safeguards in Fifth Schedule Areas, including 100% reservation of Chairperson posts at all Panchayat levels for STs, a strict distinction between 'consultation' (for land acquisition) and 'mandatory prior recommendation' (for minor mineral concessions), and Sixth Schedule-modeled district-level administration.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 4(g) of the PESA Act, 1996, the reservation of seats in the Scheduled Areas at every Panchayat shall be in proportion to the population of the communities in that Panchayat under Part IX of the Constitution, provided that the reservation for the Scheduled Tribes shall not be less than one-half (50%) of the total number of seats, and provided further that ALL seats of Chairpersons of Panchayats at all levels shall be reserved for the Scheduled Tribes.

Statement 2 is correct. PESA deliberately distinguishes between 'consultation' and 'mandatory prior recommendation'. Under Section 4(i), the Gram Sabha or the Panchayats at the appropriate level shall be 'consulted' before making the acquisition of land in the Scheduled Areas for development projects and before re-settling or rehabilitating persons affected by such projects. In contrast, under Sections 4(k) and 4(l), the prior recommendation of the Gram Sabha or the Panchayats at the appropriate level is made 'mandatory' prior to the grant of a prospecting licence or mining lease for minor minerals, as well as for the grant of concession for the exploitation of minor minerals by auction.

Statement 3 is correct. Section 4(o) of the PESA Act, 1996 explicitly stipulates that the State Legislature shall endeavour to follow the pattern of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution while designing the administrative arrangements in the Panchayats at district levels in the Scheduled Areas.

ref: Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, Sections 4(g), 4(i), 4(k), 4(l) & 4(o)

stem: With reference to the bar to interference by courts in electoral matters of local self-government institutions, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Under the Constitution of India, an election to any Panchayat or Municipality can be called in question only by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as is provided for by or under any law made by the Legislature of a State.

Statement-II: Articles 243O and 243ZG of the Constitution explicitly vest the High Court of the concerned State with exclusive original jurisdiction to try election petitions relating to Panchayats and Municipalities.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Articles 243O(b) and 243ZG(b) impose a constitutional bar against questioning Panchayat and Municipal elections except through an election petition presented to an authority designated by a State law—unlike parliamentary and assembly election petitions, the Constitution does not mandate the High Court as the original forum for local body election disputes.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Article 243O(b) (for Panchayats) and Article 243ZG(b) (for Municipalities) both stipulate that notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, no election to any Panchayat or Municipality shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as is provided for by or under any law made by the Legislature of a State.

Statement-II is incorrect. Unlike election petitions for Parliament and State Legislatures (which are tried by the High Court under Section 80A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 read with Article 329(b)), Articles 243O(b) and 243ZG(b) do NOT vest the High Court with original jurisdiction to try Panchayat or Municipal election petitions. Instead, the Constitution empowers the State Legislature, by law, to designate the authority (typically a District Judge, Civil Judge, or State Election Tribunal) before whom such election petitions are presented.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 243O & 243ZG; Laxmikanth Ch. 39 & 40

stem: With reference to the constitution of Municipalities and the specification of urban areas under Article 243Q of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The State Election Commission is the competent constitutional authority to notify a 'transitional area', a 'smaller urban area', or a 'larger urban area' after every decennial census.
opts.B: Article 243Q prescribes uniform numerical thresholds of population and population density across all States for classifying an area as a Municipal Corporation.
opts.C: A Nagar Panchayat is constituted for a smaller urban area, whereas a Municipal Council is constituted for an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area.
opts.D: The Governor may, having regard to the size of an urban area and the municipal services being provided or proposed to be provided by an industrial establishment in that area, specify it by public notification to be an Industrial Township where a Municipality may not be constituted.

core: Under Article 243Q, the Governor notifies transitional areas (Nagar Panchayats), smaller urban areas (Municipal Councils), and larger urban areas (Municipal Corporations) based on five qualitative factors, and may exempt an area from constituting a Municipality by notifying it as an Industrial Township where an industrial establishment provides municipal services.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because the Proviso to Article 243Q(1) explicitly states that a Municipality under this clause may not be constituted in such urban area or part thereof as the Governor may, having regard to the size of the area and the municipal services being provided or proposed to be provided by an industrial establishment in that area and such other factors as he may deem fit, by public notification, specify to be an Industrial Township. Option (A) is incorrect because under Article 243Q(2), it is the Governor of the State—not the State Election Commission—who specifies a transitional area, a smaller urban area, or a larger urban area by public notification. Option (B) is incorrect because Article 243Q(2) does not prescribe fixed numerical thresholds in the Constitution; rather, it mandates the Governor to have regard to five parameters: (1) population of the area, (2) density of the population therein, (3) revenue generated for local administration, (4) percentage of employment in non-agricultural activities, and (5) the economic importance or such other factors as he may deem fit. Option (C) is incorrect because under Article 243Q(1), a Nagar Panchayat is constituted for a 'transitional area' (an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area), whereas a Municipal Council is constituted for a 'smaller urban area' and a Municipal Corporation for a 'larger urban area'.

ref: Constitution of India Article 243Q; Laxmikanth Ch. 40 (Municipalities)

stem: With reference to the composition of Municipalities and the constitution of Wards Committees under Part IXA of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 243R, persons having special knowledge or experience in municipal administration nominated to a Municipality have the right to vote in ordinary meetings of the Municipality, though not in the election of its Chairperson.
2. The Constitution mandates the constitution of Wards Committees consisting of one or more wards within the territorial area of every Municipality having a population of three lakhs or more.
3. Where a Wards Committee consists of two or more wards, one of the members representing such wards in the Municipality, elected by the members of the Wards Committee, serves as its Chairperson.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the proviso to Article 243R(2)(a), nominated members having special knowledge or experience in municipal administration are constitutionally barred from voting in the meetings of the Municipality. Article 243S mandates Wards Committees in Municipalities with a population of three lakhs or more and specifies how their Chairpersons are chosen.

exp.why: Under Article 243R(2)(a)(i), the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide for the representation in a Municipality of persons having special knowledge or experience in Municipal administration. However, the proviso to Article 243R(2)(a) explicitly mandates that the persons referred to in paragraph (i) shall not have the right to vote in the meetings of the Municipality at all. By contrast, this absolute constitutional prohibition in the proviso applies only to paragraph (i) nominees and not to the ex-officio legislators (MPs, MLAs, and MLCs) mentioned in paragraphs (ii) and (iii).

Article 243S(1) lays down a mandatory constitutional threshold: there shall be constituted Wards Committees, consisting of one or more wards, within the territorial area of a Municipality having a population of three lakhs or more. Under Article 243S(2), the State Legislature makes provisions by law regarding the composition and territorial area of a Wards Committee.

Article 243S(4) directly prescribes the rule for the Chairperson of a Wards Committee: where a Wards Committee consists of one ward, the member representing that ward in the Municipality shall be the Chairperson; and where it consists of two or more wards, one of the members representing such wards in the Municipality elected by the members of the Wards Committee shall be the Chairperson.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243R and 243S; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Municipalities

stem: With reference to the District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) and the Metropolitan Planning Committee (Article 243ZE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. While not less than two-thirds of the total number of members of a District Planning Committee must be elected, not less than four-fifths of the members of a Metropolitan Planning Committee must be elected.

2. In a District Planning Committee, the rural elected representatives are chosen by and from amongst the elected members of the district-level Panchayat, whereas in a Metropolitan Planning Committee, the rural representatives are elected by and from amongst the Chairpersons of the Panchayats in the Metropolitan area.

3. For both Committees, the manner in which the Chairpersons are chosen is determined by the Legislature of the State by law, and both Chairpersons forward the recommended draft development plan to the State Government.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 243ZD and 243ZE establish distinct electoral proportions and rural electoral colleges for the District Planning Committee (DPC) and Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC): at least four-fifths of a DPC's members are elected from the district-level Panchayat and Municipalities, whereas at least two-thirds of an MPC's members are elected from Municipal members and Panchayat Chairpersons.

exp.why: The constitutional fractions for the two bodies are swapped in the statement. Under the proviso to Article 243ZD(2), not less than four-fifths (4/5th) of the total number of members of a District Planning Committee shall be elected. Conversely, under the proviso to Article 243ZE(2), not less than two-thirds (2/3rd) of the members of a Metropolitan Planning Committee shall be elected.

Under the proviso to Article 243ZD(2), the elected members of a District Planning Committee are elected by, and from amongst, the elected members of the Panchayat at the district level (Zila Parishad) and of the Municipalities in the district in proportion to the rural-urban population ratio. Under the proviso to Article 243ZE(2), the elected members of a Metropolitan Planning Committee are elected by, and from amongst, the elected members of the Municipalities and the Chairpersons of the Panchayats in the Metropolitan area in proportion to the population ratio.

Under Article 243ZD(2)(c) and Article 243ZE(2)(d), the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to the manner in which the Chairpersons of the District Planning Committee and the Metropolitan Planning Committee shall be chosen. Furthermore, under Articles 243ZD(4) and 243ZE(4), the Chairperson of every such Committee shall forward the development plan, as recommended by the Committee, to the Government of the State.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243ZD and 243ZE; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Municipalities

stem: A State Government is reviewing the legal framework of specialized urban local governance arrangements operating within its geographical boundaries and examines the following institutional profiles:
items: 1. A Notified Area Committee established for a fast-developing industrial settlement solely through an executive notification published in the State Official Gazette without enacting a separate statute, with all its members including the Chairperson nominated by the State Government.

2. A Town Area Committee created for the civic administration of a small town solely through an executive order of the Divisional Commissioner without requiring a separate Act of the State Legislature.

3. A Cantonment Board established for the municipal administration of the civilian population in a military area, functioning under the administrative control of the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs with an elected civilian President.
prompt: Which of the institutional profiles described above accurately conforms/conform to the statutory and administrative framework of Urban Local Bodies in India?
core: Unlike a Town Area Committee (which requires a separate State statute) or a Cantonment Board (a Central statutory body under the Ministry of Defence headed ex-officio by the military station commander), a Notified Area Committee is constituted by a State Gazette notification applying selected provisions of the State Municipal Act and is entirely nominated.

exp.why: A Notified Area Committee is created for an area that is either a fast-developing town due to industrialization or a town that does not yet fulfill all conditions necessary for the constitution of a regular municipality. Because it is established by an executive notification in the State Government Gazette (applying only specified provisions of the State Municipal Act), it is called a Notified Area Committee. It is neither an elected body nor created by a separate statute; all its members, including the Chairman, are nominated by the State Government.

Unlike a Notified Area Committee, a Town Area Committee is created by a separate Act of a State Legislature for the administration of a small town. Its composition, limited civic functions (such as drainage, roads, and street lighting), and whether it is wholly elected, wholly nominated, or partly elected and partly nominated are governed strictly by that separate State statute, not merely by an executive order.

A Cantonment Board is established under the provisions of the central Cantonments Act and functions under the administrative control of the Union Ministry of Defence, not the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. Furthermore, the military officer commanding the station serves as its ex-officio President, while the Vice-President is elected by the elected civilian members from amongst themselves, and the Executive Officer is appointed by the President of India.

ref: Cantonments Act, 2006; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Municipalities (Types of Urban Governments)

stem: With reference to the distribution of functional items between the Eleventh Schedule (Article 243G) and the Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W) of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. 'Public distribution system' and 'Non-conventional energy sources' are explicitly enumerated as functional items in both the Eleventh Schedule and the Twelfth Schedule.

2. 'Cattle pounds and prevention of cruelty to animals' as well as 'Vital statistics including registration of births and deaths' are enumerated under the Eleventh Schedule rather than the Twelfth Schedule.
3. 'Regulation of slaughter-houses and tanneries' and 'Fire services' are placed in the Eleventh Schedule to regulate rural agro-processing and leather clusters.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Eleventh Schedule (29 items for Panchayats under Article 243G) and the Twelfth Schedule (18 items for Municipalities under Article 243W) have distinct enumerations: items such as Cattle pounds, Vital statistics, Fire services, and Regulation of slaughter-houses and tanneries belong to the Twelfth Schedule, whereas Public distribution system and Non-conventional energy sources belong exclusively to the Eleventh Schedule.

exp.why: 'Non-conventional energy sources' (Item 15) and 'Public distribution system' (Item 28) are enumerated exclusively in the Eleventh Schedule (Article 243G) for Panchayats. Neither of these items appears among the 18 functional items listed in the Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W) for Municipalities.

Although 'Cattle pounds' is often assumed to be a rural Panchayat subject, 'Cattle pounds; prevention of cruelty to animals' (Item 15) and 'Vital statistics including registration of births and deaths' (Item 16) are specifically enumerated in the Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W) for Municipalities, and not in the Eleventh Schedule.

Both 'Fire services' (Item 7) and 'Regulation of slaughter-houses and tanneries' (Item 18) are specifically listed in the Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W) as functional matters that may be devolved to Municipalities, and do not figure in the Eleventh Schedule.

ref: Constitution of India, Eleventh Schedule (Article 243G) and Twelfth Schedule (Article 243W)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional status of Co-operative Societies under the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011:
items: Statement-I: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB of the Constitution insofar as it applies to co-operative societies operating within a single State, while upholding its operation with respect to Multi-State Co-operative Societies.

Statement-II: While Multi-State Co-operative Societies fall under Entry 44 of the Union List, co-operative societies operating within a State fall under Entry 32 of the State List, and curtailing the exclusive legislative power of States over them required ratification by at least one-half of the State Legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of severability to Part IXB (inserted by the 97th Amendment): because State co-operative societies fall exclusively under Entry 32 of the State List, restricting State legislative power over them without ratification by half the States under the proviso to Article 368(2) was unconstitutional, whereas Part IXB remains valid for Multi-State Co-operative Societies under Entry 44 of the Union List.

exp.why: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of severability to Part IXB of the Constitution (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT). It declared Part IXB inoperative regarding co-operative societies working within a single State, while holding that Part IXB continues to remain operative in respect of Multi-State Co-operative Societies (Articles 243ZR and 243ZS). The amendments to Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B also remained unaffected.

Under the Seventh Schedule, 'Co-operative societies' are an exclusive State subject under Entry 32 of List II (State List), whereas Multi-State Co-operative Societies with objects not confined to one State fall under Entry 44 of List I (Union List). By prescribing mandatory rules for board composition, elections, and supersession in Part IXB, the 97th Amendment significantly curtailed the plenary legislative power of State Legislatures over Entry 32 of List II, thereby attracting clause (b) of the proviso to Article 368(2). Because Parliament passed the 97th Amendment without obtaining ratification from at least one-half of the State Legislatures, Statement-II directly explains why the Supreme Court reached the ruling stated in Statement-I.

ref: Supreme Court Judgment in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021); Constitution of India, Part IXB and Article 368(2)

stem: With reference to the substantive provisions governing Co-operative Societies contained in Part IXB of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 243ZJ, the maximum number of directors of a co-operative society shall not exceed twenty-one inclusive of up to two co-opted expert directors, and the board must reserve two seats for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes and one seat for women.

2. Persons having experience in banking, management, or finance who are co-opted as directors to the board have the right to vote in the election of the office-bearers of the board, though they cannot themselves be elected as office-bearers.

3. Under Article 243ZL, the board of any co-operative society may be superseded or kept under suspension for up to six months on grounds of persistent default, even where there is no Government shareholding, loan, financial assistance, or guarantee.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Part IXB (Articles 243ZJ and 243ZL) caps elected directors at 21 plus up to 2 additional non-voting co-opted expert directors, reserves 1 seat for SC/ST and 2 seats for women, bars co-opted directors from voting in elections or becoming office-bearers, and strictly prohibits the supersession of any board where there is no Government shareholding, loan, financial assistance, or guarantee.

exp.why: Under the first proviso to Article 243ZJ(1) read with the first proviso to Article 243ZJ(3), the maximum number of directors shall not exceed twenty-one, and the up to two co-opted expert members are in addition to (not inclusive of) the twenty-one directors (allowing a total up to 23). Furthermore, the second proviso to Article 243ZJ(1) mandates the reservation of one seat for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes and two seats for women (not two for SC/ST and one for women) on the board of every co-operative society having individual members from such categories.

Under the second proviso to Article 243ZJ(3), co-opted expert directors shall neither have the right to vote in any election of the co-operative society in their capacity as such member, nor be eligible to be elected as office-bearers of the board.

The first proviso to Article 243ZL(1) contains an express constitutional bar: the board of any co-operative society shall not be superseded or kept under suspension where there is no Government shareholding or loan or financial assistance or any guarantee by the Government.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 243ZJ and 243ZL (Part IXB); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Co-operative Societies

stem: With reference to the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor of the concerned State is empowered to declare any area within the State to be a Scheduled Area by public notification.

2. Under the Sixth Schedule, the Governor is empowered by public notification to organize and re-organize the Autonomous Districts, including increasing or diminishing their areas or altering their boundaries.
3. The executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to a State having Fifth Schedule Areas regarding the administration of those areas.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Paragraph 6 of the Fifth Schedule, only the President of India is empowered by order to declare or alter the boundaries of a Scheduled Area (in consultation with the Governor), whereas under Paragraph 1(3) of the Sixth Schedule, the Governor is directly empowered by public notification to create, unite, or alter the boundaries of Autonomous Districts.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 6(1) of the Fifth Schedule, the expression 'Scheduled Areas' means such areas as the President may by order declare to be Scheduled Areas. Furthermore, under Paragraph 6(2), only the President—after consultation with the Governor of the State concerned—may by order direct that the whole or any specified part of a Scheduled Area shall cease to be a Scheduled Area, or increase the area, or alter and rectify boundaries. The Governor does not possess the authority to declare an area as a Fifth Schedule Area.

Under Paragraph 1(3) of the Sixth Schedule, the Governor is explicitly empowered, by public notification, to include any area in or exclude any area from the table of tribal areas, create a new Autonomous District, increase or diminish the area of any Autonomous District, unite two or more Autonomous Districts, or alter the name or define the boundaries of any Autonomous District.

Under Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule, the executive power of a State extends to the Scheduled Areas therein, subject to the provisions of the Schedule; additionally, the Governor must report to the President annually (or whenever required) regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas, and the executive power of the Union extends to the giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas.

ref: Constitution of India, Fifth Schedule (Paras 3 & 6) and Sixth Schedule (Para 1); Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: With reference to the Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) provided for under Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Tribes Advisory Council can be constituted under the Fifth Schedule only in those States that have notified Scheduled Areas within their territory.
2. It consists of not more than twenty members, of whom, as nearly as may be, three-fourths shall be the representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of the State.
3. The Governor is empowered to make rules prescribing the number of members of the Council, the mode of their appointment, and the appointment of its Chairman.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While a Tribes Advisory Council is mandatory in every State having notified Fifth Schedule Areas, Paragraph 4(1) also empowers the President to direct the establishment of a TAC in any State having Scheduled Tribes even if it has no Scheduled Areas. Its membership is capped at 20, with three-fourths reserved for ST MLAs of the State.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 4(1) of the Fifth Schedule, a Tribes Advisory Council shall be established in each State having Scheduled Areas therein and, if the President so directs, also in any State having Scheduled Tribes but not Scheduled Areas therein (for example, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Uttarakhand have constituted TACs under Presidential direction despite having no notified Scheduled Areas).

Paragraph 4(1) of the Fifth Schedule stipulates that the Tribes Advisory Council shall consist of not more than twenty members, of whom, as nearly as may be, three-fourths shall be the representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of the State. If the number of ST MLAs in the Assembly is less than the number of seats to be filled by such representatives, the remaining seats are filled by other members of those tribes.

Under Paragraph 4(3) of the Fifth Schedule, the Governor may make rules prescribing or regulating the number of members of the Council, the mode of their appointment, the appointment of the Chairman of the Council and of the officers and servants thereof, and the conduct of its meetings and its procedure in general.

ref: Constitution of India, Fifth Schedule, Paragraph 4; Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the legislative powers of the Governor under Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: While the Governor can by public notification direct that a general Act of Parliament shall not apply to a Scheduled Area without requiring the assent of the President, any Regulation made by the Governor for the peace and good government of that Scheduled Area has no legal effect until it is assented to by the President after prior consultation with the Tribes Advisory Council.

Statement-II: Under Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule, the power to make Regulations enables the Governor to enact substantive primary laws restricting land transfers and regulating money-lending, and even to repeal or amend an existing Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature in its application to the Scheduled Area.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule draws a vital structural distinction between the Governor's adaptive notification power under sub-paragraph (1) and plenary law-making power via Regulations under sub-paragraphs (2) and (3). Because Regulations can create substantive laws on tribal land and money-lending and even repeal or amend Parliamentary statutes, sub-paragraphs (4) and (5) subject Regulations to mandatory prior consultation with the Tribes Advisory Council and Presidential assent.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 5(1) of the Fifth Schedule, the Governor may by public notification direct that any particular Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area or shall apply subject to specified exceptions and modifications. This notification power under Paragraph 5(1) does not textually mandate prior TAC consultation or Presidential assent. Conversely, under Paragraphs 5(4) and 5(5), all Regulations made under Paragraph 5 must be preceded by consultation with the Tribes Advisory Council (where one exists) and must be submitted forthwith to the President, having no effect until assented to by him.

Under Paragraphs 5(2) and 5(3) of the Fifth Schedule, Regulations made by the Governor for the peace and good government of a Scheduled Area may prohibit or restrict the transfer of land by or among members of Scheduled Tribes, regulate the allotment of land, and regulate money-lending to Scheduled Tribes; furthermore, in making any such Regulation, the Governor may repeal or amend any Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature or any existing law applicable to the area. Because this Regulation-making authority constitutes extraordinary plenary legislation capable of amending Parliamentary Acts, the Constitution imposes the dual procedural safeguard described in Statement-I.

ref: Constitution of India, Fifth Schedule, Paragraph 5(1)–(5); Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: With reference to the structural composition and constitutional status of Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Every Autonomous District Council consists of not more than twenty members, of whom three-fourths are required to be sitting members of the State Legislative Assembly belonging to the Scheduled Tribes.
opts.B: The provisions of Part IX of the Constitution relating to Panchayats apply automatically to the Autonomous Districts under the Sixth Schedule, subject only to modifications notified by the State Election Commission.
opts.C: Under the general scheme of Paragraph 2 of the Sixth Schedule, an Autonomous District Council consists of not more than thirty members, of whom not more than four are nominated by the Governor and the rest are elected on the basis of adult suffrage.
opts.D: All members of an Autonomous District Council, whether elected or nominated, enjoy a fixed constitutional tenure of five years and can be removed only through a resolution passed by the State Legislative Assembly.

core: Under Paragraph 2(1) of the Sixth Schedule, the general constitutional baseline for an Autonomous District Council is a maximum of 30 members: up to 4 nominated by the Governor (who hold office during the Governor's pleasure) and the remaining 26 elected via adult suffrage for a 5-year term.

exp.why: Option C is correct: Under Paragraph 2(1) of the Sixth Schedule, each Autonomous District Council (save for specific tailored exceptions inserted for councils like the Bodoland Territorial Council) consists of not more than thirty members, of whom not more than four persons are nominated by the Governor and the rest are elected on the basis of adult suffrage. Option A is incorrect because it describes the Tribes Advisory Council under Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule (20 members, three-fourths ST MLAs), not an ADC. Option B is incorrect because Article 243M(2)(a) explicitly exempts the tribal areas referred to in Article 244(2) (Sixth Schedule areas) from the application of Part IX (73rd Amendment). Option D is incorrect because under Paragraph 2(6A) of the Sixth Schedule, only elected members hold office for a term of five years from the date appointed for the first meeting of the Council after general elections, whereas nominated members hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.

ref: Constitution of India, Sixth Schedule, Paragraph 2 & Article 243M(2)(a); Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: With reference to the application of Acts of Parliament and of the State Legislatures to the Autonomous Districts and Autonomous Regions under Paragraphs 12, 12A, 12AA, and 12B of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Across all four Sixth Schedule States—Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram—only the President of India is empowered to direct by notification that an Act of Parliament shall not apply, or shall apply with modifications, to an Autonomous District.

2. In the Autonomous Districts of Tripura and Mizoram, while the President may direct that an Act of Parliament shall not apply to an Autonomous District, the power to issue a similar direction in respect of an Act of the State Legislature vests only in the Governor.

3. An Act of the Legislature of the State of Assam with respect to any matter on which an Autonomous District Council is empowered to make laws under Paragraph 3 of the Sixth Schedule does not apply to that Autonomous District unless the District Council itself so directs by public notification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: The Sixth Schedule features a crucial State-wise asymmetry regarding who filters Union versus State laws: in Assam (Para 12), the Governor holds the notification power over both Acts of Parliament and State Acts, whereas in Meghalaya (Para 12A), Tripura (Para 12AA), and Mizoram (Para 12B), the power regarding Acts of Parliament vests in the President while the Governor exercises it only in respect of State Acts.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 12(1)(b) of the Sixth Schedule, with respect to Autonomous Districts and Autonomous Regions in the State of Assam, the power to direct by public notification that any Act of Parliament (or of the State Legislature to which clause (a) does not apply) shall not apply, or shall apply with exceptions or modifications, vests in the Governor of Assam—not the President. By contrast, in Meghalaya (Para 12A), Tripura (Para 12AA), and Mizoram (Para 12B), the power regarding Acts of Parliament vests in the President.

Under Paragraph 12AA(b) (applicable to Tripura) and Paragraph 12B(b)–(c) (applicable to Mizoram) of the Sixth Schedule, the Governor is empowered by public notification to direct that any Act of the Legislature of the State shall not apply to an Autonomous District or Region (or shall apply with modifications), whereas the President is empowered by notification to issue such directions with respect to any Act of Parliament.

Under Paragraph 12(1)(a) of the Sixth Schedule, no Act of the Legislature of the State of Assam in respect of any of the matters specified in Paragraph 3 (matters on which a District or Regional Council may make laws), and no Act of the Assam Legislature prohibiting or restricting the consumption of any non-distilled alcoholic liquor, shall apply to any Autonomous District or Region in the State unless the District Council for such district by public notification so directs (with or without exceptions or modifications).

ref: Constitution of India, Sixth Schedule, Paragraphs 12, 12A, 12AA, and 12B; Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: With reference to the judicial, fiscal, and regulatory powers of Autonomous District Councils under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The village councils or courts constituted by an Autonomous District Council under Paragraph 4 of the Sixth Schedule have automatic original jurisdiction to try all civil suits and criminal cases arising within the territorial limits of the district, even where one of the parties to the dispute is a non-tribal.

2. An Autonomous District Council has the constitutional authority under Paragraph 8 of the Sixth Schedule to assess and collect land revenue, as well as to levy and collect taxes on professions, trades, callings, employments, and on the entry of goods into a market for sale therein.

3. Regulations made by an Autonomous District Council under Paragraph 10 of the Sixth Schedule to control money-lending and trading within the district by non-tribals can be passed by a simple majority of the Council and take effect immediately without requiring the Governor's assent.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Autonomous District Councils enjoy wide fiscal powers under Paragraph 8 (land revenue, profession tax, market entry tax, ferry tolls), their village courts under Paragraph 4 are restricted to suits and cases where all parties belong to Scheduled Tribes, and their regulations controlling money-lending and trading by non-tribals under Paragraph 10 require both a three-fourths special majority of the total membership of the Council and mandatory assent of the Governor.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 4(1) of the Sixth Schedule, a Regional Council or District Council may constitute village councils or courts for the trial of suits and cases 'between the parties all of whom belong to Scheduled Tribes within such areas', to the exclusion of any court in the State. They do not enjoy general jurisdiction under Paragraph 4 over disputes involving non-tribal parties.

Under Paragraph 8(1) of the Sixth Schedule, the Regional or District Council has the power to assess and collect revenue in respect of all lands within its jurisdiction in accordance with principles followed generally by the State Government. Furthermore, under Paragraph 8(3), the District Council has the power to levy and collect taxes on professions, trades, callings, and employments; taxes on animals, vehicles, and boats; taxes on the entry of goods into a market for sale therein and tolls on passengers and goods carried in ferries; and taxes for the maintenance of schools, dispensaries, or roads.

Under Paragraph 10(1) of the Sixth Schedule, a District Council may make regulations for the control of money-lending and trading within the district by persons other than Scheduled Tribes resident in the district. However, Paragraph 10(2) mandates that no such regulation shall be made unless it is passed by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the total membership of the District Council, and Paragraph 10(3) mandates that all such regulations shall be submitted forthwith to the Governor and, until assented to by him, shall have no effect.

ref: Constitution of India, Sixth Schedule, Paragraphs 4, 8, and 10; Laxmikanth Ch. 41

stem: With reference to the administration and amendment of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Any addition, variation, or repeal of a provision of the Fifth or Sixth Schedule requires a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by a special majority of Parliament under Article 368.

2. The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act (PESA), 1996 extends the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution with modifications exclusively to the Scheduled Areas under Clause (1) of Article 244, and not to the Sixth Schedule tribal areas.
3. Under the Fifth Schedule, the executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to a State regarding the administration of the Scheduled Areas therein.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Paragraph 7 of the Fifth Schedule and Paragraph 21 of the Sixth Schedule empower Parliament to amend either Schedule by ordinary legislation passed by a simple majority, explicitly excluding such laws from the purview of Article 368. Furthermore, PESA 1996 applies solely to Fifth Schedule Areas under Article 244(1), whereas Sixth Schedule Areas have their own Autonomous District and Regional Councils.

exp.why: Under Paragraph 7 of the Fifth Schedule and Paragraph 21 of the Sixth Schedule, Parliament may from time to time by law amend by way of addition, variation, or repeal any of the provisions of the respective Schedule, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. Thus, an ordinary parliamentary law passed by a simple majority suffices.

Article 243M(1) exempts both Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas from the automatic application of Part IX. Exercising power under Article 243M(4)(b), Parliament enacted the PESA Act, 1996 to extend Part IX (with exceptions and modifications) specifically to the Scheduled Areas referred to in Clause (1) of Article 244 (Fifth Schedule States).

Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule explicitly provides that the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the administration of the Scheduled Areas therein.

ref: Constitution of India, Fifth Schedule (Paras 3 & 7), Sixth Schedule (Para 21) & Art. 243M; PESA Act, 1996

stem: With reference to the Special Provisions for certain States under Part XXI of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Article 371B : Constitution of a committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly consisting of members elected from the Hill Areas
2. Article 371C : Constitution of a committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly consisting of members elected from the tribal areas
3. Article 371F : Provision for a Legislative Assembly of not less than thirty members and protection of existing laws for the State of Sikkim
4. Article 371J : Establishment of a separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region and equitable reservation in education and public employment
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Part XXI (Articles 371 to 371J) contains asymmetric federal arrangements tailored to specific regional, tribal, and historical needs of various States. Article 371B applies to Assam's tribal area Assembly committee, whereas Article 371C applies to Manipur's Hill Areas Committee.

exp.why: Article 371B deals with the State of Assam (added by the 22nd Amendment Act, 1969), empowering the President to provide for the constitution and functions of a committee of the Legislative Assembly of Assam consisting of members elected from the tribal areas specified in Part I of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule.

Article 371C deals with the State of Manipur (added by the 27th Amendment Act, 1971), empowering the President to provide for the constitution and functions of a committee of the Legislative Assembly of Manipur consisting of members elected from the Hill Areas of that State.

Article 371F (inserted by the 36th Amendment Act, 1975) contains special provisions with respect to the State of Sikkim, mandating inter alia that its Legislative Assembly shall consist of not less than thirty members and protecting pre-merger laws in force.

Article 371J (inserted by the 98th Amendment Act, 2012) empowers the President to provide for the special responsibility of the Governor of Karnataka to establish a separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region (now Kalyana-Karnataka) along with reservation of seats in educational institutions and posts in State Government jobs.

ref: Constitution of India, Part XXI (Articles 371B, 371C, 371F, 371J); Laxmikanth on Special Provisions for Some States

stem: With reference to the comparative scope of special constitutional provisions for Nagaland (Article 371A), Mizoram (Article 371G), and Arunachal Pradesh (Article 371H), consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Article 371A protects 'ownership and transfer of land and its resources' in Nagaland from the automatic application of Acts of Parliament, Article 371G protects 'ownership and transfer of land' in Mizoram without explicitly mentioning its resources.

2. Under both Article 371A and Article 371H, the Governor of the respective State has a special responsibility with respect to law and order and exercises individual judgment as to the action to be taken after consulting the Council of Ministers.

3. Like the Legislative Assemblies of Nagaland and Mizoram, the Legislative Assembly of Arunachal Pradesh under Article 371H must pass a resolution before any Act of Parliament in respect of the religious or social practices of the indigenous tribes can apply to the State.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Articles 371A (Nagaland), 371G (Mizoram), and 371H (Arunachal Pradesh) confer distinct degrees of autonomy: while 371A and 371G grant the State Legislative Assembly veto power over Parliamentary laws on customary law and land (with 371A explicitly including 'and its resources'), only 371A and 371H vest the Governor with special responsibility and individual judgment regarding law and order.

exp.why: Under Article 371A(1)(a)(iv), no Act of Parliament in respect of 'ownership and transfer of land and its resources' shall apply to Nagaland unless its Legislative Assembly so decides by a resolution. In contrast, Article 371G(a)(iv) for Mizoram specifies 'ownership and transfer of land' and omits the phrase 'and its resources'.

Both Article 371A(1)(b) (for Nagaland) and Article 371H(a) (for Arunachal Pradesh) confer special responsibility on the Governor with respect to law and order in the State, where the Governor, after consulting the Council of Ministers, exercises individual judgment as to the action to be taken, and the Governor's decision is final unless the President directs otherwise. Article 371G (Mizoram) contains no such provision.

Unlike Article 371A (Nagaland) and Article 371G (Mizoram), Article 371H (Arunachal Pradesh) does not grant the Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly any power to block or require a prior resolution for the application of Acts of Parliament relating to religious or social practices, customary law, or land ownership.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 371A, 371G, and 371H

stem: With reference to the institutional mechanisms under Articles 371, 371D, and 371J of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Articles 371 and 371J, the Governors of Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Karnataka are directly empowered by the Constitution to establish separate regional development boards at their own discretion without requiring any prior order from the President.
2. Under Articles 371 and 371J, the annual report on the working of each regional development board is required to be laid before both Houses of Parliament by the President.

3. Under Article 371D, the power to issue an order providing for equitable opportunities and facilities in public employment and education for people from different parts of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana is vested in the Governor of the respective State.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Articles 371(2) and 371J(1), the Governor's special responsibility to establish separate regional development boards arises only when the President issues an order providing for it, and the annual working report of each board is placed before the State Legislative Assembly. Under Article 371D(1), it is the President directly—not the Governor—who issues orders ensuring equitable opportunities in public employment and education in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

exp.why: Under Article 371(2) (for Maharashtra and Gujarat) and Article 371J(1) (for Karnataka), the Governor does not possess an independent, self-executing power to establish development boards. Instead, the President may by order made with respect to the State provide for any special responsibility of the Governor for the establishment of separate development boards.

Under Article 371(2)(a) and Article 371J(1)(a), the report on the working of each development board is required to be placed every year before the State Legislative Assembly, not before both Houses of Parliament.

Under Article 371D(1), it is the President of India (and not the Governor of the State) who may by order with respect to the State of Andhra Pradesh or the State of Telangana provide, having regard to the requirements of each State as a whole, for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of the State in the matter of public employment and education.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 371(2), 371D(1), and 371J(1)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the special constitutional provisions applicable to the State of Sikkim:
items: Statement-I: Notwithstanding the general mandate under Article 170 of the Constitution, the Legislative Assembly of Sikkim is constitutionally permitted to consist of fewer than sixty members and to reserve a seat for the non-territorial Sangha constituency elected exclusively by Buddhist monks.

Statement-II: Under Article 371F of the Constitution, neither the Supreme Court nor any other court has jurisdiction in respect of any dispute or other matter arising out of any treaty, agreement, or engagement relating to Sikkim entered into before its merger with the Union of India.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article 371F (inserted by the 36th Amendment Act, 1975) begins with a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution'), which under clauses (a) and (f) enables Sikkim to have an Assembly of not less than 30 members and non-territorial Sangha representation, as upheld in R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993). While clause (m) of Article 371F separately bars judicial jurisdiction over pre-accession treaties, that jurisdictional bar is not what validates the Assembly's composition.

exp.why: Article 170(1) generally prescribes a minimum of 60 members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in a State Legislative Assembly. However, by virtue of the non-obstante clause of Article 371F along with clauses (a) and (f), the Sikkim Legislative Assembly can have a minimum of 30 members (currently 32) and reserve a seat for the non-territorial Sangha constituency (monasteries recognized at the time of merger), which the Supreme Court upheld in R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993) based on Sikkim's historical evolution.

Statement-II accurately states Article 371F(m), which ousts the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts over disputes arising out of pre-merger treaties or agreements relating to Sikkim. However, Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: in R.C. Poudyal (1993), the Supreme Court explicitly clarified that Article 371F(f) is justiciable and not shielded by clause (m), upholding the Assembly's composition and the Sangha seat on the substantive authority of the non-obstante clause and clauses (a) and (f) of Article 371F.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 371F; R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993)

stem: With reference to the Official Language of the Union under Part XVII of the Constitution of India and the Official Languages Act, 1963, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 343(1) of the Constitution, the official language of the Union is Hindi in Devanagari script and the default form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union is the Devanagari form of numerals.

2. The Committee of Parliament on Official Language constituted under Article 344(4) consists of thirty members drawn exclusively from the Lok Sabha and submits its report directly to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

3. Under the Official Languages Act, 1963, English may continue to be used, in addition to Hindi, for all the official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before the expiration of fifteen years from the commencement of the Constitution and for the transaction of business in Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Article 343(1) mandates that while the official language of the Union is Hindi in Devanagari script, the form of numerals for official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals. Furthermore, the joint Parliamentary Committee on Official Language (20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha MPs) reports to the President, and the Official Languages Act, 1963 provides for the indefinite continuation of English alongside Hindi.

exp.why: Article 343(1) explicitly stipulates that the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script, but 'the form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals', not the Devanagari form of numerals.

Under Article 344(4) and Section 4 of the Official Languages Act, 1963, the Committee of Parliament on Official Language consists of thirty members, of whom twenty are members of the Lok Sabha and ten are members of the Rajya Sabha. Moreover, under Article 344(5), the Committee submits its report to the President (not the Speaker), who causes it to be laid before each House of Parliament.

Enacted pursuant to Article 343(3), Section 3 of the Official Languages Act, 1963 provides that notwithstanding the expiration of the initial fifteen-year period (ending January 26, 1965), the English language may continue to be used, in addition to Hindi, for all official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before that day and for the transaction of business in Parliament.

ref: Constitution of India, Part XVII (Articles 343 & 344); Official Languages Act, 1963

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the official languages of States under Part XVII of the Constitution of India:
items: Statement-I: A language that is not enumerated in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution can nevertheless be legally adopted as an official language of a State or officially recognized for specified purposes within that State.

Statement-II: Both Article 345, which empowers a State Legislature to adopt by law any one or more of the languages in use in the State, and Article 347, which empowers the President to direct official recognition of a language spoken by a section of the State's population, operate independently of the Eighth Schedule.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Neither Article 345 (adoption of official languages by a State Legislature) nor Article 347 (Presidential direction for recognition of a language spoken by a section of a State's population) restricts the choice of language to those listed in the Eighth Schedule. Consequently, States have validly adopted non-Eighth Schedule languages such as English (e.g., Nagaland), Kokborok (Tripura), and Mizo (Mizoram) for official purposes.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Inclusion in the Eighth Schedule is not a constitutional prerequisite for a language to be adopted as an official language of a State. For example, English (in Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Arunachal Pradesh), Kokborok (in Tripura), Mizo (in Mizoram), and Khasi and Garo (associate official languages in Meghalaya) are legally recognized for official purposes in their respective States despite not being in the Eighth Schedule.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Article 345 states that the Legislature of a State may by law adopt 'any one or more of the languages in use in the State or Hindi' as the language or languages to be used for all or any of the official purposes of that State. Similarly, Article 347 empowers the President, if satisfied that a substantial proportion of the population of a State desires the use of any language spoken by them to be recognized by that State, to direct that such language shall also be officially recognized throughout that State or any part thereof. Neither article cross-references or limits itself to the Eighth Schedule (which is explicitly referenced only in Articles 344(1) and 351).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 344, 345, 347 & 351; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Official Language

stem: With reference to the constitutional provisions governing the language of the Supreme Court, the High Courts, and authoritative legislative texts under Article 348 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution, neither the President nor the Chief Justice of India is empowered to authorize the use of Hindi in the proceedings of the Supreme Court unless Parliament by law provides otherwise.

2. Under Article 348(2), although the Governor of a State may, with the previous consent of the President, authorize the use of Hindi or any other official language of the State in proceedings in the High Court, the proviso to that clause expressly excludes judgments, decrees, or orders passed by the High Court from its purview.

3. Where a State Legislature has prescribed any language other than English for use in Bills introduced in, or Acts passed by, the Legislature of the State, a translation of the same in the English language published under the authority of the Governor in the Official Gazette of the State is deemed to be the authoritative text thereof in the English language.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 348(1) mandates that until Parliament by law provides otherwise, all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court, and all authoritative texts of Bills, Acts, Ordinances, and delegated legislation at both Union and State levels, shall be in English. While Article 348(2) creates a constitutional exception allowing the Governor (with Presidential consent) to authorize Hindi or a State official language in High Court proceedings, its proviso carves out judgments, decrees, and orders, and no parallel executive exception exists for Supreme Court proceedings.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 348(1)(a), until Parliament by law otherwise provides, all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court shall be in the English language. Unlike High Courts (covered by the executive exception in Article 348(2)), the Constitution gives neither the President nor the Chief Justice of India any independent authority to replace English with Hindi in Supreme Court proceedings in the absence of Parliamentary legislation.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 348(2), the Governor of a State may, with the previous consent of the President, authorize the use of the Hindi language, or any other language used for any official purposes of the State, in proceedings in the High Court having its principal seat in that State. However, the proviso to Article 348(2) explicitly states: 'Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to any judgment, decree or order passed or made by such High Court.' (Note: The optional use of Hindi in High Court judgments accompanied by an English translation flows from Section 7 of the Official Languages Act, 1963 enacted by Parliament, not from Article 348(2) itself).

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 348(3), where the Legislature of a State has prescribed any language other than the English language for use in Bills introduced in, or Acts passed by, the Legislature of the State, or in Ordinances promulgated by the Governor, or in any order, rule, regulation or bye-law, a translation of the same in the English language published under the authority of the Governor of the State in the Official Gazette of that State shall be deemed to be the authoritative text thereof in the English language under this article.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 348(1), 348(2) & 348(3); Official Languages Act, 1963, Section 7

stem: With reference to the Special Directives relating to language contained in Chapter IV of Part XVII of the Constitution of India (Articles 350 to 351), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Every person is entitled to submit a representation for the redress of any grievance to any officer or authority of the Union or a State in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State, as the case may be, even if that language is not listed in the Eighth Schedule.
opts.B: Both the directive to provide facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education and the office of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities were present in the original Constitution of 1950.
opts.C: The Constitution prescribes a fixed tenure of five years for the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities and stipulates that the officer can be removed only in the manner prescribed for a Judge of a High Court.
opts.D: Under Article 350A, only the Parliament by law can issue binding directions to a State Government for securing adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups.

core: Article 350 entitles every person to submit a representation for the redress of any grievance to any officer or authority of the Union or a State in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State, without restricting this right to Eighth Schedule languages. Furthermore, Articles 350A and 350B were inserted later by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956, and the Constitution does not prescribe the tenure or removal procedure of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because Article 350 explicitly provides that every person shall be entitled to submit a representation for the redress of any grievance to any officer or authority of the Union or a State in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State, as the case may be; it is not restricted to Eighth Schedule languages. Option (B) is incorrect because Articles 350A and 350B were not in the original Constitution; they were inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956, pursuant to the recommendations of the States Reorganisation Commission. Option (C) is incorrect because Article 350B merely provides for the appointment of a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities by the President and does not lay down qualifications, tenure, salaries, or removal procedures in the Constitution. Option (D) is incorrect because under Article 350A, it is the President (and not Parliament by law) who is empowered to issue such directions to any State as he considers necessary or proper for securing the provision of mother-tongue instruction facilities at the primary stage.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 350, 350A & 350B; 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956

stem: Consider the following constitutional developments regarding the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Inclusion of Maithili and Dogri in the Eighth Schedule
2. Inclusion of Sindhi in the Eighth Schedule
3. Inclusion of Konkani and Manipuri in the Eighth Schedule
4. Alteration of the nomenclature of 'Oriya' to 'Odia' in the Eighth Schedule
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above developments, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: Originally containing 14 languages in 1950, the Eighth Schedule was expanded to 22 languages through three Constitutional Amendments: the 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi; the 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali; and the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. Subsequently, the 96th Amendment (2011) substituted 'Odia' for 'Oriya'.

exp.why: Item 1 (Inclusion of Maithili and Dogri, along with Bodo and Santhali) was enacted by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, placing it third in the chronological sequence.
Item 2 (Inclusion of Sindhi as the 15th language in the Eighth Schedule) was enacted by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1967, making it the earliest milestone among the four.
Item 3 (Inclusion of Konkani and Manipuri, along with Nepali) was enacted by the 71st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, placing it second in the chronological sequence.

Item 4 (Alteration of 'Oriya' to 'Odia' in the Eighth Schedule) was enacted by the 96th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, making it the latest milestone among the four. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2 - 3 - 1 - 4.

ref: Constitution of India, Eighth Schedule; 21st (1967), 71st (1992), 92nd (2003) & 96th (2011) Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: Consider the following table comparing specific languages in India across their recognition as a 'Classical Language' by the Government of India and their inclusion in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution (formatted as — Language : Classical Language Status : Eighth Schedule Status):
items: 1. Pali : Accorded Classical Language status : Not included in the Eighth Schedule
2. Prakrit : Accorded Classical Language status : Included in the Eighth Schedule
3. Assamese : Accorded Classical Language status : Included in the Eighth Schedule
4. Maithili : Accorded Classical Language status : Included in the Eighth Schedule
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
core: Following the October 2024 notification by the Union Cabinet adding Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali to the previous six Classical Languages (Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and Odia), India recognizes 11 Classical Languages. Crucially, Classical Language status does not require inclusion in the Eighth Schedule: Pali and Prakrit are Classical Languages of India even though neither is listed among the 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule.
