exp.why: Row 1 is correctly matched. Pali was accorded Classical Language status by the Government of India in October 2024, and it is not included among the 22 languages enumerated in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
Row 2 is incorrectly matched. Although Prakrit was accorded Classical Language status in October 2024, it is NOT included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.

Row 3 is correctly matched. Assamese was accorded Classical Language status in October 2024 (alongside Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, and Bengali) and has been included in the Eighth Schedule since the commencement of the Constitution in 1950.

Row 4 is incorrectly matched. While Maithili is included in the Eighth Schedule (added by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003), it has not been accorded Classical Language status by the Government of India.

ref: Ministry of Culture Notification on Classical Languages (October 2024); Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional mechanisms for overseeing the administration of Scheduled Areas, Scheduled Tribes, and Autonomous Districts:
items: Statement-I: Under Paragraph 14 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, the President of India appoints the Commission to examine and report on matters relating to the administration of Autonomous Districts and Autonomous Regions in a State, and causes its report to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.

Statement-II: Under Article 339 of the Constitution, the President is empowered to appoint a Commission to report on the administration of the Scheduled Areas and the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the States, and the executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to a State regarding the drawing up and execution of schemes specified in the directions to be essential for the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Constitution sharply distinguishes between the general oversight of Scheduled Areas/Scheduled Tribes under Article 339 and the specific inquiry mechanism for Sixth Schedule Autonomous Districts under Paragraph 14. While the President appoints the Commission on Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes under Article 339(1), it is the Governor of the State—and not the President—who appoints a Commission to inquire into and report on the administration of Autonomous Districts and Regions under Paragraph 14 of the Sixth Schedule, with its report laid before the State Legislature.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Under Paragraph 14(1) of the Sixth Schedule, it is the Governor of the State (not the President of India) who may at any time appoint a Commission to examine and report on any matter specified by him relating to the administration of the autonomous districts and autonomous regions in the State. Furthermore, under Paragraph 14(3), every such report, together with the recommendations of the Governor and an explanatory memorandum regarding the action proposed to be taken thereon by the Government of the State, is laid before the Legislature of the State (not Parliament).

Statement-II is correct. Under Article 339(1), the President may at any time (and was required to at the expiration of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution) by order appoint a Commission to report on the administration of the Scheduled Areas and the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the States (under which the Dhebar Commission in 1960 and the Dilip Singh Bhuria Commission in 2002 were appointed). Under Article 339(2), the executive power of the Union extends to the giving of directions to a State as to the drawing up and execution of schemes specified in the direction to be essential for the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the State, and failure to comply with such directions attracts Article 365.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 339, Article 365 & Sixth Schedule (Paragraph 14); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity

stem: With reference to the Election Commission of India (ECI) under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 324, the Election Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners, if any, as the President may from time to time fix.

2. Although the Election Commission conducts elections to the offices of the President and Vice-President, all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with such elections are inquired into and decided only by the Supreme Court.

3. The superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and Urban Local Bodies are vested in the Election Commission of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President in the ECI, whereas elections to Panchayats and Municipalities are vested in separate State Election Commissions under Articles 243K and 243ZA. Furthermore, under Article 71, the Supreme Court exercises exclusive and final jurisdiction over disputes relating to Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.

exp.why: Under Article 324(2) of the Constitution, the Election Commission shall consist of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners, if any, as the President may from time to time fix. The Constitution does not fix the numerical strength of the Commission.

While Article 324(1) charges the Election Commission of India with conducting elections to the offices of the President and Vice-President, Article 71(1) explicitly mandates that all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided only by the Supreme Court, whose decision shall be final.

The Election Commission of India does not supervise elections to Panchayats or Urban Local Bodies (Municipalities). Under Articles 243K and 243ZA (inserted by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, 1992), the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Panchayats and Municipalities are vested in a separate State Election Commission.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 71, 243K, 243ZA & 324; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Election Commission

stem: With reference to the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Search Committee constituted to prepare a panel of five persons for consideration of the Selection Committee is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary.
2. The Selection Committee that recommends appointments to the President consists of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.
3. The Selection Committee cannot consider any person outside the panel prepared by the Search Committee, and any vacancy in the Selection Committee invalidates the appointment process.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Enacted pursuant to Article 324(2) of the Constitution, the 2023 Act replaced the Supreme Court's interim mechanism in Anoop Baranwal (2023) with a statutory Selection Committee comprising the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. It also instituted a Search Committee headed by the Union Minister of Law and Justice while empowering the Selection Committee to consider candidates even outside the shortlisted panel.

exp.why: While the original Bill introduced in August 2023 proposed the Cabinet Secretary as head of the Search Committee, Section 6 of the finally enacted Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 mandates that the Search Committee is headed by the Union Minister of Law and Justice (not the Cabinet Secretary) and includes two other members not below the rank of Secretary to the Government of India having knowledge and experience in matters relating to elections.

Under Section 7(1) of the 2023 Act, the Selection Committee consists of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People (or the leader of the single largest opposition party in the Lok Sabha), and a Union Cabinet Minister to be nominated by the Prime Minister. The Chief Justice of India, who was part of the interim committee set up by the Supreme Court in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) pending parliamentary legislation, is not a member under the enacted statute.

Under Section 8(2) of the 2023 Act, the Selection Committee is expressly empowered to also consider any other person than those included in the panel prepared by the Search Committee. Furthermore, Section 7(2) stipulates that the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner or other Election Commissioners shall not be invalid merely by reason of any vacancy in or any defect in the constitution of the Selection Committee.

ref: CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, Sections 6, 7 & 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the institutional structure and tenure of the Election Commission of India:
items: Statement-I: Although the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the other Election Commissioners exercise equal voting power in decision-making and draw identical salaries, they do not enjoy identical constitutional security of tenure.

Statement-II: Under Article 324(5) of the Constitution, the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court, whereas any other Election Commissioner can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners function as co-equals in transacting business (deciding by majority vote in case of difference of opinion) and receive identical salaries and service conditions under the 2023 Act, Article 324(5) creates a structural asymmetry in removal protection. Only the CEC enjoys the rigorous parliamentary removal shield equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge, whereas other ECs can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC.

exp.why: Under the 2023 Act and established constitutional jurisprudence (T.N. Seshan v. Union of India, 1995), the CEC does not enjoy superior voting authority over the other Election Commissioners; all business is transacted unanimously as far as possible, and in case of a difference of opinion, the matter is decided according to the opinion of the majority. They also draw equal salaries (equivalent to a Judge of the Supreme Court), yet their constitutional protection against removal differs significantly.

The first and second provisos to Article 324(5) of the Constitution directly explain this asymmetry in security of tenure: the Chief Election Commissioner shall not be removed from office except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court (requiring a special majority resolution in both Houses of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity), whereas any other Election Commissioner or a Regional Commissioner can be removed from office on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 324(5); T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995); CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023

stem: With reference to the advisory and quasi-judicial powers of the Election Commission of India (ECI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Articles 103 and 192 of the Constitution, the President or the Governor is constitutionally bound to act according to the opinion of the Election Commission when deciding on the post-election disqualification of a legislator on grounds other than defection.

2. Under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, the Election Commission acts as a quasi-judicial tribunal to adjudicate disputes between rival factions of a recognised political party claiming its name and symbol.

3. Before deciding on a petition for the disqualification of a legislator on the ground of defection under the Tenth Schedule, the Presiding Officer of the House must obtain the advisory opinion of the Election Commission.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Constitution bifurcates adjudication of legislative disqualifications into two distinct tracks: general disqualifications under Articles 102(1)/191(1) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 are decided by the President/Governor strictly in accordance with the binding opinion of the ECI (Articles 103/192), whereas anti-defection disqualifications under the Tenth Schedule are decided exclusively by the Presiding Officer of the Legislature without any involvement of the ECI.

exp.why: Under Article 103 (for Members of Parliament) and Article 192 (for Members of State Legislatures), if any question arises as to whether a sitting member has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in Article 102(1) or Article 191(1) (such as holding an office of profit, unsoundness of mind, or statutory disqualifications under the RPA 1951), the President or the Governor shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and 'shall act according to such opinion'.

Under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, when the Election Commission is satisfied that there are rival sections or groups of a recognised political party each of whom claims to be that party, the Commission decides the dispute after taking into account all available facts and circumstances and hearing the representatives. As affirmed by the Supreme Court in Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1972) and Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary (2023), the ECI exercises a quasi-judicial power under Paragraph 15.

Under Articles 102(2) and 191(2) read with Paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule, any question regarding disqualification on the ground of defection is referred for the decision of the Chairman or the Speaker of such House, who acts as a tribunal (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992). The Election Commission of India has no advisory or adjudicatory role in Tenth Schedule anti-defection proceedings.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 102, 103, 191, 192 & Tenth Schedule; Election Symbols Order, 1968, Para 15

stem: With reference to the constitutional safeguards enshrined in Article 148 to insulate the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India from executive interference, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The CAG holds office during the pleasure of the President, though all administrative expenses of the office are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
opts.B: After ceasing to hold office, the CAG is eligible for reappointment to the same office for a second term, provided the cumulative tenure does not exceed six years.
opts.C: While barred from accepting executive appointments under State Governments after retirement, the CAG remains constitutionally eligible for appointment as the Chairperson of the Finance Commission.
opts.D: Once the CAG ceases to hold office, he or she is constitutionally barred from holding any further office either under the Government of India or under the Government of any State.

core: To ensure that the guardian of the public purse audits executive expenditure without fear or favour, Article 148 provides both security of tenure during service (removal only like a Supreme Court Judge) and complete insulation from executive inducement after retirement by rendering the CAG ineligible for any further office under the Union or any State Government under Article 148(4).

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because Article 148(4) of the Constitution explicitly mandates that the Comptroller and Auditor General shall not be eligible for further office either under the Government of India or under the Government of any State after he has ceased to hold his office. Option (A) is incorrect because although appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, the CAG does not hold office during the pleasure of the President and can only be removed in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court under Article 148(1). Options (B) and (C) are incorrect because the constitutional bar under Article 148(4) is absolute and precludes both reappointment and appointment to any other office of profit under the Union or State Governments.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 148; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. Comptroller and Auditor General of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India in relation to public accounts:
items: Statement-I: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India continues to compile and maintain the accounts of State Governments, even though the CAG was relieved of the responsibility of compiling the accounts of the Union Government in 1976.

Statement-II: Under Article 149 of the Constitution, the duties and powers of the CAG in relation to the accounts of the Union are prescribed by Parliament by law, whereas those in relation to the accounts of a State are prescribed by the respective State Legislature.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the Indian constitutional scheme, the CAG is a unitary constitutional authority whose duties and powers in respect of both the Union and the States are regulated exclusively by parliamentary law under Article 149. Through the 1976 amendment to the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, accounts were separated from audit at the Central level (departmentalisation of Union accounts), but the CAG continues to compile and maintain the accounts of the States.

exp.why: Under the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 as amended in 1976, the President relieved the CAG from the responsibility of compiling the accounts of the Union Government (departmentalising Union accounts under the Controller General of Accounts). However, the CAG continues to perform both accounting (compilation and maintenance of accounts) and auditing functions for the State Governments.

Under Article 149 of the Constitution, the CAG performs such duties and exercises such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union AND of the States and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament. State Legislatures have no constitutional competence to legislate on or prescribe the duties and powers of the CAG regarding State accounts.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 149; CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971

stem: With reference to the constitutional mandate and audit jurisdiction of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the Comptroller and Auditor General of Britain, the CAG of India has no prior control over the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund of India and performs only a post-facto audit after the expenditure has already been incurred.

2. While conducting a regulatory audit to verify whether expenditure conforms to the governing authority is obligatory on the CAG, the conduct of a 'propriety audit' looking into the wisdom, faithfulness, and economy of government expenditure is discretionary.

3. The audit jurisdiction of the CAG over statutory corporations is not uniform under the Constitution and depends upon the specific Acts of Parliament establishing them, because of which statutory bodies like the Reserve Bank of India and the Life Insurance Corporation of India are completely outside the CAG's direct audit.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian CAG fulfills the role of an Auditor General rather than a true 'Comptroller' with exchequer control, exercises discretionary authority over propriety audits alongside mandatory regulatory audits, and audits statutory corporations strictly according to the terms of their governing statutes.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Britain, the CAG is both Comptroller and Auditor General in the literal sense because the executive cannot draw any money from the public exchequer without the CAG's prior approval. In India, the CAG has no control over the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund of India; departments are authorized to draw money by issuing cheques without the CAG's prior sanction, and the CAG examines accounts only at the audit stage after expenditure has already taken place.

Statement 2 is correct. Legal and regulatory audit (ascertaining whether money shown in the accounts as having been disbursed was legally available for and applicable to the service or purpose to which it has been applied and whether the expenditure conforms to the authority that governs it) is obligatory on the CAG. However, 'propriety audit'—which goes beyond formality to examine the wisdom, faithfulness, and economy of expenditure and comment on wastefulness or extravagance—is discretionary for the CAG.

Statement 3 is correct. Unlike government companies (whose audit is uniformly governed by the Companies Act), the CAG's relationship with statutory corporations is governed by the respective Acts of Parliament establishing them. While some corporations (such as the Damodar Valley Corporation) are audited wholly and directly by the CAG, others like the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), State Bank of India (SBI), and Food Corporation of India (FCI) are totally subject to private professional audit and submit their annual reports and accounts directly to Parliament without CAG audit.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 149-151; CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 52

stem: With reference to the appointment, suspension, and removal of the Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission (SPSC), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Although the Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission are appointed by the Governor of the State, they can be removed from office only by the President of India.

2. Where the President has made a reference to the Supreme Court for an inquiry into the alleged misbehaviour of the Chairman or a member of an SPSC, the Governor of the State is constitutionally empowered to suspend them from office pending the final order of the President.

3. The report tendered by the Supreme Court to the President after conducting an inquiry into the misbehaviour of a member of the UPSC or an SPSC under Article 317(1) is strictly advisory in nature and is not binding on the President.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Articles 316 and 317, while the Governor appoints SPSC members and can suspend them during a pending Supreme Court inquiry, only the President possesses the power to remove them, and the findings of the Supreme Court in a misbehaviour inquiry under Article 317(1) are constitutionally binding on the President.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 316(1), the Chairman and other members of an SPSC are appointed by the Governor of the State. However, to safeguard their institutional independence from state-level executive interference, Article 317(1) and 317(3) vest the power of removal exclusively in the President of India, on the exact same grounds and in the same manner as a member of the UPSC.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 317(2) of the Constitution, in the case of the UPSC or a Joint Commission, the President may suspend from office the Chairman or any other member in respect of whom a reference has been made to the Supreme Court under Article 317(1); in the case of a State Commission (SPSC), this power of interim suspension pending the President's final order on receipt of the Supreme Court's report is explicitly vested in the Governor of the State.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Article 317(1), the President may by order remove from office the Chairman or any other member on the ground of misbehaviour only after the Supreme Court, on reference being made to it by the President, has, on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed under Article 145, reported that the Chairman or such other member ought on any such ground to be removed. Thus, the advice tendered by the Supreme Court in this inquiry is constitutionally binding on the President.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 316 and 317; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 45

stem: Consider the following statements regarding a Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC):
items: 1. Unlike the Union Public Service Commission and a State Public Service Commission, which are created directly by the Constitution, a Joint State Public Service Commission is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament on the request of the concerned State Legislatures.
2. Both the power of appointment and the power of removal of the Chairman and members of a Joint State Public Service Commission are vested in the President of India.
3. A Joint State Public Service Commission presents its annual performance report not to the President of India, but to the Governor of each of the participating States.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 315(2) authorizes the creation of a Joint State Public Service Commission, it comes into existence only through an Act of Parliament following resolutions by the participating State Legislatures; its members are appointed and removed by the President, yet it reports annually to the respective State Governors.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 315(1) directly mandates that there shall be a Public Service Commission for the Union and a Public Service Commission for each State. In contrast, under Article 315(2), if two or more States agree that there shall be one Public Service Commission for that group of States, and a resolution to that effect is passed by each House of the Legislature of each of those States, Parliament may by law provide for the appointment of a Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC). Hence, a JSPSC is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament (such as the JSPSC created for Punjab and Haryana in 1966).

Statement 2 is correct. Because a JSPSC serves two or more States simultaneously, Article 316(1) vests the power to appoint its Chairman and members in the President of India (unlike an SPSC, where the Governor appoints). Similarly, under Article 317, the power to suspend and remove the Chairman and members of a JSPSC is vested solely in the President.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 323(2) of the Constitution, it is the duty of a Joint Commission to present annually to the Governor of each of the States the needs of which are served by the Joint Commission a report as to the work done by the Commission in relation to that State, and each Governor causes a copy of the report to be laid before the Legislature of that State.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 315(2), 316, 317, and 323(2); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 45

stem: With reference to the constitutional restrictions and eligibility for further offices upon ceasing to hold office under Articles 316(3) and 319 of the Constitution of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission : Eligible for reappointment to a second term in the same office subject to the age limit of 65 years
2. Member of the Union Public Service Commission (other than Chairman) : Eligible for appointment as the Chairman of the UPSC or as the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission
3. Chairman of a State Public Service Commission : Eligible for reappointment as the Chairman of the same State Public Service Commission for a second term

4. Member of a State Public Service Commission (other than Chairman) : Eligible for appointment only as the Chairman of that same State Public Service Commission and barred from appointment to the UPSC
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Articles 316(3) and 319 establish a strict hierarchy of permissible post-retirement appointments for Public Service Commission members: no member or Chairman is ever eligible for reappointment to the exact same office for a second term, and movement is permitted only upward or laterally to Chairmanships as specified in Article 319.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Under Article 316(3), a person who holds office as a member (including Chairman) of a Public Service Commission shall, on the expiration of his term of office, be ineligible for reappointment to that office. Furthermore, under Article 319(a), the Chairman of the UPSC is completely ineligible for any further employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Under Article 319(c), a member other than the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission is eligible for appointment as the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission or as the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission (or Joint Commission), though not for any other employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Under Article 316(3) read with Article 319(b), the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission is eligible for appointment as the Chairman or any other member of the UPSC, or as the Chairman of any other State Public Service Commission, but cannot be reappointed as the Chairman of the same SPSC for a second term.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Under Article 319(d), a member other than the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission is eligible for appointment as the Chairman or any other member of the UPSC, or as the Chairman of that same SPSC or any other SPSC, though not for any other employment under the Government of India or a State Government.

ref: Constitution of India Articles 316(3) and 319; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 44 & 45

stem: With reference to the advisory jurisdiction of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 320 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Consultation with the UPSC on all disciplinary matters affecting a civil servant under Article 320(3) is mandatory, and any disciplinary order passed by the Government without consulting the UPSC is void and unenforceable in a court of law.

2. The UPSC is constitutionally exempted from being consulted as respects the manner in which appointments or posts are reserved in favour of any backward class of citizens under Article 16(4) or the manner in which effect is given to the claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under Article 335.

3. The President is empowered to make regulations specifying the matters in which it shall not be necessary for the UPSC to be consulted, provided that all such regulations are laid before each House of Parliament for not less than fourteen days and are subject to modification or repeal by Parliament.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Article 320(3) uses the word 'shall be consulted', the Supreme Court has ruled that this requirement is directory rather than mandatory; furthermore, Article 320(4) excludes reservation policy from UPSC consultation, and the Proviso to Article 320(3) read with Article 320(5) allows the President to exclude matters subject to a 14-day parliamentary laying requirement.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In State of U.P. v. Manbodhan Lal Srivastava (1957), the Supreme Court held that the provision in Article 320(3)(c) regarding consultation with the Public Service Commission on disciplinary matters is directory and not mandatory. Therefore, failure on the part of the Government to consult the UPSC does not render the disciplinary action null and void, nor does it confer any cause of action on the aggrieved public servant in a court of law.

Statement 2 is correct. Article 320(4) explicitly stipulates that nothing in clause (3) shall require a Public Service Commission to be consulted as respects the manner in which any provision referred to in Article 16(4) may be made or as respects the manner in which effect may be given to the provisions of Article 335 (claims of SCs and STs to services and posts).

Statement 3 is correct. Under the proviso to Article 320(3), the President as respects the all-India services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union may make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally, or in any particular class of case, it shall not be necessary for the UPSC to be consulted. Under Article 320(5), all such regulations made by the President must be laid for not less than fourteen days before each House of Parliament as soon as possible after they are made, and shall be subject to such modifications, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as both Houses of Parliament may make during the session in which they are so laid.

ref: Constitution of India Article 320(3), 320(4), and 320(5); State of U.P. v. Manbodhan Lal Srivastava (1957); M. Laxmikanth Ch. 44

stem: With reference to the Finance Commission constituted under Article 280 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The President can constitute a new Finance Commission only upon the completion of the full five-year period of the preceding Commission and not at any earlier time.
opts.B: The specific qualifications required for appointment as the Chairman and the four other members of the Finance Commission are explicitly enumerated in Article 280 of the Constitution.
opts.C: The Chairman and members of the Finance Commission, once their tenure expires, are constitutionally barred from reappointment to a subsequent Finance Commission.
opts.D: The Constitution itself does not prescribe the qualifications of the members of the Finance Commission and expressly empowers Parliament to determine by law both their requisite qualifications and the manner of their selection.

core: Article 280(1) empowers the President to constitute a Finance Commission every fifth year or at such earlier time as considered necessary, while Article 280(2) leaves it entirely to Parliament to prescribe by law the qualifications of the members and the manner of their selection.

exp.why: Option D is correct because Article 280(2) of the Constitution states that 'Parliament may by law determine the qualifications which shall be requisite for appointment as members of the Commission and the manner in which they shall be selected.' Pursuant to this constitutional authorization, Parliament enacted the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951, which specifies that the Chairman shall be a person having experience in public affairs and the four other members shall be selected from among persons who are/have been/are qualified to be High Court judges, or have special knowledge of finance and accounts of Government, or have wide experience in financial matters and administration, or have special knowledge of economics. Option A is incorrect because Article 280(1) explicitly permits the President to constitute the Commission at the expiration of every fifth year 'or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary'. Option B is incorrect because those qualifications are statutory (under the 1951 Act), not enumerated in Article 280. Option C is incorrect because under the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951, members hold office for such period as specified by the President in his order and are eligible for reappointment.

ref: Constitution of India Article 280; Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951; M. Laxmikanth Ch. 46

stem: With reference to the role of the Union Finance Commission in fiscal transfers to local bodies, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Union Finance Commission is constitutionally mandated to make recommendations to the President on the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the State.

Statement-II: Under Article 280 of the Constitution, the Union Finance Commission bypasses the State Consolidated Fund and directly transfers grant-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India to the bank accounts of Panchayats and Municipalities without reference to the recommendations of the State Finance Commission.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Articles 280(3)(bb) and 280(3)(c) inserted by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, the Union Finance Commission recommends measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities. These recommendations must be made on the basis of the recommendations made by the Finance Commission of the State, and funds are routed through the State Consolidated Fund rather than transferred directly by the Commission.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Clauses (bb) and (c) of Article 280(3), added by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992 respectively, explicitly make it the duty of the Union Finance Commission to make recommendations to the President as to the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the State.

Statement-II is incorrect. First, the Union Finance Commission is strictly an advisory body that makes recommendations to the President; it does not execute or disburse funds itself. Second, under Articles 280(3)(bb) and (c), the measures are specifically to augment the Consolidated Fund of the State (through which grants flow to local bodies), and must be made on the basis of the recommendations made by the Finance Commission of the State.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 280(3)(bb) & (c), Art. 281; Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth, Ch. Finance Commission

stem: With reference to a comparative analysis of the Union Finance Commission (UFC) and the State Finance Commission (SFC) under the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution, both the Union Finance Commission and a State Finance Commission are mandated to be constituted at the expiration of every fifth year by the President and the Governor respectively, to make recommendations regarding the distribution of net proceeds of taxes and grants-in-aid.

2. While the qualifications of members of the Union Finance Commission are determined by Parliament by law, the composition and qualifications of members of a State Finance Commission are explicitly specified in the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules of the Constitution.

3. Both the President (in respect of the UFC) and the Governor (in respect of the SFC) are constitutionally mandated to cause every recommendation made by the respective Commission, together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon, to be laid before the respective Legislature.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Articles 280–281 (for the Union Finance Commission) and Articles 243-I and 243-Y (for the State Finance Commission) establish strong structural symmetry in the five-year appointment cycle and the laying of reports with an explanatory memorandum. Just as Parliament by law determines the qualifications of UFC members under Article 280(2), the State Legislature by law determines the composition and qualifications of SFC members under Article 243-I(2).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 280(1) and (3), the President constitutes the Union Finance Commission at the expiration of every fifth year (or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States and grants-in-aid out of the Consolidated Fund of India. Similarly, under Articles 243-I(1) and 243-Y(1), the Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission at the expiration of every fifth year to review the financial position of Panchayats and Municipalities and recommend the distribution of net proceeds of State taxes and grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of the State.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules of the Constitution merely list the 29 and 18 functional items within the purview of Panchayats and Municipalities respectively. Under Article 243-I(2), it is the Legislature of a State that may, by law, provide for the composition of the State Finance Commission, the qualifications requisite for appointment as members thereof, and the manner in which they shall be selected.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article 281, the President shall cause every recommendation made by the UFC together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon to be laid before each House of Parliament. Under Articles 243-I(4) and 243-Y(2), the Governor shall cause every recommendation made by the SFC together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon to be laid before the Legislature of the State.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 243-I, 243-Y, 280 & 281; Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST):
items: 1. Under the Constitution, the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson and Members of the NCSC and the NCST can be prescribed only by an Act of Parliament and not by rules made by the President.

2. While investigating any matter or inquiring into any complaint, both the NCSC and the NCST are vested with all the powers of a Criminal Court of Session under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, including the power to sentence offenders to imprisonment.

3. Following the bifurcation of the erstwhile combined Commission by the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and three other Members of both the NCSC and the NCST are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Articles 338 and 338A (bifurcated by the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003), the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and three other Members of both the NCSC and NCST are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Subject to any law made by Parliament, their conditions of service and tenure of office are determined by the President by rule, and they exercise the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit during inquiries.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Article 338(2) and Article 338A(2), subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and other Members of the NCSC and NCST shall be such as the President may by rule determine.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Article 338(8) and Article 338A(8), the NCSC and NCST, while investigating any matter or inquiring into any complaint, have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit (such as summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person, requiring the discovery and production of any document, and receiving evidence on affidavits), and not the powers of a Criminal Court to convict or sentence offenders.

Statement 3 is correct. The 65th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1990 established a combined multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs, which was later bifurcated into the NCSC (Article 338) and NCST (Article 338A) by the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. Under Articles 338(3) and 338A(3), the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and three other Members of each Commission are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 338 & 338A; 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003

stem: With reference to the constitutional framework governing Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs), consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Under the Constitution of India, every State or Union Territory is empowered by law to prepare and maintain for its own purposes a list of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes, which may contain entries different from the Central List.

Statement-II: By virtue of the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021, the public notification issued by the President under Article 342A(1) specifies the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes only for the purposes of the Central Government, while Article 342A(3) expressly preserves the independent legislative competence of States and Union Territories to identify SEBCs for their own purposes.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: After the Supreme Court interpreted the 102nd Amendment (2018) as creating a single Presidential notification of SEBCs and stripping States of their power to identify OBCs, Parliament enacted the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021. It amended Article 342A(1) and (2) to clarify that the President's list is solely the 'Central List' for the purposes of the Central Government, and inserted Article 342A(3) empowering States and UTs by law to prepare and maintain their own SEBC lists.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 342A(3) of the Constitution, notwithstanding anything contained in clauses (1) and (2) of Article 342A, every State or Union Territory may, by law, prepare and maintain for its own purposes a list of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes, and the entries in such a State List may differ from the Central List.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 amended Article 342A(1) and (2) (along with inserting the Explanation to clause (2) and adding clause (3)) to clarify that the President's notification under Article 342A(1) specifies SEBCs only for the purposes of the Central Government, thereby restoring the federal power of States and Union Territories under Article 342A(3) to maintain separate State Lists of SEBCs.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 338B & 342A; 102nd (2018) and 105th (2021) Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the constitutional functions and reporting procedures of the National Commissions under Articles 338, 338A, and 338B, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Notwithstanding the cessation of the nomination of members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) continues to be constitutionally mandated under Article 338(10) to discharge similar functions in relation to the Anglo-Indian community as it does in relation to the Scheduled Castes.

2. While the Union and every State Government must consult the NCSC and the NCST on all major policy matters affecting SCs and STs respectively, a State Government is constitutionally exempted from consulting the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) when preparing and maintaining its own State List of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes under Article 342A(3).

3. Where a report of the NCSC, NCST, or NCBC relates to any matter with which a State Government is concerned, the Commission submits that report directly to the Speaker of the concerned State Legislative Assembly for being laid before the House.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 338(10), the NCSC continues to discharge functions regarding the Anglo-Indian community even after the 104th Amendment ended legislative nomination. Furthermore, the 105th Amendment added a proviso to Article 338B(9) exempting States from consulting the NCBC when preparing State SEBC lists under Article 342A(3), while all reports of NCSC/NCST/NCBC are submitted only to the President, who forwards State-related reports to the concerned Governor.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 only amended Article 334 to discontinue the reservation of seats by nomination for the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha (Article 331) and State Legislative Assemblies (Article 333). Article 338(10) remains untouched in the Constitution, continuing to mandate the NCSC to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Anglo-Indian community.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Articles 338(9), 338A(9), and 338B(9), the Union and every State Government shall consult the respective Commission on all major policy matters affecting SCs, STs, and SEBCs. However, the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 inserted a proviso to Article 338B(9) explicitly stating that nothing in that clause shall apply for the purposes of clause (3) of Article 342A (preparation and maintenance of the State List of SEBCs by a State or UT).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Articles 338(5)(d), 338(6), and 338(7) (and the parallel provisions in Articles 338A and 338B), the Commission presents all its reports to the President. Where any such report, or any part thereof, relates to any matter with which any State Government is concerned, a copy of such report is forwarded by the President to the Governor of the State, who causes it to be laid before the Legislature of the State along with an explanatory memorandum.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 338(6)-(10), 338A(6)-(9), 338B(6)-(9); 104th & 105th Constitutional Amendment Acts

stem: With reference to the Attorney General for India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To be eligible for appointment as the Attorney General for India, a person must be qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court, and he holds office during the pleasure of the President, receiving such remuneration as the President may determine.

2. When speaking and taking part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament or any Parliamentary Committee of which he may be named a member, the Attorney General enjoys all the powers, privileges, and immunities of a Member of Parliament, although he is not entitled to vote.

3. Being the highest law officer of the country, the Attorney General is categorized as a full-time government servant under the Central Civil Services Rules and is strictly debarred from engaging in any private legal practice during his tenure.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 76 of the Constitution, the Attorney General must be qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge, holds office during the pleasure of the President, and receives remuneration determined by the President. Under Articles 88 and 105(4), he can speak and participate in Parliamentary proceedings and Committees (without voting rights) with full parliamentary privileges, and since he is not a full-time government servant, he is not debarred from private legal practice (provided it is not against the Government of India).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article 76(1), the President appoints a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court to be Attorney General for India. Under Article 76(4), the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President, and receives such remuneration as the President may determine.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article 88, the Attorney General has the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote. Further, under Article 105(4), all parliamentary powers, privileges, and immunities apply to persons who have the right to speak in and take part in the proceedings of a House or any committee thereof.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Attorney General is not a full-time counsel for the Government and does not fall into the category of full-time government servants under the Central Civil Services Rules. Therefore, he is not debarred from private legal practice, subject only to specific restrictions such as not advising or holding a brief against the Government of India or defending accused persons in criminal prosecutions without the permission of the Government of India.

ref: Constitution of India Art. 76, 88 & 105(4); Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth, Ch. Attorney General of India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional qualifications for the Law Officers and the Higher Judiciary in India:
items: Statement-I: An eminent jurist who has neither held a judicial office in the territory of India nor been an advocate of a High Court for ten years can be appointed as the Attorney General for India, but cannot be appointed as the Advocate General of a State.

Statement-II: While computing the ten-year period of advocacy required to qualify for appointment as a Judge of a High Court under Article 217(2) of the Constitution, any period during which a person has held judicial office after becoming an advocate is included.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The eligibility of the Attorney General (Article 76) mirrors that of a Supreme Court Judge (Article 124(3)), which includes a 'distinguished jurist' in the opinion of the President, whereas the eligibility of an Advocate General (Article 165) mirrors that of a High Court Judge (Article 217(2)), which contains no 'distinguished jurist' category.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Article 76(1), the President appoints a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court as the Attorney General for India. Under Article 124(3)(c), a person who is in the opinion of the President a 'distinguished jurist' is qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge even without prior judicial office or ten years of High Court advocacy. Conversely, under Article 165(1), the Governor appoints a person qualified to be appointed a Judge of a High Court as the Advocate General for the State. Article 217(2) prescribes only two eligibility avenues for a High Court Judge—holding a judicial office in India for at least ten years OR being an advocate of a High Court (or two or more such Courts in succession) for at least ten years—and completely omits the 'distinguished jurist' category (an omission restored by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, after a brief introduction by the 42nd Amendment).

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. Under Explanation (a) to Article 217(2) of the Constitution, in computing the ten-year period during which a person has been an advocate of a High Court, any period during which the person has held judicial office after becoming an advocate is included. While this is a valid constitutional rule governing how the ten-year threshold is calculated under Article 217(2), it does not explain why a pure academic or eminent jurist lacking both advocacy and judicial office is ineligible to become an Advocate General; that ineligibility stems strictly from the absence of a 'distinguished jurist' clause in Article 217(2) when contrasted with Article 124(3)(c).

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 76(1), 124(3), 165(1) & 217(2); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapters on Attorney General and Advocate General.

stem: With reference to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council under Article 279A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. One-half of the total number of members of the GST Council constitutes the quorum at its meetings.

2. Every decision of the GST Council is taken by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, wherein the vote of the Central Government has a weightage of one-third of the total votes cast and the votes of all the State Governments taken together have a weightage of two-thirds of the total votes cast.

3. Under the constitutional scheme of Articles 246A and 279A as interpreted by the Supreme Court of India, all recommendations of the GST Council are mandatorily binding on Parliament and the State Legislatures when enacting primary legislation on Goods and Services Tax.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Article 279A establishes asymmetric weighted voting in the GST Council (1/3rd weightage for the Union, 2/3rds for all States combined, and a 3/4ths weighted majority threshold), so neither the Centre nor the States can unilaterally carry a resolution. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations have persuasive, collaborative value rather than a binding legislative mandate that overrides simultaneous legislative competence under Article 246A.

exp.why: Under Article 279A(7) of the Constitution, one-half of the total number of Members of the Goods and Services Tax Council shall constitute the quorum at its meetings.

Under Article 279A(9) of the Constitution, every decision of the GST Council shall be taken at a meeting by a majority of not less than three-fourths (75%) of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, in accordance with two principles: (a) the vote of the Central Government shall have a weightage of one-third (33.33%) of the total votes cast, and (b) the votes of all the State Governments taken together shall have a weightage of two-thirds (66.67%) of the total votes cast in that meeting.

In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022), the Supreme Court of India ruled that Article 246A vests both Parliament and the State Legislatures with simultaneous and equal power to enact primary laws on Goods and Services Tax. Because neither Article 246A nor Article 279A contains a non-obstante clause subordinating legislative power to the GST Council, the recommendations of the GST Council under Article 279A are products of uncoerced cooperative federalism that carry persuasive value for primary legislation, and are binding only with respect to secondary legislation/rule-making where the respective GST statutes explicitly stipulate that rules or notifications be issued 'on the recommendations of the Council'.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 246A & 279A; Supreme Court Judgment in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022).

stem: With reference to the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities under the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The office was originally incorporated in the Constitution of 1950 under Part XVI alongside the Special Officer for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
opts.B: The Constitution explicitly prescribes a fixed tenure of five years for the Special Officer and renders the incumbent ineligible for reappointment.
opts.C: The Constitution creates the office under Part XVII and vests the power of appointment in the President, but leaves the qualifications, tenure, salaries, and procedure for removal unspecified in the constitutional text.
opts.D: The Special Officer submits periodic reports directly to the respective Zonal Councils and the Inter-State Council rather than to the President of India.

core: Inserted as Article 350B in Part XVII by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 (pursuant to the States Reorganisation Commission's recommendations), the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is appointed by the President to investigate safeguards for linguistic minorities. Notably, Article 350B is entirely silent on the officer's qualifications, tenure, service conditions, and removal procedure.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct. Originally, the Constitution of India (1950) made no provision for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. Following the recommendations of the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55), the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 inserted Article 350B in Part XVII of the Constitution. Article 350B(1) states that there shall be a Special Officer for linguistic minorities to be appointed by the President, but the constitutional text does not specify the qualifications, tenure, salaries and allowances, service conditions, or procedure for removal of the officer. Option (A) is incorrect because the office was neither in the original Constitution nor placed in Part XVI (it is in Part XVII). Option (B) is incorrect because the Constitution does not prescribe a five-year tenure or bar on reappointment. Option (D) is incorrect because under Article 350B(2), the Special Officer reports to the President at such intervals as the President may direct, and the President causes all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament and sent to the Governments of the States concerned.

ref: Constitution of India, Article 350B (7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Chapter on Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

stem: Consider the following pairs of Constitutional Authorities and the specific textual provisions governing their appointment and tenure/removal under the Constitution of India:
items: 1. Comptroller and Auditor-General of India : Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, and removed only in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court

2. Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission : Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, and removed only in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court

3. Chairperson of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes : Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, with conditions of service and tenure of office determined by the President by rule subject to any parliamentary law
4. Attorney General for India : Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, and holds office for a fixed constitutional tenure of five years
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: The Constitution explicitly mandates appointment 'by warrant under his hand and seal' for the CAG (Article 148), NCSC (Article 338), NCST (Article 338A), NCBC (Article 338B), and Supreme Court/High Court Judges, but NOT for UPSC members (Article 316), the Attorney General (Article 76), or the Finance Commission (Article 280). Furthermore, while the CAG and CEC are removed like a Supreme Court Judge, the UPSC Chairman is removed on the ground of misbehaviour by the President following a binding Supreme Court inquiry under Article 317.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Article 148(1) of the Constitution, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India is appointed by the President 'by warrant under his hand and seal' and shall only be removed from office in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched on both counts. First, under Article 316(1), the Chairman and other members of the Union Public Service Commission are appointed by the President by ordinary order, without the constitutional requirement of a 'warrant under his hand and seal'. Second, under Article 317(1), the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission is NOT removed by the parliamentary process applicable to a Supreme Court Judge; instead, removal on the ground of misbehaviour is executed by order of the President after the Supreme Court, on a reference made to it by the President, has on inquiry reported that the incumbent ought on any such ground to be removed.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Under Article 338(3), the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes shall be appointed by the President 'by warrant under his hand and seal'. Under Article 338(2), subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched on both counts. Under Article 76(1), the President appoints the Attorney General for India without the constitutional mandate of a 'warrant under his hand and seal'. Furthermore, under Article 76(4), the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and does not enjoy any fixed constitutional tenure.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 76, 148, 316, 317 & 338.

stem: With reference to the financial independence of Constitutional Bodies and expenditures 'charged' upon the Consolidated Fund of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Constitution of India, the administrative expenses of both the Union Public Service Commission and the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, including all salaries, allowances, and pensions payable to their members or staff, are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.

2. Unlike the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, the Constitution does not declare the administrative expenses of the Election Commission of India or the salaries of the Election Commissioners to be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.

3. The administrative expenses and salaries of the members of the Finance Commission and the National Commission for Scheduled Castes are not charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India by the Constitution, and are instead met through voted parliamentary appropriations.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Among India's major non-judicial constitutional bodies, only the UPSC (Article 322) and the office of the CAG (Article 148(6)) have their entire administrative expenses—including salaries, allowances, and pensions of members and staff—explicitly 'charged' upon the Consolidated Fund of India by the Constitution. The administrative expenses and salaries of the Election Commission of India, Finance Commission, and National Commissions (NCSC, NCST, NCBC) are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and remain subject to parliamentary voting.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Article 322 explicitly states that the expenses of the Union Public Service Commission, including any salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the members or staff of the Commission, shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Similarly, Article 148(6) (read with Article 112(3)(e)) provides that the administrative expenses of the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of persons serving in that office, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.

Statement 2 is correct. Neither Article 324 nor Article 112(3) of the Constitution declares the administrative expenses of the Election Commission of India or the salaries of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners to be 'charged' expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India. Even though the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 equates their salary to that of a Judge of the Supreme Court, the expenditure of the Election Commission remains a voted expenditure passed in the Union Budget.

Statement 3 is correct. Neither Article 280 (Finance Commission) nor Article 338 (National Commission for Scheduled Castes) nor Article 112(3) makes the salaries or administrative expenses of these commissions a charged expenditure upon the Consolidated Fund of India. Their operational budgets are met through voted Demands for Grants under the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment respectively.

ref: Constitution of India, Articles 112(3), 148(6), 280, 322, 324 & 338.

stem: Consider the following milestones in the constitutional evolution of Constitutional Bodies in India:
items: 1. Insertion of Article 338A creating a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
2. Insertion of Article 350B creating the office of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
3. Insertion of Article 338B conferring constitutional status on the National Commission for Backward Classes
4. Insertion of Article 279A providing for the establishment of the Goods and Services Tax Council
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above constitutional developments, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The constitutional institutionalization of specialized bodies followed a distinct timeline via constitutional amendments: Article 350B (Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities) via the 7th Amendment (1956); bifurcation of the combined SC/ST Commission to insert Article 338A (NCST) via the 89th Amendment (2003); Article 279A (GST Council) via the 101st Amendment (2016); and Article 338B (NCBC) via the 102nd Amendment (2018).

exp.why: Item 1 occurred in 2003 (effective February 2004): The 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 bifurcated the erstwhile combined National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (which had been made a multi-member body by the 65th Amendment, 1990) into two distinct bodies by amending Article 338 (NCSC) and inserting Article 338A (NCST).
Item 2 occurred in 1956: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 inserted Article 350B in Part XVII of the Constitution, creating the office of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

Item 3 occurred in 2018: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 inserted Article 338B into the Constitution, elevating the National Commission for Backward Classes (earlier a statutory body established in 1993) to a Constitutional Body.

Item 4 occurred in 2016: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 inserted Article 279A into the Constitution, empowering the President to constitute the Goods and Services Tax Council. Hence, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1956) -> 1 (2003) -> 4 (2016) -> 3 (2018).

ref: Constitution of India, 7th (1956), 89th (2003), 101st (2016), and 102nd (2018) Constitutional Amendment Acts.

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately describes the legal status and organizational structure of the NITI Aayog?

opts.A: It was established as an autonomous statutory body under a parliamentary enactment replacing the Planning Commission, with the Prime Minister serving as its ex-officio Chairperson.
opts.B: It is a non-statutory executive body created by a resolution of the Union Cabinet, and its Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of Union Territories with Legislatures, and Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories.
opts.C: The Union Ministers of Home Affairs and Finance serve in the NITI Aayog only as Special Invitees nominated by the Prime Minister rather than as Ex-Officio Members.
opts.D: Its Regional Councils are permanent statutory bodies chaired by the Union Home Minister to resolve inter-state resource disputes on a continuous basis.

core: NITI Aayog is an extra-constitutional, non-statutory executive body created by a Cabinet Resolution on January 1, 2015, rather than by an Act of Parliament. Its Governing Council embodies cooperative federalism by bringing together the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers of all States and Union Territories with Legislatures, and Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct because NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) is neither a constitutional body nor a statutory body; it was created via an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet. Its Governing Council comprises the Prime Minister (Chairperson), Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of Union Territories with Legislatures (such as Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir), and Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories. Option (A) is incorrect (T1 trap) because no Act of Parliament confers statutory backing on NITI Aayog. Option (C) is incorrect because up to four members of the Union Council of Ministers (traditionally including the Home and Finance Ministers) are nominated by the Prime Minister as Ex-Officio Members, whereas Special Invitees are domain experts and specialists or sectoral ministers invited separately. Option (D) is incorrect because NITI Aayog's Regional Councils are formed for a specific tenure to address specific contingencies impacting more than one state or region and are chaired by the Chairperson of NITI Aayog or his nominee (unlike the permanent statutory Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, which are chaired by the Union Home Minister).

ref: Cabinet Resolution dated 1 January 2015; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. on NITI Aayog

stem: With reference to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as amended by the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A person who has been a Judge of the Supreme Court is eligible to be appointed as the Chairperson of the Commission, even if that person has never served as the Chief Justice of India.

2. The Chairperson and Members of the Commission hold office for a term of three years or until they attain the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier, and are barred from reappointment to the same office.

3. The Chairpersons of the National Commission for Backward Classes, the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities serve as ex-officio members of the Commission.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019 widened the talent pool for the NHRC Chairperson to include former Supreme Court Judges alongside former Chief Justices of India, reduced the tenure from five to three years while making both the Chairperson and Members eligible for reappointment, and expanded its ex-officio membership.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Prior to the 2019 Amendment, only a person who had been the Chief Justice of India was eligible to be appointed as Chairperson of the NHRC. The 2019 Amendment amended Section 3(2)(a) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 to make any person who has been the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court eligible for appointment as Chairperson.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the 2019 Amendment reduced the tenure of the Chairperson and Members from five years to three years (or until attaining the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier), it explicitly amended Section 6 of the Act to make both the Chairperson and the Members eligible for reappointment.

Statement 3 is correct. Alongside the Chairpersons of the National Commissions for Minorities, SCs, STs, and Women, the 2019 Amendment Act added the Chairpersons of the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC), the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities as deemed (ex-officio) members of the NHRC under Section 3(3).

ref: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (Sections 3 & 6) as amended by Act 19 of 2019

stem: With reference to the Selection Committee constituted for recommending the appointment of the Chairperson and Members of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The six-member Selection Committee includes the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha as ex-officio parliamentary presiding officers.
2. Both the Chief Justice of India and the Union Minister of Law and Justice serve as voting members of the Selection Committee.

3. Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, any vacancy in the Selection Committee—such as the absence of a recognized Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha—renders an appointment invalid until the vacancy is filled.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Section 4 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the six-member NHRC Selection Committee comprises the Prime Minister (Chairperson), Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Union Home Minister, Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses of Parliament, and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. No appointment is invalidated merely by reason of any vacancy in the Committee.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Because the Prime Minister chairs the Selection Committee and the Vice-President of India (ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) ranks higher than the Prime Minister in the Warrant of Precedence, protocol precludes the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha from serving under the Prime Minister. Therefore, Section 4(1)(f) of the Act includes the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, not the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Neither the Chief Justice of India nor the Union Minister of Law and Justice is a member of the Selection Committee. The Union Minister in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs is the sole Cabinet Minister alongside the Prime Minister on the Committee. A sitting Judge of the Supreme Court or a sitting Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, but the CJI does not sit on the Selection Committee.
