Statement 3 is incorrect. Section 4(2) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 explicitly provides that no appointment of a Chairperson or a Member shall be invalid merely by reason of any vacancy of any member in the Selection Committee (such as when no party has the requisite strength to claim the post of Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha).

ref: Section 4 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the powers and jurisdiction of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC):
items: Statement-I: The National Human Rights Commission cannot take cognizance of human rights violations committed more than a year prior to the filing of a complaint, nor can it directly punish guilty public servants or execute its own compensation awards as self-executing judicial decrees.

Statement-II: Section 36(2) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 statutorily bars the Commission from inquiring into any matter after the expiry of one year from the date of the alleged violation, while Section 18 restricts its post-inquiry remedial powers to making recommendations to the concerned government or authority.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although the NHRC enjoys the procedural powers of a Civil Court while conducting inquiries, its substantive jurisdiction is strictly circumscribed by the one-year limitation period under Section 36(2) and the recommendatory nature of its remedial measures under Section 18 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Despite possessing the procedural powers of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for summoning witnesses, receiving evidence on affidavits, and requisitioning public records, the NHRC cannot inquire into stale claims older than one year, nor does it possess penal power to sentence offenders or pass self-executing decrees of compensation.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The operational limitations described in Statement-I stem directly from two statutory provisions of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993: Section 36(2), which prohibits the NHRC and SHRCs from inquiring into any matter after the expiry of one year from the date on which the act constituting violation of human rights is alleged to have been committed, and Section 18, which confines the Commission after an inquiry to making recommendations to the concerned government or authority (which must report back within one month on action taken) or approaching the Supreme Court or High Court for directions.

ref: Sections 13, 18 and 36(2) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

stem: With reference to the State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A State Human Rights Commission can inquire into violation of human rights only in respect of subjects relatable to entries in List II (State List) and List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

2. In a State having a Legislative Council, the Deputy Chairman of the Council—and not its Chairman—is included along with the Leader of the Opposition in the Council as a member of the Selection Committee.
3. Although the Chairperson and Members of a State Human Rights Commission are appointed by the Governor of the State, they can be removed from office only by the President of India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, an SHRC's subject-matter jurisdiction is confined to the State and Concurrent Lists, its Selection Committee in a bicameral state includes the Chairman (not Deputy Chairman) and Leader of the Opposition of the Legislative Council, and its Chairperson and Members can be removed solely by the President.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 21(5) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, a State Commission may inquire into violation of human rights only in respect of matters relatable to any of the entries enumerated in List II (State List) and List III (Concurrent List) in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, provided the matter is not already being inquired into by the NHRC or another statutory commission.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Unlike at the Union level—where the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the Vice-President of India and therefore cannot sit on a committee chaired by the Prime Minister—at the State level, the proviso to Section 22(1) of the Act explicitly stipulates that where there is a Legislative Council in a State, the Chairman of that Council (not the Deputy Chairman) and the Leader of the Opposition in that Council shall also be members of the Selection Committee chaired by the Chief Minister.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 22(1) and Section 23 of the Act, while the Chairperson and Members of an SHRC are appointed by the Governor by warrant under his hand and seal, they can be removed from office only by order of the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (or on specified grounds such as insolvency or infirmity), identical to the removal procedure for the NHRC.

ref: Sections 21, 22 and 23 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

stem: With reference to the Central Information Commission (CIC) under the Right to Information Act, 2005 (as amended in 2019), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act statutorily guarantees the Chief Information Commissioner a fixed tenure of five years and a salary equivalent to that of the Chief Election Commissioner.

2. Following the Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019, the term of office as well as the salaries and allowances of the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners are such as may be prescribed by the Central Government.

3. While the Chief Information Commissioner is not eligible for reappointment, an Information Commissioner is eligible for appointment as the Chief Information Commissioner, subject to an aggregate tenure cap of five years across both posts.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 removed the statutory five-year tenure and statutory salary equivalence with the Election Commission for the CIC and Information Commissioners, delegating the power to prescribe their tenure and service conditions to the Central Government while retaining the statutory bar on reappointment of the CIC and the five-year aggregate cap for an IC elevated as CIC.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under the original RTI Act, 2005 prior to 2019, Section 13 provided a fixed five-year statutory tenure (subject to the 65-year age cap) and equated the salaries and allowances of the CIC and Information Commissioners with those of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners respectively. The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 removed both the fixed five-year statutory tenure and the statutory salary equivalence with the Election Commission.

Statement 2 is correct. Sections 13(1), 13(2), and 13(5) of the RTI Act, 2005, as amended by the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019, empower the Central Government to prescribe by rules the term of office and the salaries, allowances, and other terms and conditions of service of the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners (with the protection that they cannot be varied to their disadvantage AFTER appointment).

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 13(1) and the provisos to Section 13(2) of the RTI Act, 2005 (which remained intact after the 2019 Amendment), the Chief Information Commissioner is not eligible for reappointment. However, an Information Commissioner is eligible on vacating office to be appointed as the Chief Information Commissioner, provided that the aggregate term of office as Information Commissioner and Chief Information Commissioner does not exceed five years in total (and subject to the upper age limit of 65 years).

ref: Section 13 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 as amended by Act 24 of 2019

stem: With reference to the Central Information Commission (CIC) and the State Information Commissions (SICs) under the Right to Information Act, 2005, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Selection Committee that recommends the appointment of the Chief Information Commissioner at the Central level comprises the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.

2. Unlike the Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission who can be removed only by the President of India, a State Chief Information Commissioner is both appointed and removed from office by the Governor of the State after an inquiry by the Supreme Court on a reference made by the Governor.

3. Under the parent statute as currently in force, the tenure of five years and the equivalence of salary of the Chief Information Commissioner with that of the Chief Election Commissioner are statutorily guaranteed and cannot be altered by executive rules.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Right to Information Act, 2005 (as amended in 2019), the 3-member CIC Selection Committee comprises the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM (not the CJI), and their tenure and salaries are prescribed by the Central Government via rules. Unlike a State Human Rights Commission (where the President holds removal power), State Information Commissioners are both appointed and removed by the Governor after a Supreme Court inquiry.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Section 12(3) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a three-member committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister to be nominated by the Prime Minister. The Chief Justice of India is not a member of this Selection Committee.

Statement 2 is correct. While the Chairperson and Members of a State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) are appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President of India (under Section 23 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993), Sections 15(3) and 17(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 vest both the power of appointment and the power of removal of the State Chief Information Commissioner or a State Information Commissioner in the Governor of the State. Under Section 17(1), the Governor can remove them on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after the Supreme Court, on a reference made to it by the Governor, has on inquiry reported that the Commissioner ought to be removed.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended Sections 13 and 16 of the parent Act to remove the fixed five-year statutory tenure and the statutory equivalence of salaries and allowances with those of the Chief Election Commissioner/Election Commissioners. It empowered the Central Government to prescribe the tenure, salaries, and allowances of the Central and State Information Commissioners through rules (presently notified as a three-year tenure under the RTI Rules, 2019).

ref: Right to Information Act, 2005 (Sections 12, 13, 15, 16 & 17) as amended in 2019; Laxmikanth Ch. 57 & 58

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the adjudicatory and enforcement powers of the Central Information Commission (CIC):
items: Statement-I: Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, while the Central Information Commission is empowered to directly impose a daily monetary penalty up to a statutory ceiling on an erring Central Public Information Officer personally for malafide denial of information, it can only recommend and not directly execute disciplinary action against him under the applicable service rules.

Statement-II: While inquiring into any complaint under Section 18 of the Right to Information Act, 2005, the Central Information Commission is vested with the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit in respect of summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and compelling them to give oral or written evidence on oath.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Section 20 of the RTI Act, 2005, the CIC can directly impose a personal monetary penalty (Rs. 250 per day up to Rs. 25,000) on an erring CPIO, whereas disciplinary action under service rules remains within the administrative domain of the concerned cadre-controlling authority upon the CIC's recommendation. Separately, Section 18(3) grants the CIC the procedural powers of a Civil Court for conducting inquiries.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 20(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, if the CIC at the time of deciding any complaint or appeal is of the opinion that the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) has, without any reasonable cause, refused to receive an application or malafidely denied the request for information, it shall impose a penalty of Rs. 250 each day till the application is received or information is furnished, up to a total ceiling of Rs. 25,000, recoverable personally from the CPIO's salary (whereas compensation under Section 19(8)(b) is paid by the Public Authority). However, under Section 20(2), for persistent default, the CIC can only recommend disciplinary action against the CPIO under the service rules applicable to him; actual execution of disciplinary proceedings lies with the competent disciplinary authority.

Statement-II is correct, but does not explain Statement-I. Under Section 18(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, while inquiring into any matter under Section 18, the CIC has the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including summoning witnesses, compelling oral or written evidence on oath, requiring discovery and inspection of documents, and requisitioning public records. This procedural power to conduct an inquiry does not explain why the statute restricts the CIC to merely recommending (rather than executing) service-rule disciplinary action, which is grounded in preserving the administrative autonomy of the appointing/disciplinary authority under Article 311 and service jurisprudence.

ref: Right to Information Act, 2005 (Sections 18, 19 & 20); Laxmikanth Ch. 57

stem: With reference to the institutional evolution, composition, and conditions of service of the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It was originally established as a single-member statutory body in 1964 on the recommendations of the First Administrative Reforms Commission and converted into a multi-member body in 2003.
opts.B: It is a multi-member statutory body consisting of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners, who hold office for a term of four years or until they attain the age of sixty-five years, and are ineligible for any further employment under the Central or a State Government.
opts.C: While a Vigilance Commissioner is eligible for appointment as the Central Vigilance Commissioner, his combined tenure in the Commission across both posts can extend up to six years.
opts.D: The salary, allowances, and other conditions of service of the Central Vigilance Commissioner are equivalent to those of a Judge of the Supreme Court.

core: Originally set up by an executive resolution in 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee, the CVC was accorded statutory status as a multi-member body (CVC plus up to two Vigilance Commissioners) via Ordinance in 1998 and the CVC Act, 2003. Its members serve a 4-year/65-year term and are strictly barred from any post-retirement employment under the Central or State Governments.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. Under Sections 3 and 5 of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, the CVC consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner (Chairperson) and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners (Members). They hold office for a term of four years from the date on which they enter upon their office or until they attain the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, and on ceasing to hold office, they are ineligible for any diplomatic assignment or any further office of profit/employment under the Union or a State Government. Option (A) is incorrect because the CVC was created in 1964 by an executive resolution of the Government of India on the recommendations of the Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1962–64), not as a statutory body and not by the First ARC. Option (C) is incorrect because under the proviso to Section 5(2) of the CVC Act, 2003, while a Vigilance Commissioner is eligible to be appointed as the Central Vigilance Commissioner, his total term in office in both capacities cannot exceed four years in the aggregate. Option (D) is incorrect because under Section 5(4) and 5(5) of the CVC Act, 2003, the salary and allowances of the Central Vigilance Commissioner are equivalent to those of the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), and those of a Vigilance Commissioner are equivalent to those of a Member of the UPSC.

ref: Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003 (Sections 3 & 5); Laxmikanth Ch. 59

stem: With reference to the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and its relationship with the Central Bureau of Investigation (Delhi Special Police Establishment), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Selection Committee that recommends the appointment of the Central Vigilance Commissioner consists of the Prime Minister, the Union Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.

2. Under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, the Commission exercises superintendence over the functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment only insofar as it relates to the investigation of offences alleged to have been committed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

3. In the exercise of its statutory power of superintendence, the Central Vigilance Commission is empowered to direct the Central Bureau of Investigation to investigate a pending corruption case in a specific manner or file a charge-sheet against a public servant.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Section 4 of the CVC Act, 2003, the Selection Committee comprises the PM, the Union Home Minister, and the LoP in the Lok Sabha. Under Section 8 of the CVC Act, 2003 and Section 4 of the DSPE Act, 1946, the CVC's superintendence over the CBI is strictly limited to offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and the CVC is statutorily barred from directing the CBI to investigate or dispose of any case in a particular manner.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 4(1) of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, the Central Vigilance Commissioner and the Vigilance Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a three-member Committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Union Minister of Home Affairs (Member), and the Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People (Member).

Statement 2 is correct. Under Section 8(1)(a) of the CVC Act, 2003 read with Section 4(1) of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 (following the Supreme Court's directives in Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997), the superintendence of the DSPE (CBI) insofar as it relates to the investigation of offences alleged to have been committed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 vests in the Central Vigilance Commission, whereas the superintendence of the DSPE in all other matters vests in the Central Government.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the proviso to Section 8(1)(b) of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, while exercising the powers of superintendence over the Delhi Special Police Establishment (CBI), the Commission shall not exercise powers in such a manner so as to require the DSPE to investigate or dispose of any case in a particular manner. This statutory safeguard protects the investigative autonomy of the investigating officer from external interference in deciding whether to file a charge-sheet or closure report.

ref: Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003 (Sections 4 & 8); DSPE Act, 1946 (Section 4); Laxmikanth Ch. 59 & 60

stem: With reference to the structural composition and eligibility criteria of the Lokpal under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Lokpal consists of a Chairperson and such number of Members, not exceeding eight, out of whom at least fifty per cent shall be Judicial Members.
2. Not less than fifty per cent of the Members of the Lokpal shall be from amongst persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities, and women.

3. A person is eligible to be appointed as a non-judicial Member of the Lokpal if he has attained the minimum age of thirty-five years and possesses not less than fifteen years of special knowledge and expertise in matters relating to anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, or finance.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 3 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 mandates a Chairperson and up to 8 Members, with a dual 50% rule: 50% must be Judicial Members and not less than 50% must belong to SC, ST, OBC, Minorities, and Women. Non-judicial Members must be at least 45 years old and possess at least 25 years of specialized domain expertise.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 3(2) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Lokpal consists of a Chairperson and such number of Members, not exceeding eight, out of whom fifty per cent shall be Judicial Members (who must be or have been a Judge of the Supreme Court or the Chief Justice of a High Court).

Statement 2 is correct. Under the proviso to Section 3(2)(b) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, not less than fifty per cent of the Members of the Lokpal shall be from amongst persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities, and women.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Section 3(3)(b) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, a non-judicial Member must be a person of impeccable integrity and outstanding ability having special knowledge and expertise of not less than twenty-five years (not 15 years) in matters relating to anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance including insurance and banking, law, and management. Furthermore, under Section 3(4)(c), a person is not eligible to be appointed as Chairperson or Member unless he has attained the minimum age of forty-five years (not 35 years) on the date of assuming office.

ref: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Section 3); Laxmikanth Ch. 61

stem: With reference to the appointment mechanism of the Chairperson and Members of the Lokpal under Section 4 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Selection Committee for the appointment of the Chairperson and Members of the Lokpal includes the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Union Minister of Home Affairs, and the Chief Justice of India.

2. The Selection Committee is statutorily required to constitute a Search Committee of at least seven persons of standing to prepare a panel of candidates, in which not less than fifty per cent of the members must belong to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities, and women.
3. No appointment of a Chairperson or a Member of the Lokpal can be invalidated merely by reason of any vacancy in the Selection Committee.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Section 4 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the 5-member Selection Committee comprises the PM, the Speaker of Lok Sabha, the LoP in Lok Sabha, the CJI (or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by him), and an eminent jurist (excluding both the Rajya Sabha Chairman and the Home Minister). It is assisted by a Search Committee of at least 7 members with a 50% diversity mandate.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under Section 4(1) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the five-member Selection Committee consists of: (a) the Prime Minister (Chairperson); (b) the Speaker of the House of the People (Lok Sabha); (c) the Leader of Opposition in the House of the People; (d) the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by him; and (e) one eminent jurist, as recommended by the Chairperson and the first three Members, to be nominated by the President. Unlike the NHRC Selection Committee, neither the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha nor the Union Minister of Home Affairs is a member of the Lokpal Selection Committee.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Section 4(3) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Selection Committee shall, for the purposes of selecting the Chairperson and Members of the Lokpal and for preparing a panel of persons to be considered for appointment, constitute a Search Committee consisting of at least seven persons of standing and having special knowledge and expertise, provided that not less than fifty per cent of the members of the Search Committee shall be from amongst persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities, and women.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 4(2) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, no appointment of a Chairperson or a Member shall be invalid merely by reason of any vacancy in the Selection Committee.

ref: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Section 4); Laxmikanth Ch. 61

stem: With reference to the jurisdiction of the Lokpal over the Prime Minister under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An inquiry against the Prime Minister can be initiated if a Bench of not less than three Members of the Lokpal approves it by a simple majority.

2. Any inquiry conducted by the Lokpal against the Prime Minister must be held in camera, and if the Lokpal concludes that the complaint deserves to be dismissed, the records of the inquiry shall not be published or made available to anyone.
3. Allegations of corruption against the Prime Minister relating to defence procurement, fiscal policy, and public order are statutorily excluded from the jurisdiction of the Lokpal.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Section 14 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 places the Prime Minister within the ambit of the Lokpal, subject to five strict subject-matter exclusions and heightened procedural safeguards requiring full-bench consideration, a two-thirds approval threshold, and mandatory in-camera proceedings.

exp.why: Under Section 14(1)(a)(ii) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Lokpal cannot inquire into any matter against the Prime Minister unless the full bench of the Lokpal, consisting of its Chairperson and all Members, considers the initiation of inquiry and at least two-thirds of its members approve such inquiry. A three-member bench acting by simple majority is insufficient.

Under Section 14(1)(a)(iii) of the Act, any such inquiry against the Prime Minister shall be held in camera, and if the Lokpal comes to the conclusion that the complaint deserves to be dismissed, the records of the inquiry shall not be published or made available to anyone.

Section 14(1)(a)(i) excludes only five specific subject-matter domains from the Lokpal's jurisdiction in relation to the Prime Minister: international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space. Defence procurement and fiscal policy are not among the statutorily excluded subjects.

ref: Section 14, Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; Laxmikanth Ch. 63

stem: Consider the following procedural stages prescribed under Section 20 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 upon the receipt of a complaint of corruption against a public servant:
items: 1. Consideration of the investigation report by a Bench of not less than three Members of the Lokpal to grant sanction to file a charge-sheet before the Special Court.
2. Ordering a preliminary inquiry by the Inquiry Wing or any agency to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists for proceeding in the matter.
3. Directing an investigating agency to carry out a full investigation into the alleged offence.

4. Calling for an explanation and affording an opportunity of being heard to the concerned public servant by a Bench of the Lokpal to determine whether a prima facie case exists to order an investigation.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct statutory sequence in which the stages given above occur?
core: Section 20 of the Lokpal Act mandates a structured four-step filter—Preliminary Inquiry, Audi Alteram Partem hearing before a 3-Member Bench, Full Investigation, and Prosecution Sanction by a 3-Member Bench—to prevent frivolous prosecution while bypassing executive sanction.

exp.why: This is the fourth and final stage (Step 4): under Section 20(6) and 20(7), after the investigating agency submits its completion report, a Bench of not less than three Members of the Lokpal considers the report and may grant sanction to its Prosecution Wing or the investigating agency to file a charge-sheet before the Special Court.

This is the first stage (Step 1): under Section 20(1)(a), on receipt of a complaint, the Lokpal may first order a preliminary inquiry against any public servant by its Inquiry Wing or any agency (including the CBI) to ascertain whether there exists a prima facie case for proceeding in the matter.

This is the third stage (Step 3): under Section 20(3)(a), after considering the preliminary inquiry report and hearing the public servant, if the Bench decides that a prima facie case exists, it directs any agency (including the CBI) to carry out a full investigation.

This is the second stage (Step 2): under the proviso to Section 20(1) and Section 20(3), before ordering a full investigation, a Bench of not less than three Members of the Lokpal must call for the explanation of the public servant and afford an opportunity of being heard to determine whether a prima facie case exists.

ref: Section 20, Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013

stem: Consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the Central Government, which cannot unilaterally extend the jurisdiction of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to investigate offences within a State without that State Government's consent, the Supreme Court and the High Courts can direct the CBI to investigate a crime anywhere in a State without obtaining the consent of the State Government.

Statement-II: While Entry 80 of the Union List and Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 subject the executive extension of a central police force's jurisdiction in a State to the consent of the State Government in deference to 'Police' being a State List subject, statutory restrictions cannot curtail the constitutional power of judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights vested in the Supreme Court under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Section 6 of the DSPE Act, 1946 operationalizes the federal limitation in Entry 80 of the Union List by requiring State consent for the Central Government to extend CBI jurisdiction to a State, but the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench held that this statutory bar cannot fetter constitutional courts acting under Articles 32 or 226.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, the Central Government cannot direct the CBI to exercise powers and jurisdiction in any area in a State (other than a Union Territory) without the consent of the Government of that State. However, in State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that the Supreme Court and High Courts can direct the CBI to investigate a cognizable offence in a State without that State's consent.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Entry 80 of List I permits Parliament to extend the jurisdiction of a police force outside its area only with the consent of the host State Government because 'Police' is an exclusive State List subject (Entry 2, List II). However, judicial review and enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Articles 32 and 226 form part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution, which ordinary statutory limitations like Section 6 of the DSPE Act cannot restrict.

ref: Entry 80 List I & Entry 2 List II; Section 6, DSPE Act 1946; State of West Bengal v. CPDR (2010)

stem: With reference to the appointment and tenure of the Director of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Selection Committee that recommends the appointment of the Director of the CBI consists of the Prime Minister, the Union Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
2. Once appointed, the Director of the CBI is guaranteed a minimum statutory tenure of two years, regardless of the date of his normal superannuation.

3. Under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (Amendment) Act, 2021, the tenure of the Director of the CBI can be extended by up to one year at a time on the recommendation of the Selection Committee, subject to a maximum total tenure of five years including the initial appointment.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Sections 4A and 4B of the DSPE Act, 1946, the CBI Director is appointed on the recommendation of a three-member committee comprising the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and CJI (or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by him), with an assured 2-year minimum tenure extendable annually up to 5 years total.

exp.why: Under Section 4A(1) of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 (as amended by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013), the Selection Committee for the Director of the CBI comprises the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the Leader of the single largest opposition party), and the Chief Justice of India (or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by him). The Union Minister of Home Affairs is not a member of this committee.

Under Section 4B(1) of the DSPE Act, 1946 (codifying the Supreme Court's mandate in Vineet Narain v. Union of India), the Director of the CBI shall, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the rules relating to his conditions of service, continue to hold office for a period of not less than two years from the date on which he assumes office.

Under the provisos inserted into Section 4B(1) by the Delhi Special Police Establishment (Amendment) Act, 2021, the initial two-year tenure of the Director may, in public interest and on the recommendation of the Selection Committee for reasons recorded in writing, be extended up to one year at a time, provided that no such extension shall be granted after the completion of a period of five years in total including the initial appointment.

ref: Sections 4A & 4B, Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 (as amended in 2013, 2014 & 2021)

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding statutory offices and their specific appointment or removal mechanisms:
items: 1. Chairperson of the Lokpal : The President can refer a complaint of misbehaviour to the Supreme Court for inquiry upon receiving a petition signed by at least 100 Members of Parliament.
2. Central Vigilance Commissioner : Appointed on the recommendation of a six-member Selection Committee that includes the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

3. Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission : Appointed on the recommendation of a three-member Selection Committee consisting solely of the Prime Minister, the Union Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
4. Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission : Appointed by the Governor of the State, but can be removed from office only by the President of India.
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Statutory bodies in India exhibit distinct institutional designs: the NHRC uses a broad 6-member parliamentary-executive selection committee (including the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman), whereas the CVC uses a compact 3-member committee (PM, Home Minister, and LoP in Lok Sabha).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under Section 37(2) of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Chairperson or any Member of the Lokpal shall not be removed from office on grounds of misbehaviour unless the Supreme Court, on a reference made to it by the President on a petition signed by at least one hundred Members of Parliament, has on inquiry reported that the person ought to be removed.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched (swapped with Pair 3). Under Section 4(1) of the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, the Central Vigilance Commissioner is appointed on the recommendation of a three-member Selection Committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Union Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched (swapped with Pair 2). Under Section 4(1) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the Chairperson and Members of the NHRC are appointed on the recommendation of a six-member committee comprising the Prime Minister, Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Union Home Minister, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha, and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Under Sections 22 and 23 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, although the Chairperson and Members of a State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) are appointed by the Governor of the State, they can be removed from office only by the President of India (and not by the Governor) on the same grounds and through the same Supreme Court inquiry procedure applicable to the NHRC.

ref: Lokpal Act 2013 (Sec 37); Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 (Sec 4, 22, 23); CVC Act 2003 (Sec 4)

stem: With reference to the organizational structure and functioning of NITI Aayog, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Regional Councils under NITI Aayog are formed for a specified tenure to address specific issues and contingencies impacting more than one State or a region, and are convened by the Prime Minister and chaired by the Chairperson of NITI Aayog or his nominee.

2. The structural framework of NITI Aayog provides for a maximum of four part-time members selected from leading universities and research organizations on a rotational basis, and a maximum of two ex-officio members from the Union Council of Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister.

3. The Chief Executive Officer of NITI Aayog is appointed by the Prime Minister for a fixed tenure in the rank of Secretary to the Government of India, and its 'Team India Wing' comprises representatives from every State and Central Ministry to serve as a permanent platform for national collaboration.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: NITI Aayog operates as an executive think-tank featuring issue-specific Regional Councils with fixed tenures, up to four Union Ministers as ex-officio members, up to two rotational part-time academic members, and three specialized functional wings (Research, Consultancy, and Team India).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Unlike the permanent statutory Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (which are chaired by the Union Home Minister), NITI Aayog's Regional Councils are constituted for a specified tenure to address specific issues and contingencies impacting more than one State or a region. They are convened by the Prime Minister, comprise the Chief Ministers of States and Lt. Governors of UTs in the region, and are chaired by the Chairperson of NITI Aayog or his nominee.

Statement 2 is incorrect because the numerical caps are swapped. Under the Cabinet Secretariat Resolution constituting NITI Aayog, there is a provision for a maximum of TWO part-time members (from leading universities, research organizations, and other relevant institutions in an ex-officio capacity on a rotational basis) and a maximum of FOUR ex-officio members from the Union Council of Ministers to be nominated by the Prime Minister.

Statement 3 is correct. The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of NITI Aayog is appointed by the Prime Minister for a fixed tenure in the rank of Secretary to the Government of India. Further, NITI Aayog houses three specialized wings—Research Wing, Consultancy Wing, and Team India Wing—where the Team India Wing comprises representatives from every State and Ministry to institutionalize cooperative federalism.

ref: Cabinet Secretariat Resolution dated 1 January 2015; Laxmikanth Ch. 56 (NITI Aayog)
